design_detail: Case study of US newspaper coverage: a cross-sectional search and content analysis of the online archives of the 50 largest US newspapers with available archives, for stories on the September 2002 publication of a primate study reporting MDMA-induced dopaminergic neurotoxicity (Ricaurte et al., 2002) and on its September 2003 retraction. The units are newspapers (50) and stories, not people. Analyses: proportions of newspapers covering each event, word counts, Fisher's exact tests comparing retraction stories between newspapers that covered both events (14) and those that covered only the retraction (6), and simple logistic regression of coverage on circulation. The PDF is the online-first version (published online 26 November 2020): a publisher's cover page, then the article numbered pp. 1-7; the 2021 issue prints it as pp. 104-110 (issue pagination not checked). Anchors cite the online-first PDF's own page numbers. The 2002 paper and its retraction notice are not in this batch; what this article says about them is its authors' description.
can_establish: How many of these 50 newspapers ran stories on the publication and on the retraction, how long the stories were, and which elements the retraction stories contained, as coded by the authors.
cannot_establish: Why coverage differed, whether the coverage influenced legislation or research, how the public understood either event, or anything about the effects of MDMA on the brain.

sample.recruitment: Newspapers, not people: the 50 largest US newspapers for which online archives were available through Newspapers.com or the newspapers' own websites, taken in order from a 2007 circulation list (Infoplease, 2007); because some lacked archives, the list was descended to rank 64 (Methods, 1st paragraph, pp. 2-3; Table 1, p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Newspapers without available online archives were skipped and replaced by the next largest.
sample.demographics: Not applicable; Table 1 lists the 50 newspapers in order of circulation.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. Editors' calculation: 14 of the 64 largest newspapers were skipped for lack of archives.
sample.selection_effects: The frame is a 2007 ranking applied to coverage in 2002-2003, and newspapers without online archives were left out; the authors list their inability to search all of the 50 largest newspapers as a limitation (Discussion, 7th paragraph, p. 5). Television, magazines, wire services and online media are outside the frame, and where in each paper a story appeared was not analysed.

exposure.measurement: The events covered: the September 2002 publication and the September 2003 retraction. Stories were found by archive searches combining the terms MDMA, ecstasy, Ricaurte, monkey, dopamine, Johns Hopkins and retraction; where these found nothing, all articles mentioning MDMA or ecstasy from September to November 2002 and September to November 2003 were read (Methods, 2nd paragraph, p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Coverage of the publication compared with coverage of the retraction in the same 50 newspapers; the content of retraction stories compared between the 14 newspapers that covered both events and the 6 that covered only the retraction.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense. Newspaper characteristics that could explain coverage (science staff, use of wire stories, editorial policy) were not recorded; only circulation was tested.

outcomes.instruments: Whether each newspaper ran a story on each event; word counts; a content analysis of the 20 retraction stories for 17 reporting components (Table 2, p. 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: No coding manual, coder description, blinding or inter-rater reliability is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Retraction reporting is called balanced (Abstract; Discussion, 5th paragraph, p. 5) without a definition; lack of context is judged from which of the 17 components a story contained.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 15 Fisher's exact comparisons (two components were present in every story), none significant, the lowest p being 0.06.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the coders are not identified.

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions without confidence intervals: publication covered by 26 of 50 newspapers (52%; editors' calculation, Wilson 95% CI 38.5% to 65.2%) and the retraction by 20 of 50 (40%; 27.6% to 53.8%); 14 of the 26 newspapers that covered the publication covered the retraction (54%; 35.5% to 71.2%). The publication-versus-retraction difference is not tested; editors' calculation from the discordant newspapers (12 covered only the publication, 6 only the retraction): exact McNemar p=0.24. Mean word counts 482 (SD 303) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193) for retraction stories, not tested; editors' calculation, Welch t=1.17, p=0.25, treating the stories as independent. Circulation was not associated with coverage of the publication (p=.25) or of the retraction (p=.84); no coefficients are given.
analysis.selective_reporting: The 14-of-26 figure conditions on newspapers that had already covered the publication; the symmetric figure, that 14 of the 20 newspapers covering the retraction (70%) had covered the publication (editors' calculation), is not given. The underlying data are available from the first author on request (Data availability statement, p. 5).
analysis.power: Not discussed. With 14 against 6 newspapers in the content comparison, only very large differences could have been detected.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A few more of these 50 newspapers covered the publication (26) than the retraction (20); about half of those that had covered the publication (14 of 26) also covered the retraction, while 6 covered only the retraction. Retraction stories were somewhat shorter on average, with wide spread. Every retraction story reported that the original findings had suggested one night's use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism and that a mix-up of compounds made them erroneous. None of the publication-versus-retraction differences was tested, and the content comparison found no significant difference.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the overall decrease moderate and the lower retraction coverage among newspapers that had covered the publication concerning, and calls retraction stories balanced. The discussion explains the difference by the sensational AAAS press release, the parkinsonism angle, the media narrative of the time and the late-Friday release of the retraction, none of which was tested, and closes by suggesting that sensational coverage of the erroneous findings may have slowed the development of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (Discussion, 8th paragraph, p. 5). It also states, citing only a 2014 commentary by Doblin and colleagues for the regulatory point, that evidence of dopaminergic toxicity of MDMA in humans has not materialized since the retraction (Discussion, 6th paragraph, p. 5). The second author directs the organization that sponsors the Phase 3 trials the discussion mentions. The same causal suggestion frames the study's rationale: the Introduction says the 2002 publication may have influenced the passage of anti-drug legislation aimed at recreational MDMA use and slowed efforts to gain regulatory approval for MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (p. 2), sourced to the sponsoring organization's own documents and a journal editorial. The abstract also states that the retraction stories were balanced but shorter, which the paper does not test.

timeline.event: Publication of the primate study (Ricaurte et al., 2002), with a university announcement and an AAAS press release (as described here, p. 2).
Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin criticizing the study, and the authors' reply (June 2003).
Retraction (September 2003), as described here: methamphetamine instead of MDMA given to all but one animal because of a labelling error.
Earlier case study of the media coverage of another retracted paper (Rada, 2005, as cited; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: A single descriptive case study; the authors compare it with one earlier case study and a survey of retraction coverage (Rada, 2005, 2007), neither read here.

funding.funder: This work was unfunded (Funding, p. 6).
funding.declared_conflicts: Disclosure statement (p. 5): Dr. Barnett has received no funding from pharmaceutical companies or organizations involved in MDMA therapeutic research; Dr. Doblin is the founder and executive director of the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS), which funds research assessing the therapeutic potential of MDMA and other psychedelic compounds.
funding.affiliations_note: Barnett: Cleveland Clinic, Ohio; Doblin: MAPS, Santa Cruz, California. As the article itself reports, MAPS criticized the original study, asked NIDA to investigate and obtained the released documents (p. 2), and sponsors the Phase 3 trials mentioned in the discussion (p. 5); Doblin also co-wrote one of the 2003 letters criticizing the study (card sc_mithoefer_2003). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the counts.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered content analysis of the coverage of many retracted and comparable non-retracted studies, with archive searches checked against a second source, two independent coders unaware of the hypothesis, reliability statistics, and paired tests with intervals for the publication-versus-retraction difference.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Large US newspapers are a reasonable frame for print coverage, but the ranking is from 2007 rather than 2002-2003 and papers without online archives were replaced by smaller ones.
A census of the largest newspapers with archives rather than a sample; whether lack of archives is related to coverage is unknown (14 of the top 64 skipped, editors' calculation).
Fifty newspapers give proportions with intervals of roughly 14 percentage points either way; the content comparison of 14 against 6 newspapers is far too small for its tests.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Table 1 lists the newspapers; the archive sources and search terms are given.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 50 newspapers were searched and every retraction story was coded.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Keyword archive searches with a manual fallback for two three-month windows; the sensitivity of the searches was not checked; no search date and no second searcher are reported.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: No coding scheme, coders, blinding or inter-rater reliability are reported for the content analysis, and balanced reporting is not defined.

The main comparison (publication against retraction coverage, paired by newspaper) and the word-count difference are not tested and no intervals are given; 15 uncorrected Fisher tests compare 14 with 6 newspapers.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: No response rate applies; the availability of archives is covered under items 1 and 2.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The counts are simple and probably close to right for these 50 newspapers, but the searches were not validated, the content coding is unreported, the coders are not named although both authors' affiliations bear on the topic, and the central comparison was not tested. The counts may be cited as a description of these newspapers' coverage; the judgments of balance and the explanations for the difference may not. What the article says about the 2002 study and its retraction is second-hand and should be cited as its description.

key_findings.finding: As the article describes the original study: published in Science in September 2002 by Ricaurte, McCann and colleagues at Johns Hopkins University, funded by NIDA, in which MDMA was given to 10 non-human primates to model human use; the authors report that it found severe dopaminergic and less severe serotonergic neurotoxicity and that two of the animals died, and that the dopaminergic finding was new and raised the possibility of parkinsonism.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the 2002 paper was not read. The authors of the 2002 study wrote in 2003 that one of ten monkeys died (card sc_mithoefer_2003).

key_findings.finding: As described: the Johns Hopkins Gazette announced that the researchers had found extensive damage to brain dopamine neurons in primates at doses it likened to those young adults take at all-night dance parties; the AAAS press release was titled as a study finding that ecstasy causes brain damage and closed with its chief executive likening use to Russian roulette with brain function; the New York Times wrote that the amount some take in a single night may cause permanent brain damage. MAPS and Mithoefer et al. (2003) criticized the findings, and Ricaurte et al. defended them, saying their results differed from earlier studies because of a novel protocol.

As described: in September 2003, one year after publication, Science issued a retraction in which Ricaurte and colleagues wrote that methamphetamine rather than MDMA had been used to treat all but one study animal, because of a labelling error (Ricaurte et al., 2003b); MAPS then asked NIDA to investigate all work done by the group since the mislabelled supply was received.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; the retraction notice was not read.

key_findings.finding: As described: NIDA issued no report, but in January 2004, in response to a Freedom of Information Act request by MAPS, released documents listing affected projects and indicating that another article would be retracted; a Nature editorial noted that the publication had received far more US media coverage than the retraction and discussed its possible influence on the passage of the Illicit Drug Anti-Proliferation Act; MAPS reported that a psychotherapy trial in Spain was shut down and approval efforts in the United States hampered.

Of 50 newspapers, 26 (52%) ran a story on the publication and 20 (40%) on the retraction; 6 (12%) covered the retraction without having covered the publication; of the 26 that covered the publication, 14 (54%) covered the retraction. Circulation was not associated with coverage of the publication (p=.25) or of the retraction (p=.84).

Mean word count 482 (SD 303; range 69-1260) for publication stories and 396 (SD 193; 86-837) for retraction stories. In newspapers covering both events, 550 (SD 271; 188-1260) against 386 (SD 205; 86-837); publication-only newspapers 404 (SD 331; 69-1038); retraction-only newspapers 420 (SD 177; 124-652).
key_findings.note: Editors' check: the subgroup means recombine to the overall means (14 x 550 + 12 x 404 over 26 gives 483; 14 x 386 + 6 x 420 over 20 gives 396).

key_findings.finding: All 20 retraction stories reported that the original findings had suggested that one night's MDMA use could cause brain damage or parkinsonism and that a mix-up of study compounds made the results erroneous; 14 (70%) mentioned long-standing scientific controversy, 13 (65%) earlier criticism, 11 (55%) that animals died, 11 (55%) that the laboratory blamed its supplier, 8 (40%) McCann's regrets, 7 (35%) earlier research suggesting serotonergic damage, 7 (35%) allegations of political motives, 5 (25%) NIDA funding; 4 (20%) each a critic's quotation, the laboratory's statement that its earlier MDMA findings were unaffected, the university's statement that Ricaurte remained in good standing, McCann's continuing concerns about MDMA, and Ricaurte's statement that the laboratory had not verified the compounds; 3 (15%) his denial of political influence; 2 (10%) that Leshner had defended the findings. No component differed significantly between the 14 and the 6 newspapers (Fisher's exact test, p from 0.06 to 1.00).
key_findings.note: Editors' check: every percentage in Table 2 matches its count, and the Fisher p values recomputed for five rows (0.06, 0.16, 0.27, 0.35, 0.61) agree.

key_findings.finding: The authors judge the retraction stories balanced but often short of context, such as quotations from the study's authors or critics, the allegations of political influence, and earlier research suggesting serotonergic damage after recreational use.

The authors state that debate continues over whether serotonergic damage associated with recreational use applies to pharmaceutical-grade MDMA (citing Doblin et al., 2014, and Parrott, 2013, 2014) and over long-term neurocognitive deficits (citing among others Parrott, 2011, Lyvers, 2011, and Halpern et al., 2004, 2011), and that evidence of MDMA-induced dopaminergic toxicity in humans has not materialized since the retraction.
key_findings.note: An assertion without citation of human studies; the source given for the regulatory point is a commentary (Doblin et al., 2014). The Parrott (2013) cited here is a different paper (Human Psychopharmacology 28:289-307, per the reference list) from the review carded in this batch as parrott_2013.

key_findings.finding: Limitations given by the authors: archives could not be searched for all of the 50 largest US newspapers, the AAAS press release for the retraction could not be obtained, and the placement of stories within newspapers was not analysed. As quoted from a Nature editorial, the retraction was issued late on Friday 5 September, giving low-key coverage.

reporting_issues.issue: The article says two of the primates died, whereas the authors of the 2002 study wrote in their 2003 reply that one of ten monkeys given the regimen died of complications related to hyperthermia (Mithoefer et al., 2003, p. 1504).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of deaths should not be cited from either source without the original paper or its retraction notice.

reporting_issues.issue: The 14-of-26 figure (newspapers covering the publication that also covered the retraction) is framed as much lower retraction coverage, but it conditions on having covered the publication; the symmetric figure, 14 of the 20 newspapers covering the retraction (70%) having covered the publication, is not reported (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline contrast is partly a product of how the subset was chosen; the untested 52% against 40% is the fair comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list gives Parrott (2011) as Addiction 106:1365-1268 and Fisk et al. (2011) as Addiction 106:1268-69; the PDF of Parrott (2011) shows that letter at pp. 1365-1368 and the Fisk et al. letter beginning on p. 1368.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor citation errors; use the DOIs.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods name the archive sources and the search terms and describe a manual search of two three-month windows as a fallback, but give no date on which the archives were searched and no second searcher or verification of the searches.
reporting_issues.consequence: The counts, which are the only part of this study the encyclopedia cites, cannot be reproduced against the same archive state, and single-searcher coverage cannot be checked (JBI item 6).

disagreements.resolution: Checked the Methods at pp. 2-3: the sources, terms and manual fallback are given, and no search date or duplicate searching is mentioned anywhere. Added as a reporting issue.

design_detail: Correspondence (Neuropsychopharmacology 2012;37:1072-1073), single author: a reply to a letter by Krebs and Johansen that criticized the author's group's fMRI study of cortical excitability in people who used MDMA (Bauernfeind et al., 2011). Five running-text paragraphs, acknowledgments, competing interests and seven references; no data. The Krebs and Johansen letter and the Bauernfeind et al. study were not read; both are described here only as this reply describes them. Received 16 August 2011, accepted 19 August 2011, published 13 February 2012 (PMC article notes and publisher page).
can_establish: How the author of a cross-sectional imaging study answers a methodological critique of it, and what he accepts and disputes about the limits of cross-sectional designs.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA changes brain activation or serotonergic function in people: the reply gives no numbers from either the original analysis or the critics' reanalysis.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter). The study defended enrolled people with between 3 and 155 episodes of MDMA use and a control group (3rd paragraph); group sizes are not given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The reply cites mainly the author's own group's work (five of seven references) and does not report the critics' reanalysis in numbers.

exposure.measurement: Not described beyond lifetime episodes of MDMA use (3 to 155 in the study defended; 3rd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime episodes only, as a study characteristic (3 to 155).
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not given.

comparison.controls: A control cohort is mentioned but not described (3rd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The reply accepts that traits such as impulsivity may predispose people to MDMA use (4th paragraph) but argues that serotonergic effects of MDMA are likely irrespective of such pre-existing differences.

outcomes.instruments: BOLD fMRI activation in the study defended; functional connectivity in a further study of the group (Salomon et al., 2011); impulsivity in a prospective study cited (de Win et al., 2007).
outcomes.validity_norms: The author reads increased task-evoked activation as a possible marker of reduced neural efficiency and compensatory effort (2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable; no outcome is analysed in the letter.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not discussed.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None given, either for the original correlations or for the critics' reanalysis.
analysis.selective_reporting: The reply describes the critics' reanalysis (the MDMA group and controls in one correlation, no association found) and argues it is inappropriate, but reports no figures from either analysis.
analysis.power: Not discussed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As the reply describes them, people with little MDMA use tended to show activation somewhat below the control mean and people with much use activation above it, so the MDMA group as a whole did not clearly differ from controls; the claimed dose-response relationship is a correlation within the MDMA group, on ranked data. The prospective impulsivity finding is cited in one sentence without numbers.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The author speaks of a strong dose-response relationship between lifetime MDMA exposure and brain activation (3rd paragraph) and states his belief that MDMA-induced serotonergic neurotoxicity likely changes mood and behaviour irrespective of pre-existing differences (4th paragraph), while agreeing that large prospective studies are needed to confirm or refute cross-sectional findings (5th paragraph). A pattern that goes below control values at low exposure and above them at high exposure is not what a simple damage model predicts, and the reply offers no test of it.

timeline.event: Prospective cohort of people starting ecstasy use, cited for an increase in impulsivity after first use (de Win et al., 2007, as described in this letter; not read).

fMRI study of cortical excitability defended here (Bauernfeind et al., 2011); as Parrott (2013) describes it, no significant group differences in any region, with lifetime use associated with greater activation in some regions.
Letter by Krebs and Johansen criticizing that study and reporting a reanalysis of its raw data (not read; described only by this reply).

replication.where_it_stands: An unresolved exchange: the critics' reanalysis and the authors' correlations within the MDMA group are both described without numbers in the material read here. Both sides agree that prospective studies are needed.

funding.funder: NIDA/NIH grants R01 DA01537 and R21 DA020149 to the author, and NCRR/NIH Vanderbilt CTSA grant UL1 RR024975 (Acknowledgments, as printed).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author received publication royalties from Lippincott Williams and Wilkins, and consultant income from the Southwest Michigan First Life Science Fund, the University of West Alabama, Novo Nordisk, the Treatment Research Institute and Shire Pharmaceuticals (competing interests statement).
funding.affiliations_note: Psychiatric Neuroimaging Program, Vanderbilt Addiction Center, Vanderbilt University School of Medicine, Nashville. The letter defends the author's own study, and five of its seven references are from his group. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the letter.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective imaging cohort that measures cortical activation and serotonin transporter binding before first use and again after use begins, with use verified, a retested non-using control group, and the dose-response model (including how controls enter it) stated before analysis.

domains.note: A reply letter; no search, and references chosen to support the defended study.
The cited studies, including the prospective impulsivity finding, are not appraised and no numbers are given.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Five of seven references are the author's group's work, and the letter defends one of them.
The causal statement is labelled as the author's belief, but it is placed beside data that cannot support it.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against MDMA-related changes in brain function
domains.note: The critics' case and the pre-trait explanation are acknowledged, but the critics' reanalysis is not shown and is dismissed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The reply may be cited for the author's acknowledgement that prospective studies are needed and for his account of the dispute; it is not evidence that MDMA alters brain activation.

key_findings.finding: The author agrees with the critics on the need for well-controlled longitudinal studies to address the potential neurotoxic effects of recreational MDMA, while saying their concerns were addressed in the original report.

On a press-release comparison with early Alzheimer's disease: the group had noted that increased task-evoked activation in people who used MDMA overlaps with findings in people at risk of Alzheimer's disease, possibly a marker of reduced neural efficiency; the author states that he neither proposes a common cause nor suggests that people who use MDMA will develop dementia at higher rates.

The critics combined the MDMA group and controls in one correlation and found no association between MDMA exposure and activation. The author replies that people with little use tend to fall somewhat below the control mean and people with much use above it, that the study included people with 3 to 155 episodes of use, and that including controls therefore obscures what he calls a strong dose-response relationship, evident with ranked data. No figures are given. He adds that the relationship is evident when ranked data are used, to account for the non-parametric distribution of lifetime exposure; no coefficient, interval or sample size is given for either analysis.

The author accepts that impulsivity may predispose to MDMA use but argues that MDMA's serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates is well established, that he knows of no evidence that humans are less vulnerable, and that a prospective study found incident MDMA use associated with increased impulsivity (de Win et al., 2007), so that elevated impulsivity is not solely a pre-existing trait.
key_findings.note: The prospective finding is cited without numbers and was not read; the reference's title concerns brain imaging in people new to ecstasy.

key_findings.finding: The author states that large, well-controlled prospective studies are needed to confirm or refute cross-sectional findings, while holding that well-designed cross-sectional imaging studies are informative.

reporting_issues.issue: Neither the critics' reanalysis nor the original correlations within the MDMA group are reported in numbers, so the claimed strong dose-response relationship cannot be checked from the letter. The letter also gives no group sizes, no abstinence interval and no distribution of exposure beyond the range of 3 to 155 episodes, so nothing in it can be checked or re-analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The letter cannot be cited for the size or existence of a dose-response relationship.

reporting_issues.issue: The prospective study is cited in the text as de Winn et al., 2007, and in the reference list as de Win et al. (2007).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor spelling slip.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence that MDMA has a well-established ability to cause serotonin neurotoxicity in non-human primates, and that the author knows of no evidence that humans are less vulnerable, carries no citation of its own; the citations in that paragraph are to the author's group's human imaging work and to a prospective cohort. The closing paragraph cites two reviews for animal evidence in general (Cowan et al., 2008; Reneman et al., 2006).
reporting_issues.consequence: The one general statement about primate neurotoxicity in this letter is unsourced at the place it is made, so it cannot be cited for that evidence; the primate studies themselves have not been read.

design_detail: Cross-sectional field study in Salt Lake City, Utah. 52 people who had used ecstasy at least 17 times (30 with 17 to 50 episodes, 22 with more than 50) and 59 who had never used it, all from the all-night dance (rave) scene, with strict limits on lifetime use of other drugs and alcohol, and with abstinence and undisclosed drug use checked by breath, urine and hair tests at the testing visit. Battery of 15 neuropsychological tests (40 scored measures in Table 2); linear regression adjusted for age, gender, race/ethnicity, four family-of-origin variables, childhood conduct disorder and childhood ADHD. Designed as a replication, in a fresh sample, of the same group's 2004 pilot study. Read as the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central.
can_establish: Whether, among people from the same dance scene with minimal exposure to other drugs and alcohol, a history of ecstasy use of the size reported here (median 43.5 episodes) goes with detectable differences on a broad cognitive battery at least 25 days after last use, and which large differences can be ruled out for heavier use.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy causes or does not cause cognitive change (no testing before use); the effects of much heavier use (only 6 people reported 150 or more episodes); differences of medium size on most measures (for heavier use, a medium effect is excluded on 5 of the 14 measures analysed, left in play on 8 and left exactly at the margin on 1); or results in people who use ecstasy together with other drugs, who are most people who use it.

sample.recruitment: Case finders advertised at raves and other places frequented by the Salt Lake City all-night dance scene; telephone screening included irrelevant questions to hide the criteria, and people turned down were not told why (Materials and Methods › Participants, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). About 1500 people screened by telephone, about 250 qualified for the baseline visit, 116 met all criteria and completed testing, and 5 were excluded for drugs found in hair or urine (Results, 1st paragraph). Payment: $100 for the baseline visit, $100 for testing and $150 after the urine and hair results were confirmed (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 5th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 to 45; at least 17 lifetime episodes of ecstasy use or none; native English speakers; at least 10 all-night dance parties (awake until at least 4:30 AM). Excluded: more than 100 lifetime episodes of cannabis use or more than 10 of any other illicit drug class, more than 50 lifetime episodes of alcohol intoxication, clinically significant head injury or medical illness affecting cognition, and current psychoactive medication; psychiatric disorders were not excluded (Participants, 2nd paragraph). The criteria were relaxed for 6 people near the end (cocaine 15 and 20 times; other hallucinogens 11, 14 and 22 times; cannabis 250 times) (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Comparison group vs ecstasy group (Table 1): men 64.4% vs 57.7% (p = 0.56); white 91.5% vs 76.9% (p = 0.04); father's education high school or less 27.1% vs 53.9% (p = 0.006), mother's 27.1% vs 61.5% (p < 0.001); parents' income $30,000 or less 27.1% vs 30.8%; median age 24 vs 22 years (p = 0.06); current major depression 6.8% vs 5.8%; current anxiety disorder 15.3% vs 9.6%.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single testing). Of about 1500 people screened, 111 were analysed; the characteristics of those not tested are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: A highly selected sample: people who used ecstasy with little other drug or alcohol use, chosen from a dance scene with a comparison group from the same scene. The ecstasy group had attended more all-night parties (median 98 vs 45, p = 0.005), more often had parents with little education, and had lower vocabulary scores (Table 1; Table 2). Exposure was modest (median 43.5 episodes).

exposure.measurement: Semi-structured interview on lifetime episodes, doses and settings of ecstasy use and lifetime use of alcohol and other drugs (Baseline Evaluation). At testing: breathalyzer and urine dipstick (cannabis, opioids, cocaine, barbiturates, amphetamines, benzodiazepines, phencyclidine), exclusion if positive; urine sent to an outside laboratory for MDMA; hair (or axillary hair) tested for drugs over the past 90 days; results discarded if urine was positive for MDMA or hair positive for a drug the person had denied (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime ecstasy episodes median 43.5 (interquartile range 27 to 87.3) (Table 1); groups of 17 to 50 and more than 50 episodes (Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph); only 6 people reported 150 or more episodes (Discussion, 6th paragraph). Amounts per episode were collected but are not reported. Tablet content unknown.
exposure.polysubstance: Kept low by the exclusion limits and checked by breath, urine and hair tests; residual differences in Table 1: lifetime marijuana intoxications median 10 (interquartile range 4 to 30) vs 1 (0 to 6), p < 0.001; cigarettes a day median 0 in both, p = 0.04; lifetime alcohol intoxications 10 vs 10. Marijuana use was not among the adjustment variables; a repeat analysis without the 6 people over the drug limits gave very similar results (Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 10 days without ecstasy, other illicit drugs or all-night parties required before testing (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 1st paragraph); observed minimum 25 days since last ecstasy use, 3 people (6%) under 40 days, median 121 days (interquartile range 60 to 209) (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).

comparison.controls: 59 people who had never used ecstasy, from the same dance scene (at least 10 all-night parties), under the same exclusion limits.
comparison.matching: Not individually matched; adjusted by linear regression for age, gender, race/ethnicity, parents' combined education, parents' income, family history of psychiatric disorder, family history of substance use disorder, childhood conduct disorder and childhood ADHD score (Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph). Verbal IQ and current depression scores were added only in a check of the strategy-application result.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No testing before ecstasy use. Vocabulary and verbal IQ, which the authors treat as signs of premorbid ability, were lower in the ecstasy group (Table 2); childhood ADHD and conduct disorder were assessed retrospectively.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Minimal by design (lifetime marijuana intoxications median 1; alcohol intoxications median 10).

outcomes.instruments: WAIS-R Vocabulary, Digit Span, Digit Symbol and Block Design; Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure; Wisconsin Card Sorting Test; Trail Making A and B; Raven's Progressive Matrices; FAS verbal fluency; Stroop; California Verbal Learning Test, second edition; WMS-III Logical Memory, Verbal Paired Associates and Spatial Span; Revised Strategy Application Test; computerized Iowa Gambling Task; Grooved Pegboard; plus the Beck Depression Inventory (Neuropsychological Testing Visit, 4th paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: No comparison with published norms is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Adjusted mean differences between groups (non-using minus ecstasy group); no definition of impairment. Equivalence-type bounds (from 90% confidence intervals) for the heavier-use group on 14 chosen measures (Statistical Analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table 4).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, by stated choice: the authors judge Bonferroni correction too conservative and ask readers to bear multiple testing in mind (Statistical Analyses, 3rd paragraph). 40 counts the measures in Table 2; each was also compared for the two use subgroups (Table 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Whole ecstasy group vs comparison group, adjusted differences (comparison minus ecstasy group, 95% CI; Table 2): verbal memory near zero, e.g. CVLT trials 1-5 total 61.6 vs 60.6, -0.5 (-4.2 to 3.2), p = 0.79; WMS-III logical memory delayed 31.1 vs 29.4, 0.7 (-2.4 to 3.8), p = 0.65; verbal paired associates delayed 6.8 vs 6.8, 0.1 (-0.7 to 0.8). Significant (uncorrected): vocabulary 52.9 vs 45.8, 4.7 (1.1 to 8.4), p = 0.01; digit symbol 72.7 vs 64.5, 7.1 (1.0 to 13.2), p = 0.02; spatial span forward 9.7 vs 9.0, 0.8 (0.0 to 1.6), p = 0.04; non-dominant-hand pegboard 67.2 vs 72.4 s, -5.0 (-9.3 to -0.7), p = 0.02; borderline Raven's 2.2 (0.0 to 4.3), p = 0.05, and digits backwards 0.9 (0.0 to 1.9), p = 0.05; verbal IQ 108.4 vs 99.3, 6.0 (-0.2 to 12.2), p = 0.06. Heavier use (more than 50 episodes, n = 22) vs comparison group (Table 3): proportion of brief items on the Revised Strategy Application Test 88.5 vs 79.5%, 8.7 (3.1 to 14.4), p = 0.003; non-dominant pegboard 67.2 vs 75.6 s, -8.4 (-13.9 to -2.8), p = 0.003; vocabulary 5.0 (0.2 to 9.8), p = 0.04. 17 to 50 episodes (n = 30): Raven's 3.0 (0.5 to 5.4), p = 0.02; digit symbol 8.4 (1.4 to 15.3), p = 0.02; vocabulary 4.6 (0.4 to 8.8), p = 0.03; WCST categories 0.9 (0.1 to 1.7), p = 0.03; spatial span forward 0.9 (0.0 to 1.8), p = 0.04. Within the ecstasy group, more lifetime episodes (log scale) went with fewer brief items, coefficient -1.4 (-2.3 to -0.4), p = 0.004, Pearson r = -0.37 (Results, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1). Bounds for heavier use (Table 4): the largest Cohen's d not excluded ranged from 0.37 to 0.76. Editors' calculation: adjusted standardized differences for the whole group, about 0.48 for vocabulary, 0.50 for digit symbol and -0.05 for CVLT total; for heavier use about 0.81 for brief items and 0.92 for the pegboard; of the 40 adjusted differences in Table 2, 29 point towards lower performance in the ecstasy group, 8 towards higher and 3 are zero (a count only: the measures are correlated, so this is not a test); in Table 4, a medium effect (d 0.5) is excluded on 5 of the 14 measures, with one bound at exactly 0.50 and the other 8 from 0.53 to 0.76.
analysis.covariates: Age, gender, race/ethnicity, parents' education, parents' income, family history of psychiatric disorder, family history of substance use disorder, childhood conduct disorder, childhood ADHD score. Not adjusted for lifetime all-night parties, marijuana use or verbal IQ (verbal IQ and depression score only in a check of the strategy-application result).
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 2 and 3 are titled representative test scores, without saying whether every scored variable is shown. Several checks are reported only in words: the simplified model and the analysis without the 6 people over the drug limits (very similar), the strategy-application result adjusted for verbal IQ and depression (virtually unchanged), and the exploratory analyses behind calling the pegboard difference chance (not shown) (Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph). The equivalence bounds cover 14 measures chosen for the heavier-use group only (Table 4).
analysis.power: No power calculation. The equivalence bounds (Table 4) show what the comparison of 22 people with heavier use and 59 without could exclude: Cohen's d of 0.8 or more on all 14 chosen measures, and of 0.5 or more on 5 of them, with one bound at exactly 0.50 and 8 from 0.53 to 0.76 (editors' count from Table 4).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Adjusted differences were small and mostly non-significant across 40 measures, including all verbal-memory measures; the significant differences (uncorrected) were lower vocabulary, digit symbol and spatial span and a slower non-dominant hand in the whole ecstasy group, and fewer brief strategy items, a slower non-dominant hand and lower vocabulary with heavier use; within the ecstasy group more episodes went with fewer brief items. Most point estimates lean towards lower scores in the ecstasy group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that they failed to demonstrate marked residual cognitive effects, give both possible readings (a false negative, or that ecstasy by itself does not generally produce lasting residual neurotoxicity) and state that the question remains incompletely resolved (abstract; Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs). Each significant difference is set aside as premorbid (vocabulary), chance (differences seen only with lighter use; the pegboard, on analyses not shown) or possibly premorbid impulsivity (strategy application), while non-significant results are read as no difference; the claim that even a medium effect could be excluded on many measures (Results, 3rd paragraph) holds for 6 of 14. The cross-sectional design cannot show that the lower vocabulary predates use.

timeline.event: Pilot study by the same group (23 people who used ecstasy, 16 who did not, minimal other drug use): heavier use (60 to 450 episodes) went with differences in processing speed, strategic self-regulation and executive function, lighter use with almost none (as described in the Introduction, 4th paragraph).

Gouzoulis-Mayfrank and colleagues, 38 people followed over 18 months: those who stopped (17) did not improve and those who continued (21) did not deteriorate (as described in the Discussion, 4th paragraph) (reference 62 of this paper; the attribution was checked in the reference list by the second reader).
Prospective study of people starting ecstasy use: smaller verbal-memory gains after a median of 1.5 tablets, which this paper says raises doubt about a causal role (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
This study: of the pilot's differences with heavier use, only strategic self-regulation recurred.
Letter re-interpreting these findings as consistent with serotonergic neurotoxicity (title as recorded; not read by this reader).
Commentary on this study (title: strengthening the case against functionally significant serotonergic neurotoxicity; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: This study is itself the replication of the 2004 pilot, and reproduced only the strategy-application difference with heavier use. It is the main study of people who used ecstasy with minimal other drug use among the papers read in this batch; a published letter and a commentary on it are read separately. No independent replication is described in the papers read here.

funding.funder: US National Institute on Drug Abuse grant DA017953 (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: None of the authors reports conflicts of interest, and none reports support from the tobacco, alcohol, pharmaceutical or gaming industries in association with this study (Footnotes).
funding.affiliations_note: McLean Hospital and Harvard Medical School (Belmont and Boston, Massachusetts); University of New Mexico (Author information). Recorded as a flag for closer reading only.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people from the same scene tested before first use, with hair-verified exposure across a wide range including heavy use, a pre-specified primary outcome and an equivalence margin set in advance, so that both the presence and the absence of medium-sized differences can be shown.

domains.note: Many premorbid and family variables adjusted for; residual differences in marijuana use and party attendance not adjusted; lower vocabulary in the ecstasy group may reflect premorbid ability (which would bias towards finding differences) or an effect of use.
Lifetime episodes self-reported and tablet content unknown, but abstinence and undisclosed use of other drugs checked by breath, urine and hair tests.
About 111 of 1500 screened; a deliberately unusual group of people who used ecstasy with little else; characteristics of those excluded not reported.
None described.
5 tested people excluded by design for positive drug tests; no other missing data reported.
Standardized tests, but blinding of the tester to group is not reported.
Representative tables, 40 measures without correction, checks reported without numbers, equivalence bounds for chosen measures only.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design addresses the main confounders of this literature (other drug use, verified abstinence, comparison from the same scene, family and childhood variables), so the small differences are less likely to be explained by polydrug use than in most studies. Concerns remain about residual confounding, unreported tester blinding and selective presentation, and the sample's modest exposure limits what the null results can exclude. The study may be cited for small or absent differences on most tests after moderate ecstasy use with minimal other drug use, and for the exclusion of large differences with heavier use; it may not be cited as showing that ecstasy has no lasting effect, or that medium-sized effects are excluded.

key_findings.finding: Of about 1500 people screened by telephone, about 250 qualified for baseline, 116 completed testing and 5 were excluded for drugs found in hair or urine, leaving 52 people who had used ecstasy and 59 who had not; criteria were relaxed for 6 people.

Ecstasy use: lifetime episodes median 43.5 (interquartile range 27 to 87.3); days since last use median 121 (60 to 209), minimum 25, 3 people under 40; 30 people with 17 to 50 episodes and 22 with more than 50.

The ecstasy group more often had parents with high-school education or less (father 53.9% vs 27.1%, p = 0.006; mother 61.5% vs 27.1%, p < 0.001), was less often white (76.9% vs 91.5%, p = 0.04), had attended more all-night parties (median 98 vs 45, p = 0.005) and reported more marijuana intoxications (median 10 vs 1, p < 0.001).

Memory measures did not differ after adjustment: CVLT trials 1-5 total 61.6 vs 60.6, difference -0.5 (95% CI -4.2 to 3.2), p = 0.79; WMS-III logical memory immediate 0.7 (-3.6 to 5.0) and delayed 0.7 (-2.4 to 3.8); verbal paired associates delayed 0.1 (-0.7 to 0.8); Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall 0.8 (-1.8 to 3.4).

Significant (uncorrected) whole-group differences: vocabulary 4.7 (1.1 to 8.4), p = 0.01; digit symbol 7.1 (1.0 to 13.2), p = 0.02; spatial span forward 0.8 (0.0 to 1.6), p = 0.04; non-dominant-hand pegboard -5.0 s (-9.3 to -0.7), p = 0.02; borderline Raven's (p = 0.05) and digits backwards (p = 0.05); verbal IQ 6.0 (-0.2 to 12.2), p = 0.06.

Heavier use (more than 50 episodes, n = 22) vs no use: fewer brief items on the Revised Strategy Application Test, 79.5 vs 88.5%, difference 8.7 (3.1 to 14.4), p = 0.003, virtually unchanged after further adjustment for verbal IQ and depression score; slower non-dominant-hand pegboard, -8.4 s (-13.9 to -2.8), p = 0.003; lower vocabulary 5.0 (0.2 to 9.8), p = 0.04; no other differences.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (comparison vs heavier-use columns); Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Lighter use (17 to 50 episodes, n = 30) vs no use: lower Raven's 3.0 (0.5 to 5.4), digit symbol 8.4 (1.4 to 15.3), vocabulary 4.6 (0.4 to 8.8), Wisconsin categories 0.9 (0.1 to 1.7) and spatial span forward 0.9 (0.0 to 1.8), p = 0.02 to 0.04; the authors note these appeared with lighter but not heavier use.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (comparison vs lighter-use columns); Results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Within the ecstasy group, more lifetime episodes (log-transformed) went with fewer brief items: coefficient -1.4 (-2.3 to -0.4), p = 0.004, adjusted for age, gender and race/ethnicity; Pearson r = -0.37; not driven by outliers on inspection of the scatterplot.
key_findings.note: Figure 1 is an image; values were not read from it.

key_findings.finding: For heavier use vs no use, the equivalence analysis covers the 14 measures on which the two groups did not differ significantly; the largest effect not excluded at the 0.05 level ranges from Cohen's d 0.37 (Wisconsin perseverations) to 0.76 (spatial span total). The authors say a large effect (d 0.8) could be excluded on all of them and a medium effect (d 0.5) on many.
key_findings.note: Table 4 lists, for the 14 measures on which heavier use and no use did not differ significantly, the largest effect that could be excluded at the 0.05 level: in ascending order the printed values are 0.37, 0.40, 0.48, 0.49, 0.49, 0.50, 0.53, 0.54, 0.55, 0.58, 0.64, 0.66, 0.69 and 0.76 (14 values; 0.49 appears twice). A large effect (d 0.8) is excluded on all 14. A medium effect (d 0.5) is excluded on 5 (bounds below 0.50); one bound is exactly 0.50 (Iowa Gambling Task), where a medium effect is not excluded; and 8 bounds run from 0.53 to 0.76. The bounds above 0.50 cluster in working memory and visuospatial span (spatial span total 0.76, digits backwards 0.69, digit symbol 0.66, block design 0.64), the domain in which Murphy et al. (2009) report the most consistent differences, so the null is much tighter for verbal memory than for span tasks.

key_findings.finding: The authors read the lower vocabulary as a premorbid difference, since vocabulary is generally preserved after neurological insults, and the differences seen only with lighter use, and the pegboard difference, as likely chance; strategic self-regulation is their only consistent finding, possibly reflecting reflection impulsivity, which they say may predate use.

The authors note their results conflict with their own pilot, possibly because the pilot's heavier-use group was tested after shorter median abstinence (59.5 vs 121 days), because of unmeasured confounders or by chance.
key_findings.note: This study is the authors' own attempt to replicate their 2004 pilot in a fresh, larger sample, and of the pilot's differences with heavier use only strategic self-regulation recurred: a failed self-replication, which is the single most important fact about the paper for the contested question.

key_findings.finding: The authors give two readings: a false negative, perhaps because only 6 participants had 150 or more episodes or few had predisposing factors; or that ecstasy by itself does not generally produce lasting residual neurotoxicity; and they conclude that the question remains incompletely resolved.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say that even a medium effect (d of 0.5 or more) could be excluded on many measures. Table 4 lists, for the 14 measures on which heavier use and no use did not differ significantly, the largest effect that could be excluded at the 0.05 level: in ascending order the printed values are 0.37, 0.40, 0.48, 0.49, 0.49, 0.50, 0.53, 0.54, 0.55, 0.58, 0.64, 0.66, 0.69 and 0.76 (14 values; 0.49 appears twice). A large effect (d 0.8) is excluded on all 14. A medium effect (d 0.5) is excluded on 5 (bounds below 0.50); one bound is exactly 0.50 (Iowa Gambling Task), where a medium effect is not excluded; and 8 bounds run from 0.53 to 0.76. So many covers 5 of 14 strictly, or 6 if the bound of exactly 0.50 is counted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The null results are less informative than the text suggests: medium-sized differences with heavier use remain possible on most measures shown.

reporting_issues.issue: The pegboard difference with heavier use (p = 0.003) is called likely due to chance on the basis of exploratory analyses that are not reported, and several robustness checks are reported only in words.
reporting_issues.consequence: The basis for discounting significant differences cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison group's SD for the proportion of brief items is 8.8 in Table 2 and 8.7 in Table 3, for the same 59 people.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor transcription difference.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 2 and 3 are titled representative test scores; whether all scored variables are shown is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible selective presentation of outcomes.

design_detail: Invited-style commentary (Addiction 2011;106:787-788), single author, published alongside Halpern et al. (2011). Four running-text paragraphs, a declaration of interests and 18 references; no sections, methods or data. Argues that Halpern et al.'s study, designed to limit confounding by other drug use, strengthens the case against functionally significant serotonergic neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy, and that the one difference found is compatible with pre-existing traits. Locators count the four paragraphs from the start of the text.
can_establish: What the author argues about Halpern et al. (2011) and about pre-existing traits as an explanation for test differences, and which studies he cites for it.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy does or does not cause lasting serotonergic damage: the commentary adds no data, and its central argument (pre-drug traits) is offered as a possibility.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The study discussed is Halpern et al. (2011): people who used ecstasy, selected for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol, and non-using controls recruited from the same rave subculture (1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the author chooses the studies discussed.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The commentary cites the null and pre-trait side of the literature and the author's own earlier critiques (refs 2, 7, 11); it does not discuss the PET studies of the serotonin transporter published from 2008 to 2010 that the other letters in this batch cite (McCann et al., 2008; Kish et al., 2010).

exposure.measurement: Not described in the commentary beyond the selection of the Halpern et al. sample for low exposure to other drugs.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not given; the commentary refers only to heavy and moderate subgroups.
exposure.polysubstance: Presented as the study's main strength: the ecstasy group was selected for low exposure to other illicit drugs and alcohol, unlike most studies, in which confounding by other substances could not be ruled out (1st paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not given.

comparison.controls: As described: non-using controls who belonged to the rave subculture like the ecstasy group (1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: As described: analyses adjusted for demographic and other factors, for example attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (1st paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The commentary's central point: impulsivity, weaker executive control and lower serotonergic function before any drug use may predispose to heavier drug use, so the people who used most heavily would on average be more impulsive even without neurotoxicity (2nd and 3rd paragraphs). It cites one prospective study in which test performance in people who had not used ecstasy predicted later first use (ref 12).

outcomes.instruments: As described: a battery of 15 neuropsychological tests, of which the Revised Strategy Application Test (RSAT) is the only one discussed (1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: The commentary notes that poor RSAT performance in people with brain injury has been read as deficient prefrontal inhibitory control over reward-driven responding (2nd paragraph, ref 8).
outcomes.operationalization: A clear indication of poorer performance is not defined; no p values or effect sizes are given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not discussed.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None given.
analysis.selective_reporting: Reports only the RSAT difference in the heavier subgroup. It does not mention the non-dominant-hand pegboard difference in the same subgroup, which in Halpern et al.'s Table 3 has the same p value (0.003), or the overall-group differences on five tests at p of 0.05 or below (checked by this reader in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Tables 2 and 3); Halpern et al. themselves call the RSAT result their only consistently significant finding and the pegboard result likely due to chance.
analysis.power: Not discussed; the commentary does not say how large an effect the study could have detected.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The commentary's evidence is one cross-sectional study with few differences, an argument that pre-existing traits could explain the one it discusses, an analogy with fenfluramine, a cross-sectional comparison read as recovery of transporter binding after abstinence, and two within-person studies of controlled exposure described as finding no deficits without sample sizes or designs.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The commentary calls Halpern et al. possibly the most informative retrospective study to date and concludes that, once controlled within-person studies are replicated, MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy may be shown to be a "chimera" (4th paragraph), with Halpern et al.'s findings already supporting that outcome. A null result in a sample of 52 (22 in the heavier subgroup), without effect sizes, is presented as support for absence of harm, and the within-person evidence cited is a conference abstract (ref 17) and a small therapy pilot trial (ref 18).

timeline.event: Critique of the 2004 pilot study by the same author (Lyvers and Hasking, 2004), cited as ref 2.
Halpern et al. (2011), the study discussed.
Letter reading the same study as consistent with neurotoxicity.

replication.where_it_stands: Opposite reading of the same data to Parrott (2011). The argument from pre-existing traits is plausible but untested in this commentary; the within-person exposure studies it relies on are few and small.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Declaration of interests: None.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Bond University, Gold Coast, Australia. The author had criticized the 2004 pilot study (ref 2) and cites three of his own papers (refs 2, 7, 11).

what_would_settle_it: Prospective within-person studies that measure cognition and serotonin transporter binding before and after exposure, large enough to exclude small effects, both in clinical-trial participants and in people who start using ecstasy on their own, with a retested non-using control group.

domains.note: A commentary; no search, studies chosen by the author.
Halpern et al.'s design is appraised; the within-person studies and the fenfluramine imaging study are not.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of 18 references are the author's own, including his critique of the pilot study.
The pre-trait argument is offered as a possibility, but the closing paragraph treats absence of evidence as support for absence of harm.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against functionally significant serotonergic neurotoxicity
domains.note: Under-represented: the transporter imaging studies, the pegboard difference and the other overall-group differences in the study discussed.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The commentary is a well-argued statement of the confounding problem in cross-sectional studies, and may be cited for that argument and for what it says about Halpern et al.'s design. It should not be cited as evidence that ecstasy is free of lasting effects.

key_findings.finding: Of the 15 tests in Halpern et al. (2011), chosen because other studies had reported differences on them, the author counts only the Revised Strategy Application Test as clearly poorer, in the heavier subgroup but not the moderate one, compared with controls. He credits the study with selecting people for low exposure to other drugs and alcohol, recruiting controls from the same rave subculture and adjusting for demographic factors and childhood ADHD, and calls it possibly the most informative retrospective study to date.

The author argues that lower strategy-application performance in the heavier subgroup fits pre-drug traits: low serotonergic function has been linked to impulsivity, which is linked to low prefrontal activation, reward sensitivity, signs of frontal dysfunction and heavier substance use; and a prospective study found that test performance in people who had not yet used ecstasy predicted later first use (ref 12, Schilt et al., 2009, on decision making).
key_findings.note: The prospective study is described in one sentence; it was not read here.

key_findings.finding: The author states that the evidence for functional signs of serotonergic neurotoxicity remains mixed (refs 4-7, 13), and that transporter deficiencies in people who use ecstasy appear to recover with abstinence (ref 16, Thomasius et al., 2003), unlike those reported years after fenfluramine (ref 15). He argues that the same traits attributed by some to neurotoxicity may predispose to heavier use, and that retrospective studies cannot separate the two.
key_findings.note: Ref 16 compared people currently using and people who had stopped, at one time point, as Parrott (2013, p. 11 of the in-press PDF) describes it; the recovery is a cross-sectional inference. The persistence half of the fenfluramine contrast is a PET study of people treated years earlier (reference 15); the statements about animal doses, the number of people prescribed the drug and its withdrawal come from a legal and technical book (reference 14; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: The author proposes within-person comparisons before and after controlled experimental exposure as the way to resolve the question, states that the few examples so far found no deficits (ref 17, Ludewig et al., 2003, a conference abstract; ref 18, Mithoefer et al., 2010, a pilot randomized trial in PTSD), and concludes that Halpern et al.'s findings support the view that MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in people who use ecstasy may prove illusory.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary says only the strategy-application test clearly differed in the heavier subgroup, but in Halpern et al.'s Table 3 the non-dominant-hand pegboard difference in that subgroup has the same p value (0.003); Halpern et al. judged it likely chance on exploratory analyses (checked in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Table 3 and Discussion, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: The study's results are presented as cleaner than its tables show; claims should cite the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Recovery of transporter binding with abstinence is cited to a study that compared people currently using and people who had stopped, at a single time point (ref 16), not to repeated scans of the same people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The recovery statement is open to the same selection problems as other cross-sectional comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The within-person evidence (refs 17-18) is a conference abstract in a journal supplement and a small pilot trial; neither sample size nor whether any neurotoxicity measure was taken is stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that controlled exposure has not produced deficits cannot be weighed from the commentary.

reporting_issues.issue: The fenfluramine comparison, which runs through the third paragraph, rests for its factual content on reference 14, a legal and technical book (O'Donnell, Drug Injury: Liability, Analysis and Prevention, Lawyers and Judges Publishing, 2005): that the drug lowers brain serotonin in laboratory animals at lower effective doses than MDMA, that it was prescribed to tens of millions of people and that it was withdrawn in 1997 over heart-valve damage. The imaging half of the comparison is a peer-reviewed study (reference 15, a PET study of people treated years earlier with fenfluramine or dexfenfluramine).
reporting_issues.consequence: Under METHODS §3.1 a book is never the sole source of an empirical claim, so the dose comparison with MDMA and the prescribing figures cannot be carried into a claim from this commentary.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence attributing the greater research interest in people who use ecstasy, compared with people who took fenfluramine, to political reasons carries no citation; it is the commentary's one attribution of motive, and it sits in the paragraph the claims cite.
reporting_issues.consequence: An unsourced statement of motive should not be carried into a claim or a debate box.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary does not mention the equivalence analysis of the study it discusses (that study's Table 4), which is its quantitative answer to how large an effect could be ruled out: a large effect (d 0.8) is excluded on all 14 measures analysed, a medium effect (d 0.5) on 5, with one bound at exactly 0.50 and the other 8 from 0.53 to 0.76.
reporting_issues.consequence: The case against functionally significant neurotoxicity is made from a count of significant tests rather than from the precision the study reports, which leaves medium-sized differences in play on most of the measures analysed.

Statements about Halpern et al. (2011) were checked against its PMC full text (PMC3053129).
