design_detail: Controlled cross-sectional inpatient study at a clinical research centre (Johns Hopkins, Baltimore). 30 people who had used MDMA on at least 25 occasions and 28 controls who had never used it were admitted after at least 2 weeks of agreed abstinence and kept on a low-monoamine diet. Outcomes: lumbar CSF monoamine metabolites (5-HIAA, HVA, MHPG) on the third morning; prolactin response to intravenous L-tryptophan; ischaemic pain by the tourniquet test; personality questionnaires (Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire, Buss-Durkee Hostility Inventory, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire). No tests of memory or thinking.
can_establish: That this self-referred group of people who had used MDMA many times had lower lumbar CSF 5-HIAA than this control group under standardized inpatient conditions, and whether neuroendocrine, pain and personality measures differed between the two groups.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the lower 5-HIAA (no pre-use measure, and much heavier use of other drugs in the MDMA group that was not adjusted for); that the lower metabolite level reflects loss of serotonin nerve terminals rather than lower serotonin turnover (the authors write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from CSF data alone, p. 135); any effect on memory or thinking (none was measured); or how much use matters (5-HIAA was not related to any measure of use).

sample.recruitment: MDMA group self-referred: they telephoned one of the investigators after learning of ongoing MDMA research at the Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions. Controls were referred by people in the MDMA group or recruited from the Baltimore/Washington area. Telephone screen, then medical, neurological and psychiatric screening on admission (Methods › Subjects, p. 130).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MDMA group: good health and MDMA used on at least 25 occasions; earlier use of other drugs allowed. Controls: the same health criteria and no MDMA exposure. Both groups excluded for past or present major medical illness, pregnancy, HIV seropositivity, history of psychosis, current major depressive disorder and current alcohol or drug dependence (p. 130).
sample.demographics: Controls: mean age 27.8 (SD 7.8), education 16.5 (2.8) years; MDMA group: 32.3 (13.6) and 15.2 (2.0). Men in the MDMA group had less education than control men, 14.8 (1.6) vs 17.2 (2.6) years, marked significant (Table 1, p. 131; group x gender interaction F(1, 53) = 4.4, p = .04, p. 132). The text states that there were no significant socioeconomic, ethnic, racial or occupational differences, without data (Results › Demographics, p. 132).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single admission). The prolactin analysis includes 51 of the 58 participants (control women 7 of 11, control men 16 of 17, MDMA women 10 of 12), with no explanation (Table 5, p. 133).
sample.selection_effects: The MDMA group selected itself by contacting an MDMA research programme, and the authors describe its members as often strong advocates of the drug's benefits (p. 136); some controls were referred by them. Lifetime use of other drugs was far more common in the MDMA group (cocaine 80% vs 29%, LSD and other hallucinogens 87% vs 32%, benzodiazepines 60% vs 21%; Table 3, p. 131). Exclusion of current depression, psychosis and dependence makes both groups healthier than many people who use MDMA.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: a telephone interview, an MDMA questionnaire (number of occasions, usual amount, frequency, last use, highest amount), a standardized drug-history questionnaire and the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (p. 130). Urine and blood drug screens were taken on arrival; their results are not reported. Tablet content was not tested.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported (Table 2, p. 131): 94.4 (SD 90.6) occasions, range 25 to 300; duration 4.98 (2.96) years, range 0.5 to 16; frequency 4.16 (4.79) times a month, range 0.15 to 20; time since last use 17.9 (24.7) weeks, range 2 to 104. The usual amount per occasion is misprinted and cannot be read (see reporting issues). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Allowed, and described only as any lifetime exposure by drug class (Table 3, p. 131), MDMA group vs controls: non-MDMA amphetamines 43% vs 14%, cocaine 80% vs 29%, benzodiazepines 60% vs 21%, sedative-hypnotics 33% vs 4%, LSD and other hallucinogens 87% vs 32%, cannabis 93% vs 73% as printed (22 of 28 is 79%), solvents 27% vs 29%, opiates 53% vs 32%, PCP 13% vs 7%. Frequency and recency of other drug use, alcohol and tobacco are not reported, and no analysis adjusts for other drug use. The authors argue that other drugs are unlikely to explain the CSF finding because controls also used them, to a lesser extent, and few drugs outside the amphetamine class are selectively neurotoxic (p. 136).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks of agreed abstinence from all recreational drugs, with urine and blood screens on arrival (results not reported); time since last MDMA use 17.9 (24.7) weeks, range 2 to 104 (Table 2, p. 131). Lumbar puncture between 8 and 10 AM on the third morning of the stay, after an overnight fast and bed rest (p. 130).

comparison.controls: 28 healthy volunteers with no MDMA exposure, referred by MDMA participants or recruited locally; other recreational drug use allowed (p. 130).
comparison.matching: The Results call the groups well matched for age, height, weight and sex ratio (p. 132) and the Discussion calls the controls matched also for education and other drug use (p. 135); Table 1 shows less education in MDMA men and Table 3 more lifetime use of most other drug classes in the MDMA group. CSF analyses were adjusted for age and height only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure before MDMA use of CSF metabolites, personality or cognition. The authors argue against a premorbid explanation because people with psychiatric disorders involving serotonin were screened out and the groups did not differ on standardized psychiatric measures (p. 136); those psychiatric data are not shown.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Yes: cannabis 22 of 28 (printed 73%), LSD and other hallucinogens 32%, opiates 32%, cocaine 29%, solvents 29%, benzodiazepines 21% (Table 3, p. 131).

outcomes.instruments: CSF 5-HIAA, HVA and MHPG by high-performance liquid chromatography with electrochemical detection; control and MDMA samples processed and assayed together without knowledge of group (p. 130); intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation 2.3% and 4.7% for 5-HIAA (Table 4, p. 133). Prolactin before and after 7 g intravenous L-tryptophan (basal level, peak change, area under the curve) (pp. 130-131). Submaximum-effort tourniquet ischaemic pain: sensitivity, endurance, tolerance (p. 131). Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire, Buss-Durkee Hostility Inventory, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (pp. 131-132).
outcomes.validity_norms: Control CSF values are said to lie within the ranges reported for controls in other studies (p. 132). The use of lumbar CSF 5-HIAA as a marker rests on monkey studies cited by the authors, which they say show that it detects, but underestimates, serotonin damage produced by MDMA (p. 130).
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity is inferred from lower CSF 5-HIAA and from the absence, in the MDMA group, of the usual negative correlation between height and CSF 5-HIAA (pp. 132, 135); no direct measure of serotonin nerve terminals. No cognitive outcome.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni multivariate intervals for the personality measures only; Duncan's multiple range test for post hoc comparisons (p. 132). No correction across the CSF, neuroendocrine, pain and personality families. 16 counts the outcomes named in the Results (3 metabolites, 3 prolactin measures, 3 pain measures, 4 MPQ scales, 1 hostility scale, 2 EPQ scales); the questionnaires have more subscales than are reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: CSF assays blind to group (p. 130). Not reported for the other measures; the personality measures are self-report.

analysis.effect_sizes: CSF 5-HIAA: controls 15.2 (SD 7.9; range 4.8 to 37.3) vs MDMA group 10.3 (3.1) ng/ml; one-way ANCOVA with age and height, F(1, 54) = 11.6, p = .001; 2 x 2 group x gender ANCOVA, group F(1, 52) = 14.9, p < .001, interaction F(1, 52) = 5.1, p < .03 (Results › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph, p. 132; Table 4, p. 133). Women 18.7 (9.3) vs 10.1 (2.6), 46% lower; men 13.4 (5.8) vs 10.8 (2.6), 20% lower (p. 132; Table 4). Editors' calculation from Table 4: 32% lower overall; unadjusted difference 4.9 ng/ml (95% CI 1.7 to 8.1, Welch t test); standardized difference about 0.82 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.35) with the pooled SD, or 0.62 with the control SD (the two SDs differ more than twofold); men alone 2.6 ng/ml (-0.6 to 5.8), p about .10; women alone 8.6 (2.2 to 15.0), p about .01. HVA: 27.4 (21.3; range 8.1 to 117.9) vs 19.4 (7.8) ng/ml; group F(1, 52) = 6.9, p = .01, interaction F(1, 52) = 4.3, p = .04; lower only in MDMA women vs control women, 18.7 (7.0) vs 34.8 (29.9) (pp. 132-133); editors' calculation, unadjusted Welch tests: p about .07 overall and about .11 in women. MHPG 8.5 vs 8.5, no effects (p. 133). Height and 5-HIAA: r = -.42 (p = .03) in controls and r = .18 (p = .34) in the MDMA group (p. 132); editors' calculation: the two correlations differ (Fisher z = 2.27, p about .02). 5-HIAA and number of MDMA exposures r = -0.2, p = .33; not significantly correlated with duration or frequency of use or time since last use, coefficients not given (p. 132). Season: no effect (F(3, 50) = .89, p = .45). Prolactin: no drug effects on peak change or area under the curve (p. 133; Table 5). Pain: gender effects only are reported (p. 134; Table 6). Personality: MPQ control scale higher (less impulsive) in the MDMA group, F(1, 52) = 9.21, p = .004; Buss-Durkee indirect hostility lower, F(1, 52) = 7.4, p = .009, the difference coming from control women; EPQ impulsivity and sociability no differences (p. 134).
analysis.covariates: Age and height for CSF metabolites; age, basal prolactin and plasma tryptophan for prolactin; age and education for personality (Methods, p. 132; the MPQ paragraph names age only, p. 134). Other drug use, education (for CSF), diet before admission, smoking and alcohol were not adjusted for.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports lower impulsivity (p = .004) from the MPQ control scale but not that the EPQ impulsivity subscale showed no difference (p. 134). Correlations between CSF 5-HIAA and personality scales are given as p values only, without coefficients (p. 134). For pain endurance and tolerance only gender effects are reported, although Table 6 shows lower values in MDMA men than in control men (p. 134). The arrival drug-screen results are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 30 and 28 participants and the wide spread of control values, the interval for the 5-HIAA difference is wide: about 11% to 53% below the control mean (editors' calculation from the Welch interval).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Lumbar CSF 5-HIAA was about a third lower in 30 self-referred people who had used MDMA many times than in 28 controls. The difference was clear in women (12 vs 11) and is not marked as significant in men; it was unrelated to the number of occasions, duration, frequency or recency of use. HVA was lower only in women; prolactin and pain responses did not differ; and the MDMA group scored as less impulsive and less hostile, the opposite of what low CSF 5-HIAA goes with in the clinical groups the authors cite.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the summary present the CSF finding as suggesting that serotonin neurotoxicity may be a complication of MDMA use, and the summary says MDMA neurotoxicity "may generalize to humans" (p. 136); the title states serotonin neurotoxicity as the subject of the finding. The Discussion describes the controls as matched for education and other drug use (p. 135), which Tables 1 and 3 contradict, and sets aside other drugs and premorbid factors by argument, not analysis (p. 136). The neurotoxicity reading rests on the similarity to CSF decrements in MDMA-treated monkeys (pp. 135-136); the authors also write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from CSF data alone (p. 135). The personality differences, opposite to the expected direction, are read post hoc as support for serotonin modulating these traits (abstract; pp. 135-136).

timeline.event: Peroutka and colleagues: CSF monoamine metabolites in people who used MDMA recreationally; no reduction in 5-HIAA (as described in this paper's introduction, p. 130, which notes the setting was not controlled).
Ricaurte and colleagues: preliminary report of reduced CSF 5-HIAA in people previously exposed to MDMA (as described, p. 130; setting not controlled).
This study: controlled inpatient comparison, 30 vs 28.

Ung et al. cite this study, with a 1999 study from the same group (not read), for reduced CSF 5-HIAA as support for possible serotonin neurotoxicity, and also cite it as indirect human evidence of dopamine-system damage (pp. 274, 281), although the HVA difference was confined to women.

replication.where_it_stands: Before this study one uncontrolled CSF study had found lower 5-HIAA and one had not (as described on p. 130). Later CSF studies are not among the papers read in this batch; a 2026 review cites this study and a 1999 study by the same group for reduced CSF 5-HIAA (Ung et al., 2026, p. 281; the 1999 study not read). Independent replication of the controlled CSF finding is not documented in the papers read here. The study measured no memory or thinking outcome, so it cannot be cited on the cognition claims.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service research grant R01DA05938 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, and General Clinical Research Center grant 5M01RR02719 (Acknowledgments, p. 136).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: National Institute of Mental Health (Bethesda), Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions (Baltimore) and Concordia University (Montreal). The neurotoxicity reading leans on monkey studies by the senior author (cited on pp. 130 and 135-136), and the MDMA group was recruited through contact with him about MDMA research (p. 130). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study measuring CSF 5-HIAA and a direct marker of serotonin nerve terminals (for example serotonin transporter imaging) before and after people begin regular MDMA use, against people who use the same other drugs but not MDMA, with exposure confirmed by hair analysis, testing of memory and thinking, and a dose-response analysis across a wide range of use.

domains.note: Other drug use far more common in the MDMA group (cocaine, hallucinogens, benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, amphetamines) and not adjusted for; less education in MDMA men; diet before admission, smoking and alcohol not reported; premorbid serotonin function unknown.
Self-reported number of occasions and amounts, tablet content unknown, usual amount misprinted; arrival drug screens not reported.
Self-referred MDMA group in contact with an MDMA research programme, described by the authors as often strong advocates of the drug; some controls referred by them.
Time since last use ranged from 2 weeks to 2 years with abstinence verified only on arrival (results not shown); 5-HIAA was not related to time since last use.
CSF data complete for 58; prolactin data missing for 7 of 58 without explanation.

For CSF 5-HIAA: standardized diet, time of day and bed rest, assays blind to group, low assay variation. The personality outcomes would be some concerns (self-report by people the authors describe as advocates).

Several analysis models (one-way, group x gender, group x season); the abstract selects the MPQ control scale over the null EPQ impulsivity result; personality correlations reported without coefficients.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The CSF measurement itself is careful (inpatient stay, low-monoamine diet, fixed time of sampling, blind assays), but the comparison is confounded by much heavier use of other drugs in a self-selected MDMA group, with no adjustment and no measure before use; the difference rests mainly on women, and 5-HIAA showed no relation to any measure of MDMA use. The study may be cited for lower lumbar CSF 5-HIAA in this group under controlled conditions. It may not be cited as showing that MDMA damages serotonin neurons, that the deficit is dose-related, or that MDMA affects memory or thinking.

key_findings.finding: Lumbar CSF 5-HIAA was 10.3 (SD 3.1) ng/ml in 30 people who had used MDMA at least 25 times vs 15.2 (7.9; range 4.8 to 37.3) in 28 controls; ANCOVA with age and height F(1, 54) = 11.6, p = .001; group x gender ANCOVA group F(1, 52) = 14.9, p < .001. Editors' calculation: about 32% lower; unadjusted difference 4.9 ng/ml (95% CI 1.7 to 8.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › CSF Monoamine Metabolites › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph (p. 132); Table 4 (p. 133)

key_findings.finding: The difference depended on sex (group x gender F(1, 52) = 5.1, p < .03): 46% lower in women (10.1 vs 18.7 ng/ml; 12 vs 11), marked significant, and 20% lower in men (10.8 vs 13.4; 18 vs 17), not marked significant in Table 4. Control women had higher 5-HIAA than control men.
key_findings.locator: Results › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph (p. 132); Table 4 and its footnotes (p. 133)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, unadjusted Welch tests: men 2.6 ng/ml (95% CI -0.6 to 5.8), p about .10; women 8.6 (2.2 to 15.0), p about .01. The authors explain the sex difference by greater exposure in women rather than greater susceptibility: women reported about 115 occasions against 85 for men and weighed less while reporting the same amount per occasion (p. 135). That explanation sits against the absence of any relation between 5-HIAA and the number of exposures within the group (r = -0.2, p = .33).

key_findings.finding: CSF 5-HIAA was not significantly related to the number of MDMA exposures (r = -0.2, p = .33), duration or frequency of use, or time since last use (coefficients not given).

Height correlated negatively with CSF 5-HIAA in controls (r = -.42, p = .03) but not in the MDMA group (r = .18, p = .34); the authors read the missing gradient as a sign that MDMA damages ascending more than descending serotonin projections.
key_findings.note: No test of the difference between the two correlations is reported; editors' calculation, Fisher z = 2.27, p about .02.

key_findings.finding: Season had no effect on CSF 5-HIAA and no interaction with group (F(3, 50) = .89, p = .45).

CSF HVA (a dopamine metabolite): 27.4 (21.3; range 8.1 to 117.9) in controls vs 19.4 (7.8) ng/ml; group F(1, 52) = 6.9, p = .01, group x gender F(1, 52) = 4.3, p = .04; lower only in MDMA women than control women (18.7 vs 34.8, control SD 29.9), not in men (22.1 vs 24.6). MHPG did not differ (8.5 vs 8.5).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, unadjusted Welch tests: p about .07 overall and about .11 in women; the control-women SD of 29.9 suggests one or more very high values.

key_findings.finding: Prolactin before and after intravenous L-tryptophan showed gender effects but no significant drug effects on peak change or area under the curve.
key_findings.note: Table 5 shows the MDMA groups numerically above the control groups on the post-tryptophan peak (women 33.8 vs 30.3, men 14.8 vs 13.4), so the neuroendocrine result is not only non-significant but in the opposite direction to the blunting reported in 1988 and set aside here.

key_findings.finding: The authors explain the normal prolactin response by possible recovery of serotonin axons to the hypothalamus in the months after exposure, citing monkey work, and note that participants had last used MDMA about 18 weeks earlier, some up to 2 years; they offer as an alternative that the serotonin deficit behind the lower 5-HIAA may be too small or wrongly placed to produce a neuroendocrine effect.
key_findings.note: Second-hand for the monkey evidence (not read). This is the only reversibility argument in the paper and is relevant to the tolerance and recovery questions (METHODS §8, section 5).

key_findings.finding: Ischaemic pain: gender effects on sensitivity (F(1, 54) = 5.7, p = .02) and tolerance (F(1, 54) = 4.9, p = .03); no effect of group on sensitivity; no significant effects of group or gender on endurance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pain Measures, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Personality: the MDMA group scored higher on the MPQ control scale (less impulsive; F(1, 52) = 9.21, p = .004) and lower on Buss-Durkee indirect hostility (F(1, 52) = 7.4, p = .009; both MDMA subgroups lower than control women, neither different from control men); no differences on the EPQ impulsivity and sociability subscales.
key_findings.locator: Results › Personality Measures (MPQ; BDHI; EPQ paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: Lifetime use of other drug classes, MDMA group (30) vs controls (28): cocaine 24 (80%) vs 8 (29%); LSD and other hallucinogens 26 (87%) vs 9 (32%); benzodiazepines 18 (60%) vs 6 (21%); sedative-hypnotics 10 (33%) vs 1 (4%); non-MDMA amphetamines 13 (43%) vs 4 (14%); opiates 16 (53%) vs 9 (32%); cannabis 28 (93%) vs 22 (printed 73%).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, Fisher exact tests: cocaine and hallucinogens p < .001, benzodiazepines p about .004, sedative-hypnotics p about .006, amphetamines p about .02; cannabis p about .14.

key_findings.finding: MDMA use as self-reported: 94.4 (SD 90.6) occasions (range 25 to 300) over 4.98 (2.96) years, 4.16 (4.79) times a month; last use 17.9 (24.7) weeks before admission (range 2 to 104).

Men in the MDMA group had less education than control men (14.8 vs 17.2 years, marked significant; group x gender interaction F(1, 53) = 4.4, p = .04); the age difference (32.3 vs 27.8 years) was not significant (F(1, 54) = 2.31, p = .13).

The authors write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from CSF data alone and base the neurotoxicity reading on similar CSF 5-HIAA decrements in MDMA-treated monkeys with known serotonin deficits; they describe the controls as matched for age, height, weight, gender, education and other drug use.

The authors consider and set aside three alternatives: a premorbid condition (screening for psychiatric disorders), other drugs (controls also used them, to a lesser extent) and changes in serotonin turnover unrelated to toxicity (similar CSF findings in monkeys); they also raise biased questionnaire answers by people who were often strong advocates of MDMA.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the usual amount as 170 (SD .82) mg with a range of 0.5 to 4, and a footnote saying it was estimated from the number of capsules or tablets taken; a mean of 170 cannot lie outside a range of 0.5 to 4, and the unit appears to be tablets or capsules, not mg. The Discussion refers to a usual amount of one tablet or capsule (p. 135).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample's usual amount per occasion cannot be stated from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives cannabis use in controls as 22 (73%); 22 of 28 is 79%, and 73% matches no whole number out of 28.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either the count or the percentage is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the controls as matched for education and other drug use (p. 135), but Table 1 marks lower education in MDMA men (14.8 vs 17.2 years) and Table 3 shows more lifetime use of most other drug classes in the MDMA group (p. 131).
reporting_issues.consequence: The main finding is presented as free of confounders that the paper's own tables show were not matched; no analysis adjusts for them.

reporting_issues.issue: The alienation interaction is printed as F(1, 52) = 4.4, p = .004; an F of 4.4 on 1 and 52 degrees of freedom gives p of about .04 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either the F or the p value is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports a significant overall group effect on HVA (F(1, 52) = 6.9, p = .01), but Table 4 does not mark the overall HVA difference; the women's difference rests on a control-women SD of 29.9 with control values up to 117.9 ng/ml, and unequal-variance tests are not significant (editors' calculation, p about .07 overall and .11 in women).
reporting_issues.consequence: The HVA finding, used later as indirect evidence of dopamine-system damage (Ung et al., 2026, p. 274), is fragile.

reporting_issues.issue: The group x season ANCOVA is reported with F(3, 50); a 2 x 4 design with two covariates in 58 people leaves 48 error degrees of freedom (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the model fitted may differ from the one described.

reporting_issues.issue: The prolactin analysis includes 51 of 58 participants (control women 7 of 11) without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Missing data in the functional measure that was expected to show a deficit; the null result is less informative for women.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations between CSF 5-HIAA and personality scales are reported as p values only, without coefficients; the Discussion then speaks of a negative correlation between CSF 5-HIAA and control, which was not significant (p = .06 in women).
reporting_issues.consequence: The strength of these relations cannot be judged, and a non-significant result is treated as a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods state that personality measures were analysed with age and education as covariates (p. 132); the MPQ paragraph names age only (p. 134). The reported degrees of freedom (52) fit two covariates.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the description of the model.

reporting_issues.issue: For pain endurance and tolerance the text reports gender effects only, but Table 6 shows MDMA men below control men on both (endurance 9.9 vs 12.2; tolerance 114 vs 157); group and interaction statistics for these measures are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that the groups resembled each other in their response to ischaemic pain may not hold for men.

design_detail: Exchange of letters in Science (6 June 2003, vol. 300, pp. 1504-1505): a letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin criticizing the 2002 report of severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity in primates given MDMA (Ricaurte et al., 2002), followed on the same pages by the reply of Ricaurte, Yuan, Hatzidimitriou, Cord and McCann. The letter is one paragraph with 16 references; the reply has five paragraphs and 15 references. No data. The PDF also carries unrelated letters on p. 1503 (smallpox modelling) and p. 1505 (research fraud and gun control), which are not part of this card. The exchange predates the 2003 retraction of the primate study; the 2002 paper and its retraction notice are not in this batch and are described here only as these letters and Barnett and Doblin (2021) describe them.
can_establish: What critics and the authors of the 2002 primate study argued about it in June 2003, before its retraction, and which human studies each side cited.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA damages dopamine or serotonin neurons in people: neither letter presents data, and the study under discussion was later retracted (as Barnett and Doblin, 2021, report).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letters). The study discussed gave MDMA, as then believed, to ten monkeys (reply, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Each side cites the studies that support its position; the reply relies largely on its authors' own work (refs 9-13 of the reply).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported here as numbers. The two sides disagree on whether the regimen in the primate study modelled common human use; the reply argues that the dosing pattern, not only the amount, determined which neurotransmitter systems were affected in the animals.
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed for the human studies cited.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not discussed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed by either side.

outcomes.instruments: Cited human measures: brain dopamine transporter imaging (letter refs 7-8), a post-mortem case (ref 9), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dopamine metabolites (refs 10-12), serotonin transporter and memory in clinical studies (refs 3, 15, 16).
outcomes.validity_norms: The reply argues that CSF homovanillic acid (HVA) is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity (reply, 3rd paragraph, refs 11-12).
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None given, except the reply's counts of US emergency-room visits related to MDMA (500 in 1994, about 4500 in 2000) and its statement that one of ten monkeys died.
analysis.selective_reporting: The letter describes the earlier CSF studies by the same research group as finding no reduced dopamine metabolites; one of the three it cites (McCann et al., 1994) reports lower CSF HVA in its MDMA group (see reporting issues). The reply does not correct this.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Two opposed readings of a primate study, each supported by selected citations: the critics cite imaging and post-mortem reports of normal dopamine markers and earlier CSF findings in people who used MDMA heavily; the authors cite mouse studies, their own primate observation that the pattern of dosing changed the toxic profile, and dopamine-transporter reductions in people who had used methamphetamine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter states that there is no credible evidence linking amphetamine-type prescription drugs to Parkinson's disease and that clinical MDMA research has been conducted without evidence of toxicity; its support for the first is a news-service item (ref 14), and the reply states that none of the three studies cited for the second measured neurotoxicity. The reply concludes that the data are insufficient to say clinical MDMA research carries no risk of monoaminergic injury. In September 2003 the primate paper was retracted because, as its authors then reported, all but one animal had received methamphetamine rather than MDMA (Barnett and Doblin, 2021, p. 2 of the online-first PDF): the reply's argument from the primate data, written before that discovery, therefore concerned animals that had mostly been given another drug.

timeline.event: Ricaurte et al. (2002) report severe dopaminergic and less severe serotonergic neurotoxicity in ten primates given what the title calls a common recreational dose regimen of MDMA (as described by Barnett and Doblin, 2021, and in this exchange).
This exchange (6 June 2003), before the retraction.
Retraction in Science (September 2003): methamphetamine rather than MDMA had been given to all but one animal because of a labelling error, as reported by Barnett and Doblin (2021).
Study of US newspaper coverage of the publication and of the retraction.

replication.where_it_stands: The primate dopamine finding that both letters argue about was withdrawn with the retraction. The human points raised in the exchange (dopamine markers in people who used MDMA heavily, the sensitivity of CSF HVA) remain to be judged from the primary studies, which are not cards in this batch except McCann et al. (1994).

funding.funder: Not reported for either letter.
funding.declared_conflicts: No statements of interests are printed for either letter.
funding.affiliations_note: Letter: Michael Mithoefer (Mount Pleasant, South Carolina), Lisa Jerome and Richard Doblin (Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, MAPS; the corresponding address is a MAPS e-mail). Barnett and Doblin (2021, p. 5 of the online-first PDF) describe Doblin as the founder and executive director of MAPS, which funds research on the therapeutic potential of MDMA. Reply: the authors of the criticized study (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine). Both sides had a stake in the outcome; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount either.

what_would_settle_it: For the human question the letters raise: dopamine transporter imaging and CSF metabolite measures in people with heavy MDMA use and little stimulant use, against matched controls and with repeat measures over abstinence; for the animal question: replication in primates with the identity of the drug verified.

domains.note: Letters; citations chosen by each side.
The letter misdescribes one of its own CSF sources and relies on a news item; the reply does not appraise the studies it cites.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The reply rests mainly on its authors' own studies, including the one under criticism.
Both sides go beyond their citations: absence of risk on one side, parkinsonism-like features on the other.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against dopamine neurotoxicity of MDMA in people
domains.note: Each letter is one-sided, but together the exchange presents both positions.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to letters (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used for the exchange as a whole. It may be cited for what each side argued before the retraction; it is not evidence on whether MDMA damages dopamine or serotonin neurons.

key_findings.finding: The letter argues that because people rarely die from MDMA use, the high mortality among the primates suggests the study did not model a common recreational regimen, which calls its interspecies scaling into question; it also says the paper's position conflicts with an earlier monkey study by the same group (ref 6).
key_findings.locator: Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin (left column, one paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Route in the animal work: the critics say the same group had earlier reported that, in squirrel monkeys, MDMA given by injection under the skin was about twice as neurotoxic as MDMA given by mouth, which they treat as inconsistent with the group's present position that the oral route offers little or no protection. The reply answers that it cites every study addressing the question: three found no protective effect and a fourth found protection that varied by brain region. These are laboratory-animal study conditions, reported here only as the two sides describe them.
key_findings.locator: Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin (left column); Response, 2nd paragraph (middle column)
key_findings.note: This is the letter's second charge of internal inconsistency, alongside the mortality argument. None of the animal studies was read.

key_findings.finding: The letter says the paper raises the possibility that even one night's recreational use may cause dopamine toxicity and a higher risk of Parkinson's disease, but does not cite studies finding normal dopamine (with reduced serotonin) in people who used MDMA heavily: two imaging studies of the dopamine transporter (refs 7-8) and a post-mortem examination of one person (ref 9); and that earlier studies by Ricaurte and McCann in people who used MDMA heavily did not find reduced dopamine metabolites in CSF (refs 10-12).
key_findings.locator: Letter (left column), middle of the paragraph
key_findings.note: Contradicted for ref 11 by that study's own table; see reporting issue 0.

key_findings.finding: The letter states that the dopamine changes reported are long-known potential effects of d-amphetamine and d-methamphetamine, available on prescription for over 80 years; that there is no credible evidence linking these drugs to Parkinson's disease or to more early-onset Parkinson's disease (ref 14, a New Scientist news item); and that clinical MDMA research has been conducted without evidence of toxicity, including no detectable change in serotonin transporter or memory (refs 3, 15, 16).
key_findings.locator: Letter (left column), end of the paragraph

key_findings.finding: Reply: interspecies dose scaling was not used in the recent studies; one of ten monkeys given the regimen died of complications related to hyperthermia, from which the authors say no firm conclusion about mortality can be drawn given the sample size; isolated human deaths with prominent hyperthermia have been described (refs 2-5); and US emergency-room visits related to MDMA rose from 500 in 1994 to about 4500 in 2000, a significant portion involving raised body temperature.
key_findings.note: The two emergency-department figures carry no citation: none of the reply's 15 references is a surveillance source, and no year-by-year denominator is given, so the rise cannot be interpreted and must not be used as an epidemiological figure (METHODS §10).

key_findings.finding: Reply: the letter ignores mouse studies showing MDMA dopamine neurotoxicity (ref 10) and the study's central observation that changing the pattern of dosing changed the toxic profile in primates (from serotonin alone to dopamine and serotonin); because the human studies cited did not take patterns of use into account, their groups were probably heterogeneous and dopamine markers, including the transporter, would not be expected to differ; and CSF HVA is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity (refs 11-12).

Reply: methamphetamine and d-amphetamine are dopamine neurotoxins with no evidence that they cause parkinsonism, but past methamphetamine use has been associated with lower dopamine transporter levels in living, abstinent people (refs 13-15) and with motor slowing (ref 15), features seen in parkinsonism.
key_findings.locator: Response, 4th paragraph (p. 1504 right column, continued on p. 1505)
key_findings.note: This is the only human evidence the reply brings to the dopamine question, and it is about methamphetamine, not MDMA: the species-and-drug gap matters for cl_mdma_dopamine_human, where the yes side would otherwise appear to have human data.

key_findings.finding: Reply: of the three references the letter gives for clinical research without toxicity, one is an unpublished conference presentation, one is an exchange of letters about interspecies dose scaling, and one is a Phase I study of two doses and placebo in which no neurotoxicity measures were taken; the authors remain of the opinion that the data do not show that clinical MDMA research can be done without risk of monoaminergic neural injury.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says earlier studies by Ricaurte and McCann found no reduced dopamine metabolites in CSF (refs 10-12). Ref 11 is McCann et al. (1994), whose Table 4 shows CSF HVA of 19.4 (SD 7.8) ng/ml in 30 people who used MDMA against 27.4 (SD 21.3) in 28 controls, with a significant group effect (F[1,52]=6.9, p=.01) and a group-by-sex interaction: lower in women who used MDMA, not different in men (checked by this reader in the McCann et al. 1994 PDF, pp. 132-133; the abstract of that paper mentions only 5-HIAA). The reply accepts the letter's description and argues instead that CSF HVA is an insensitive marker.
reporting_issues.consequence: The letter's argument from normal CSF dopamine metabolites is not accurate for at least one of its sources; the lower HVA in that study is itself a finding the CSF claims for this monograph should report.

reporting_issues.issue: Mortality in the primate study is described differently in the sources read: the letter speaks of high mortality, the reply says one of ten monkeys died, and Barnett and Doblin (2021, p. 2 of the online-first PDF) say two of the animals died. The 2002 paper itself was not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any statement about deaths in the primate study must name its source and should be checked against the paper or its retraction notice.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter's support for the absence of any Parkinson's link is a news-service item (ref 14), and the reply states that none of the three sources cited for the absence of toxicity in clinical research measured neurotoxicity; the letter's reference list shows one of them to be a conference paper (ref 16).
reporting_issues.consequence: The letter's two strongest reassurances rest on sources that cannot carry them.

reporting_issues.issue: Crossref lists G. A. Ricaurte among the authors of this item because the letter and the reply share a DOI and pages; the letter is signed by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin and the reply by Ricaurte and four colleagues (already noted on the reference record).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the reply as part of the same item, naming its authors in the text.

The CSF statement was checked against McCann et al. (1994), PDF pp. 129 and 132-133.

design_detail: Described by its authors as a critical review; classified here as a systematic review without meta-analysis (as for sc_lappin_2017) because it reports its search (PsycINFO and Medline, July to September 2008, no date limits, 46 search terms pairing 'ecstasy' and 'MDMA' with the names of executive tasks and with 'visuospatial', 'word fluency' and 'verbal fluency'), explicit eligibility criteria and a structured extraction of all 33 included studies (Table 2). Synthesis is narrative and by counting studies, within four executive processes (updating, shifting, inhibition, access to long-term memory) and visuospatial memory; no appraisal of the included studies' risk of bias and no statistical synthesis. Many of the updating and visuospatial studies are the review authors' own.
can_establish: Which executive working memory tasks have and have not shown differences between people who use ecstasy, not intoxicated at testing, and comparison groups in the studies found up to 2008, and how those studies tried to control for other drug use.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy causes executive deficits (all but one included study were cross-sectional or quasi-experimental); the size of any deficit (no effect sizes were pooled); or that the pattern is free of selection and publication bias (no appraisal, English-language peer-reviewed studies only, many by the reviewers themselves); or anything about memory in general: the review covers only tasks empirically mapped onto updating, shifting, inhibition and access to long-term memory, plus memory for the spatial position of elements of a display, and states that studies reporting differences on other executive tasks were therefore not included (p. 173), so verbal list-learning tests, which carry the verbal-memory literature and the later meta-analysis, are outside it.

sample.recruitment: Two databases searched July to September 2008 with no date limits (Method › Identification of Studies, p. 160); 59 studies found and screened against the criteria, 33 included (p. 161). Included studies were mostly from the UK, with others from Germany, the Netherlands, Spain, Hong Kong and the USA; samples community-recruited or predominantly student (Table 2, pp. 162-166).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: New empirical findings or attempted replications on a task empirically linked to an executive process (Table 1, p. 160) or on memory for the spatial location of single elements of a display; peer-reviewed journals; English; a stated minimum time since last ecstasy use, so that testing under the influence was excluded. Excluded: review articles, conference and thesis abstracts, and results reported only as composite measures (p. 161).
sample.demographics: Not applicable at review level. Group sizes in Table 2 range from about 10 to over 100; mean ages mostly early twenties.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases with task-specific terms, English only, no grey literature or reference-list searching reported, and who screened and extracted is not stated. Eight of the nine updating studies are by some combination of the review's authors (p. 161), and samples overlap between several of them (27 of the 44 people in one study were also in another, p. 161; 27 of 104 in a third, p. 170).

exposure.measurement: As reported by the primary studies (self-reported lifetime tablets or episodes); where none was reported, the reviewers recorded an implied estimate from the data available (Data Extraction, p. 161).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mean lifetime use in Table 2 from about 20 exposures to more than 1,000 tablets; time since last use from about 1 day to more than 2 years (Table 2, pp. 162-166).
exposure.polysubstance: Recorded for each study as polydrug-using, cannabis-using, near-drug-naive or drug-naive comparison groups, together with the statistical controls used (ANCOVA, matched groups, exclusion of people exposed to a drug, correlations) (Data Extraction, p. 161; Table 2). Cannabis was present in every ecstasy group except in one Hong Kong study, and was relatively rare in one US study (p. 173).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinent means not under the influence at testing, even if use was fairly recent (Introduction, p. 160); minimum intervals in the included studies ranged from about a day to months (Table 2).

comparison.controls: Varies by study: polydrug-using, cannabis-using, near-drug-naive or drug-naive comparison groups (Table 2).
comparison.matching: Recorded per study in Table 2 (group designs and covariates).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review states that cross-sectional designs make it impossible to rule out pre-existing differences as a cause of performance differences; only one included study was prospective (pp. 172-173).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Mostly yes (polydrug or cannabis-using comparison groups).

outcomes.instruments: Tasks listed in Table 1 (p. 160): updating (letter memory, spatial sequences, tone monitoring, computation span, reading span, consonant updating, operation span, keep track, random number generation), shifting (Wisconsin Card Sorting, plus/minus, number/letter, local/global), inhibition (random letter and number generation, Stroop, Tower of Hanoi or London, antisaccade, stop signal), access to long-term memory (Chicago word fluency, random letter generation; the FAS task added as a close variant), and spatial-location memory tasks.
outcomes.validity_norms: The mapping of tasks to executive processes is taken from latent-variable and factor-analytic studies (Miyake et al.; Fisk and Sharp) (p. 160).
outcomes.operationalization: A deficit is a statistically significant difference between groups on a dependent variable, as reported by the primary study; studies are counted as showing or not showing a deficit on each task.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates; the reviewers decided statistical analysis would not serve their aim of mapping deficits across executive processes (Results › Overview, p. 161). Figures given: the largest updating difference among 5 studies reporting span scores was 2.48 span items, 2.75 in people abstinent for at least 6 months vs 5.23 in polydrug controls (Wareing et al., 2005, as summarized, p. 161); computation span deficits were reported in 7 of 9 updating studies (p. 161); deficits in visuospatial tasks in 11 of 18 studies and none in 12 (some studies in both, Tables 3 and 4, pp. 170-171).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable at review level; the primary studies' covariates are recorded in Table 2.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review's own selection of tasks excludes studies of other executive tasks that reported deficits (p. 174). Several findings are discussed in terms of the authors' own studies. No list of the 26 excluded studies is given.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 33 mostly small cross-sectional studies, differences between people who use ecstasy and comparison groups were reported most often on computation span and consonant updating (mostly the reviewers' own studies) and on visuospatial tasks with higher processing demand; shifting tasks rarely showed differences; inhibition and access to long-term memory gave inconsistent results; and the links between deficits and amounts of ecstasy or other drugs were inconsistent.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say evidence of deficits was strongest for updating of verbal material and for demanding visuospatial tasks, that shifting appears relatively immune and that inhibition and access to long-term memory are unclear (pp. 159, 172), which matches the vote counts. The review calls the updating effects fairly robust (p. 167) while noting in the same summary that correlations with ecstasy and other drug use were inconsistent and that controlling for cannabis removed deficits on two other updating tasks (pp. 167-168). It does not flag that most of the updating evidence comes from its own authors' overlapping samples, and its conclusion that cross-sectional designs are a necessary means (p. 173) is not matched by any appraisal of their risk of bias.

timeline.event: Wareing and colleagues report impaired random letter generation in 10 people currently using and 10 who had stopped using ecstasy, with mean lifetime use above 1,000 tablets; two later studies by the same team did not replicate it (as summarized, pp. 169-170).

Halpern and colleagues' pilot in a region with low exposure to other drugs: a Wisconsin Card Sorting difference only for 11 people with heavier use (as summarized, p. 168); this is the pilot, not the larger 2011 study by the same group, which did not reproduce the Wisconsin or spatial-span differences (card sc_halpern_2011).
Wareing and colleagues: computation span 2.75 vs 5.23 span items in people abstinent at least 6 months vs polydrug controls (as summarized, p. 161).
Prospective cohort of people starting ecstasy use: no visuospatial (line orientation) difference; the only genuinely prospective study among the 33 (pp. 166, 172).
This review.

A later systematic review restricted to at least 6 months of abstinence could not pool executive function and found mostly no significant differences between abstinent and MDMA-naive groups, with a trend in four studies by the same author (Ung et al., 2026, pp. 279-280). This review's Table 2 is the comparison source for the Wareing entries that the 2026 review transcribes differently (card sc_ung_2026, reporting issues).

replication.where_it_stands: A map of which executive tasks have shown differences, up to 2008. Its central updating result rests mainly on the reviewers' own overlapping samples and has not been tested by an independent pooled analysis in the papers read in this batch. The later review of sustained abstinence (Ung et al., 2026) did not pool executive function.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Edge Hill University, Liverpool John Moores University and the University of Central Lancashire (p. 159). The authors wrote eight of the nine updating studies and several of the visuospatial studies they review (p. 161; Table 2). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered systematic review with meta-analysis of the same executive tasks, with independent duplicate screening and risk-of-bias appraisal and with each sample counted once; and new studies of updating tasks by independent groups, with matched polydrug controls and testing before use.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (people who use ecstasy, not intoxicated at testing), comparison groups, and outcomes (named executive tasks and spatial-location memory) are specified (pp. 159-161).
No protocol is mentioned.
Cross-sectional and the one prospective study were included without an explanation of the choice of designs before the Discussion's argument that cross-sectional designs are necessary (p. 173).
Two databases with stated terms and dates, but English only and peer-reviewed only without justification, no reference-list, grey-literature or expert searching (pp. 160-161).
Not described.
Extraction is described (p. 161), but not who did it or whether two people did.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: 59 studies screened and 33 included; the 26 excluded are not listed.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives for every study the country, sample source, group sizes and ages, time since last use, lifetime use, comparison groups' drug use, tasks, statistical controls and main findings (pp. 162-166).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No appraisal tool; control of other drug use and the testing of ANCOVA assumptions are discussed study by study, but selection bias and the other bias domains are not assessed.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
No statistical synthesis.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No statistical synthesis.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion considers the cross-sectional designs, residual confounding by cannabis and other drugs, and the limits of ANCOVA when interpreting the findings (pp. 172-173).
Inconsistent findings across tasks are discussed in terms of task demands, dependent variables, control of cannabis and time since last use (pp. 167-172).
No statistical synthesis; publication bias is not discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding or conflict-of-interest statement, although the authors review many of their own studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because four critical items are not met: no protocol (item 2), a restricted search (item 4), no list of excluded studies (item 7) and no risk-of-bias appraisal (item 9); items 11, 12 and 15 do not apply. The review is transparent about its search, criteria and data (Table 2 is a usable catalogue) and its conclusions follow its vote counts, but the vote counts are not weighted by study quality or sample overlap, and much of the positive updating evidence is the reviewers' own. It may be cited for which tasks have and have not shown differences up to 2008 and for the only prospective study being the only one; it may not be cited for the size of any deficit or for a causal effect of ecstasy.

key_findings.finding: 33 studies were included from 59 found in PsycINFO and Medline (searched July to September 2008), all but one cross-sectional; inclusion required peer-reviewed English-language reports and a minimum time since last ecstasy use.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Conclusions (p. 159); Method › Identification of Studies, 1st paragraph (begins p. 160, continues p. 161) and 2nd paragraph (p. 161)

key_findings.finding: Updating: 9 studies, all but one by some combination of the review's authors; 7 reported computation span deficits; of 5 reporting span scores, the largest difference was 2.48 span items (2.75 in people abstinent for at least 6 months vs 5.23 in polydrug controls). Samples overlap: 27 of 44 people in one study were also in another.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Updating, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Computation span deficits remained when cannabis, alcohol and nicotine (and in one study amphetamine and cocaine) were controlled by ANCOVA, and after excluding people exposed to amphetamine, cocaine or poppers; but correlations of performance with ecstasy and cannabis use were inconsistent across studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Updating, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The reviewers call the updating effects on computation span and consonant updating fairly robust, noting deficits in people abstinent at least 6 months after more than 400 tablets on average; but correlations with use of ecstasy and other drugs were not consistent, and controlling for cannabis left no ecstasy-related deficit on two other updating tasks (reading span, keep track).
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Updating, 5th and 6th paragraphs (6th begins p. 167, continues p. 168)

key_findings.finding: Shifting: 6 studies; no differences on plus/minus or number/letter tasks or on the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test where other drug use was controlled by matched groups; in one study polydrug controls did worse than people using ecstasy; the only Wisconsin difference came from 11 people with heavier use in a region where cultural and religious norms limited exposure to other drugs. The reviewers find little evidence of impaired shifting.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Shifting, 1st to 3rd and 5th paragraphs
key_findings.note: The one Wisconsin difference comes from Halpern et al. (2004), the pilot study of 23 people who had used ecstasy and 16 who had not, in its subgroup of 11 people with heavier use; the same pilot supplies the spatial-span entry in Table 3. It is not the 2011 study of the same group carded here as sc_halpern_2011, which did not reproduce either difference. Any use of this review's tallies alongside that study needs the distinction.

key_findings.finding: Inhibition: 17 studies; standard Stroop measures showed no deficit in 6 of 8 Stroop studies and equivocal results in 2, including a Hong Kong study of 100 people who used ecstasy but no other illicit drugs, in which performance was not significantly worse after correction for multiple comparisons; an early random letter generation deficit (10 people currently using and 10 who had stopped) was not replicated. The reviewers find little evidence of impaired inhibition.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Executive Inhibition, 1st paragraph (begins p. 168, continues p. 169), 5th paragraph (pp. 169-170) and 6th paragraph (p. 170)
key_findings.note: The Hong Kong study (Yip and Lee, 2005, as summarized on pp. 169-170) is a second sample of people who used ecstasy with minimal other drug use, alongside Halpern et al. (2011): 100 people who had used ecstasy (mean 35.84 lifetime tablets, SD 13.21) and no other illicit drugs, with regular alcohol and tobacco use excluded, against 100 apparently drug-naive controls; a discriminant analysis classified the groups by response time, but after correction for multiple comparisons performance was not significantly worse and estimated consumption did not correlate with it. Second-hand here; the primary study was not read.

key_findings.finding: Access to long-term memory: the Chicago word fluency task showed deficits in 3 studies (overlapping samples); the FAS task showed deficits in 3 studies and none in 3; the reviewers call the results contradictory.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Access to LTM, 2nd to 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Visuospatial memory: 18 studies; 11 reported a deficit or a relation with ecstasy use on at least one measure (Table 3) and 12 reported none on some task (Table 4); deficits were reported in people abstinent at least 6 months in 2 studies and in groups with mean lifetime use of 149.69 and 169 tablets; the reviewers link deficits to tasks with higher executive demand.
key_findings.locator: Results › Ecstasy and Visuospatial Memory, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 170-171), 4th paragraph (p. 172); Tables 3 and 4 (p. 171)

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: deficits seem particularly evident in updating of verbal and visuospatial material and in visuospatial tasks with high executive demand; shifting appears relatively immune; evidence for inhibition and access to long-term memory is weak and ambiguous.

Only one included study was genuinely prospective (people tested before first ecstasy use); the others were cross-sectional or quasi-experimental, which makes it impossible to rule out pre-existing differences; the reviewers argue that prospective studies are slow and risk too little use by follow-up, and that experimental exposure would be unethical.

Cannabis was present in all ecstasy groups except in the Hong Kong study; ANCOVA removes variance shared between ecstasy and the covariate, so interactions cannot be studied, and its results are invalid without homogeneity of regression, which several studies did not report.
The reviewers note that laboratory tasks are proxies for everyday behaviour and that evidence of everyday cognitive problems in people who use ecstasy is self-reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the prospective study of people starting ecstasy use as reporting mean use of 3.2 tablets after 3 years (p. 173); in that study follow-up took place within 3 years of baseline, a mean of 11.1 months later in the ecstasy group (Schilt et al., 2007, p. 731).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstates the length of follow-up of the only prospective study.

reporting_issues.issue: Overlapping samples are noted for some updating and word-fluency studies (27 of 44; 27 of 104), but studies are still counted separately in the tallies of studies showing deficits.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of independent samples behind the updating and word-fluency findings is smaller than the study counts suggest.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 159-175 (all pages; Tables 1-4 read in the text layer, and Table 2 checked on rendered pages because the text layer drops its plus-minus signs; no supplementary material)

disagreements.first_pass: That ecstasy causes executive deficits (all but one included study were cross-sectional or quasi-experimental); the size of any deficit (no effect sizes were pooled); or that the pattern is free of selection and publication bias (no appraisal, English-language peer-reviewed studies only, many by the reviewers themselves).
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the review's scope excludes other executive tasks and verbal list learning (p. 173); without this the card is easy to cite for memory in general.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at pp. 173-174: the review states the restriction and says studies reporting deficits on other executive tasks were not included. Added to cannot_establish, which is where a later reader looks before citing the review.

disagreements.first_pass: (absent)

disagreements.resolution: Checked in Table 2 (p. 164) and Table 3 (p. 171): both entries are Halpern et al. [30], 2004, with 23 and 16 participants and subgroups of 11 and 12. Added as a note, because the 2011 study is in this batch and did not reproduce them (card sc_halpern_2011).

disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the Hong Kong study is a second minimal-polydrug sample alongside Halpern et al. (2011) and is relevant to cl_mdma_minimal_polydrug, which speaks of a single such study.
