design_detail: Letter to the editor (Addiction 2011;106:1365-1368). Single author. The letter's text runs from p. 1365 to p. 1367 and its reference list ends at the top of p. 1368, where a separate letter by Fisk, Murphy, Montgomery and Wareing begins (that letter is not part of this card). It re-interprets Halpern et al. (2011), a cross-sectional study of people who used ecstasy with minimal exposure to other drugs, as consistent with serotonergic neurotoxicity. Evidence used: the letter's reading of Halpern et al.'s tables, a 2009 Health Technology Assessment meta-analysis (Rogers et al., 2009), the author's own earlier review (Parrott, 2006) and model, and a short list of imaging and electrophysiology studies. No methods, no search, no new data; 25 references. The letter has no sections; locators count its nine running-text paragraphs from the start of the letter (block quotations are not counted).
can_establish: What the author argues about Halpern et al. (2011), and which numbers from that study and from other papers he uses to argue it.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy causes the test differences the letter discusses: it adds no data, and its reading of the cited studies is the author's own.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letter). The study discussed is Halpern et al. (2011): people in Salt Lake City who used ecstasy and reported comparatively slight use of other drugs, against similar-aged occasional rave attendees who had never used ecstasy (p. 1365, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the author chooses which findings and studies to discuss.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The letter discusses the Halpern et al. results that fit the author's model and cites mainly studies reporting deficits (refs 7-20), including several from the author's group. It does not mention that Halpern et al. attribute the lower vocabulary score of their ecstasy group to premorbid ability (checked by this reader in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph).

exposure.measurement: As reported from Halpern et al. (2011): self-reported lifetime occasions of use; median 43.5 lifetime occasions; median 121 days since last use (pp. 1365-1366).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime occasions only, as reported: median 43.5; subgroups with fewer than 50 and with 50 or more lifetime occasions; 6 of the 22 people in the heavier subgroup had used on 150 or more occasions (p. 1366, 6th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The letter stresses the light use of other drugs in the ecstasy group: median 10 lifetime alcohol intoxications, median 10 lifetime cannabis intoxications, median 0 cigarettes a day (interquartile range 0-0.3) (pp. 1365-1366, 4th paragraph). It does not give the control group's figures; in Halpern et al.'s Table 1 (checked by this reader, PMC HTML) alcohol intoxications were the same in both groups (median 10) and cannabis intoxications were higher in the ecstasy group (median 10 against 1).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Median 121 days since last ecstasy use, as reported (p. 1366, 8th paragraph, bracketed note).

comparison.controls: As reported: similar-aged occasional rave attendees who had never used ecstasy and had some slight use of other drugs (p. 1365, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not discussed in the letter.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The letter does not discuss pre-use differences between the groups. It counts the ecstasy group's lower vocabulary score among the impairments (p. 1366, 5th paragraph), although vocabulary is usually read as an index of premorbid ability, as Halpern et al. themselves read it.

outcomes.instruments: As listed from Halpern et al. (2011): Wechsler Memory Scale spatial span, WAIS digit-symbol, vocabulary and digits backwards, grooved pegboard, trail-making A and B, California verbal learning test, Revised Strategy Application Test (p. 1366). From Rogers et al. (2009): RAVLT immediate and delayed word recall, RBMT immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards, and NART IQ (p. 1365, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: Any test with a lower group mean at p<0.05 is called an impairment or deficit; no norms or clinical cut-offs are used.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: The letter rejects Halpern et al.'s reading of their uncorrected multiple comparisons as probable chance findings (p. 1366, 5th paragraph) but applies or proposes no correction itself.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None given. The letter cites p values only: for Halpern et al.'s overall comparison, spatial span forwards P<0.04, digit-symbol P<0.02, vocabulary P<0.01, digits backwards P<0.05 and grooved pegboard with the non-dominant hand P<0.02 (p. 1366, 5th paragraph); the pegboard difference P=0.02 overall and P=0.003 for the heavier subgroup (p. 1366, 7th paragraph); from Rogers et al. (2009), pooled digit span P=0.017 against polydrug-using controls and pooled verbal immediate recall P<0.001 over 27 studies (p. 1365, 2nd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Lists the overall-group differences at p of 0.05 or below but not that most of Halpern et al.'s 15 tests did not differ, and treats the vocabulary difference as a drug effect. It reports that the two subgroups did not generally differ and that the moderate subgroup was sometimes more impaired (p. 1366, 6th paragraph), without saying that this pattern runs against a dose-related effect on those tests. It also makes no mention of the study's equivalence analysis (its Table 4), which is that study's own quantitative answer to how large an effect it could rule out, and which shows a medium effect excluded on 5 of 14 measures, with one bound at exactly 0.50 and 8 from 0.53 to 0.76.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The letter's own numbers describe a study in which a few of many tests were lower in the ecstasy group at p values between 0.01 and 0.05 without correction for multiple comparisons, in which the lighter and heavier subgroups mostly did not differ, and in which one of the lower scores (vocabulary) is a measure usually taken to reflect ability before drug use. Two tests (strategy application and the non-dominant-hand pegboard) were lower in the heavier subgroup.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter concludes that Halpern et al. have shown MDMA to be cognitively damaging even under conditions the author calls neuroprotective, and that the study confirms rather than refutes neurotoxicity (p. 1367, 9th paragraph). It treats the light other-drug use of the sample as the reason the deficits were modest. Causal language is drawn from an uncorrected cross-sectional comparison; the alternative readings that Halpern et al. give (premorbid differences, chance) are named only to be rejected.

timeline.event: Pilot study of people who used ecstasy with minimal other drug use, with deficits only in the heavier-use subgroup (Halpern et al., 2004, as described in this letter, p. 1366); critique by Lyvers and Hasking (2004), cited by Lyvers (2011).
Halpern et al. (2011): 52 people who used ecstasy and 59 non-using rave attendees; few differences on 15 tests.
Commentary reading the same study as strengthening the case against functionally significant neurotoxicity.
This letter, and on the same page a separate letter by Fisk, Murphy, Montgomery and Wareing criticizing the sample and the choice of tests (not carded).
The same author's narrative review describes Halpern et al. (2011) differently from this letter (see card sc_parrott_2013, reporting issues).

replication.where_it_stands: The letter is one side of a published disagreement over the same data set; the other side is the original authors' reading and Lyvers (2011). Neither side adds data. The disagreement turns on uncorrected p values and on whether pre-existing differences explain the few lower scores, which a cross-sectional design cannot settle.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: No declaration of interests is printed for this letter. The "Declarations of interest: None" on p. 1368 belongs to the following letter by Fisk et al.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Swansea University, UK. The argument is framed by the author's own earlier review (Parrott, 2006) and bio-energetic stress model, and the author is a co-author of two of the studies cited in support (Fox et al., 2002; Burgess et al., 2011). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the letter.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort that tests people before and after they start using ecstasy, with minimal use of other drugs, measures premorbid ability (including vocabulary) at baseline, pre-registers a small set of primary tests with correction for multiple comparisons, and retests a non-using control group over the same interval.

domains.note: A letter: no search or selection criteria; studies are chosen to support the argument.
The cited studies reporting deficits are not appraised; Halpern et al.'s own explanations (premorbid ability, chance) are dismissed without analysis.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The interpretive frame is the author's own review and model; two supporting studies are co-authored by him.
A causal conclusion (cognitively damaging) is drawn from uncorrected cross-sectional differences, and the model is used as if it were evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a drug effect in the study discussed
domains.note: Under-represented: the many tests that did not differ, the lack of a consistent subgroup gradient, and the premorbid reading of the vocabulary difference, and the study's equivalence analysis (its Table 4).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a letter (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The letter is an advocacy re-reading of one study. It may be cited for the author's argument and for the numbers it quotes from Halpern et al. (2011), which this reader found to match that study's Table 2 for the five tests listed; it should not be cited as evidence that ecstasy caused the differences.

key_findings.finding: Thesis: the author argues that the modest deficits found by Halpern et al. (2011) are consistent with current knowledge of MDMA's adverse cognitive effects and neurotoxic properties, and concludes that the study confirms rather than refutes MDMA neurotoxicity, even with careful use.

As reported from the meta-analysis by Rogers et al. (2009): marked variation across studies; pooled digit span lower in people who used ecstasy than in polydrug-using controls (P=0.017); pooled verbal immediate recall composite lower over 27 studies (P<0.001); 6 of 7 meta-analysed variables (RAVLT immediate and delayed recall, RBMT immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards) lower, and NART IQ not different.
key_findings.locator: 2nd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the meta-analysis was not read; no effect sizes or intervals are given in the letter.

key_findings.finding: The author's earlier review named four factors behind variable findings (lifetime dose, intensity of use per session, environmental co-stimulation and other drugs) and reported that groups with fewer than about 50 lifetime occasions were generally not significantly impaired while groups above it often were; Halpern et al.'s median was 43.5 lifetime occasions.

Other drug use in Halpern et al.'s ecstasy group, as reported: median 10 lifetime alcohol intoxications, median 10 lifetime cannabis intoxications and median 0 cigarettes a day (interquartile range 0-0.3); the author describes the sample as relatively health-conscious and careful in its drug use.
key_findings.locator: 4th paragraph, continued at the top of p. 1366 (left column)

key_findings.finding: Five tests lower in the ecstasy group than in controls in Halpern et al.'s Table 2, as listed: Wechsler Memory Scale spatial span forwards P<0.04, WAIS digit-symbol P<0.02, WAIS vocabulary P<0.01, WAIS digits backwards P<0.05, grooved pegboard non-dominant hand P<0.02. The author rejects Halpern et al.'s reading that such differences are probably chance findings from uncorrected multiple comparisons. He notes that trail-making B and California verbal learning, tests he says are often impaired, did not differ.
key_findings.note: Checked by this reader against Halpern et al. (2011), PMC HTML, Table 2: the five tests and p values match (printed there as 0.04, 0.02, 0.01, 0.05 and 0.02). Raven's matrices, also at p=0.05 in that table, is not listed.

key_findings.finding: Subgroups: with moderate use defined as fewer than 50 and heavy use as 50 or more lifetime occasions, the two subgroups did not generally differ, and on some measures the moderate subgroup was more impaired; only 6 of the 22 people in the heavier subgroup had used on 150 or more occasions, and the subgroups' lifetime use was not reported. The Revised Strategy Application Test showed a dose-related impairment, which Halpern et al. read as poorer strategic self-regulation and perhaps greater reflection impulsivity.
key_findings.locator: 6th paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Grooved pegboard: no difference with the dominant hand; with the non-dominant hand the ecstasy group was slower than controls (P=0.02) and the heavier subgroup more so (P=0.003 against controls). Halpern et al. thought this probably chance; the author reads it as a deficit in higher cognitive control.

Imaging evidence cited for serotonergic deficits: a review concluding that lower serotonin transporter (SERT) density is the most robust finding (Cowan, 2007); a PET study of 49 people abstinent from ecstasy and 50 controls with SERT binding lower in every cortical region (-19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), associated with cumulative lifetime use and maximum use on one occasion, persisting after control for confounds including other drug use, and correlated with cognitive performance (Kish et al., 2010); SERT-cognition correlations (McCann et al., 2008); and one fMRI and one ERP study.
key_findings.locator: 8th paragraph (p. 1366, right column, continued on p. 1367)
key_findings.note: Second-hand descriptions of studies not read here.

key_findings.finding: Halpern et al.'s median time since last ecstasy use was 121 days, which the author takes to make the findings relevant to lasting toxicity.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the letter's quotations of Halpern et al. differ in wording from the source: the letter has the differences "report chance associations" introduced by "More probably", where Halpern et al. write "More likely" and "represent"; and it has the pegboard difference "due probably to chance", where the source says "likely due to chance" and attributes this to exploratory analyses (checked in Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Discussion, 1st paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the meaning is close, but the quotations should be re-checked against the source before reuse.

reporting_issues.issue: Vocabulary is counted among the drug-related impairments, but Halpern et al. report the lower vocabulary score as a group characteristic (Results, 2nd paragraph) and attribute it to premorbid ability (Discussion, 1st paragraph); the letter does not mention this.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the five differences offered as evidence of neurotoxicity is more plausibly a pre-existing difference; the case for neurotoxicity rests on four uncorrected p values.

reporting_issues.issue: P values are printed as inequalities (P<0.04 and so on) where the source gives exact values, and digits backwards at p=0.05 is called significant while Raven's matrices at the same p=0.05 is not listed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the threshold for calling a test impaired is applied inconsistently.

reporting_issues.issue: The same author's 2013 review describes Halpern et al. (2011) differently: it says the heavier subgroup was impaired on spatial span forwards and digit span backwards, whereas this letter (correctly, by Halpern et al.'s Tables 2 and 3) attributes these differences to the overall group and says the subgroups did not generally differ.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should cite Halpern et al.'s tables, not either description by this author; see card sc_parrott_2013.

reporting_issues.issue: From two medians of the study discussed (98 lifetime all-night parties and 43.5 lifetime ecstasy occasions) the letter infers that for the majority of those visits the participants were not using ecstasy. Medians of two different distributions cannot be subtracted in this way for individuals, and no individual-level figures are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The inference carries the letter's argument that this sample was at the careful end of the spectrum, which is in turn the basis for reading small differences as evidence of damage.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter gives the study's moderate subgroup as fewer than 50 lifetime occasions; in the study itself the moderate subgroup is 17 to 50 episodes, because at least 17 lifetime episodes was an entry criterion (Halpern et al., 2011, PMC HTML, Participants and Statistical Analyses).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as printed, the moderate subgroup appears to include very light use, which the study excluded by design.

reporting_issues.issue: The 800% rise in cortisol used to argue that this sample was protected is a measurement from the author's own study of people dancing at clubs after taking MDMA (the letter's reference 6), not a measurement in the participants of the study under discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: A figure from another sample is used as if it described the study's participants on their drug-free nights.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1365-1368 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2011_ReinterpretationOfHalpern.pdf), all pages read and pp. 1366-1368 rendered; the letter by Fisk et al. on p. 1368 read only to separate it from this letter. Quotations and numbers attributed to Halpern et al. (2011) were checked against that paper's PMC full text (PMC3053129) in this reader's own browser tab.

disagreements.first_pass: (not on the card)
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 32): the letter subtracts two medians to argue that most rave visits were drug-free, and that inference carries its argument.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 1366: the inference is as described, from the two medians, with no individual data. Added as a reporting issue.

disagreements.first_pass: (not on the card)
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 32): the letter's phrasing drops the floor of the moderate group's range.
disagreements.resolution: Checked in Halpern et al. (2011) at the source: entry required at least 17 lifetime episodes and the moderate group is 17 to 50. Added as a reporting issue.

disagreements.first_pass: (not on the card)
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 32): the 800% cortisol increase is from the author's own dance-club study, not from the participants of the study discussed.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 1366 and the letter's reference 6: the figure is from that study. Added as a reporting issue.

disagreements.first_pass: Lists the overall-group differences at p of 0.05 or below but not that most of Halpern et al.'s 15 tests did not differ, and treats the vocabulary difference as a drug effect. It reports that the two subgroups did not generally differ and that the moderate subgroup was sometimes more impaired (p. 1366, 6th paragraph), without saying that this pattern runs against a dose-related effect on those tests.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 32): a letter arguing that real deficits are present should be recorded as having left out the study's own precision estimate (Table 4).
disagreements.resolution: Checked the letter in full: Table 4 is never mentioned. Added to selective reporting and to the balance domain; the domain judgment is unchanged.

design_detail: Narrative review, single author (Neuroscience and Biobehavioral Reviews 2013;37:1466-1484). The PDF on file is the uncorrected in-press proof, numbered pp. 1-19 with proof line numbers in the margins; anchors cite its own page numbers (of the in-press PDF) and line numbers. No methods section, search strategy or inclusion criteria; the review is organized around its stated core hypothesis that people abstinent from ecstasy will show deficits in functions modulated by serotonin (§1.2). It covers animal neurotoxicity (§2.1), human imaging (§2.2), memory and higher cognition including the role of other drugs (§3.2-3.5), vision, awareness, psychiatric symptoms, psychomotor function, prenatal exposure and other functions (§3.6-3.11), brain activity during tasks (§4), practical implications (§5) and the author's explanatory model (§6). Four overview tables list functions and selected references without numbers. No quantitative synthesis.
can_establish: Which studies, as the author summarizes them, report functional differences between people who use ecstasy and controls, and how the author's serotonergic-neurotoxicity model accounts for them.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy causes lasting serotonergic damage or the functional differences: the review has no systematic search, does not appraise the studies it cites, and several of its descriptions are inaccurate when checked against the primary papers.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Most studies cited are cross-sectional comparisons of people abstinent from ecstasy, who mostly also used other drugs, with non-using or polydrug-using controls; a few prospective studies are described (§3.2, 3rd and 4th paragraphs, p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated; the author chooses studies that illustrate deficits in functions with a serotonergic component.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection follows the stated core hypothesis (§1.2, p. 2) and favours studies reporting deficits; roughly 30 of the references are the author's own or co-authored (editors' approximate count). The critiques of this literature cited by other papers in this batch (Lyvers and Hasking, 2004; Gouzoulis-Mayfrank and Daumann, 2006; Lyvers, 2011; the Krebs and Johansen correspondence answered by Cowan, 2012) are not cited, and null findings appear mainly as qualifications.

exposure.measurement: Varies across the cited studies; mostly self-reported lifetime use, with hair analysis in one cited PET study (Kish et al., 2010; §2.2, 2nd paragraph, p. 4).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime use as reported in the cited studies, for example a mean of 3.2 tablets in total in one prospective cohort and a mean of 13.5 tablets over a year in another (p. 6), and light, moderate and heavy lifetime-use subgroups elsewhere. Reported here only as study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: Discussed in §3.5 (p. 7): the author states that it has become standard to control for other drugs through polydrug-using control groups or covariance, and that deficits generally remain after such control; interactions with other drugs are not covered. He also notes that deficits were generally strongest against non-using controls (§3.5, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinent at testing in most cited studies; durations are rarely given in the review.

comparison.controls: Non-using controls (people who use only legal drugs such as alcohol or tobacco) and polydrug-using controls (people who use cannabis or other illicit drugs), as defined for Rogers et al. (2009) (§3.5, 3rd paragraph, p. 7).
comparison.matching: Not systematically reported for the cited studies.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mostly not discussed. The review reports that one group's authors called for prospective studies because premorbid differences might explain their cross-sectional findings (Daumann et al., 2006; §4.2, p. 12), that psychiatric disorders mostly preceded ecstasy or amphetamine use in a large prospective survey (Lieb et al., 2002; §3.8, p. 9), and that earlier authors noted premorbid and predisposition factors (§6.1, p. 14), but it does not apply these points to the cognitive findings.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Polydrug-using controls in many cited studies (§3.5).

outcomes.instruments: As cited: word-list and prose recall (RAVLT, Rivermead, California Verbal Learning), prospective-memory tasks and questionnaires, working-memory tasks, Tower of London and other complex tasks, social-intelligence scales; serotonin transporter (SERT) binding by PET and SPECT; EEG, ERP and fMRI measures; psychiatric scales and diagnoses; sleep, pain and other measures (Tables 1-4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed; no study is compared with population norms, except that IQ was not lower in Rogers et al. (2009) (§3.5, p. 7).
outcomes.operationalization: A deficit or impairment is any statistically significant group difference reported by a cited study; the review does not define clinical impairment.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not discussed for the cited studies.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not discussed.

analysis.effect_sizes: Second-hand only. From meta-analyses as summarized: Laws and Kokkalis (2007), 26 studies, short-term memory d -0.63, long-term memory -0.87, verbal memory -1.00, visual memory -0.27 (§3.2, 2nd paragraph, p. 5); Rogers et al. (2009), deficits on six memory measures against both non-using and polydrug-using controls but not on IQ (§3.5, p. 7). From imaging as summarized: SERT -19% to -46% across the cortex and -21% in the hippocampus in 49 people who used ecstasy against 50 controls (Kish et al., 2010; p. 4). No intervals, heterogeneity statistics or publication-bias assessments are given.
analysis.selective_reporting: Unsystematic selection guided by the core hypothesis; critiques not cited (see sample.selection_effects).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As summarized: lower average scores on memory and complex tasks in people abstinent from ecstasy in many but not all cross-sectional studies, normal performance on most simple tasks, small declines on some memory tests in two prospective cohorts with low use, lower SERT binding in most imaging studies, and associations of several measures with lifetime use. Persistence after stopping is uncertain on the author's own account.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions present the differences as functional deficits caused by serotonergic neurotoxicity, for example that MDMA-induced serotonergic neurotoxicity can impair memory (§6.2, 3rd paragraph, p. 15) and that the original model has been confirmed (§6.2, 1st paragraph, p. 14), and treat abstinent people who use ecstasy as having documented neurotoxicity (§5.3, p. 14). The practical-implications passage extends the laboratory differences to impairment in almost every occupation (§6.2, 5th paragraph, p. 15) without any study of occupational outcomes. Causal verbs are drawn from cross-sectional data, and the same section concedes that whether the problems endure cannot be answered on current evidence (§6.2, 6th paragraph, p. 15).

timeline.event: Prospective cohort of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, with incident use associated with a decline in verbal memory.
Critical review of executive working memory, summarized in this review (§3.4).
Study of people who used ecstasy with minimal exposure to other drugs, summarized in this review (§3.5).
The same author's letter on Halpern et al. (2011), which describes that study differently from this review.
Systematic review and meta-analysis of neurocognition after sustained abstinence (online 2025), read by the other reader of this batch.

replication.where_it_stands: The fullest statement in this batch of the view that recreational ecstasy causes serotonergic neurotoxicity with functional consequences. Its descriptions of individual studies should be checked against the primary papers before they are cited.

funding.funder: Not reported. The acknowledgements state only that the article was written during a sabbatical at the Centre for Human Psychopharmacology, Swinburne University, Melbourne (p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the in-press proof.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, Swansea University, UK. The explanatory model and roughly 30 of the cited studies are the author's own or co-authored; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Large prospective cohorts that measure memory and SERT binding before first use and repeatedly afterwards, with hair-verified use, a retested non-using control group and follow-up after people stop, analysed with pre-specified outcomes; and studies that relate within-person change in SERT binding to within-person change in memory.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; selection guided by the stated hypothesis.
No appraisal; several descriptions are wrong when checked (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The model is the author's, and roughly 30 references are his own or co-authored.
The model is said to be confirmed, causal verbs are used for cross-sectional findings, and occupational impairment is asserted without data.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against serotonergic neurotoxicity and functional deficits
domains.note: Critiques of the literature are not cited; null and premorbid findings are reported but treated as compatible with the model.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is a useful map of the literature reporting deficits and of the author's model, and may be cited for those. Its figures are second-hand, several are misreported, and claims should cite the primary studies or systematic reviews instead; any claim resting only on this review stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: the review states that declarative memory, prospective memory and higher cognitive skills are often impaired in people abstinent from ecstasy, that deficits are often related to lifetime dose (slight in light use, more pronounced in heavy use), and that abstinent people who use ecstasy can show deficits in a wide range of functions with a serotonergic component.

Scope: the author describes the empirical literature as still fairly limited, with neurocognition the only area extensively studied, and states the review's core hypothesis that abstinent people who use ecstasy will show deficits in functions modulated by serotonin.

Animal findings and their interpretation: serotonergic neurotoxicity after MDMA is described as robust in many laboratory species since the mid-1980s, with distal loss of serotonin axon terminals the predominant hypothesis; the review reports an alternative reading, neuroadaptive change without terminal loss, and a call for a clearer definition of neurotoxicity (Biezonski and Meyer, 2011), who nonetheless conclude that MDMA can be called neurotoxic in the sense of causing serotonergic dysfunction.

Human imaging: the first studies, in the late 1990s, found reduced serotonergic markers in people abstinent from ecstasy compared with non-using controls; the evidence was critically reviewed in the mid-2000s for the specificity of the markers; not every study found deficits, a variation attributed to lifetime dose, duration of abstinence, radioligand, brain region, sex, polydrug use and sample size; reviews concluded that lower SERT density is the most robust finding.

Kish et al. (2010), as summarized: 49 people with moderate ecstasy use against 50 non-using controls; SERT binding lower in every cortical region (-19% to -46%) and in the hippocampus (-21%), related to the extent of use, after control for many confounds (recent use checked by hair analysis; other drugs, sex, gene polymorphism and chronic tolerance monitored). Studies of heavier use also found subcortical reductions.

Other drugs: the author argues that SERT changes are probably due to MDMA rather than other drugs, citing a post-mortem case of one person who used ecstasy (and also cocaine and heroin) with striatal serotonin 60% to 77% lower and normal dopamine (Kish et al., 2000), and a PET study in which a group preferring MDMA had SERT binding lower by 56% in the neocortex, 19% in the pallidostriatum and 32% in the amygdala, correlated with lifetime MDMA use, while a group preferring hallucinogens showed no change (Erritzoe et al., 2011).
key_findings.note: The review's argument that the transporter changes are due to MDMA rather than other drugs rests partly on a theoretical claim, that most other recreational drugs do not have strong serotonergic effects (proof lines 211-217), and partly on the single post-mortem case and the hallucinogen comparison described here. No analysis is presented.

key_findings.finding: Two imaging studies summarized with null or mixed results: an fMRI study of cortical excitability found no significant group difference in any brain region, with lifetime use associated with greater activation in some regions (Bauernfeind et al., 2011); in a prospective imaging study of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, the 59 who had used it by follow-up at 17 months (mean 6.0 tablets, median 2.0) did not differ from 56 controls in SERT, which the author attributes to the very low use, but differed on blood-volume and diffusion measures (de Win et al., 2008).
key_findings.note: The de Win et al. (2008) cohort appears to be the same 188-person Netherlands XTC Toxicity cohort as Schilt et al. (2007) (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Cerebrospinal fluid: one study is summarized as finding that more use per month went with lower immediate verbal and delayed visual memory, and that lower CSF 5-HIAA went with poorer memory (Bolla et al., 1998). The review does not discuss CSF 5-HIAA group differences otherwise.

Memory meta-analyses as summarized: Laws and Kokkalis (2007), 26 studies with calculable effect sizes: short-term memory d -0.63, long-term memory -0.87, verbal memory -1.00, visual memory -0.27; Rogers et al. (2009), over 100 studies: deficits significant against both non-using and polydrug-using controls, with strength varying by task; Nulsen et al. (2010): poorer performance in all memory domains, with drug-naive or polydrug-using controls.
key_findings.note: Second-hand; none of the meta-analyses was read; no intervals or heterogeneity given. Rogers et al. (2009) is a Health Technology Assessment systematic review of observational evidence (Health Technology Assessment 13(6), 1-315), not a primary study; cite that synthesis rather than this review's description of it.

key_findings.finding: Small prospective series as summarized: 15 people tested a year apart, during which their lifetime use rose from an average of 19 to 55 occasions, declined on Rivermead paragraph recall but not on two WAIS subtests (Zakzanis and Young, 2001); at 2 years, the 8 who had stopped were unchanged or improved and the 7 who continued were unchanged or worse, with the Rivermead overall memory score rising from 19.9 to 22.9 in those who stopped and falling from 17.4 to 9.2 in those who continued (Zakzanis and Campbell, 2006).
key_findings.note: No retested control group; editors' calculation: the fall in the continuing group is 47%, not over 50% as the review says.

key_findings.finding: Prospective cohorts as summarized: of 149 people almost naive to ecstasy at baseline, 23 who had used a mean of 13.5 tablets over the following year were compared with 43 cannabis-using controls; most tasks did not differ, but figural visual recognition (immediate and delayed) was poorer (Wagner et al., 2013). Of 188 people who had not used ecstasy, 58 who then used an average of 3.2 tablets were compared with 60 who did not; there were no baseline differences, and at retest the ecstasy group was worse on immediate and delayed verbal recall and verbal recognition (Schilt et al., 2007).
key_findings.note: The retest interval for Schilt et al. is misreported (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Working memory: a review of 33 studies (Murphy et al., 2009) is summarized as finding performance normal on most working-memory tasks, executive shifting and most inhibition tasks unaffected, and deficits most apparent on tasks requiring updating of verbal information and on visuospatial tasks needing processing beyond storage.

Lifetime-use gradient as summarized: in one study, Tower of London planning time per solution was 6.5 s in polydrug-using controls, 8.9 s with low, 9.8 s with medium and 15.3 s with high lifetime ecstasy use, and correct answers on a spatial memory task fell with lifetime use (Fox et al., 2001).

Other drugs: the author states that deficits generally remain after control for polydrug use; in Rogers et al. (2009) people who used ecstasy showed deficits on all six memory measures (RAVLT immediate and delayed, RBMT immediate and delayed prose recall, digit span forwards and backwards) against both non-using and polydrug-using controls, IQ was not lower than in polydrug-using controls, and deficits were generally strongest against non-using controls.
key_findings.note: Rogers et al. (2009) is a Health Technology Assessment systematic review of observational evidence (Health Technology Assessment 13(6), 1-315), not a primary study; cite that synthesis rather than this review's description of it.

key_findings.finding: Studies with minimal other drug use as summarized: in Halpern et al. (2004) the light-use subgroup did not differ from non-using controls, while the heavy-use subgroup was poorer on Wisconsin card sorting, Stroop interference and the Revised Strategy Application test; in Yip and Lee (2005), who excluded people with illicit polydrug histories, basic working memory was normal and verbal memory, non-verbal memory and complex attention were poorer; in Halpern et al. (2011) the overall group had few deficits, and the heavier subgroup is said to have been impaired on spatial span forwards, digit span backwards, the strategy test and the non-dominant-hand pegboard.
key_findings.note: The description of Halpern et al. (2011) is partly wrong (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Summary of the cognitive evidence: many simple cognitive skills are not impaired, and even on tasks that often show deficits they are not universally found; in Rogers et al. (2009) individual studies of digit span and of verbal immediate recall were a mixture of significant and non-significant results, with significant pooled estimates; the author suggests sample size, participant selection and control of error variance as reasons.

Pre-existing psychiatric differences as summarized: in a prospective survey of 2462 young people aged 14-24 at baseline and reassessed 4 years later, people who had used ecstasy or amphetamines had higher rates of almost all DSM-IV disorders, which in most cases preceded the drug use (Lieb et al., 2002); childhood anxiety and depression predicted later ecstasy use in 1580 Dutch young people (Huizink et al., 2006) but not in 2143 Australian young people (odds ratio 1.0; Alati et al., 2007).

Pregnancy (§3.10): the review summarizes a prospective cohort of 28 women who used ecstasy (group mean 25 tablets) around conception and in the first trimester, against 68 women who used other psychoactive drugs in pregnancy; it reports lower scores on the Bayley Psychomotor Developmental Index and other psychomotor ratings at 4 months, a relation with the amount used, continuing differences at 12 and 24 months in the children of the women who had used most, and no differences in other child behavioural or psychological ratings (Singer et al., 2012a, 2012b, 2013). It also cites a report of more congenital abnormalities, mainly cardiac and musculo-skeletal, among women who had used ecstasy in pregnancy (McElhatton et al., 1999).
key_findings.note: Second-hand: none of these studies was read, the comparison group also used other drugs, and the review gives no intervals.

key_findings.finding: SERT and cognition: two PET studies (described as fMRI) are summarized as finding SERT reductions and associations with cognition: memory performance associated with SERT binding in dorsolateral prefrontal, orbitofrontal and parietal cortex (McCann et al., 2008), and poorer short-term memory, mental flexibility and speed associated with SERT loss in the insula and hippocampus, with simple tasks unimpaired and complex tasks impaired (Kish et al., 2010).
key_findings.note: The direction of the McCann et al. association is worded inconsistently (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Current against former use as summarized: in a PET study, people who had stopped using ecstasy showed some selective memory deficits against controls while people currently using did not, whereas on imaging the current group differed from polydrug-using controls and the former group did not (Thomasius et al., 2003).

An electrophysiology study found higher loudness dependence of auditory evoked potentials in people abstinent from ecstasy, related to cumulative use; its authors noted that prospective studies were still needed because premorbid differences between groups might explain the cross-sectional findings (Daumann et al., 2006, as summarized).

Tolerance and stopping (§5.2): the review states that people who use ecstasy typically stop on their own after a few years, that in a survey of 430 people the most frequently reported long-term effect was tolerance, with 90% reporting a decline in the drug's effect with repeated use (Verheyden et al., 2003a), and that a follow-up study of reasons for stopping reported the same decline (Verheyden et al., 2003b). The author's hypothesis is that loss of serotonin function reduces the subjective effect, which in turn leads to heavier patterns of use; he presents this as his own model, not as a tested finding.
key_findings.locator: §5.2 Quitting Ecstasy/MDMA and serotonergic neurotoxicity, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (proof lines 1267-1309)
key_findings.note: Second-hand: the surveys were not read. Recorded because tolerance is a standard question on every monograph (METHODS §8, section 5) and no other source in this batch covers it.

key_findings.finding: Early proposals: the review reports that earlier authors noted that premorbid factors should be considered (Gerra et al.) and that serotonergic effects might be modulated by predisposition (Schifano, 2000), and quotes a 2002 review stating that, because of methodological problems, no conclusions could yet be established on ecstasy toxicity in the human brain (Kish et al., 2002). The next section states that recent findings have confirmed the original model.

Model: in many aspects of behaviour people abstinent from ecstasy are not impaired; most basic cognitive, visual and psychomotor skills remain intact, the degree of loss is often subtle, and the overall memory system is described as retained while serotonergic neurotoxicity is said to impair memory.

Practical implications: the author argues that most occupations need memory, planning and organization and are therefore likely to be impaired, giving examples of occupations and concluding that it is difficult to think of any occupational activity that would not be impaired; no study of occupational outcomes is cited.

Persistence: a case study is summarized of one man whose problems had not resolved after 7 years of abstinence (Soar et al., 2004); the author states that whether the problems endure over time cannot be answered on current evidence, that there are some indications that they do (Morgan et al., 2002) but the data are very limited, and that prospective studies with imaging and comprehensive functional measures are needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Two PET studies of SERT (McCann et al., 2008; Kish et al., 2010; their PET methods are named in their titles in the review's own reference list) are called fMRI studies, in Table 4 and in §4.1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mislabelled method; fMRI cannot measure SERT. Cite the studies by their own methods.

reporting_issues.issue: Halpern et al. (2011) is misdescribed: the review says the heavier-use subgroup was impaired on spatial span forwards and digit span backwards, but in Halpern et al.'s Table 3 neither differs in that subgroup (p=0.18 and 0.15); spatial span forwards differed in the overall group (p=0.04) and the moderate subgroup (p=0.04), and digits backwards only in the overall group (p=0.05) (checked by this reader, PMC HTML, Tables 2-3). The author's own 2011 letter gives the correct pattern. The citation Halpern et al. (2011a,b) also points to a 2011b reference that is a different study of emergency-department morbidity by other authors named Halpern (reference list, p. 16).
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's account of the minimal-polydrug study overstates a dose gradient; claims must cite Halpern et al.'s tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The Schilt et al. (2007) cohort is said to have been retested 18-36 months later; Schilt et al. report a mean retest interval of 11.1 months (SD 6.2) in the ecstasy group and 19.1 months (SD 7.5) in controls (Schilt et al. PDF, p. 731). The review also omits that study's statement that the scores of the people who started using stayed within the normal range (its abstract, p. 728), and presents de Win et al. (2008) as a separate prospective study, although Schilt et al. describe their study as part of the Netherlands XTC Toxicity study with a baseline sample of 188 (pp. 728-729), the same study name and number the review gives for de Win et al., so the two appear to report one cohort; that cohort's mean age was 22 years (Schilt et al., p. 728), not teenagers as the review says.
reporting_issues.consequence: The prospective evidence presented as two studies appears to be one cohort, with unequal retest intervals that the review does not mention; claims should rest on Schilt et al. directly.

reporting_issues.issue: The decline in the 7 continuing participants of Zakzanis and Campbell (2006), from 17.4 to 9.2, is 47% (editors' calculation), described as over 50% on p. 6 and as 50% lower than baseline on p. 15; there was no retested control group, and the 8 who stopped improved from 19.9 to 22.9, which may include practice effects.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small overstatement of an uncontrolled change in seven people.

reporting_issues.issue: The direction of the SERT-memory association is worded inconsistently: §4.1 says memory performance was inversely associated with SERT binding (which, read literally, means lower binding with better memory), while Table 4 says lower SERT went with poorer memory and the same paragraph calls it a positive association between deficits and serotonergic reductions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction must be taken from McCann et al. (2008) itself.

reporting_issues.issue: A survey of 329 people is summarized with the majority (n=136, 46%) changing their behaviour alone; 136 is 41% of 329, and 46% is not a majority (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor and outside the claims of this batch; another sign that the review's figures need checking at source.

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF is the uncorrected in-press proof, with open author queries (Q1-Q3) and a list of uncited references (p. 15); whether the printed article (pp. 1466-1484) corrected any of these errors was not checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: Anchors cite the proof's page numbers; the editor should check the printed version before publication.

reporting_issues.issue: The prospective cohort summarized at p. 6 as Wagner et al. (2013) has no entry in the proof's reference list: the only occurrences of that surname are co-authorships of other cited papers (Bosch et al., 2013; Mithoefer et al., 2011; Quednow et al., 2004). A reader cannot identify one of the two prospective cohorts the review relies on.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's second prospective cohort cannot be traced from this source; claims must not describe it as a second cohort on this basis (see cl_mdma_prospective). Whether the printed article supplies the entry was not checked.

Descriptions of Halpern et al. (2011) were checked against its PMC full text (PMC3053129), and of Schilt et al. (2007) against its PDF in this batch.

design_detail: Prospective cohort within the Netherlands XTC Toxicity (NeXT) study. 188 ecstasy-naive volunteers aged 18 to 35 who intended to start using ecstasy were tested between April 2002 and April 2004, then sent drug-use questionnaires every 3 months for about 18 months. Within 3 years, people who had started using ecstasy and persistently ecstasy-naive people individually matched on sex, age and verbal IQ were retested with the same battery by an examiner blind to ecstasy use. Analysed: 58 people who started using ecstasy and 60 who did not; 12 test scores covering attention, working memory, verbal and visual memory and visuospatial ability.
can_establish: Whether, among young adults who intended to try ecstasy and had the same test scores beforehand, those who went on to use small amounts changed differently on memory and other tests over about one to one and a half years from those who did not.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused the smaller verbal-memory gains (not randomized; the groups differed in cannabis and cocaine use, in retest interval and, in the wider cohort, in sensation seeking); that the change reflects neurotoxicity (no brain measure in this paper); whether it lasts, grows with heavier use or reverses after stopping (one retest after very little use); or that it matters in daily life (all scores stayed in the normal range).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers aged 18 to 35 who were considering starting ecstasy use soon, recruited April 2002 to April 2004 by targeted site sampling (dance events, youth fairs, universities, colleges, parks), a project website and internet campaign, and snowball sampling; main inclusion criterion an intention to probably or certainly use ecstasy for the first time in the near future, preferably with one or more friends who already did. Paid 100 or 150 euros per session (Methods › Participants, p. 729).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: earlier ecstasy use, a major medical, neurological or neuropsychiatric disorder or cognition-affecting medication in the last year, pregnancy, intravenous drug use. Required abstinence from psychoactive substances for at least 2 weeks and from alcohol for at least 1 week before each examination, checked by urinalysis (p. 729).
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group at baseline: 25 men and 33 women, age 21.8 (SD 3.1), DART-IQ 103.4 (9.0); comparison group: 25 men and 35 women, 21.5 (2.1), 105.5 (10.2). Most had senior general secondary education or vocational college (45 of 58 vs 55 of 60) (Table 1, p. 731). Similar on sex (chi-square 0.03, p = .88), age (t = -0.67, p = .50), verbal IQ (t = 1.18, p = .24) and education (U = 1563, p = .13) (p. 731).
sample.attrition: Of 188, 158 returned the last drug-use questionnaire (30 refused or could not be reached); 64 of the 158 reported starting ecstasy and 59 of them attended the follow-up session; 61 matched controls were chosen from the 94 who stayed naive (p. 730). One person who had started using ecstasy was excluded for a cocaine-positive urine test and one control for dyslexia and attention-deficit disorder diagnosed in youth (p. 731). Dropouts and the 5 people who started using ecstasy but did not attend are not compared with those analysed.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers selected for an intention to use ecstasy, more educated and intelligent than young adults in general and, by the authors' account, highly motivated (p. 734). The comparison group consists of people who did not start despite intending to, chosen by matching only after those who had started using ecstasy were known, so they were retested later. In the wider cohort, starting ecstasy went with higher sensation seeking (p. 733).

exposure.measurement: Self-report on validated substance-use questionnaires sent every 3 months and at follow-up: cumulative number of tablets and weeks between first and last use (Methods › Independent Variables, p. 730). Urinalysis before sessions for recent use. No hair testing; tablet content not tested (the authors cite Dutch pill testing showing that 95% of tablets sold as ecstasy in 2003 and 2004 contained MDMA as the major component, p. 734).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: At follow-up, cumulative 3.2 (SD 5.2) tablets, median 1.5, range 0.5 to 30; time since first tablet 18.6 (17.6) weeks; time since last tablet 11.8 (12.0) weeks, median 7.9, range 2 to 59; duration of use printed as 6.8 (12.5) weeks, median 0.0, range 0 to 12 (Table 1, p. 731; see reporting issues). The text describes use over a mean of 1.6 months within an average follow-up of 11.1 months (p. 731). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine use in the last year measured at both sessions and entered as log-transformed covariates (pp. 730-731). Cannabis was higher in the ecstasy group at baseline (mean 48.8 vs 17.2 joints in the last year, medians 15.8 vs 15.5; U = 1363, p = .04) and at follow-up (53.6 vs 20.5 joints, U = 1089, p < .001), and cocaine at follow-up (1.4 vs 0.3 times, U = 1436, p = .006); amphetamine at follow-up 2.9 (SD 20.5, range 0 to 156) times vs none (Table 1, p. 731). A sensitivity analysis excluded everyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines, leaving 43 and 57 (p. 732).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks from psychoactive substances and 1 week from alcohol before each session, checked by urinalysis (p. 729); last ecstasy use 11.8 (12.0) weeks before follow-up, minimum 2 weeks (Table 1, p. 731).

comparison.controls: 60 persistently ecstasy-naive members of the same at-risk cohort, individually matched on sex, age and verbal IQ measured with the Dutch Adult Reading Test (p. 729).
comparison.matching: Matched on sex, age and DART-IQ (p. 729); similar on education (p. 731). The abstract also describes the groups as matched on use of substances other than ecstasy (p. 728), which Table 1 contradicts for cannabis and cocaine.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Cognition was measured before use in both groups and did not differ. Sensation seeking, impulsivity and depression were measured in the wider cohort but are not covariates here (p. 733); sleep, lifestyle and the settings of use were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Yes, at lower levels: cannabis (mean 17.2 joints in the last year at baseline), alcohol, tobacco and a little cocaine (0.3 times); no amphetamine (Table 1, p. 731).

outcomes.instruments: Paced Auditory Serial Addition Test at 2.4 s and 1.6 s; Dutch adaptation of Digit Span forward and backward; Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (sum of 5 learning trials of 15 words, delayed recall and recognition after 20 minutes); computerized Memory for Designs (elements over 5 trials, number of trials, delayed reproduction), split into two parallel versions; Mental Rotation Task; adapted Judgment of Line Orientation (pp. 729-730).
outcomes.validity_norms: Performance of all participants remained within the normal range of a sex- and age-comparable general population (p. 732). Parallel versions are described for Memory for Designs only (p. 730); whether a different word list was used for the retest of the RAVLT is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Change from baseline to follow-up, analysed with ecstasy use and sex as fixed factors and age, DART-IQ, log-transformed use of other substances and the baseline score as covariates; RAVLT recognition, near ceiling, was dichotomized into any decline vs none and analysed by logistic regression (p. 730).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; p < .05 for every test, and the dose-response correlations were one-tailed (pp. 730, 732). Editors' calculation: with a Bonferroni threshold for 12 outcomes (p < .0042), none of the three significant group results (p = .02 to .03) would remain.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The examiner was blind to whether a participant had used ecstasy (p. 729).

analysis.effect_sizes: Change scores, ecstasy group (58) vs comparison group (60), with adjusted regression coefficients (Table 2, p. 732): RAVLT immediate recall +0.86 (SD 5.5) vs +3.90 (5.8) words, B 2.23 (95% CI 0.17 to 4.29), F(1, 108) = 4.62, p = .03, partial eta squared 0.04; delayed recall -0.52 (1.8) vs +0.65 (1.8) words, B 0.63 (0.05 to 1.22), F(1, 108) = 4.67, p = .03, partial eta squared 0.04; recognition: any decline in 22.4% vs 6.7%, odds ratio 5.87 (Wald chi-square 5.62, p = .02; the table prints 1.77 (1.36 to 25.37), see reporting issues). No differences on Memory for Designs, Digit Span, PASAT, Judgment of Line Orientation or Mental Rotation (p = .21 to .85). Baseline: no differences on any test (multivariate F(12, 96) = 0.73, p = .72, partial eta squared 0.08) (p. 731). Sensitivity analysis without anyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines (43 vs 57): delayed recall effect F(1, 92) = 6.62, p = .01, partial eta squared 0.07 (p. 732). Dose-response within the ecstasy group (one-tailed): cumulative tablets with delayed recall change r = -0.24, p = .04, and recognition change r = -0.29, p = .02, not immediate recall (r = -0.16, p = .12); partial correlations controlling for age, IQ, sex and other substances, recognition r = -0.30, p = .02, delayed recall r = -0.21, p = .08; logistic regression for recognition decline, log-transformed tablets odds ratio 15.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 210.14), raw tablets 1.30 (0.96 to 1.75), p = .09; no association with duration of use or time since last use (p. 732). Editors' calculation from Table 2: unadjusted standardized differences in change about 0.54 (immediate recall) and 0.65 (delayed recall); adjusted coefficients divided by the change-score SD about 0.39 and 0.35; recognition decline in 13 of 58 vs 4 of 60 people (crude odds ratio 4.0, risk difference 16 percentage points); two-tailed p for the dose correlations about .07 (delayed recall) and .03 (recognition).
analysis.covariates: Sex (fixed factor), age, DART-IQ, log-transformed use of alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, amphetamines and cocaine, and the baseline score (p. 730). Not adjusted for the difference in retest interval or for sensation seeking.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The paper refers to a separate design article for the NeXT study (ref. 48, not read); no registration of hypotheses or outcomes is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 12 outcomes are reported in Table 2. The sensitivity analysis excluding people who had used cocaine or amphetamines is reported for delayed recall only, not for immediate recall or recognition (p. 732). Recognition was analysed as a dichotomy in the group comparison but as a continuous change score in the dose correlations (pp. 730, 732).
analysis.power: Not reported. The confidence intervals of the significant adjusted differences reach close to zero (0.17 words for immediate recall, 0.05 for delayed recall) and the recognition odds ratio interval runs from 1.36 to 25.37.

interpretation_gap.results_show: With no differences before use, people who started using ecstasy (median 1.5 tablets) gained less than the comparison group on word-list learning and delayed recall at retest, and more of them lost any points on recognition (13 vs 4 people, on a test where almost everyone scores about 30 of 30); 9 other scores did not differ; all scores stayed in the normal range; the ecstasy group was retested about 8 months sooner and used more cannabis and cocaine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that even a first low cumulative dose of ecstasy is associated with decline in verbal memory (p. 728), and the conclusion calls the finding "suggestive for Ecstasy-induced neurotoxicity" (p. 734). For immediate recall the ecstasy group did not decline (58.7 to 59.6 words); it gained less than the comparison group, whose gain the authors call a normal retest effect (p. 732). No brain measure is reported in this paper. The abstract says the groups were matched on use of substances other than ecstasy, while the Methods matched on sex, age and verbal IQ only and Table 1 shows more cannabis and cocaine in the ecstasy group. Against this, the authors state that the design offers no indisputable evidence of causality, that the immediate clinical relevance is limited and that the study cannot say whether the effects remain after quitting (pp. 728, 733-734).

timeline.event: This study: the first prospective cohort of people tested before their first ecstasy use.

Murphy et al. name it the only genuinely prospective study among 33 studies of executive and visuospatial memory, with no visuospatial (line orientation) difference, and describe mean use as 3.2 tablets after 3 years (pp. 166, 172-173).
Halpern et al. note that the median of 1.5 tablets at follow-up raises doubt about a causal role of ecstasy (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
Ung et al. cite it among studies reporting neurocognitive impairment in people with light use (p. 282).

replication.where_it_stands: No replication with the same design is described in the papers read in this batch; whether one exists has not been checked. Murphy et al. (2009) note that prospective studies in this field take years and risk too little use by follow-up, and that experimental exposure would be unethical (pp. 172-173). The finding remains a single small-effect result after very little use.

funding.funder: Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development (ZonMw), grant 310-00-036, Addiction Program (p. 734).
funding.declared_conflicts: Financial disclosure: none reported (p. 734).
funding.affiliations_note: Amsterdam Institute for Addiction Research; Academic Medical Center, University of Amsterdam; University Medical Centre Utrecht; Bonger Institute of Criminology. Recorded as a flag for closer reading only.

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective cohort with longer follow-up and a wide range of later use, retesting the comparison group at the same intervals with parallel test forms, hair-verified exposure, adjustment for cannabis, cocaine and sensation seeking, one pre-registered primary memory outcome, and further retests after people stop.

domains.note: Baseline cognition equal and the baseline score adjusted for; other substances measured at both sessions and adjusted for; but cannabis and cocaine use rose more in the ecstasy group, and sensation seeking, sleep and lifestyle were not adjusted for.
Self-reported tablets of unknown content, very little variation (median 1.5); the duration row of Table 1 is internally inconsistent.
At-risk volunteers; 16% lost before follow-up and 5 of the 64 people who started using ecstasy not retested; controls chosen by matching from 94 after those who had started using ecstasy were known.
No intervention after exposure is described.
Those lost to follow-up and the people who started using ecstasy but did not attend are not compared with those analysed.
Blind examiner and standardized tests, but the retest interval differed by 8 months between groups, a parallel RAVLT form is not reported, and recognition was at ceiling and dichotomized.
12 outcomes without correction; sensitivity analysis shown for one outcome; one-tailed dose tests.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is the strongest design among the papers read: cognition was measured before any ecstasy use, the groups were matched and equal at baseline, and the examiner was blind. The overall judgment is high because several concerns act together on a small effect whose intervals reach almost to zero: differential retest intervals, residual confounding by cannabis and cocaine, possible practice effects on a repeated word list, and 12 uncorrected outcomes. The study may be cited for smaller verbal-memory retest gains after very little ecstasy use in this cohort. It may not be cited as showing that ecstasy damages memory or serotonin neurons, or that the change is lasting or clinically meaningful.

key_findings.finding: Before any ecstasy use, the 58 people who later started and the 60 who did not showed no significant difference overall on the 12 test scores in one multivariate analysis of covariance (F(12, 96) = 0.73, p = .72, partial eta squared 0.08); the 12 scores were not tested one by one at baseline.
The Methods state that the same participants also underwent brain imaging, analysed and described by other investigators in separate articles, within the same project.
key_findings.note: This is the paper's own evidence that the imaging cohort published as de Win et al. (2008) is this same 188-person sample, which a narrative review in this batch presents as a second prospective cohort (card sc_parrott_2013, reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: RAVLT immediate recall (sum of 5 trials) changed by +0.86 (SD 5.5) words in the ecstasy group vs +3.90 (5.8) in the comparison group (58.7 to 59.6 vs 57.8 to 61.7); adjusted B 2.23 (95% CI 0.17 to 4.29), F(1, 108) = 4.62, p = .03.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (p. 731); Table 2, RAVLT immediate row (p. 732)

key_findings.finding: RAVLT delayed recall changed by -0.52 (SD 1.8) words vs +0.65 (1.8) (13.8 to 13.2 vs 13.5 to 14.1, of 15); adjusted B 0.63 (95% CI 0.05 to 1.22), F(1, 108) = 4.67, p = .03.
key_findings.locator: Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (p. 731); Table 2, RAVLT delayed recall row (p. 732)

key_findings.finding: RAVLT recognition (of 30, mean scores 29.95 to 29.66 vs 29.88 to 29.93): any decline in 22.4% vs 6.7% of people; logistic regression odds ratio 5.87 (Wald chi-square 5.62, p = .02).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, RAVLT recognition row and footnote (p. 732); Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 731, continues p. 732)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 13 of 58 vs 4 of 60 people; crude odds ratio 4.0.

key_findings.finding: No group differences in change on Memory for Designs (immediate, trials, delayed), Digit Span forward and backward, PASAT at 2.4 s and 1.6 s, Judgment of Line Orientation or Mental Rotation (p = .21 to .85); no sex x ecstasy interaction on RAVLT scores.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 732); Results › Neuropsychological Testing, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 731, continues p. 732)

key_findings.finding: After excluding everyone who had used cocaine or amphetamines (43 people who had started using ecstasy, 57 controls), the delayed recall effect remained significant (F(1, 92) = 6.62, p = .01, partial eta squared 0.07); cocaine and amphetamine use had a covariance effect on delayed recall, alcohol, tobacco and cannabis did not.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: 15 of the 58 people in the ecstasy group and 3 of the 60 controls were excluded as having used cocaine or amphetamines.

key_findings.finding: Within the ecstasy group, cumulative tablets correlated with change in delayed recall (r = -0.24, p = .04) and recognition (r = -0.29, p = .02) but not immediate recall (r = -0.16, p = .12), all one-tailed; after adjustment only recognition remained (partial r = -0.30, p = .02; delayed recall -0.21, p = .08); recognition decline with log-transformed tablets odds ratio 15.18 (95% CI 1.10 to 210.14), with raw tablets 1.30 (0.96 to 1.75), p = .09; no association with duration of use or time since last use.
key_findings.locator: Results › Relationship Between Neuropsychological Test Performance and Amount of Ecstasy Use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: two-tailed p about .07 for delayed recall and .03 for recognition. The odds ratio of 15.18 for recognition decline with log-transformed tablets has an interval from 1.10 to 210.14, spanning more than two orders of magnitude; it must never be quoted without that interval and cannot carry a dose-response claim.

key_findings.finding: Use at follow-up: 3.2 (SD 5.2) tablets in total, median 1.5, range 0.5 to 30, over a mean of 1.6 months; last use 11.8 (12.0) weeks before retest (median 7.9). Time between sessions 11.1 (6.2) months in the ecstasy group vs 19.1 (7.5) in the comparison group (t = 6.30, p < .001).
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of the Sample and Substance Use, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Other substances: cannabis higher in the ecstasy group at baseline (48.8 vs 17.2 joints in the last year, p = .04) and at follow-up (53.6 vs 20.5, p < .001), cocaine higher at follow-up (1.4 vs 0.3 times, p = .006); smoking, alcohol, amphetamines and cocaine similar at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Characteristics of the Sample and Substance Use, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Overall test performance of all participants remained within the normal range of a sex- and age-comparable general population.

The authors list alternatives to an ecstasy effect: cannabis, cocaine and amphetamine use, sensation seeking (higher in people who started using ecstasy in the wider cohort), depression and expectancy from the information given at entry; and limitations: no indisputable evidence of causality, self-reported medical history, unmeasured lifestyle and settings, longer follow-up for controls (argued not to explain the result because retest effects shrink with time), uncontrolled tablet content and a well-educated, motivated sample; and, in the other direction, that a well-educated sample makes a decrease in cognitive function harder to detect (the brain-reserve argument), so that the study may have underestimated an effect of ecstasy.
key_findings.locator: Comment, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 732) and 6th paragraph (begins p. 733)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives duration of ecstasy use as 6.8 (SD 12.5) weeks with median 0.0 and range 0 to 12. With 58 values between 0 and 12 and at least half at 0, the mean can be at most 6.0 and the SD at most about 6 (editors' arithmetic). The text's mean period of 1.6 months fits a mean of about 6.8 weeks, so the printed range is probably wrong.
reporting_issues.consequence: The spread of duration of use cannot be read from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the recognition result as B 1.77 (95% CI 1.36 to 25.37). 1.77 is the logarithm of the odds ratio of 5.87 given in the text and the table footnote, while the interval is the interval of the odds ratio itself (its logarithms, 0.31 and 3.23, centre on 1.77; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as printed, the estimate and its interval are on different scales; the odds ratio is 5.87 (95% CI 1.36 to 25.37).

reporting_issues.issue: Memory for Designs rows in Table 2 do not fit their own means: for number of trials the comparison group's mean fell from 3.4 to 3.1 but its change score is printed as +0.10; for delayed reproduction its mean rose from 20.8 to 20.9 but its change is printed as -0.33, with change SDs of 1.8 although the score SDs are 0.5 and 0.3 (an SD of a difference cannot exceed 0.8 here; editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Errors in non-significant rows; they do not affect the verbal-memory results but lower confidence in the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that the groups were matched on use of substances other than ecstasy (p. 728); the Methods matched on sex, age and verbal IQ (p. 729), and Table 1 shows more cannabis (baseline and follow-up) and cocaine (follow-up) in the ecstasy group (p. 731).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates the comparability of the groups; other drug use was adjusted for statistically, not matched.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract describe the ecstasy group as having minimal exposure to other drugs, but 15 of 58 had used cocaine or amphetamines (editors' arithmetic from the sensitivity analysis), one person reported 156 amphetamine uses, and cannabis use was higher than in the comparison group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minimal is relative to earlier studies; the sensitivity analysis without people who had used cocaine or amphetamines covers delayed recall only.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that low doses are associated with decreased verbal memory function is described as decline, but immediate recall did not fall in the ecstasy group (58.7 to 59.6 words); the difference is a smaller practice gain than in the comparison group.
reporting_issues.consequence: Decline is accurate for delayed recall and recognition only; for immediate recall the finding is a smaller improvement.
