design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (inverse variance, Hedges' g) of neurocognitive performance in people who had used MDMA recreationally and had been abstinent from it for at least 6 months, compared with people still using MDMA (at least 7 days since last use) and with MDMA-naive comparison groups. 14 studies included (11 cross-sectional case-control studies, 3 prospective cohorts); 5 entered a meta-analysis of learning and memory; the other domains (executive function, complex attention, language, perceptual-motor) were summarized narratively by DSM-5 neurocognitive domain. Protocol on the Open Science Framework, registered 18 March 2023 and revised 30 November 2023. Published online 2025, issue 2026.
can_establish: How people abstinent from MDMA for at least 6 months compared with people still using it and with MDMA-naive comparison groups on learning and memory tests in the studies published up to August 2024, and how few and how heterogeneous those studies are.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the lower scores or that scores do not recover after stopping (the comparisons are between different people, mostly at one time point, with no measure before use); whether longer abstinence helps (the authors did not test it, p. 279); or the size of any effect in a defined population (4 or 5 studies per estimate with heterogeneity of 80 to 96%).

sample.recruitment: Database search (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane, Web of Science, PsycINFO, CINAHL) from inception to 9 August 2024, developed with a hospital librarian, plus reference lists of included articles (Material and methods › Search strategy, p. 274; Table 1, p. 275). 8172 records, 5631 after removing duplicates, 214 sought, 213 assessed in full, 14 included; 3 more from citation searching all excluded (Figure 1, p. 275). Studies came from the UK (7), the Netherlands, Australia and Germany (2 each) and Canada (1) (Results › Study characteristics, p. 276).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: humans who used MDMA recreationally with a group abstinent from MDMA for at least 6 months; any current-use comparison group at least 7 days after last use; standardized neurocognitive tests; peer-reviewed publications only; all languages eligible. Excluded: studies where MDMA was given with another substance or medication, and global cognitive screening tools (pp. 275-276). Excluded full texts by reason in Figure 1: acute effects or washout under 7 days 72, no group abstinent more than 6 months 72, non-standardized tool 18, abstract only 17, unclear abstinence 10, others 10 (p. 275).
sample.demographics: Table 2 (pp. 277-278): group sizes from 3 to 182; mean ages mostly in the twenties; mean lifetime use above 100 tablets in 9 studies (up to 500 to 600 in some) and below 100 in 1; minimum abstinence 6 months in 8 studies, 12 months in 1, 18 months in 2, 24 months in 2 and 48 months in 1 (pp. 276, 279).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Peer-reviewed publications only, with no grey literature or registry search; the evidence is weighted towards UK case-control studies, four of them by the same first author with the same abstinent participants (p. 280). In every study the current and abstinent MDMA groups had used other drugs; most comparison groups had too, and only one study, the largest, had a completely drug-naive comparison group (pp. 276, 279).

exposure.measurement: As reported by the primary studies: mean lifetime tablets in almost all, a range only in one, a minimum in another, no quantity in one (p. 276); the review notes reliance on self-report for exposure in 12 of the 14 studies (p. 279).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: No dose-response analysis, because most participants would be classified as having heavy use (more than 100 lifetime tablets) and the study with the lowest exposure (36 to 69 tablets on average) also had the longest abstinence (p. 282).
exposure.polysubstance: All current and abstinent MDMA groups had histories of other drug use; most comparison groups did as well; two studies used comparison groups using only alcohol and tobacco and one (Taurah et al., 2014; 154, 157 and 182 people) a completely drug-naive group (pp. 276, 279; Table 2). Not addressed in the meta-analysis, which pooled unadjusted group means; the authors list polysubstance use as a limitation and note that the comparison groups' drug use was often much lower (p. 282).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinent groups at least 6 months by inclusion; current-use groups at least 7 days since last use (p. 275). Minimum periods by study as above (p. 279).

comparison.controls: MDMA-naive comparison groups, mostly people who used other drugs; people still using MDMA as a second comparison.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level; the appraisal found concerns about matching in all case-control studies and about comparability of abstinent and control groups in all studies (p. 279).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No included study measured cognition before MDMA use began; the authors raise pre-existing characteristics such as trait impulsivity as a possible explanation for differences (p. 282).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Mostly yes (polysubstance comparison groups); none in the largest meta-analysed study.

outcomes.instruments: Standardized neuropsychological tests classified by a clinical neuropsychologist into DSM-5 neurocognitive domains (learning and memory, executive function, complex attention, language, perceptual-motor, social cognition); the classification is in Supplemental Appendix A-1 (not read) (p. 276).
outcomes.validity_norms: Primary-study quality rated by two independent raters with the Joanna Briggs Institute checklists for case-control and cohort studies, plus a global rating of poor or fair (p. 276); all 3 cohorts and 6 of 11 case-control studies poor, 5 case-control studies fair (p. 279). Item-level ratings are in Supplemental Appendix B (not read).
outcomes.operationalization: Pooled standardized mean differences (Hedges' g) between groups for overall learning and memory and for verbal and visual immediate and delayed memory; how several measures from one study were combined into the overall estimate is not described.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 11 counts the pooled estimates in Table 3 (p. 280).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening of titles, abstracts and full texts by two independent reviewers with a third for disagreements (p. 274); quality rated by two independent raters (p. 276); whether data extraction was done by one or two people is not described (p. 276).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 3 (p. 280), Hedges' g with 95% CI and I2. Current vs abstinent: overall 0.03 (-0.35 to 0.41), 5 studies, I2 79.77%; verbal immediate 0.00 (-0.46 to 0.47), 4 studies, I2 36.89%; verbal delayed 0.24 (-1.17 to 1.66), 4 studies, I2 92.23%; visual immediate -0.01 (-0.49 to 0.47), 2 studies, I2 14.79%; visual delayed -0.17 (-0.62 to 0.27), 2 studies, I2 0%. Abstinent vs MDMA-naive: overall -1.37 (-2.65 to -0.09), 4 studies, I2 96.02%; verbal immediate -1.22 (-3.63 to 1.18), 3 studies, I2 94.18%; verbal delayed -1.30 (-4.15 to 1.54), 3 studies, I2 95.54%. Current vs MDMA-naive: overall -1.06 (-1.98 to -0.15), 4 studies, I2 94.58%; verbal immediate -0.41 (-0.88 to 0.06), 3 studies, I2 28.37%; verbal delayed -1.16 (-2.58 to 0.26), 3 studies, I2 90.45%. Sensitivity analysis without the poor-quality cohort: the current vs abstinent result unchanged (p. 279). No tau-squared, prediction intervals or study weights are given in the article (forest plots are in Supplemental Appendices C and D, not read).
analysis.covariates: None at review level; unadjusted group means were pooled.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Science Framework protocol registered 18 March 2023 and revised 30 November 2023 (p. 274); the reference list gives its title as a systematic review (revised protocol) (p. 285). The protocol was not read, so whether the meta-analysis and an analysis by length of abstinence were planned, and any deviations, could not be checked; the article reports no deviations.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only learning and memory were pooled, the other domains being judged too heterogeneous (p. 276), although the pooled comparisons with MDMA-naive groups have I2 of 95 to 96%. The planned contrast of longer abstinence was not done (p. 279), yet its result is stated in the abstract and conclusion (pp. 273, 282). Publication bias was not assessed.
analysis.power: Not addressed. 2 to 5 studies per estimate; some groups very small (an abstinent group of 3 in Morgan, 1999; Table 2, p. 277).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 4 heterogeneous studies, both current and abstinent groups scored lower than MDMA-naive groups on overall learning and memory (g -1.06 and -1.37, with intervals reaching -0.15 and -0.09 and I2 of 95 and 96%); every verbal-memory subtest interval included zero; and abstinent groups did not differ from current groups (g 0.03, -0.35 to 0.41). Executive function, attention, language and perceptual-motor results could not be pooled and were mostly null or inconsistent; the 3 small cohorts, all of poor quality, disagreed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state that a longer period of abstinence did not demonstrate greater improvement or recovery (pp. 273, 282), but the Results say that the effect of longer abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested (p. 279). The Results say the verbal subcategory analyses showed both abstinent and current groups performing "significantly more poorly" than MDMA-naive controls (p. 279), while every one of these intervals in Table 3 includes zero (p. 280). The Discussion reads the cross-sectional comparison of different people as showing that 6 months of abstinence is insufficient for people who have stopped to reach naive-level performance (p. 282), and argues that learning and memory changes are specific to MDMA, a comparison the review did not make. Against this, the authors state that their results do not confirm permanent damage or that it is due to neurotoxic effects of MDMA, that the findings are of low quality, and that pre-existing differences could explain them (pp. 273, 282).

timeline.event: Cited for reduced CSF 5-HIAA (with a 1999 study by the same group, not read) and as indirect human evidence of dopamine-system damage (pp. 274, 281).

Earlier meta-analyses described in the introduction (Verbaten, 2003; Laws and Kokkalis, 2007; Kalechstein et al., 2007; Zakzanis et al., 2007; Nulsen et al., 2010; Roberts et al., 2016) report poorer memory, most consistently verbal, in people who use MDMA; none restricted to sustained abstinence (pp. 273-274; not read).
Prospective study of people starting ecstasy use cited as reporting impairment after light use (p. 282).

Muller et al. meta-analysis of 16 neuroimaging studies: lower serotonin transporter density in 8 of 13 regions, and a positive association with time abstinent that the review says rests largely on one small study (p. 281; not read).
This review: the first, by its authors' account, restricted to at least 6 months of abstinence (pp. 274, 282).

replication.where_it_stands: The review's learning-and-memory estimates rest on 4 or 5 studies with very high heterogeneity, and the authors call the findings low quality. Overlap with the earlier meta-analyses of the same cross-sectional literature was not assessed in the review and has not been checked here. The question of recovery with abstinence cannot be answered from cross-sectional comparisons between people who still use and people who have stopped.

funding.funder: The authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication (p. 283).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared (p. 283).
funding.affiliations_note: Metro North Mental Health (Queensland Health), the University of Queensland, West Moreton Hospital and Health Service, Queensland Centre for Mental Health Research and QIMR Berghofer (p. 273). Recorded as a flag for closer reading only.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that test cognition before MDMA use and then repeatedly in people who continue and people who stop, with retested comparison groups, hair-verified exposure and abstinence, and an individual-participant analysis relating change in scores to time since stopping, against people who use the same other drugs.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (recreational MDMA use, at least 6 months abstinent), comparators (current use, MDMA-naive), outcomes (neurocognitive domains) stated (p. 275).

Open Science Framework protocol registered March 2023 and revised November 2023, before the search ended in August 2024; the protocol was not read, its cited title names a systematic review only, and no deviations are reported.
Case-control and cohort studies were included without an explanation of the choice of designs.

Six databases with a librarian-developed strategy (Table 1), reference lists, all languages, search within 24 months of publication; but the restriction to peer-reviewed publications is not justified and no grey literature, registries or experts were searched. Judged as written for unjustified publication restrictions (decision p-amstar2-item4); a lenient reading would give partial yes. The overall rating does not depend on this item.
Two authors independently screened titles, abstracts and full texts, with a third reviewer for discrepancies (p. 274).
Pre-defined extraction variables are listed, but who extracted the data, and whether two people did, is not described (p. 276).

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives the number of exclusions by reason; no list of excluded studies appears in the article, and none of the named supplements is described as holding one (supplements not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 2 gives design, group sizes, age, sex, MDMA use, comparison-group substance use, domains and minimum abstinence; setting, recruitment and the specific tests are not tabulated, and several entries are inconsistent (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: JBI checklists by two independent raters, covering confounding, matching and exposure measurement (p. 279); selection of the reported result is not covered; item-level ratings only in a supplement (not read).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.

Random-effects inverse-variance pooling of unadjusted group means from non-randomized studies, without justification for combining unadjusted data; pooled despite I2 of 95 to 96% with 4 studies, although high heterogeneity was the stated reason for not pooling the other domains; the handling of several measures per study in the overall estimate is not described; a cohort study was pooled with case-control studies without explanation.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis excluding the only poor-quality study in the meta-analysis left the current vs abstinent result unchanged (p. 279); the comparisons with MDMA-naive groups contain only studies rated fair. Minimal, but it meets the item.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The abstract, critical appraisal and conclusion state that the findings are low quality and call for caution (pp. 273, 279, 282), and the limitations discuss confounding by other drug use and pre-existing traits (p. 282), although parts of the Discussion still overstate the results.
I2 is reported and heterogeneity in recruitment, populations, tests and confounding is named as a limitation (p. 282), but no subgroup, meta-regression or other investigation of its sources was done.
Not investigated or discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (p. 283).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence because more than one critical item is not met: no list of excluded studies (item 7), pooling of unadjusted data with extreme heterogeneity (item 11) and no assessment of publication bias (item 15), and, as written, an unjustified restriction to peer-reviewed publications (item 4); items 2 and 9 are partly met and item 13 is met. This is a judgment about how far the pooled numbers can be trusted, not about the value of the question: the review is registered, searched widely without language limits, screened in duplicate and states its low certainty. Its pooled estimates should be read as describing a small, heterogeneous set of cross-sectional comparisons. It may be cited for those comparisons and for the absence of any analysis of longer abstinence; it may not be cited for recovery or its absence, or for a causal effect of MDMA.

key_findings.finding: 14 studies met the criteria (11 cross-sectional case-control, 3 prospective cohorts): 8 assessed learning and memory, 10 executive function, 5 complex attention, 2 language, 1 perceptual-motor function, none social cognition.

Learning and memory meta-analysis of 5 studies with, as stated, 228 people currently using MDMA, 218 abstinent at least 6 months and 229 MDMA-naive comparison participants; studies were left out for insufficient data (2) or participants already represented (1).
key_findings.note: Table 2 group sizes for the same 5 studies sum to 241, 208 and 231 (editors' arithmetic; the cohort study has no naive group); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Current vs abstinent (at least 6 months): no difference in overall learning and memory, g 0.03 (95% CI -0.35 to 0.41), 5 studies, I2 79.77%, unchanged when the poor-quality cohort was excluded; verbal and visual subtests also near zero (g -0.17 to 0.24, all intervals including zero).
key_findings.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (p. 279); Table 3 (p. 280)

key_findings.finding: Abstinent vs MDMA-naive: overall learning and memory g -1.37 (95% CI -2.65 to -0.09), 4 studies, I2 96.02%; current vs MDMA-naive: g -1.06 (-1.98 to -0.15), 4 studies, I2 94.58%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (p. 279); Table 3 (p. 280)

key_findings.finding: Verbal memory subtests vs MDMA-naive groups: abstinent immediate -1.22 (-3.63 to 1.18) and delayed -1.30 (-4.15 to 1.54), 3 studies each, I2 94 to 96%; current immediate -0.41 (-0.88 to 0.06) and delayed -1.16 (-2.58 to 0.26). All four intervals include zero.
key_findings.note: The text says these subcategory analyses showed significantly poorer performance (p. 279); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Because of the small sample, the effect of longer durations of abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested.
key_findings.locator: Results › Learning and memory, 2nd paragraph (last sentence)

key_findings.finding: Of the three learning-and-memory studies not pooled, two case-control studies found impairment despite 12 to 24 months of abstinence, while a small 2-year prospective study of poor quality found memory improved in people who stopped and worsened in people who continued (Zakzanis and Campbell, 2006).

Executive function (10 studies): the two prospective studies (poor quality) found neither improvement nor deterioration after 18 months of abstinence; seven case-control studies found no significant difference between abstinent and MDMA-naive groups; four by the same author with the same abstinent participants showed a trend for abstinent groups to score between current-use groups and controls; the four are among the seven, so those seven studies rest on at most four independent samples and the ten executive-function studies on at most seven.
key_findings.locator: Results › Executive function, 1st paragraph (begins p. 279, continues p. 280)

key_findings.finding: Complex attention (5 cross-sectional studies): 4 of 5, including the largest, found no significant differences between current, abstinent and MDMA-naive groups; one found both MDMA groups poorer than controls on serial 7s. Language (2 studies) mixed; perceptual-motor (1 small study) a small improvement in people who stopped; social cognition no studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Complex attention; Language; Perceptual motor function; Social cognition

key_findings.finding: Quality: all 3 cohorts and 6 of 11 case-control studies rated poor, 5 fair; comparability of abstinent and control groups questioned in all studies and matching in all case-control studies; exposure assessed by self-report in 12 of 14.

Polysubstance use: in all studies both MDMA groups had used other drugs; most comparison groups had too; two used alcohol- and tobacco-using controls, and only one (Taurah et al., 2014) a completely drug-naive comparison group.
key_findings.locator: Results › Patterns of MDMA use and other drug use, 1st paragraph (begins p. 276, continues p. 279)

key_findings.finding: Abstinence minima: 6 months in 8 studies, 12 months in 1, 18 months in 2, 24 months in 2, 48 months in 1; the study with the lowest exposure (mean 36 to 69 tablets) also had the longest abstinence, so dose and abstinence are confounded across studies; no dose-response analysis was done.
key_findings.locator: Results › Duration of abstinence (p. 279); Discussion, 6th paragraph (begins p. 281, continues p. 282)
key_findings.note: The review gives its reason for not doing a dose-response analysis: most participants in the included studies would count as heavy use under the usual definition of more than 100 lifetime tablets (p. 282). That is also the reason the review cannot speak to lighter use.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that their results do not definitively confirm permanent damage or that it is due to neurotoxic effects of MDMA, that the conclusions rest on variable, low-quality findings, and that pre-existing traits may explain differences.

As summarized in the Discussion (studies not read): a meta-analysis of 16 neuroimaging studies found lower serotonin transporter density in 8 of 13 regions, with a positive association between transporter density and time abstinent that the review says rested largely on one small study, which it names as Selvaraj et al. (2009) (Muller et al., 2019); and a study of people abstinent about 2.5 years found possible transporter recovery without recovery of verbal memory (Thomasius et al., 2006), a study the review itself excluded from its evidence base because the washout in its current-use comparison group was shorter than 7 days.
key_findings.note: Both figures are second-hand. The parenthesis in the first half names the meta-analysis; the single small study behind the abstinence association is Selvaraj et al. (2009), which a reader would otherwise take to be Muller et al.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results state that the verbal immediate and delayed subcategory analyses showed both abstinent and current MDMA groups performing significantly more poorly than MDMA-naive controls (p. 279), but all four intervals in Table 3 include zero (p. 280).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text overstates the subcategory results; only the overall estimates exclude zero, and only just.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and conclusion state that a longer period of abstinence did not demonstrate greater improvement or recovery (pp. 273, 282), but the Results say the effect of longer abstinence beyond 6 months was not tested (p. 279).
reporting_issues.consequence: A headline conclusion rests on an analysis that was not done; the only basis is the cross-sectional current vs abstinent comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The meta-analysis totals do not add up: the text gives 228 current, 218 abstinent and 229 MDMA-naive participants in 5 studies and 74, 51 and 47 in the 4-study verbal subset (p. 279). Adding the largest study's Table 2 sizes (154, 157 and 182) to the subset gives 228 and 229 but 208, not 218; and Table 2's sizes for the four smaller studies sum to 87, 51 and 49 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of abstinent participants in the meta-analysis is uncertain (208 or 218).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 contains internal errors: in Taurah et al. (2014) the abstinent group is 66% men and 24% women, and in Ward et al. (2006) the current and comparison groups are 29% and 61%, and 23% and 67%, neither summing to 100; the abstinent group of Potter et al. (2013) is n = 17 but given as 4 men and 11 women with the same age as Morgan et al. (2002), whose row it appears to repeat.
reporting_issues.consequence: Study characteristics cannot be relied on without the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's entries for the Wareing studies differ from those printed by Murphy et al. (2009, Table 2), whose authors include the primary authors: the sample sizes and lifetime tablets given here for Wareing et al. (2004a, verbal working memory) and (2004b, visuospatial memory) are those Murphy et al. give for the other paper, and Wareing et al. (2005) has 291.33 lifetime tablets here vs 591.33 in Murphy et al. Two further mismatches: this table prints the same standard deviation (718.44) for the 2004b and 2005 rows, where Murphy et al. give 681.49 for the earlier study; and the comparison group of Wareing et al. (2007) is aged 22.85 here against 22.58 in Murphy et al.
reporting_issues.consequence: Likely transcription errors in this review; the primary studies have not been read, so which version is right is not settled.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results describe Zakzanis and Campbell (2006) as a 2-year study with findings at 18 months (pp. 279-280) and Table 2 gives its minimum abstinence as 24 months (p. 278); the language section reports vocabulary change at 18 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence and follow-up periods of this study are unclear from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says Taurah et al. (2014) observed impairments in learning and memory and executive functioning that did not improve despite an average of 5 years of abstinence, and refers to no improvement up to 5 years of follow-up (pp. 281-282); Table 2 lists that study as cross-sectional and assessing learning and memory and complex attention only, and the executive-function section does not include it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A cross-sectional study is described as showing absence of improvement over time, and in a domain it did not assess.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction cites McCann et al. (1994) as indirect human evidence of dopamine-system damage (p. 274); in that study the dopamine metabolite HVA was lower only in women and not on unequal-variance testing (card sc_mccann_1994).
reporting_issues.consequence: Overstatement of the dopamine evidence; not used in this review's analyses.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 273-285 (issue version, all pages; Figure 1, Table 2 and Table 3 checked on rendered pages; Supplemental Appendices A-D, including forest plots and item-level quality ratings, not read)

disagreements.first_pass: Executive function (10 studies): the two prospective studies (poor quality) found neither improvement nor deterioration after 18 months of abstinence; seven case-control studies found no significant difference between abstinent and MDMA-naive groups; four by the same author with the same abstinent participants showed a trend for abstinent groups to score between current-use groups and controls.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the four Wareing studies share the same abstinent participants, so the ten executive-function studies rest on at most seven independent samples and the seven case-control studies reported as null include those four; METHODS §6.3 requires overlapping evidence to be stated wherever studies are counted.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 280: the review lists the same seven studies as finding no difference and then says four of these, by the same primary author, share the same abstinent participants. The arithmetic (seven studies, at most four samples; ten studies, at most seven samples) follows from the review's own lists and is added to the finding.

disagreements.first_pass: (absent)
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the reason the review gives for not doing a dose-response analysis is worth recording beside the fact that it was not done.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 282: the reason is as the reader states. Added as a note, with the consequence for lighter use, which the review does not draw.

disagreements.first_pass: As summarized in the Discussion (studies not read): a meta-analysis of 16 neuroimaging studies found lower serotonin transporter density in 8 of 13 regions, with a positive association with time abstinent that rested largely on one small study (Muller et al., 2019); one study of people abstinent 2.5 years found possible transporter recovery without recovery of verbal memory (Thomasius et al., 2006).

Missed: Thomasius et al. design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (tabulation and vote counting) of randomized trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD, said to follow PRISMA, not registered and without a protocol (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, online 2025, pp. 1–13). CINAHL, PubMed, Medline, PsycInfo and the Cochrane Library were searched in March 2023 with keywords for clinical trials published in peer-reviewed journals in 2002–2022, and the search was rerun in May 2025. Six trials were analysed (two pilot trials, two phase 2 dose-response trials and the two phase 3 trials; 280 participants), all linked to MAPS; two pooled analyses retracted in August 2024 and one long-term follow-up were tabulated but excluded. Outcomes summarised: CAPS change and loss of diagnosis at each trial's primary end point, long-term follow-up, adverse events, suicidality, blinding and other limitations, and dropout.
can_establish: Which randomized trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD were found in the databases searched up to May 2025, and how the authors summarised their direction of effect, adverse events, suicidality, blinding and dropout.
cannot_establish: A pooled effect size or its uncertainty (no meta-analysis); a validated risk-of-bias appraisal of the trials (no tool was used); anything outside the trial publications (no registries, regulatory documents or grey literature); and, because of transcription errors, the trial numbers themselves, which should be taken from the trial reports.

sample.recruitment: Database search (see design), run by a librarian as non-financial support; titles and abstracts screened independently by two reviewers (Methods, p. 2; Other information, p. 10).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: randomized controlled trial design, PTSD treatment condition and MDMA-AT (Methods, p. 2). Of the 26 records, 14 were eliminated (6 on mechanisms in healthy controls, 6 outside the scope, 1 not specific to MDMA-AT, 1 abstract only); the 2025 rerun added one article (Mitchell et al., 2023). Of the 13 articles so identified, four more were eliminated: three for focusing on secondary outcomes (Ching et al., 2022; Nicholas et al., 2022; Ponte et al., 2021) and one randomized trial (Bouso et al., 2008) for outcome measures inconsistent with the others, in part because it was conducted outside the United States, so that all analysed trials used the CAPS. Two retracted pooled analyses (Mithoefer et al., 2019; Jerome et al., 2020) and a long-term follow-up overlapping another trial (Mithoefer et al., 2013) were then left out of the analysis (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Analysed trials: mean age 37.2 to 42.0 years; 66.4% female; baseline CAPS thresholds from 28 or more to 50 or more; three trials with an inactive placebo and three with low-dose MDMA as an active placebo; four of six trials 90% to 100% White, the two phase 3 trials more diverse (p. 3; p. 8; Tables 1 and 5).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; the review reports dropout of 7.1% to 16.7% in the trials (p. 8).
sample.selection_effects: Peer-reviewed journals only (2002–2022 in the first search), five databases, no trial registries, regulatory documents, reference-list searches or grey literature; one randomized trial excluded after the fact for its outcome measure. Every trial found, including the excluded Bouso et al. (2008), which lists the MAPS founder among its authors, is linked to MAPS, so the review cannot speak to independent evidence; and its search keywords included the sponsor's name (MAPS) and 'breakthrough therapy', with no stated combination, so the absence of trials without a MAPS link may partly reflect the search. Table 1 lists six phase 2 registrations under the pooled analyses, two of which (NCT01958593, the trial at the site of the ethical violation, and NCT01689740) correspond to no analysed study; the review does not say whether their results were sought.

exposure.measurement: As tabulated from the trial reports: MDMA in two or three experimental sessions with MAPS-manualized therapy, against an inactive placebo (three trials) or low-dose MDMA as an active placebo (three trials) (p. 3; Table 1).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (Table 1, p. 3): initial active doses of 75, 100 or 125 mg in the phase 2 and pilot trials, with low-dose MDMA of 25, 30 or 40 mg as active placebo; the two phase 3 trials are listed only by the first session's initial dose of 80 mg, whereas the trial reports give 80 mg in session 1 and 120 mg in sessions 2 and 3, each followed by a supplemental half-dose. The text counts the 160 active-dose participants as those given an initial dose of 40 mg or more, a threshold that would include the 40 mg active-placebo arm, which the 160 excludes (editors' sum of Table 1); Table 2 gives that active placebo as 40 mg in its efficacy column and 30 mg in its clinical-response column; the Appendix gives 80–120 mg per session for MAPP1 (pp. 3, 4, 13).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed, beyond noting that MAPP2 excluded substance use disorders other than mild cannabis or alcohol use (Appendix, p. 13).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo (Mithoefer et al., 2011; Mitchell et al., 2021, 2023) or low-dose MDMA as an active placebo (Oehen et al., 2013; Ot'alora et al., 2018; Mithoefer et al., 2018), with the same therapy in both arms (p. 3).
comparison.matching: Not applicable (review).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable (review).

outcomes.instruments: CAPS (CAPS-IV or CAPS-5) change at each trial's primary end point; proportion no longer meeting PTSD criteria; long-term follow-up; adverse events as each trial reported them (different instruments and time windows); C-SSRS suicidality; blinding (correct guesses), sample size, diversity, conflicts of interest and bias-reduction steps; dropout (pp. 2–8; Tables 2–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review notes that adverse-event reporting varied substantially between trials and measures, making synthesis difficult (p. 4; p. 9).
outcomes.operationalization: Efficacy is the number of trials with a statistically significant CAPS difference (vote counting) and the range of loss-of-diagnosis percentages; no effect sizes are pooled or tabulated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests were done. The count of 6 covers CAPS change, loss of diagnosis, long-term follow-up, adverse events, suicidality and dropout.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; each trial's blinding is tabulated (Table 5).

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled and no confidence intervals. Vote count: 5 of 6 trials found a significantly greater CAPS decrease with MDMA; Oehen et al. (2013) did not reach significance (p = 0.0666, Appendix p. 12). Loss of diagnosis at the primary end point: 41.7% to 85.7% in active-dose arms vs 25.0% to 33.3% in placebo arms, excluding Oehen et al. (2013), in which all 12 participants still met criteria (p. 4; Table 2). Long-term follow-up: 41.6% to 100% no longer meeting criteria (p. 4). Dropout 7.1% to 16.7% (p. 8).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The authors state that the review was not registered and no protocol was prepared (Other information, p. 10).
analysis.selective_reporting: The placebo-arm loss-of-diagnosis results of the two phase 3 trials are not tabulated (Table 2, p. 4), and the stated placebo range omits MAPP2's 47.6% (20 of 42); serious, severe and special-interest adverse events are summarised unevenly across trials.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A tabulation of six MAPS-linked trials (280 participants: four small pilot or phase 2 trials and the two phase 3 trials), without pooling, risk-of-bias tool or certainty rating. Five of six favoured MDMA significantly; by the review's own count, four of six had functional unblinding, all had conflicts of interest with MAPS, four had very small samples, and adverse-event reporting was inconsistent. Several numbers in its tables differ from the trial reports.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the findings support MDMA-AT as a viable treatment option and that it appeared well tolerated (Abstract, p. 1). The Discussion says the trials supported its safe and effective use, calls the two phase 3 trials well designed and sufficient for the FDA's two-trial paradigm, suggesting the treatment could be considered for approval (p. 8), and, while accepting functional unblinding as a valid concern, states without a source that “researchers considered it unlikely that unblinding alone could explain the magnitude and durability” of the gains (p. 9). The main conclusion cites the retracted Mithoefer et al. (2019) among its supporting trials (p. 8). The claim that five studies with long-term follow-up showed maintained or improved gains rests on uncontrolled follow-ups, mostly after open-label crossover (Appendix). The conclusion still calls for larger, more diverse trials and an active placebo (p. 10).

timeline.event: MAPP1, phase 3 trial analysed in the review.
MAPP2, phase 3 trial added by the 2025 rerun of the search.

Retraction, on 10 August 2024, of the pooled phase 2 analyses by Mithoefer et al. (2019) and Jerome et al. (2020), and of a third analysis by Feduccia et al. (2020) that this review does not name; the notices give grounds the review leaves out (reporting issues).
This review (received December 2024, accepted September 2025).

replication.where_it_stands: The review adds no data and, because of its errors and lack of appraisal, cannot replace the trial reports; it is useful mainly for its inventory, which by May 2025 found no randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD without a link to MAPS, from a search whose keywords included MAPS (their combination is not reported).

funding.funder: No funding (Funding, p. 10); a librarian ran the database searches as non-financial support (Other information, p. 10).
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors (Disclosure statement, p. 10).
funding.affiliations_note: Psychology Department, Colorado State University – Pueblo (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review with meta-analysis of all randomized trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, including trial-registry results and regulatory documents, with duplicate extraction, RoB 2 assessments that address unblinding, pooled effects with intervals, and GRADE certainty ratings.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: The stated criteria are design, condition and intervention only; comparator and outcomes are not specified, and the restriction to trials using the CAPS was added after screening (p. 2).
Not registered, no protocol (p. 10).
Randomized trials only, explained as the valid evidence on safety and efficacy (Rationale and objective, p. 2).

Five databases and keywords given, but publication restrictions (peer-reviewed journals, 2002–2022) are not justified and no full strategy, trial registry, regulatory document, reference-list search or expert contact is reported (p. 2); the keywords include the sponsor's name (MAPS) and 'breakthrough therapy', and the rerun, called the same exact search, must have changed the 2002–2022 limits to find MAPP2 (2023), which is not reported.
Two reviewers screened titles and abstracts independently (p. 2); how disagreements were resolved is not stated.

The Methods say only that reviewers created tables; the abstract's statement that data were independently reviewed does not describe duplicate extraction, and several extracted numbers differ from the trial reports.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Exclusions after the first selection are named with reasons (four articles, two retracted analyses and one follow-up), but the 14 earlier exclusions are given only as counts by reason, and the reason for excluding the Bouso et al. (2008) trial departs from the stated criteria (p. 2).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives design, sample size, CAPS threshold, sex, age, arms and initial doses and number of sessions; country, setting, timing of the primary end point and follow-up length are not tabulated, and some entries are wrong.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No tool was used; Table 5 lists blinding, sample size, diversity, conflicts of interest and bias-reduction steps, but allocation concealment, missing data and selective reporting are not assessed (pp. 7–8).

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: MAPS is named for every trial (Table 5; p. 8), though as a conflict of interest rather than as funder.
No meta-analysis; vote counting only.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled results.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The limitations section names expectancy, small samples and conflicts of interest (p. 8), but the conclusions call the phase 3 trials well designed and the treatment safe and efficacious, and dismiss unblinding with an unsourced statement (pp. 8–9).
The one discordant trial is attributed speculatively to rater differences (p. 8); differences in comparator (active or inactive placebo), number of sessions and population are not examined.
No quantitative synthesis; the review also does not ask whether registered phase 2 trials without separate publications exist.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: No funding and no conflicts declared (p. 10).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items are not met (2, protocol; 4, search; 9, risk-of-bias assessment) and a fourth (13) is not met, with item 7 only partly met, which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. Beyond the instrument, the review contains many transcription errors (reporting issues) and cites a retracted analysis in its main conclusion. It may be cited for its inventory of published randomized trials up to May 2025 (from a search whose keywords included MAPS) and, second-hand, for the fact of the 2024 retractions (not their grounds, which the notices give) and for the FDA advisory panel's concerns; it should not be cited for any trial result, which should come from the trial reports.

key_findings.finding: Search and selection: CINAHL, PubMed, Medline, PsycInfo and the Cochrane Library searched in March 2023 (clinical trials in peer-reviewed journals, 2002–2022), with the keywords breakthrough therapy, MDMA, PTSD, post-traumatic stress disorder, MDMA-AT and Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS) and no stated Boolean combination, and again in May 2025; 26 unique records, 12 meeting criteria after independent screening by two reviewers, 14 eliminated; the rerun gave 12 more records and one inclusion (MAPP2); four further articles were eliminated, three for secondary outcomes and one trial (Bouso et al., 2008) for using other outcome measures, partly because it was run outside the United States.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Two tabled articles, Mithoefer et al. (2019) and Jerome et al. (2020), were retracted in August 2024 because they included data from a site where a serious ethical violation occurred, identified in Table 1 as MP4, NCT01958593; they are shown in Table 1 but excluded from all calculations, as is the long-term follow-up by Mithoefer et al. (2013).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study and participant characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 2); Table 1 and its footnote (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Six trials analysed with 280 participants: 160 (57.1%) in active-dose MDMA arms and 120 (42.9%) given an inactive or active placebo; three trials used an inactive and three a low-dose active placebo; three used two and three used three experimental sessions; mean age 37.2 to 42.0 years; 66.4% female.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study and participant characteristics, 2nd paragraph (starts on p. 2, continues on p. 3); Table 1 (p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Efficacy: 5 of 6 trials (83.3%) found a significantly greater CAPS decrease with MDMA; Oehen et al. (2013) found a non-significant decrease. Loss of diagnosis at the primary end point 41.7% to 85.7% in active-dose arms vs 25.0% to 33% in placebo arms, except Oehen et al. (2013), where all 12 still met criteria; Table 2 gives 28 of 42 (67%) for MAPP1 and 37 of 52 (71.2%) for MAPP2 without their placebo results.
key_findings.locator: Efficacy of MDMA-AT for PTSD, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Adverse events: reporting varied substantially between trials and measures; muscle tightness or jaw clenching was among the top three events on MDMA in all six trials and headache the most common on placebo; Table 3 lists, for MAPP1, muscle tightness 29 (63%) vs 5 (11%), decreased appetite 24 (52%) vs 5 (11%), nausea 14 (30%) vs 5 (11%), hyperhidrosis 9 (20%) vs 1 (2%) and substance use 3 (6%) vs 0, rows that cannot be traced to the trial article (whose counts are only in an unread supplement) and that differ in places from the trial registry (muscle tightness 28 vs 6, hyperhidrosis 10 vs 1); and for MAPP2 the rows of that trial's Table 2 with rounded percentages, except that feeling cold (11 vs 3) is missing.
key_findings.locator: Safety of MDMA-AT: adverse events (p. 4, right column, and p. 6, left column); Table 3 (pp. 5–6)

key_findings.finding: Suicidality: four trials reported C-SSRS data; lifetime positive ideation 83.7% to 96.4%; in the two phase 3 trials the number with ideation never exceeded baseline in either arm; suicidal behaviour during the study was reported only in a placebo participant (MAPP1).
key_findings.locator: Risk of suicidality (p. 6, right column, to p. 8, left column); Table 4 (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Blinding: blinding was maintained or partly maintained in 2 of 6 trials, both with an active placebo; the review states that in the other four, correct guesses by active-dose participants ranged from 90% to 95%, indicating functional unblinding in 66.7% of trials. Table 5 gives 95% of participants correct for Mithoefer et al. (2011), 58.1% to 72.7% for Ot'alora et al. (2018), no formal assessment for MAPP1 and 94.2% (MDMA) and 75% (placebo) for MAPP2.

Limitations named by the review: conflicts of interest with MAPS in all trials (financial support to investigators, study drug, input on design), very small samples (12 to 28) in four trials, limited diversity, and possible expectation bias, observer expectancy and selective reporting.
Dropout: 16.7% (Oehen et al., 2013) and 7.1% (Ot'alora et al., 2018); the review gives 9% for both phase 3 trials, with four dropouts from each arm in MAPP1 and 1 vs 8 in MAPP2.
key_findings.note: MAPP1's report shows 4 of 46 on MDMA and 7 of 44 on placebo not completing treatment; the review's four per arm matches the participants without an 18-week assessment in MAPP1's CONSORT diagram (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: FDA advisory panel, as described without a citation: the panel voted against recommending MDMA-AT, concluding that the data did not sufficiently show efficacy and that benefits did not outweigh risks; its concerns included potential functional unblinding, lack of standardized psychotherapy across sites, suicidal ideation, cardiovascular risk and potential misuse; the review adds that an ethical violation in one trial, publicly documented on YouTube, led to the retraction of multiple articles.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph starting on p. 9 (right column)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the trials support MDMA-AT as potentially safe and efficacious; the two phase 3 trials meet the FDA's minimum two-trial paradigm; functional unblinding is a valid concern but said to be unlikely to explain the gains; future trials should be larger and more diverse, track sessions, drug effects, adverse events, suicidality and misuse more consistently, and consider an active placebo.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 8) and 3rd paragraph starting on p. 9; Conclusion and future implications (p. 10)

key_findings.finding: Not registered, no protocol, no funding, no declared conflicts of interest.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says seven randomized trials with 280 participants were identified and six were analysed for efficacy; the Results analyse six trials, whose sample sizes (20, 12, 28, 26, 90, 104) alone sum to 280.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the seventh is apparently the excluded long-term follow-up, which is not a separate trial.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated placebo range for loss of diagnosis, 25.0% to 33.3%, omits MAPP2's placebo result of 47.6% (20 of 42), and Table 2 gives neither phase 3 trial's placebo figure (MAPP1: 32%, 12 of 37).
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast between arms is overstated; in MAPP2 nearly half of placebo completers lost the diagnosis.

reporting_issues.issue: The review states that correct guesses by active-dose participants ranged from 90% to 95% in four trials, but its own Table 5 gives 58.1% for one of them (Ot'alora et al., 2018) and no rate for MAPP1, which did not assess blinding.
reporting_issues.consequence: Only two trials support the stated range; the unblinding conclusion is still supported by the MAPP2 survey and the 2011 pilot.

reporting_issues.issue: MAPP1's dropout is given as 9% with four dropouts from each arm. This matches the participants without an 18-week (T4) assessment in MAPP1's CONSORT diagram (4 of 46 and 4 of 44, three placebo participants having given off-treatment values), not treatment discontinuation, which was 4 of 46 on MDMA and 7 of 44 on placebo (12% of 90), plus one withdrawal before dosing; for MAPP2 the review counts treatment discontinuation (1 vs 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: The between-arm difference in MAPP1 treatment discontinuation is hidden, and the review's two phase 3 dropout figures measure different things.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 gives MAPP1's suicidality events of special interest as three suicidal ideation on MDMA and two ideation plus one self-harm on placebo (three, not the five stated); the trial's Table 2 gives two ideation and one self-harm with ideation on MDMA, and three ideation and two with suicidal behaviour or self-harm on placebo. For MAPP2, Table 4 gives a baseline rate of 15 of 104 (14.4%), which does not appear in the trial report, and lists as during-study values the 13 of 53 and 12 of 51 that the trial reports at the final preparation session.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the trial reports for suicidality figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives MAPP1 events in 4 participants as 5% (4 of 46 is 8.7%) in four rows, and muscle tightness as 29 vs 5, while the trial registry gives 28 vs 6 (over a longer window); the review's source for MAPP1's adverse events is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Percentages in the table cannot be relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: The text defines the 160 active-dose participants by an initial-dose threshold that would also take in one trial's active-placebo arm, which the count excludes; Table 2 itself gives that active placebo (Ot'alora et al., 2018) as 40 mg in its efficacy column and 30 mg in its clinical-response column, while Table 1 gives 40 mg (30 mg is the active placebo of Mithoefer et al., 2018); and Table 1 gives the phase 3 trials only their first-session initial dose (see the exposure field).
reporting_issues.consequence: The tabulated exposure of the phase 3 trials is incomplete; use the trial reports.

reporting_issues.issue: Long-term follow-up results are summarised as 41.6% to 100% no longer meeting criteria 12 months or longer after the study, but the 100% is the 2011 pilot's 7 of 7 at 2 months (Table 2); the follow-ups mostly came after open-label crossover, so no placebo group remained.
reporting_issues.consequence: The durability statement in the abstract and Discussion is not supported as written.

reporting_issues.issue: The main conclusion cites Mithoefer et al. (2019), one of the two retracted analyses the review says it excluded; the review names the retracting journal as the Journal of Psychopharmacology, while the DOIs it gives and its reference list place both articles in Psychopharmacology.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the retractions from the notices (Crossref), not from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Appendix says about 61% of MAPP2 participants were ethnically diverse, which is the sum of two overlapping percentages (33.7% other than White and 26.9% Hispanic or Latino).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Sex counts differ between Table 1 and Table 5 for three studies (Oehen et al., 2013: 2 M, 10 F vs 3 M, 7 F; Ot'alora et al., 2018: 9 M, 19 F vs 9 M, 16 F; Mithoefer et al., 2013: 3 M, 16 F vs 3 M, 13 F); the text says three studies reported treatment-related adverse events but names two.
reporting_issues.page: pp. 3, 4, 7 (Tables 1 and 5; Safety of MDMA-AT, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor transcription errors.

reporting_issues.issue: The reference list names the journal of both phase 3 trials as Naturopathic Medicine; unresolved typesetting queries (marked AQ) remain in the published Appendix; the FDA is called the Federal Drug Administration, and the abstract says the FDA voted, while the Discussion describes an advisory panel vote, for which no source is cited.
reporting_issues.consequence: Signs of limited editorial checking; the advisory panel's vote and concerns should be taken from primary regulatory sources.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2025 rerun is called the same exact search, yet with the stated 2002–2022 limits it could not have found MAPP2 (published 2023), the one article it added; the changed date limits are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The rerun cannot be reproduced from the report.

reporting_issues.issue: The review gives as the reason for the retractions that the two analyses included data from a site where a serious ethical violation occurred (p. 2), and says the violation was publicly documented on YouTube (p. 9, no source). The retraction notices give two grounds the review leaves out: that the authors knew of the violations at the MP4 site when they submitted and neither disclosed them nor removed that site's data, and that a competing interest was not fully declared; the review does not name the third retracted analysis (Feduccia et al.), speaking on p. 9 only of the retraction of multiple articles.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the notices, not this review, for the retractions and their grounds.

design_detail: Qualitative story-completion study (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs, online first 10 October 2025, article pages 1-11; received 30 January, revised 9 July, accepted 30 July 2025). Not a commentary: 30 veterans with a previous PTSD diagnosis receiving care at one VA hospital in the north-eastern United States listened to a vignette about 'Chris', a combat veteran whose doctor offers him a clinical trial of MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT), and completed the story aloud in answer to five open prompts (reaction, prior knowledge, questions and concerns, hopes, decision; Appendix, p. 11). Recordings were transcribed and coded by three authors (43 codes); coders also rated each participant's willingness and familiarity on 0-100 scales; codes were correlated (Kendall's tau) with demographics, story length, drug use, PCL-5 and PHQ-9. Table 1 (code definitions, examples, frequencies) and Table 2 (correlations above |0.30|). The Introduction and Discussion contain background statements about the phase 3 trials and the 2024 FDA decision, taken from other sources, which this card records separately.
can_establish: Which questions, hopes and concerns these 30 veterans voiced, as coded by the authors, when asked to imagine a fellow veteran being offered MDMA-assisted therapy in a trial.
cannot_establish: How common any of these attitudes is among veterans with PTSD, what the participants themselves would decide, or anything about the efficacy, blinding or safety of MDMA-assisted therapy: the statements about the trials and the FDA are background from other sources (news reports for the FDA) or unreferenced.

sample.recruitment: Veteran patients of one VA hospital in the north-eastern United States (the procedures were approved by the IRB of the Stratton VA Medical Center, Albany). How participants were identified, approached and selected, how many declined, and whether they were paid are not reported.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All 30 reported a previous diagnosis of, and treatment for, PTSD; no other criteria are reported.
sample.demographics: Ages 30-77 (mean 51.03, SD 14.49). Education: some college 14 (46.7%), college graduate 10 (33.3%), graduate degree 4 (13.3%), some high school 1 (3.3%), high school diploma or equivalent 1 (3.3%). PCL-5 19-65 (mean 43.67, SD 10.91); PHQ-9 8-21 (mean 14.70, SD 3.74). Lifetime use of 1 to 8 of 11 listed substance classes (mean 3.37, SD 2.19), past-year use 0 to 7 (mean 1.57); lifetime use of 0 to 3 of four psychedelics listed (MDMA, LSD, ketamine, psilocybin; mean 0.77), past-year 0 to 3 (mean 0.23).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one session).
sample.selection_effects: One site; recruitment not described; 29 of 30 White and 25 of 30 men. The authors note that more articulate or temperamentally open veterans may be overrepresented and that one BIPOC participant limits generalizability. Saturation is asserted from the sample size (9-17 interviews usually suffice) rather than assessed in these data.

exposure.measurement: Self-report: yes/no lifetime and past-year use of alcohol, cannabis, cocaine, amphetamine, MDMA, LSD, ketamine, opiates, sedatives, inhalants and psilocybin; summed as counts. No quantities or frequencies.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable to the participants. The vignette (Appendix) describes the treatment as several preparatory meetings with the people who would sit with the patient during the drug's effects, three sessions with MDMA, and later sessions to discuss the experience; no doses are given.
exposure.polysubstance: Counts of substances ever used and used in the past year were used as correlates of the codes.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported.

comparison.controls: None (qualitative design). Comparisons are correlations between codes and participant characteristics.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Participants' own prior knowledge of MDMA-AT was not asked; 'familiarity' was rated by coders from the transcripts.

outcomes.instruments: Story-completion vignette with five open prompts (Appendix); PCL-5 (Cronbach's alpha 0.86, McDonald's omega 0.85); PHQ-9 (alpha 0.53, omega indeterminate); 43 codes generated top-down from the prompts and bottom-up from the responses and defined in Table 1; coder-rated willingness and familiarity (0-100).
outcomes.validity_norms: Inter-rater agreement: Cohen's kappa 0.65 to 1.00 across codes, with four codes below conventional reliability (reported anyway); Kendall's tau between raters 0.76 (familiarity) and 0.77 (willingness).
outcomes.operationalization: A theme is a code present in at least 3 of the 30 stories (27 themes). 'Wrong information' is a statement about MDMA treatment given as fact that the coders judged clearly incorrect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Codes were correlated with willingness, familiarity, story length, lifetime and past-year drug use, PCL-5, PHQ-9 and demographic variables; 'given the number of analyses' only Kendall's tau values above |0.30| are reported, without p-values. n_outcomes_tested counts the codes defined.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable in the usual sense; the coders were authors who also generated the codes, and the interviewer (CH) helped generate the initial codes. No blinding of coders to participant characteristics is reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive frequencies (Table 1) and Kendall's tau values (Table 2) without p-values or intervals; for example willingness with familiarity 0.431, willingness with the code 'Skeptical' -0.699, story length with asking about booster sessions 0.499.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published protocol is mentioned; IRB approval at the Stratton VA Medical Center.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists 27 themes and the two ratings although 43 codes were defined; two codes used in Table 2 and the text (Skeptical, Microdosing) are not defined in Table 1, and the PHQ-9 correlations given in the text are not in Table 2 (see reporting issues). The authors state that they report all details because the project is exploratory.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the sample size is justified by published saturation estimates, not by an assessment of saturation in these data.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Hope came up in 20 of 30 stories (18 with reasonable positive hopes, 2 alluding to little hope); stories asked about side effects (19), the rationale for the treatment (15), the shortcomings of other treatments (14), subjective effects (13) and addictive potential (12); a third raised continuity of care (10). Coder-rated willingness averaged 69.5 of 100 and familiarity 40.08. Therapist abuse was mentioned in 1 story, microdosing and sitters in 4 each; 4 stories stated clearly wrong information about the treatment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and most of the discussion stay close to these counts. Two statements go beyond them: the closing sentence says the results suggest that targeted information can increase veterans' understanding, although no information was given or tested and although the Discussion had concluded that targeted information seems less necessary than brief, broad psychoeducation (p. 6, 3rd paragraph; p. 8), and the Discussion states that the FDA's 2024 rejection 'explicitly cited weaknesses in safety documentation and reporting of adverse events' with no source (p. 6). The vignette itself opens with a research project suggesting that MDMA helps, and one prompt asks about hopes; the authors acknowledge that the prompts may have created a demand for hope or optimism. The Discussion also recommends materials that emphasize that the treatment helped people with PTSD who did not respond to other interventions (p. 7, 5th paragraph), an efficacy statement without a citation.

timeline.event: MAPP1 (Mitchell et al., 2021), cited in the Introduction for a between-group effect size of d = 0.91.
MAPP2 (Mitchell et al., 2023), cited for d = 0.70 and for a more diverse sample.

FDA advisory committee meeting and rejection of the application, described in the Introduction from news reports (Jacobs, 2024; Jarow, 2024a, 2024b) and a JAMA piece (Marks, 2024), none read for this card.
This study (received January 2025; published online October 2025).

replication.where_it_stands: A first exploratory study at one site. The authors propose a survey built from these themes, in larger and more diverse samples, as the next step.

funding.funder: The authors report no funding for this work; it used resources and facilities of the Samuel S. Stratton VA Medical Center, Albany, New York.
funding.declared_conflicts: No potential conflict of interest was reported by the authors.
funding.affiliations_note: Mitch Earleywine: University at Albany, SUNY; Caitlin Holley and Stacey Farmer: Albany Stratton VA Medical Center; Henry MacConnel: Mount Sinai Hospital, New York. The interviewer (CH) works at the VA medical center where the participants receive care; the paper does not describe her relationship to the participants. Earleywine's earlier studies of the credibility of psychedelic and ketamine treatments are cited (Earleywine, Altman and De Leo, 2022; Low and Earleywine, 2022, 2024; Kamilar-Britt, Gordis and Earleywine, 2023).

what_would_settle_it: For how common these concerns are: a survey of a large, diverse sample of veterans with PTSD, recruited by a stated method, with items built from these themes. For the background statements on the trials and the FDA: the trial reports and the FDA's own documents, not this paper.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: Indirect story completion suits an exploration of attitudes that people may not state about themselves; the vignette and prompts are printed in full.
One VA site; recruitment and refusals unreported; almost all White and mostly men; saturation asserted from the literature rather than assessed.

Recorded and transcribed; but the vignette opens with a favourable research finding and one prompt asks about hopes, which the authors acknowledge may create a demand for optimism; in trying to avoid stereotypes, the vignette did not emphasize the blissful side of the subjective effects.

The interviewer works at the hospital where the participants receive care and helped generate the codes; no reflexive account of interviewer or coders' views, although the first author has published on the credibility of psychedelic treatments.
IRB approval at the Stratton VA Medical Center and informed consent; data shared on request under VA policy.

Several coders with kappa reported (0.65 to 1.00) and four codes below conventional reliability kept; many correlations with no p-values or correction; codes missing from Table 1; text and tables disagree in places; codes are declared orthogonal because chi-square tests gave no p < .001 (p. 3), an unusual criterion among many tests, and Table 2 shows no code-code correlations to support the Discussion's statement that the codes did not correlate with one another.
Frequencies and an example quotation for each theme; but the inconsistencies between text and tables, and the closing inference about targeted information, are not grounded in the data.
The authors state the limits plainly: one BIPOC participant, possibly more articulate or open veterans, civilians may differ.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a qualitative study with the editors' qualitative checklist (METHODS §5.3). The design suits the question and the authors are candid about its limits, but recruitment is undescribed, the vignette and prompts lean toward hope, and the reporting of codes and correlations is inconsistent. The paper may be cited for which concerns these 30 veterans voiced (side effects, rationale, addictive potential, continuity of care) and how rarely therapist misconduct came up; it is not evidence on how common those concerns are, and its statements about the trials and the FDA decision are second-hand background (news reports) or unreferenced, to be cited, if at all, only as what this paper says.

key_findings.finding: Thirty veteran patients took part (25 men, 5 women; 29 White, 1 of African descent), aged 30-77 (mean 51.03, SD 14.49); all reported a previous diagnosis of, and treatment for, PTSD. Education: some college 14, college graduate 10, graduate degree 4, some high school 1, high school diploma 1.
PCL-5 scores ranged 19-65 (mean 43.67, SD 10.91); 26 of 30 were above the 31-33 range recommended for intervention; alpha 0.86. PHQ-9 ranged 8-21 (mean 14.70, SD 3.74), with alpha 0.53.
key_findings.locator: Measures › PTSD symptom severity; Depressive symptom severity (left column)

key_findings.finding: Coding produced 43 codes, of which 4 did not reach conventional reliability; Cohen's kappa ranged 0.65 to 1.00. Twenty-seven themes appeared in at least 3 of the 30 stories. Only one participant mentioned therapist abuse; four mentioned microdosing and four sitters.

Frequencies of the commonest codes: hope 20 (67%), side effects 19 (63%), rationale for the treatment 15 (50%), shortcomings of other treatments 14 (46%), subjective effects 13 (43%), addictive potential 12 (40%), continuity of care 10 (33%), impact on psychosocial function 9 (30%), difficulty of the experience 9 (30%); retraumatization 6 (20%); stigma 7 (23%); wrong information 4 (13%); concern about drug tests 4 (13%); access to VA services 3 (10%).
key_findings.note: Hope's 20 (67%) counts 18 stories with reasonable positive hopes and 2 that allude to having little hope (Table 1's definition).

key_findings.finding: Coder-rated willingness to try the treatment ranged 15-100 (mean 69.5, SD 21.21) and familiarity with it 0-90 (mean 40.08, SD 28.73); the two correlated at 0.431 (Kendall's tau).
key_findings.locator: Results › Codes (p. 3, right column, continued on p. 5, left column); Results › Covariation (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: Correlations above |0.30| (Table 2): longer stories more often mentioned booster sessions (0.499), ongoing maintenance (0.468), triggering of drug problems (0.451) and shortcomings of other treatments (0.405); willingness correlated with retraumatization -0.425 and with skepticism -0.699; familiarity with skepticism -0.376 and with side effects -0.384; PCL-5 with the view that veterans are reluctant to try new treatments 0.344. No p-values are given.
Background statement about the phase 3 trials: in MAPP1 and MAPP2, MDMA-AT produced large between-group effect sizes on CAPS-5 (d = 0.91 and d = 0.70), citing Mitchell et al. (2021, 2023).
key_findings.note: Second-hand; to be checked against the trial reports (other first reader). The reference list gives volume, issue and pages for both trials that differ from Crossref (reporting issue 5).

key_findings.finding: Background statement about the FDA: the FDA rejected the application (Marks, 2024) after a split vote of an independent advisory committee, whose concerns, as reported by news sources (Jacobs, 2024; Jarow, 2024a, 2024b), included maintaining the blind given MDMA's psychoactive effects, whether the long-term safety data were sufficient, ethical concerns about therapist behaviour during trials, the difficulty of separating the effects of MDMA from the accompanying psychotherapy, and generalizability given the homogeneity of the samples.
key_findings.note: Second-hand, from news reports and a JAMA piece; no vote counts are given.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion states that the FDA's 2024 rejection of the new drug application explicitly cited weaknesses in safety documentation and in the reporting of adverse events; no source is given for this statement.

Misconceptions in the stories: at least one veteran seemed to confuse the duration of MDMA's effects with ketamine's, one questioned how an illicit drug could work as a prescription, one believed MDMA would remove the need to discuss traumatic events, and one thought the treatment required self-injection.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the stimuli may create demands despite the indirect method; the vignette did not emphasize the blissful side of the subjective effects; the prompt about hopes may create a demand for optimism; one BIPOC participant; more articulate or open veterans may be overrepresented; civilians may differ.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs (right column; the 9th continues on p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests: no funding; work supported with resources and facilities of the Samuel S. Stratton VA Medical Center; no potential conflict of interest reported.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 defines 27 themes and the two ratings, although 43 codes are reported; two codes that appear in Table 2 and in the text, 'Skeptical' and 'Microdosing', are not defined in Table 1, although microdosing was mentioned by 4 participants, above the threshold of 3 used for themes. Table 1's note says that capitalized codes are those in Table 2, but Table 2 also lists codes not capitalized in Table 1 (for example Side Effects, Neophobic, Difficulty).
reporting_issues.consequence: The full code list cannot be reconstructed; the counts of themes and codes do not reconcile.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says lifetime drug use increased with 'Wrong Information' (0.339) and 'Microdosing' (0.313), but Table 2 places 0.339 for Wrong Information under current (past-year) drug use and 0.313 for Microdosing under lifetime use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text and table disagree on which drug-use measure correlated with wrong information.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports correlations of PHQ-9 depression scores with 'Neophobic' (0.315), 'Retrauma' (0.356) and 'Hope' (0.427), but Table 2, headed as listing all correlations above |0.30| among codes and key variables, has no PHQ-9 column and no row for Hope. The Discussion also lists treatment-outcome research among the codes linked to story length, while Table 2's word-count column has ongoing maintenance but no outcome-rate code.
reporting_issues.consequence: Correlations given only in the text cannot be checked against the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Rater agreement for the willingness and familiarity ratings is given as Kendall's tau 0.76 and 0.77 in Coding, and as kappa above 0.75 in Results; percentages in Table 1 are rounded inconsistently (14 of 30 printed as 46% and 8 of 30 as 26%, but 20 of 30 as 67% and 5 of 30 as 17%; editors' calculation: 46.7%, 26.7%, 66.7%, 16.7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages should be recomputed from the counts if cited.

reporting_issues.issue: In the reference list, MAPP1 is given as Nature Medicine 27 (5):720-28 and MAPP2 as 29 (9):2020-29 with 'double-blind' in its title; the Crossref records used by this project give 27(6):1025-1033 and 29(10):2473-2480, and MAPP2's title as 'a randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial'. The author lists also differ from Crossref's (Doblin is listed third for MAPP1; Lake and Sherwood appear among MAPP2's authors).
reporting_issues.consequence: The trial effect sizes quoted (d = 0.91 and 0.70) should be taken from the trial reports, not from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes 'a review of 10 trials' showing pre/post differences and lower dropout (Tedesco et al., 2021), but the reference listed under that name is a preliminary discourse analysis of therapeutic change in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement is not supported by the reference as listed; not to be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the FDA's rejection explicitly cited weaknesses in safety documentation and adverse-event reporting has no source; the FDA's decision letter is not cited, and the sources given for the advisory committee are news reports.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cannot be used as evidence of the FDA's reasons; the regulator's documents are needed.

reporting_issues.issue: Two further background statements carry no citation: that the FDA granted MDMA-AT breakthrough status in 2017 (p. 1, Introduction, 2nd paragraph) and that the treatment helped people with PTSD who did not respond to other interventions (p. 7, Discussion, 5th paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither is citable from this paper.

design_detail: Retraction note, not a study (Psychopharmacology vol. 241, p. 2403, November 2024 issue; published online 10 August 2024; open access, CC BY), retracting Feduccia, Jerome, Mithoefer and Holland, 'Discontinuation of medications classified as reuptake inhibitors affects treatment response of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy' (Psychopharmacology 238:581-588; published online 21 November 2020). Two short paragraphs, no data. Read on the publisher's page (link.springer.com, reached through doi.org) in the app's browser; the Crossref records of the notice and of the retracted article were read in the same tab. Card design 'narrative-review' is the schema's closest category for an editorial notice. Reference id assigned by this reader (first author in Crossref plus year); the reference record is to be built by the editor from the Crossref line added to the cache.
can_establish: That Psychopharmacology retracted this article on 10 August 2024, the grounds the editors gave, and which authors agreed or disagreed with the retraction.
cannot_establish: What the protocol violations at the MP4 site were, how much of the article's data came from that site, or whether its findings would change without those data: the notice gives none of these.

Mithoefer, MAPS Public Benefit Corporation, Santa Cruz, CA (Mithoefer also Medical University of South Carolina); Julie Holland, private practice, New York.

what_would_settle_it: For the article's question: the analysis re-run without the MP4 site's data and published with the reasons for the retraction; for the programme as a whole, the regulator's assessment of the site's data.

The notice is the primary record of the retraction and its stated grounds and may be cited for both; it gives no account of the violations and no reanalysis.
