key_findings.locator: Article header; 'The Original Article was published on' line

key_findings.finding: The editors retracted the article after they were informed of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at the MP4 study site by researchers associated with the project. The authors then confirmed that they had known of these violations when they submitted the article but did not disclose this to the journal or remove that site's data from their analysis.

The authors also did not fully declare a potential competing interest: two of the authors are affiliated with MAPS PBC, a subsidiary wholly owned by MAPS. Citing the article's funding declaration, the notice states that MAPS fully funded and provided the MDMA that was used in the trial, and that MAPS PBC organised the trial.
Allison A. Feduccia agrees with the retraction but disagrees with the wording of the notice; Lisa Jerome, Michael C. Mithoefer and Julie Holland disagree with the retraction.

The notice's Crossref record (vol. 241, issue 11, page 2403; online 10 August 2024, print November 2024; authors Feduccia, Jerome, Mithoefer, Holland) carries an update-to link of type 'retraction', from both Retraction Watch and the publisher, dated 10 August 2024, pointing to 10.1007/s00213-020-05710-w; that article's record carries the matching updated-by link, its title now begins 'RETRACTED ARTICLE', and its print issue is given as February 2021 (vol. 238, issue 2, pp. 581-588).

reporting_issues.issue: The notice cites the original as Psychopharmacology (2020) 238:581-588; Crossref gives the print issue of volume 238 as February 2021, the 2020 date being the online date.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the retracted article cannot support claims in any case (METHODS §4.3).

reporting_issues.issue: The notice says 'the authors' confirmed knowing of the violations at submission, without saying which authors; three of the four authors disagree with the retraction.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the notice's wording; do not attribute the confirmation to any named author.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice says the editors were informed of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at the MP4 study site 'by researchers associated with this project', a phrase that can name either who informed the editors or whose conduct it was; the BMJ reads it as conduct by researchers. The notice gives no date for when the editors were informed or for the violations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the notice's own wording and do not resolve the ambiguity. For timing, the sponsor's own public statement of an ethical violation by former MAPS-sponsored investigators is dated 24 May 2019 by its URL (Mahase, 2024, reference 5; not read); whether it concerns MP4 is not stated in the sources read.

design_detail: Matters Arising (Nature Medicine 27:1689–1690, published online 11 October 2021) by three authors, responding to MAPP1 (Mitchell et al., 2021). Seven running-text paragraphs and 10 references, without methods or new data; a third page carries the author contributions and competing interests. Argues that calling MDMA-assisted therapy a breakthrough requires benchmarking against first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies (or testing in people who did not respond to them), patient-relevant outcomes, longer follow-up, larger safety samples and attention to therapy time and cost. Locators count paragraphs from the start of the text on each printed page.
can_establish: What the authors argue about how MAPP1 should be benchmarked, and which comparison figures they cite for it.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy is more or less effective, safe or cost-effective than trauma-focused psychotherapies: the letter adds no data and compares effect sizes and remission rates across trials with different comparators and populations.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The study discussed is MAPP1, 90 adults with severe PTSD.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable; the authors chose the comparison sources (two guidelines, three meta-analyses, two trials and one narrative review).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The psychotherapy effect sizes cited are against wait-list, usual care or other controls in other populations (including complex PTSD and female rape survivors), and the remission figures come from cognitive-therapy trials and a meta-analysis of CBT (described by the letter as for PTSD; its reference title names adult anxiety disorders); no evidence on psychotherapy outcomes in people like MAPP1's participants (severe, chronic, comorbid PTSD, nearly all with earlier therapy) is cited.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. The letter describes MAPP1's therapy: three 90-minute preparatory sessions, three 8-hour MDMA sessions each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions, two therapists throughout (p. 1689, 6th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not discussed.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: The letter's benchmark: first-line trauma-focused psychotherapies (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR, trauma-focused CBT), compared through effect sizes and remission rates from other trials.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: standardized mean differences on PTSD symptoms; remission or loss of diagnosis; adverse effects; therapy time; cost-effectiveness.
outcomes.operationalization: No outcomes of its own.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the letter does not discuss MAPP1's blinding.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed. Cited (p. 1689): MAPP1 SMD 0.91 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.37); sertraline 0.51 (0.38 to 0.64), paroxetine 0.36 (0.28 to 0.49) and trauma-focused psychotherapies 0.83 (0.69 to 0.97) against control (Lee et al., 2016); EMDR 2.07 (1.44 to 2.70) and trauma-focused CBT 1.46 (1.05 to 1.87) against wait-list (Mavranezouli et al., 2020); in complex PTSD against usual care, CBT 0.90 (0.68 to 1.11), exposure 1.05 (0.58 to 1.52) and EMDR 1.26 (interval printed as 0.512.01) (Karatzias et al., 2019); post-treatment remission of about 46% to over 70% with two versions of cognitive therapy (Ehlers et al., 2014) and about 53% (45% to 61%) in a meta-analysis the letter describes as of CBT for PTSD (its reference title, Springer et al., 2018, names adult anxiety disorders); at long-term follow-up only 22.2% (cognitive processing therapy) and 17.5% (prolonged exposure) still had a diagnosis (Resick et al., 2012).
analysis.selective_reporting: The letter cites MAPP1's 33% remission (MDMA arm, completers) but not its 67% loss of diagnosis or the placebo arm's 5% remission, and sets MAPP1's effect against an active control beside psychotherapy effects against wait-list or usual care.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A methodological argument: a breakthrough claim needs comparison with first-line psychotherapies or tests in people who did not respond to them, patient-relevant outcomes, mid- and long-term follow-up, and larger, longer safety evaluation; the supporting figures come from other trials and populations. The editors' check of the therapy time is consistent: 3 × 90 + 3 × 480 + 9 × 90 minutes = 2,520 minutes, equal to 28 sessions of 90 or 42 of 60 minutes.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter says psychological interventions “attain similar or elevated symptom reduction compared with that due to MDMA-assisted psychotherapy” and that remission rates are higher for several first-line treatments (p. 1689, 3rd and 4th paragraphs); both are cross-trial comparisons in which MAPP1's effect is relative to placebo plus the same intensive therapy, whereas the psychotherapy effects are relative to wait-list, usual care or other controls in different populations. It states that MDMA's abuse potential and adverse effects are substantial even with limited use, citing one narrative review (p. 1689, 5th paragraph). It does not discuss MAPP1's blinding or expectancy, its adverse-event recording or its use of completer denominators.

timeline.event: MAPP1, the trial discussed.
Reply by the MAPP1 authors: comparison with psychotherapies is not part of a regulatory phase 3 programme; pragmatic studies should be done.
MAPP2 again compared MDMA with placebo plus the same therapy; no benchmark against a first-line psychotherapy.

replication.where_it_stands: The benchmark the letter asks for has not been done in the sources read: both phase 3 trials compared MDMA with placebo plus the same therapy, and Brett & Bynum (2025) found no randomized trial with a psychotherapy comparator.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests (Competing interests, third page of the PDF).
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, NTNU, and St. Olav's Hospital, Trondheim (Halvorsen); CHU Rennes, INSERM CIC 1414, University of Rennes (Naudet); Department of Brain and Behavioral Sciences, University of Pavia (Cristea). J.Ø.H. and I.A.C. conceptualized the arguments and J.Ø.H. wrote the first draft. None of the 10 references is by the authors.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial comparing MDMA-assisted therapy with a first-line trauma-focused psychotherapy of matched therapist time, or testing it in people who did not respond to an adequate course of such therapy, with blinded assessment, quality of life and at least 12 months of follow-up.

domains.note: A letter; sources chosen by the authors, no search.

The cited meta-analyses and trials are not appraised, and the different control conditions and populations behind the effect sizes and remission rates are not discussed, although the comparison depends on them.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 10 references is by the authors.
The need for benchmarking is argued as principle; the statement that MDMA's abuse potential and adverse effects are substantial even with limited use rests on one narrative review.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how MDMA-assisted therapy compares with first-line psychotherapies
domains.note: Under-represented: that MAPP1's comparison arm received the same intensive therapy; dropout and non-response with trauma-focused psychotherapies; and MAPP1's blinding problem, which bears on its effect size and is not raised.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a commentary (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the worst domains. The letter is a clear statement of the benchmarking argument and can be cited for that argument and for its description of MAPP1's therapy time (which the editors' arithmetic confirms). Its comparative effect sizes and remission rates are cross-trial figures against different controls and should not be cited as evidence that psychotherapies are as effective as or more effective than MDMA-assisted therapy.

key_findings.finding: The authors argue that a treatment labelled a breakthrough should be evaluated against first-line psychological interventions, or in prespecified subgroups of people who do not improve with them, because guidelines (American Psychological Association; NICE) recommend trauma-focused psychotherapies (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR, trauma-focused CBT) as first-line treatments for PTSD.

Comparative figures cited: MAPP1 SMD 0.91 (95% CI 0.44 to 1.37), which MAPP1 contrasted with the modest effects of medicines, given here from a meta-analysis (Lee et al., 2016) as sertraline 0.51 (0.38 to 0.64) and paroxetine 0.36 (0.28 to 0.49), with trauma-focused psychotherapies at 0.83 (0.69 to 0.97) against control in the same meta-analysis; EMDR 2.07 (1.44 to 2.70) and trauma-focused CBT 1.46 (1.05 to 1.87) against wait-list; in complex PTSD against usual care, CBT 0.90 (0.68 to 1.11), exposure 1.05 (0.58 to 1.52) and EMDR 1.26.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: Remission: against MAPP1's 33% post-treatment remission, the letter cites about 46% to over 70% for two versions of cognitive therapy, about 53% (95% CI 45% to 61%) in a meta-analysis of CBT, and long-term follow-up in which 22.2% (cognitive processing therapy) and 17.5% (prolonged exposure) of an intent-to-treat sample of female rape survivors still had the diagnosis.
key_findings.note: Editors' arithmetic: the 22.2% and 17.5% of Resick et al. still meeting criteria mean 77.8% and 82.5% without the diagnosis at long-term follow-up in an intent-to-treat sample; the like-for-like MAPP1 figure is loss of diagnosis (61% of the dosed MDMA arm, by the editors' calculation), not its 33% remission among completers.

key_findings.finding: Adverse effects: serious adverse effects of MDMA were rare in MAPP1, but rare events are hard to evaluate in small phase 3 trials without long-term follow-up; citing one review, the authors call MDMA's abuse potential and adverse effects substantial even with limited use and ask regulators to rely on more than a single small study for a post-approval risk-management plan.

Therapy time: MAPP1's psychotherapy amounted to the equivalent of 28 sessions of 90 minutes or 42 of 60 minutes, with two therapists in every session, against 8 to 16 sessions of 60 to 90 minutes with one therapist (or up to 20 hours) for first-line psychotherapies, half or less.
key_findings.note: Editors' check: 3 × 90 + 3 × 480 + 9 × 90 = 2,520 minutes, which is 28 × 90 and 42 × 60.

key_findings.finding: What the authors ask for: a phase 3 programme with large pragmatic studies and adequate comparators such as trauma-focused psychotherapies, or tests in rigorously prespecified subgroups who did not respond to adequate courses of them; patient-relevant outcomes such as quality of life; mid- and long-term follow-up; and safety investigation in larger samples over longer periods.
The authors declare no competing interests.

reporting_issues.issue: The confidence interval for EMDR in complex PTSD is printed as 0.512.01, without a separator (presumably 0.51 to 2.01).
reporting_issues.consequence: Trivial typesetting error.

reporting_issues.issue: The remission comparison sets MAPP1's 33% (14 of 42 completers on MDMA, its strictest outcome) against figures from other populations and definitions, including a meta-analysis that the letter describes as of CBT for PTSD but whose title (reference 8, Springer et al., 2018) concerns adult anxiety disorders, so whether its 53% is a PTSD figure cannot be checked from the letter.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison cannot show that remission is higher with first-line psychotherapies in people like MAPP1's participants.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says the cost-effectiveness of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy had not yet been formally evaluated, although MAPP1 itself cites a 2020 cost-effectiveness analysis (its reference 11) and the trial authors' reply says an evaluation based on the phase 3 design was under review.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not to be cited for the absence of economic evaluations.

design_detail: Retraction note, not a study (Psychopharmacology vol. 241, p. 2407, November 2024 issue; published online 10 August 2024; open access, CC BY), retracting the article by Jerome, Feduccia, Wang, Hamilton, Yazar-Klosinski, Emerson, Mithoefer and Doblin reporting long-term follow-up outcomes of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD in a longitudinal pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (Psychopharmacology 237:2485-2497; published online 4 June 2020; full title in Crossref). Two short paragraphs, no data. Read on the publisher's page (link.springer.com, reached through doi.org) in the app's browser; the Crossref records of the notice and of the retracted article were read in the same tab. Card design 'narrative-review' is the schema's closest category for an editorial notice. Reference id assigned by this reader (first author in Crossref plus year); the reference record is to be built by the editor from the Crossref line added to the cache.
can_establish: That Psychopharmacology retracted this pooled long-term follow-up analysis of six phase 2 trials on 10 August 2024, the grounds the editors gave, and which authors agreed, disagreed or did not respond.
cannot_establish: What the protocol violations at the MP4 site were, which of the six trials the site belonged to, how much of the pooled data came from it, or whether the long-term findings would change without those data: the notice gives none of these.

interpretation_gap.claimed: The notice claims nothing beyond its grounds and the authors' positions. It speaks of 'this trial', although the article, by its title, pooled six phase 2 trials.

timeline.event: The article is published online (4 June 2020; print issue August 2020 per Crossref).
This retraction note (10 August 2024), issued the same day as the notes for two other phase 2 analyses from the same programme (Feduccia et al., 2024; Mithoefer et al., 2024).
The BMJ reports the three retractions (Mahase, 2024).

replication.where_it_stands: Retracted. Under METHODS §4.3 the retracted article cannot support any claim, including claims about long-term outcomes after MDMA-assisted therapy; this notice may be cited for the fact of the retraction and its stated grounds.

funding.funder: Not applicable (notice). The notice states, from the article's funding declaration, that MAPS fully funded and provided the MDMA used and that MAPS PBC organised the trial.
funding.declared_conflicts: Per the notice, the authors did not fully declare a potential competing interest: several of the authors are affiliated with either MAPS or MAPS PBC, a subsidiary wholly owned by MAPS.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliations listed with the notice: Lisa Jerome, Allison A. Feduccia, Julie B. Wang and Amy Emerson, MAPS Public Benefit Corporation(s), Santa Cruz, CA; Scott Hamilton, Stanford School of Medicine; Berra Yazar-Klosinski and Rick Doblin, Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, Santa Cruz, CA; Michael C. Mithoefer, Medical University of South Carolina.

what_would_settle_it: For the article's question: the long-term follow-up re-analysed without the MP4 site's data and published; for the programme as a whole, the regulator's assessment of the site's data.

domains.note: Not a review: the notice reports the editors' own decision on one article, so nothing is selected.
The notice does not say how the violations were established, which of the six trials the site belonged to, or how much of the pooled data came from it.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Cites only the retracted article.
States the decision and its grounds without speculation.

domains.domain: Balance of views on the retraction (the authors' positions)
domains.note: Records which authors agree, which disagree and which did not respond.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to retraction notices; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used as the closest available, its domains read as questions about the notice as a source. The notice is the primary record of the retraction and its stated grounds and may be cited for both; it gives no account of the violations and no reanalysis.

key_findings.finding: Retraction note published 10 August 2024 (Psychopharmacology 241, p. 2407; issue date November 2024) for the original article published on 4 June 2020, cited in the notice as Psychopharmacology (2020) 237:2485-2497, doi 10.1007/s00213-020-05548-2.
key_findings.locator: Article header; 'The Original Article was published on' line

key_findings.finding: The editors retracted the article after they were informed of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at the MP4 study site by researchers associated with the project. The authors then confirmed that they had known of these violations when they submitted the article but did not disclose this to the journal or remove that site's data from their analysis.

The authors also did not fully declare a potential competing interest: several of the authors are affiliated with either MAPS or MAPS PBC, a subsidiary wholly owned by MAPS. As the article's funding declaration stated, MAPS fully funded and provided the MDMA used, and MAPS PBC organised the trial.

Allison A. Feduccia agrees with the retraction but disagrees with the wording of the notice; Michael C. Mithoefer, Lisa Jerome, Berra Yazar-Klosinski and Rick Doblin disagree with the retraction; the remaining authors did not respond to the publisher's correspondence (editors' reading of the author list: Julie B. Wang, Scott Hamilton and Amy Emerson).
key_findings.locator: Retraction note text, 2nd paragraph; author list

key_findings.finding: The notice's Crossref record (vol. 241, issue 11, page 2407; online 10 August 2024, print November 2024; eight authors, Jerome first) carries an update-to link of type 'retraction', from both Retraction Watch and the publisher, dated 10 August 2024, pointing to 10.1007/s00213-020-05548-2; that article's record carries the matching updated-by link, its title now begins 'RETRACTED ARTICLE', and its print issue is given as August 2020 (vol. 237, issue 8, pp. 2485-2497).

reporting_issues.issue: The notice refers to 'this trial' and to data generated by the MP4 site, although the article, by its title, is a pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials; it does not say which of them included the MP4 site or how much of the pooled data came from it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the problem in the pooled long-term data cannot be judged from the notice.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice says 'the authors' confirmed knowing of the violations at submission, without saying which authors; four authors disagree with the retraction and three did not respond.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the notice's wording; do not attribute the confirmation to any named author.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice says the editors were informed of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at the MP4 study site 'by researchers associated with this project', a phrase that can name either who informed the editors or whose conduct it was; the BMJ reads it as conduct by researchers. The notice gives no date for when the editors were informed or for the violations.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the notice's own wording and do not resolve the ambiguity. For timing, the sponsor's own public statement of an ethical violation by former MAPS-sponsored investigators is dated 24 May 2019 by its URL (Mahase, 2024, reference 5; not read); whether it concerns MP4 is not stated in the sources read.

design_detail: 'Insights' commentary in European Neuropsychopharmacology (vol. 70, 2023, pp. 19-20; received 8 January, revised 31 January, accepted 2 February 2023) by Santiago Madero (Hospital Clinic of Barcelona, IDIBAPS) and Oscar D. Alvarez (Parc Sanitari Sant Joan de Deu), on the premise, promise and challenges of MDMA-assisted therapy (MDMA-AT) for PTSD. Six paragraphs of running text (three beginning on p. 19, three on p. 20; paragraph numbers in the locators count from the start of the piece), 10 references, no tables, figures or new data. Written after the first phase 3 trial was published and before the second was (the second is described from the sponsor's top-line announcement).
can_establish: What two Spanish clinicians, one of them a principal investigator in the sponsor's trials, argued in early 2023 about MAPP1, the sponsor's regulatory plans, the risks of MDMA-assisted therapy, how it should be delivered, and its cost-effectiveness.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy works or is safe: no data are presented, the first trial is summarized in one sentence without numbers beyond 'as much as two thirds', and the safety, regulatory and economic statements are unreferenced or second-hand.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary). The trial cited (Mitchell et al., 2021) is described as the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site phase 3 trial, in patients with severe PTSD; no sample size is given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Sources chosen to support the argument: the first trial, the sponsor's treatment manual (Mithoefer, 2017), a review by Sessa, Higbed and Nutt (2019), a favourable modelling study (Avanceña et al., 2022) and a favourable review (Gonda et al., 2022). Two critical pieces (Yaden et al., 2022; Hall and Humphreys, 2022) are cited in one paragraph without detail. The second phase 3 trial is described from the sponsor's announcement, without a reference.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (commentary).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not given. The piece describes MDMA-AT as sessions with MDMA, in an optimal setting with non-directive therapists, preceded by preparation and followed by integration sessions (p. 20, 4th paragraph); no doses or numbers of sessions are stated.
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. The trial's comparison is given as placebo, without saying that both arms received the same therapy.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed.

outcomes.instruments: CAPS-5 is named as the trial's measure; no scores are given.
outcomes.operationalization: 'No longer meeting criteria for PTSD after completing treatment' is given for 'as much as two thirds' of the MDMA arm, without a count, a week or the corresponding figure for the placebo arm; 'after completing treatment' points to completers.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not discussed: blinding, expectancy and functional unblinding are not mentioned.

analysis.effect_sizes: None from the trial, beyond 'as much as two thirds' of the MDMA arm no longer meeting PTSD criteria. The economic figures are second-hand model outputs (Avanceña et al., 2022): with access for 25-75% of eligible patients with chronic and severe PTSD over 10 years, 43,000 to 106,000 deaths averted, 3.3-8.2 million quality-adjusted life years gained and 109 to 266 billion US dollars in net savings for the US health-care system.
analysis.selective_reporting: The safety statement (no adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation) has no citation of its own, repeats the trial's abstract and does not say how such events were assessed. The second phase 3 trial is reported only as announced top-line results meeting primary and secondary endpoints, without a reference. The model's assumptions (comparator, drug price) are not mentioned.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: No data. The piece summarizes the first trial's direction of effect in one sentence (a significant CAPS-5 reduction compared with placebo; up to two thirds of the MDMA arm no longer meeting PTSD criteria) and relays the sponsor's announcements about the second trial and its regulatory plans.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors write that approval by the FDA was very likely within the next year and a half (p. 19) and that the phase 2 and 3 trials have shown MDMA might revolutionize PTSD treatment, with benefits beyond all existing pharmacotherapies (p. 20, citing a review); by August 2024 the FDA had rejected the application (Mahase, 2024, published 13 August 2024). The safety profile is called favourable because the trial did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation, in a sentence without a citation of its own that repeats the trial's abstract, and without saying how these were recorded. The piece's account of the first trial (randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site; a significant attenuation in CAPS-5 score against placebo; no such adverse events) follows that abstract without appraisal. Modelled projections of deaths averted and money saved are presented as what an analysis shows. The final paragraph warns of a hype bubble and of debate over lowered standards in major journals publishing psychedelic trials, without applying either concern to the trials it describes.

timeline.event: FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation for the sponsor's programme, based on pooled phase 2 data, as stated by the commentary.
MAPP1, the first phase 3 trial (Mitchell et al., 2021).
Avanceña, Kahn and Marseille (2022), modelling study of expanded access to MDMA-assisted therapy in the USA, cited for the economic figures (not read).
This commentary (accepted 2 February 2023), citing the second phase 3 trial only from top-line results.
MAPP2, the second phase 3 trial, published later in 2023 (Mitchell et al., 2023).
The BMJ reports that the FDA rejected the application and that Psychopharmacology retracted three phase 2 analyses (Mahase, 2024).

replication.where_it_stands: The forecast of FDA approval within about 18 months of early 2023 was not borne out (Mahase, 2024). The European phase 3 trial planned for 2024 and a possible EMA approval from 2026 are forecasts whose outcome is not covered by the sources read here.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: O.A. is a principal investigator for the phase IIB and III clinical trials in the MAPS-sponsored MDMA-AT trials for PTSD and reports no other conflicts; S.M. reports none.
funding.affiliations_note: Santiago Madero: University Hospital Clinic of Barcelona, Psychiatry and Psychology Department, Bipolar and Depressive Disorders Unit, IDIBAPS; Oscar D. Alvarez: Parc Sanitari Sant Joan de Deu Hospital, Sant Joan de Deu Research Foundation. One author is an investigator in the trial programme whose results the piece summarizes. The economic figures come from a model whose authors include Elliot Marseille, who in 2025 declares consulting fees from MAPS PBC/Lykos (Marseille and Mitchell, 2025, p. 3). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: The peer-reviewed trial reports read in full, with blinding, expectancy and adverse-event recording examined; independent replication; the regulator's own review documents; and, for the economic claims, models that use a standard-of-care comparator and realistic prices, with their assumptions published.

domains.note: A short commentary; no search, and sources chosen to support the argument.
Neither the trial nor the cost model is appraised; the safety statement and the second trial's results are unreferenced.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the 10 references is by the authors; one author's role as a trial investigator is declared (see funding).
Regulatory forecasts, a mechanistic metaphor (the helioscope) and modelled projections sit beside the trial result as if of the same standing.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the benefits and risks of MDMA-assisted therapy (limitations of the trials under-represented)
domains.note: Risks, therapist training, hype and lowered journal standards are acknowledged, but no specific limitation of the trials is named.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to commentaries (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The piece may be cited for what its authors argued and forecast in early 2023, including their recommendations on certified centres, screening and therapist training. It is not evidence on efficacy, blinding or adverse events, and its economic figures are second-hand model outputs.

key_findings.finding: Lifetime prevalence of PTSD is given as 1.3% to 12% depending on the population studied (Shalev et al., 2017; second-hand).

History as told by the authors: Merck developed MDMA in 1912; Alexander Shulgin resynthesized it in 1976; hundreds of therapists then gave MDMA and saw patients make, in a few sessions, progress that normally took years (no citation); it spread to the night scene as ecstasy; in October 1986 the DEA classified it in Schedule I, which the authors say was done without convincing academic arguments, and research was then hugely restricted.
key_findings.note: Nutt and de Wit (2021, p. 951) date the criminalization to 1985; see reporting issue 3.

key_findings.finding: MAPS has led clinical research of MDMA-AT since the early 2000s; pooled data from all MAPS-sponsored phase 2 trials led to the FDA Breakthrough Therapy designation in 2017 and to multi-site phase 3 trials.
key_findings.locator: 3rd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: MAPP1 (2021), described as the first randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multi-site phase 3 trial in severe PTSD, is said to show a significant reduction in CAPS-5 score compared with placebo, with as much as two thirds of patients in the MDMA arm no longer meeting criteria for PTSD after completing treatment.
key_findings.note: No count, week or placebo-arm figure is given; 'after completing treatment' points to completers, and as a figure for completers two thirds agrees with the 28 of 42 (67%) of MAPP1, while the share of everyone randomized and dosed was 61% (editors' calculation). The sentence follows the wording of the MAPP1 abstract.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that the safety profile of MDMA appears favourable because it did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation. The sentence carries no citation of its own; it follows the sentence citing Mitchell et al. (2021) and repeats almost word for word that trial's abstract. How these events were assessed is not described.

The sponsor had completed the second phase 3 trial (USA, Canada, Israel) and announced positive top-line results meeting its primary and secondary endpoints (no reference); it planned to submit a new drug application in the third quarter of 2023, and the authors judged approval very likely within the next year and a half. MAPS had trained therapists in seven European countries (Netherlands, Czech Republic, Germany, Portugal, Spain, Norway and England) for a phase 3 trial to start in 2024, and EMA approval might follow as early as 2026.

Proposed mechanism and delivery: sessions in an optimal setting with non-directive therapists, preceded by preparation and followed by integration; the pharmacological and subjective effects of MDMA are said to impair the fear response selectively while leaving other cognitive processes relatively spared (Mithoefer, 2017; Sessa et al., 2019); Hasler's 'helioscope' hypothesis (2022) is offered as a model of how psychedelics let people look at what they otherwise could not.

Risks: MDMA-AT has inherent risks, which the authors say increase in recreational settings (abuse potential, triggering of psychiatric disorders, especially in people with pre-existing vulnerabilities such as psychotic disorders). They recommend that after approval administration be limited to certified centres with defined safety screening and a centralized pharmacy, with trained therapists under supervision, and name therapist training as probably the main limit on availability.

Economic figures quoted from a modelling study (Avanceña et al., 2022): increasing access to MDMA-AT to 25-75% of eligible patients with chronic and severe PTSD over 10 years could avert 43,000 to 106,000 deaths, gain 3.3-8.2 million quality-adjusted life years and save 109 to 266 billion US dollars net for the US health-care system.
key_findings.note: Model outputs, second-hand; the model's comparator and price assumptions are not given.

key_findings.finding: The authors write that the phase 2 and 3 findings show MDMA might revolutionize the treatment of PTSD, with benefits beyond all current pharmacotherapies (Gonda et al., 2022), and cite a scientometric analysis showing a trend toward clinical testing of MDMA, psilocybin and ketamine with psychotherapy (Solmi et al., 2022).

They add that psychedelic research appears to be caught in a hype bubble driven largely by media and industry interests (Yaden et al., 2022) and that there has been debate over major medical journals lowering their standards for psychedelic trials (Hall and Humphreys, 2022), a combination they say could prove disastrous unless research keeps the highest ethical and scientific standards.
Declaration of competing interest: O.A. is a principal investigator for the phase IIB and III MAPS-sponsored MDMA-AT trials for PTSD; S.M. declares none.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the trial did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation has no citation of its own; it follows the sentence citing Mitchell et al. (2021) and repeats almost word for word that trial's abstract, so it is the trial authors' own conclusion restated without appraisal, and it does not say how such events were looked for.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cannot be used as evidence on adverse events; the trial report and the critiques of its adverse-event recording are needed. Its wording means no excess over placebo, not absence: MAPP1 recorded suicidality events of special interest in 3 of 46 on MDMA and 5 of 44 on placebo.

reporting_issues.issue: The second phase 3 trial's results are reported from the sponsor's top-line announcement, without a reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the published trial report (Mitchell et al., 2023) instead.

reporting_issues.issue: The commentary dates Schedule I classification of MDMA by the DEA to October 1986; Nutt and de Wit (2021, p. 951) date its criminalization to 1985. Neither cites a scheduling document.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dates of US scheduling should come from the legal-status sources (section 13).

reporting_issues.issue: 'As much as two thirds' of the MDMA arm no longer meeting PTSD criteria after completing treatment is given without a count, a week or the placebo-arm figure; the phrase points to completers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable as a remission or loss-of-diagnosis rate; as a completers' share it is consistent with the trial report (28 of 42), and the between-arm difference and the share of everyone randomized must come from the trial report.

reporting_issues.issue: Modelled projections (deaths averted, quality-adjusted life years, net savings) are presented as what a recent analysis shows, without the model's comparator or price assumptions.
reporting_issues.consequence: These are model outputs, not observed outcomes; see the cost-effectiveness critique (Marseille and Mitchell, 2025) for what such results depend on.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 19-20 (PDFs/MDMA/Madero_2023_PremisePromiseChallenges.pdf): read in full, including the declaration of competing interest and the reference list; both pages rendered.

disagreements.first_pass: No denominator, time point or placebo-arm figure is given; to be checked against the trial report (other first reader).
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 35: confirmed; the note needs one fix: the source does give a time reference, after completing treatment, which points to completers; what it lacks is a count, a week and the placebo-arm figure; two thirds agrees with the completers' 28 of 42.
disagreements.resolution: Checked p. 19, 3rd paragraph and the MAPP1 report (28 of 42 completers). Note corrected.

disagreements.first_pass: The authors write that the safety profile of MDMA appears favourable because the trial did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation; no source is cited and the way these events were assessed is not described.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 35: corrected. 'No source is cited' is literally true of the sentence but misleads: it repeats the MAPP1 abstract's own summary after the sentence citing the trial; its wording means no excess over placebo, not absence.
disagreements.resolution: Checked p. 19, 3rd paragraph against the MAPP1 abstract on the publisher's page: the sentence follows the abstract's wording. Corrected.

disagreements.first_pass: The statement that the trial did not induce adverse events of abuse potential, suicidality or QT prolongation has no citation and does not say how such events were looked for.

design_detail: News article in The BMJ (BMJ 2024;386:q1798, published 13 August 2024; one printed page with 7 references) by Elisabeth Mahase, on the retraction of three MDMA-assisted therapy papers by Psychopharmacology and the FDA's rejection of Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application. Sources cited: the three retraction notices (refs 1-3), a New York Times report (ref 4), a MAPS statement (ref 5), a CBC report (ref 6) and the final summary minutes of the FDA advisory committee meeting of 4 June 2024 (ref 7); company statements are quoted without references. The article has an unheaded opening section (5 paragraphs) and a section headed 'FDA rejects Lykos Therapeutics' application' (7 paragraphs). The PDF's second page is a permissions notice.

cannot_establish: What the FDA's own review found or why it decided as it did (its decision letter and review documents are not cited; the advisory committee minutes are summarized in one sentence without vote counts), or what the protocol violations were (the article relies on press reports for this).

interpretation_gap.claimed: The headline joins the two events ('as FDA rejects'), but the text gives the journal's reasons for the retractions, which concern researchers' conduct at one site and undisclosed interests, not the FDA review, and says only that the retractions came after the decision. Its statement that the retracted research did not form part of the application is introduced with 'reports show' and has no source.

key_findings.finding: Three papers on MDMA-assisted psychotherapy were retracted by Psychopharmacology because of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct by researchers at a study site (article published 13 August 2024).

According to the retraction notices (refs 1-3), the authors were aware of the violations when they submitted the articles but did not disclose them or remove the affected data from their analyses; all three papers related to phase 2 randomized controlled trials of MDMA-assisted therapy and had similar authors.

The notices did not say what the violations were; reports (ref 4, a New York Times article of 12 August 2024; ref 5, a 2019 MAPS statement announcing an ethical violation by former MAPS-sponsored investigators) suggest that an investigator at one study site had an unethical sexual relationship with a trial participant; in a 2018 lawsuit settled out of court the participant said she had been sexually assaulted, and the investigator said the relationship was consensual (ref 6, a CBC report of March 2022).
key_findings.note: Ref 6's title concerns a trial in British Columbia; the article does not name the site, and the notices call it MP4; the sources read do not say whether these are the same site.

key_findings.finding: The journal said some authors had not fully declared competing interests, including that many were affiliated with MAPS or its subsidiary MAPS Public Benefit Corporation, now known as Lykos Therapeutics; MAPS fully funded the trials and provided the MDMA, and Lykos Therapeutics organised them.
key_findings.note: The notices themselves say 'two of the authors' (feduccia_2024) or 'several of the authors' (jerome_2024, mithoefer_2024); see reporting issue 3.

key_findings.finding: The retractions came after the US FDA rejected Lykos Therapeutics' new drug application for MDMA capsules for the treatment of PTSD; no date for the decision is given.

key_findings.finding: According to the final summary minutes of the FDA Psychopharmacologic Drugs Advisory Committee meeting of 4 June 2024 (ref 7, dated 30 July 2024), most committee members did not believe the available data showed the drug was effective in people with PTSD, and all but one said its benefits did not outweigh its risks. No vote counts are given.

design_detail: Commentary in Psychedelics (vol. 2, 2025, article 100002, three pages; received 14 March, revised 13 July, accepted 30 July, available online 5 August 2025; open access, CC BY) by Elliot Marseille (UC Berkeley, Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics) and Jennifer Mitchell (San Francisco VA Medical Center; University of California San Francisco), critiquing the Lykos-funded cost-effectiveness analysis of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD by Stanicic et al. (2024, PLoS One), which was not read. Besides argument, it reports new runs of the authors' own earlier model (Marseille et al., 2020, 2022) as single numbers, without the model's structure, inputs, tables or uncertainty analysis. 13 references. Paragraph numbers in the locators count running-text paragraphs within each printed section.
can_establish: What two authors of earlier cost-effectiveness models of MDMA-assisted therapy, both with declared financial ties to the sponsor, argue about the sponsor-funded analysis: that its comparator, its drug price, its scope of costs and its threshold drive its result.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy is cost-effective: the sponsor's analysis is described rather than reproduced, the authors' new figures are reported without their model or its uncertainty, and none of the sources it uses compares MDMA-assisted therapy with standard treatments in a trial.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (commentary on a modelling study). The analysis critiqued drew its health outcomes and PTSD-care use from trial data, with 17 months of follow-up from MAPP2 and its long-term extension (MPLONG), as the commentary states.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The sponsor's model is compared only with the authors' own models; no economic evaluation by anyone else is cited. Several factual statements rest on news or trade sources (the FDA decision on a CNN report; Lykos's fundraising on a Lucid News article; therapist shortages on a Psychedelic Alpha piece).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (commentary).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Trial and model conditions as the commentary describes them: three MDMA sessions, each with two clinicians for 8 hours, within a course of therapy; the sponsor's model priced the drug at 12,000 US dollars per dose for three doses (36,000 for the drug alone, therapy not included), and costed the whole treatment at 48,376 dollars, against 11,537 dollars in the authors' own earlier analyses (2020 and 2022; the commentary says 'in our study' without saying which) (pp. 1-2). No amounts of MDMA are given.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: The sponsor's model compared MDMA-assisted therapy with the same therapy given with placebo. The authors' own models use standard of care as the comparator, which in their base case carries no new costs and no change in health status (p. 1).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Incremental cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY); time to break even for payers; dominance (lower cost with better health).
outcomes.operationalization: Cost-effectiveness judged against willingness-to-pay thresholds of 150,000 US dollars per QALY (the sponsor's analysis) and about 100,000 (preferred by the authors).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As stated, without intervals: sponsor's model, about 84,000 US dollars per QALY for MDMA-assisted therapy versus placebo-therapy over five years. Authors' model: break-even at 3.8 years in their 2022 analysis at a much lower drug price; about 8.4 years with the sponsor's 36,000-dollar drug cost; 160 dollars per QALY over five years with the drug priced at 10,500 dollars for the course; dominant at any drug cost below 10,320 dollars; a drug price about 12% lower would allow therapists' hourly rate to rise from 147 to 200 dollars.
analysis.selective_reporting: The new model runs are reported without methods, inputs or sensitivity analyses. The sponsor's analysis is credited with trial-based estimates and a documented fall in health-care use without any of its numbers other than the ratio, the threshold and the prices.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Arithmetic and model outputs showing that, in these models, the result depends heavily on the drug's price and on what MDMA-assisted therapy is compared with; no new data.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the sponsor's analysis methodologically rigorous but of limited relevance to decision-makers, and says alternative modelling suggests that at about 10,500 dollars MDMA therapy could be extremely cost-effective, around 160 dollars per QALY, or even cost-saving. Those figures come from the authors' own model, whose base-case comparator brings no new costs and no change in health status (p. 1); the commentary does not say how much of the improvement seen with MDMA-assisted therapy its model credits to the treatment, nor show what happens if standard care itself improves health. It notes that no head-to-head trial against standard treatments exists, yet presents its comparison with standard care as the more accurate one. Neither model, as described, allows for the possibility that the trial effect was inflated by unblinding or expectancy.

timeline.event: Marseille et al. (2015), on alternative approaches to cost-effectiveness thresholds, cited for the weakness of the WHO three-times-GDP heuristic (not read).
Marseille, Kahn, Yazar-Klosinski and Doblin (2020), cost-effectiveness of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD (cited; not read).
Marseille, Mitchell and Kahn (2022), updated cost-effectiveness using findings from a phase 3 trial: break-even for payers at 3.8 years (as stated here; not read).
FDA declines to approve MDMA-assisted therapy in August 2024, as reported by CNN (McPhillips, 2024) and cited here.
Stanicic, Zah, Grbic and De Angelo (2024), the Lykos-funded cost-effectiveness analysis critiqued here (PLoS One; not read).
This commentary (available online 5 August 2025).

replication.where_it_stands: No economic evaluation independent of both the sponsor and the authors of the earlier models is among the sources read for this batch; all the models described come from the sponsor or from authors with declared ties to it.

funding.funder: No funding was received for this commentary.
funding.declared_conflicts: Elliot Marseille has received consulting fees from MAPS PBC/Lykos. Jennifer Mitchell has received research support from MAPS PBC/Lykos.
funding.affiliations_note: Elliot Marseille: UC Berkeley, Collaborative for the Economics of Psychedelics; Jennifer Mitchell: Staff for Research and Development, SFVAMC, and Departments of Neurology and Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, Weill Institute for Neurosciences, University of California San Francisco. The authors critique a rival analysis and offer their own models (2020, 2022; the 2022 model co-authored by both) as the alternative. The second author has the same name and the same affiliations as the first author of the two phase 3 trial reports: the Departments of Neurology and of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences of the University of California San Francisco (MAPP1 and MAPP2, Author information) and the San Francisco VA Medical Center (MAPP2); MAPP1 records MAPS PBC funding for that author during the study. The commentary does not mention a role in the trials, whose effects both the sponsor's and the authors' models take as given. The authors declare that ChatGPT was used to edit the manuscript and to develop responses to reviewers. Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A cost-effectiveness analysis independent of the sponsor and of earlier modellers with ties to it, comparing MDMA-assisted therapy with the evidence-based treatments people with PTSD actually receive (using trial or indirect-comparison estimates for both, with the trials' blinding problems allowed for), counting all health-care costs, publishing its inputs and running probabilistic sensitivity analyses over a range of drug prices; ultimately, a pragmatic trial against standard care that collects costs.

domains.note: A commentary on one analysis; the only alternatives offered are the authors' own models.

The sponsor's analysis is appraised on comparator, price, scope of costs and threshold, and its strengths are acknowledged; the authors' own model is not appraised and its new outputs are unreported in method.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The alternative figures come entirely from the authors' own models (2020, 2022), and the threshold argument cites their own 2015 paper; the second author also has the same name and university departments as the first author of both phase 3 trials whose effects both models take as given (editors' comparison).
New model outputs are given without methods; the motives behind the sponsor's price and the possibility that some patients need fewer MDMA sessions are speculative.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on the cost-effectiveness of MDMA-assisted therapy (uncertainty about the size of the trial effect under-represented)
domains.note: Both the sponsor's and the authors' models take the trials' effects at face value; that unblinding or expectancy might have inflated the effect, which would make the therapy less cost-effective, is not considered.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to commentaries (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The piece may be cited for what the cost-effectiveness question turns on as these critics state it (comparator, drug price, scope of costs, threshold, time horizon) and for its description of the sponsor's analysis, labelled as second-hand. Its own figures are outputs of a model whose inputs are not published here; they are not evidence that MDMA-assisted therapy saves money.

key_findings.finding: The analysis critiqued (Stanicic et al., 2024) was funded by Lykos Therapeutics and appeared after the FDA declined to approve MDMA-assisted therapy in August 2024 (citing a CNN report). The authors name two critical limitations: an inappropriate comparator and a pricing strategy that threatens access.

The sponsor's model compared MDMA-assisted therapy with an identical therapy regimen given with placebo, which the authors call appropriate for regulatory approval but not informative for payers, because people with PTSD usually receive evidence-based psychotherapies (prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, EMDR) or SSRIs (sertraline, paroxetine), not placebo plus the trial's intensive therapy (described in the exposure field).
key_findings.locator: Inappropriate choice of comparator, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: The authors acknowledge that head-to-head trial data against standard treatments are lacking. Their own earlier models used standard of care as comparator; in the base case the comparator carried no new costs and no change in health status, and the whole MDMA treatment cost 11,537 US dollars against 48,376 in the sponsor's model, mainly because of a much lower drug cost; this gave net savings at the five-year horizon.
key_findings.locator: Inappropriate choice of comparator, 2nd paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: The sponsor's analysis reported an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of about 84,000 US dollars per QALY for MDMA versus placebo-therapy, under its threshold of 150,000 dollars per QALY.
key_findings.locator: Inappropriate choice of comparator, 2nd paragraph (p. 1, right column, continued on p. 2, left column)

key_findings.finding: Strengths credited to the sponsor's analysis: health outcomes and PTSD-care use estimated from clinical-trial data rather than the literature, and 17 months of follow-up from the MAPP2 and MPLONG trials; a documented reduction in health-care use among people treated with MDMA. Limitation: only PTSD-specific health-care costs were counted, leaving out emergency, inpatient and comorbidity costs.
key_findings.locator: Methodological strengths despite flawed comparator, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)

key_findings.finding: The authors call the 150,000-dollar threshold defensible but at the high end of values in use, weakly justified by the WHO three-times-GDP heuristic, and say about 100,000 dollars per QALY better reflects consensus; at either threshold, 84,000 dollars per QALY may not convince payers.
key_findings.locator: Methodological strengths despite flawed comparator, 3rd paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: Pricing: the sponsor's model priced MDMA at 36,000 US dollars for the full course of the drug, therapy excluded (the per-dose price is in the exposure field). With this drug cost in the authors' model, payers' break-even moves from 3.8 years (their 2022 analysis, at a much lower price) to about 8.4 years, beyond the average enrolment period of most US health plans. With the drug priced at 10,500 dollars for the course, their model gives 160 dollars per QALY over five years, and below 10,320 dollars treatment is dominant (better health at lower cost).
key_findings.locator: Drug pricing: a critical policy concern, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (left column)
key_findings.note: Outputs of the authors' model, reported without inputs or uncertainty intervals.

key_findings.finding: Workforce: a drug price about 12% lower would allow therapists' hourly rate to rise from 147 US dollars (the rate in the sponsor's model) to 200, which the authors argue could help recruitment and retention.
key_findings.locator: Drug pricing: a critical policy concern, 3rd paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)

key_findings.finding: On the sponsor: Lykos (formerly MAPS PBC), a public benefit corporation, raised over 140 million US dollars in philanthropy and more than 100 million from investors to fund the phase 3 trials and the approval process (Harrison and Jordan, 2024); bringing a drug to market is said to cost 500 million to 1 billion dollars (no source); the sponsor's analysis did not give recovery of research costs as a reason for its price, and the authors judge the price misaligned with the company's stated mission.
key_findings.locator: Drug pricing: a critical policy concern, 4th paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Policy conclusions: payers need comparisons with treatments used in practice (or at least indirect comparisons); a 36,000-dollar drug cost risks a two-tiered system; the authors suggest charging only for the MDMA sessions actually given, on the untested assumption that some patients might need fewer than the protocol's maximum; and call for models with realistic comparators, all health-care costs and balanced pricing.
key_findings.locator: Policy implications and conclusions, 2nd to 6th paragraphs (p. 2, right column, to p. 3, left column)

key_findings.finding: Declared interests: Elliot Marseille has received consulting fees from MAPS PBC/Lykos; Jennifer Mitchell has received research support from MAPS PBC/Lykos; no funding for this study. ChatGPT was used to edit the manuscript and to develop responses to reviewers.
key_findings.locator: Conflict of interest and source of funding; Declaration of Generative AI (right and left columns)

reporting_issues.issue: The new model results (break-even at about 8.4 years with the sponsor's drug cost; 160 US dollars per QALY at 10,500 dollars; dominance below 10,320 dollars; therapist rate rising from 147 to 200 dollars with a 12% lower price) are given without the model's inputs, structure or uncertainty.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be checked from the paper; cite them only as the authors' model outputs.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors reject the placebo-therapy comparator as unrealistic, but their own base-case comparator assumes no new costs and no change in health status for people receiving standard care; the paper does not report how its results change if standard care improves health, which another source in this batch reports for the psychotherapies named (effect sizes over one standard deviation; Earleywine et al., 2025, p. 1, citing Cusack et al., 2016).
reporting_issues.consequence: The more favourable figures depend on this assumption as well as on the lower price; the critique shows how sensitive the result is to the comparator, not which comparator result is right.

reporting_issues.issue: The FDA decision is dated to August 2024 from a CNN report, and the cost of bringing a drug to market (500 million to 1 billion dollars) is attributed to unnamed analysts.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the regulator's own documents for the decision and its date.
