verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9548934 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2 as text, author contributions, conflicts, funding, reference list; Figure 1 is an image whose legend only was read; the three supplements (.docx) were not read). Crossref record read in this reader's tab.

design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects pairwise meta-analyses (PROSPERO CRD42022355572) of side effects of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in phase 2 and 3 studies across psychiatric indications, searched to 30 October 2023 in PubMed, EMBASE, PsycINFO, MEDLINE and CENTRAL. 13 studies (333 unique participants) in the review, 8 randomized trials (298 participants) in the meta-analyses, analysed separately for phase 2 (spontaneously reported expected reactions and treatment-emergent adverse events) and phase 3 (treatment-emergent adverse events and adverse events of special interest). Also assessed the reporting of harms against CONSORT Harms 2022 and compared adverse-event counts in publications with those in ClinicalTrials.gov. Independent academic review (University of Melbourne), funded by the Australian Medical Research Future Fund.
can_establish: Which side effects were reported more often with MDMA than with placebo or low-dose MDMA in the published trials up to October 2023, how complete and standardized the reporting of harms was, and how many registered adverse events were missing from the publications.
cannot_establish: Rates of side effects per person (the unit of the pooled 'any side effect' outcomes is unclear), rare or delayed harms (studies small and short, most data from PTSD trials of one sponsor), or harms outside the trials' screened populations.

sample.recruitment: Database search from inception to 30 October 2023 (search re-run just before the final analysis), English-language peer-reviewed articles of MDMA given with psychotherapy for a psychiatric condition; phase 1 studies without psychotherapy excluded (Methods › Search strategy; Inclusion and exclusion criteria).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: one or more MDMA doses combined with psychotherapy to treat a target psychiatric condition, any design. Excluded: studies without psychotherapy, papers without original data, conference abstracts, book chapters, animal studies.
sample.demographics: Table 1, by study: PTSD in 10 of 13 studies (8 PTSD trials or open studies plus the long-term follow-up and the couples study with one partner with PTSD), autistic adults with social anxiety (Danforth 2018, 12), alcohol use disorder (Sessa 2021, open-label, 14), and a Swiss case series with various treatment-resistant disorders (Oehen & Gasser 2022, 50, of whom 6 received MDMA only). Ages 31 to 48 on average; percentage female from 17 to 100.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; withdrawal for any reason was analysed as an outcome.
sample.selection_effects: Restrictive search string (MDMA AND psychotherapy or therapy AND 'safe' or 'side' or 'adverse', without truncation shown), English and peer-reviewed only, no search of trial registries for studies. The randomized trial in anxiety with a life-threatening illness (Wolfson et al., 2020), cited in the review's introduction, is not among the included studies. The evidence is mostly from trials funded by one sponsor (MAPS), as the authors note.

exposure.measurement: MDMA-assisted psychotherapy as delivered in each study (Table 1): one to three MDMA sessions with preparatory and integration psychotherapy; doses in the MDMA groups were pooled.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed in Table 1: oral MDMA from 50 mg (Bouso 2008, one session) to 125 to 150 mg (Oehen 2013), with optional supplemental half doses in most trials; phase 3 trials 80 mg in the first session and 120 mg in later ones plus optional half doses.
exposure.polysubstance: Prior MDMA or ecstasy use was extracted: from 0% (Bouso; Danforth) to 51.0% lifetime (MAPP2 placebo arm); not reported in several studies (Table 1).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo (Bouso, Danforth, Mitchell 2021 and 2023, Mithoefer 2011) or low-dose MDMA as active placebo (25 mg Oehen 2013, 30 mg Mithoefer 2018, 40 mg Ot'alora 2018), pooled together as 'control' (Methods › Data synthesis, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Side effects as each study defined them: in phase 2, 'spontaneously reported reactions' from a list of reactions expected from healthy-volunteer studies, during sessions and for 7 days after, and treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs: events not on the list or lasting more than 7 days), including psychiatric TEAEs; in phase 3, TEAEs over the whole treatment period and adverse events of special interest (cardiac, suicidality, abuse, misuse or diversion). Withdrawal for any reason. Reporting quality: 17-item CONSORT Harms 2022 checklist, adequate if 70% or more.
outcomes.validity_norms: Most studies relied on passive monitoring of spontaneous reports (11 of 13); one used the UKU side-effect scale (Bouso); eight used the C-SSRS for suicidality (Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects).
outcomes.operationalization: Odds of experiencing an outcome with MDMA against control, Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; 64 outcomes meta-analysed at p < 0.05, of which the significant ones are shown in Fig. 2 and the rest in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level. Screening of titles and abstracts by one reviewer; full texts by two independent reviewers; extraction by one reviewer checked by a second; RoB 2 and CONSORT Harms scoring by two reviewers independently; GRADE by two reviewers.

analysis.effect_sizes: Phase 2: any side effect during medication sessions OR 1.67 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.49), p = 0.01, 45% against 30%; in the 7 days after OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), p = 0.007, 46% against 31%; anxiety OR 4.7 and jaw clenching OR 4.8 during sessions (intervals in Fig. 2, an image, not extracted); in PTSD studies anxiety OR 4.1 during sessions and 4.8 in the 7 days after; no difference in TEAEs or psychiatric TEAEs, except lower odds of any TEAE with MDMA in the PTSD subgroup (OR 0.5, two studies with low-dose controls). Phase 3: any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), p < 0.001, 16% against 5%; 13 specific TEAEs more likely; no difference in suicidality or cardiac adverse events of special interest; none for abuse, misuse or diversion. Withdrawal: no difference. Heterogeneity described as low; I2 values are in Fig. 2 and the supplement (not extracted).
analysis.covariates: Subgroup analyses of PTSD against non-PTSD studies; sensitivity analyses by method of side-effect assessment and number of medication sessions, which did not change the results.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42022355572; PRISMA reporting. The article does not say whether any analysis departed from the protocol (protocol not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only primary outcomes and significant secondary outcomes are reported in the text and Fig. 2; the other secondary outcomes are in Supplementary Table 3 (not read).
analysis.power: Publication bias not assessed (10 or fewer studies per analysis); the authors note that rare events such as cardiac or suicidality events were unlikely to reach significance.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In mostly PTSD trials, mostly funded by one sponsor, MDMA was associated with more frequent expected side effects during and in the week after sessions (phase 2) and with more treatment-emergent adverse events of 13 named kinds over treatment (phase 3), without differences in psychiatric TEAEs, suicidality or cardiac events of special interest, or withdrawal; certainty very low to moderate; seven of eight trials at high risk of bias; no trial reported harms adequately; more than half the registered non-serious adverse events and 4 of 13 serious adverse events were missing from the publications.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusion say side effects were largely transient and mild or moderate, and the authors call for caution, independent trials and post-marketing studies. The severity and transience statements rest on how the primary trials described their events; the review itself graded no severity data. Calling the review comprehensive and 'across indications' overstates its reach: one randomized trial outside PTSD was included, and one known randomized trial outside PTSD was not.

timeline.event: Breeksema et al. systematic review of adverse events with psychedelics and MDMA (no meta-analysis) finds mostly transient acute and late adverse events and poor assessment of harms.
Kisely et al. meta-analysis of psilocybin and MDMA trials, cited by this review as an earlier meta-analysis of side effects (not read here).
This review (published online 23 April 2024), before the August 2024 retraction of two analyses it cites (Jerome et al., 2020, and Mithoefer et al., 2019).
Commentary on this review in the same journal (Murray, 2024; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The only meta-analysis of MDMA-assisted therapy side effects across indications found here. Its direction agrees with the phase 3 trial reports read by the project (sc_mitchell_2021, sc_mitchell_2023) and with Breeksema et al. (2022), but it pools mostly the same sponsor's trials; its 'any side effect' estimates are of uncertain unit; and its registry comparison is the most useful original contribution.

funding.funder: Medical Research Future Fund of Australia (MRF2010957); open access funded by CAUL.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: University of Melbourne (Melbourne School of Psychological Sciences; Centre for Youth Mental Health and Orygen). None of the authors ran the included trials.

what_would_settle_it: Independent trials outside PTSD and outside one sponsor's programme that assess side effects systematically (structured checklists at fixed times, including between sessions and at long-term follow-up), report all events by arm with denominators, and register them; and an individual-participant-data meta-analysis with the participant as unit of analysis.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (psychiatric conditions), intervention (MDMA with psychotherapy), comparator (control) and outcomes (side effects, withdrawal) are stated.
PROSPERO CRD42022355572; the article does not report whether the analyses followed the protocol or justify any deviation.
All designs combining MDMA with psychotherapy, with the reason phase 1 studies are excluded.

Five databases, but English-language and peer-reviewed articles only without justification, a narrow search string, no registry, grey-literature or reference-list searching for studies, and an eligible randomized trial (Wolfson et al., 2020) that the review cites but does not include.
Titles and abstracts screened by one reviewer; only full texts by two.
Extraction by one reviewer checked for accuracy and completeness by a second.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article lists only the five studies excluded from the meta-analyses (Table S2) and shows the flow in Fig. 1 (an image); whether the supplement lists the excluded full texts with reasons could not be checked (supplement not read).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 gives population, doses, controls, prior MDMA use and how side effects were assessed and reported; settings and follow-up periods are given only partly.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 in duplicate for the eight randomized trials (kappa 1.00); the five non-randomized studies in the review were not appraised for risk of bias.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported for the included studies, although the authors note that most were sponsored by one advocacy group.

Random-effects Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios, but the unit of analysis of the 'any side effect' outcomes is not stated and cannot be the participant (16% with any TEAE on MDMA in phase 3, while 58.5 to 63% had muscle tightness alone); event counts per session and participant counts appear side by side in Table 1; placebo and low-dose MDMA controls are pooled.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Seven of eight trials at high risk; no analysis of the effect of risk of bias on the estimates (sensitivity analyses concern assessment method and number of sessions).

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The authors stress high risk of bias and very low to moderate certainty and ask for cautious interpretation.
Heterogeneity reported as low; phase 2 and 3 analysed separately because of different reporting; PTSD subgroups; the active-control issue discussed.
Not assessed because 10 or fewer studies per analysis; possible sources (small studies from one advocacy sponsor) are mentioned but not investigated.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and the absence of competing interests are stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence when more than one critical item fails: here the search (4), the statistical methods (11) and publication bias (15); item 7 is provisional (supplement not read) but cannot change the rating. This judges the pooled numbers as unbiased summaries, not the review's usefulness: its registry comparison, its CONSORT Harms audit and its tabulation of the trials' side-effect data are valuable and are what claims should cite, with the pooled odds ratios as indicating direction only.

key_findings.finding: 13 studies with 333 unique participants met the criteria; 5 without a control group were excluded from the meta-analyses; the remaining 8 randomized trials (298 participants) reported 138 safety outcomes, of which 64 had data from at least two studies.

Included studies (Table 1): randomized trials in PTSD (Bouso 2008, 6; Mithoefer 2011, 20; Oehen 2013, 12; Mithoefer 2018, 26; Ot'alora 2018, 28; Mitchell 2021, 90; Mitchell 2023, 104) and in autistic adults with social anxiety (Danforth 2018, 12); non-randomized: an open-label PTSD study (Jardim 2021, 3), a pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials (Jerome 2020, 107), an uncontrolled couples study with one partner with PTSD (Monson 2020, 12), a Swiss case series of various treatment-resistant disorders (Oehen & Gasser 2022, 50) and an open-label alcohol use disorder study (Sessa 2021, 14).
key_findings.note: Jerome et al. (2020) was retracted in August 2024; its rows must not be cited. The randomized trial in anxiety with a life-threatening illness (Wolfson et al., 2020) is cited in the Introduction but not included.

key_findings.finding: Phase 2 trials: any side effect during medication sessions OR 1.67 (95% CI 1.12 to 2.49), 45% against 30%; in the 7 days after OR 1.59 (1.12 to 2.24), 46% against 31%; anxiety (OR 4.7) and jaw clenching (OR 4.8) during sessions more likely with MDMA; in PTSD studies anxiety OR 4.1 during sessions and 4.8 in the following 7 days.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Phase two studies, side effects during and 7 days following medication sessions; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2 legend
key_findings.note: The percentages cannot be shares of participants with any side effect (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Phase 2 trials: no difference in any treatment-emergent adverse event or psychiatric TEAE; in PTSD studies only, lower odds of any TEAE with MDMA (OR 0.5), from two studies whose controls were low-dose MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Results › Phase two studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Phase 3 trials (194 participants): any TEAE OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46), 16% against 5%; more likely with MDMA: muscle tightness, decreased appetite, nausea, excessive perspiration, feeling cold, restlessness, dilated pupils, jaw clenching or tight jaw, uncontrolled eye movements, feeling jittery, non-cardiac chest pain or discomfort, blurred vision and chills.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Results › Phase three studies › Treatment emergent adverse events, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Phase 3: no difference in adverse events of special interest for suicidality or cardiac function; no AESIs for MDMA abuse, misuse or diversion reported. Withdrawal for any reason: no difference across all studies or in PTSD studies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Phase three studies › Adverse event of special interest; Phase 2 and 3 studies › Withdrawal

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (RoB 2, outcome side effects): 7 of the 8 meta-analysed trials high, 1 some concerns (Danforth 2018); measurement of the outcome the domain most often high; kappa 1.00. GRADE: very low for all phase 2 primary outcomes, low for two and moderate for one phase 3 primary outcome, moderate for withdrawal.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Certainty of evidence

key_findings.finding: No trial adhered adequately (70% or more) to CONSORT Harms 2022; median adherence 50% (range 21% to 64%); no trial reported effect sizes with precision for harms or absolute and relative effects.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adherence to CONSORT Harms 2022; Table 2

key_findings.finding: ClinicalTrials.gov against publications: 1487 non-serious adverse events in the registers against 661 in the articles (5 trials comparable) and 13 serious adverse events against 9 (8 trials); the 4 unpublished serious events were all in MDMA groups (metastases to the central nervous system, clavicle fracture, syncope, suicidal behaviour). 56% of non-serious and 31% of serious registered events were not in the articles; the phase 3 reports listed only events with at least a twofold difference between arms.
key_findings.locator: Results › Comparison of adverse events published versus reported on ClinicalTrial.gov; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Measurement: 11 of 13 studies relied on passive monitoring of spontaneous reports; one used a structured side-effect scale (UKU, Bouso 2008); eight used the C-SSRS. Phase 2 trials collected expected reactions separately from TEAEs; phase 3 trials reported only TEAEs over the treatment period.
key_findings.locator: Results › Systematic review: measurement of side effects; Systematic review: reporting of side effects

key_findings.finding: Authors' limits: conclusions only for acute and short-term side effects, insufficient data on longer-term risks; highly selective samples; small studies sponsored largely by a single advocacy group; implementation outside trials likely to increase side effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The proportions given for 'any' side effect cannot be shares of participants: in phase 3, 16% of MDMA participants are said to have had a TEAE, while Table 1 lists muscle tightness alone in 63% (Mitchell 2021) and 58.5% (Mitchell 2023) of MDMA participants; in phase 2, 45% with any side effect during sessions, while Table 1 lists anxiety during MDMA sessions in 59% to 89% of MDMA participants in individual trials. The unit of analysis is not stated; with 194 phase 3 participants, the narrow interval for OR 3.51 (2.76 to 4.46) also suggests that events or participant-by-event entries were counted.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Phase two studies; Results › Phase three studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled 'any side effect' odds ratios cannot be read as odds per person and their intervals are probably too narrow; claims should cite them for direction only, and use trial-level percentages for frequencies.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports some studies' side effects as numbers of events and percentages of sessions (Jardim 2021, Mithoefer 2011, Oehen 2013, Monson 2020) and others as participants; the Methods do not say how these were combined in the meta-analyses.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Methods › Data synthesis, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Adds to the uncertainty about the unit of analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: Wolfson et al. (2020), a randomized trial of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for anxiety with a life-threatening illness, is cited in the Introduction (reference 7) as evidence of potential in other conditions, but is not among the 13 included studies, and no reason is given in the article.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Introduction, 1st paragraph; Table 1; reference list)
reporting_issues.consequence: The review is not complete for indications other than PTSD; non-PTSD randomized data rest on one trial of 12 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Two sources since retracted are used: the pooled long-term follow-up by Jerome et al. (2020) is an included study (Table 1, the review's only long-term harm data, including 9.6% using ecstasy or MDMA after treatment), and the phase 2 outcome categories are defined with reference to Mithoefer et al. (2019). Both were retracted in August 2024, after this review was published; PMC now marks them.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Methods › Data synthesis, 3rd paragraph; references 28 and 44)
reporting_issues.consequence: The long-term harm data in Table 1 must not be cited; the meta-analyses are unaffected because the follow-up had no control group.

reporting_issues.issue: Bouso et al. is dated 2008 in Table 1 and the reference list but 2011 in the header of Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC11224236 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2 as text, figure legends, author contributions, funding, competing interests, reference list; Figs. 1 to 3 are images whose legends only were read; Supplementary Material (.docx) and Supplementary Tables 3 and 8 (.xlsx) not read). Crossref record read in this reader's tab.

design_detail: Exploratory phase 2, single-site, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding pilot (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396) at the Los Angeles Biomedical Research Institute at Harbor-UCLA, February 2014 to April 2017. Twelve autistic adults with marked to very severe social anxiety (LSAS of 60 or more) were randomized to MDMA (8, in two dose subgroups of 4) or an inactive lactose placebo (4) in two blinded 8-hour experimental sessions about a month apart, with three 60- to 90-minute preparatory sessions (including mindfulness skills adapted from dialectical behavior therapy) and three integrative sessions after each; primary outcome the change in LSAS total from baseline to one month after the second session, rated by one blinded independent rater; follow-up 6 months after the last session, when the blind was broken (open-label sessions for the placebo group not reported). Sponsored and funded by MAPS, organized by MAPS PBC, with additional private donors.
can_establish: Whether, in 11 analysed autistic adults with severe social anxiety, two MDMA sessions within psychotherapy were followed by a larger fall in interview-rated social anxiety than the same psychotherapy with an inactive placebo, with a very imprecise estimate; and which acute reactions and vital-sign changes were more frequent with MDMA in 8 people.
cannot_establish: How large any effect of MDMA is, or whether it differs from participants knowing their allocation (they guessed correctly in 22 of 23 sessions) or from expectation; whether a dose matters (4 per subgroup, pooled in the paper); durability beyond 6 months; rare harms; or effects in autistic people with intellectual disability, those under 21, those with prior MDMA use, or those not physically healthy or psychologically stable, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Internet advertisements, word of mouth and clinician referrals, mainly online; advertisements were placed in autism forums and community outreach was used to limit self-selection and expectancy from drug-interest forums (Methods › Screening, eligibility, and participants, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 6th paragraph). Fig. 1 (read from the figure image): 49 preliminary telephone screens, 25 excluded, 24 assessed in person, 12 excluded, 12 enrolled and randomized.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 21 or older; LSAS of 60 or more; autism confirmed with the ADOS-2 Module 4; MDMA-naive by self-report; physically healthy and psychologically stable; full criteria only in the supplement, not read (Methods › Screening, eligibility, and participants, 1st paragraph). One MDMA participant was found after randomization to have been enrolled with hypertension and a pre-study substance use disorder within the exclusion window and was withdrawn (Fig. 1 footnote; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.3 (SD 8.8); 10 men and 2 women, both women in the MDMA group; 6 White, others Latino/Hispanic, Asian/Pacific Islander, Middle Eastern or mixed; 25% non-heteronormative sexual orientation; baseline LSAS 69 to 125; earlier psychotherapy in most (psychodynamic 10 of 12); earlier antidepressants 7, stimulants 4, anxiolytics 3; lifetime C-SSRS positive ideation 7, serious ideation 1, suicidal behaviour 2 (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2).
sample.attrition: One of 8 MDMA participants withdrawn as ineligible after randomization; the remaining 7 and all 4 placebo participants completed the primary assessment and the 6-month follow-up; their baseline scores were kept and missing data were not imputed (Fig. 1; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers able to engage with online advertisements, mostly men, aged 21 or older, without prior MDMA use, and willing to take MDMA in a trial; the authors note possible self-selection and expectancy effects (Discussion › Limitations, 6th paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in two blinded experimental sessions (arrival about 09:30, drug about 10:30 after progressive muscle relaxation, end late afternoon) in a room designed to reduce sensory distress, with a pair of therapists; participants went home with a study support partner and returned next morning for integration; seven daily telephone checks after each session (Methods › Experimental sessions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Post-session follow-up, 1st paragraph; Safety monitoring, 1st paragraph). MDMA was synthesized by David Nichols at Purdue University and compounded with lactose into capsules identical to the placebo (Methods › Trial design, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: one MDMA subgroup (4) received 75 mg at the first session and 100 mg at the second, the other (4) 100 mg and 125 mg; placebo was lactose of equivalent weight; no participant declined the dose increase; no supplemental dose is described (Methods › Trial design, 2nd paragraph). The subgroups were pooled for analysis (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants had to be MDMA-naive by self-report, which could not be verified; drug screens at baseline and before experimental sessions; Table 2 lists polysubstance dependence, alcohol abuse and substance use among comorbid diagnoses in single participants (current or past not stated); concomitant psychiatric medicines during follow-up could have affected 6-month outcomes (Results › Demographics; Table 2; Discussion › Limitations, 5th paragraph). One MDMA participant who had stopped escitalopram about 2 months earlier showed no physiological or subjective response although MDMA was found in plasma (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Inactive lactose placebo with the same psychotherapy (Methods › Trial design, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized 2:1 (8 and 4); the randomization procedure and allocation concealment are not described in the main text (a randomization monitor is thanked in the Acknowledgments). Baseline LSAS 91.8 (15.8) on MDMA vs 83.3 (11.9) on placebo; both women in the MDMA group (Tables 1 and 3).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; expectations were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not reported by group beyond Table 2's comorbidity lists.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS, 24-item semi-structured interview) by one independent rater at baseline, 1 day, 2 weeks and 4 weeks after each experimental session and at 6 months. Secondary (exploratory, descriptive): BDI-II, Perceived Stress Scale, Interpersonal Reactivity Index, Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, STAI, TAS-20, TASIT, Emotion Regulation Questionnaire. Vital signs before and hourly for 6 to 7 hours after dosing; adverse events, spontaneously reported reactions during sessions and for 7 days, C-SSRS at the start and end of treatment days, hourly subjective units of distress (Methods › Trial design, 3rd paragraph; Assessments; Pharmacodynamic measures; Safety monitoring).
outcomes.validity_norms: LSAS severity bands used in Table 3: 0 to 54 normal, 55 to 65 moderate, 66 to 80 marked, 81 to 95 severe, 96 or more very severe (Table 3 footnote d); response defined post hoc as a fall of 20 points or more, from prior LSAS studies (Results › Clinical response, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: a larger fall in LSAS total from baseline to one month after the second session on MDMA than on placebo, by independent-samples t test; Cohen's d for an independent-groups pretest–posttest design (Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not needed for the two inferential tests (primary endpoint and 6-month follow-up); the eight secondary measures were presented descriptively (in the supplement, not read).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants, therapists and the independent rater were described as blind; the single rater never attended experimental sessions and participants were asked not to reveal their beliefs; the rater's guesses were not recorded. Participants guessed wrongly in only 1 of 23 sessions (one of eight placebo sessions); the two therapists guessed wrongly in 2 and 1 of 8 placebo sessions and in 2 of 15 MDMA sessions each (Results › Blinding, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: LSAS change −44.1 (SD 14.8) on MDMA (n = 7) vs −19.3 (18.8) on placebo (n = 4); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037, 95% CI of the difference 1.92 to 47.87; placebo-subtracted Cohen's d 1.4 (CI −0.074 to 2.874). Six months: −47.7 (14.7) vs −23.3 (18.0); t(9) = 2.454, P = 0.036, CI 1.92 to 47.01; d 1.1 (−0.31 to 2.53) (Results › Clinical response, 1st paragraph; Table 3). Editors' calculations from the printed means and SDs: difference 24.8 points, t(9) = 2.44, P = 0.038, CI 1.8 to 47.8; an approximate 95% CI for d = 1.4 of 0.04 to 2.76. LSAS fall of 20 points or more: 6 of 7 on MDMA vs 2 of 4 on placebo (Table 3). Registry, by dose: 75/100 mg change −51.0 (8.19), 100/125 mg −39.0 (17.57), placebo −19.3 (18.77).
analysis.covariates: None; unadjusted change scores (baseline LSAS 4 to 8 points higher on MDMA).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396: first submitted 6 December 2013, posted 11 December 2013, before the actual start (11 April 2014); a dose-finding phase 2 pilot; registered primary outcomes: LSAS total at one month after experimental session 2 and its change from baseline; no secondary outcomes registered; results posted 14 October 2020, reported by dose group. The paper pools the two dose groups and lists eight secondary measures (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: The dose-group results, the point of a dose-finding design, are not reported in the paper (only in the registry, where the lower-dose group improved more); the eight secondary measures are reported only descriptively in the supplement (not read); outcomes of the placebo group's open-label MDMA sessions are not presented.
analysis.power: No power calculation; a pilot of 12 (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: With 7 analysed on MDMA and 4 on placebo, interview-rated social anxiety fell by about 44 points on MDMA and 19 on placebo one month after the second session (difference about 25 points, 95% CI about 2 to 48), and the difference was similar at 6 months. Participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions. MDMA raised blood pressure, pulse and temperature during sessions and was followed more often by anxiety, difficulty concentrating, fatigue, headache and low mood; there were no serious adverse events. In the registry, the lower-dose group improved more than the higher-dose group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the trial "demonstrated rapid and durable improvement in social anxiety symptoms" and calls the effect size very large (Abstract › Results and Conclusions), although the printed interval of d includes zero. The Limitations conclude that double-blinding with an inactive placebo was adequate because one participant and both investigators made incorrect guesses (Discussion › Limitations, 4th paragraph), whereas participants were right in 22 of 23 sessions. The Discussion says long-term follow-up failed to detect any deleterious outcomes (Discussion, 8th paragraph) on 11 people, and the Conclusions say feasibility and safety were successfully established. The authors do acknowledge that observable drug effects may contribute to efficacy and that the sample limits claims (Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 4th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Danforth et al., Prog Neuropsychopharmacol Biol Psychiatry: rationale and design of this trial (on the project's evidence map; not read).
This pilot trial (online 8 September 2018).
Results posted on ClinicalTrials.gov (14 October 2020), by dose group.

replication.where_it_stands: One pilot trial of 12 people. The project's evidence map lists a completed trial in social anxiety disorder without autism (NCT05138068; protocol Lear et al., 2023) and a completed laboratory study in autistic adults with posted results (NCT04053036), neither with a publication among the sources read.

funding.funder: Sponsored and funded by MAPS, a 501(c)(3) non-profit; MAPS PBC, wholly owned by MAPS, organized the trial; additional private funding from Richard S. Ross, Lars Skovlund, The Betsy Gordon Foundation, Frances Vaughn and Angeles Arrien (Funding information).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: Alicia Danforth and Charles Grob received research funds from MAPS PBC as clinical investigators; Allison Feduccia, Lisa Jerome and Amy Emerson were salaried full-time employees of MAPS PBC; Berra Yazar-Klosinski was a salaried full-time employee of MAPS; Nick Walker was paid by MAPS as an independent consultant (Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Four of eight authors were sponsor employees; the sponsor's staff monitored the data and a sponsor statistician reviewed the analysis (Acknowledgments). The registry now names Resilient Pharmaceuticals as sponsor. The paper's Crossref record carries no correction or retraction (read 2026-10-17).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered randomized trial in autistic adults with social anxiety, comparing MDMA with an active placebo within the same psychotherapy, with prespecified dose arms, measured expectancy, a blinding check of participants and raters, and follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: The method of randomization and allocation concealment is not described in the main text; baseline differences in 12 people (LSAS 91.8 vs 83.3; both women in the MDMA arm) are compatible with chance.

One MDMA participant was enrolled in breach of the exclusion criteria and withdrawn; participants were almost all aware of their allocation, which could change how they engaged with the psychotherapy; two needed an extra preparatory session.
One of 8 in the MDMA arm (12.5%) has no outcome, after post-randomization withdrawal for ineligibility; no imputation or sensitivity analysis; in a trial of 12 a single participant matters.

The LSAS was given by one blinded rater, but it scores participants' own reports of fear and avoidance, and participants identified their allocation in 22 of 23 sessions; knowledge of allocation could plausibly have influenced the reports. The rater's blinding was not checked.

Prospectively registered with the LSAS as primary outcome, but the registry reports it by dose group while the paper reports only the pooled comparison, and the registry's posted denominators do not match the paper's.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The overall judgment is high because the primary outcome rests on participants' reports while their allocation was evident in almost every session, and expectancy was not measured; other domains add concerns in a trial of 12. The trial can be cited for the observed LSAS changes with their wide interval, for the acute reactions and vital-sign changes seen in 8 people given MDMA, and for the absence of serious adverse events; it cannot be cited for the size of an effect of MDMA, for dose, or for durability or safety beyond this small group.

key_findings.finding: Flow (read from the Fig. 1 image): 49 telephone screens, 25 excluded, 24 assessed in person, 12 excluded, 12 randomized (4 placebo, 8 MDMA); one MDMA participant withdrawn for enrolment with hypertension and a pre-study substance use disorder within the exclusion window; 4 placebo and 7 MDMA participants completed the primary assessment and the 6-month follow-up.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image, with footnote); Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, LSAS total: placebo 83.3 (SD 11.9) at baseline and 64.0 (13.3) one month after the second session, change −19.3 (18.8); MDMA 91.8 (15.8) and 46.4 (15.2), change −44.1 (14.8); t(9) = 2.451, P = 0.037, CI 1.92 to 47.87; placebo-subtracted d 1.4 (CI −0.074 to 2.874).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations: difference 24.8 points (CI 1.8 to 47.8, t(9) = 2.44); approximate CI for d 0.04 to 2.76. MDMA n = 7 after baseline (Table 3 footnote c).

key_findings.finding: Six-month follow-up: placebo 60.0 (17.4), change −23.3 (18.0); MDMA 42.9 (20.4), change −47.7 (14.7); t(9) = 2.454, P = 0.036, CI 1.92 to 47.01; d 1.1 (CI −0.31 to 2.53); within the MDMA group, primary endpoint to 6 months t(6) = 1.117, P = 0.307.
key_findings.locator: Results › Clinical response, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3

key_findings.finding: LSAS fall of 20 points or more at the primary endpoint: 6 of 7 (85.7%) on MDMA vs 2 of 4 (50.0%) on placebo in Table 3; the text gives 6 of 8 (75%) vs 2 of 4. Severity at the primary endpoint: 5 MDMA participants and 2 placebo participants in the normal range.
key_findings.locator: Table 3; Results › Clinical response, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blinding: participants guessed their allocation wrongly in one of 8 placebo sessions and in none of the 15 MDMA sessions (right in 22 of 23); one therapist was wrong in 2 of 8 placebo and 2 of 15 MDMA sessions, the other in 1 of 8 and 2 of 15. One MDMA participant had no physiological or subjective response (MDMA confirmed in plasma) and both investigators guessed placebo.

Vital signs: mean peak systolic blood pressure (P = 0.021), pulse (P = 0.015) and temperature (P < 0.001) higher on MDMA; maximum pulse 114 bpm and maximum temperature 37.7 °C; no systolic pressure above 180 or diastolic above 110 mmHg; values back to pre-drug levels by session end without intervention.

Reactions during the two blinded sessions, MDMA (n = 8) vs placebo (n = 4): anxiety 6 (75.0%) vs 1; difficulty concentrating 5 (62.5%) vs 1; fatigue, headache and sensitivity to cold 4 (50.0%) each vs 0 to 1. Over the next 7 days: fatigue 5 (62.5%) vs 2, headache 5 (62.5%, one severe) vs 1, difficulty concentrating 4 (50.0%) vs 0, low mood 4 (50.0%) vs 2, lack of appetite 3 (37.5%) vs 0. No serious adverse events.

Psychiatric adverse events from the first session to the primary endpoint, MDMA vs placebo: depressed mood 2 (25.0%) vs 0; suicidal ideation 2 (25.0%) vs 1 (25.0%), pre-existing in medical history; anxiety, depression, panic attack and panic reaction 1 each on MDMA; moderate events on MDMA included anxiety, depression, suicidal ideation and panic attack; positive suicidal ideation occurred during two MDMA sessions and resolved by the next day.

Registry results by dose group (LSAS one month after session 2): 75/100 mg 34.3 (10.41), change −51.0 (8.19); 100/125 mg 55.5 (11.47), change −39.0 (17.57); placebo 64.0 (13.34), change −19.3 (18.77); posted denominators 4, 4 and 3. Registered 6 December 2013, before the start on 11 April 2014; no secondary outcomes registered; no serious adverse events or deaths; other adverse events in 1 of 4, 4 of 4 and 1 of 4, to the end of stage 2 (about 10 months).
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02008396 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures; Results › Outcome Measures, Adverse Events
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: weighting the two dose groups by 3 and 4 reproduces the paper's pooled MDMA values (46.41 and −44.14); the posted denominators of 4, 4 and 3 do not.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: small sample and wide range of scores; too small to compare doses; inactive placebo with observable drug effects, which might contribute to efficacy; prior MDMA abstinence could not be verified; undisclosed drug use and concomitant psychiatric medicines during follow-up could affect 6-month outcomes; possible self-selection and expectancy from recruitment.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentages for the MDMA group mix denominators of 7 and 8: in Table 3 the primary-endpoint severity categories give 5 (71.4%) normal but 1 (12.5%) moderate and 1 (12.5%) marked, and the change categories give 4 (57.1%), 2 (28.6%) and 1 (12.5%); in Table 4 low mood and thirst are 2 (28.6%) while anxiety is 6 (75.0%), and 7-day irritability is printed as 1 (25.0%) in the MDMA column (1 of 8 is 12.5%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite counts with their denominator rather than the printed percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: The rate of a 20-point LSAS fall on MDMA is 6 of 8 (75%) in the Results text but 6 of 7 (85.7%) in Table 3 and the Discussion.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Clinical response, 2nd paragraph; Table 3; Discussion, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the analysed denominator is 7.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed interval for the placebo-subtracted d at the primary endpoint (−0.074 to 2.874) includes zero, although the t test gives P = 0.037 and the interval of the raw difference (1.92 to 47.87) excludes zero; the editors' approximate interval for d is 0.04 to 2.76. The abstract calls d = 1.4 very large without noting its width.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Results; Results › Clinical response, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The standardized effect is extremely imprecise; cite the raw difference with its interval.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 41.67% of participants had generalized anxiety disorder and 66.67% a history of depression, while Table 2 lists generalized anxiety in 2 (16.6%) and 'anxiety' in 4 (33.3%); Table 2's 'Other' pre-study medication total is 2 (16.6%) although the groups show 0 and 3.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comorbidity description is internally inconsistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The registry's posted results give the primary outcome by dose group with denominators of 4, 4 and 3 (placebo 3), while the paper analyses 7 MDMA and 4 placebo participants; the placebo values are the same in both. Weighting the dose groups 3 and 4 reproduces the paper's pooled values (editors' calculation), so the registry's denominators appear mislabelled. The registry also shows the lower-dose group improving more (−51.0) than the higher-dose group (−39.0), which the paper does not report.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Results › Outcome Measures); PMC HTML (Table 3; Methods › Statistical analysis)
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper's pooled result is consistent with the registry's subgroup data; there is no sign of a dose–response in these tiny groups.

reporting_issues.issue: One participant randomized to MDMA had been enrolled despite exclusion criteria (hypertension and a recent substance use disorder), found only after randomization; the analysis that leaves this participant out is labelled intention-to-treat.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Fig. 1 footnote; Methods › Statistical analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 3 footnote a)
reporting_issues.consequence: A modified intention-to-treat analysis of 11 of 12 randomized; screening missed an exclusion in 1 of 12 enrolled.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC6208958 (all sections, Tables 1 to 5, figure legends, the Fig. 1 CONSORT image viewed at its PMC address, funding and conflicts), read in this reader's own browser tab; ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT02008396 (API v2) for registration, outcomes, posted results and adverse events; the Crossref record for the DOI. The supplementary files (ESM 1, Word; ESM 2, PDF) were not read because they are downloads; Fig. 2 values were not extracted.

design_detail: Systematic review and Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42023469014; PRISMA-NMA) of randomized trials of oral monotherapy with psilocybin, LSD, MDMA, ayahuasca or escitalopram in adults with depressive symptoms, searched to 12 October 2023 in MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Embase, PsycINFO, ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO ICTRP without language restriction. Primary outcome: change in depressive symptoms converted to HAMD-17 points (minimal important difference 3 points); secondary: all-cause discontinuation and severe adverse events. To allow for unblinding, the placebo arms of psychedelic trials, the placebo arms of escitalopram trials and extremely low doses of psychedelics are separate nodes; the two parts of the network are joined by one head-to-head trial (psilocybin against escitalopram). 19 studies: 15 psychedelic trials (811 participants) and 5 escitalopram trials (1968). This card concerns the MDMA results. Independent academic review (Taiwan), funded by the National Science and Technology Council.
can_establish: How large the reduction in depressive symptoms with MDMA-assisted treatment was against the placebo arms of psychedelic trials, and how it compares, through the network, with placebo responses in antidepressant trials and with other psychedelics, in the trials available up to October 2023.
cannot_establish: An effect of MDMA on depression as a disorder (the MDMA trials enrolled mostly people with PTSD), a fair comparison with the placebo response in antidepressant trials (indirect, through one psilocybin trial, across different populations and therapies), or long-term effects (acute outcomes only).

sample.recruitment: 3104 unique records; 42 full texts; 26 excluded (reasons in appendix 3, not read); 3 added by manual search; 19 eligible (Results › Characteristics of included study). Study characteristics are in etable 1 of the appendix (not read).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Randomized parallel or crossover trials (first phase only) in adults with clinically diagnosed depression (major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, other psychiatric disorders with comorbid clinical depression) or with life-threatening diagnoses and depressive symptoms, using validated depression scales; psychedelics as oral monotherapy without concomitant antidepressants; escitalopram fixed-dose placebo-controlled trials with at least two doses (up to 20 mg/day). Excluded: follow-up studies, healthy volunteers, conference abstracts, editorials, reviews, case reports and series, duplicate data; ketamine (Methods › Study selection).
sample.demographics: Psychedelic trials: mean age 42.49, 54.2% women (440 of 811); escitalopram trials: 39.35, 62.5% women (1230 of 1968).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; all-cause discontinuation was an outcome.
sample.selection_effects: The authors state that participants in the MDMA trials were predominantly diagnosed with PTSD, while the escitalopram trials enrolled people with major depressive disorder (Strengths and limitations, 2nd paragraph). The MDMA trials cited in the article are Mithoefer 2011, Mithoefer 2018, Ot'alora 2018, Mitchell 2021 (cited as its 2023 reprint in Focus) and Wolfson 2020; the second phase 3 trial (Mitchell 2023) is not cited, and the list of included trials (etable 1) was not read.

exposure.measurement: Psychedelic arms as given in each trial, with the psychological support or psychotherapy the trials used (protocols in etable 2, not read).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Dose categories defined by the review for MDMA: high, 100 mg or more; extremely low, 40 mg or less; low, between (Methods › Data synthesis, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed at review level; concomitant antidepressants excluded by the eligibility criteria.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Three reference nodes: placebo response in psychedelic trials (inactive placebo arms), placebo response in escitalopram trials (assumed by the authors to reflect adequate blinding), and extremely low doses of psilocybin or MDMA (taken to approximate the effect of the accompanying psychotherapy).
comparison.matching: Not applicable. Transitivity was examined by comparing effect modifiers and by checking that escitalopram's effect was similar in placebo-controlled trials and in the head-to-head trial (0.64, 95% CrI −4.41 to 5.40).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: HAMD-17, MADRS or BDI-II in that order of preference, all converted to HAMD-17 points by a validated method; standard deviations of change imputed with a correlation of 0.5 where missing (0 in a sensitivity analysis). Severe adverse events: death, hospital admission, significant or persistent incapacity, congenital anomaly, suicide attempt.
outcomes.validity_norms: Minimal important difference 3 HAMD-17 points (Hengartner and Plöderl, 2022); certainty rated with GRADE for network meta-analysis (minimally contextualized).
outcomes.operationalization: Mean difference in change scores (95% credible interval) for depression; odds ratios for discontinuation and severe adverse events.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the authors interpret only differences whose credible interval excludes zero and that exceed 3 points.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Screening, extraction (each checked by another author) and RoB 2 assessment were done independently by two authors.

analysis.effect_sizes: MDMA results, HAMD-17 points (Fig. 2, values read from the figure image, which prints them): against the placebo arms of psychedelic trials, high-dose MDMA 5.32 (95% CrI 2.26 to 8.32; SMD 0.42), low-dose 4.92 (−0.26 to 9.94; 0.73), extremely low dose 2.11 (−1.63 to 5.71; 0.29); against the placebo arms of escitalopram trials, high-dose 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78; 0.08), low-dose 1.13 (−4.85 to 7.00), extremely low dose −1.68 (−6.49 to 3.20); against extremely low-dose psilocybin, high-dose MDMA 1.36 (−3.08 to 5.84). High-dose psilocybin against high-dose MDMA 4.98 (1.23 to 8.67; SMD 0.32). For reference, the placebo arms of escitalopram trials did better than those of psychedelic trials by 3.79 (0.77 to 6.80). No intervention had more all-cause discontinuation or severe adverse events than placebo in psychedelic trials (efigure 11, not read).
analysis.covariates: Network meta-regression on sex, age, baseline severity, disorder type and follow-up period (credible intervals for age, women and baseline severity crossed zero; etable 3 not read); sensitivity analyses for major depressive disorder only, excluding high risk of bias, adjusting for baseline severity, and correlation 0.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42023469014; reasons for protocol changes are in appendix 5 (not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: The MDMA results appear only in Fig. 2 and the appendix; the text reports them as falling short of the authors' criteria.
analysis.power: The authors note that 15 psychedelic trials are few and that publication-bias tests have little power; Egger, Begg and Thompson-Sharp tests and funnel plots did not show asymmetry.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against the placebo arms of the psychedelic trials, mostly PTSD trials for MDMA, high-dose MDMA reduced depressive symptoms by about 5 HAMD-17 points, above the 3-point threshold; against the placebo response seen in escitalopram trials, reached only indirectly through one psilocybin trial and across different populations, the difference was about 1.5 points with a credible interval including zero; no excess of discontinuation or severe adverse events.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions concern psilocybin; for MDMA the authors' reading is that its benefit is not distinguishable from the placebo response in antidepressant trials, from which they infer that effects in psychedelic trials may be overestimated because of unsuccessful blinding. This inference rests on the assumption that the antidepressant-trial placebo response represents what adequately blinded psychedelic trials would show, an assumption that cannot be tested in these data, while MDMA's trials differed from escitalopram's in diagnosis, therapy and outcome scale.

timeline.event: Ko et al. meta-analysis of psychedelic therapy for depressive symptoms reports large standardized effects (1.37 to 3.12), which this review sets out to correct for unblinding (cited as background; not read).
This network meta-analysis (BMJ, 21 August 2024).

replication.where_it_stands: The only network meta-analysis read here that places MDMA among other depression treatments. Its MDMA estimates concern depressive symptoms in mostly PTSD trials of one sponsor; it can be cited for the size of the difference against the trials' own placebo arms and for the uncertainty that appears once that placebo is replaced, through the network, by the placebo response of antidepressant trials.

funding.funder: National Science and Technology Council, Taiwan (NSTC 112-2314-B-016-036-MY2 and NSTC 112-2314-B-002-210-MY3); the funder had no role in the study.
funding.declared_conflicts: ICMJE forms: support from the National Science and Technology Council for the submitted work; no financial relationships with organisations that might have an interest in the work in the previous three years; no other relationships or activities.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Taiwanese hospitals and universities, the University of Greenwich and Deakin University; none ran the included trials.

what_would_settle_it: Randomized trials of MDMA-assisted therapy in people whose primary diagnosis is major depressive disorder, with an active placebo, measured blinding and expectancy, and ideally a direct comparison with an antidepressant or an established psychotherapy.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults with depressive symptoms; psychedelics and escitalopram; placebo nodes; depression change, discontinuation, severe adverse events.
PROSPERO CRD42023469014; protocol changes are explained in appendix 5, not read.
Randomized trials only, first period of crossover trials to avoid carry-over.
Four databases and two trial registries without language restriction, grey literature and reference lists; consultation of experts not described.
Two authors independently, with a third for disagreements.
Two authors independently, each reviewed by another author.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: reasons for the 26 full-text exclusions are said to be in appendix 3, which was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: study characteristics are in etable 1 of the appendix, not read; the article gives only aggregate characteristics.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 2 by two authors independently. No psychedelic trial was judged at high risk overall, although the review's own premise is that unblinding biases these trials; the authors address unblinding through separate placebo nodes instead.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Provisional: not in the article; possibly in etable 1 (not read).

Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis with transitivity checks, global and local inconsistency tests and convergence checks; the separation of placebo nodes is explicit. For MDMA, comparisons with the antidepressant-trial nodes depend on a single head-to-head psilocybin trial.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: A sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk studies was run, though no study was rated high; results similar.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Unblinding is the organising concern of the interpretation.
Network meta-regression on effect modifiers; major depressive disorder subgroup; differences between MDMA (PTSD) and escitalopram (MDD) populations discussed.
Comparison-adjusted funnel plots and Egger, Begg and Thompson-Sharp tests, with their limited power discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding and ICMJE declarations given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: three items (7, 8 and 10) could be judged only from the appendix, which was not read; if appendix 3 lacks a list of excluded studies, confidence falls to low. No critical item is known to fail. AMSTAR 2 does not capture the main limit for MDMA, which is indirectness: the MDMA trials concern depressive symptoms in people with PTSD (and anxiety with a life-threatening illness), with intensive psychotherapy, and their comparison with antidepressant-trial placebo responses is entirely indirect through one psilocybin trial. Cite it for MDMA's estimates as printed, with that framing.

key_findings.finding: 19 eligible studies: 15 psychedelic trials with 811 participants (mean age 42.5, 54.2% women) and 5 escitalopram trials with 1968 participants (one head-to-head trial counted in both); search to 12 October 2023 without language restriction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Characteristics of included study; Methods › Data sources and searches

key_findings.finding: Dose categories for MDMA: high 100 mg or more, extremely low 40 mg or less, low in between, based on two three-arm trials in which 125 mg was the high dose and 30 to 40 mg the active control.

Against the placebo arms of psychedelic trials (HAMD-17 points): high-dose MDMA 5.32 (95% CrI 2.26 to 8.32), SMD 0.42; low-dose MDMA 4.92 (−0.26 to 9.94), SMD 0.73; extremely low-dose MDMA 2.11 (−1.63 to 5.71), SMD 0.29.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 2, upper panel (values printed in the figure image)
key_findings.note: Read from the figure image of the PMC article, which prints the estimates beside the forest plot.

key_findings.finding: Against the placebo arms of escitalopram trials: high-dose MDMA 1.53 (−2.79 to 5.78), SMD 0.08; low-dose 1.13 (−4.85 to 7.00), SMD 0.14; extremely low dose −1.68 (−6.49 to 3.20), SMD −0.18. Only high-dose psilocybin (6.52, 3.19 to 9.57) and escitalopram 10 and 20 mg (1.86 and 1.82, intervals excluding zero) differed from this reference.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 2, middle panel (values printed in the figure image); Results › Network meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Against extremely low-dose psilocybin: high-dose MDMA 1.36 (−3.08 to 5.84), low-dose 0.96 (−5.11 to 6.96), extremely low-dose −1.85 (−6.76 to 3.02). High-dose psilocybin against high-dose MDMA 4.98 (1.23 to 8.67), SMD 0.32.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 2, lower panel (values printed in the figure image); Results › Network meta-analysis, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The placebo response in antidepressant trials exceeded that in psychedelic trials by 3.79 HAMD-17 points (0.77 to 6.80), SMD 0.2; the authors treat this as evidence that placebo arms of psychedelic trials do worse because of unsuccessful blinding.
key_findings.locator: Results › Network meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results › Transitivity assumption

key_findings.finding: No intervention was associated with more all-cause discontinuation or severe adverse events than placebo in psychedelic trials.
key_findings.locator: Results › All cause discontinuation and severe adverse event

key_findings.finding: In the MDMA trials, participants' accuracy in guessing their arm ranged from about 60% to 90% (citing Mithoefer 2018, Ot'alora 2018, Mitchell 2021, Mithoefer 2011 and Wolfson 2020).
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations: only acute effects extracted; participants in the MDMA trials were predominantly diagnosed with PTSD whereas escitalopram trials enrolled people with major depressive disorder; few psychedelic trials; extremely low doses may not be pure placebos; biases in the single head-to-head trial can propagate through the network.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Strengths and limitations of this study, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias (RoB 2): no psychedelic trial (0 of 15) and no escitalopram trial (0 of 5) at high overall risk; GRADE certainty for most comparisons moderate or low (efigure 13, not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias of the included studies; Results › Network meta-regression and publication bias

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives high-dose psilocybin against the antidepressant-trial placebo response as 6.45 (3.19 to 9.41), while the Results text and Fig. 2 give 6.52 (3.19 to 9.57).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract, Results; Results › Network meta-analysis, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite the Results and Fig. 2 values.

reporting_issues.issue: Risk-of-bias percentages are miscounted: high risk in randomization is printed as 0% with k = 15 (it should be k = 0), and some concerns in selection of the reported result as 67% with k = 1 (1 of 15 is 7%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Risk of bias of the included studies)
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the distribution (0 high, 1 some concerns, 14 low) can be read from the counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Standardized mean differences are not comparable between rows: in Fig. 2, low-dose MDMA's 4.92 points corresponds to SMD 0.73 and high-dose MDMA's larger 5.32 points to 0.42, and the placebo-response difference of 3.79 points to 0.20, so each standardization uses a different standard deviation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the HAMD-17 point differences, not the SMDs, to compare treatments; the text's 'large to small' change for psilocybin also mixes standardizations.

reporting_issues.issue: The first phase 3 MDMA trial (Mitchell et al., 2021) is cited as its 2023 reprint in Focus rather than the original article, and the second phase 3 trial (Mitchell et al., 2023, published in September 2023, before the search date) is not cited at all; which MDMA trials entered the network is shown only in etable 1 (not read).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (references 38 to 40; Discussion › Comparison with other studies, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The composition of the MDMA evidence cannot be confirmed from the article; the senior author may wish to save the appendix.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC11337322 (all sections, figure legends, contributors, funding, competing interests, reference list); Fig. 2 read as the image the PMC article links to (https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/9a3f/11337322/15ffa467d0a6/hsut078607.f2.jpg), whose printed estimates were transcribed; Figs. 1 and 3 not read for values; the web appendix (PDF, 4.8 MB) was not opened. Crossref record read in this reader's tab.

design_detail: Critical narrative review (Annual Review of Psychology 76:143-165; read as the NIH author manuscript in PMC) of the therapeutic evidence for ketamine, MDMA, psilocybin and LSD, by four addiction and drug-policy researchers (Stanford/VA, Oregon Health & Science University, University of Queensland). No search strategy; explicit minimum standard for the evidence discussed: randomized trials in people with diagnosed disorders with more than 15 participants per condition. For MDMA only the two phase 3 PTSD trials meet it. Includes 'warnings to the wise' boxes on hype, bias and money, a section on mechanisms, and a policy section on regulation, including Australia's 2023 decision. No retracted source is cited.
can_establish: What a critical review applying a minimum standard concludes about the therapeutic evidence for MDMA and other psychedelics, which MDMA trials meet that standard, and which design weaknesses (blinding, expectancy, enrolment, follow-up) it identifies.
cannot_establish: Completeness (no systematic search), the size of any effect (no pooling), or anything about MDMA for indications other than PTSD, for which no trial met the standard and none is discussed.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The evidence for MDMA comprises the two phase 3 trials (Mitchell et al., 2021, 2023).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Randomized controlled trials of people with diagnosed disorders with more than 15 participants in each condition; open-label trials and trials with failed or unassessed blinding included with cautions; claims about consciousness, creativity or social goals excluded; ayahuasca, mescaline, ibogaine and DMT judged to lack enough high-quality evidence to review (Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 3rd paragraph; Definitions and Scope, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors under a stated threshold, without a search; the threshold excludes all MDMA studies outside the two phase 3 PTSD trials.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As described for the first phase 3 trial: three sessions of MDMA (80 to 180 mg per session) 4 weeks apart (study conditions as reported by the review).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None computed; results described in words, with the MAPP2 blinding figures and severe adverse event percentages.
analysis.selective_reporting: The review discusses only trials meeting its threshold, by design.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors argue that meta-analyses of very small trials inflate effects.

interpretation_gap.results_show: For MDMA, two sponsor-run phase 3 trials found larger falls in PTSD scores than placebo with the same therapy; blinding was not tested in the first, failed in the second, and expectancy may account for some or all of the difference; severe adverse events were more frequent on MDMA in the second.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review concludes that MDMA for PTSD is a positive signal that warrants replication in stronger studies and should not be taken as definitive. This is consistent with its own appraisal. Its prediction that approval was likely was overtaken before print (see reporting issues), and its policy section states predictions as near-certainties.

timeline.event: First phase 3 trial (MAPP1).
Burke and Blumberger's commentary raises the expectancy concern that this review cites.
Second phase 3 trial (MAPP2), the first with a blinding survey.
13 August 2024: the BMJ reports the FDA's rejection of the application and three retractions (Mahase, 2024); this review, published online in December 2024, still predicts approval.

replication.where_it_stands: A critical narrative review that may be cited for its argument and its threshold-based finding that only the two phase 3 PTSD trials qualified for MDMA; claims resting only on it stay at draft (METHODS §6.3).

funding.funder: Acknowledgements: Keith Humphreys, Esther Ting Memorial Professorship and grants from the Department of Veterans Affairs, the National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Wu Tsai Neurosciences Institute; Todd Korthuis, NIDA grant UG1DA015815; Wayne Hall, emeritus professor at a centre with core funding from the Australian Commonwealth Department of Health.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported in the author manuscript (no disclosure statement printed).
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are addiction and drug-policy researchers who have written critically about medical cannabis; their own papers are cited for the policy arguments, not for the efficacy evidence.

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered, independently run trials of MDMA-assisted therapy with active placebos, measured expectancy and blinding, representative participants (fewer with prior psychedelic experience) and long-term follow-up, in PTSD and in any other proposed indication.

domains.note: Explicit, reproducible threshold for the evidence discussed, but no search strategy, databases or dates.
Each trial discussed is appraised for blinding, sample size, comparator, expectancy and follow-up.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors' own work is cited for arguments about hype and policy, not for the efficacy evidence.

The evidence sections are cautious, but the policy section states predictions as near-certainties (post-approval practice will resemble the medical cannabis industry) and attributes Australia's decision to lobbying without cited evidence.

domains.domain: Balance of the case for and against efficacy (the trialists' replies to the expectancy critique are not presented)
domains.note: The positive trial results are reported, but counter-arguments from the trialists are not; the review is avowedly sceptical.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3). This is a careful critical review with an explicit threshold, useful for its appraisal of design weaknesses and for the observation that, for MDMA, only the two sponsor-run PTSD phase 3 trials met a modest standard. It is not a systematic synthesis and gives no effect sizes; claims citing it alone stay at draft.

key_findings.finding: Minimum standard for the evidence discussed: randomized controlled trials of people with diagnosed disorders, with more than 15 participants in each condition; open-label trials and trials whose blinding was not assessed or failed are discussed with cautions.
key_findings.locator: Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: As an illustration of the evidence base, Kisely et al.'s (2023) meta-analysis of psilocybin and MDMA screened 837 studies and found 14 randomized trials, only one with at least 30 participants and none demonstrating successful blinding.
key_findings.locator: Minimal research quality standards imposed in this review, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: For MDMA the review discusses only the two phase 3 PTSD trials, run by a consortium assembled and funded by MAPS, which the review calls an advocacy organization; no MDMA trial in another indication meets its standard.
key_findings.locator: Safety and Effectiveness of Psychedelic Drugs › MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 1st paragraph; Definitions and Scope, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: First trial: the mean CAPS-5 change was significantly larger with MDMA, but blinding was not formally tested; the trial's argument that at least 10% guessed their arm wrongly implies that up to 90% could have guessed it, which raises the concern that expectancy biased the results (citing Burke and Blumberger, 2021; Flameling et al., 2023).
key_findings.locator: MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Second trial (53 MDMA, 51 placebo): severe adverse events in 9.4% on MDMA against 3.9% on placebo; large decreases in CAPS-5 in both groups, larger with MDMA; blinding assessed formally: 75% on placebo and 94.2% on MDMA correctly guessed their assignment, so expectancy may account for some or all of the difference; an ICER report argued that enrolment may have been skewed toward people with strong faith in MDMA.
key_findings.locator: MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: 'Severe' refers to graded severity, not to serious adverse events.

key_findings.finding: Summary: MDMA for PTSD is one of the positive signals; because of absent successful blinding and likely expectancy effects, none of these signals should be taken as definitive without replication in methodologically stronger studies, all of which warrant such replication.
key_findings.locator: Summary of Effectiveness Evidence for Psychedelic Medicines, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: On dependence: apart from ketamine and perhaps MDMA, psychedelic drugs do not seem to have significant addictive liability; MDMA is described as possibly addictive.
key_findings.locator: Definitions and Scope, 1st paragraph; Word to the Wise #5 (box)

key_findings.finding: Australia's Therapeutic Goods Administration in 2023 allowed authorized psychiatrists to prescribe MDMA for PTSD (and psilocybin for intractable depression) under its Special Access Scheme, a decision the review says went against the advice of the TGA's own expert panel and was opposed by the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists and the Australian Psychological Society.
key_findings.locator: Policy Implications › Australia as a case study in regulatory failure, 1st and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Research priorities: better blinding with assessment and reporting of expectancy and blinding in every trial; more representative participants (about half of trial patients have used psychedelics, against about 10% of the general population, per Nayak et al., 2023, and Krebs and Johansen, 2013); longer follow-ups.

reporting_issues.issue: The MDMA section predicts that FDA approval was likely in the near future; the FDA had rejected the application by 13 August 2024, when the BMJ reported it (mahase_2024), months before this review was published online (December 2024) and in print (January 2025), and the text was not updated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 5th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The regulatory statement is outdated; it does not affect the appraisal of the trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The first trial's therapy is described as 3 hours of manualized therapy before the first dose and three weekly 90-minute sessions after each dosing session; the trial report, as carded by the project, describes three 90-minute preparatory sessions and three 90-minute integration sessions after each experimental session (sc_mitchell_2021).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (MDMA for post-traumatic stress disorder, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor second-hand inaccuracy; cite the trial report for the design.

cannot_establish: What the ethical violation was, how it affected the data, or whether the analysis's conclusions hold: the notice gives none of this, and it says the journal's investigation of the human-subjects ethics questions was inconclusive.

interpretation_gap.results_show: An editorial decision: the authors asked in early 2024 to remove four MP-4 participants treated by a pair of therapists involved in an ethical violation that caused a protocol deviation; the journal and Wiley investigated, agreed to a correction and issued the expression of concern because the authors' failure to report the violation at submission was judged improper, while the investigation of human-subjects ethics was inconclusive.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The notice claims nothing beyond its grounds; it states that all authors agree with it.

timeline.event: October 2018: report from Chesapeake IRB (now Advarra) to MAPS Public Benefit Corporation (now Lykos Therapeutics) on the ethical violation, as the notice reports.
May 2019: the violation is publicly announced; December 2019: the article is submitted without notifying the journal (per the notice).
March 2022: Advarra's follow-up report finds that the deviation and violation occurred during the trial as well as during the long-term follow-up (per the notice).

Early 2024: the authors contact the journal (per the notice). 10 August 2024: Psychopharmacology retracts three other phase 2 analyses of the same sponsor; Jerome, Mithoefer and Feduccia, authors of this article, are authors of all three (author lists in the Crossref records of the retraction notes feduccia_2024, jerome_2024 and mithoefer_2024).
3 December 2024: this expression of concern and the correction (jts_2025b) are published.

replication.where_it_stands: In force. The article is not retracted and may be cited, with the notice, for its corrected figures (sc_jts_2025b); the notice itself may be cited for the journal's decision and the timeline it states.

funding.funder: Not applicable (notice).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not applicable. The notice states that MAPS Public Benefit Corporation (now Lykos Therapeutics) received the IRB reports and finalized a clinical study report before the authors contacted the journal.
funding.affiliations_note: The two therapists involved were not co-authors of the article (per the notice).

what_would_settle_it: Publication of the IRB findings and of the sponsor's clinical study report for MP-4, and an independent reanalysis of the pooled phase 2 data with the affected site's data handled transparently.

The notice relies on reports the authors shared and does not describe the violation or its effect on the data.
