States the decision, its grounds and the dates without speculation.

domains.domain: Balance of the parties' accounts (the authors' account at submission and the IRB's later findings are both given)
domains.note: The notice gives the authors' account at submission (violation thought to have occurred after treatment) and the March 2022 finding that it occurred during the trial as well.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to an editorial notice; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used, its domains read as questions about the notice as a source. It is the primary record of the expression of concern and may be cited for the decision, its grounds and its dates; it gives no account of the violation itself.

key_findings.finding: Expression of concern for Ponte et al. (2021), issued by agreement between the Editor-in-Chief, the International Society for Traumatic Stress Studies and Wiley; published 3 December 2024 (Journal of Traumatic Stress 38(3):555).
key_findings.locator: Notice header; 2nd paragraph (the first after the citation of the article)

key_findings.finding: The authors asked the journal to remove the data of 4 participants of the MP-4 study (NCT01958593, October 2014 to October 2016), in which an ethical violation by a pair of therapists, who treated 4 of the 6 MP-4 participants included, caused a deviation from the protocol; neither therapist was a co-author.

Timeline given by the notice: a report from Chesapeake IRB (now Advarra) to MAPS Public Benefit Corporation (now Lykos Therapeutics) in October 2018; public announcement of the violation in May 2019; submission of the article in December 2019 without notifying the journal, the violation being described at the time as having occurred after treatment, during long-term follow-up, and all participants being included under the intention-to-treat principle; Advarra's March 2022 follow-up report found that it had occurred during the trial as well; the authors contacted the journal in early 2024, after a compliance review by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of British Columbia and the finalization of the sponsor's clinical study report.

Decision: all data provided by the two therapists are removed by correction (10.1002/jts.23098); the expression of concern is issued because the authors' conduct in not initially reporting the violation was judged improper, while the investigation into violations of Wiley's and the journal's ethical guidelines on human-subjects research proved inconclusive; all authors agree with the notice.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice refers to the 4 MP-4 participants as 4 of 6 'included in the MP-4 study', while the correction says 4 of 6 MP-4 participants 'out of the 68 participants included in the pooled analysis'; the article's pooled sample was 63.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Notice, 2nd paragraph); correction, Description and explanation
reporting_issues.consequence: The denominator of 68 in the correction is unexplained (see sc_jts_2025b).

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12416979 (the whole notice), read with the article (PMC8453707) and the correction (publisher HTML, free access). Crossref record read in this reader's tab: no authors; update-to link to 10.1002/jts.22696 of type expression_of_concern.

design_detail: Correction notice with a reanalysis, not a new study: 'Correction to Sleep Quality Improvements After MDMA-Assisted Psychotherapy for the Treatment of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder', Journal of Traumatic Stress 38(3), pp. 557-569 (first published 3 December 2024; free access on Wiley Online Library; no authors listed in Crossref). It lists each change made to Ponte et al. (2021) after removing the 4 MP-4 participants treated by the two therapists involved in an ethical violation: revised abstract figures, methods text, Tables 1 to 3, Figures 1 to 3 (images, not read for values), Discussion sentences and the supplementary table. Card design 'narrative-review' follows the project's precedent for errata (sc_fda_2024b); the reanalysed results it reports inherit the risk-of-bias appraisal of the study (sc_ponte_2021, RoB 2 high). Reference id assigned by this reader (journal abbreviation and print year).
can_establish: The corrected figures of the pooled sleep analysis without the four affected participants, and which results and methods changed.
cannot_establish: Whether the remaining data are unaffected by the sponsor's handling of the MP-4 site, or why the model specification was changed beyond the removal of data; the correction gives no reason for either.

sample.recruitment: As in Ponte et al. (2021); four MP-4 participants removed.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As in Ponte et al. (2021).
sample.demographics: Corrected Table 1: mean age 40.62 (SD 11.74); 31 men (52.5%); 86.4% White; mean PTSD duration 231.64 months; combat trauma 37.3%, sexual assault 33.9%, child abuse 23.7%, accident 11.9%, other 45.8%; lifetime suicidal ideation 86.4%; earlier ecstasy use 30.5%.
sample.attrition: Corrected blinded-endpoint analysis: 14 controls and 44 active participants for CAPS-IV and PSQI (Table 2 note a); open-label analysis N = 58.
sample.selection_effects: Removal of the participants of one therapist pair; the removed four included the only participants given 0 mg, so no inactive placebo remains in the comparison.

exposure.measurement: As in Ponte et al. (2021).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: control doses revised from 0 to 40 mg to 25 to 40 mg MDMA; active doses unchanged (75 to 125 mg).
exposure.polysubstance: As in Ponte et al. (2021).

comparison.controls: Low-dose MDMA (25, 30 or 40 mg) with the same psychotherapy; the 'placebo/control' label is replaced by 'control' throughout.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: PSQI and CAPS-IV, as in Ponte et al. (2021).
outcomes.operationalization: As in Ponte et al. (2021).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, as in the original.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: As in Ponte et al. (2021).

analysis.effect_sizes: Corrected blinded endpoint: CAPS-IV change −34.93 (SD 26.66) against −11.07 (16.85), p = .003, Hedges' g 0.96 (95% CI 0.33 to 1.59); PSQI change −3.51 (5.08) against +0.50 (3.25), p = .008, g 0.85 (0.23 to 1.47); sleep quality component g 0.96 (0.33 to 1.59), sleep latency 0.70 (0.08 to 1.32), daytime dysfunction 1.21 (0.57 to 1.85), the other four components with intervals including zero. 3-point PSQI drop: 24 active (53.3%) against 2 controls (14.3%), χ2 6.85, N = 57, p = .008. Open-label (N = 58): PSQI least-squares means 12.59, 8.18 and 7.09; treatment exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029; CAPS-IV 88.22, 42.46 and 35.28; exit to 12 months −7.18 (SE 2.60), p = .008; CAPS-IV and PSQI change correlated r = .372 (n = 54).
analysis.covariates: The base mixed model now has time as the only fixed effect (baseline CAPS-IV and study removed); no candidate covariate met the p ≤ .01 cut-off (age no longer retained).
analysis.preregistration_detail: As in the original: analyses not preregistered.
analysis.selective_reporting: The subgroup result (a 3-point PSQI drop at the primary endpoint associated with lower CAPS-IV at treatment exit and 12 months) is removed because it was no longer significant at treatment exit; the 12-month result is not reported. The change of model specification is described but not explained.
analysis.power: Not addressed.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After removing four participants, the blinded comparison still favours full-dose over low-dose MDMA on self-reported sleep (about 4 PSQI points, g 0.85, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.47) and on CAPS-IV; the 12-month open-label figures are similar to the original; one subgroup result and the age covariate are no longer significant; the comparator is now low-dose MDMA only.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The correction states that removing the data does not compromise the conclusions, and that directionality and interpretation are unaffected.

timeline.event: Original article (Ponte et al., 2021, published online 10 June 2021).
This correction and the expression of concern (jts_2025a), 3 December 2024.

replication.where_it_stands: The corrected figures replace the original ones for any citation of the sleep analysis; they remain subject to the study's high risk of bias and to the expression of concern.

funding.funder: Not applicable (correction).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not stated in the correction; see the original article's author note (all authors paid by MAPS or MAPS PBC).
funding.affiliations_note: No authors are listed for the correction; its text ends with an apology in the first person plural.

what_would_settle_it: A trial-by-trial reporting of the sleep outcome, the reasons for the change of model, and an independent reanalysis of the pooled data; ultimately a prespecified sleep outcome in an independently run, adequately blinded trial.

domains.note: Not a review; the correction lists changes to one article.

Read as a question about the correction's own documentation: each change is listed, but the change of model specification is not explained and the corrected trauma-type rows of Table 1 cannot follow from removing four participants.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Concerns only the article it corrects (and revises figures quoted from the authors' own pooled phase 2 analysis).
Asserts that the conclusions are not compromised while a subgroup result and a covariate result disappear.

domains.note: Stresses unchanged directionality; the loss of the 12-month subgroup result is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a correction notice; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used as a check on how the correction documents its changes. The corrected results themselves are those of the pooled analysis, appraised on sc_ponte_2021 with RoB 2 (overall high). Cite the corrected numbers from this notice, never the original ones, together with the expression of concern.

key_findings.finding: Reason: during MP-4 (NCT01958593, October 2014 to October 2016) an ethical violation by a pair of therapists with one of the participants caused a protocol deviation; the pair treated 4 of the 6 MP-4 participants, whose data are removed. Sample revised from 63 to 59 (active 47 to 45; control 16 to 14), the control range from 0 to 40 mg to 25 to 40 mg, because the removed participants were the only ones on 0 mg (placebo).

key_findings.finding: Corrected PSQI components: sleep quality +0.29 against −0.65 (p = .003), sleep latency +0.29 against −0.33 (p = .027), daytime dysfunction +0.21 against −0.86 (p < .001); duration, efficiency, disturbance and use of sleep medication with intervals including zero.

reporting_issues.issue: The correction says the pair of therapists treated 4 of 6 MP-4 participants 'out of the 68 participants included in the pooled analysis reported in the original manuscript', but the original analysis included 63 participants, and 63 minus 4 is the corrected 59.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Description and explanation for this correction, 1st paragraph; new supplementary text)
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure of 68 is unexplained; the counts 63 and 59 are the ones consistent with the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The corrected Table 1 trauma-type counts cannot result from removing four participants: combat falls from 45 of 63 (16 controls, 29 active) to 22 of 59 (8 and 14), 'other' from 44 to 27, sexual assault from 29 to 20 and child abuse from 19 to 14, each a fall of more than 4; the other rows of Table 1 (sex, race, prior ecstasy use, suicidality) change by no more than the four removed people allow. The zopiclone row of Table 1 is also missing from the corrected table.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (corrected Table 1; Sample characteristics, revised text) against PMC HTML (original Table 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the original or the corrected trauma data are wrong; the sample's trauma profile (for example, the share with combat trauma) cannot be cited from either version.

reporting_issues.issue: The correction describes the revised insomnia figures as reflecting updates to Mithoefer et al. (2019) 'in an ongoing correction update', although that paper had been retracted on 10 August 2024, four months before the correction was published.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Summary of corrections made, Discussion, 4th paragraph change)
reporting_issues.consequence: The insomnia figures come from a retracted analysis and must not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The corrected 3-point response footnote gives 24 (53.3%) and 19 (42.2%) of the active group (percentages of 45, counts adding to 43) while the table gives n = 44; the χ2 of 6.85 could not be reproduced from the printed counts (editors' calculation 7.34 without and 5.76 with continuity correction).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (corrected Table 2, notes a and b)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the counts (24 and 2) with their denominators; the test statistic is uncertain.

design_detail: Investigator-initiated, open-label, single-group phase 2 proof-of-principle trial (EudraCT 2021-000805-26; protocol published as Kvam et al., 2022) at Østfold Hospital Trust, Norway, recruiting January 2023 to May 2024: 12 adults with moderate to severe major depressive disorder received three 90-minute preparatory sessions, two all-day MDMA sessions about 4 weeks apart with an overnight stay, telephone follow-up and three 90-minute integration sessions after each, with an inner-directed MDMA-assisted therapy approach; primary outcome the change in clinician-rated MADRS from baseline to about 8 weeks after the second MDMA session (about 12 weeks after baseline), secondary the Sheehan Disability Scale. A corrigendum (Kvam et al., 2026; card sc_kvam_2026a) corrects one participant's post-treatment MADRS score; this card gives the corrected values. Funded by the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority; Lykos Therapeutics provided the MDMA and an unconditional grant. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest, appraised with ROBINS-I.
can_establish: That two open-label MDMA sessions within a structured psychotherapy programme could be given to 12 people with major depressive disorder without dropouts or serious adverse events, and how far their clinician-rated depression and functional impairment fell over about 12 weeks.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA, the eleven or so psychotherapy sessions, expectation (participants were almost all self-referred), regression to the mean (entry required a MADRS of at least 20 at baseline) or natural fluctuation produced the fall (no control group, raters not blind); whether improvement lasts (reported separately at 7 months); rare harms; or effects in people with psychotic features, bipolar disorder, personality disorders, substance use disorders, serious suicide risk or cardiovascular risk, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Self-referrals and referrals from general practitioners, psychiatrists or psychotherapists; 11 of the 12 self-referred and 1 was referred by a study therapist; no referral from other professionals was eligible (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph). Fig. 1 (read from the figure image): 86 telephone-screened, 65 excluded after telephone screening, 21 screened, 6 screening failures, 15 enrolled, 3 early terminations before dosing, 12 completed dosing session 1 and the primary end point.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: DSM-5 major depressive disorder, single or recurrent, without psychotic features, current episode longer than 12 weeks and shorter than 2 years; MADRS of 20 or more at enrolment and again at the baseline visit (V3); age 18 or older. Excluded: psychotic disorders, mania, personality disorders, eating disorders with purging, substance use disorders, serious suicide risk, pregnancy, recent electroconvulsive therapy or ketamine, and medical conditions made risky by raised blood pressure or heart rate (Method › Participants, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Procedures, 2nd paragraph). The EU register adds the exclusion of people who had used ecstasy more than 10 times in 10 years or at all within 6 months of the first session, or had been in a MAPS-sponsored MDMA trial (registry record).
sample.demographics: 7 women and 5 men; mean age 44.1 (SD 9.2); 11 White, 1 Asian; 2 of non-Norwegian origin; mean 18.6 years of education; 11 with recurrent MDD, mean 16.1 years (10.4) since the first episode; baseline MADRS 29.6 (4.9), 10 moderate and 2 severe; comorbid PTSD 3 (25.0%) and ADHD 3 (25.0%); previous antidepressants 9 (75.0%), 8 tapering ongoing psychotropic medicines; previous psychological treatments 5.5 courses (3.3) and 223.1 sessions (333.9; median 88.5); 7 on sick leave in the past 3 months; previous MDMA use 1 (8.3%) (Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Three of 15 enrolled stopped before dosing (reasons not given in this paper, which refers to the protocol article); no early terminations, dropouts or losses after dosing; all 12 dosed reached the primary end point (Fig. 1; Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Almost all self-referred, highly educated and with long histories of psychotherapy; the authors note that self-referral may have raised expectations and exaggerated the pre–post differences (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Analysis is of the 12 who were dosed, not the 15 enrolled.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to all: three 90-minute preparatory sessions and a baseline visit; psychotropic medicines tapered after enrolment; two MDMA sessions about 4 weeks apart, each about 8 hours with a pair of therapists, ended by a study physician's assessment, with an overnight stay; four telephone calls in the following week and three 90-minute integration sessions over the next 4 weeks; therapists were three psychologists and a psychiatrist (three trained for a sponsored PTSD trial); adherence to the therapy manual was not rated (Method › Procedures, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 7th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: first session an initial dose of 80 mg MDMA, second session 120 mg (all participants accepted the increase), each with a supplemental half of the initial dose offered 90 to 120 minutes later; all but one participant took the supplement in both sessions (Method › Procedures, 3rd paragraph). The route is not stated in this paper.
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorders were excluded; AUDIT and DUDIT did not change (3.3 to 3.3; 0.6 to 0.1); no adverse events related to MDMA use outside the study were reported (Table 2; Results › Safety, 6th paragraph). During the treatment period six participants took psychotropic medicines for other conditions (two resumed lisdexamfetamine; others hydroxyzine, zopiclone, alimemazine or oxazepam; one codeine for a rib fracture), and two received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for adverse events (Results › Safety, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; ongoing psychotropic medicines were tapered after enrolment in 8 of 12 (Table 1).

comparison.controls: None: change from the baseline visit to the outcome visit about 8 weeks after the second MDMA session.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (single group).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; the authors state that without a control group they cannot tell whether the response was due to the treatment, expectancy or natural fluctuation (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Primary: MADRS (clinician-rated). Secondary: Sheehan Disability Scale (SDS). Exploratory: BDI-II, Bergen Insomnia Scale, PCL-5, GAD-7, AUDIT, DUDIT; responders (MADRS reduction of 50% or more) and remitters (MADRS 12 or less). Safety: adverse events recorded by the therapists with the sub-investigator; treatment-emergent adverse events and psychotropic co-medication during and for 2 days after dosing and through treatment; C-SSRS, any deterioration from baseline being recorded as an adverse event; adverse events of special interest (cardiac, serious suicidal ideation or behaviour, abuse potential); blood pressure, heart rate and temperature before each dose and at the end of sessions (Method › Outcome measures, 1st to 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments. MADRS raters were affiliated with the hospital but not the study team; not fully blinded, though said to be largely unaware whether an assessment was before or after treatment (Method › Procedures, 5th paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Mean change from baseline to the outcome visit, tested with the two-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test, with 95% CIs from 4,000 bootstrap resamples of the mean change; a mixed-effects model for repeated BDI-II (Method › Statistics, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Ten pre–post tests in Table 2 (MADRS, SDS total and two SDS items, BDI-II, GAD-7, PCL-5, BIS, AUDIT, DUDIT) plus the BDI-II mixed model.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Open label. The authors say raters were neither completely independent nor blinded, so rater bias may have inflated the MADRS change; adverse events were reported to the therapy team, which may have led to under-reporting (Discussion, 7th paragraph).

analysis.effect_sizes: Corrected values (corrigendum): MADRS 29.6 (SD 4.9) at baseline and 10.3 (8.3) at the outcome visit; mean change −19.3 (SD 8.3; s.e. 2.4), bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7, z = −3.06, P < 0.001 (the original article printed the outcome as 9.7, SD 10.0). Among the 9 without comorbid PTSD, mean change −18.1 (8.8). SDS 21.3 (6.1) to 9.7 (9.2), change −11.7 (SD 7.6), CI −7.6 to −15.8, P = 0.001. Responders 9 of 12 (75.0%) and remitters 9 of 12 (75.0%). Exploratory: BDI-II 33.5 to 12.0 (−21.5; −14.0 to −29.0); GAD-7 13.8 to 6.0 (printed difference −9.0); PCL-5 36.4 to 25.4 (−11.0; −2.4 to −19.6); BIS 28.9 to 12.6 (−16.3); BDI-II mixed model −0.19 points per day (95% CI −0.24 to −0.15) (Results › Primary outcome; Secondary outcome; Exploratory analysis; Table 2; corrigendum). Within-group changes only; no comparison exists.
analysis.preregistration_detail: EU Clinical Trials Register, EudraCT 2021-000805-26: record first entered 4 August 2021, ethics opinion 25 June 2021, competent authority decision 19 November 2021, before recruitment (January 2023); an open-label phase 2 feasibility study sponsored by Østfold Hospital Trust; main objective the mean change in MADRS from visit 4 (baseline) to visit 13 (about 12 weeks after baseline); secondary endpoint feasibility measured by a 15-item subjective-effects visual analogue scale; status ongoing, no results posted (registry record, read on clinicaltrialsregister.eu on 2026-10-17). The article reports SDS as its secondary outcome and does not report the registered subjective-effects scale; it takes baseline MADRS at visit 3; it calls safety and feasibility the primary objectives. The protocol article (2022) was not read.
analysis.selective_reporting: Adverse-event lists, vital signs and suicidal-ideation trajectories are only in the supplementary files (PDF, Word and PowerPoint downloads), not read; the registered subjective-effects endpoint is not reported.
analysis.power: No power calculation; a proof-of-principle sample of 12.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 12 people with moderate to severe, mostly recurrent depression, clinician-rated depression fell from about 30 to about 10 on the MADRS some 8 weeks after the second of two open-label MDMA sessions within an intensive psychotherapy programme; 9 of 12 met both response and remission thresholds and functional impairment fell. No one dropped out after dosing and there were no serious adverse events, but six participants had a worsening in the intensity of suicidal ideation recorded as adverse events and two needed benzodiazepines and zopiclone after dosing. There is no comparison group, the raters knew everyone had been treated, and expectations were probably high, so none of the change can be attributed to MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the study provided "indications of efficacy" (Abstract › Conclusion). The Discussion says the authors demonstrated that MDMA-assisted therapy can be safely administered to people with major depressive disorder (Discussion, 1st paragraph) and compares the 9 of 12 responders and remitters with the loss of PTSD diagnosis in 67% and 71% of the MDMA arms of the two phase 3 trials (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), a comparison across designs, outcomes and populations; it attributes part of the improvement to participants' work on traumatic material, which is not tested (Discussion, 2nd paragraph). The Limitations state that without a control group the response cannot be attributed to the treatment rather than to expectancy or natural fluctuation, and that the trial cannot draw conclusions about efficacy (Discussion, 7th and 8th paragraphs).

timeline.event: Kvam et al., Front Psychiatry: the study protocol (on the project's evidence map; not read here).
This proof-of-principle trial (online 11 July 2025).
Kvam et al., Br J Psychiatry: corrigendum correcting one participant's post-treatment MADRS score (card sc_kvam_2026a).
Kvam et al., J Psychiatr Res: seven-month follow-up of the same 12 participants (on ScienceDirect, not readable in this session; not read).
Ai et al. and Kvam et al., Br J Psychiatry: a commentary on this trial and the authors' reply (on the project's evidence map; not read).

replication.where_it_stands: One open-label trial of 12 people, from one team; no randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for depression is among the sources read. The authors call for randomized trials.

funding.funder: Investigator-initiated; funded by the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority (project 2021007); Lykos Therapeutics provided the study drug and an unconditional grant (Funding). The protocol was written with a template from Lykos Therapeutics, and two authors secured the agreement with Lykos (Author contributions).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: MDMA was provided by Lykos Therapeutics; T.-M.K. received a lecture honorarium from Lundbeck; L.H.S. is employed by Axon Clinic; O.A.A. is a consultant for Cortechs.ai and has received speaker honoraria from Janssen, Lilly, Lundbeck and Sunovion; I.W.G. runs an online training programme in MDMA-assisted therapy through his clinic Psykologvirke; several authors at Østfold Hospital (T.-M.K., I.W.G., L.H.S., O.A.A.) received research support from Lykos Therapeutics for an MDMA-assisted therapy trial for PTSD (Declaration of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The first author and two other authors were study therapists (Author contributions); one author sells training in the therapy. The authors used ChatGPT to improve parts of the text (Acknowledgements). Data available on reasonable request (Data availability).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in major depressive disorder comparing the same psychotherapy with MDMA against an active placebo, with blinded independent raters, measured expectancy, an independent adverse-event assessor and follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: No comparison group. The package includes about eleven psychotherapy sessions, itself an effective treatment for depression; entry required a MADRS of 20 or more at baseline, inviting regression to the mean; expectations were probably high. MDMA's contribution cannot be estimated.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Eleven of 12 self-referred and one referred by a study therapist; the analysis covers the 12 dosed, not the 15 enrolled (3 stopped before dosing).
Same protocol for all; all accepted the second-session increase and all but one took the supplements.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Six participants took psychotropic medicines for other conditions during treatment, two received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for adverse events, three needed seven extra visits, and adherence to the manual was not assessed.
All 12 dosed participants reached the primary end point.

MADRS raters were not blind and not fully independent, as the authors state; secondary and exploratory outcomes are self-reports by people who knew they had taken MDMA; adverse events were recorded by the therapists.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Prospectively registered with the MADRS change as the main objective, but the registered secondary endpoint (a subjective-effects scale) is replaced by the SDS, and one primary-outcome value had to be corrected after publication.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence of the effect of MDMA-assisted therapy on depression the study is at critical risk of bias: it has no comparison group, the treatment includes substantial psychotherapy, and enrolment at a high score invites regression to the mean; unblinded rating adds a serious concern that the authors acknowledge. The paper can be cited for feasibility (no dropouts after dosing), for the observed fall in MADRS in 12 people, and for the adverse events recorded, including worsening suicidal ideation in some participants; it cannot be cited for efficacy, for comparison with other treatments, or for durability.

key_findings.finding: Flow (read from the Fig. 1 image): 86 telephone-screened, 65 excluded, 21 screened, 6 screening failures, 15 enrolled, 3 early terminations before dosing, 12 dosed, none lost afterwards; 12 reached the primary end point. Recruitment January 2023 to May 2024; 11 self-referred, 1 referred by a study therapist.
key_findings.locator: Fig. 1 (CONSORT diagram, image); Results › Feasibility, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Baseline: 7 women and 5 men, mean age 44.1 (SD 9.2); 11 White; 11 with recurrent MDD; mean 16.1 years since the first episode; MADRS 29.6 (4.9), 10 moderate and 2 severe; comorbid PTSD 3 and ADHD 3; previous antidepressants 9 (75.0%); 8 tapered ongoing psychotropic medicines; mean 223.1 previous psychotherapy sessions (median 88.5); SDS 21.3 (6.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › Demographics and baseline characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Primary outcome, corrected: MADRS 29.6 (SD 4.9) at baseline and 10.3 (8.3) at the outcome visit about 8 weeks after the second MDMA session; mean change −19.3 (SD 8.3), bootstrap 95% CI −14.9 to −23.7, Wilcoxon z = −3.06, P < 0.001. Among the 9 participants without comorbid PTSD the mean change was −18.1 (8.8).
key_findings.locator: Results › Primary outcome, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (MADRS row); corrigendum (PMC13051208), corrected Table 2
key_findings.note: The original article printed the outcome mean as 9.7 (SD 10.0), which did not match the printed change (29.6 − 9.7 = 19.9); the corrigendum's 10.3 does. The abstract gives the interval as −14.8 to −23.8.

key_findings.finding: Secondary outcome: SDS 21.3 (6.1) to 9.7 (9.2); mean change −11.7 (SD 7.6), 95% CI −7.6 to −15.8, z = −3.02, P = 0.001.
Responders (MADRS reduction of 50% or more): 9 of 12 (75.0%); remitters (MADRS 12 or less): 9 of 12 (75.0%); the corrigendum says these counts are unaffected by the correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Exploratory analysis, 1st paragraph; corrigendum, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exploratory outcomes, baseline to the termination visit: BDI-II 33.5 (9.6) to 12.0 (14.8), −21.5 (−14.0 to −29.0); GAD-7 13.8 (4.2) to 6.0 (5.4), printed difference −9.0 (−6.0 to −12.0); PCL-5 36.4 (17.0) to 25.4 (19.7), −11.0 (−2.4 to −19.6); Bergen Insomnia Scale 28.9 (7.5) to 12.6 (10.5), −16.3; AUDIT 3.3 to 3.3 and DUDIT 0.6 to 0.1, no significant change.

Adverse events: 10 of 12 had at least one; 46 events, 45 treatment-emergent (one, a deterioration in suicidal ideation, occurred before the study drug); 15 moderate and 31 mild; no serious or severe adverse events, no adverse events of special interest, no discontinuations or hospitalisations; most common were headache, increased suicidal ideation and jaw muscle tightness; the 3 non-responders had 25 events (13 moderate) and the 9 responders 21 (2 moderate); 39 of 46 resolved within a week (mean duration 7.3 days, SD 17.6, median 1.0).

Adverse events needing treatment: ten needed psychotherapeutic support at scheduled visits; three participants needed seven extra visits; two participants received benzodiazepines and zopiclone for anxiety and insomnia within 2 days after dosing (one also a benzodiazepine later); paracetamol for eight headaches.

Suicidality: no serious suicidal ideation (C-SSRS 4 or 5) and no suicidal behaviour; one participant's ideation score increased over the study; six participants (12 adverse events) had a worsening in the intensity of suicidal ideation; no ideation was reported during dosing sessions; group means never exceeded the 6-month baseline measured at screening.

No cardiovascular adverse events or arrhythmias; transient rises in blood pressure, heart rate and body temperature during sessions (values only in Supplementary Fig. 5, not read); no adverse events related to MDMA use outside the study.

Limitations stated by the authors: no control group, so response cannot be attributed to the treatment rather than expectancy or natural fluctuation; raters neither completely independent nor blinded, so rater bias may have inflated the MADRS change; adverse events reported to the therapy team, so possibly under-reported; adherence to the manual not assessed; a self-referred sample with possibly elevated expectations.

Registration: EudraCT 2021-000805-26, first entered 4 August 2021; open-label phase 2 feasibility study; main objective the mean change in MADRS from visit 4 (baseline) to visit 13 (about 12 weeks); secondary endpoint feasibility measured by a 15-item subjective-effects visual analogue scale; ongoing, no results posted.

design_detail: Uncontrolled long-term follow-up of one cohort: the 19 people who received MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in the first US randomized phase 2 trial for chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD (Mithoefer et al., 2011; NCT00090064; 12 randomized to MDMA and 7 of the 8 placebo participants who crossed over to open-label MDMA afterwards), plus descriptive data on the one placebo participant who never received MDMA. The follow-up was added by protocol amendment after the trial had started; the first follow-up assessments took place 5 years after study initiation, and each participant was assessed once, 17 to 74 months after the last MDMA session. Within-person comparison of the CAPS and IES-R scores obtained 2 months after the second MDMA session with the follow-up scores, plus an unvalidated questionnaire written by the investigators on benefits, harms, later treatment, drug use and perceived cognition. Sponsored and funded by MAPS. Read as the PMC author-deposited version of the SAGE article (CC BY).
can_establish: What the PTSD symptom scores, reported benefits and harms, later treatments and drug use of these 19 treated participants looked like, on average and one by one, a mean of about 4 years after their last MDMA session.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted psychotherapy caused the long-term outcome (there is no comparison group at follow-up, and most participants had later psychotherapy or psychiatric medicines), whether the average stability would hold in larger or less selected samples, or whether harm, dependence or cognitive decline were absent (a single yes/no question and self-reports from 19 people).

sample.recruitment: All 20 participants of the first randomized trial (Mithoefer et al., 2011) were mailed a consent form and a letter asking them to take part; all 20 took part (Methods and materials › Subjects, 3rd paragraph). The original trial enrolled people with chronic, treatment-resistant PTSD, in most cases from sexual abuse or assault (Subjects, 1st paragraph); how they were recruited is not restated here.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: As in the original trial, which is not restated in this article. The Discussion gives a CAPS of 50 or more as the original entry criterion (Discussion, 3rd paragraph); the notes to Table 2 show that two MDMA-arm participants had CAPS 56 and 62 at enrolment and 43 after medication washout, the post-washout score being the one reported.
sample.demographics: The 19 MDMA-treated participants: 16 women and 3 men, mean age at enrolment 41.0; the 17 who completed the CAPS (including the participant who never received MDMA): 14 women and 3 men, mean age 42.3 (Subjects, 4th paragraph). Mean duration of PTSD symptoms more than 19 years (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph). Other demographics are in the original report.
sample.attrition: 3 of 19 MDMA-treated participants (16%) did not complete the CAPS and IES-R: one moved and was lost after answering the questionnaire; two declined, one of whom had shown the smallest CAPS reduction at 2 months and feared the testing would trigger symptoms, the other citing family stress (Subjects, 5th paragraph). All 20 completed the questionnaire.
sample.selection_effects: A small, highly selected group of treatment-resistant volunteers from a single private-practice trial. The crossover group consists of placebo participants who had not recovered with psychotherapy alone (the one who had recovered did not cross over and is excluded from the analysis). Follow-up intervals vary from 17 to 74 months because the follow-up was added late by amendment. Non-completers were compared with completers only on two questionnaire ratings, in groups of 16 and 3.

exposure.measurement: MDMA-assisted psychotherapy as delivered in the original trial: two 8-hour MDMA sessions 3 to 5 weeks apart with weekly non-drug psychotherapy, non-directive, following the sponsor's treatment manual; by a protocol amendment the last eight participants recruited (five in the double-blind and three in the crossover stage) had a third MDMA session, which came after the 2-month score used as this study's reference point (Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study design, 3rd paragraph; Table 2 notes).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Doses are not given in this article; the authors refer to the original report (Mithoefer et al., 2011), not read. Two or three sessions in all, by mouth.
exposure.polysubstance: At follow-up, by questionnaire under a certificate of confidentiality: cannabis by 8 participants (from 'once' to 'occasionally'), psilocybin mushrooms by 1 (frequency not reported), all of whom had used these substances before enrolment; one participant used 'ecstasy' once in a quasi-therapeutic setting. Participants had not been asked to abstain after the trial (Methods › Outcome measures, 3rd paragraph; Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period). Psychiatric medicines: 12 of 19 at study entry and at follow-up (Results › Psychiatric medications; Table 4). The authors call the MDMA pure; manufacture is not described here.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: the outcome was measured 17 to 74 months after the last MDMA session.

comparison.controls: None at follow-up. The comparison is within person: CAPS and IES-R 2 months after the second MDMA session against the same participants' follow-up scores. The randomized comparison of the original trial ended before the crossover; the one participant who never received MDMA is reported separately (CAPS 14 at 2 months and 16 at follow-up; IES-R 5 and 15).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Intervening life events, reasons for continuing psychotherapy and treatments received outside those asked about were not measured; the authors suggest asking about life events in future questionnaires (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).

outcomes.instruments: CAPS (DSM-IV global severity and diagnostic status), given in person or by phone by the same independent rater who rated the original trial; IES-R, self-report by post; an unvalidated follow-up questionnaire written by the investigators (degree of benefit and persistence of benefit on 1 to 5 scales, a list of benefits, one yes/no question on harm, later psychotherapy and psychiatric medicines, use of 'ecstasy' and other illicit substances, perceived change in cognition, free comments). The NEO PI-R was given but is held back for a separate publication (Methods › Outcome measures; Study design, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: CAPS and IES-R are established instruments; the questionnaire is not validated, as the authors say (Discussion, 4th paragraph). Relapse is defined as a CAPS score above 50, the original entry cut-off.
outcomes.operationalization: Durability: no statistically significant difference between mean scores 2 months after the second MDMA session and at follow-up. Relapse: CAPS above 50. Harm: answering yes to whether one was harmed by taking part. Drug problems and cognitive decline: the participants' own answers to the questionnaire.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. The six tests are CAPS and IES-R at 2 months against follow-up, two against three MDMA sessions for each, and completers against non-completers for degree and persistence of benefit; the rest is descriptive.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the rater knew that every participant analysed had received MDMA; the rater, Mark Wagner, is the second author and was paid by the sponsor to act as the independent rater (conflict-of-interest statement). All other outcomes are self-reports.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes reported. CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) at 2 months and 23.7 (22.8) at follow-up, matched t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; IES-R 19.8 (19.5) and 22.1 (21.8), t 0.4, df 15, p = 0.72 (Table 1). Editors' calculation from the 16 completers' individual scores in Table 2, which reproduce the printed means and SDs: mean change −0.9 points (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9, paired t), SD of the individual changes 31.4; 6 of 16 improved and 3 worsened by 10 points or more (by 14, 44 and 85 points). Mean pre-MDMA CAPS of the same 16 was 77.9 (for crossover participants the score after the placebo stage).
analysis.covariates: None. Two against three MDMA sessions were compared (CAPS t 0.2, df 14, p 0.83; IES-R t 0.7, df 14, p 0.48) and found not different, which was used to justify comparing everyone at 2 months after the second session (Study design, 3rd paragraph).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The original trial is registered (NCT00090064, Acknowledgments). The follow-up was added by protocol amendment, approved by the Copernicus Group IRB, after the trial had started; no registration of the follow-up outcomes or analysis plan is mentioned (registry not read).
analysis.selective_reporting: NEO PI-R results withheld for a separate paper; the full questionnaire and all comments are online supplements on the sponsor's website (not read). The reference time point was chosen after a non-significant comparison of two against three sessions in 16 people.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 16 completers. The authors state that the sample is too small to compare participants who continued treatment with those who did not (Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 of 19 treated participants, mean CAPS a mean of about 4 years after the last MDMA session was similar to the mean 2 months after the second session (23.7 against 24.6), with wide individual variation: two scores above 50 counted as relapses, and nine changes of 10 points or more in either direction. Three did not complete the CAPS. At follow-up 8 of 19 were in psychotherapy and 12 of 19 took psychiatric medicines. All 19 reported some benefit and none answered yes to having been harmed, on an unvalidated questionnaire; one reported using ecstasy once. There was no comparison group.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title announces "absence of harmful effects or drug dependency", which rests on one yes/no question and self-reported drug use in 19 people, with no structured assessment of substance use disorder and no cognitive testing at follow-up. The Discussion reads the non-significant difference in 16 people as an enduring benefit of the treatment (the data are compatible with anything from a 17.6-point improvement to a 15.9-point worsening, editors' calculation) and argues that the improvement is not easily attributed to placebo or spontaneous remission, while the Limitations concede that there was no meaningful control group and that later psychotherapy and medicines confound the result. The Conclusions call the methodology rigorous and state that the results indicate a "favorable long-term risk/benefit ratio" (Conclusions, 1st paragraph).

timeline.event: Original randomized trial of 20 participants (Mithoefer et al., 2011, Journal of Psychopharmacology), the cohort followed here; not in the project's references.
This follow-up, 17 to 74 months after the last MDMA session.

A pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials by an overlapping author group (Jerome et al., 2020, Psychopharmacology) appears; it was retracted on 10 August 2024 and is not evidence (METHODS §3.2).

Ponte et al. report 12-month open-label sleep and CAPS data pooled from four other phase 2 trials of the same sponsor; an expression of concern and a correction (4 participants removed) followed in December 2024.
The second phase 3 trial reports outcomes to 18 weeks only.

replication.where_it_stands: The only peer-reviewed long-term (more than 1 year) follow-up of a randomized MDMA trial that the project has found and that is not retracted. It describes one small cohort without a comparison group, and the same sponsor's later pooled follow-up was retracted. It can be cited for what was observed in these participants, not for an effect of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy at follow-up.

funding.funder: The Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies (MAPS), a non-profit organization (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The sponsor played a role in the study design, data analysis and writing of the report; the investigators collected the data. Three authors (Yazar-Klosinski, Jerome, Doblin) are employed by the sponsor. Michael Mithoefer is a medical monitor for other MDMA studies of the sponsor; he and Ann Mithoefer were paid by the sponsor for conducting this research and for work on a treatment manual, investigator training and protocols for further studies. The sponsor paid Mark Wagner for acting as the independent rater (Footnotes › Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The follow-up CAPS was administered by the second author, who was paid by the sponsor; the questionnaire was written by the investigators; the statistics author is a private biostatistics consultant (affiliation 7). The first two Mithoefers practise privately in Mount Pleasant, SC, and are affiliated with MAPS clinical research (author information).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial with long-term follow-up planned from the start, at fixed intervals, in which the comparison group is followed as long (or a randomized comparison with an established trauma-focused psychotherapy), with blinded raters, structured assessment of substance use disorders and cognition, and full recording of later treatments and life events.

domains.note: No comparison group at follow-up: whether scores stayed low because of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, later psychotherapy (8 of 19) or medicines (12 of 19), the natural course or life events cannot be separated, as the authors acknowledge.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Every MDMA-treated participant of the trial was approached and took part, but the crossover arm contains only placebo participants who had not recovered with therapy alone, and the treated cohort is a highly selected treatment-resistant group.
Who received two or three MDMA sessions is recorded for each participant (Table 2).

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: After the reference point, 8 participants had a third MDMA session; during follow-up most had other treatment (psychotherapy, psychiatric medicines) and 8 used cannabis; none of this is accounted for in the analysis.

3 of 19 (16%) without CAPS, for reasons that may relate to the outcome (one feared symptoms would be triggered and had responded least); analyses are completers only, with a worst-case count given in text.

The CAPS rater knew all analysed participants had received MDMA, was paid by the sponsor and is a co-author; ratings by phone or in person; harms, drug use and cognition rest on an unvalidated self-report questionnaire written by the investigators.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Follow-up added by amendment with no reported analysis plan; NEO PI-R withheld; reference time point justified after the fact by a non-significant subgroup comparison.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-I judges a study's ability to estimate an intervention's effect. Without a comparison group at follow-up, and with co-interventions in most participants, this follow-up cannot estimate the long-term effect of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (critical confounding), and its outcome measurement is unblinded and partly unvalidated. It remains usable as a description of what was observed in these 19 people: mean CAPS similar to the 2-month score, wide individual variation, two relapses, and three participants without data. Claims may cite it in that descriptive sense only, never for an effect or for an absence of harm or dependence.

key_findings.finding: Cohort: 20 people randomized in the original trial (12 MDMA, 8 placebo with the same psychotherapy); 7 of the 8 placebo participants accepted open-label MDMA afterwards, so 19 received MDMA; the eighth had recovered with psychotherapy alone. The last eight recruited had a third MDMA session (8 had three sessions, 11 had two).
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study design, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Follow-up added by protocol amendment; all 20 took part. 20 completed the questionnaire and 17 the CAPS and IES-R, of whom 16 had received MDMA (16 women and 3 men among the 19 MDMA-treated, mean age at enrolment 41.0). Three MDMA-treated participants did not complete the measures: one moved, two declined (one with the smallest earlier CAPS reduction feared the testing would trigger symptoms; one cited family stress).
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 3rd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Timing: CAPS and IES-R 17 to 74 months after the final MDMA session (mean 45.4, SD 17.3, n = 17); questionnaire 10 to 74 months after completion (mean 40.8, SD 19.2, n = 20). The first follow-up assessments came 5 years after study initiation, so intervals vary widely.
key_findings.locator: Methods and materials › Subjects, 6th paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: In the 16 MDMA-treated completers, CAPS 24.6 (SD 18.6) 2 months after the second MDMA session and 23.7 (SD 22.8) at follow-up, t 0.1, df 15, p = 0.91; IES-R 19.8 (19.5) and 22.1 (21.8), t 0.4, df 15, p = 0.72.
key_findings.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Two of the 16 completers (13%) had CAPS above 50 at follow-up, which the authors call relapse to moderate-to-severe PTSD; counting the three non-completers as negative outcomes as well gives 5 of 19 (26%). The Discussion restates this as 14 of 19 (74%) with sustained reductions in the worst case and up to 17 of 19 (89%) at best.
key_findings.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Editors' calculation from the individual scores (Table 2), which reproduce Table 1's means and SDs: mean change from 2 months to follow-up −0.9 points (95% CI −17.6 to 15.9; paired t −0.11), SD of individual changes 31.4. Six of 16 improved by 10 points or more (largest 53 points) and three worsened by 10 points or more (by 14, 44 and 85 points; the two relapses went from 16 to 60 and from 6 to 91).
The participant who never received MDMA had a sustained response to psychotherapy with placebo: CAPS 14 at 2 months and 16 at follow-up; IES-R 5 and 15.
key_findings.locator: Results › CAPS and IES-R, 3rd paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Questionnaire (19 MDMA-treated): all reported some benefit and all answered no to having been harmed by taking part. Degree of benefit: 11 (58%) rated it 5 ('large'), mean 4.3; persistence: 8 (42%) said benefits had lasted and continued to grow, 4 (21%) that some but not most had lasted, mean 3.8, median 4. Most endorsed benefits: general well-being and increased self-awareness 17 (89%) each, less excessive vigilance and less avoidance 15 (79%) each, fewer nightmares, flashbacks or intrusive memories 13 (68%), improved sleep 12 (63%).
key_findings.locator: Results › LTFU questionnaire results for 19 PTSD subjects › Degree of benefit, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Later treatment: at enrolment 16 of 19 (84%) were in psychotherapy, at follow-up 8 of 19 (42%), most often EMDR (4) and cognitive behavioural therapy (3). Psychiatric medicines: 12 of 19 at entry and at follow-up; mean number of medicines 1.7 at entry and 1.3 at follow-up. The authors call this the most important confounder of the durability finding.
key_findings.locator: Results › Participation in psychotherapy; Results › Psychiatric medications; Table 4; Discussion › Limitations, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The text prints 58% for 12 of 19 (which is 63%); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Drug use during follow-up (self-report under a certificate of confidentiality): cannabis by 8 ('once' to 'occasionally'), psilocybin mushrooms by 1, all of whom had used them before enrolment; one participant used 'ecstasy' once in a quasi-therapeutic setting and reported no interest in repeating it outside a legal therapeutic context. Participants had not been asked to abstain. No participant is reported to have developed a substance use problem; there was no structured assessment.
key_findings.locator: Results › Questions about illicit drug use during LTFU period; Methods and materials › Outcome measures, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Risk of substance abuse

key_findings.finding: All participants answered yes to whether more MDMA sessions would have been helpful. On perceived cognition, none reported a decline; 7 reported no change and 13 an improvement (self-report only; no testing at follow-up).
key_findings.locator: Results › Opinion about additional sessions; Results › Cognitive function

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: no meaningful control group, because all but one participant ended up receiving MDMA, so natural history or uncontrolled variables could explain the results; follow-up intervals varied because the follow-up was added late; later psychotherapy and medicines preclude a definite conclusion about long-term benefit; blinding in the original trial had been transparent to the investigators and most participants.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Limitations, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Discussion › Symptom improvement and other benefits reported on our LTFU Questionnaire, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods say the 2-month and follow-up scores were compared with independent t tests and independent Mann-Whitney U tests, although they are the same participants; the abstract and Table 1 report a matched t with df 15.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Methods and materials › Study design, 1st paragraph; Abstract; Table 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the editors' paired calculation from Table 2 gives the printed t of about 0.1, so the reported result stands; the Methods text is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: Psychiatric medicines: the text gives 58% (12/19) on medicines at entry and at follow-up, but 12 of 19 is 63%. In Table 4, participant 10's follow-up row shows an 'other' medicine (code f, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) but a follow-up total of 0, and the follow-up column total is 23 while the category totals add up to 24; the text's mean of 1.3 medicines corresponds to 24 of 19, and 12 participants are on a medicine at follow-up only if participant 10 is counted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small: use the counts (12 of 19 at both times), not the percentage; the follow-up total in Table 4 is one short.

reporting_issues.issue: Perceived cognition: 7 participants with no change and 13 with improvement add up to 20, but the section reports on the 19 MDMA-treated participants.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two counts is wrong, or the non-MDMA participant is included; these self-reports should not be cited as counts.

reporting_issues.issue: Persistence of benefit: the text gives a median of 5 for the whole group, for the 16 CAPS completers and for the 3 non-completers, but Table 3 shows only 8 of 19 rating persistence 5 (median 4); a median of 5 among 16 completers would need at least 9 such ratings.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › LTFU questionnaire results › Degree of benefit, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3)
reporting_issues.consequence: The completer versus non-completer comparison of persistence (p = 0.18) cannot be reconciled with Table 3; cite Table 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion gives the relapse rate as 'a minimum of 11% of the CAPS completers', but 2 of 16 completers is 13%, as the Results say; 11% is 2 of 19.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Results › CAPS and IES-R, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite 2 of 16 completers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract presents the 17-to-74-month interval (mean 45.4, SD 17.3) as the follow-up of the 16 MDMA-treated completers, but the Methods give it for n = 17, including the participant who never received MDMA; from Table 2, the 16 completers' intervals average 45.6 months (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract; Methods and materials › Subjects, 6th paragraph; Table 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for the claim; noted for accuracy.

reporting_issues.issue: For the 8 participants who had a third MDMA session, the '2-month' reference score was taken before that session (Table 2 notes), so the comparison mixes scores after the full treatment with scores after part of it.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 2 notes; Methods and materials › Study design, 3rd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: For these participants the follow-up change includes the effect of the third session; the stability of the mean is partly built from different starting points.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3573678 (all sections, Tables 1 to 4 as text, Table 4 cell structure checked in the page's DOM, author information, funding and conflict-of-interest footnotes, reference list; Figure 1 is an image whose legend only was read; the online questionnaire and comments supplements on the sponsor's website were not read). Crossref record read in this reader's tab.

design_detail: Uncontrolled phase 1/2 open-label treatment-development trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172, named in the Acknowledgments; MAPS protocol MPVA-1) of MDMA-facilitated cognitive-behavioural conjoint therapy (CBCT) for PTSD in six heterosexual couples in which one partner had chronic PTSD: a condensed version of the 15-session CBCT protocol delivered over 7 weeks, with two all-day sessions in which both partners took MDMA, two co-therapists (one expert in MDMA therapy, one in CBCT), and assessments before, at mid-treatment, after treatment and at 3 and 6 months; growth-curve models and within-group effect sizes. Brief report (no Results subsections beyond two). The setting is not stated here; the companion paper on secondary outcomes from the same six couples (Wagner et al., 2021) gives a private practice clinic in Charleston, South Carolina. Funded by MAPS. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest, and the card uses ROBINS-I as the batch brief directs for non-randomized intervention studies.
can_establish: That MDMA could be given to both members of six couples within a condensed course of CBCT without serious adverse events or dropouts, and what happened to PTSD symptoms, depression, sleep and relationship satisfaction in these 12 people over 6 months.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA added anything to CBCT, an established therapy that improves PTSD on its own (there is no CBCT-alone or placebo arm); whether any change is due to the treatment rather than natural course, regression to the mean or expectation; rare harms; or effects in couples other than White, heterosexual, mostly relationally satisfied couples treated by the developers of the therapy.

sample.recruitment: Not described in this report.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: One partner with current PTSD on the CAPS-5 for at least 6 months; both partners at least 18, generally healthy, proficient in English, willing to stay off psychiatric medicines during the study, to follow food, drink and nicotine restrictions before MDMA sessions, to use birth control if able to become pregnant, to be video-recorded and not to join other trials. Excluded: acute psychosis, acute mania, substance use disorder, pregnancy or nursing, weight under 48 kg (Method › 1.1 Participants, 1st paragraph). The companion paper adds no active suicidal planning or intent and no severe partner aggression, and specifies no current substance use disorder (Wagner et al., 2021).
sample.demographics: Mean age about 47 (patients 47.1, SD 12.5; partners 46.6, SD 11.2); all White ('Caucasian'); all heterosexual couples; 4 of 6 patients men; 5 of 6 patients with multiple traumas (index trauma childhood sexual abuse 3, childhood physical abuse or neglect 2, adult combat 1); all patients with comorbid diagnoses and earlier drug and psychological treatment; 3 of 6 patients in current psychotherapy; at baseline 2 patients and 3 partners relationally distressed (Couples Satisfaction Index below 104.5) (Method › 1.1 Participants, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: All six couples completed the protocol; there were no missing clinician PTSD interviews; across the other self-report measures and occasions 86% of assessments were completed (2. Results, 1st paragraph; Method › 1.3 Assessment, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Couples willing to take MDMA together, to stop psychiatric medicines and to be video-recorded, treated by the developers of the therapy and of MDMA-assisted therapy; all White and heterosexual; most patients had long histories of treatment. Expectations were probably high and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to all: CBCT sessions 1 to 3 in person the day before the first MDMA session, sessions 4 and 5 on the morning of it, the MDMA session (6 to 8 hours) and an integration session the next morning; sessions 6 to 9 by secure video over 2.5 weeks; sessions 10 and 11 the day before the second MDMA session, then the second MDMA session and an integration session; sessions 12 to 15 weekly by video; 7 weeks in all. MDMA sessions were timed to follow the communication-skills work and to fall in the middle of the cognitive work (Method › 1.2 Treatment, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: each partner took 75 mg MDMA in the first session and 100 mg in the second, with an optional supplemental half-dose 1.5 hours later in both sessions; participants were told the supplement could prolong the therapeutic window (Method › 1.2 Treatment, 2nd paragraph). The companion paper gives the supplements as 37.5 mg and 50 mg (Wagner et al., 2021).
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorder was an exclusion criterion, yet Table 1 lists a substance use disorder among SCID-5 diagnoses in 3 of 6 patients and 1 partner, without saying whether these are past diagnoses (Table 1; reporting issues). Other drug use during the study is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; psychiatric medicines were stopped for the study.

comparison.controls: None: within-person change from pre-treatment to mid-treatment, post-treatment and 3- and 6-month follow-ups.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (single group).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; without a comparison group, the effect of CBCT itself, the natural course, regression to the mean and expectation cannot be separated from any effect of MDMA.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: CAPS-5 (clinician-rated, by independent assessors trained to reliability); PCL-5, patient and partner versions; Couples Satisfaction Index (CSI), with its overall relationship-happiness item also given at each visit. Secondary: BDI-II, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Emotion Regulation Questionnaire (reappraisal and suppression), Trauma and Attachment Belief Scale (TABS). SCID-5 at baseline. Adverse events from enrolment to treatment completion and at 3 and 6 months; spontaneously reported experiences and listed effects on session days and contact days (Method › 1.2 Treatment, 2nd paragraph; 1.3 Assessment, 1st to 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated measures; relational distress defined as a CSI total below 104.5 (Table 1 footnote).
outcomes.operationalization: Change over time in growth-curve models with log-transformed days since baseline, fixed slopes and random intercepts; within-group Cohen's d from pre-treatment to each time point, computed on the models' estimated means and the raw pooled SDs (Method › 1.4 Analyses).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Twelve outcome models (CAPS-5, patient and partner PCL-5, BDI-II, PSQI, two ERQ subscales, TABS, patient and partner CSI, patient and partner relationship happiness) (Table 3).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None possible: every participant received MDMA, and the independent CAPS-5 assessors knew it; the self- and partner-reports come from people who had taken MDMA. Two authors (Monson and Wagner) were paid to provide the treatment (COI Statements).

analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172: actual start 3 July 2016, first submitted 16 August 2016, posted 23 August 2016 (about six weeks after the start). Registered primary outcome: CAPS-5 total severity at the primary endpoint (visit 16, about 2 months) and its change from baseline; PCL-5 (patient and partner), CSI, BDI-II, PSQI, TABS and ERQ are registered as secondary outcomes, whereas the article calls PCL-5 and CSI primary self-report outcomes. Results posted 19 July 2021 (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: The adverse-event and reaction tables are in two supplementary Word files, not read because they are downloads; the article names only the most common reactions. The registry's adverse-event list (5% threshold) was read instead.
analysis.power: No power calculation; a treatment-development pilot of six couples.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six couples given a condensed course of an established couple therapy for PTSD with two MDMA sessions for both partners, clinician-rated PTSD fell from about 41 to 19 after treatment and 16 at 6 months (model estimates), five of six patients no longer met PTSD criteria, depression, sleep and relationship satisfaction improved, all couples finished, and no serious adverse event was reported. With no comparison arm none of this can be attributed to MDMA rather than to CBCT, time or expectation.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says MDMA "holds promise as a facilitator of CBCT to achieve more robust and broad effects" (Abstract). The Discussion says the combination may potentiate the treatment effects, that its effect sizes were greater than those of individual MDMA-assisted therapy (citing the pooled phase 2 analysis that PMC marks as retracted) and on par with or greater than CBCT alone, and that the largest effects at 6 months suggest MDMA facilitation may confer ongoing benefits (Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs): comparisons of within-group effects in six people with other studies' results. The Discussion itself calls these comparisons tentative, and the Limitations say the lack of randomization or control severely limits the conclusions (Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).

timeline.event: Wagner, Mithoefer, Mithoefer & Monson, J Psychoactive Drugs: a case example of the combined treatment (cited in this report; not read).
This report: primary outcomes of the six-couple uncontrolled trial.

replication.where_it_stands: One uncontrolled trial of six couples, reported in two papers by the same team. The project's evidence map lists a pilot of a brief MDMA-enhanced CBCT (Morland et al., 2026; read by this reader, card sc_morland_2026) and a registered randomized trial of conjoint therapy with and without MDMA (NCT06044675, recruiting); no controlled result exists in the sources read.

Data are openly available on the Open Science Framework (osf.io/7fuwd) (Data sharing statement); not inspected here.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of CBCT with MDMA against CBCT with an active placebo, in couples with PTSD from more diverse backgrounds, with therapists other than the developers, blinded independent assessors, measured expectancy and follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: No comparison group, and the treatment includes a full course of CBCT, which the authors describe as efficacious on its own; any contribution of MDMA cannot be separated from CBCT, time, regression to the mean or expectation.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Self-selected couples willing to take MDMA together, most relationally satisfied at baseline; recruitment is not described.
All received the same protocolized treatment.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Three of six patients were in current psychotherapy at baseline (Table 1) and the report does not say whether this continued; doses of the optional supplements taken are not reported.
No missing clinician interviews; 86% completion of the other self-reports.
Outcomes rated by participants and partners who had taken MDMA, and by assessors who knew everyone had; the therapists include the first two authors, one of whom developed the therapy.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Registered about six weeks after the start; PCL-5 and CSI, registered as secondary, are presented as primary; the registered CAPS-5 endpoint is reported, but the registry's posted endpoint mean (16.3) differs from the article's estimated mean (19.37).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that MDMA adds to CBCT, the study is at critical risk of bias: it has no comparison arm, and the therapy it adds MDMA to is itself an efficacious treatment. Unblinded self-, partner- and assessor-ratings add serious concerns. The paper can be cited for feasibility (all six couples completed), for the absence of serious adverse events in 12 people, and for the observed changes as a description; it cannot be cited for MDMA's contribution or for comparisons with other treatments.

key_findings.finding: Six heterosexual couples (12 people), one partner in each with PTSD; mean age about 47; all White; 4 of 6 patients men; all patients with comorbid diagnoses and earlier treatment; 2 patients and 3 partners relationally distressed at baseline.

All couples completed the protocol and there were no serious adverse events; the most common reactions after MDMA sessions in patients and partners were diminished appetite, anxiety, headache and jaw tightness (counts only in the supplementary tables, not read).

Clinician-assessed PTSD (CAPS-5, estimated means): 41.42 (SD 5.76) before treatment, 19.37 (13.71) after, 17.43 (17.14) at 3 months and 15.52 (15.22) at 6 months; growth-model B = −4.64, P < .001; within-group d 2.10, 1.88 and 2.25. All but one patient had a sustained remission of the clinician-assessed PTSD diagnosis.
key_findings.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3
key_findings.note: Editors' check: d = 2.10 equals the change of 22.05 divided by the root mean square of the two SDs (10.52).

key_findings.finding: Self-rated PTSD (PCL-5): 62.64 (6.35) to 23.96 after treatment and 17.20 at 6 months, B = −8.14, P < .001, d 2.72 to 3.59; partner-rated PTSD: 49.58 (8.52) to 21.54 and 16.64, B = −5.90, P < .001, d 1.85 to 2.72.
key_findings.locator: 2. Results › 2.1 PTSD and patient comorbid outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 2 and 3

key_findings.finding: Patient depression (BDI-II) 32.91 (8.75) to 12.75 after treatment and 9.23 at 6 months, B = −4.24, d 1.50 to 2.53; sleep (PSQI) 14.24 (3.54) to 10.37 and 9.69, B = −0.81, P < .01, d 0.88 to 1.18; emotion regulation, reappraisal B = 1.38 and suppression B = −1.12, both P < .01; trauma-related beliefs (TABS) B = −12.01, P < .01, d 0.98 to 1.17.

key_findings.finding: Relationship satisfaction (CSI): patients 105.37 (13.39) to 127.00 after treatment and 130.78 at 6 months, B = 4.55, P < .05, d 0.82 to 1.22; partners 98.10 (50.81) to 125.34 and 130.10, B = 5.73, P < .05, d 0.64 to 0.80. Both relationally distressed patients were satisfied after treatment; one patient satisfied at baseline was dissatisfied afterwards (the one who kept the PTSD diagnosis); one of three distressed partners stayed distressed (that patient's partner). Relationship happiness: patients B = 0.35, partners B = 0.33, both P < .001.

key_findings.finding: Registry results: CAPS-5 at the primary endpoint 16.3 (SD 13.71) and change from baseline −25.7 (13.89), n = 6. Adverse events (5% threshold): every patient and every partner had at least one non-serious event from enrolment to 2 months after the last MDMA session (for example nausea, decreased appetite and fatigue in 2 patients each; anxiety in 1 patient and 1 partner), 2 patients and 2 partners in the 6-month follow-up period; no serious events or deaths; the list includes a spontaneous abortion in one partner during the follow-up period, entered as non-serious.

key_findings.finding: Limitations as stated: no randomization or control condition, which severely limits the conclusions; expert therapists in each modality, which limits generalizability; too small to examine moderators or mechanisms; a phase 2 randomized trial is being prepared.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentages that six people cannot produce: Table 1 gives 4 male patients as 60% (4 of 6 is 66.7%) and depressive and anxiety disorders in 4 partners as 60%; the text says 60% of patients had received trauma-focused therapy and 40% dialectical behaviour or cognitive-behavioural therapy; the text says 50% of partners had a mental health condition, while Table 1 lists a depressive disorder in 4 of 6 partners.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample description is internally inconsistent; cite counts, not percentages.

reporting_issues.issue: Substance use disorder was an exclusion criterion, but Table 1 lists it among SCID-5 diagnoses in 3 of 6 patients and 1 partner (and anorexia nervosa in one of each), without saying whether these are past diagnoses; the companion paper specifies no current substance use disorder.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably lifetime diagnoses, but the report does not say.

reporting_issues.issue: Three of six patients were in current psychotherapy at baseline (Table 1); the report does not say whether it continued during the trial.
reporting_issues.consequence: A possible co-intervention.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the ERQ suppression effect as d = 1.12 to 1.20 at post-treatment and follow-ups, but Table 3 gives 0.91 at post-treatment; the BDI-II slope (B = −4.24) has no P value; the Discussion compares 'd = .82' for patients with 'g = .64' for partners.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (2. Results › 2.1, 2nd paragraph; Table 3; 3. Discussion, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The registry's posted CAPS-5 endpoint mean is 16.3 (SD 13.71), while Table 2 gives an estimated post-treatment mean of 19.37 with the same SD; for every secondary outcome the registry's posted means equal the article's 'estimated means' to two decimals (for example PSQI 14.24 and 10.37; BDI-II 32.91 and 12.75).
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Results › Outcome Measures); PMC HTML (Table 2)
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which values are observed and which model-estimated; the within-group effect sizes depend on which they are.

reporting_issues.issue: PCL-5 and the Couples Satisfaction Index, registered as secondary outcomes, are called primary self-report outcomes in the article; registration followed the actual start by about six weeks.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Method › 1.3 Assessment, 2nd paragraph); registry record (Outcome Measures; Status)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor outcome switching in emphasis.
