key_findings.finding: Funding: Heroic Hearts Project grant; MDMA supplied by Resilient Pharmaceuticals (formerly Lykos Therapeutics); VA career development awards for two authors.

reporting_issues.issue: The account of relational distress is incomplete and ambiguous: six of eight veterans and six of eight partners are said to have been distressed at baseline and four of each to have improved clinically; the next sentence, about 'the remaining two veterans and one of the remaining partners', describes people who began and stayed nondistressed, and the last partner is said to have begun nondistressed and deteriorated. What happened to the two distressed veterans and two distressed partners who did not improve clinically is not stated, and 'remaining' reads as if it referred to them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Presumably those four stayed distressed, but the text does not say; cite the reliable-change counts and the four of six who improved.

reporting_issues.issue: Treatment-emergent adverse events are defined as events during or within 2 days after MDMA administration (Methods), but the most frequent ones are reported as those within 7 days of an MDMA session (Results).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (METHOD › Measures › Safety endpoints › Adverse event tracking; RESULTS › Safety › AEs, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The window behind the reported percentages is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered primary time frame is baseline to 6 months after treatment, but the article reports the change to the end of treatment as its main effect and the follow-up only as a rebound; the PCL-5 and PCL-C results, named as secondary endpoints, are not given; the registry calls this open-label pilot phase 3.
reporting_issues.page: registry record (Design; Outcome Measures); publisher HTML (METHOD › Measures; RESULTS)
reporting_issues.consequence: The registered outcome has to be reconstructed (about a 10-point net fall, editors' arithmetic).

reporting_issues.issue: Effect sizes come from estimated marginal means of models that controlled for baseline levels of each outcome, a within-group change model; the standardizer is not stated, and the printed d for CAPS-5 (−1.25) cannot be reproduced from the printed raw change (16.1, SD 11.4) or baseline SD (10.56).
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Data analysis, 1st paragraph; RESULTS › PTSD symptom severity)
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the raw changes and counts rather than the d values.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jts.70126 (open access, CC BY-NC-ND; all sections, figure notes, author note and open practices statement), read in this reader's own browser tab; ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT05979844 (API v2) for registration and outcomes; the Crossref record for the DOI. Supplementary Tables S1 and S2 were not read (downloads); Figs 1 to 4 are images and no values were taken from them.

design_detail: Exploratory secondary analysis of the first phase 3 trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for severe PTSD (MAPP1; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03537014; 15 sites in the US, Canada and Israel; card sc_mitchell_2021): change in self-reported hazardous alcohol use (AUDIT) and drug use (DUDIT) from baseline, before randomization, to study termination, compared between MDMA with manualized therapy and inactive placebo with the same therapy, in the 82 of 90 participants with both assessments. Read as the accepted author manuscript in PubMed Central (NIHMS1847922), not the publisher's version. Sponsored and fully funded by MAPS; organized by MAPS PBC.
can_establish: Whether, within a randomized trial in people with severe PTSD and little current alcohol or drug problem, AUDIT and DUDIT scores changed differently with MDMA-assisted therapy than with placebo plus the same therapy over about 4 months.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy treats alcohol or other substance use disorders (no participant had a current alcohol use disorder and other current substance use disorders were excluded); whether consumption itself changed (the AUDIT and DUDIT are screening questionnaires, and their recall window was 12 months at baseline but only the time since treatment ended at termination); or longer-term substance use, including later MDMA use.

sample.recruitment: As in MAPP1 (card sc_mitchell_2021); participants recruited 7 November 2018 to 26 May 2020 (3.1 Sample characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Severe PTSD (CAPS-5 of 35 or more, symptoms for at least 6 months); psychiatric disorders and alcohol and substance use disorders in the last 12 months assessed with the MINI; current mild alcohol or cannabis use disorder, or moderate disorder in early remission for 3 months, allowed; any other substance use disorder within 12 months excluded; past disorders more than 12 months before allowed (2.2 Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Of the 82: 64.6% women; 80.3% White; mean age 41.4 (12.2); past alcohol use disorder 21 (25.6%) and no current one; past substance use disorder 14 (17.1%); current mild cannabis use disorder 2 (both on placebo); any alcohol use (AUDIT 1 or more) 69 (84.2%); any drug use (DUDIT 1 or more) 48 (58.5%); baseline CAPS-5 43.8 (6.0) (3.1 Sample characteristics, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Three MDMA and 4 placebo participants withdrew; analyses use the 82 with both baseline and termination AUDIT or DUDIT (complete cases) (3.1 Sample characteristics, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: The trial population had little current alcohol or drug disorder: no participant with even a mild alcohol use disorder was recruited, although permitted (4. Discussion, 2nd paragraph); results say nothing about people with substance use disorders.

exposure.measurement: As in MAPP1: after medication taper, three 90-minute preparatory sessions, randomization, three 8-hour experimental sessions with MDMA or placebo, each followed by three 90-minute integration sessions over 3 to 4 weeks; participants, site staff and sponsor blinded until database lock (2.3 Intervention, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: in each of three sessions a divided dose, 80 mg plus 40 mg in the first session and 120 mg plus 60 mg in the second and third, the supplement 1.5 to 2 hours after the initial dose; supplements and the increase could be withheld or declined; placebo on the same schedule (2.3 Intervention, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: The outcomes are the alcohol and drug-use questionnaires themselves; cannabis was the only drug with a permitted current (mild) disorder (2.2 Participants).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo with the identical therapy (2.1 Study design; 2.3 Intervention).
comparison.matching: Randomized (MAPP1). In the 82 analysed, baseline AUDIT 4.26 (4.28) on MDMA vs 2.83 (3.27) on placebo (Table 1; text P = .10); the authors report no significant group differences at baseline.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison.

outcomes.instruments: AUDIT (10 items, 0 to 40; hazardous alcohol use) and DUDIT (11 items, 0 to 44; drug use and drug-related problems), self-reported at baseline with the standard 12-month lookback and at study termination with instructions altered to cover the time since the end of treatment; CAPS-5, adapted SDS, BDI-II and modified C-SSRS from the parent trial for correlations (2.4 Outcome measures, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Screening instruments, not diagnostic, with cited validity across populations (2.4 Outcome measures).
outcomes.operationalization: Between-group difference in change scores from baseline to termination, by t test and models with and without adjustment for the baseline score; Hedges' g for significant effects; Pearson correlations of AUDIT change with CAPS-5, SDS and BDI-II (2.5 Statistical methods, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; two exploratory outcomes, each tested with and without baseline adjustment, plus correlations.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Self-report by participants who, in MAPP1, very probably knew their allocation (card sc_mitchell_2021); blinding of participants was not formally assessed in MAPP1.

analysis.effect_sizes: AUDIT change: −1.02 (SD 3.52) on MDMA vs +0.40 (2.70) on placebo, F printed as (80, 1) = 4.20, P = 0.0436, Hedges' g = 0.45; after adjustment for baseline AUDIT, P = 0.52. Within groups: MDMA 4.09 (4.16) at baseline and 3.24 (3.36) at termination (P = .30); placebo 2.80 (3.18) and 3.23 (3.65) (P = .57). DUDIT change: −1.36 (3.00) vs −0.78 (5.39), F printed as (80, 1) = 0.37, P = 0.5452, g = 0.13 with a printed 95% CI of 0.013 to 0.89; within groups MDMA 2.70 to 1.33 (P = .10), placebo 3.45 to 2.70 (P = .53). AUDIT change correlated with baseline CAPS-5 in the MDMA group only (r = .32, P = .04) (3.2 AUDIT and DUDIT scores, 1st paragraph; Abstract). Editors' calculation from the printed change means and SDs: difference 1.42 AUDIT points, t(80) = 2.04, g about 0.45, matching the printed F and g.
analysis.covariates: Baseline score in the adjusted models.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The parent trial is registered (NCT03537014); AUDIT and DUDIT were exploratory measures, not registered outcomes, and their results were not reported in the main trial paper (card sc_mitchell_2021). No analysis plan for this secondary analysis is cited.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract and highlights report only the unadjusted AUDIT result (P = 0.0436); the baseline-adjusted result (P = 0.52) appears only in the Results and Discussion.
analysis.power: No power calculation for these outcomes; the authors note that the narrow distribution of AUDIT scores limited the ability to detect change (4. Discussion, 2nd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 82 people with severe PTSD and no current alcohol use disorder, AUDIT scores fell by 1.0 point on MDMA and rose by 0.4 on placebo (on a 0 to 40 scale); the difference was significant without adjustment but not after adjusting for the MDMA group's higher baseline (P = 0.52). DUDIT changes did not differ. The termination questionnaires covered only the period since treatment ended, against 12 months at baseline.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says MDMA-assisted therapy was associated with a "significantly greater reduction" in AUDIT change scores, without the adjusted result, and concludes that it may lead to subclinical improvements in alcohol use and does not appear to increase the risk of illicit drug use (Abstract). The highlights speak of greater decreases in alcohol consumption, which the AUDIT does not measure directly. The Discussion says the reduction in alcohol use may be uniquely associated with MDMA-assisted therapy and that the protocol did not show an increased risk of substance use, abuse or dependence, or of MDMA use, during and 2 months after treatment (4. Discussion, 1st and 4th paragraphs); MDMA use is not reported separately in the paper, and the supporting long-term follow-up it cites (Jerome et al., 2020) is marked retracted in PMC. The Discussion acknowledges that the adjusted effect was not significant and that the sample without alcohol use disorder limits interpretation (4. Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

timeline.event: MAPP1 main report (Mitchell et al.); AUDIT and DUDIT were exploratory and not reported there.
This secondary analysis (online 11 February 2022).

replication.where_it_stands: A single exploratory analysis; the authors announce long-term follow-up data on AUDIT, DUDIT and MDMA craving and use (4. Discussion, 4th paragraph), not among the sources read. The MAPP1 card records, from the registry, a 'substance use' adverse event in 3 of 46 MDMA and 0 of 44 placebo participants, which this paper does not mention.

funding.funder: MAPS sponsored the trial, provided the MDMA and fully funded it from private and foundation donations; MAPS PBC, its wholly owned subsidiary, organized the trial (Acknowledgments; Role of funding sources).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: JBW, AC and AE received salary support for full-time employment with MAPS PBC; BY-K and RD for full-time employment with MAPS; CRN, JM and SK received funding from MAPS PBC during this and other studies; CRN is also paid for contract work as an MDMA-assisted therapy trainer (Declaration of Competing Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: A sponsor employee (JBW) carried out the statistical analysis; sponsor staff oversaw data collection (CRediT statement).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in people with PTSD and a current alcohol use disorder, with consumption measured by timeline follow-back over equal windows and verified biologically, blinded raters and follow-up of at least 12 months, reporting any later MDMA or other drug use.

domains.note: Central randomization in MAPP1 (card sc_mitchell_2021); the higher baseline AUDIT on MDMA (P = .10) is compatible with chance.
As in MAPP1: participants probably aware of allocation through drug effects; the analysis concerns the effect of assignment among those with data.
Eight of 90 (9%) excluded as incomplete, complete-case only; reasons for withdrawal could relate to substance use.
Self-reported questionnaires by participants who probably knew their allocation, and a recall window that changed from 12 months to the period since treatment ended between the two measurements.
Unregistered exploratory outcomes; the unadjusted and baseline-adjusted analyses disagree (P = 0.0436 and 0.52) and the abstract reports only the significant one.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Randomized, but the outcomes are exploratory self-reports with a changed recall window in a largely unblinded trial, and the reported effect depends on the choice between two analyses. The paper can be cited for the small size of the AUDIT and DUDIT changes in both arms and for the absence of a detectable increase in drug-use scores over about 4 months in people without current substance use disorders; it cannot be cited for an effect on alcohol use, for any population with a substance use disorder, or for long-term drug use.

key_findings.finding: Of 90 randomized and dosed in MAPP1, 82 (42 MDMA, 40 placebo) had baseline and termination AUDIT or DUDIT; none had a current alcohol use disorder; 21 (25.6%) a past alcohol use disorder, 14 (17.1%) a past substance use disorder, 2 placebo participants a current mild cannabis use disorder.

AUDIT change from baseline to study termination: −1.02 (SD 3.52) on MDMA vs +0.40 (2.70) on placebo, P = 0.0436, Hedges' g = 0.45 unadjusted; not significant after adjusting for baseline AUDIT (P = 0.52). Baseline AUDIT did not differ significantly (P = .10).
key_findings.locator: 3.2 AUDIT and DUDIT scores, 1st paragraph; Abstract › Results

key_findings.finding: Within-group AUDIT: MDMA 4.09 (4.16) at baseline and 3.24 (3.36) at termination (P = .30, g = .22); placebo 2.80 (3.18) and 3.23 (3.65) (P = .57, g = .13).
key_findings.note: These baseline means differ from Table 1 (4.26 and 2.83), and 4.09 to 3.24 is a fall of 0.85, not the printed −1.02 (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: DUDIT change: −1.36 (3.00) on MDMA vs −0.78 (5.39) on placebo, P = 0.5452, g = 0.13 (printed 95% CI 0.013 to 0.89); within groups MDMA 2.70 (4.31) to 1.33 (3.14), placebo 3.45 (4.46) to 2.70 (6.33).
key_findings.locator: 3.2 AUDIT and DUDIT scores, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Recall windows: AUDIT and DUDIT were given at baseline with the standard 12-month lookback and at study termination with instructions to cover the time since the end of treatment.
AUDIT change was not correlated with baseline or change in CAPS-5, BDI-II or SDS overall; in the MDMA group it correlated with baseline CAPS-5 (r = .32, P = .04; data not shown).

Limitations stated: no participant with even a mild current alcohol use disorder was recruited, although permitted; the narrow distribution of AUDIT scores limited detection of change; the exploratory, non-AUD sample limits clinical interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: The adjusted analysis that removes the AUDIT effect (P = 0.52) is absent from the abstract and highlights, which report only the unadjusted P = 0.0436.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract; Highlights; 3.2 AUDIT and DUDIT scores, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates the finding.

reporting_issues.issue: Baseline AUDIT means differ between Table 1 (4.26 and 2.83) and the Results text (4.09 and 2.80), and the text's MDMA means (4.09 to 3.24) imply a change of −0.85, not the printed −1.02; Table 1 has 42 MDMA participants although 46 minus 3 withdrawals is 43.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; 3.1 Sample characteristics, 1st paragraph; 3.2 AUDIT and DUDIT scores, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The analysed sets for the two questionnaires may differ; the change scores cannot be reconstructed from the printed means.

reporting_issues.issue: The DUDIT effect is printed as g = 0.13 with a 95% CI of 0.013 to 0.89, an interval excluding zero for a test with P = 0.5452; F statistics are printed with their degrees of freedom reversed, as F (80, 1).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (3.2 AUDIT and DUDIT scores, 1st paragraph; Abstract)
reporting_issues.consequence: The DUDIT interval cannot be right; cite the P value and the change scores.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 arithmetic: White participants total 66 although the groups give 37 and 28 (65, which matches the printed 80.25% of 81 with race reported); past substance use disorder on placebo is 6 printed as 12.50% (6 of 40 is 15.0%); veterans 15 printed as 19.29% (15 of 82 is 18.3%). The Discussion gives a baseline DUDIT of 2.51 (3.39), range 1 to 15, which matches no figure in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the sample description has several typographical errors.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites the pooled long-term follow-up of the phase 2 trials (Jerome et al., 2020), marked retracted in PMC's reference list, for limited abuse potential in clinical settings.
reporting_issues.consequence: That support cannot be used (METHODS §3.2).

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9750500, the accepted author manuscript (NIHMS1847922), all sections, Table 1 and figure legend, read in this reader's own browser tab; the publisher's version of record on ScienceDirect could not be opened in the app's browser and was not compared; the Crossref record for the DOI; the MAPP1 study card (sc_mitchell_2021) for the parent trial's design and registry. Fig. 1 values were not extracted.

design_detail: Historical narrative review (Drug Science, Policy and Law, vol. 4, published online 11 April 2018; free access on the SAGE site) of the use of MDMA in psychotherapy in the United States from 1977 to 1985, when it was legal and unscheduled, and of the scheduling process, by a single author, a psychiatrist and historian of psychedelic therapy. Sources: memoirs and books by early practitioners and their associates (for example Stolaroff, 2004; Shulgin and Shulgin), conference reports, a self-published and later journal-published follow-up of patients (Greer and Tolbert, 1986), an unpublished study (Kueny, 1980), an informal therapist survey (ARUPA, 1984), an unapproved physiological study (Downing, 1986), court records, press reports, interviews and personal communications. No search strategy, no appraisal of the cited reports, no quantitative synthesis. Also describes session practices and guidelines of the period, which this card does not reproduce.
can_establish: Who used MDMA in psychotherapy before it was scheduled, in what settings and with what stated aims, what early reports and testimonies claimed, how the 1984 to 1988 scheduling unfolded, and which abuses by therapists were documented.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted psychotherapy helped or harmed patients in that period: the outcome evidence described is uncontrolled reports, testimonies and one small follow-up, relayed without appraisal; the numbers of people treated come from memoirs, interviews and the author's own extrapolation.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (historical review).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated; the author's selection of sources.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Sources are mostly practitioners, advocates and their circles (the Boston group, ARUPA, EMDL, MAPS founders); regulators' and critics' positions are given briefly; some figures rest on personal communications with more than 10 informants.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable; the review describes therapeutic practices of the period in prose.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Doses of the period are mentioned in the article; not reproduced here.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: Not applicable.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The only outcome figures described: Greer and Tolbert's follow-up of 29 patients (no serious side effects or negative after-effects found; 23 reported positive changes in attitude lasting from 1 week to the 2-year follow-up), and an informal survey in which 15 of 16 therapists judged MDMA valuable.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable; the review relays proponents' accounts of benefit and safety without appraisal, while also documenting two cases of sexual abuse by therapists.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A history: a few dozen US therapists used MDMA in psychotherapy between about 1977 and 1985, with caseloads reported in memoirs and interviews; outcome evidence consisted of uncontrolled reports and testimonies; two therapists sexually abused patients during MDMA sessions; the DEA's administrative law judge recommended against Schedule I, the DEA overruled him, and research applications were then blocked until 1992.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls MDMA's properties "benign, feeling-enhancing, and nonhallucinatory" and says the pioneers laid the groundwork for later studies; the review states that the safety profile was very good overall and side effects all mild, judgments that rest on practitioners' reports rather than on studies able to detect harms. The estimate of more than 60,000 people treated underground from 1985 to 2017 is the author's extrapolation from informants, presented with caveats.

timeline.event: 27 July 1984: the DEA proposes placing MDMA in Schedule I; therapists and EMDL request a hearing (per this review).
Hearings; the administrative law judge recommends against Schedule I and the DEA overrules him; the WHO Expert Committee recommends international control while urging research (per this review).
Greer and Tolbert publish their follow-up of 29 patients (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs), the main outcome report of the period (not read).
The 'Grinspoon window' (22 December 1987 to 22 March 1988) closes; the DEA holds that accepted medical use requires FDA approval (per this review).
The first FDA-approved study of MDMA in humans begins, in healthy volunteers, after earlier applications were placed on clinical hold (per this review).
Long-term follow-up of the first randomized trial of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for PTSD.

replication.where_it_stands: A useful historical account by one author, consistent in outline with the 1985 to 1986 primary documents on the project's list (not read here). Claims about the history may cite it as a narrative review; claims about efficacy or safety in that period should not.

funding.funder: The author received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication.
funding.declared_conflicts: The author declared no potential conflicts of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: The author has written several histories of MDMA and psycholytic therapy, some with Benzenhöfer, which this review cites for background.

what_would_settle_it: For the history: the primary documents of 1985 to 1986 (the hearing record, the judge's recommended ruling, the WHO committee report, the early clinical papers) read directly. For the clinical question the history raises: controlled trials, which began only in the 2000s.

domains.note: No search or selection criteria; sources chosen by the author, many of them memoirs, interviews and personal communications.
Uncontrolled reports and therapists' testimonies of benefit and safety are relayed without appraisal.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The author's earlier histories are cited for background, not as evidence of effects.
The underground-treatment estimate is labelled as such, but judgments of safety and benefit are stated as findings.

domains.domain: Balance of the history (regulators' and critics' views of the early claims are under-represented)
domains.note: Documents the abuse cases and the WHO's methodological reservation, but presents the case for therapeutic use mainly through its proponents; the DEA's and FDA's reasoning is summarized in a sentence or two.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to narrative reviews (METHODS §5.3). As history the review is informative and dated; as evidence about effects it is second-hand and unappraised. Cite it for who did what and when, and for the scheduling sequence it describes; any claim resting only on it stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: A few dozen psychotherapists, mostly in California and elsewhere on the West Coast, used MDMA in psychotherapy between about 1977 and 1985, when it was neither an FDA-approved drug nor a controlled substance; in California and some other states a physician could use it legally if self-synthesized, with informed consent and a peer-reviewed protocol.
key_findings.note: The abstract and title say 1977, the Discussion 1978.

key_findings.finding: Reported caseloads (from memoirs, interviews and the practitioners' own accounts): Leo Zeff gave MDMA to about 4000 people over 12 years and trained more than 150 therapists (Stolaroff, 2004); George Greer and Requa Tolbert treated more than 80 patients from 1980 to 1985; Rick Ingrasci 100 patients in about 150 sessions, one-third with couples, including 11 people with cancer; Claudio Naranjo more than 30 patients by 1984; Deborah Harlow more than 200 clients before 1985.
key_findings.locator: Leo Zeff—The Secret Chief, 2nd paragraph; George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 1st paragraph; Rick Ingrasci: MDMA in couples and patients with life-threatening illnesses, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Claudio Naranjo, 2nd paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The main outcome report described is Greer and Tolbert's follow-up of 29 patients (self-published 1983, published 1986): no serious side effects or negative after-effects were found, and 23 reported positive changes in attitude lasting between 1 week and the follow-up time of 2 years; there was no comparison group.
key_findings.locator: George Greer's work with MDMA in psychotherapy, 5th paragraph (author's paragraphs; block quotations not counted)

key_findings.finding: Other early evidence: an unpublished exploratory study of nine people given one MDMA session each (Kueny, 1980); a 1984 survey of 16 therapists for ARUPA, in which 15 judged MDMA valuable in augmenting psychotherapy and all claimed negligible complications and low abuse potential, used as evidence at the hearings; and a 1984 study of 21 people with prior MDMA experience, run without FDA or institutional review board approval, reporting dose-dependent rises in blood pressure of 20 to 40 mm Hg and no complications.
key_findings.locator: Kueny's 1980 study, 1st paragraph; A survey of MDMA therapists, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; The first psychophysiological study of MDMA in humans, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Two therapists, Rick Ingrasci and Francesco DiLeo, initiated sexual contact and intercourse with patients during MDMA sessions; both were sued and lost their licences; DiLeo's patient was later diagnosed with PTSD and anxiety and awarded damages by a Maryland court (1991). According to Harlow, the Ingrasci case led to the rule of male-female co-therapist teams in later studies.
key_findings.locator: Physical abuse in MDMA-assisted psychotherapy, 1st, 2nd and 4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Scheduling: on 27 July 1984 the DEA recommended Schedule I; a hearing was requested and held in 1985; the administrative law judge concluded that MDMA did not have to be placed in Schedule I (therapeutic potential, could be handled without grave dangers under medical supervision, no high abuse potential, not proven toxic in humans); the DEA overruled him; an appeal suspended the scheduling from 22 December 1987 to 22 March 1988, after which the DEA held that accepted medical use requires FDA approval.
key_findings.locator: Therapists opposed to the scheduling of MDMA in 1985, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, which recommended international control of MDMA in late 1985, found the reports of therapeutic usefulness intriguing but methodologically inadequate and urged countries to facilitate research (WHO, 1985).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs (the WHO statement is a block quotation)

key_findings.finding: After scheduling, five applications to the FDA to study MDMA (1986 to 1988) were placed on clinical hold on grounds of possible neurotoxicity; a protocol for anxiety in terminal cancer was rejected in 1992; the first FDA-approved MDMA study in humans, in healthy volunteers, began in 1992. In Switzerland, five members of a physicians' society were permitted to use MDMA and LSD in psychotherapy from 1988 to 1993.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 8th paragraph; MDMA therapy goes underground, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The indications explored by the early therapists (trauma, anxiety associated with terminal cancer, psychoneuroses and couples) were also those taken up in later research.
key_findings.locator: Indications, precautions, and session guidelines, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The author estimates, from more than 10 informants and assumed session numbers, that more than 60,000 people may have been treated with MDMA in underground therapy from 1985 to 2017, an estimate he calls probably conservative and that cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The start of the period is 1977 in the title and abstract and 1978 in the Discussion; the section on underground therapy says European work began in the late 1970s, before scheduling, under a heading about going underground after it.
reporting_issues.page: publisher HTML (Title; Abstract; Discussion, 1st paragraph; MDMA therapy goes underground, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; dates in a history claim should be given as 'from the late 1970s'.

verification.source_read: Publisher full text (HTML), https://doi.org/10.1177/2050324518767442 (journals.sagepub.com article page, free access; all sections, block quotations, declaration of conflicting interests and funding; reference list scanned). Crossref record read in this reader's tab.

design_detail: Sponsor's secondary analysis of pooled individual data from four randomized, double-blind phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy for chronic PTSD (MP-8 and MP-12 in the United States, MP-4 in Canada, MP-9 in Israel; NCT01958593, NCT01211405, NCT01689740, NCT01793610; data collected January 2012 to March 2017), the four of six phase 2 trials that included the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Blinded comparison at the primary endpoint (1 to 2 months after two blinded sessions): participants pooled into an 'active' group (75 to 125 mg MDMA, n = 47) and a 'control' group (0 to 40 mg, n = 16) by unstratified t tests; then, after unblinding and open-label crossover, an uncontrolled mixed-model analysis of all participants at treatment exit and 12-month follow-up. Analyses not preregistered. An expression of concern (jts_2025a) and a correction (jts_2025b) were published on 3 December 2024; the correction removed the four MP-4 participants treated by a pair of therapists involved in an ethical violation, leaving 59 (45 active, 14 control at 25 to 40 mg, no inactive placebo). Read as the PMC copy (CC BY-NC), with both notices read in full.
can_establish: Whether self-reported sleep quality improved more over 1 to 2 months after two sessions with full-dose MDMA than with low-dose MDMA in these trials, as reanalysed after the correction, and how sleep and PTSD scores changed, without a comparison group, to 12 months after open-label treatment.
cannot_establish: An effect of MDMA on sleep separate from expectancy (blinding was not assessed and the outcome is self-reported), any effect at 12 months (everyone had received full-dose MDMA by then), or objective sleep changes; and, after the expression of concern, it cannot be taken as independent of the sponsor's handling of the MP-4 site.

sample.recruitment: Referrals by health professionals, internet advertisements and word of mouth; civilians, veterans and first responders aged 18 or older with an inadequate response to at least one pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy; three private-practice sites and one government-funded psychiatric hospital (Method › Participants and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: PTSD for at least 6 months and CAPS-IV total severity of 50 or more (MP-8, MP-12, MP-9) or 60 or more (MP-4); anxiety and depression allowed; excluded: past or current psychotic disorders, bipolar I, borderline personality disorder, eating disorders with active purging, substance use disorder within 60 days (6 months for MP-4), major medical conditions except controlled hypertension or treated hypothyroidism, pregnancy, lactation or no effective contraception, weight under 48 kg. Psychiatric medicines were tapered and stopped, except as-needed anxiolytics and sedative-hypnotics between sessions, gabapentin for pain and ADHD medicines (Participants and Procedure, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Original sample (63): mean age 40.8 (SD 11.5); 34 men (54.0%); 85.7% White; mean PTSD duration 225 months; combat trauma 71.4%; lifetime suicidal ideation 87.3%; earlier ecstasy use 28.6% (Results › Sample Characteristics; Table 1). The groups differed: combat trauma 100% of controls and 61.7% of the active group, PTSD duration 155 against 249 months. The corrected Table 1 gives other trauma figures (combat 37.3% of 59), which cannot follow from removing four people (see reporting issues).
sample.attrition: Modified intention-to-treat set: participants with at least one blinded session and at least one follow-up assessment; one participant without a baseline PSQI was omitted. The PSQI was added by amendment in MP-8, so 6 of 26 MP-8 participants have no PSQI; PSQI at the primary endpoint for 45 of 47 active participants (Participants and Procedure, 6th paragraph; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Table 2 note).
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-resistant volunteers; a large share combat veterans and first responders; 28.6% had used ecstasy before. Pooling trials with different allocation ratios and control doses produced groups that differ at baseline. The correction removed four participants of one site because of an ethical violation by their therapists.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in two blinded 8-hour sessions 3 to 5 weeks apart, each followed by three 90-minute integrative sessions, after three 90-minute preparatory sessions with a co-therapist team, using the sponsor's manual; overnight stay with a night attendant. After unblinding at the primary endpoint, full-dose participants (except in MP-9) had one more open-label session, and control and 75 mg participants crossed over to two (MP-9) or three open-label full-dose sessions (Participants and Procedure, 4th to 6th paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth; active doses 75, 100 or 125 mg, control doses 0, 25, 30 or 40 mg (25, 30 or 40 mg after the correction), each followed by an optional supplemental half dose; MDMA from David Nichols, Purdue University (MP-8, MP-12) or Lipomed (MP-4, MP-9), in equivalent-weight capsules with lactose.
exposure.polysubstance: Substance use disorder in the previous 60 days (6 months for MP-4) excluded. Prior ecstasy use 18.8% of controls and 31.9% of the active group (Table 1). Sleep aids on the nights of blinded sessions were given only in the active group: 6 of 46 after session 1 and 5 of 46 after session 2 (Results › Blinded Endpoint, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the primary endpoint was 1 to 2 months after the second blinded session.

comparison.controls: Pooled 'control' group: participants randomized within their trial to 0, 25, 30 or 40 mg MDMA with the same psychotherapy (after the correction only 25 to 40 mg: the removed MP-4 participants were the only ones on 0 mg). The 75 mg group, counted as active in the blinded comparison, also crossed over to open-label full doses.
comparison.matching: Randomized within each trial, but the pooled comparison uses unstratified independent-samples t tests across trials with different allocation ratios and control doses; the groups were defined by the protocols' dose designations and 'by inspection of posttreatment CAPS-IV scores' (Data Analysis, 1st paragraph), citing the pooled phase 2 analysis by Mithoefer et al. (2019), retracted in 2024.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparison within trials; across the pooled groups trauma type and PTSD duration differ (Table 1). Expectancy was not measured.

outcomes.instruments: PSQI (19 items, seven components, global score 0 to 21; past month), at baseline, primary endpoint, treatment exit and 12 months; CAPS-IV (0 to 136) rated by an independent rater who was not present during the psychotherapy sessions (Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: The authors cite a cut-off of 5 for poor sleep and adopt a 3-point drop as clinically meaningful; Cronbach's alpha in this sample .63 at baseline, .71, .69 and .80 later (corrected .65, .72, .70, .80).
outcomes.operationalization: Improvement in sleep quality: larger fall in the PSQI global score from baseline to primary endpoint in the active group; a 3-point drop counted as clinically meaningful.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: CAPS and PSQI totals, seven PSQI components, the 3-point responder comparison, the three open-label mixed-model contrasts and the CAPS-PSQI correlation, plus covariate screening, all at alpha 0.05.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The CAPS-IV rater was independent of the therapy; the PSQI is self-reported. Blinding of participants was not assessed.

analysis.effect_sizes: Original: CAPS-IV change −34.0 (SD 26.5) active against −12.4 (16.4) control, p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 printed with 95% CI −5.18 to 6.93; PSQI change −3.53 (5.03) against +0.56 (3.05), p = .003, g 0.88 printed with CI −0.27 to 2.03 (Table 2). Editors' recalculation from Table 2: g 0.88 with 95% CI 0.29 to 1.47 for CAPS-IV and 0.28 to 1.47 for PSQI. Corrected (jts_2025b): CAPS-IV −34.93 (26.66) against −11.07 (16.85), g 0.96 (0.33 to 1.59); PSQI −3.51 (5.08) against +0.50 (3.25), p = .008, g 0.85 (0.23 to 1.47); 3-point PSQI response 24 of 45 (53.3%) against 2 of 14 (14.3%). Open-label (corrected, N = 58): PSQI least-squares means 12.59, 8.18 at treatment exit and 7.09 at 12 months; treatment exit to 12 months −1.09 (SE 0.49), p = .029; CAPS-IV 88.22, 42.46 and 35.28.
analysis.covariates: Original mixed model: time, baseline CAPS-IV and study as fixed effects, participant random; candidate covariates (age, PTSD duration, sex, race, prior ecstasy use) screened one at a time at p ≤ .01; age retained (p = .017). The correction drops baseline CAPS-IV and study from the base model and reports that no candidate covariate met the cut-off.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Open Practices Statement: the four trials were registered, but the analyses were not formally preregistered; the article nonetheless carries a 'Preregistered Research Designs' badge linked to the trial registrations.
analysis.selective_reporting: Grouping of doses partly by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores. The correction removed the subgroup result (a 3-point PSQI drop predicting lower CAPS-IV at treatment exit and 12 months) because it was no longer significant at treatment exit, without reporting the 12-month result, and changed the model specification.
analysis.power: None; the authors state the pilot trials were not powered for this exploratory analysis.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In four pooled phase 2 trials of one sponsor, self-reported sleep quality improved more 1 to 2 months after two blinded sessions in the full-dose group than in the low-dose (and, originally, placebo) group: by about 4 PSQI points, with half of the full-dose group improving by 3 points or more against one in seven controls. After open-label full-dose treatment for all, scores were lower again at 12 months than at treatment exit by about 1 point, without a comparison group. The outcome is self-reported, blinding was not assessed, and the data were corrected in 2024 after an ethical violation at one site.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the trials provide evidence for beneficial effects of MDMA-assisted psychotherapy in treating sleep disturbance. The Discussion calls the change from treatment exit to 12 months an enduring, clinically meaningful benefit, although that change (about 1 point) is below the authors' own 3-point threshold and comes from uncontrolled open-label data, and suggests the therapy may be "particularly suited for promoting sleep regulation" (Discussion, 8th paragraph). The correction states that removing the data "does not compromise the conclusions", although one subgroup result disappeared.

timeline.event: The first phase 2 trial's follow-up reports improved sleep on a questionnaire item in 12 of 19 participants (Mithoefer et al., 2013).
Pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials (Mithoefer et al., 2019), cited here for the dose grouping and for insomnia rates; retracted on 10 August 2024.
This pooled sleep analysis (published online 10 June 2021).

Expression of concern and correction (3 December 2024): the four MP-4 participants treated by two therapists involved in an ethical violation are removed; the journal judges the authors' non-disclosure improper.

replication.where_it_stands: The only analysis of sleep in the MDMA trials found here. It rests on the sponsor's own pooled data, carries an expression of concern, and cites a retracted pooled analysis for its dose grouping; its blinded comparison is with low-dose MDMA after the correction. Cite the corrected figures, with the notice.

funding.funder: Not stated as a funding statement. The trials were run by MAPS and MAPS Public Benefit Corporation (copyright of the article is held by MAPS Public Benefit Corporation).
funding.declared_conflicts: Author note: Ponte previously received salary support from MAPS as a full-time employee; Jerome is a full-time employee of MAPS Public Benefit Corporation; Hamilton received salary support from MAPS PBC as a biostatistician; Mithoefer received research funds from MAPS PBC as investigator, medical monitor and trainer; Yazar-Klosinski is a full-time employee of MAPS; Feduccia is a full-time employee of MAPS PBC; Vermetten received salary support from MAPS PBC as an investigator.
funding.affiliations_note: Every author is or was paid by the sponsor. The corresponding author is on the MAPS PBC Safety Team. Jerome, Mithoefer and Feduccia are authors of all three phase 2 analyses retracted in August 2024, and Hamilton and Yazar-Klosinski of two of them (author lists in the Crossref records of the three retraction notes).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial with sleep as a prespecified outcome, an active placebo, assessment of blinding and expectancy, objective sleep measures (actigraphy or polysomnography) and a controlled follow-up beyond the end of treatment, run independently of the sponsor.

domains.note: Each trial was randomized, but the pooled comparison is unstratified across trials with different allocation ratios and control doses, producing baseline imbalances (combat trauma 100% against 61.7%; PTSD duration 155 against 249 months).
Participants and therapists probably knew the dose from its effects (not assessed); sleep aids on session nights only in the active group.
PSQI missing for 6 of 26 MP-8 participants (added by amendment) and for two active participants at the primary endpoint; the open-label analyses rely on a mixed model.
The PSQI is self-reported and participants probably knew their dose; expectancy was not measured.
Analyses not preregistered; dose groups defined partly by inspecting post-treatment CAPS-IV scores; the correction changed the model and dropped a subgroup result.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The blinded comparison rests on randomization within trials, but its outcome is self-reported with probable unblinding and its analysis choices were made without a plan, partly after inspecting outcomes. The 12-month results are uncontrolled. The expression of concern and the correction add that one site's data were affected by an ethical violation that the authors did not disclose at submission. Cite the corrected blinded comparison for a short-term difference in self-reported sleep against low-dose MDMA, with these caveats, and the open-label results only descriptively.

key_findings.finding: Four randomized, double-blind phase 2 trials at four sites (MP-8, MP-12 in the United States; MP-4 in Canada; MP-9 in Israel), data collected January 2012 to March 2017; the two earliest phase 2 trials did not include the PSQI and are not in this analysis. Original pooled sample 63: 47 active (75 to 125 mg) and 16 control (0 to 40 mg).
key_findings.locator: Method › Participants and Procedure, 1st paragraph; Abstract; Data Analysis, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: After the 2024 correction: 59 (45 active, 14 control at 25 to 40 mg); see sc_jts_2025b.

key_findings.finding: Dose groups were pooled according to the trials' designation of doses as control or active and by inspection of post-treatment CAPS-IV scores, citing the pooled analysis by Mithoefer et al. (2019), which the reference list in PMC marks as retracted; blinded comparisons used independent-samples t tests, with no power analysis.
key_findings.locator: Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; References (Mithoefer et al., 2019)

key_findings.finding: Original blinded endpoint (1 to 2 months after the second blinded session): CAPS-IV change −33.98 (SD 26.46) active against −12.38 (16.38) control, p = .003; PSQI change −3.53 (5.03) against +0.56 (3.05), p = .003, Hedges' g 0.88 for both; 3-point PSQI drop in 25 active (printed 53.2%) against 2 controls (12.5%), χ2 8.87, N = 61, p = .003.
key_findings.locator: Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Table 2 and its notes
key_findings.note: Superseded by the corrected values (sc_jts_2025b). The printed confidence intervals for g are wrong (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: PSQI components at the blinded endpoint (original): sleep quality −0.62 against +0.19 (p = .006), sleep latency −0.42 against +0.38 (p = .005), daytime dysfunction −0.82 against +0.25 (p < .001); duration, efficiency, disturbance and use of sleep medication not significantly different.

On the nights of blinded sessions, no control participant received a sleep aid; in the active group (n = 46) 3 received zolpidem, 2 melatonin and 1 zopiclone after session 1, and 4 zolpidem and 1 melatonin after session 2.

Open-label analysis of everyone (original, N = 62): CAPS-IV least-squares mean 88.50 at baseline, 42.97 at treatment exit and 36.43 at 12 months (exit to 12 months −6.53, SE 2.50, p = .011); PSQI 12.65, 8.37 and 7.34 (exit to 12 months −1.03, SE 0.46, p = .029); 21 participants had a PSQI of 5 or lower at 12 months against 2 at baseline; change in CAPS-IV and PSQI from baseline to treatment exit correlated r = .371 (n = 58).
key_findings.locator: Results › Open-Label Endpoints: Treatment Exit and Long-Term Follow-Up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3; Figure 3 legend
key_findings.note: Uncontrolled: all had received full-dose MDMA by then. Corrected values in sc_jts_2025b.

key_findings.finding: The CAPS-IV sleep items were not removed, so part of the CAPS-PSQI correlation is built into the measures, as the authors note; limitations named: small, mostly White sample (85.7%), self-reported outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Open Practices Statement: the four trials were registered (NCT01958593, NCT01211405, NCT01689740, NCT01793610); the analyses were not formally preregistered; data available only through a data-use proposal to MAPS.
Every author was paid by MAPS or MAPS PBC (author note); no separate funding statement is printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% confidence intervals printed for Hedges' g in the original Table 2 do not fit the effect sizes or the p values: CAPS-IV g 0.88 with CI −5.18 to 6.93 and PSQI g 0.88 with CI −0.27 to 2.03 (including zero despite p = .003); sleep efficiency and sleep disturbance have intervals excluding zero (0.05 to 0.70; 0.25 to 0.60) although p = .191 and .124. Editors' recalculation from the table's means, SDs and group sizes: 0.29 to 1.47 (CAPS-IV), 0.28 to 1.47 (PSQI), −0.20 to 0.95 (efficiency), −0.18 to 0.97 (disturbance).
reporting_issues.consequence: The original intervals cannot be used; the corrected Table 2 (jts_2025b) gives plausible intervals.

reporting_issues.issue: The share of active participants with a 3-point PSQI drop is printed as 53.2% (25 of 47) and 42.6% (20 of 47) for the rest, which add to 95.7%; only 45 active participants had PSQI data, so the share is 25 of 45 (55.6%). The corrected footnote repeats the pattern: 24 (53.3%) and 19 (42.2%) use 45 as denominator although the table gives n = 44 and the counts add to 43; the printed χ2 of 6.85 could not be reproduced from those counts (editors' calculation 7.34, or 5.76 with continuity correction).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Blinded Endpoint, 1st paragraph; Table 2 note b); correction, Table 2 note b
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite counts rather than these percentages; the direction of the difference is not in doubt.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 (original) prints unlabelled counts and percentages (27, 44.3%; 34, 55.7%) beside the baseline and treatment-exit CAPS rows, while the rows for a 3-point PSQI drop to 12 months are empty; the numbers appear to belong to those empty rows. The corrected Table 3 gives 35 (60.3%) yes and 15 (25.9%) no, percentages of N = 58 although only 50 have data (35 of 50 is 70%).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 12-month responder figures are unclear in both versions; state counts with their denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The subgroup differences in CAPS-IV for participants with a 3-point PSQI drop are given as least-squares means with 'SD' 7.06 and 6.00; with p = .046 and p < .001 these are standard errors (editors' check: −14.41/7.06 gives z of about 2.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: Mislabelled; the result was withdrawn in the correction anyway.

reporting_issues.issue: The treatment-exit to 12-month PSQI change is p = .029 in Table 3 and p = .030 in the text and abstract; the primary endpoint is '1 month' after the second blinded session in the Figure 2 note and '1 to 2 months' in the Methods.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 3; Results › Open-Label Endpoints, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 note; Method › Participants and Procedure, 6th paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor.

reporting_issues.issue: The article carries a 'Preregistered Research Designs' badge, while its Open Practices Statement says the analyses were not formally preregistered; the badge links to the trial registrations.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Open Practices Statement; Open Research Badges)
reporting_issues.consequence: The badge should not be read as preregistration of this analysis.

reporting_issues.issue: The analysis relies on a retracted paper: the dose grouping cites Mithoefer et al. (2019), and the Discussion takes insomnia rates on session nights from it (38% control against 29% MDMA, and 47% against 36% the next day; revised in the correction to 34% and 29%, 44% and 31%). The correction (December 2024) describes these revisions as reflecting an ongoing correction of that paper, which had been retracted on 10 August 2024.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Method › Data Analysis, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph); correction, Discussion changes
reporting_issues.consequence: The insomnia figures from the retracted analysis must not be cited; the grouping method depends on a retracted source.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8453707 (all sections, Tables 1 to 3 as text, figure legends, Open Practices Statement, author note, article notes, reference list; Figures 1 to 3 are images whose legends only were read; the supplementary table, a .docx file, was not read, its content being reproduced in the correction). Read together with the expression of concern (PMC full text PMC12416979) and the correction (publisher full text, https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/jts.23098, free access). Crossref records of all three read in this reader's tab.

design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with meta-analyses (update, pub2, of review CD015383; protocol published 2022) of psychedelic-assisted therapy against placebo or active comparators for anxiety, depression and existential distress in adults with life-threatening diseases. Randomized trials only; CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase and two trial registers searched on 30 March 2024 without language or date restrictions, with reference checking, citation searching and contact with authors and experts. Six crossover trials (149 randomized, 140 analysed), first-period data only: five of classical psychedelics (psilocybin, LSD), pooled, and one of MDMA (Wolfson et al., 2020; 18 participants), analysed alone. Risk of bias with Cochrane RoB 1; certainty with GRADE. This card concerns mainly the MDMA comparison. Funded by NIHR Cochrane infrastructure funding.
can_establish: What the randomized evidence up to March 2024 shows, and how certain it is, for MDMA-assisted therapy against placebo for anxiety, depression, quality of life and serious harms in people with a life-threatening illness: one small trial.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA-assisted therapy reduces anxiety or depression in this population (one trial of 18, intervals including no effect), any effect beyond about a month (outcomes after crossover are uncontrolled), or rare harms.

sample.recruitment: Search on 30 March 2024 by the Cochrane PaPaS information specialist: 440 database records and 13 registry records, 304 after deduplication, 30 full texts; 6 studies (17 records) included, 6 excluded, 7 ongoing (Results › Results of the search).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Randomized trials (including crossover and cluster) of adults with anxiety, depression or existential distress (diagnosed or above questionnaire thresholds) and a life-threatening disease, any setting; interventions with a psychedelic at any dose plus preparatory and integration therapy; comparators placebo, active placebo or active treatment. The protocol's restriction to palliative care (more than 75% incurable) was changed post hoc to 'life-threatening disease' (Differences between protocol and review).
sample.demographics: Wolfson 2020: mean age 54.9 (SD 7.9), 14 of 18 women (77.8%), 15 White (83%); life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness, life expectancy of at least 9 months, STAI-Trait above 45; prior MDMA use 7 of 13 (MDMA arm) and 3 of 5 (placebo arm); single centre, USA, outpatients, 2015 to 2018 (Characteristics of included studies › Wolfson 2020). Across the six trials: ages 36 to 64, USA and Switzerland.
sample.attrition: Wolfson 2020: no dropouts at the primary assessment (12 of 13 MDMA participants after the open-label third session).
sample.selection_effects: All participants volunteered for psychedelic trials, many with prior use of the drug; most were White. PsycINFO was not searched. A registered randomized MDMA trial in anxiety with advanced-stage cancer (NCT00252174, terminated for lack of funds and participants) enrolled two people, both in its low-dose arm (ClinicalTrials.gov record read by this reader), so it adds no comparative data; the review does not mention it.

exposure.measurement: Wolfson 2020: two day-long blinded experimental sessions 2 to 4 weeks apart with nine 60- to 90-minute non-drug psychotherapy sessions (three before the first session and three after each), then an open-label crossover (Characteristics of included studies › Wolfson 2020).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed in the review: by mouth, 125 mg MDMA followed by an optional 62.5 mg 90 to 150 minutes later; comparator 125 mg lactose (labelled 'active placebo group' in the table). The review's summary gives the MDMA range as 75 to 125 mg plus or minus 62.5 mg.
exposure.polysubstance: Concomitant opiates allowed; psychiatric medicines and ongoing primary treatment of the illness excluded (Wolfson 2020 table).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; primary outcomes about 1 month after the second blinded session.

comparison.controls: Wolfson 2020: inactive placebo (lactose) with the same psychotherapy; the five classical-psychedelic trials used low-dose psilocybin or LSD, niacin or placebo.
comparison.matching: Not applicable at review level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Anxiety (STAI-T and STAI-S, 20 to 80; others planned), depression (BDI or BDI-II, 0 to 63; HADS-D), existential distress (Demoralisation Scale and others), quality of life, spirituality, treatment-related serious adverse events and grade 3 or 4 adverse events; two time windows, 1 to 12 weeks and more than 3 months after the intervention.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard self-report instruments; for MDMA no existential-distress or spirituality measure was used. Quality of life in Wolfson 2020 measured with the Global Assessment of Functioning (independent rater) and FACIT subscales.
outcomes.operationalization: Mean differences of change scores from baseline, with standard errors computed assuming no correlation between pre- and post-treatment values, which widens the intervals (Methods › Measures of treatment effect).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; GRADE certainty rated per outcome.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Selection, extraction and RoB 1 assessment by two authors independently with a third adjudicating; GRADE by two authors.

analysis.effect_sizes: MDMA (Wolfson 2020, 18 participants, 1 month after the second session): STAI-T mean difference −14.70 (95% CI −29.45 to 0.05); STAI-S −16.10 (−33.03 to 0.83); BDI-II −6.30 (−16.93 to 4.33); GAF 75.1 against 72.8 at 1 month (p = 0.52) and FACIT subscales (p 0.15 to 0.87) not different; no treatment-related serious or grade 3 or 4 adverse events; all very low certainty. For comparison, classical psychedelics pooled over five trials: STAI-T −8.41 (−12.92 to −3.89), STAI-S −9.04 (−13.87 to −4.21), BDI −4.92 (−8.97 to −0.87; 4 trials), SMD for depression −0.43 (−0.79 to −0.06), low certainty; heterogeneity low.
analysis.covariates: Subgroups psilocybin against LSD only (no difference); planned subgroups by number of sessions and medical condition not possible; fixed-effect sensitivity analyses gave the same estimates.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol (Schipper 2022). Deviations reported: post hoc widening of the population from palliative care to life-threatening disease, first-period crossover data only, change scores, and other methods clarifications (Differences between protocol and review).
analysis.selective_reporting: None apparent; all prespecified outcomes are reported, including those not measured for MDMA.
analysis.power: Imprecision is the main reason for very low certainty for MDMA: one trial of 18 with intervals including no effect; the authors downgraded twice for it.

interpretation_gap.results_show: One randomized trial of 18 people with a life-threatening illness found point estimates favouring MDMA by about 15 points on trait and state anxiety and 6 points on depression, with 95% intervals reaching zero or beyond (computed conservatively by the review), no treatment-related serious adverse events and common transient side effects; certainty very low.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusions describe the MDMA evidence as very uncertain and inconclusive, which matches the data. The Results text, however, states that anxiety and depression 'did not decrease' with MDMA, which reads an imprecise result as an absence of effect.

timeline.event: Wolfson et al. randomized pilot trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for anxiety with a life-threatening illness (Scientific Reports), the only MDMA trial in this review.
Protocol and first version of this Cochrane review (CD015383).
This update (pub2, 12 September 2024); seven ongoing trials identified, none of MDMA.

replication.where_it_stands: The highest-quality review of the question, but for MDMA it rests on one trial of 18 people; no further randomized MDMA trial in this population was published or ongoing by March 2024 according to the review.

funding.funder: National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), via Cochrane Infrastructure funding to the Cochrane Pain, Palliative and Supportive Care Review Group; no internal sources.
funding.declared_conflicts: SS and CB: members of the Swiss Medical Society for Psycholytic Therapies (SÄPT). KN: contract consulting for Acuta Capital Partners (discontinued). YS: research grant from the Swiss National Science Foundation. YB: research grants from Sunstone Therapies and Cy Biopharma, consulting fees from Reunion Neuroscience, unpaid advisory board member of Reset Pharma. GS: consulting fees from Roche. VP and ML: none.
funding.affiliations_note: The included MDMA trial was funded by MAPS and its authors received salaries from MAPS (Wolfson 2020 table). One of the review's clinical peer reviewers, Bessel van der Kolk, is an author of the second phase 3 MDMA trial for PTSD (author list of Mitchell et al., 2023, in its Crossref record).

what_would_settle_it: A larger randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in people with a life-threatening illness and clinically significant anxiety, with a parallel (not crossover) design or a secondary open-label crossover, an active placebo, measured expectancy and blinding, existential-distress outcomes, and follow-up beyond 3 months.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population, interventions, comparators and outcomes explicit.
Published Cochrane protocol (2022); deviations listed and justified.
Randomized trials only, with the reason given.

CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP, no language or date limits, reference and citation searching, experts and authors contacted, search 6 months before publication; PsycINFO not searched.
Two authors independently, third adjudicating.
Two authors independently with a piloted form.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Characteristics of excluded studies: six, with reasons.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Characteristics of included studies tables, including setting, dates, doses and funding.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: RoB 1 in duplicate covering sequence generation, concealment, blinding, attrition and selective reporting; unblinding judged high in all six trials.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Funding and conflicts of each trial in its table.
Random-effects inverse-variance meta-analysis of first-period data; conservative standard errors; MDMA analysed separately (one trial, not pooled).

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: All trials at high risk, so the planned restriction to low-risk trials was impossible and no other analysis of its impact was made; handled through GRADE downgrading.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Unblinding discussed at length and certainty downgraded for it.
Heterogeneity low; clinical diversity of populations and therapy paradigms discussed.
Not assessed because few trials were expected, and its likely impact is not discussed; registers were searched for ongoing trials.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Declarations of interest and sources of support given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: AMSTAR 2 gives low confidence when one critical item fails: here publication bias (15), neither investigated nor discussed. Otherwise the review meets Cochrane standards. For the MDMA question the flaw matters little, because the MDMA result is one trial taken from its publication, not a pooled estimate; that result is itself very uncertain. Cite the review for the MDMA trial's estimates as the review computed them (conservatively), for the absence of other randomized MDMA trials in this population up to March 2024, and for its certainty ratings.

key_findings.finding: Six randomized crossover trials, 149 randomized and 140 analysed: Gasser 2014 (12 randomized, 11 analysed), Griffiths 2016 (56, 51), Grob 2011 (12), Holze 2022 (20), Ross 2016 (31, 28), Wolfson 2020 (18 randomized and analysed); one evaluated MDMA (Wolfson 2020); USA and Switzerland; funding from organisations that promote psychedelic-assisted therapy, none from drug companies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Description of studies › Included studies, 1st paragraph; Abstract, Main results

key_findings.finding: Wolfson 2020: 18 randomized (13 MDMA, 5 placebo), single US centre, 2015 to 2018, outpatients; mean age 54.9, 77.8% women; life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness with STAI-Trait above 45; prior MDMA use 54% and 60%; two blinded sessions with nine psychotherapy sessions; funded by MAPS, authors salaried by MAPS. Risk of bias: low for sequence generation and concealment, high for blinding of participants, personnel and outcome assessment (more than 80% guessed their assignment correctly; outcomes mostly self-reported), low for attrition and selective reporting (primary outcome prespecified in NCT02427568).
key_findings.locator: Characteristics of included studies › Wolfson 2020 (study characteristics and risk-of-bias table)

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC11390284 (abstract, plain language summary, both summary-of-findings tables, background, methods, results with Tables 3 and 4 as text, discussion, conclusions, characteristics of included, excluded and ongoing studies, differences between protocol and review, contributions, sources of support, declarations of interest, data and analyses table; forest plots and risk-of-bias figures are images whose captions only were read; search-strategy appendices skimmed). ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT00252174 (API v2) read for the registry check. Crossref record read in this reader's tab.

design_detail: Secondary analysis of a single-arm, open-label feasibility trial (the Bristol Imperial MDMA in Alcoholism study, BIMA; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778, phase 1; EudraCT 2016-002547-42 per the registry) in 14 adults with alcohol use disorder who had recently completed detoxification, all given an eight-week course of ten psychotherapy sessions of which sessions 3 and 7 included MDMA. The safety and tolerability results were published earlier (Sessa et al., 2021, J Psychopharmacol; not read here, not free). This paper reports a binomial test and a Bayesian re-expression of one binary outcome (a reduction of two WHO drinking risk levels from baseline to 3 months after treatment) and pre–post changes in self-reported craving, quality of life, sleep, self-compassion and empathy at 3 months. Sponsor Imperial College London; funded by the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest (an uncontrolled before–after study of one treated group), and the card uses ROBINS-I as the batch brief directs for non-randomized intervention studies.
can_establish: What happened to self-reported drinking risk levels, craving, sleep, quality of life, self-compassion and empathy over about five months in 14 detoxified adults with alcohol use disorder who received an eight-week psychotherapy course including two MDMA sessions, and how often a two-level fall in WHO drinking risk was seen in this group.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA, the psychotherapy, the preceding detoxification, the natural course after detoxification, regression to the mean or expectation produced any of these changes (there is no comparison group and no blinding); whether the changes last beyond 3 months (the registered 6- and 9-month outcomes are not reported here); or anything about people the study excluded (people taking antidepressants who were unwilling to stop, serious suicide risk, psychotic or personality disorders, cardiovascular or severe liver disease, regular ecstasy use, other drug dependence) or about non-White populations.

sample.recruitment: Not described in this paper, which refers to Sessa et al. (2021) for full details (Materials and methods › Participants; Procedure, 1st paragraph). The registry describes detoxified patients with alcohol use disorder at a Bristol and Imperial study (registry record, Identification; Eligibility).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Registry: primary DSM-5 diagnosis of alcohol use disorder; successful alcohol detoxification (no longer drinking); age 18 to 65; a supportive significant other who could accompany the participant or help collect follow-up data; English proficiency. Excluded: lack of capacity; psychotic disorder, bipolar I or personality disorder; serious suicide risk (C-SSRS and clinical judgement); cardiac disease, hypertension, stroke, severe liver disease, epilepsy, malignant hyperthermia; regular ecstasy use (for example more than five times in five years or at least twice in the 6 months before the study); medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 or interact with MDMA, including MAO inhibitors, several SSRIs and regular benzodiazepines, unless stopped for the 8-week course; regular use of or dependence on other drugs; pregnancy or breast-feeding (registry record, Eligibility). The paper's own summary of the criteria (antidepressants unless titrated off, serious suicide risk, psychotic or personality disorders, cardiovascular and severe liver disease) agrees (Discussion › Limitations, 2nd paragraph). The paper's own sentence on age is corrupted in the PMC text (reporting issues).
sample.demographics: 8 men and 6 women; mean age 48 years; all White British (Results › Demographics, 1st paragraph). Other characteristics, including baseline drinking, are only in Sessa et al. (2021), not read.
sample.attrition: The abstract says all 14 completed the eight-week course (Abstract › Methods). The WHO risk-level analysis uses all 14 (Table 1); the questionnaire analyses at 3 months use 11 to 14 participants (Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends) with no account of the missing data.
sample.selection_effects: People who had already succeeded in detoxification, had a supportive significant other and were willing to take MDMA in a research setting; regular ecstasy use, other drug dependence and much psychiatric and physical comorbidity excluded; all White British. Fourteen of an estimated 20 in the registry. Expectations of benefit were probably high and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to everyone: an eight-week recovery-based therapy course of ten psychotherapy sessions using motivational interviewing and third-wave cognitive-behavioural elements, with MDMA in sessions 3 and 7 and psychotherapy alone in the other sessions; participants stayed overnight in the treatment centre after each MDMA session (Materials and methods › Procedure, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Future directions, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). Good Manufacturing Practice MDMA from Sterling Pharmaceuticals, formulated into capsules by the Pharmacy Manufacturing Unit at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust (Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth in two sessions (3 and 7) of the eight-week course, an initial dose of 125 mg followed by a booster of 62.5 mg; capsules of 62.5 mg (Materials and methods › Procedure, 2nd paragraph; Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph). How many participants took the booster is reported only in Sessa et al. (2021).
exposure.polysubstance: Regular use of or dependence on other drugs (benzodiazepines, synthetic cannabinoids, cocaine, heroin) and regular ecstasy use were exclusion criteria (registry record, Eligibility). The registry says illicit drug use and any recreational MDMA use after the trial would be recorded; neither is reported in this paper.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants had completed alcohol detoxification before the course. Drinking afterwards was measured by Timeline Followback, a self-report interview; no biological verification is reported (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level, 1st paragraph).

comparison.controls: None. Each participant's 3-month values are compared with their own baseline. The paper does not state which period the baseline drinking covers; the registry describes the drinking comparison as pre-detoxification (screening) levels against later visits (registry record, Outcome Measures, 'Change in Drinking behaviour').
comparison.matching: Not applicable (single group).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; without a comparison group the natural course after detoxification, the psychotherapy itself, regression to the mean (people enrolled at a low point) and expectation are all uncontrolled.

outcomes.instruments: Timeline Followback (TLFB), alcohol units converted to WHO drinking risk levels; Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS; five items scored 0 to 6); Obsessive Compulsive Drinking Scale (OCDS; 14 items, obsessive and compulsive subscales); SF-36 (eight domains scored 0 to 100, plus reported change in health); four items derived from the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index combined into one sleep-disturbance score; Self-Compassion Scale (26 items); Interpersonal Reactivity Index (IRI; four 7-item subscales) (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level; PROMs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated questionnaires, except the sleep score, which uses four items derived from the PSQI rather than the PSQI itself (Materials and methods › PROMs › Sleep). The two-level reduction in WHO risk drinking levels is presented as an endpoint accepted by the EMA as an intermediate harm-reduction endpoint and in the FDA's outcome-assessment qualification process, not yet fully qualified (Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Treatment success: a reduction of two WHO drinking risk levels from baseline to 3 months after treatment, from TLFB units (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level). The questionnaires: change from baseline to 3 months.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni correction within questionnaires that have several subscales (OCDS, SF-36, IRI); none across questionnaires. Editors' count of 19 tests in the text: the WHO risk-level outcome, PACS total, two OCDS subscales, eight SF-36 domains and the reported-change item, the sleep score, the Self-Compassion Scale total and four IRI subscales. The authors acknowledge possible Type I error inflation and call the findings hypothesis-generating (Materials and methods › Data analysis, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open-label; all outcomes self-reported or, for the TLFB, collected by the study team, with participants and staff aware of the treatment.

analysis.effect_sizes: WHO risk level: 9 of 14 achieved a two-level reduction at 3 months; binomial test against 50%, proportion .64, P = .423, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87; mean posterior success rate 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat Beta(1,1) prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with a Beta(1,3) prior called sceptical (Results › Bayesian analysis…, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 1). Editors' check: two-sided exact binomial P = 0.424 and Clopper–Pearson interval 0.351 to 0.872; posteriors Beta(10,6), mean 0.625, highest-density interval 0.40 to 0.85, and Beta(10,8), mean 0.556, 0.33 to 0.77 (the printed intervals match highest-density intervals). Questionnaires, 3 months vs baseline (Wilcoxon signed-rank, differences with 95% CI and rank-biserial r): PACS 5.50 (0.5 to 13), P = .031, r .781; OCDS obsessive 5.00 (2.00 to 8.50), P = .006, r .868, compulsive 5.00 (1.00 to 9.00), P = .021, r .769; sleep score 2.00 (7.54e-6 to 3.00), P = .041, r .648; Self-Compassion Scale 12.1 (9.09 to 14.4), P < .001, r 1.00; IRI personal distress 0.5 (0.143 to 0.929), P = .009, r .945; SF-36 subscales not significant after correction (Results, subsections). Within-group changes only; no between-group effect exists.
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778 was first submitted on 31 January 2019 and first posted on 12 November 2019, after the study's actual start (18 April 2018): retrospective registration (the EudraCT number 2016-002547-42 is listed but that register was not read). Registered primary outcome: safety and tolerability (completion of the course, acceptance of the booster dose, adverse events). Registered secondary outcomes include change in drinking behaviour by TLFB (pre-detoxification screening levels against session 10 and 3, 6 and 9 months), SF-36, PSQI, SIP, GAD-7, PHQ-9, IRI, Self-Compassion Scale, PACS, OCDS, prescribed medication use and recreational MDMA use, each at 3, 6 and 9 months. The two-level WHO risk-level endpoint and the Bayesian analysis are not registered outcomes; the sleep measure reported is four PSQI-derived items rather than the PSQI; no results are posted (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only the 3-month time point is reported for registered outcomes that were planned at 3, 6 and 9 months; SIP, GAD-7, PHQ-9, prescribed medication use and recreational MDMA use are not reported here (anxiety and depression results are said to be in Sessa et al., 2021); the full statistics for the questionnaires are only in a supplementary Word file (Tables S1 to S12), not read because it is a download; Figs 2 and 3 are images and no values were extracted from them.
