analysis.power: No power calculation; a feasibility sample of 14 (registry estimate 20). The authors call the sample small and the analysis exploratory (Discussion › Limitations, 1st paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one uncontrolled group of 14 detoxified adults with alcohol use disorder, 9 had drinking at least two WHO risk levels lower 3 months after an eight-week psychotherapy course with two MDMA sessions than at baseline, which the registry describes as drinking before detoxification; the Bayesian analysis restates 9 of 14 as a posterior success rate of 0.55 to 0.63 depending on the prior and adds no comparison. Self-reported craving, a four-item sleep score, self-compassion and one empathy subscale improved between baseline and 3 months in the 11 to 14 people with data; quality-of-life subscales did not survive correction. None of these changes can be attributed to MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract presents the Bayesian analysis as a useful harm-reduction interpretation of drinking (Abstract › Conclusions). The Discussion compares the 55% to 63% success rate with 68% from secondary analyses of the COMBINE study and Project MATCH and says the results suggest MDMA-assisted psychotherapy "may produce clinically meaningful reductions in alcohol consumption" comparable with established treatments (Discussion, 2nd paragraph): a comparison across studies with different populations, baselines and treatments, made from a single-arm study. It says MDMA's acute prosocial effects "appear to persist" because self-compassion and personal distress improved (Discussion, 5th paragraph), a causal reading of pre–post change without a control. The Limitations call the findings hypothesis-generating and ask for randomized placebo-controlled trials, measurement of unblinding and expectancy, and long-term follow-up (Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).

timeline.event: Sessa et al., J Psychopharmacol: the safety and tolerability report of the same 14 participants, with drinking and mood outcomes to 9 months (cited by this paper; not read here because it is not free; DOI 10.1177/0269881121991792).
This paper: Bayesian re-expression of the two-level WHO risk-level outcome at 3 months (9 of 14) and 3-month questionnaire changes.

replication.where_it_stands: One open-label study of 14 people, reported twice by the same group. No randomized or otherwise controlled trial of MDMA-assisted therapy in alcohol use disorder was among the sources read; the project's evidence map lists protocols of two trials in people with both PTSD and alcohol use disorder (Eaton et al., 2024; Morley et al., 2026), not read here.

funding.funder: The Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust funded the entire clinical trial (Funding). Sponsor: Imperial College London (Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph; Ethics statement). The Methods state that Awakn Life Sciences Corporation has exclusive rights to the data from 'the Phase 2b' (Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: HT was a Senior Research Officer at Drug Science, collaborating with industry partners developing medical psychedelics, and was seconded to Awakn Life Sciences, positions no longer held at submission; DJN is Chief Scientific Officer of Awakn Life Sciences; CJAM was seconded to Awakn Life Sciences and the University of Exeter has licensed intellectual property from her work to Awakn; 'BS, LH, SO, CD, SW, BS' declare no conflicts (Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Seven of nine authors are at Imperial College London; Ben Sessa is listed as an independent consultant (Contributor Information). A company in which the senior author is Chief Scientific Officer holds exclusive data rights, and the first author was seconded to it. Data available on reasonable request from the first author (Data availability).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered randomized trial in adults with alcohol use disorder, after detoxification, comparing the same psychotherapy with MDMA against an active comparator, with the drinking baseline taken after detoxification, drinking verified biologically (for example phosphatidylethanol), blinding and expectancy measured, independent outcome assessors, and follow-up for at least 12 months.

domains.note: No comparison group. The drinking outcome is compared with a baseline that the registry places before detoxification, so the change mixes detoxification, the psychotherapy, the natural course after detoxification and regression to the mean with any effect of MDMA; none of these can be separated in a single-arm design.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Participants entered after successful detoxification and had to have a supportive significant other; selection on early success could favour good outcomes, though it bears more on who the results apply to than on the pre–post change itself.
Everyone received the same protocolized course with two MDMA sessions.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-interventions between the end of the course and 3 months (other alcohol treatment, medicines, mutual-help groups) are not reported in this paper; booster acceptance is only in Sessa et al. (2021).
Questionnaire analyses at 3 months use 11 to 14 of 14 participants without any account of who was missing or why; how missing TLFB data were handled for the WHO risk-level outcome is not stated.
All outcomes are self-reported (TLFB interview and questionnaires) by participants who knew they had received MDMA, collected by the unblinded study team, with no biological verification of drinking.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Retrospective registration; the two-level WHO risk-level endpoint and the Bayesian analysis are not registered; registered 6- and 9-month results and several registered measures are not reported; the sleep measure differs from the registered PSQI.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence about the effect of MDMA-assisted therapy, the study is at critical risk of bias because it has no comparison group and its drinking baseline appears to precede detoxification (registry), so the before–after change cannot be attributed to the intervention, still less to MDMA. Missing questionnaire data without explanation, self-reported unblinded outcomes and an unregistered endpoint add serious concerns. The paper can be cited for what was observed in this small open-label group (9 of 14 with a two-level fall in WHO drinking risk at 3 months; changes in self-reported craving, sleep and self-compassion) and for the fact that no controlled evidence exists; it cannot be cited for efficacy, for comparison with standard treatments, or for durability.

key_findings.finding: Fourteen participants with alcohol use disorder who had recently been detoxified completed an eight-week course of ten psychotherapy sessions, two of them with MDMA; 8 men and 6 women, mean age 48, all White British.
Two-level reduction in WHO drinking risk from baseline to 3 months after treatment: 9 of 14 participants; binomial test against an expected 50%, proportion .64, P = .423, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.87.
key_findings.locator: Results › Bayesian analysis of World Health Organization drinking risk level at 3 months follow-up, 1st paragraph; Table 1
key_findings.note: Editors' check: exact two-sided P = 0.424; Clopper–Pearson 95% CI 0.351 to 0.872.

key_findings.finding: Bayesian analysis of the same 9 of 14: mean posterior success rate 0.63 (credible interval 0.40 to 0.85) with a flat Beta(1,1) prior and 0.55 (0.33 to 0.77) with a Beta(1,3) prior, described as sceptical, with a mean of 25% chosen from typical placebo response rates of 25% to 40% in mental health trials.
key_findings.locator: Table 1; Results › Bayesian analysis of World Health Organization drinking risk level at 3 months follow-up, 2nd paragraph; Materials and methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' check: posteriors Beta(10,6), mean 0.625, 95% highest-density interval 0.40 to 0.85, and Beta(10,8), mean 0.556 (printed 0.55), 0.33 to 0.77. The posterior is an estimate of the success rate in this single group; it involves no comparison.

key_findings.finding: Craving at 3 months vs baseline (n = 13): PACS total difference 5.50 (95% CI 0.5 to 13), P = .031, rank-biserial r .781; OCDS obsessive subscale 5.00 (2.00 to 8.50), P = .006, r .868; OCDS compulsive subscale 5.00 (1.00 to 9.00), P = .021, r .769.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drinking behavior at 3 months follow-up, 1st paragraph; Fig. 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Quality of life (SF-36, n = 11): energy/fatigue, emotional well-being, social functioning, pain, general health and reported change in health rose nominally at 3 months, but no subscale remained significant after Bonferroni correction.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Quality of life, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Sleep (four PSQI-derived items, n = 14): difference 2.00 (95% CI 7.54e-6 to 3.00), P = .041, r .648, lower scores meaning less disturbance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Sleep, 1st paragraph; Materials and methods › PROMs › Sleep; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Self-Compassion Scale total (n = 13): increase of 12.1 (95% CI 9.09 to 14.4), P < .001, r 1.00; IRI (n = 12): only the personal distress subscale changed, falling by 0.5 (0.143 to 0.929), P = .009, r .945.
key_findings.locator: Results › Quality of life, sleep, well-being, and psychosocial functioning measures › Self-compassion, 1st paragraph; › Empathy, 1st paragraph; Fig. 3 legend

key_findings.finding: Analysis: Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank tests with 95% CIs around the differences; Bonferroni correction only within questionnaires with several subscales; the authors acknowledge possible Type I error inflation, call the findings hypothesis-generating rather than evidence of efficacy, and say larger randomized placebo-controlled trials, measurement of unblinding and expectancy, and long-term follow-up are needed.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Data analysis, 3rd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: The Discussion compares the 55% to 63% success rate with the 68% of patients reaching a two-level WHO risk reduction at the end of treatment in secondary analyses of the COMBINE study and Project MATCH, calling the results comparable with established treatments.

Registry: NCT04158778 (BIMA), single-group open-label, phase 1, estimated enrollment 20; actual start 18 April 2018, first submitted 31 January 2019, first posted 12 November 2019; primary outcome safety and tolerability; secondary outcomes include change in drinking by TLFB from pre-detoxification (screening) levels to session 10 and 3, 6 and 9 months, and SF-36, PSQI, SIP, GAD-7, PHQ-9, IRI, Self-Compassion Scale, PACS, OCDS and recreational MDMA use at 3, 6 and 9 months; no results posted; status unknown (last update 2019).
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04158778 (API v2) › Identification; Status; Design; Outcome Measures; Eligibility

key_findings.finding: Funding and interests: the Alexander Mosley Charitable Trust funded the entire trial; sponsor Imperial College London; Awakn Life Sciences holds exclusive rights to the data; the senior author is Chief Scientific Officer of Awakn, and the first author and another author were seconded to it.
key_findings.locator: Funding; Conflict of interest; Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Two sentences are corrupted in the PMC full text: the summary of the original study's drinking results at 9 months runs from '11 participants were drinking <14' straight into unrelated words, and the age criterion reads 'aged 18 study details and finding recently undergone detoxification'. The page's HTML contains the damaged text itself (a '<' character appears to have swallowed the words between it and a later '>').
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Introduction, 2nd paragraph; Materials and methods › Procedure, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The 9-month drinking figures and the age range cannot be cited from this paper; they must come from Sessa et al. (2021) or the registry (age 18 to 65).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Discussion give the success probability as 55% to 63% 'based upon either a flat or skeptical prior respectively', which pairs 55% with the flat prior; Table 1 and the Results give 0.63 for the flat prior and 0.55 for the sceptical one.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Results; Discussion, 1st paragraph; Table 1)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The Beta(1,3) prior is described as a gentle distribution excluding 0% and 100% with a mean of 25%; its density is highest at 0% and falls to zero only at 100% (editors' check). It is called sceptical, but it only lowers the prior success rate in this single group; it does not express scepticism about an effect relative to any comparison.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Fig. 1 legend; Results › Bayesian analysis…, 2nd paragraph; Materials and methods › Data analysis, 2nd paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The sceptical-prior result says no more than the flat one: about 9 in 14 reached the endpoint, with no comparator.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper does not say which period the baseline drinking covers; the registry describes the drinking comparison as pre-detoxification (screening) levels against later visits, and every participant had been detoxified before the course.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level); registry record (Outcome Measures)
reporting_issues.consequence: If the baseline precedes detoxification, much of the two-level fall would be expected after detoxification alone; the endpoint cannot be read as an effect of the course.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says all 14 completed the course, but the questionnaire analyses at 3 months have 13 (PACS, OCDS, Self-Compassion Scale), 11 (SF-36), 14 (sleep) and 12 (IRI) participants, with no account of the missing data.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Abstract › Methods; Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends)
reporting_issues.consequence: Complete-case results of unknown selection; with 11 to 14 people one or two missing values can change a result.

reporting_issues.issue: The registered outcomes are change in drinking by TLFB and full questionnaires at 3, 6 and 9 months; the paper reports an unregistered endpoint (two-level WHO risk-level reduction) and its Bayesian re-expression, only the 3-month time point, and a four-item sleep score instead of the registered PSQI; registration was retrospective (first submitted January 2019, nine months after the actual start, posted November 2019).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Materials and methods › WHO risk drinking level; PROMs › Sleep); registry record (Status; Outcome Measures)
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting of outcome and time point cannot be excluded.

reporting_issues.issue: The conflict-of-interest statement lists 'BS' twice among authors with no conflicts (Ben Sessa and Balázs Szigeti share the initials), and the Methods say Awakn Life Sciences has exclusive rights to the data 'from the Phase 2b', while this is a phase 1 open-label feasibility study (registry).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Conflict of interest; Materials and methods › Approvals and drug source, 1st paragraph); registry record (Design)
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear which author each declaration refers to and which data the commercial rights cover.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12148347 (all sections, Table 1, figure legends, funding, conflict-of-interest and contribution statements), read in this reader's own browser tab; ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT04158778 (API v2) for registration and registered outcomes; the Crossref record for the DOI. The supplementary file (Word document, Tables S1 to S12) was not read because it is a download; Figs 1 to 3 are images and no values were taken from them.

design_detail: Secondary-outcome report of the same uncontrolled pilot trial as Monson et al. (2020): six heterosexual couples in which one partner had PTSD, treated with a condensed 7-week course of cognitive behavioral conjoint therapy (CBCT) for PTSD with two full-day MDMA sessions for both partners, at a private practice clinic in Charleston, South Carolina. Outcomes before, at mid-treatment, after treatment and at 3 and 6 months: relationship aggression (CTS-2), post-traumatic growth (PTGI, self- and collateral-report), partner accommodation (SORTS), relationship quality (QRI), social intimacy (MSIS), psychosocial functioning (IPF) and empathy (IRI); growth-curve models and within-group effect sizes. No registration number is given in this paper; the primary report names NCT02876172. Funded through donations to MAPS. The schema has no single-arm-trial design; 'case-series' is the closest, appraised with ROBINS-I.
can_establish: What happened to self- and partner-reported relationship, growth, functioning and empathy measures over 6 months in six couples given CBCT with two MDMA sessions, and that minor psychological aggression did not rise in this small group with low baseline aggression.
cannot_establish: Whether any change is due to MDMA, to CBCT or to time and expectation (no comparison group); whether the intervention is safe for couples with relationship aggression (severe aggression was excluded and baseline aggression was low); or anything about couples other than White, mixed-gender couples.

sample.recruitment: Not described here; the paper refers to Monson et al. (2020) for the full study description (Method › Participants, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both partners 18 or older, with no current substance use disorder, no active suicidal planning or intent, no mania, psychosis or severe partner aggression (severe aggression on the CTS-2 sexual coercion or physical aggression subscales was exclusionary); all psychiatric medicines tapered off; medical screening for essential hypertension, cardiac disorder and other major medical conditions (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph; Measures › Relationship Aggression Outcomes).
sample.demographics: Average age about 47; all White; all mixed-gender couples; patients: two women, all with comorbid diagnoses and earlier psychological and drug treatment for PTSD, five of six with multiple traumas; partners: four women, 50% with psychological diagnoses (Method › Participants, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: No dropout is reported; the paper says every outcome had at most one or two missing data points (at most 30%) at any assessment (Data Analyses, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: As in Monson et al. (2020): self-selected couples willing to take MDMA together, treated by the developers of the therapy; relationship depth was already high at baseline, which the authors attribute to self-selection (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Assigned treatment, given to all: CBCT for PTSD over 7 weeks (five modules in 1.5 days before MDMA session one, six between the two MDMA sessions, four weekly after the second) with two full-day MDMA sessions in reclining chairs with eyeshades, headphones and music, alternating inward focus with conversation with the therapists and partner; MDMA sessions placed after the communication-skills work and in the middle of trauma processing (Method › Procedure, 1st to 4th paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: 75 mg MDMA in the first session with an optional supplemental 37.5 mg 1.5 hours later; 100 mg in the second session with an optional 50 mg at 1.5 hours; both partners dosed (Method › Procedure, 4th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Current substance use disorder excluded (Method › Participants, 1st paragraph); drug use during the study not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None: within-person change over time.
comparison.matching: Not applicable (single group).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable as such; CBCT itself, time, regression to the mean and expectation are uncontrolled.

outcomes.instruments: CTS-2 (39 tactics, used and experienced; negotiation, psychological aggression, physical assault, sexual coercion, injury); PTGI (21 items; completed by both partners about the patient, the partner version edited into a collateral report for this study); SORTS (14 items, partner only, frequency and intensity of accommodation, 0 to 4); QRI (25 items; support, conflict, depth); IPF (80 items; higher scores mean more impairment); MSIS (17 items); IRI (28 items; perspective taking, fantasy, empathic concern, personal distress) (Measures, all subsections).
outcomes.validity_norms: Published internal consistencies are cited for each measure; the collateral-report version of the PTGI is new to this study and has no validation reported (Measures › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Change over time in growth-curve models (log-transformed days since baseline; fixed slopes and random intercepts, kept for parsimony because the better-fitting random-slope model did not converge in most cases); within-group Cohen's d from pre-treatment to each time point on estimated means and raw pooled SDs (Data Analyses, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Editors' count of the models reported: six CTS-2 models (patients' minor psychological aggression, minor physical assault, emotional and cognitive negotiation; partners' emotional and cognitive negotiation), PTGI 2, SORTS 1, QRI 6, MSIS 2, IPF 2, IRI 8.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: all measures are self- or partner-reports by people who had taken MDMA.

analysis.effect_sizes: Growth-model slopes (B, SE) and within-group d ranges (mid-treatment to 6 months): PTGI rated by patients B = 7.30 (1.56), d 1.44 to 2.00, and by partners B = 7.63 (1.49), d 1.76 to 2.74, both P < 0.001; SORTS (partners) B = −3.86 (1.36), P < 0.01, d 1.01 to 1.78; QRI support, patients B = 0.06 (0.03), P = 0.041, partners B = 0.08 (0.03), P = 0.029; QRI conflict, patients P = 0.062, partners B = −0.09 (0.03), P = 0.002; QRI depth not significant; MSIS intimacy, patients B = 4.12 (1.32), P = 0.005, d 0.93 to 1.31, partners B = 3.10 (1.03), P = 0.007, d 0.41 to 0.68; IPF, patients B = −3.20 (0.69), P < 0.001, d 0.95 to 1.26, partners P = 0.299; IRI empathic concern, patients B = 0.69 (0.32), P = 0.037, d 0.58 to 0.95, partners and other subscales not significant; CTS-2, patients' minor psychological aggression B = −0.98 (0.21), P < 0.001, d 1.06 to 1.56, no change in minor physical assault, other aggression models not estimable (Results, all subsections; Tables 1 and 2).
analysis.preregistration_detail: This paper gives no registration; the primary report names ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02876172, whose registered secondary outcomes (read for the Monson et al. card) do not include the CTS-2, PTGI, SORTS, QRI, IPF, MSIS or IRI.
analysis.selective_reporting: These relational measures are not registered outcomes of the trial; models for several CTS-2 scales could not be estimated because of infrequent endorsement.
analysis.power: No power calculation; six couples.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In six couples who completed CBCT with two MDMA sessions, patients' post-traumatic growth (rated by both partners), partners' accommodation, perceived support, social intimacy, patients' psychosocial functioning and empathic concern improved between baseline and 6 months; relationship depth, most empathy subscales and partners' functioning did not change; minor psychological aggression fell in patients. None of these changes can be attributed to MDMA, and the printed SORTS means are a copy of another measure (reporting issues).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings suggest that CBCT with MDMA "has significant effect on relational and growth outcomes" in this pilot sample (Abstract). The Discussion says the results demonstrate that the combination provides improvements for both partners and the relationship and that the intervention is safe and does not increase the risk of relational or interpersonal harm (Discussion, 1st paragraph), and that a feeling of connection during MDMA sessions likely played a role in improved intimacy, though not formally tested (Discussion, 4th paragraph). The Limitations acknowledge that, by design, no conclusion about efficacy relative to placebo or to either component alone can be drawn (Discussion, 5th paragraph).

timeline.event: Monson et al., Eur J Psychotraumatol: primary outcomes of the same six couples (not independent of this paper).
This paper: relational and growth outcomes.

replication.where_it_stands: Same sample as Monson et al. (2020); no independent or controlled study of these relational outcomes is among the sources read.

funding.funder: Donations to MAPS; a MAPS-sponsored study, and the funder had input into the study design (Footnotes › Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: CM receives royalties from Guilford Press for the CBCT manual; AW, MM, AM and CM received salary support from MAPS for the study; MM and AM sit on the advisory board of Awakn Life Sciences; the remaining author declares no conflicts (Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The authors designed and ran the study (Author Contributions); the first and last authors are among the therapy's developers. Raw data available from the authors (Data Availability Statement).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of CBCT with MDMA against CBCT with an active placebo, with registered relational outcomes, observer-rated couple interaction, measured expectancy and a follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: No comparison group; the intervention includes a full course of CBCT, so no change can be attributed to MDMA.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Self-selected couples, already high in relationship depth; severe aggression excluded.
Same protocol for all.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Co-interventions are not reported here (the primary report shows three of six patients in current psychotherapy at baseline).
Up to one or two of six values missing per assessment for some outcomes; which ones is not reported.
Self- and partner-reports by people who took MDMA, about a therapy delivered by its developers; one measure (collateral PTGI) was adapted for this study without validation.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: None of these outcomes is registered; 27 models without correction; the SORTS means printed in Table 1 are not the SORTS data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: An uncontrolled secondary analysis of six couples: as evidence that MDMA improves relationships it is at critical risk of bias. It can be cited for the observed course of these self-reports and for the absence of an increase in minor aggression in this small, low-aggression sample; it cannot be cited for effects of MDMA, for safety in couples with aggression, or for the SORTS values in Table 1.

key_findings.finding: Same six couples as the primary report; patients two women and four men, partners four women and two men; all White and mixed-gender; treated at a private practice clinic in Charleston, South Carolina.

Post-traumatic growth of the patient: rated by patients 19.40 (SD 10.29) before treatment, 64.17 (32.43) after and 63.50 (27.36) at 6 months, B = 7.30 (SE 1.56), d 1.44 to 2.00; rated by partners 14.60 (15.77), 55.75 (16.46) and 55.67 (15.32), B = 7.63 (1.49), d 1.76 to 2.74; both P < 0.001.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Partner accommodation (SORTS): B = −3.86 (SE 1.36), P < 0.01, d 1.01 to 1.78; the means printed for SORTS in Table 1 (49.58 [8.52] before treatment to 16.64 [14.84] at 6 months) are identical, value for value, to the partner-rated PCL-5 means in the primary report's Table 2.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (SORTS row); Table 2
key_findings.note: The modelled result (B, d) may be right, but the printed SORTS means cannot be cited (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Relationship quality (QRI): support improved for patients (B = 0.06, P = 0.041; d 0.68 to 0.94) and partners (B = 0.08, P = 0.029; d 0.47 to 0.81); conflict fell for partners (B = −0.09, P = 0.002) but not significantly for patients (P = 0.062); depth did not change (patients P = 0.171, partners P = 0.093).
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Relationship Quality Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2
Results › Outcomes › Relationship Quality Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Tables 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Psychosocial functioning (IPF, higher = more impairment): patients 52.35 (14.48) to 35.94 after treatment and 34.14 at 6 months, B = −3.20 (0.69), P < 0.001, d 0.95 to 1.26; partners no significant change (B = −0.67, P = 0.299). Empathy (IRI): patients' empathic concern rose (B = 0.69, P = 0.037, d 0.58 to 0.95); no change in partners' empathic concern or in personal distress, fantasy or perspective taking for either partner.
key_findings.locator: Results › Outcomes › Psychosocial Functioning Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Tables 1 and 2

key_findings.finding: Relationship aggression (CTS-2): patients' minor psychological aggression fell (B = −0.98, SE 0.21, P < 0.001, d 1.06 to 1.56); no significant change in patients' minor physical assault; the other aggression models could not be estimated because these items were rarely endorsed; negotiation strategies did not change.
key_findings.locator: Results › Safety Outcomes › Relationship Aggression, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The SORTS (partner) row of Table 1 reproduces exactly the partner-rated PCL-5 estimated means and SDs of the primary report (Monson et al., 2020, Table 2): 49.58 (8.52), 26.38 (19.37), 21.54 (19.67), 19.08 (16.18), 16.64 (14.84). The SORTS growth estimate (B = −3.86) and effect sizes (1.01 to 1.78) differ from the PCL-5 ones (B = −5.90; 1.55 to 2.72).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1; Results › Outcomes › Trauma-Related Outcomes, 1st paragraph)
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed SORTS means are a copying error and cannot be cited; whether the modelled SORTS results were computed on the right data cannot be checked from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is titled 'Estimated means and standard deviations', but its footnote says raw means and standard deviations are presented, while Table 2's footnote says the effect sizes were computed from least-squares means estimated from growth models.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Table 1 title and footnote; Table 2 footnote)
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether Table 1 holds observed or estimated values; recomputing the effect sizes from it may not reproduce Table 2.

reporting_issues.issue: Missing data are described as at most 1 to 2 data points, 'maximum 30%', per assessment; 2 of 6 is 33%. Several Table 1 means (for example PTGI 19.40 and 14.60 before treatment) can only come from five people.
reporting_issues.consequence: Some time points rest on five of six participants.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper calls the treatment safe and says it does not increase the risk of relational or interpersonal harm, but severe aggression was an exclusion criterion, baseline aggression was low, and most partner aggression models could not be estimated.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Discussion, 1st paragraph; Measures › Relationship Aggression Outcomes; Results › Safety Outcomes)
reporting_issues.consequence: The safety statement concerns six low-aggression couples only.

reporting_issues.issue: The background cites the pooled phase 2 analysis (Mithoefer et al., 2019; reference 22), which PMC's reference list marks as retracted, for the promising results of individual MDMA-assisted therapy.
reporting_issues.consequence: Background only; not used by the card.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8273271 (all sections, Tables 1 and 2, figure legend, funding, conflicts, contributions), read in this reader's own browser tab, with the SORTS row checked in the page's table markup; compared with the primary report (Monson et al., 2020, PMC7748057, read the same day); the Crossref record for the DOI. Fig. 1 values were not extracted.

design_detail: Phase 2 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial with an open-label crossover (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02427568), at one outpatient psychiatric clinic in San Anselmo, California, run from April 2015 to May 2018 (enrolment May 2015 to February 2017). Eighteen adults with moderate to severe anxiety related to a life-threatening illness (17 with cancer) were randomized about 1:3 to an inactive placebo (5) or MDMA (13) in two day-long experimental sessions 2 to 4 weeks apart, within manualized non-directive psychotherapy with a co-therapist pair (three preparatory and three integration sessions per experimental session). Primary outcome: change in STAI-Trait from baseline to one month after the second experimental session, when the blind was broken; the MDMA group then had one open-label MDMA session and the placebo group crossed over to three, with follow-up 6 and 12 months after the last session (uncontrolled). Sponsored and fully funded by MAPS, organized by MAPS PBC.
can_establish: Whether, in 18 people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, two MDMA sessions within psychotherapy were followed one month later by a larger fall in self-reported trait anxiety than the same psychotherapy with an inactive placebo, with a very imprecise estimate; which acute and next-week reactions were more frequent with MDMA in these 13 people.
cannot_establish: Whether there is a real difference (the 95% interval of the difference includes zero, with 5 people on placebo); how much of any difference reflects knowing one's allocation (86% of session guesses were correct) or the higher baseline anxiety of the MDMA group; whether benefits last (the 6- and 12-month data are uncontrolled after the crossover); rare harms; or effects in people with untapered psychiatric medicines, cardiovascular disease, brain tumours, ongoing first-line cancer treatment or a life expectancy under nine months, who were excluded.

sample.recruitment: Referrals from healthcare professionals, word of mouth and internet advertisements (Methods › Study design and participants, 2nd paragraph); the registry adds printed advertisements. Fig. 1 (read from the figure image): 110 preliminary telephone screens, 88 excluded for not meeting eligibility criteria or lost to contact, 22 in-person assessments, 1 excluded after the in-person screen, 21 enrolled, 3 discontinued after enrolment (1 unable to taper anxiolytic medicines, 1 unable to meet scheduling requirements, 1 deemed unfit by the investigator), 18 randomized. The main reasons for exclusion at telephone screening were living outside the study area and being too unwell to take part (Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults aged 18 or older with a life-threatening cancer or non-dementing neurological illness, ongoing or in remission with risk of recurrence, a life expectancy of at least nine months, anxiety primarily related to the illness on the SCID-I/P, and a STAI-Trait score of at least 45 of 80 (the text says 'scores … of 45'). Excluded: ongoing primary treatment such as initial chemotherapy; uncontrolled hypertension, significant cerebrovascular or cardiovascular disease, brain tumours, renal disease, dementing illness, type I or II diabetes, history of hyponatremia or hyperthermia, weight under 48 kg, pregnancy or lactation; psychotic disorders, bipolar I, dissociative identity disorder, eating disorders with active purging; inability to taper psychiatric medicines safely. Prescribed opioids were allowed, and people with substance use disorders in remission for at least 60 days could enrol (Methods › Study design and participants, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Mean age 54.9 (SD 7.9); 14 women (77.8%); 15 White (83.3%); 17 with neoplasms and 1 with a musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorder as the qualifying illness; histories of anxiety 83.3%, major depression 77.8%, PTSD 72.2%, insomnia 61.1%; prior ecstasy use 10 of 18 (55.6%), last use more than 10 years before in 6 of them; baseline STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) and STAI-State 57.4 (10.9) (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: All 18 were assessed at the primary endpoint and analysed by intention to treat (Fig. 1; Table 2 footnote). After the primary endpoint one MDMA participant stopped treatment because of cancer recurrence and died about a year later; 17 were followed at 6 and 12 months (Fig. 1; Table 3 footnote; Results, 6th paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected, mostly White women with cancer living near one California clinic, well enough for day-long sessions and overnight stays, willing to stop psychiatric medicines and take MDMA; most had psychiatric histories and over half had used ecstasy before. Expectations of benefit were probably high and were not measured.

exposure.measurement: Assigned study drug in two blinded experimental sessions of about 8 hours, 2 to 4 weeks apart, with non-directive therapy by the same male–female co-therapist team, eyeshades and music, and an overnight stay with a night attendant; three 60- to 90-minute preparatory sessions before and integration sessions after each experimental session (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Procedures, 1st to 4th paragraphs). MDMA was manufactured by David Nichols (Purdue University) and compounded with lactose placebo into capsules of identical appearance and weight (Methods › Randomization and masking, 2nd paragraph). The optional supplemental dose was taken in all but one session (Results, 5th paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as printed: by mouth, 125 mg MDMA (or 125 mg lactose placebo) per session, with an optional supplemental 62.5 mg (or placebo) offered 1.5 to 2.5 hours later; two blinded sessions, then one open-label MDMA session (MDMA group) or three open-label MDMA sessions (placebo group) on the same schedule (Methods › Study design and participants, 1st paragraph; Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph; Procedures, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).
exposure.polysubstance: Psychiatric medicines had to be tapered. Seven of 18 (39.0%) took an opioid medicine during the study; six stopped it at least 3 days before and 2 days after each MDMA session, and one MDMA participant took tramadol but not within 24 hours of a session (Results, 1st paragraph). People with substance use disorders in remission for at least 60 days were eligible; drug screens were done before sessions (Methods › Study design and participants, 3rd paragraph; Procedures, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the primary outcome was assessed about one month after the second experimental session.

comparison.controls: Inactive placebo (125 mg lactose) with the identical psychotherapy (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph).
comparison.matching: Randomized about 1:3 with a web-based system and numbered containers, monitored by staff who did not communicate with the site (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph). With 5 and 13 people the groups differed at baseline: STAI-Trait 57.4 (5.2) vs 62.5 (7.3), STAI-State 51.8 vs 59.5, PTSD history 2 of 5 (40.0%) vs 11 of 13 (84.6%), anxiety history 60.0% vs 92.3%, insomnia 40.0% vs 69.2% (Table 1). The primary analysis compared change scores without adjustment for baseline (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd paragraph).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a randomized comparison; expectations of treatment were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Prior ecstasy use 3 of 5 on placebo vs 7 of 13 on MDMA (Table 1); opioid use not reported by group.

outcomes.instruments: Primary: STAI-Trait (20 items, 20 to 80), self-reported. Secondary: STAI-State; BDI-II; PSQI; Posttraumatic Growth Inventory (PTGI, with the illness as the reference event); MADRS and GAF, both by an independent blinded rater; FACIT-Sp (four subscales and additional concerns); Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ); Death Attitude Profile (DAP, five subscales); Self-Compassion Scale (SCS). Safety: spontaneously reported expected reactions during sessions and on seven daily telephone contacts afterwards, adverse events throughout, C-SSRS at each in-person visit and on two telephone days, vital signs every 30 minutes for 4 hours and hourly thereafter (Methods › Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Procedures, 3rd and 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated instruments; STAI-Trait of 45 or more taken as moderate to severe anxiety (Methods › Study design and participants, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.operationalization: Benefit: a larger fall in STAI-Trait from baseline to one month after the second blinded session on MDMA than on placebo, by independent-samples t test of change scores; effect size Hedges' g (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Alpha 0.05 two-tailed for every test; the pooled t test or the Satterthwaite test chosen by a Folded F test of variances (Methods › Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph). Editors' count of 20 between-group tests at the primary endpoint in Table 2: STAI-Trait, STAI-State, BDI-II, PSQI, PTGI, MADRS, GAF, SCS, FFMQ, five DAP and five FACIT scores; plus 18 repeated-measures ANOVAs on the pooled follow-up data.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants, investigators and an independent rater were masked (Methods › Randomization and masking, 1st paragraph). The primary outcome is self-reported. At the end of each blinded session participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions (86.1%) and the co-therapists in 32 of 36 (88.9%) (Results, 8th paragraph). The MADRS and GAF were rated by an independent rater blind to group (Methods › Procedures, 4th paragraph); the rater's guesses were not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: STAI-Trait change −23.5 (SD 13.2) on MDMA vs −8.8 (14.7) on placebo, P = 0.0558; Hedges' g 1.03, printed 95% CI −5.25 to 7.31 (Results, 2nd paragraph; Table 2; Abstract). Editors' calculations from the printed means and SDs: difference 14.7 points (95% CI −0.5 to 29.9; pooled t(16) = 2.06, P = 0.057); approximate 95% CI for g −0.05 to 2.12. Without the one placebo participant whose score fell by 35 points, P = 0.0066 (post hoc). Secondary at the primary endpoint (Table 2): PTGI +12.9 vs −2.6, P = 0.04, printed g 0.50; FFMQ +0.4 vs 0, P = 0.04, printed g 0.67; PSQI −3.6 vs −0.2, P = 0.05; STAI-State −22.1 vs −6.0, P = 0.10; BDI-II −20.9 vs −14.6, P = 0.36; MADRS −10.5 vs −7.0, P = 0.41; GAF +6.6 vs +3.0, P = 0.52; SCS, DAP and FACIT not significant. Editors' calculation for PTGI with the pooled SD: g about 0.73 (the printed P values for PTGI, FFMQ and PSQI match the unequal-variance test). Pooled uncontrolled follow-up (n = 17): STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) at baseline, 36.4 (9.5) at treatment exit, 33.6 (8.3) at 6 months and 34.2 (10.3) at 12 months, F(3,48) = 51.39, P < 0.0001 (Table 3; Results, 4th paragraph).
analysis.covariates: None; change scores compared without adjustment for the baseline imbalance in STAI-Trait (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd paragraph; Table 1).
analysis.preregistration_detail: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02427568: first submitted 13 April 2015, first posted 28 April 2015, before the actual start (14 May 2015). Registered primary outcome: change in STAI-Trait from baseline to the primary endpoint one month after the second experimental session, as reported; registered secondary outcomes match the measures in Table 2. Results posted 2 August 2021, with the same STAI-Trait values (−8.8 [14.7] and −23.5 [13.2]; endpoint 48.6 and 38.9). The record now names Resilient Pharmaceuticals as sponsor. The record's history of changes was not read (registry record, read through the ClinicalTrials.gov API v2 on 2026-10-17).
analysis.selective_reporting: The registered primary analysis is reported, but a post hoc analysis without one placebo participant (P = 0.0066) is presented in the Results, the Discussion and the Limitations as the likely reason for non-significance. Open-label session outcomes and adverse events are in the supplement (eTables), not read because the supplement is a Word download.
analysis.power: No power calculation: a feasibility study, sample size based on the phase 2 PTSD studies (Methods › Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph). With 5 controls the trial could detect only very large differences.

interpretation_gap.results_show: One month after two sessions, self-reported trait anxiety had fallen by 23.5 points on MDMA and 8.8 on placebo; the difference of 14.7 points has a 95% interval from about −0.5 to 30 (editors' calculation), so the trial cannot tell a large benefit from none. The MDMA group started 5 points more anxious, most participants and therapists could tell which pill had been given, and the primary outcome is self-reported. After everyone had MDMA, scores stayed lower at 6 and 12 months, with no control group. Jaw clenching, thirst, sweating, dry mouth and headache in sessions, and fatigue, extra sleep need and insomnia in the following week, were more frequent on MDMA; no serious adverse event was attributed to MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Discussion attributes the non-significant primary result to one placebo participant with a large improvement, citing P = 0.0066 without that person, and to 2 placebo participants who believed they had MDMA (Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs), without weighing the much larger unblinding in the MDMA group or its higher baseline. It says the stable 6- and 12-month scores suggest the potential for benefits of up to a year or more, while acknowledging the lack of a control group (Discussion, 2nd paragraph), and that the durability "demonstrates benefits might extend beyond the acute treatment effects" (Discussion, 4th paragraph). It calls MDMA-assisted psychotherapy a safe treatment in this sample in which the benefits outweighed the costs (Discussion, 5th paragraph); the Conclusions call it possibly safe and feasible. The abstract reports the non-significant result (P = .056) with an effect-size interval that is impossible (Abstract).

timeline.event: This trial: the first randomized trial of MDMA-assisted therapy for anxiety with a life-threatening illness (18 participants).
Barone et al., Front Psychiatry: a qualitative analysis of this trial's participants (on the project's evidence map; not read here).

replication.where_it_stands: One small pilot trial. The project's evidence map lists a registered trial in advanced-stage cancer (NCT00252174) that was terminated with results posted but no publication found, and a protocol for a double-blind trial in advanced cancer (EMMAC; Bhagavan et al., 2024); neither was read here. The Cochrane review covering psychedelic-assisted therapy in life-threatening disease (Schipper et al., 2024) is with the other reader of this batch.

funding.funder: MAPS, a 501(c)(3) non-profit organization, provided the MDMA and fully funded the study; MAPS PBC, its wholly owned subsidiary, organized the trial; MAPS and MAPS PBC assisted with study design, monitoring of study data, analysis, management and interpretation of data, preparation, review and approval of the manuscript and the decision to submit; the funder had no role in collecting data or conducting the study (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: P.W. received contractual support from MAPS as principal investigator; J.A., S.C. and E.S. were paid by MAPS as therapists in the study; E.W. was paid by MAPS as the independent rater; A.F., L.J., J.W. and A.E. were salaried full-time employees of MAPS PBC; B.Y.-K. and R.D. were salaried full-time employees of MAPS; S.H. received research funds from MAPS PBC as biostatistician; M.M. was paid as medical monitor (Competing interests).
funding.affiliations_note: Every author was paid by the sponsor in some role, including the independent rater, the therapists and the biostatistician responsible for the integrity of the data and analyses (Author contributions; Competing interests). The site is the principal investigator's own clinic (Center for Transformational Psychotherapy, San Anselmo; Author information). The paper's Crossref record carries no correction, expression of concern or retraction (read 2026-10-17).

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered, adequately powered multi-site randomized trial in people with anxiety related to a life-threatening illness, comparing MDMA with an active comparator within the same psychotherapy, with baseline-adjusted analysis, independent raters, measured expectancy and blinding, and a controlled follow-up of at least 6 months.

domains.note: Web-based randomization with numbered containers, managed by staff with no contact with the site; allocation concealed. The baseline imbalances (STAI-Trait 62.5 vs 57.4; PTSD history 84.6% vs 40.0%) are compatible with chance in 18 people, but because the analysis compares unadjusted change scores, the more anxious MDMA group had more room to improve.

Participants and therapists probably knew the allocation (correct guesses in 86.1% and 88.9% of sessions); the same co-therapy team delivered all sessions. Analysis by intention to treat, with no departures from the protocol reported up to the primary endpoint.
All 18 assessed at the primary endpoint.

The primary outcome is self-reported by participants who in most sessions correctly identified what they had received, in a trial whose volunteers were probably expecting benefit; knowledge of allocation could plausibly influence reported anxiety in both arms, in opposite directions. Expectancy was not measured.

Prospectively registered; the registered primary outcome and analysis are reported and agree with the posted results. The post hoc analysis excluding one placebo participant is extra, not a substitute, but it is given prominence; the 20 secondary tests are uncorrected (relevant to secondary results, not to this judgment).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-concealed randomized comparison, but the primary outcome is participant-reported in a trial where allocation was evident in most sessions, so the measurement domain is high and with it the overall judgment. The trial is also extremely small (5 controls), its primary difference is not statistically significant and its interval includes no difference. It can be cited for the observed change scores, for the frequency of acute and next-week reactions on MDMA in 13 people, and for the absence of serious adverse events attributed to MDMA; it cannot be cited for efficacy, for durability (the follow-up is uncontrolled) or for rare harms.

key_findings.finding: Flow (read from the Fig. 1 image): 110 telephone screens, 88 excluded at that stage, 22 assessed in person, 1 excluded, 21 enrolled, 3 discontinued before randomization, 18 randomized (5 placebo, 13 MDMA); all 18 completed the primary assessment; 5 and 12 completed the open-label stage and the 6- and 12-month follow-ups, 1 MDMA participant having stopped because of disease progression.
key_findings.note: The text says 92 of 110 failed telephone screening; Fig. 1 shows 88 excluded at telephone screening and 4 more before randomization (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Baseline, placebo vs MDMA: age 53.2 (10.5) vs 55.5 (7.0); women 4 of 5 vs 10 of 13; STAI-Trait 57.4 (5.2) vs 62.5 (7.3); STAI-State 51.8 (5.3) vs 59.5 (11.9); history of PTSD 2 (40.0%) vs 11 (84.6%), anxiety 3 (60.0%) vs 12 (92.3%), major depression 3 (60.0%) vs 11 (84.6%); prior ecstasy use 3 (60.0%) vs 7 (53.9%).

Primary outcome, STAI-Trait change from baseline to one month after the second blinded session: −23.5 (SD 13.2) on MDMA (n = 13) vs −8.8 (14.7) on placebo (n = 5), P = 0.0558; endpoint scores 38.9 (10.6) vs 48.6 (12.6); Hedges' g 1.03 with a printed 95% CI of −5.25 to 7.31.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculations: difference 14.7 points, 95% CI −0.5 to 29.9 (pooled t(16) = 2.06, P = 0.057); approximate 95% CI for g −0.05 to 2.12. The printed interval for g cannot be right (reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Placebo change scores ranged from −1 to −35 (median −3, IQR 1.0); MDMA change scores from −43 to +1 (median −27, IQR 13.0). Excluding the one placebo participant with −35, the group difference would have been P = 0.0066 (a post hoc analysis).

Secondary outcomes at the primary endpoint, MDMA vs placebo change: PTGI +12.9 (23.2) vs −2.6 (6.1), P = 0.04, printed g 0.50; FFMQ +0.4 (0.6) vs 0 (0.2), P = 0.04, printed g 0.67; PSQI −3.6 (5.4) vs −0.2 (1.3), P = 0.05; STAI-State −22.1 (17.9) vs −6.0 (15.8), P = 0.10; BDI-II −20.9 (13.8) vs −14.6 (8.6), P = 0.36; MADRS −10.5 (8.2) vs −7.0 (7.2), P = 0.41; GAF +6.6 (9.7) vs +3.0 (12.5), P = 0.52; SCS P = 0.21; DAP and FACIT subscales P = 0.15 to 0.88.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: with the pooled SD the PTGI g is about 0.73; the P values for PTGI, FFMQ and PSQI match the unequal-variance (Satterthwaite) test, which the Methods allow.

key_findings.finding: Uncontrolled follow-up of both groups after three MDMA sessions (n = 17): STAI-Trait 61.1 (7.0) at baseline, 36.4 (9.5) at treatment exit, 33.6 (8.3) at 6 months, 34.2 (10.3) at 12 months, F(3,48) = 51.39, P < 0.0001; BDI-II 30.2 (10.8) to 3.0 (2.5), 3.2 (3.1) and 4.3 (4.0); MADRS 19.4 (7.5) to 4.1 (4.4), 3.6 (2.5) and 3.5 (3.2). Pairwise comparisons with baseline were not significant for any DAP subscale or for FACIT social/family well-being.

Expected reactions during the two blinded sessions, MDMA (n = 13) vs placebo (n = 5): jaw clenching 11 (84.6%) vs 1 (20.0%), thirst 11 (84.6%) vs 2 (40.0%), dry mouth 9 (69.2%) vs 1, perspiration 9 (69.2%) vs 0, headache 8 (61.5%) vs 1, lack of appetite 4 (30.8%) vs 0, anxiety 3 (23.1%) vs 0. In the following 7 days: fatigue 12 (92.3%) vs 3 (60.0%), needing more sleep 12 (92.3%) vs 2 (40.0%), insomnia 9 (69.2%) vs 2 (40.0%), low mood 8 (61.5%) vs 3 (60.0%), anxiety 8 (61.5%) vs 2 (40.0%), jaw clenching 8 (61.5%) vs 1; these decreased over the week.

Psychiatric adverse events from the first drug session to the day before session 3: anxiety, depressed mood, depression and dissociation in 1 MDMA participant each, insomnia 2 vs 1; no serious suicidal ideation or behaviour on the C-SSRS. Peak body temperature was the only vital sign that differed (37.3 [0.7] vs 36.9 [0.3] °C); no elevation needed medical intervention. One MDMA participant stopped after the primary endpoint because of cancer recurrence and died about a year later (five serious events related to the cancer and its treatment); two others had serious events from cancer progression during follow-up; none was attributed to MDMA.

Blinding: at the end of each blinded session participants guessed their allocation correctly in 31 of 36 sessions (86.1%) and the co-therapists in 32 of 36 (88.9%); three participants guessed wrongly at least once, two of them on placebo who guessed MDMA.

Registration and posted results: NCT02427568 first submitted 13 April 2015 and posted 28 April 2015, before the start on 14 May 2015; primary outcome change in STAI-Trait from baseline to the primary endpoint; results posted 2 August 2021 with the same STAI-Trait values; the adverse-event module lists 1 death and 3 participants with serious events in the MDMA group's 12-month follow-up period, all cancer-related terms (invasive ductal breast carcinoma, chordoma, spinal cord paralysis, meningitis, sepsis, cerebrovascular accident).
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02427568 (API v2) › Status; Outcome Measures; Results › Participant Flow, Outcome Measures, Adverse Events

key_findings.finding: Design rationale: the sample size was based on the phase 2 PTSD studies, with no power calculation; the Discussion cites, among the PTSD reports its safety findings agree with, the pooled phase 2 analysis (reference 53, Mithoefer et al., 2019), which PMC marks as retracted.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Statistical analyses, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 5th paragraph; References, 53

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% CI printed for Hedges' g (−5.25 to 7.31, in the abstract and the Results) is impossible for a standardized difference between groups of 13 and 5 with g = 1.03; the editors' approximate interval is −0.05 to 2.12, and the raw difference is 14.7 points (95% CI −0.5 to 29.9).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed interval cannot be cited; the correct interval still includes no effect.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results say 92 of 110 screened people failed the inclusion criteria at telephone screening and then that three more were excluded after enrolment; Fig. 1 shows 88 excluded at telephone screening, 1 after the in-person screen and 3 after enrolment (92 not randomized in all).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; cite Fig. 1 for the flow.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of placebo participants who believed they had received MDMA is given as 2 of 5 (Discussion, 1st paragraph) and as '2 of 3 placebo participants' (Discussion, 6th paragraph); the Results say three participants guessed wrongly, two of whom were on placebo.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results, 8th paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs)
reporting_issues.consequence: Two of five placebo participants guessed MDMA at least once; the limitation paragraph misstates the denominator.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the long-term reduction in anxiety was assessed by the MADRS, a depression scale; says there were significant gains in FACIT social and family well-being, although Table 3's comparisons with baseline give P = 0.72, 0.66 and 0.72; and says DAP fear of death, neutral acceptance and approach acceptance improved, although every pairwise comparison with baseline in Table 3 has P ≥ 0.10 (only the overall ANOVAs were significant).
reporting_issues.consequence: These statements are not supported by the paper's own tables.

reporting_issues.issue: For the PTGI the printed Hedges' g is 0.50, while the printed means and SDs give about 0.73 with the pooled SD (editors' calculation); the PTGI SD of the MDMA change is 23.3 in the text and 23.2 in Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; effect sizes for secondary outcomes should be recomputed rather than cited.

reporting_issues.issue: A post hoc analysis without one placebo participant (P = 0.0066) is presented three times as the likely reason the primary result was not significant; nothing in the Methods prespecifies outlier handling, and the participant's improvement is a valid observation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 1st and 6th paragraphs; Methods › Statistical analyses)
reporting_issues.consequence: The prespecified result (P = 0.056, interval including no difference) is the one to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The registry's participant flow shows all 13 MDMA participants completing the overall study, while Fig. 1 shows one who stopped after the primary endpoint because of disease progression.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the registry's period probably ends at the primary endpoint.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC7686344 (all sections, Tables 1 to 4 as text, figure legends, the Fig. 1 CONSORT image viewed at its PMC address, funding, competing interests and contributions), read in this reader's own browser tab; ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT02427568 (API v2) for registration, outcomes, participant flow and adverse events; the Crossref record for the DOI. The supplementary Word file (eTables 1 to 6) was not read because it is a download; Fig. 2 values were not extracted.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 9 men with previous recreational MDMA experience, run as outpatients. Each session lasted two days: 100 mg MDMA on day 1 and a second 100 mg dose 24 hours later, or matching placebo on both days, with at least a week between the two sessions. Physiological measures, psychomotor performance, 21 visual analogue scales, the Addiction Research Center Inventory, plasma cortisol and prolactin, and plasma and urine concentrations of MDMA and its metabolite MDA were measured repeatedly for 24 hours after each dose, with further plasma samples at 30 and 48 hours and urine to 72 hours. Peak effects and 6-hour areas under the curve were compared by two-way repeated-measures analysis of variance with drug condition and administration (first or second) as factors, with Tukey post-hoc tests and a three-way analysis including time.
can_establish: How the acute effects and plasma concentrations of a second 100 mg dose of MDMA taken 24 hours after a first compare with the first, within the same people against their own placebo days, under double-blind conditions.
cannot_establish: What happens at the intervals people actually use (the authors say 2-8 hours is the recreational pattern and that extrapolation to shorter intervals is difficult), after more than two doses, at larger doses, in women (none were studied), or over repeated weekends; and whether the smaller-than-expected effects reflect tolerance rather than ceiling effects on the rating scales and on pupil diameter, which the authors raise as an alternative.

sample.recruitment: Men recruited by word of mouth; the study was run at a municipal medical research institute in Barcelona (Materials and methods > Volunteers, p. 365).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Recreational use of MDMA on at least five previous occasions; medical screening by physician interview, physical examination, laboratory tests, urinalysis and electrocardiogram; psychiatric screening by structured DSM-IV interview excluding schizophrenia, psychosis and major affective disorder. Ten men were enrolled and one was excluded because his dextromethorphan phenotyping showed he was not an extensive metabolizer of the enzyme that clears MDMA, leaving nine (p. 365).
sample.demographics: Nine men, mean age 23 years (range 21-33), mean weight 73.3 kg (range 60.6-86.5), mean height 177 cm (range 168-189), with an average of 26 previous MDMA experiences (range 6-100). All but two smoked tobacco; all had used other stimulants, cannabis or hallucinogens; none met DSM-IV criteria for abuse or dependence other than nicotine, and none had a history of adverse reactions to MDMA (p. 365).
sample.attrition: No dropouts after enrolment; the one excluded participant was removed before the sessions on the basis of enzyme phenotyping.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, young, healthy, experienced with MDMA and screened to be fast metabolizers of it; people who metabolize MDMA slowly, who are the group most exposed to accumulation, were deliberately excluded, and women were not studied.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory in identical opaque capsules and measured directly: plasma and urine MDMA and MDA by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, sampled at baseline, 20, 40, 60 and 90 minutes and 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 and 24 hours after each dose, plus 30 and 48 hours after the second, with urine collected in four intervals to 24 hours and again to 72 hours (pp. 365-366).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral racemic MDMA 100 mg on day 1 followed by oral racemic MDMA 100 mg 24 hours later, or placebo on both days, supplied by the Spanish Ministry of Health and prepared by the institution's pharmacy (p. 365).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were asked to refrain from any drug for two weeks before and during the study, with urine screening for opiates, cocaine metabolite, amphetamines and cannabinoids before each session; smoking was allowed only from 6 hours after dosing, and the paper attributes part of the late heart-rate rise in all conditions to smoking and meals (pp. 365-367).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Overnight fast and drug-free urine screen before each session day; at least one week between the two two-day sessions. At the 24-hour point most participants still had measurable MDMA in plasma from the first dose, averaging 12 ng/mL (p. 370).

comparison.controls: The same men in a placebo-placebo session, with each active day compared against its own temporal placebo (first dose against first placebo, second against second); the first and second placebo days were also compared with each other and differed only at three isolated time points on two performance measures.
comparison.matching: Within-person, randomized, double-blind crossover with at least a week between sessions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person against the same person's placebo session.

outcomes.instruments: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, oral temperature and pupil diameter (Haab gauge) at 13 time points to 24 hours; simple reaction time, digit-symbol substitution and the Maddox-wing measure of extraocular balance; 21 visual analogue scales and the 49-item short-form Addiction Research Center Inventory with its five subscales; plasma cortisol and prolactin by immunoassay to 6 hours (pp. 365-366).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard human-pharmacology battery used by this laboratory in earlier MDMA studies; the visual analogue scales have no external norms and the questionnaire subscales are validated in Spanish.
outcomes.operationalization: Acute tolerance is not formally defined or tested: the authors infer 'some degree of tolerance' where effects after the second dose were similar to the first despite higher plasma concentrations, and the absence of sensitization where no effect exceeded what the concentration predicted.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at the family level: every variable was tested on three parameters (peak, 6-hour area under the curve, and the time course), with Tukey post-hoc comparisons at each time point, at p<0.05 (p. 366).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind with identical capsules; blinding integrity was not assessed, and 100 mg of MDMA in men with an average of 26 previous experiences is likely to have been recognizable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Effects are reported as F values with p values in Table 1 and as peak changes in the text; standardized effect sizes are not given. Pharmacokinetics (Table 2, n=9): MDMA area under the curve 1452 (SD 771) ng.h/mL after the first dose and 2564 (SD 762) after the second, a ratio of 1.77 (+77%, p<=0.001); peak concentration 180 (SD 33) and 232 (SD 39) ng/mL, a ratio of 1.29 (+29%, p<=0.001); elimination half-life 7.0 h (SD 2.2) and 8.8 h (SD 1.5); elimination constant 0.112 (SD 0.054) and 0.081 (SD 0.017) per hour. For the metabolite MDA: area under the curve 157 (SD 55) and 259 (SD 81), ratio 1.64 (+64%); peak 11 (SD 3) and 15 (SD 4) ng/mL, ratio 1.40 (+40%). Physiological peaks: systolic pressure +25 mm Hg after the first dose and +34 after the second; diastolic +10 and +20; heart rate +16 and +22 beats/min. Cortisol peak 14.11 against 21.08 microgram/mL, about 49% higher, with the area under the curve about 75% higher.
analysis.covariates: None; effects were expressed as change from each day's baseline before analysis.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned. The study was approved by the local institutional review board and authorized by the Spanish Ministry of Health (number 98/112), and conformed to Spanish clinical-trial law (pp. 364-365, 375).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists only the variables that reached significance somewhere, so the number of scales tested and found null can only be inferred; the Addiction Research Center Inventory and visual analogue time courses appear in figures without printed values.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. The authors state in their limitations that nine participants may not have had enough power to show differences in some variables, and that several questionnaire scales were near their ceiling.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first produced plasma concentrations far above simple accumulation (area under the curve 77% higher, peak 29% higher) and effects that were slightly larger than after the first dose on blood pressure, some subjective scales and cortisol, but smaller than those concentrations would predict; on pupil diameter, the Maddox-wing measure, one questionnaire subscale and prolactin the second dose produced the same response as the first. Hypertensive episodes (above 140 mm Hg systolic) occurred in 6 of 9 men after the first dose and 8 of 9 after the second, lasting on average 1 h against 1.4 h, and the two episodes of sinus tachycardia both followed the second dose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that effects after the second administration were higher than after the first but lower than expected, and attributes the concentration rise to metabolic inhibition lasting at least 24 hours; the discussion says the unchanged responses suggest 'the possible appearance of some degree of tolerance'. This is appropriately hedged. The weaker point is that the tolerance reading rests on comparing an effect with an expectation that is not modelled: no concentration-effect relation is fitted, so 'lower than expected' is a judgement rather than a measurement, and the authors' own alternative explanation (ceiling effects on the scales and on pupil diameter) is not ruled out.

timeline.event: The same group, 50 mg then 100 mg two hours apart in 10 men: concentrations above dose proportionality again, with heart rate and the wanted subjective effects lower than the concentrations predicted
Two 100 mg doses 4 hours apart (Farre et al., 2015): peak concentrations roughly doubled while the two effect-time profiles were very similar
A 60 mg booster 2 hours after 120 mg: 1.5-fold higher peak concentration, effects prolonged by about an hour, peak effects unchanged

replication.where_it_stands: The finding that a second dose raises concentrations more than simple accumulation predicts, while effects rise less than concentrations do, has now been reproduced at 24-hour, 4-hour and 2-hour intervals and with a booster design, by two independent groups. The specific 24-hour finding rests on this study alone.

funding.funder: Grants from the Generalitat de Catalunya (2001SGR00407) and the Fondo de Investigacion Sanitaria (98/0181 and 01/1336) (p. 375).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Institut Municipal d'Investigacio Medica and two Barcelona universities; the same group published the 2-hour-interval study (Peiro et al., 2013) and the 4-hour-interval study, so those are not independent replications of each other.

what_would_settle_it: A dose-ranging repeated-dose study that fits a concentration-effect model for each measure, so that 'lower than expected' becomes a measured shift in the concentration-response curve rather than a judgement; including women, people who metabolize MDMA slowly, intervals of 2-8 hours and scales without ceiling effects.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two sessions)
domains.note: Described as randomized and crossover, but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described and no period effect is reported.
At least one week between sessions, which is many half-lives, and the two placebo days behaved alike except at three isolated time points on two measures.
Double-blind with identical capsules, but blinding integrity was not tested and the active condition produced unmistakable effects in men with substantial previous MDMA experience.
All nine men completed both sessions; the one exclusion happened before dosing, on the basis of enzyme phenotyping.

Cardiovascular measures, pupil diameter, hormones and plasma concentrations are objective; the subjective scales that carry much of the tolerance argument are self-reports whose blinding cannot be assumed, and the authors state several were near their ceiling.
No protocol or pre-specified primary outcome; about forty outcomes tested on three parameters each without family-level correction; Table 1 shows only variables that reached significance somewhere.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is a well-run within-person, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover with objective pharmacokinetic measurement and matched placebo days, and the pharmacokinetic finding is internally strong (paired tests, p<=0.001, consistent in plasma and urine). The concerns are the untested blind, the number of uncorrected comparisons, and that the tolerance interpretation compares effects with an unmodelled expectation. The source can be cited for the size of the concentration rise after a second dose 24 hours later, for the direction of the cardiovascular and subjective changes, and for the observation that some measures did not increase; it cannot be cited for the size of any tolerance, for shorter intervals, for more than two doses, or for women.

key_findings.finding: A second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first produced plasma concentrations well above simple accumulation: area under the curve 2564 ng.h/mL (SD 762) against 1452 (SD 771), a ratio of 1.77 (77% higher), and peak concentration 232 ng/mL (SD 39) against 180 (SD 33), a ratio of 1.29 (29% higher); both paired comparisons at p<=0.001. The elimination constant fell (0.112 to 0.081 per hour) and the half-life rose (7.0 h, SD 2.2, to 8.8 h, SD 1.5).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, MDMA rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 370)

key_findings.finding: The metabolite MDA rose in parallel: area under the curve 259 ng.h/mL (SD 81) against 157 (SD 55), a ratio of 1.64 (64% higher), and peak 15 ng/mL (SD 4) against 11 (SD 3), a ratio of 1.40 (40% higher), both p<=0.001; urinary recoveries of both compounds were also higher after the second dose.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, MDA rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, last paragraph (p. 370)

key_findings.finding: At the 24-hour point, just before the second dose, most participants still had measurable MDMA in plasma, averaging 12 ng/mL.

Blood pressure rose more after the second dose: the peak increase in systolic pressure was 34 mm Hg against 25 after the first dose, and in diastolic pressure 20 against 10; the differences were significant only at some time points in the first 2 hours. Heart rate rose 22 beats/min against 16, significant only at 40 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'In reference to physiological parameters' (p. 367, right column); Figure 1 (p. 368)

key_findings.finding: Cardiovascular incidents were more common after the second dose: systolic pressure above 140 mm Hg was reached by 6 of 9 men after the first dose and 8 of 9 after the second, with mean episode duration 1 h (range 0.5-2) against 1.4 h (range 0.5-3); two men met criteria for sinus tachycardia (above 100 beats/min), both after the second dose, lasting 15-30 minutes.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'In reference to physiological parameters' (p. 367, right column)

key_findings.finding: Subjective effects were slightly larger after the second dose, but significantly so on few scales: 'stimulated' (peak, area under the curve and time course), 'high', 'any effect', 'changes in lights', 'changes in hearing' and four questionnaire subscales, mostly on the time course rather than the peak. No hallucinations or psychotic symptoms occurred after either dose.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'Subjective effects after administrations' (p. 370, left column); Table 1 (pp. 368-369); Figures 3-4 (pp. 371-372)

key_findings.finding: Several measures did not increase at all with the second dose despite the higher concentrations: pupil diameter, the Maddox-wing measure of extraocular balance, the amphetamine subscale of the questionnaire and plasma prolactin. Cortisol, by contrast, rose further: peak 21.08 against 14.11 microgram/mL, about 49% higher, with the area under the curve about 75% higher.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph on pupil diameter (p. 367) and the paragraph beginning 'Plasma hormone concentrations' (p. 370); Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'The pharmacological effects after the second administration' (p. 373)

key_findings.finding: The authors calculate that if the first dose's residual exposure is subtracted, the expected rise in area under the curve would be 39%, against the 77% observed, which they attribute to inhibition of MDMA's own metabolism lasting at least 24 hours.

Psychomotor performance did not differ between the two doses: both slightly reduced the number of digit-symbol responses and both produced similar extraocular tension, with no effect on reaction time.
key_findings.locator: Results > Pharmacological effects, the paragraph beginning 'Psychomotor performance results' (p. 370, left column); Figure 2 (p. 369)

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints a standard deviation beneath each median time to peak concentration (2 h with 0.26 for the first dose, 25.5 h with 0.33 for the second; 4 h with 6.88 and 28 h with 2.71 for the metabolite), although the legend and methods state that the time to peak was analysed by a rank test and reported as a median.
reporting_issues.consequence: A standard deviation around a median cannot be interpreted, and for the metabolite the value (6.88) is larger than the median itself (4 h); these dispersion figures should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed ratios do not all follow from the printed means: the metabolite's peak ratio is given as 1.40 (40%) while the rounded means (15 and 11 ng/mL) give 1.36, and the elimination half-life rises from 7.0 to 8.8 hours without a significance marker although the elimination constant it is derived from is discussed as having decreased.
reporting_issues.consequence: The ratios are presumably computed from unrounded individual values; a claim should cite the ratio with its significance marker rather than recomputing from the rounded table means, and should not describe the half-life change as significant.

reporting_issues.issue: Times to peak concentration are given from the start of the session rather than from each dose (2 h and 25.5 h; 4 h and 28 h for the metabolite), which the table does not state.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as time since the second dose, the second-dose peak is at 1.5 hours, slightly earlier than the first dose's 2 hours; a reader taking 25.5 h at face value would misreport the time course.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion lists the subjective scales that differed between doses as including 'changes in lights and sounds, changes in hearing', while the results list 'changes in lights' (peak and time course) and 'changes in hearing' (time course); there is no separate 'sounds' scale among the 21 listed in the methods.
