reporting_issues.consequence: Minor wording drift between results and discussion; the results list and Table 1 should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 includes only variables that reached significance in at least one comparison, so the denominator for the subjective findings (21 visual analogue scales and five questionnaire subscales, each tested on three parameters) is not visible in the table.
reporting_issues.consequence: The number of comparisons behind the handful of significant subjective differences is larger than the table suggests, and the paper applies no family-level correction.

reporting_issues.issue: The study's central interpretation, that effects were lower than expected given the concentrations, is not supported by a fitted concentration-effect relation; the authors note in their own limitations that ceiling effects on the questionnaire scales and on pupil diameter could produce the same pattern.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of acute tolerance from this study should be stated as an unchanged or slightly increased response despite higher concentrations, with the ceiling-effect alternative named.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 364-375 (PDFs/MDMA/Farre_2004_RepeatedDosesPharmacology.pdf), full text; Table 2 (p. 370) is printed sideways and was read from a rotated render of the page, and Table 1 (pp. 368-369) was read in the extracted text and checked against the page images.

design_detail: Phase 1 double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover in healthy volunteers at a Swiss university hospital, with three 10-hour dosing sessions at least 28 days apart in counterbalanced order: 120 mg MDMA followed two hours later by a 60 mg booster; 120 mg MDMA followed by placebo; and placebo followed by placebo. The primary outcome was the duration of any subjective drug effect, defined as the cumulative time a visual analogue rating of 'any drug effect' stayed above 10%. Secondary outcomes were other subjective ratings and mood, adverse effects by a 50-item complaint list at the end of the session and at 3 and 7 days, well-being and insomnia questionnaires, blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and temperature, and plasma concentrations of MDMA, MDA, HMMA, oxytocin and neurophysin I. Repeated-measures analyses of variance with Tukey post-hoc tests; registered as NCT05809271.
can_establish: Whether a 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg MDMA, the regimen used in most MDMA-assisted-therapy trials, lengthens the acute response, raises its peak, changes plasma concentrations, or adds adverse effects, in the same healthy people against their own single-dose and placebo sessions.
cannot_establish: Whether a booster helps anyone therapeutically (no patients and no clinical outcome); what happens after more than two doses, at other intervals, or in people with hypertension or other illness; and whether the unchanged peak effects reflect tolerance rather than a ceiling on the rating scales, since no concentration-effect model is fitted and the hysteresis analysis that illustrates acute tolerance is in a supplement this reader did not open.

sample.recruitment: Volunteers recruited through the trial registry, advertisement and word of mouth, at the University Hospital Basel; study run between 17 November 2023 and 25 March 2025 (Methods > Study design; Results > Participants and blinding).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 18-65 with a body mass index of 18-29. Excluded: pregnancy or breastfeeding, any past or current major psychiatric disorder by a structured DSM-5-based interview, a first-degree relative with a psychotic disorder, medication that could interact with MDMA, chronic or acute physical illness, smoking more than 10 cigarettes a day, drinking more than 15 standard drinks a week, lifetime MDMA use on more than 20 occasions, and any illicit drug use except cannabis within 2 months. Urine drug testing at screening and once during the study.
sample.demographics: Twenty-three completers (12 men, 11 women), mean age 35 years (SD 13), mean body weight 67 kg (SD 12). Ten (43%) had used MDMA before, on average 5.3 times (SD 3.8). Fuller baseline characteristics are in a supplementary table that was not read for this card.
sample.attrition: Two of 25 dropped out after their first session; both were women, both had received the booster condition as their first session and first ever MDMA experience, and both had intense headache and nausea during the session followed by weeks of anxiety, restlessness and impaired concentration, one with reduced ability to work for several months. Their complaint scores are reported separately and are excluded from the within-person comparisons.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy, mostly young volunteers screened to exclude psychiatric history, illness and heavy drug use, with little MDMA experience; the authors name the lack of generalizability to patients, particularly those with hypertension or other conditions, as a limitation. Because the two people with the worst reactions left after one session, the within-person comparisons of adverse effects are made among those who tolerated the drug.

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the hospital and measured directly: plasma MDMA, MDA and HMMA every 30 minutes for 6 hours and hourly thereafter by a validated method, with non-compartmental pharmacokinetics.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral racemic MDMA hydrochloride in 20 mg capsules made to Good Manufacturing Practice, measured content 20.74 mg (SD 0.47, n=10), with mannitol placebo capsules. The first dose was given at about 9 a.m. and the second exactly two hours later: 120 mg then 60 mg, 120 mg then placebo, or placebo then placebo.
exposure.polysubstance: Heavy drinking and smoking were exclusions, illicit drug use other than cannabis within two months was an exclusion, participants were asked to abstain during the study period and urine drug testing was done at screening and once during the study.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 28 days between sessions; sessions began after an overnight stay at home, with a standardized breakfast before the first dose. No breath or urine result is reported per session beyond the single in-study test.

comparison.controls: The same people in a placebo-placebo session and in a single-dose session; the booster condition is compared with both.
comparison.matching: Within-person, randomized and counterbalanced crossover with washout of at least 28 days.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person.

outcomes.instruments: Single-item 100 mm visual analogue scales, unidirectional (any drug effect, good drug effect, bad drug effect, drug liking, stimulated, drug high, anxiety) and bidirectional (emotional, talkative, happy, open, trust, close to others, wanting to be alone or with others), with 'any', 'good' and 'bad' drug effect every 15 minutes and the rest at 16 time points to 9 hours; the Adjective Mood Rating Scale at 5 time points; a 50-item List of Complaints at baseline, end of session and 3 and 7 days; the General Health Questionnaire-12, the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale and the Insomnia Severity Index at baseline and 3 and 7 days; blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and tympanic temperature; plasma MDMA, MDA, HMMA, oxytocin and neurophysin I.
outcomes.validity_norms: Validated instruments with published German versions and ranges given for each; the visual analogue scales are this group's standard measures with no external norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Effect duration is operationalized as the cumulative time the 'any drug effect' rating stays above 10%; acute tolerance is operationalized as effects subsiding while concentrations remain high, illustrated in a supplementary hysteresis plot rather than tested.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: One primary endpoint is declared (duration of any drug effect) and the rest are secondary; within each analysis, three conditions are compared by repeated-measures analysis of variance with Tukey post-hoc tests, but there is no correction across the many secondary outcomes.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind, with participants knowing the three conditions but not the order, and blinding kept to the end-of-study visit. Blinding was measured and largely failed for the drug itself: every participant identified the placebo condition correctly, and 35 of 46 MDMA conditions (76%) were identified correctly straight after the session, rising to 40 of 46 (87%) by the end of the study.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard deviations for every subjective and adverse-effect outcome, F values with 2 and 44 degrees of freedom (consistent with 23 participants and three conditions) and post-hoc significance markers. Primary outcome: duration 5.6 h (SD 1.8) with the booster against 4.6 h (SD 1.5) with the single dose and 0.2 h (SD 0.5) with placebo (F=173, p<0.001; booster against single dose p<0.01). Peak 'any drug effect' 83 (SD 21) against 85 (SD 20), not significant, with the area under the effect curve 318 (SD 127) against 255 (SD 130), p<0.05. Peak 'good drug effect' 86 (SD 29) against 87 (SD 19), not significant. Pharmacokinetics as geometric means with ratios: peak MDMA concentration 387 ng/mL (95% CI 351-426) with the booster against 253 (228-280) with the single dose, ratio 1.50 (90% CI 1.43-1.57); exposure to 9 hours 2339 against 1564 ng.h/mL, ratio 1.47 (1.40-1.54); half-life 7.2 h in both; time to peak 4 h against 2.8 h. A sample size of 20 was calculated for 80% power to detect a within-person effect of about 0.66.
analysis.covariates: None; within-person analyses of variance. Exploratory descriptive stratification by sex, body weight (under or at least 65 kg) and age.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov as NCT05809271; the paper names the primary endpoint as the duration of the 'any drug effect' rating and reports it first. The registry record itself was not opened for this card, so the registered outcome could not be compared with the reported one.
analysis.selective_reporting: Much of the detail sits in supplementary tables and figures (baseline characteristics, blinding, the full subjective-effects table, mood ratings, the hysteresis plot illustrating acute tolerance, autonomic effects, oxytocin values, symptom frequencies, the stratified complaint scores, the two dropouts' scores and laboratory results); the main text reports autonomic effects only in words. This reader did not open the supplement, so those values are not in this card.
analysis.power: Prospective calculation: 20 participants for 80% power to detect a within-person difference of about 0.66 at a two-sided 5% level; 23 completed. The study is powered for its primary endpoint, not for the adverse-effect comparisons, where the authors report differences as nominally higher after the booster without reaching significance.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg lengthened the subjective effect by about an hour (5.6 against 4.6 hours) and raised the area under the effect curve for several ratings, while leaving peak ratings unchanged, even though peak plasma concentration and 9-hour exposure were about 1.5 times those of the single dose. Blood pressure, heart rate and temperature were likewise prolonged but not raised at the peak; oxytocin was higher at 4 and 6 hours. Acute and 3-day adverse-effect scores were higher after both MDMA conditions than placebo and did not differ between them, with complaint scores nominally but not significantly higher after the booster.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that acute MDMA effects can be prolonged by a booster, as intended in therapy trials, and that whether this translates into clinical benefit remains to be investigated: an unusually disciplined statement. The discussion reads the unchanged peaks against higher concentrations as acute pharmacodynamic tolerance. That reading is reasonable and consistent with the hysteresis plot the paper cites, but the peak ratings were already at 83-87 out of 100, so a ceiling on the scales cannot be separated from tolerance in these data; the paper does not raise that alternative for the subjective peaks, although it applies the same logic to the autonomic measures where no ceiling applies. The statement that the regimen was overall well tolerated sits beside two people, both women receiving the booster as a first MDMA experience, who left with weeks of psychological symptoms.

timeline.event: Two 100 mg doses 24 hours apart: exposure 77% higher after the second dose with several responses unchanged
Fifty mg then 100 mg two hours apart: concentrations above dose proportionality, heart rate and wanted effects not raised
Two 100 mg doses 4 hours apart (Farre et al., 2015): peak concentrations doubled while the two effect-time profiles were very similar

replication.where_it_stands: This is the first direct test of the booster regimen used in MDMA-assisted-therapy trials. Its central observation, effects that do not rise with concentration after a second dose, agrees with three earlier Spanish studies at other intervals; the new findings are the prolongation of about an hour and the absence of any added peak effect or clear added harm.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation grant 32003B_185111 to the senior author, the University Hospital Basel, and Lykos Therapeutics, Inc. (Funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: The senior author is a consultant for Mind Medicine, Inc. and Lykos Therapeutics, Inc.; the other authors declare none. After the study finished, University Hospital Basel granted Lykos Therapeutics the right to use the data to support regulatory submissions, and the paper states that Lykos had no role in planning or conducting the study or writing the manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: University Hospital Basel and University of Basel. A company developing MDMA as a medicine part-funded the study and holds rights to the data for regulatory use, and the question studied, whether the booster dose in its trial regimen is justified, bears on that development. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A trial in patients receiving MDMA-assisted therapy, randomized to the booster or to a matched placebo booster, with the clinical outcome as the endpoint, so that the extra hour of acute effect can be weighed against any added harm; and, for the tolerance question, a design with scales that do not reach ceiling and a fitted concentration-effect model.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three sessions)
domains.note: Order was randomized and counterbalanced and randomization, packaging and labelling were done by the manufacturer, but the sequence-generation method and concealment are not described in the main text and no period effect is reported.
At least 28 days between sessions, far beyond the 7.2-hour half-life.

Blinding was measured and largely failed: all participants identified placebo correctly and 76% of MDMA sessions were identified correctly immediately afterwards. The primary outcome is a self-rating of drug effect, so expectancy cannot be excluded, although the comparison of interest (booster against single dose) is between two conditions both felt as active.

Two of 25 left after one session and are excluded from within-person comparisons; both had the booster and both had strong adverse reactions, so the adverse-effect comparison is biased toward tolerability. Pharmacokinetic analyses retain them (n=25 for the booster, 23 for the single dose), and half-life rests on 15-16 profiles.

Plasma concentrations, oxytocin, blood pressure, heart rate and temperature are objective and measured with validated methods; the primary outcome is self-rated on an unblindable scale, and its threshold (10% of the scale) is a convention rather than a validated cut-off.

Registered in advance with a declared primary endpoint reported first, a prospective power calculation, and both positive and negative findings, serious adverse events and dropouts reported in detail.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: This is the best-designed of the repeated-dose MDMA studies read here: registered, powered, counterbalanced, with 28-day washouts, objective pharmacokinetics and full reporting of adverse events, including two dropouts that a less careful paper would have left out. The overall judgment is set by blinding, which the authors themselves measured and found largely broken, in a study whose primary outcome is a self-rating; the dropout pattern also leaves the tolerability comparison favourable by construction. The source can be cited for the booster's effect on duration, peak effects, concentrations, oxytocin and adverse effects in healthy volunteers, and for the observation that peak effects did not rise with 1.5-fold higher concentrations; it cannot be cited for clinical benefit, for patients, or for the size of acute tolerance.

key_findings.finding: The booster lengthened the subjective effect by about an hour: duration of 'any drug effect' above the 10% threshold was 5.6 h (SD 1.8) with the booster, 4.6 h (SD 1.5) with the single 120 mg dose and 0.2 h (SD 0.5) with placebo (F(2,44)=173, p<0.001; booster against single dose p<0.01).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects, 1st paragraph; Table 1, 'Any drug effect' duration row
key_findings.note: The abstract gives the single-dose standard deviation as 1.2 h and Table 1 as 1.5 h.

key_findings.finding: Peak subjective intensity did not rise with the booster: peak 'any drug effect' 83 (SD 21) against 85 (SD 20) and peak 'good drug effect' 86 (SD 29) against 87 (SD 19), neither significant, while the areas under the effect curves were larger with the booster for 'any drug effect' (318, SD 127, against 255, SD 130; p<0.05) and for openness, trust, talkativeness and wanting to be with others.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Emax and AUEC rows; Results > Acute subjective effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations rose in proportion to the total dose: peak MDMA 387 ng/mL (95% CI 351-426) with the booster against 253 (228-280) with the single dose, a geometric mean ratio of 1.50 (90% CI 1.43-1.57); exposure to 9 hours 2339 against 1564 ng.h/mL, ratio 1.47 (1.40-1.54); elimination half-life 7.2 h in both conditions; time to peak 4 h against 2.8 h.

The authors read the combination of 1.5-fold higher concentrations with unchanged peak effects as acute pharmacodynamic tolerance, noting that subjective and physiological effects had subsided within the 9-hour observation while concentrations remained high, with the mean concentration at discharge after the booster exceeding the mean peak after the single dose.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects, last sentence; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: The hysteresis plot said to illustrate this is in Supplementary Figure S2, which was not read for this card.

key_findings.finding: Autonomic effects followed the same pattern: blood pressure, heart rate, rate-pressure product and body temperature rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo, and lasted longer after the booster without a higher maximum. No systolic pressure above 180 mm Hg and no temperature above 40 degrees Celsius occurred in any participant.
key_findings.note: The values are in Supplementary Table S11 and Supplementary Figure S6, which were not read; the main text gives only this description.

key_findings.finding: Adverse effects were more common after both MDMA conditions than placebo and did not differ significantly between booster and single dose: complaint scores were 22 (SD 15) and 20 (SD 13) acutely against 4.4 (SD 5.3) for placebo, and 16 (SD 16) and 17 (SD 16) over days 0-3 against 7.7 (SD 13). The most frequent acute complaints were tiredness, lack of appetite, bruxism and headache; vomiting occurred in 3 of 23 (13%) in the booster condition and 2 (9%) in the single-dose condition. Somatic complaints faded by days 3 and 7 while psychological ones (rumination, fatigue, inner tension, restlessness) persisted.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, List of complaints rows; Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Two of 25 participants (8%) left after one session, both women who had received the booster as their first MDMA experience: both had intense headache and nausea during the session and then weeks of anxiety, restlessness, tension or impaired concentration, one with reduced capacity for work improving over several months. One serious adverse event occurred, acute angle-closure glaucoma during a single-dose session in a participant later found to have narrow angles, with full recovery. Two men (9%) reported brief flashback-like recurrences of mild drug effects in the following days.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 3rd-4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In exploratory, descriptive analyses complaint scores were nominally higher in women and in people under 65 kg, particularly after the booster, and vomiting occurred only in women, all weighing 57-63 kg; the authors note that sex and body weight could not be separated in this sample.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, last sentence of the 1st paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Blinding largely failed: every participant identified the placebo condition correctly, 35 of 46 MDMA conditions (76%) were identified correctly immediately after the session and 40 of 46 (87%) by the end of the study.

Oxytocin and its carrier protein rose under both MDMA conditions against placebo, and were higher at 4 and 6 hours after the booster than after the single dose; the two measures correlated closely (r=0.86, p<0.0001).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the single-dose effect duration as 4.6 +/- 1.2 h while Table 1 gives 4.6 +/- 1.5 h for the same measure; the booster value (5.6 +/- 1.8 h) and the p value (0.001) agree.
reporting_issues.locator: Abstract; Table 1, 'Any drug effect' duration row
reporting_issues.consequence: The dispersion of the primary outcome differs between abstract and table; the table value should be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The pharmacokinetic table retains the two dropouts, giving n=25 for the booster condition and n=23 for the single dose, while every pharmacodynamic analysis uses the 23 completers; half-life and clearance rest on 15-16 profiles because the 9-hour observation was too short to characterize elimination in everyone, which the paper states.
reporting_issues.locator: Table 3 legend and n columns; Results > Pharmacokinetics
reporting_issues.consequence: The concentration comparison and the effect comparison are not made in exactly the same people, and the half-life figures rest on a subset; the ratio columns (n=23) are the ones to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The peak subjective ratings against which acute tolerance is argued are already 83-87 out of 100, and the paper does not consider a ceiling on the scales as an alternative explanation for the unchanged peaks, although it names scale ceilings nowhere and applies the same reasoning to autonomic measures where no ceiling applies.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of acute tolerance should rest on the autonomic and duration data as much as on the subjective peaks, since a rating that is already near the top of its scale cannot rise further.

reporting_issues.issue: Most of the quantitative detail is in supplementary tables and figures that the main text only summarizes, including all autonomic values, the mood ratings, the hysteresis plot cited as evidence of acute tolerance, the complaint-symptom frequencies and the stratified analyses.
reporting_issues.locator: Results > Autonomic effects; Results > Acute subjective effects, last sentence; Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects
reporting_issues.consequence: Several statements in this card can be anchored only to the main text's wording, not to numbers; a second reader with the supplement should check the autonomic and hysteresis claims.

reporting_issues.issue: The two participants who dropped out, both of whom had the booster, are excluded from the within-person adverse-effect comparison, which then shows no significant difference between booster and single dose.
reporting_issues.locator: Results > Acute and subacute adverse effects, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
reporting_issues.consequence: The tolerability comparison is made among those who completed all three sessions; the two worst reactions, both in the booster condition, are reported separately and in words. The finding of no added harm from the booster should always be reported with those two cases.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the area under the effect curve for 'talkative' in the single-dose condition is 3.5 (SD 110), close to the placebo value of 4.7 (SD 22), although the same condition's peak rating is 23 (SD 19).
reporting_issues.consequence: The bidirectional scales subtract the area below baseline from the area above, so a large negative phase can cancel the peak; these area values are not comparable with the unidirectional ones and should not be quoted as a measure of effect size.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC13451183 (Translational Psychiatry 2026;16:402), read in the browser pane; Tables 1-3 render as text and were read in full, Figures 1-2 are images and no values were taken from them. The supplementary PDF was not read, and every statement that depends on it is marked in the card.

design_detail: Single-author narrative review of chronic tolerance to recreational MDMA, covering subjective reports of declining effect, dose escalation across groups of people with different amounts of past use, binge patterns (stacking and boosting), and candidate mechanisms (liver enzymes, neuroadaptation, behavioural tolerance and serotonergic neurotoxicity). No search strategy, databases, dates, selection criteria or appraisal of the cited studies are reported. The review states at the outset that no laboratory study has given a series of MDMA doses to humans, for ethical reasons, so that chronic tolerance cannot be studied in humans under blind, placebo-controlled conditions, and that the human evidence therefore comes from surveys and interviews of people who use ecstasy recreationally.
can_establish: What the survey and interview literature up to 2004 reported about declining subjective efficacy, dose escalation and bingeing among people who use ecstasy, and what mechanisms had been proposed; it is a map of that literature and of its gaps.
cannot_establish: Whether tolerance to MDMA develops, how fast, to which effects, or by what mechanism: every human figure in the review is self-reported by people who used tablets of unknown content, in cross-sectional comparisons of groups with different amounts of past use, with no measurement of dose, no blinding and no prospective follow-up. It also cannot separate tolerance from the other reasons people take more tablets (tablet strength, setting, polydrug use, expectation).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable: a review. The human studies it summarizes are surveys and interview studies of people who use ecstasy recreationally, recruited through clubs, universities, the internet and a dance magazine's readership, with samples from 52 to about 1151 people.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: No inclusion or exclusion criteria are stated; studies appear to have been chosen by the author's knowledge of the field.
sample.demographics: Not applicable; the samples summarized are mostly young adults with roughly equal numbers of men and women, in Australia, the United Kingdom, the United States and continental Europe.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The review's own selection is unsystematic, and about half of the empirical comparisons it rests on come from the author's own research group (Parrott and Lasky 1998; Parrott et al. 2000, 2001, 2002a, 2002b; Fox et al. 2001a, 2001b, 2002; Scholey et al. 2004, whose first author lists the reviewer as second author). The underlying samples are self-selected people willing to report illegal drug use, with the heaviest use reported by those recruited at clubs and raves.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported numbers of tablets, in lifetime occasions, tablets per occasion and maximum tablets per occasion or per week; no biological verification anywhere, and no measurement of the MDMA content of the tablets taken.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported as study conditions of the surveys summarized: typically one tablet or half a tablet on a first occasion, 1.2-2.0 tablets per occasion for regular use, 3.1-3.7 for the most experienced groups, with maxima of 5 to more than 20 tablets in a session in survey subgroups and 20-40 tablets a weekend in three case histories. Most use is oral; the review notes that about 30% of one Australian sample had snorted MDMA and about 16% had injected it.
exposure.polysubstance: Addressed directly: people who use ecstasy are described as using several drugs, with heavier use linked to a wider range of other drugs; the review states that the contribution of polydrug use to tolerance is unclear and that stimulants might foster cross-tolerance. Tablet content is discussed at length, with the proportion containing MDMA rising to about 80-100% by the late 1990s and average content in United Kingdom forensic samples falling from about 102 mg in 1991 to 73 mg in 2001.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable to the dose-escalation data; some of the cognitive studies it cites tested people after a period of abstinence, which is not specified here.

comparison.controls: Within the studies summarized, comparisons are between groups of people with different amounts of past ecstasy use, and in a few studies against people who had never used it.
comparison.matching: Mostly none; the review singles out Verkes et al. (2001) for comparing moderate and heavy groups matched on duration of use and on cannabis, cocaine, amphetamine and alcohol use.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No study cited has a measurement before first use, so the characteristics that lead some people to escalate and others not are unmeasured; the review raises this as an open question.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Varies by study and is usually not controlled; the review treats polydrug use as a limitation it cannot resolve.

outcomes.instruments: Questionnaire and interview measures of self-reported tolerance, tablets per occasion, maximum tablets, bingeing (defined in one study as continuous use without sleep for 48 hours or more), and self-attributed problems; in the animal literature, serotonin syndrome scores, locomotor activity, operant test batteries, self-administration and post-mortem serotonergic markers.
outcomes.validity_norms: Self-report of illegal drug use without biological verification; tolerance is assessed by asking people whether they feel they have become tolerant, which mixes the pharmacological question with expectation and recall.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Chronic tolerance' is operationalized three ways: people saying effects have declined, people taking more tablets per occasion than less experienced people, and people reporting binge patterns. Only the first is a direct report of reduced effect.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: the review reports the primary studies' statistics (two chi-square tests for the internet-study tables and an analysis of variance for the three-group comparison) without reanalysis.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; none of the human data is blinded, and the review says plainly that blind, placebo-controlled study of chronic tolerance in humans has not been done.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates and no effect sizes. The figures carried forward are group means and percentages from individual surveys: 1.8 tablets per occasion now against 1.2 when starting (430 people using ecstasy regularly, Verheyden et al. 2003a); 1.45 against 1.80 tablets on a Saturday night in novice and regular groups of 15 each (Parrott and Lasky 1998); 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets per occasion and maxima of 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7) across groups defined by lifetime use of 1-99, 100-499 and 500 or more tablets (14, 14 and 11 people; p<0.01 for the maximum, p<0.10 for the usual dose); a normal dose of 1-2 tablets reported by 100% of 109 in the novice group, 84% of 136 in the moderate group and 62% of 37 in the heaviest group, and a maximum of 10 or more tablets in a week by 0%, 9% and 35% (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, p<0.001); 3.1 against 2.0 tablets per occasion in 21 heavy and 21 moderate club-goers; and 58% of 1151 dance-magazine readers reporting tolerance, with about 85-95% of 430 people using it regularly reporting declining effects.
analysis.covariates: None; the review does not reanalyse.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable to a narrative review; no protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The one study whose pattern runs against dose escalation (Fox et al. 2001b, where the longer-using group took slightly fewer tablets per occasion) is reported and discussed, which counts in the review's favour; but no systematic account is given of how many studies were considered and how many are cited, and two of the three mechanism sections rest on animal work selected without criteria.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across surveys, people who have used ecstasy more report taking more tablets per occasion and much larger maxima than people who have used it less, and a large majority of people using it regularly say the drug's wanted effects have declined with repeated use. Those same comparisons also show that problems attributed to ecstasy rise with lifetime use. All of this is self-reported and cross-sectional, and one study found no dose escalation with longer use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review concludes that chronic tolerance to ecstasy in humans is 'a robust empirical phenomenon', that it often develops rapidly, and that serotonergic neurotoxicity is a plausible and partly unique mechanism for it. The first clause goes beyond what cross-sectional self-report can show: people who escalate may differ from those who do not in ways measured nowhere, the tablets themselves vary in content, and the review itself states that the question cannot be studied in humans under controlled conditions. The neurotoxicity mechanism is argued from animal studies and from a correlation between reported use and reported problems, and the review is explicit that it is a hypothesis.

timeline.event: Two 100 mg doses 24 hours apart in a laboratory: the second dose produced slightly larger effects than the first but smaller than its higher plasma concentrations predicted, with pupil, Maddox-wing and prolactin responses unchanged
Fifty mg followed by 100 mg two hours later: blood pressure and temperature rose in line with concentration while heart rate and the wanted subjective effects did not
A 60 mg booster two hours after 120 mg prolonged effects by about an hour without raising peak effects, despite 1.5-fold higher peak concentrations

replication.where_it_stands: The within-session part of the question, which this review explicitly sets aside, has since been studied in controlled laboratory conditions by three groups; the chronic question it addresses is still answered only by surveys, and no prospective human study of repeated recreational use has been published that would settle it.

funding.funder: Not reported: the article carries no funding statement.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, University of Wales Swansea. A large share of the empirical comparisons the review relies on are the author's own studies, which the review does not flag.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study following people from their first occasions of ecstasy use, with repeated measurement of the dose actually taken (by tablet analysis or hair or plasma measurement), of the subjective response, and of the setting, so that a decline in effect can be separated from changes in tablet content, context and expectation; in the laboratory, a repeated-dosing design at intervals of days to weeks, which has not been done in humans.

domains.note: No databases, dates, search terms or selection criteria are reported; studies appear to have been chosen by the author's familiarity with the literature.

No formal appraisal. Survey percentages and group means are carried forward without discussion of response rates, recruitment or recall, and a case report of one person's use is quoted at length alongside survey data.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Most of the dose-escalation comparisons (Parrott and Lasky 1998; Fox et al. 2001a, 2001b; Parrott et al. 2000, 2001, 2002a, 2002b; Scholey et al. 2004) are the author's own work, and the review does not say so.

The neurotoxicity mechanism is repeatedly labelled as a hypothesis and the limitations section is candid about polydrug use and unknown tablet content; but the overview states that chronic tolerance is a robust empirical phenomenon without restating that every human datum is self-reported.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against tolerance to MDMA
domains.note: Alternative explanations for taking more tablets (falling tablet strength is examined and set aside; changing setting, expectation, polydrug use and self-selection are not) receive much less space than the tolerance account, and the animal studies that found sensitization rather than tolerance are given a paragraph against several pages for tolerance.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3), so the editors' checklist is used. The review is valuable as a map: it is explicit that controlled human study of chronic tolerance does not exist, it collects the survey figures in one place, and it reports the one study whose pattern runs the other way. Its selection is unsystematic, it leans heavily on the author's own studies without saying so, and the balance between the tolerance account and its alternatives is uneven. It should be cited for the existence and content of the survey literature, for the dose figures as reported by those surveys, and for the statement that no controlled human study of repeated MDMA dosing over days existed in 2005; claims about tolerance itself should cite the primary studies, and any claim resting only on this review stays at draft and says its figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3).

key_findings.finding: The review states that there are no laboratory studies giving a series of MDMA doses to humans, because of concerns about serotonergic neurotoxicity, and that it is therefore not possible to investigate chronic tolerance to MDMA in humans under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions; all human evidence in the review comes from studies of people who use ecstasy recreationally.
key_findings.locator: The paragraph beginning 'The pharmacodynamic effects of single doses of MDMA' and the one following it (left column)

key_findings.finding: Self-reported tolerance is common in surveys: 58% of 1151 readers of a dance magazine reported tolerance to ecstasy, and among 430 people who had been using it for about four years, around 85-95% reported a decline in subjective efficacy, described by the authors of that study as the most frequently reported long-term effect. An earlier survey found that 67% of people who had taken it on six or more occasions said positive effects decreased and negative effects increased with successive doses.
key_findings.locator: Subjective reports of tolerance and diminishing responsiveness to MDMA, 2nd-3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Reported dose rises with past use. In 430 people using ecstasy regularly, current use averaged 1.8 tablets a session against 1.2 when they began; across three groups defined by lifetime use (1-99, 100-499 and 500 or more tablets; 14, 14 and 11 people) the usual dose was 1.8 (SD 0.9), 2.2 (SD 1.1) and 3.7 (SD 3.8) tablets and the maximum ever taken 3.6 (SD 1.5), 5.1 (SD 2.0) and 10.9 (SD 8.7), with the maximum differing significantly (p<0.01) and the usual dose only at p<0.10.
key_findings.locator: Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 74); Table 1 (p. 74)
key_findings.note: The text gives the highest group's usual dose as 3.7 tablets and its maximum as 10.7, while Table 1 prints 3.7 (SD 3.8) and 10.9 (SD 8.7); the table values are used here.

key_findings.finding: In an internet study of 282 people, a normal dose of 1-2 tablets was reported by 100% of 109 in the novice group (1-9 lifetime occasions), 84% of 136 moderate (10-99) and 62% of 37 in the heaviest group (100 or more), while a maximum of 10 or more tablets in one week was reported by 0%, 9% and 35% of the three groups (chi-square 39.40 and 169.99, df 4, both p<0.001). In the same sample, self-attributed problems rose with lifetime use: depression 33%, 54% and 65%; memory problems 19%, 52% and 73%; weight loss 10%, 37% and 48%.

One study runs against the escalation pattern: two groups differing mainly in how long they had used ecstasy (3.9 against 10.9 years) and in lifetime consumption (223 against 811 tablets) reported similar doses per occasion, with the longer-using group taking slightly fewer (2.1 against 2.5 tablets, not significant). The review draws from this that long-term use is not invariably linked to dose escalation.
key_findings.locator: Dosage escalation in recreational Ecstasy users, last paragraph

key_findings.finding: Binge patterns are described from survey work: taking several tablets at once ('stacking') and repeated tablets over an evening or successive days ('boosting'), with 76% of people using more than weekly having binged at least once against 16% of those using less than monthly; by a stricter definition (continuous use without sleep for 48 hours or more) about a third of 329 people using ecstasy regularly had binged in the previous six months, and those who had reported more physical and psychological side-effects and more days of recent use.

The review reports that falling tablet strength does not explain rising tablet counts: in United Kingdom forensic samples the average MDMA content per tablet was about 102, 90, 103, 99, 100 and 88 mg from 1991 to 1996 and 75, 77, 82, 74 and 73 mg from 1997 to 2001, a fall of about 20% across the mid-1990s with stable values before and after, and two other national surveys found variation without a systematic trend.
key_findings.locator: The paragraph beginning 'A related problem is the issue of dosage' (right column)

key_findings.finding: On mechanisms, the review reports a specialist's view that MDMA's main metabolizing enzyme is not inducible and is largely inactivated by a single dose, so that any tolerance must be pharmacodynamic rather than pharmacokinetic, and that no repeated-dose study of liver enzymes had been done; the animal literature is mixed, with some studies showing tolerance to behavioural and serotonin-syndrome measures and two showing the opposite (sensitization).
key_findings.locator: Animal data on putative underlying mechanisms, 1st paragraph (p. 76) and the paragraphs on behavioural measures (pp. 76-77)
key_findings.note: The enzyme statement is a personal communication quoted in the review, not a published result.

key_findings.finding: The review proposes that serotonergic axon-terminal loss may itself cause the loss of effect, so that reduced efficacy, dose escalation and rising problems develop together, and states that this is an additional possible factor rather than an alternative to the usual mechanisms; it also notes that intermittent use in cool, quiet settings may limit how fast tolerance develops.
key_findings.locator: Serotonergic neurotoxicity and chronic tolerance to MDMA, last two paragraphs (p. 78); Overview, last paragraph (p. 80)

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the most experienced group's average maximum as 10.7 tablets per occasion while Table 1 on the same page prints 10.9 (SD 8.7); the usual dose is 3.7 in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small discrepancy in a figure that is quoted widely; the table value should be used.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports the lifetime-use groups as 'Low 1-99, Medium 100-499, High 500+' tablets with 14, 14 and 11 people and a two-tailed significance of p<0.10 for the usual dose, yet the running text describes the usual-dose difference without that qualification.
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose-per-occasion difference across lifetime-use groups in that study did not reach conventional significance; only the maximum did.

reporting_issues.issue: Tables 2 and 3 describe the same internet study and the same participants: Table 2 gives group sizes of 109, 136 and 37, which sum to the 282 people the text near Table 3 reports, and Table 3's legend states that it is the same study and participants as Table 2.
reporting_issues.consequence: Consistent, but the reader should note that the dose figures and the problem figures come from one sample, so the correlation between heavier use and more problems within that sample is not independent evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: A large share of the empirical comparisons are the author's own studies, and the review nowhere states this.
reporting_issues.consequence: The convergence of the cited findings is weaker than it appears, because the studies share investigators, recruitment routes and measures (METHODS 6.3, overlapping evidence).

reporting_issues.issue: A statement central to the mechanism argument, that MDMA's main metabolizing enzyme cannot be induced and is inactivated by a single dose, is sourced to a personal communication from 2002 and includes a dosing recommendation in the quoted text.
reporting_issues.consequence: An unpublished opinion is doing load-bearing work in the mechanism section; it cannot be checked, and the dosing sentence inside it must not be carried into the encyclopedia.

reporting_issues.issue: Case histories of three people using 20-40 tablets a weekend, including one injecting large amounts, are presented beside survey percentages without a change of register.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take extreme case reports as representative; they are selected cases from a clinic, and the review's own surveys put the common pattern at one to three tablets.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 71-83 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2005_ChronicToleranceReview.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3; reference list read for the authorship of the cited studies.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 10 men with recreational MDMA experience. Two sessions a week apart with a two-week washout: in one, placebo capsules at 9 a.m. and 100 mg MDMA two hours later; in the other, 50 mg MDMA at 9 a.m. and 100 mg MDMA two hours later. The comparison of interest is therefore the response to the same 100 mg dose with and without a 50 mg dose two hours earlier. All pharmacodynamic measures were expressed as change from the baseline before the first capsule, and both the peak effect and the area under the curve were taken over the window 2-6 hours, that is, after the 100 mg dose, with repeated-measures analyses of variance and post-hoc t tests at each time point. Plasma MDMA, MDA and the metabolites HMMA and HMA were measured to 50 hours, with compartmental modelling used to estimate the 50 mg dose's contribution to total exposure.
can_establish: Whether a 50 mg dose two hours earlier changes the plasma concentrations, metabolite pattern and acute response to a 100 mg dose of MDMA in the same men, at an interval the authors chose to resemble recreational redosing.
cannot_establish: What a second equal dose does (the two doses differed, 50 then 100 mg, so the design is not a repeat of the same dose); what happens after more than two doses or at larger doses; effects in women, who were not studied; and whether the smaller-than-expected responses are tolerance rather than ceiling effects, which the authors name as an alternative, or an artefact of the first dose's effects still being present when the second was given, which they also name.

sample.recruitment: Recruited from the surrounding community by word of mouth; the study was run at a hospital research institute in Barcelona (Materials and methods > Subjects, 1st paragraph, p. 884).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Recreational experience of ecstasy on 5-50 occasions without serious adverse reaction, no abuse or dependence on other substances by DSM-IV criteria other than nicotine; general medical examination, psychiatric interview, laboratory tests, urinalysis and electrocardiogram to exclude medical or psychiatric conditions; only people phenotyped as extensive metabolizers of the enzyme that clears MDMA were included. Two further men took part in a pilot condition (50 plus 75 mg) whose data are not shown (p. 884).
sample.demographics: Ten men, mean age 24.9 years (range 22-35), weight 70.7 kg (range 57.5-81.6), height 177.7 cm (range 171-190). All had used cannabis, 83.3% cocaine, 75% LSD, 25% other amphetamines and 50% other substances such as ketamine or GHB; all but two smoked (under 20 cigarettes a day); average alcohol intake 9.4 units a week (range 1-25) (p. 884).
sample.attrition: None reported: all ten completed both sessions and the paper states that no participant needed specific treatment or special care.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, young, healthy, experienced with MDMA and selected to be fast metabolizers of it; people who metabolize it slowly, the group in whom accumulation would be greatest, were excluded by design, and women were not studied. The percentages of previous drug use (83.3%, 75%) do not correspond to whole numbers out of ten (see reporting issues).

exposure.measurement: Drug given in the laboratory in identical opaque capsules and measured directly: plasma MDMA, MDA, HMMA and HMA by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry at 18 time points from baseline to 50 hours after the first capsule (p. 886).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral racemic MDMA supplied by the Spanish Ministry of Health in 50 mg capsules. Session A: two placebo capsules at 9 a.m., then 100 mg (two active capsules) at 11 a.m. Session B: 50 mg (one active and one placebo capsule) at 9 a.m., then 100 mg at 11 a.m. (pp. 884-885).
exposure.polysubstance: Participants were asked to avoid psychoactive drugs for at least three days before and throughout the study and caffeine or alcohol for 48 hours before each session, with a urine screen for opiates, cocaine metabolite, amphetamines and cannabinoids on arrival; smoking was allowed only from 6 p.m. (pp. 884-885).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Overnight fast and a drug-free urine screen before each session; sessions once a week with a two-week washout between them. In the repeated-dose session, MDMA from the 50 mg dose was still present when the 100 mg dose was given: peak 84.71 ng/mL and 79.92 ng/mL at the 2-hour point (p. 889).

comparison.controls: Within-person: the same men received 100 mg alone (after placebo) and 100 mg preceded by 50 mg. There is no placebo-only session, so the 2-6 hour effects are compared between two active conditions rather than against placebo.
comparison.matching: Within-person randomized, double-blind crossover with a two-week washout.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable: every comparison is within person.

outcomes.instruments: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate, oral temperature and pupil diameter; digit-symbol substitution, simple reaction time, the Pauli test and the Maddox-wing device; 21 visual analogue scales and the 49-item short-form Addiction Research Center Inventory with five subscales; plasma concentrations of MDMA and three metabolites. Pharmacodynamic measures were taken at 16-17 time points to 26 hours (pp. 885-886).
outcomes.validity_norms: The laboratory's standard battery, used in its earlier MDMA studies; subjective scales have no external norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Tolerance is operationalized informally as effects after the second dose that are lower than the plasma concentrations would predict; no concentration-effect model is fitted, and 'expected' is judged against dose proportionality.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at the family level: each variable was tested on peak, area under the curve and time course, with post-hoc t tests at each time point, at p<0.05 (p. 886).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind with identical capsules; blinding integrity was not assessed, and participants with MDMA experience are likely to have detected the 50 mg dose, since its effects were measurable before the second capsule.

analysis.effect_sizes: Means with standard deviations are printed for every outcome in Table 1 (n=10, change from baseline over 2-6 hours) and for pharmacokinetic parameters in Tables 2 and 3. Key contrasts, single 100 mg against 50+100 mg: systolic pressure peak 29.50 (SD 9.69) against 33.30 (SD 4.13) mm Hg, not significant, with the area under the curve 49.35 (SD 24.28) against 72.96 (SD 22.12), p=0.029; diastolic peak 11.85 (SD 13.83) against 18.90 (SD 12.33), not significant, area under the curve 18.81 against 46.82, p=0.015; heart-rate peak 33.50 (SD 11.87) against 33.05 (SD 13.25) and area under the curve 57.75 against 69.98, both not significant; temperature peak 0.20 against 0.56 degrees Celsius and area under the curve 0.50 against 1.61, both not significant; pupil diameter peak 3.39 against 3.74 mm, not significant, area under the curve 9.42 against 11.92, p=0.037. Pharmacokinetics: peak MDMA concentration 202.92 ng/mL (SD 30.30) against 311.16 (SD 66.48), p<0.001; exposure to 50 hours 2890.73 against 4426.60 microgram.h/L; half-life 10.41 h (SD 3.55) against 10.48 (SD 2.12); the 50 mg dose contributed 0.30 (SD 0.01) of total exposure and the 100 mg dose 0.67 (SD 0.13). Against dose proportionality, peak concentration was 12.8% and exposure 16.2% higher than expected, while the metabolite HMMA was 38.2% lower at peak and 29.8% lower in exposure.
analysis.covariates: None; all measures expressed as change from the pre-first-capsule baseline.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the protocol was approved by the local research ethics committee and authorized by the Spanish Ministry of Health (pp. 884-885).
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 shows only variables with a significant difference somewhere, so the wanted subjective effects (euphoria, liking, stimulation on the visual analogue scales) appear only as the statement that they did not differ; the pilot condition's data are not shown; figures carry no printed values.
analysis.power: No sample-size calculation. The authors state in their limitations that the sample size may limit the power to show differences, alongside ceiling effects on several scales.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Giving 50 mg two hours before a 100 mg dose raised peak MDMA concentration by about half (203 to 311 ng/mL) and exposure by about 50%, somewhat more than dose proportionality predicts (+12.8% peak, +16.2% exposure), while the metabolite HMMA fell well below proportionality, consistent with inhibition of MDMA's own metabolism. Blood pressure, temperature and pupil diameter were higher in the repeated-dose condition on the area under the curve or at scattered time points, whereas heart rate did not differ in peak or area under the curve, and none of the wanted subjective effects (euphoria, liking, stimulation) differed in peak or area; one perceptual scale was lower after the repeated dose.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion say that effects on heart rate and subjective variables were lower than expected given the concentrations achieved, 'suggesting a possible tolerance phenomenon', and that blood-pressure and temperature effects were in the expected range. The data support the contrast between measures that tracked concentration and measures that did not; 'lower than expected' remains a judgement against dose proportionality rather than against a fitted concentration-effect curve, and the authors list three alternatives themselves: scale ceilings, ceiling effects in pupil diameter and heart rate, and the fact that the second dose was given while the first dose's effects were still present.

timeline.event: The same group, two 100 mg doses 24 hours apart: exposure 77% higher after the second dose, with pupil, Maddox-wing, amphetamine-subscale and prolactin responses unchanged
The same group, two 100 mg doses 4 hours apart (Farre et al., 2015): peak concentrations roughly doubled while the two effect-time profiles were very similar
An independent group, 60 mg booster 2 hours after 120 mg: 1.5-fold higher peak concentration, effects about an hour longer, peak effects unchanged

replication.where_it_stands: The pattern of more-than-proportional concentrations with less-than-proportional effects after a second dose has now been seen at 2, 4 and 24 hours by this group and, with a booster design, by an independent Swiss group. The specific 50-then-100 mg comparison rests on this study alone.

funding.funder: Grants from the Generalitat de Catalunya (2001SGR00407, 2005SGR00032, 2009SGR718) and the Fondo de Investigacion Sanitaria (98/0181 and 01/1336) (p. 892).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: IMIM-Hospital del Mar and two Barcelona universities, the same group and partly the same authors as Farre et al. (2004); the two studies are not independent of each other.

what_would_settle_it: A repeated-dose study using the same dose twice at the intervals people actually redose, with a placebo-only session so that each dose can be compared with placebo, a fitted concentration-effect model for each measure, scales that do not reach ceiling, and both sexes, so that a shift of the concentration-response curve can be measured rather than inferred.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the two sessions)
domains.note: Described as randomized and crossover, but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described and no period effect is reported.
Two weeks between sessions, which is far longer than the drug's half-life of about 10 hours.

Double-blind in form, but in the repeated-dose session the 50 mg dose produced measurable effects and concentrations (84.71 ng/mL) before the second capsule, so experienced participants could tell the two sessions apart, and the main outcomes are self-rated.
All ten men completed both sessions, with no missing data reported.

Cardiovascular measures, temperature, pupil diameter and plasma concentrations are objective; the subjective scales that carry the tolerance interpretation are self-rated, and the authors report ceiling effects on several.

No protocol; about forty outcomes each tested three ways without correction; Table 1 lists only variables that reached significance somewhere, so the wanted subjective effects appear only as a null statement; and both tables and figures contain mislabelling (see reporting issues).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is a proper within-person double-blind crossover with objective pharmacokinetics, and the metabolic finding is clear and consistent with the group's earlier work. The overall judgment is set by the blinding, which cannot hold once the first dose is felt, and by reporting: the key subjective null results are not tabulated, the significance markers rest on many uncorrected tests, and at least three labels in the tables and figures are wrong. The source can be cited for the concentration and metabolite findings at a 2-hour interval, for blood pressure, temperature and pupil diameter rising with the added dose, and for heart rate and the wanted subjective effects not rising; it cannot be cited for the size of any tolerance, for equal repeated doses, or for women.

key_findings.finding: Adding 50 mg two hours before a 100 mg dose raised peak MDMA concentration from 202.92 ng/mL (SD 30.30) to 311.16 (SD 66.48), p<0.001, and exposure from 2 to 50 hours from 2890.73 to 4426.60 microgram.h/L, with no change in half-life (10.41 h, SD 3.55, against 10.48, SD 2.12), time to peak, volume of distribution or clearance.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, MDMA rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 889)

key_findings.finding: The rise was greater than dose proportionality predicts: peak concentration was 12.8% and exposure 16.2% above the expected values obtained by fitting the plasma concentrations to a one-compartment model, while the metabolite HMMA was 38.2% lower at peak and 29.8% lower in exposure than proportionality predicts, and all metabolic ratios fell significantly except MDA to MDMA.

Blood pressure was higher in the repeated-dose condition on the area under the curve but not at the peak: systolic peak 29.50 (SD 9.69) against 33.30 (SD 4.13) mm Hg, not significant, with the area under the curve 49.35 (SD 24.28) against 72.96 (SD 22.12), p=0.029; diastolic peak 11.85 (SD 13.83) against 18.90 (SD 12.33), not significant, area under the curve 18.81 (SD 21.09) against 46.82 (SD 27.82), p=0.015. Every one of the ten men reached blood pressure above 140/90 mm Hg.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, SBP and DBP rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st paragraph (p. 888)

key_findings.finding: Heart rate did not rise with the extra dose: peak 33.50 beats/min (SD 11.87) against 33.05 (SD 13.25) and area under the curve 57.75 (SD 30.11) against 69.98 (SD 40.02), neither significant, with differences only at two scattered time points (2.3 and 5 hours, p=0.004 for the time course).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, HR rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st paragraph (p. 888)

key_findings.finding: Temperature and pupil diameter rose modestly: peak temperature change 0.20 degrees Celsius (SD 0.52) against 0.56 (SD 0.44) and area under the curve 0.50 against 1.61, neither significant but with significant differences at 2.3, 2.6 and 3 hours; pupil diameter peak 3.39 mm (SD 0.58) against 3.74 (SD 0.87), not significant, area under the curve 9.42 (SD 1.83) against 11.92 (SD 3.33), p=0.037. No hyperthermia occurred.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, T and PD rows (p. 887); Results > Physiological measures, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 888)

key_findings.finding: None of the wanted subjective effects differed significantly in peak or area under the curve between the two conditions. The only subjective differences were on the euphoria subscale (one time point), the dysphoria subscale (area under the curve and one time point), the amphetamine-like subscale (one time point) and a perceptual scale for changes in colours, which was lower in the repeated-dose condition (area under the curve 18.90, SD 22.73, against 7.70, SD 12.13; p=0.042). The sedation and stimulant subscales did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, subjective rows (p. 887); Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (p. 888)

key_findings.finding: Psychomotor performance showed no difference in peak or area under the curve on any test; total reaction time was longer in the repeated-dose condition at one time point (peak increase 34.7 ms against 54.2 ms; difference at 3 hours, p=0.009).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, RT total rows (p. 887); Results > Psychomotor performance (p. 888)

key_findings.finding: The modelling attributes 0.30 (SD 0.01) of total MDMA exposure in the repeated-dose session to the 50 mg dose and 0.67 (SD 0.13) to the 100 mg dose; before the second capsule, the 50 mg dose had produced a peak of 84.71 ng/mL with 79.92 ng/mL still present at 2 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, contribution rows; Results > Pharmacokinetics, 1st paragraph (p. 889)

key_findings.finding: No serious adverse reactions, hyperthermia, moderate or severe hypertension, tachycardia, hallucinations or psychotic episodes occurred, and no participant required specific treatment.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the area under the curve from time 0 to the last measured concentration for the repeated-dose condition as 446.88 microgram.h/L, which is impossible beside that condition's own exposure from 2 to 50 hours (4426.60), its exposure to infinity (4781.13) and the same figure in Table 3 (4460.88, with the identical standard deviation of 958.90).
reporting_issues.consequence: A digit is lost in Table 2; Table 3's value of 4460.88 is the correct one, and anyone quoting Table 2 for this parameter would understate exposure tenfold.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 3 the rows labelled HMMA and HMA carry values that fit the opposite labels: HMMA is printed as 129.20 microgram.h/L and HMA as 2365.09, while Figure 2 shows the HMMA curve peaking near 160 ng/mL and the fourth panel near 5 ng/mL, and the text treats HMMA as the main metabolite of the inhibited enzyme pathway. The printed sums are consistent either way, since HMMA plus HMA is 2494.29 in both readings.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two metabolite rows appear to be transposed; a claim about either metabolite's absolute exposure should not be taken from Table 3 without the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: Both lower panels of Figure 2 are labelled HMMA, although the legend states that the panels show MDA, HMMA and HMA; the two panels differ by a factor of about thirty in scale.
reporting_issues.consequence: The fourth panel is HMA mislabelled; the mislabelling is what makes the transposition in Table 3 detectable.

reporting_issues.issue: The statistical-analysis section names the conditions as 'M100 or M150' and the post-hoc comparison as 'M100 vs. M50+150', although the abbreviation list and every table define the repeated condition as M50+100, a total of 150 mg.
reporting_issues.consequence: The labels in the methods do not match the conditions actually given; a reader could take M150 to be a single 150 mg dose.

reporting_issues.issue: The legend of Table 3 attributes its p values to analysis of variance, while the statistical-analysis section states that pharmacokinetic parameters and metabolic ratios were compared by paired t test (and time to peak by a rank test).
reporting_issues.consequence: The test behind the metabolite comparisons cannot be determined from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The sample is described as ten men, but the reported proportions of previous drug use are 83.3%, 75%, 25% and 50%, which correspond to fractions of twelve rather than ten (83.3% is 10 of 12).
reporting_issues.consequence: The drug-history percentages appear to include the two men from the pilot condition whose data are otherwise not shown; the proportions should not be read as applying to the ten analysed participants.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, the perceptual scale for changes in colours has a significant analysis-of-variance result for the time course (p=0.044) with the time-point entry printed as 'none'.
reporting_issues.consequence: A significant overall test with no significant time point; the finding should not be reported as a difference at any particular time.

reporting_issues.issue: There is no placebo-only session, so every effect reported in the 2-6 hour window is a comparison between two active conditions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study measures what the extra 50 mg adds, not what MDMA does against placebo; the absolute effect sizes in Table 1 are changes from a pre-drug baseline without a placebo correction for time of day, meals and fatigue.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 883-893 (PDFs/MDMA/Peiro_2012_RepeatedDoses2hApart.pdf), full text; Tables 1-3 were read in the extracted text and checked cell by cell against rendered images of pages 887, 889 and 890, and Figure 2's panel labels were checked on the rendered page 890.

design_detail: Prospective cohort within the Netherlands XTC Toxicity (NeXT) study (Brain 2008;131:2936-2945). 188 people who had never used ecstasy but were judged likely to start were imaged at baseline between 2002 and 2004, then followed with questionnaires. After a mean of about 17 months, imaging was repeated in 59 people who had begun using ecstasy and in 56 matched people who had not. Four imaging measures were compared: [123I]beta-CIT SPECT for serotonin transporter binding, proton MR spectroscopy for brain metabolites, diffusion tensor imaging for fractional anisotropy and apparent diffusion coefficient, and perfusion-weighted imaging for relative cerebral blood volume. Follow-up values were compared by linear regression adjusted for the baseline value, then for sex, baseline verbal IQ and follow-up age, education, alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine and tobacco.
can_establish: That in people who had used on average 6 tablets (median 2) and were scanned a mean of about 19 weeks after their last tablet, serotonin transporter binding and brain metabolites did not change relative to people who did not start, while small differences appeared in diffusion measures in the thalamus and frontoparietal white matter and in blood volume in globus pallidus and putamen; and that the two groups did not differ on any imaging measure before anyone had used ecstasy.
cannot_establish: That heavier use leaves transporter binding unchanged (the doses here are very low and the tracer is insensitive, as the authors say); that the diffusion and perfusion differences are damage, are lasting, or are caused by MDMA rather than by the other drugs that rose more in this group; or that the absence of a transporter difference excludes a smaller one (no equivalence margin, intervals span the measured range).

sample.recruitment: Targeted site sampling, advertisement and snowball sampling in the Netherlands, 2002-2004, of people aged 18-35 who had never used ecstasy but intended to or had friends who used it (p. 2937).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: under 18 or over 35, past ecstasy use, severe physical or mental illness, psychotropic medication, pregnancy, intravenous drug use. Abstinence from psychoactive substances for at least 2 weeks and alcohol for 1 week before each session, checked by urine screen; nobody was excluded for a positive screen (p. 2937).
sample.demographics: At baseline 77 men and 111 women, mean age 21.7 (SD 3.0). At follow-up: 25 men and 34 women in the group that had started, 23 men and 33 women in the group that had not; age 23.0 and 23.1; Dutch adult reading test IQ 103.5 and 105.3 (Table 1, p. 2940).
sample.attrition: Of 188 at baseline, 158 (84%) returned follow-up drug questionnaires; 64 had started using ecstasy and 59 of these (92%) were re-imaged; 56 of the 94 who had not started were selected as matched comparisons. Not every person has complete data for every imaging method (Ns per method in Table 2, p. 2941).
sample.selection_effects: The cohort is self-selected by intention to start using ecstasy, so both groups are at higher risk than the general population; the comparison group was selected from the non-starters to match on sex, verbal IQ and cannabis use, which is a matched rather than random comparison; 30 people were lost before the follow-up questionnaires.

exposure.measurement: Validated Dutch drug-use questionnaires at baseline and follow-up, with four postal questionnaires in between; urine enzyme immunoassay for amphetamines, MDMA, opioids, cocaine, benzodiazepines, cannabis and alcohol before each session (pp. 2937-2938).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Cumulative use between baseline and follow-up: mean 6.0 tablets (SD 11.6), median 2, range given as 0.5-80 in the Results and 1-80 in the Discussion; 54% had taken one tablet or less and 17% ten or more; duration of use 20.4 (23.8) weeks; time since first tablet 39.2 (23.4) weeks (Table 1, p. 2940; Results, p. 2939; Discussion, p. 2943).
exposure.polysubstance: Between baseline and follow-up the group that started also increased alcohol (p=0.036), cannabis (p=0.029), amphetamine (p=0.047) and cocaine (p=0.017) relative to the comparison group; all effects of ecstasy remained significant after adjustment for these (Table 1, p. 2940; Results, p. 2939).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks from psychoactive substances, verified by urine screen; mean time since last tablet 18.7 weeks (SD 17.5) (Table 1, p. 2940).

comparison.controls: 56 people from the same baseline cohort who did not start using ecstasy, individually matched on sex, age, verbal intelligence and cannabis use (p. 2937).
comparison.matching: Individual matching on sex, verbal IQ and cannabis use; the interval between sessions was shorter in the group that started (15.9 vs 18.3 months, p=0.024).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Almost none: this is the one design among the imaging studies with a pre-use measurement, and the groups did not differ on any imaging parameter, substance use or transporter genotype at baseline.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparison group also used alcohol, tobacco, cannabis and occasionally cocaine; their use rose less over follow-up (Table 1, p. 2940).

outcomes.instruments: [123I]beta-CIT SPECT 4 h after injection, specific-to-non-specific binding ratios in midbrain, thalamus and frontal, occipital and temporal grey matter, cerebellum as reference, with region-of-interest and voxel-by-voxel analyses; 1H-MRS (NAA/Cr, Cho/Cr, mI/Cr) in mid-frontal and mid-occipital grey matter and left frontoparietal white matter; diffusion tensor imaging (fractional anisotropy, apparent diffusion coefficient) in thalamus, putamen, globus pallidus, caudate and frontoparietal white matter; perfusion-weighted imaging (relative cerebral blood volume) in those regions plus four cortical regions (pp. 2938-2939).
outcomes.validity_norms: The SPECT tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and, as the authors note, animal work shows it underestimates MDMA-induced transporter loss; the striatal regions were not analysed because binding there is not serotonergic at 4 h. No normative values for any measure.
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity is operationalized as a change over follow-up in any of the four imaging measures relative to the comparison group.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, deliberately: the authors state that they had a priori hypotheses and did not correct, to limit false negatives, while acknowledging the risk of false positives (p. 2943).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; image processing was largely automated (spatial normalization, segmentation, template regions).

analysis.effect_sizes: Serotonin transporter binding, regression coefficients for the group that started versus the comparison group, adjusted for baseline (Table 2, p. 2941): midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal grey matter -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed); none significant, and the voxel-by-voxel analysis also found nothing. Brain metabolites: all nine comparisons non-significant. Significant differences: fractional anisotropy in thalamus -8.16 (-15.30 to -1.02) and frontoparietal white matter -8.23 (-14.35 to -2.10), both x1000; fractional anisotropy in globus pallidus +23.19 (3.65 to 42.73); apparent diffusion coefficient in thalamus +3.68 (0.67 to 6.69) x10-5 mm2/s; relative cerebral blood volume in globus pallidus -0.083 (-0.154 to -0.012) and putamen -0.058 (-0.110 to -0.006). Percentage changes were under 5%. No dose-response relation with cumulative tablets within the group that started.
analysis.covariates: Model 1 adjusted for the baseline value; model 2 added sex, baseline verbal IQ, follow-up age, years of education and use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine and tobacco; all significant effects persisted (p. 2939).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A design paper for the NeXT study was published in 2005 (de Win et al., Int J Methods Psychiatr Res 14:167-185) and is cited for methods, but no trial-registry record or pre-specified analysis plan is cited; the design paper was not read here.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 32 region-by-measure comparisons are tabulated with intervals, including the many null results.
analysis.power: Not formally calculated; the authors state that power may have been insufficient for SPECT and spectroscopy given the very low doses, and that the SPECT tracer may be too insensitive (p. 2943).

interpretation_gap.results_show: After people had taken a median of 2 ecstasy tablets, serotonin transporter binding and brain metabolites were unchanged relative to matched people who did not start, while four small differences appeared in diffusion and perfusion measures, each under 5% and within the normal range for the age group, with no relation to the number of tablets taken.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title speaks of 'sustained effects of ecstasy on the human brain' and the abstract concludes that the findings suggest effects on brain microvasculature, white-matter maturation and possibly axonal damage, and that neurotoxicity of even low doses cannot be excluded (abstract, p. 2936). The Discussion concedes that the study offers no undisputable evidence of causality, that no dose-response was found, that confounding by other substances cannot be fully excluded, that no correction for multiple comparisons was applied, and that the changes may be reversible adaptations (pp. 2943-2944). The headline claim therefore rests on 6 of 32 comparisons, uncorrected, in the absence of the transporter change the study was designed to detect.

timeline.event: Cognitive results from the same cohort: a smaller gain in verbal memory in those who had started using ecstasy
Companion paper from the same cohort on the thalamus (de Win et al., Br J Psychiatry 193:289-296); not read here.
Cross-sectional PET in people with heavier use finds cortical and hippocampal reductions
Review places this null result beside the dose-related reductions found in heavier use

replication.where_it_stands: No second prospective imaging cohort of people starting to use ecstasy has been published; this remains the only study with pre-use brain measurements, and its transporter null is routinely read as showing that very low doses do not produce a detectable transporter change rather than that no change occurs.

funding.funder: Netherlands Organization for Health Research and Development (ZonMw 310-00-036); a BSIK grant from the Dutch Ministry of Education, Culture and Science for one author's informatics work (Funding, p. 2944).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (searched in the text extraction of all pages).
funding.affiliations_note: Academic Medical Center Amsterdam and Utrecht; the same group published the Lancet SPECT study of 2001 (Reneman et al.), whose authors are co-authors here.

what_would_settle_it: The same prospective design with a selective PET tracer rather than [123I]beta-CIT, in people who go on to heavier use, with repeated scanning over years and pre-specified outcomes, so that a transporter change and its reversal could be observed in the same people.
