domains.note: Baseline imaging, substance use and genotype did not differ, which removes most premorbid confounding; but use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamine and cocaine rose more in the group that started, and the adjustment for these is by self-report.
Self-reported tablets with urine screens at sessions only; tablet content unverified, though the authors cite national monitoring that over 95% of Dutch tablets contained MDMA.

People selected for intending to start using ecstasy; 30 of 188 lost before follow-up questionnaires and 5 of 64 starters not re-imaged; the comparison group was selected by matching from the non-starters.
None.
Complete data were not available for every method in every person (for example SPECT in 53 and 57 of the two groups), and the reasons are described only as technical problems or refusal.

The SPECT tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and is described by the authors as probably too insensitive for small changes; the diffusion and perfusion measures are non-specific; no blinding of processing is reported.
All comparisons are tabulated, which is good practice, but 32 tests were run without correction and the title and abstract are built on the 6 that reached p<0.05.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The design is the strongest available for this question, and the pre-use equivalence of the groups is a real strength; the weaknesses are the insensitive transporter tracer, very low doses, uncorrected multiplicity and a headline built on small differences in non-specific measures. It can be cited for the absence of a detectable transporter change after a median of 2 tablets and for the baseline equivalence of the groups, not for the presence of neurotoxicity.

key_findings.finding: Serotonin transporter binding did not differ at follow-up in any region: midbrain 0.036 (95% CI -0.068 to 0.140), thalamus -0.001 (-0.077 to 0.076), frontal -0.003 (-0.036 to 0.31 as printed), occipital -0.018 (-0.051 to 0.015), temporal -0.009 (-0.053 to 0.35 as printed); the voxel-by-voxel analysis also showed no effect.
key_findings.note: The upper limits for frontal (0.31) and temporal grey matter (0.35) are printed as such in Table 2 and checked on the rendered page; given the coefficients and lower limits they are almost certainly misprints for 0.031 and 0.035 (see reporting issues). The occipital and frontal binding ratios are close to zero in both groups (0.03 to 0.06), so percentage differences computed from them, as later reviews do, are not meaningful.

key_findings.finding: Brain metabolite ratios (NAA/Cr, Cho/Cr, mI/Cr in three voxels) showed no effect of starting to use ecstasy.

Fractional anisotropy fell in the thalamus (-8.16, 95% CI -15.30 to -1.02, x1000) and frontoparietal white matter (-8.23, -14.35 to -2.10) and rose in the globus pallidus (+23.19, 3.65 to 42.73); the apparent diffusion coefficient rose in the thalamus (+3.68, 0.67 to 6.69); relative cerebral blood volume fell in the globus pallidus (-0.083, -0.154 to -0.012) and putamen (-0.058, -0.110 to -0.006).
key_findings.note: All changes were under 5% and, as the paper says, within the normal range of the age group; part of each difference comes from an increase in the comparison group over follow-up.

key_findings.finding: The two groups did not differ on any imaging parameter, on substance use or on serotonin-transporter genotype at baseline, before anyone had used ecstasy.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Characteristics of the sample and substance use' (p. 2939); Table 2, baseline columns (p. 2941)

key_findings.finding: Cumulative use was a mean of 6.0 tablets (SD 11.6), median 2; 54% had taken one tablet or less and 17% ten or more; mean time since the last tablet was 18.7 weeks (SD 17.5).
Within the group that started, there was no relation between cumulative tablets and any follow-up imaging measure.
All significant effects persisted after adjustment for sex, baseline verbal IQ, age, education and use of alcohol, cannabis, amphetamines, cocaine and tobacco.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction says the 59 people who started were compared with 58 people who remained ecstasy-naive, while the abstract, Methods and Table 1 give 56.
reporting_issues.consequence: Internal inconsistency in the sample size of the comparison group; the tabulated analyses use 56 (and fewer for individual imaging methods).

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the upper confidence limits for transporter binding in frontal grey matter (0.31) and temporal grey matter (0.35) are printed with one digit too few for their own rows: the coefficients are -0.003 and -0.009 with lower limits -0.036 and -0.053, and every other interval in the table is symmetrical about its coefficient.
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as printed, the frontal interval would span -0.036 to 0.31 on a measure whose group means are 0.00 and 0.01, which is not credible; the intended values are almost certainly 0.031 and 0.035. Checked on the rendered page, where the figures read 0.31 and 0.35. Anyone quoting these intervals should say which reading they use.

reporting_issues.issue: The cumulative dose range is given as 0.5-80 tablets in the Results and as 1-80 in the Discussion.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the median of 2 tablets is the figure that matters for interpretation.

reporting_issues.issue: No correction for multiple comparisons was applied to 32 region-by-measure tests, by explicit choice.
reporting_issues.consequence: With 32 tests, one or two results at p<0.05 would be expected by chance; six were found, four of them in the same two measures, so the pattern is not purely chance, but individual findings (for example the increase in pallidal anisotropy) are fragile.

reporting_issues.issue: The interval between the two sessions was shorter in the group that started than in the comparison group (15.9 vs 18.3 months, p=0.024), and several of the significant differences arise partly from increases in the comparison group over that interval.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper itself reads the white-matter difference as failure of normal maturation in the group that started; a difference in follow-up time between groups works in the same direction and is not adjusted for.

reporting_issues.issue: The title and abstract present 'sustained effects on the human brain' and possible axonal damage although the study's primary serotonergic measures were null and no dose-response was found.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusion that is most often quoted from this paper is weaker than it appears; the Discussion's own caveats are not carried into the abstract.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 2936-2945 (all pages; Table 2 checked on the rendered page 2941)

design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (Archives of General Psychiatry 2011;68:562-576) in Copenhagen comparing serotonin transporter binding ([11C]DASB, non-displaceable binding potential) and 5-HT2A receptor binding ([18F]altanserin, binding potential of specific binding) in 24 people who used MDMA and/or hallucinogens and 21 people who did not. The drug group was split by the ratio of lifetime exposures into 14 whose use was mainly MDMA and 10 whose use was mainly hallucinogens. Regions were drawn automatically on each person's MRI; the primary outcome was a volume-weighted neocortical average, with pallidostriatum, midbrain, amygdala and thalamus for the transporter. Dose-response and abstinence were examined within the drug group by regression on the logarithm of lifetime exposures and of days since last use, including a log-logistic model.
can_establish: That transporter binding was markedly lower in the group whose use was mainly MDMA than in both the hallucinogen-preferring group and the comparison group, that it was not lower in the hallucinogen-preferring group, that binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime MDMA tablets in every region except the midbrain, and that binding was higher in people whose last MDMA use was longer ago in subcortical regions but not in neocortex.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the reduction (cross-sectional, self-selected groups); that the subcortical relation with time since last use is recovery within a person (it compares different people, as the paper says); that the neocortex does not recover (a null in a noisy, low-binding region); or that the small cortical 5-HT2A difference is real, since it disappeared when two control outliers were removed.

sample.recruitment: Fliers, advertisements on relevant websites and word of mouth from other participants; face-to-face screening with drug-use questionnaires and the SCAN 2.1 psychiatric interview (pp. 562-563).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18-35, at least 12 lifetime exposures to MDMA or hallucinogens and use within the year before the scan; no drug use for 7 days before the scan. Comparison group excluded for more than 15 lifetime cannabis exposures or any other illicit drug use. Excluded for neurological or psychiatric disorders and any previous antidepressant or antipsychotic use (p. 563).
sample.demographics: Drug group 21 men and 3 women, mean age 24.6 (SD 4.0); comparison group 17 men and 4 women, 24.0 (3.4). The MDMA-preferring group had less education (p=0.04 across the three groups), started smoking earlier and smoked more (4.3 pack-years vs 1.0 in both other groups, p=0.02) (Table 1, p. 564; Table 3, p. 567).
sample.attrition: Altanserin data could not be quantified in 3 drug-group participants and 1 control because of a technical failure in blood metabolite analysis, leaving 21 and 20 for the receptor analysis (p. 564).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers recruited through drug-related websites and word of mouth; group membership is defined after the fact by the ratio of MDMA to hallucinogen exposures, so the 'hallucinogen-preferring' group is also a group with lighter MDMA use (median 24 lifetime tablets) rather than an MDMA-naive group.

exposure.measurement: Copenhagen Substance Screening Questionnaire and modified Danish versions of the Customary Drinking and Drug Use Record and Lifetime Drinking History; urine screens every 2-3 days for the 7 days before scanning; gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of a 3.5-cm scalp hair segment covering about 3 months (pp. 563-564).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: MDMA-preferring group: median 635 calculated lifetime tablets (mean 1296, SD 1801, range 33-6590), 236 lifetime sessions, 3.3 use days a month, 4.3 tablets in a typical session, 268 mg of powder in a typical session, regular use for 72 months. Hallucinogen-preferring group: median 24 lifetime tablets (mean 60, range 6-362), 18 sessions, 0.3 use days a month, 1.8 tablets per session. Powder was converted to tablets by dividing milligrams by 60, the average Danish tablet content at the time (Table 1, p. 564; p. 563).
exposure.polysubstance: All 24 in the drug group had used cannabis; the MDMA-preferring group had used amphetamine and cocaine more recently and more often in the past 3 months (p=0.02 to 0.04); 9 of 14 had used GHB and 8 of 14 ketamine. Methamphetamine was not found in hair and is described as almost absent from the Danish market; cocaine is associated with higher, not lower, transporter binding (Table 1, p. 564; p. 573).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 7 days with negative urine screens; actual time since last MDMA, median 44 days in the MDMA-preferring group (mean 57, SD 62, range 11-258) and 96 days in the hallucinogen-preferring group (mean 122, range 30-293) (Table 1, p. 564).

comparison.controls: 21 people of similar age and sex with at most 15 lifetime cannabis exposures and no other illicit drug use (p. 563).
comparison.matching: Age- and sex-matched by design; not matched on education or smoking, which differed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measurement; the paper considers and rejects a premorbid difference as less likely on the strength of animal experiments and the dose-response relation (p. 573), which is an argument, not a measurement.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Up to 15 lifetime cannabis exposures; no other illicit drugs; 4 of 21 were current smokers.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB PET (90-min dynamic scan, multilinear reference tissue model MRTM2, cerebellum as reference) for the transporter; [18F]altanserin PET under steady-state conditions with arterial plasma for the 5-HT2A receptor; 3-T MRI for automatic region definition and grey-matter segmentation (pp. 564-565).
outcomes.validity_norms: [11C]DASB is selective for the serotonin transporter; the authors report published test-retest reliability for cortical regions (intraclass correlations 0.55-0.85) and note that cortical binding is low and noisy (p. 572). No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: Serotonergic status is operationalized as regional binding potential; 'recovery' as a positive regression coefficient of binding on the logarithm of days since last MDMA use, across people.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Tukey correction for the three-group comparisons of the five transporter regions; the dose-response and abstinence regressions are reported uncorrected (pp. 565-566).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; region definition was automatic and model-based (p. 565).

analysis.effect_sizes: Group differences in transporter binding: pallidostriatum F=7.89, p=0.001; neocortex F=23.05, p<0.001; amygdala F=16.58, p<0.001; thalamus F=2.6, p=0.08; midbrain not significant. The MDMA-preferring group was lower than the comparison group by 19% in pallidostriatum, 32% in amygdala and 56% in neocortex (regionally 40% orbitofrontal to 73% occipital), with differences in binding-potential units of 0.30 (95% CI 0.09-0.50) in pallidostriatum, 0.15 (0.09-0.20) in neocortex and 0.49 (0.28-0.71) in amygdala; the hallucinogen-preferring group did not differ from controls. Dose-response within the drug group: a doubling of lifetime tablets corresponded to a fall in binding of 0.021 in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), 0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), 0.067 in thalamus (p=0.006) and 0.075 in amygdala (p<0.001); no relation in midbrain. Abstinence: a doubling of days since last MDMA corresponded to higher binding of 0.14 in pallidostriatum (0.05-0.23, p=0.004), 0.12 in amygdala (0.04-0.21, p=0.008) and 0.11 in thalamus (0.002-0.22, p=0.046), with no relation in neocortex (0.005, -0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67); with adjustment for lifetime tablets the pallidostriatal (0.11, 0.02-0.19, p=0.02), amygdala (0.07, 0.01-0.14, p=0.02) and midbrain (0.10, 0.01-0.19, p=0.02) relations held and the thalamic one did not (p=0.17). From the log-logistic model, pallidostriatal binding in a person with the median lifetime use would reach the control average after an estimated 212 days (lower 95% limit 91 days; upper limit beyond a human lifespan). 5-HT2A receptor binding in the combined drug group was 9% lower in neocortex than in controls (medians 1.51 vs 1.66, Mann-Whitney p=0.03), but p=0.10 after excluding two controls with very high values, and the three-group comparison was not significant (p=0.07).
analysis.covariates: Age, body mass index, daylight minutes on the scan day, education and recent use of amphetamine, cocaine and cannabis were each tested as covariates; none was significant and none changed the group effects materially (p. 566).
analysis.selective_reporting: All five transporter regions and the receptor analyses are reported, including the null results in midbrain and in the hallucinogen-preferring group, and the sensitivity analysis that weakens the receptor finding.
analysis.power: Not reported. The groups are small (14, 10 and 21), and the paper notes that the cortical receptor reduction was modest and might be a power problem.

interpretation_gap.results_show: People whose drug use was mainly MDMA had markedly lower transporter binding than people who used mainly hallucinogens and than people who used neither, with a graded relation to lifetime tablets, and higher binding in those whose last use was longer ago in subcortical regions but not in neocortex; cortical 5-HT2A binding was slightly lower in the drug groups, a difference that did not survive the removal of two control outliers.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that MDMA but not hallucinogen use 'is associated with changes in the cerebral presynaptic serotonergic transmitter system', that the association is mediated by a direct presynaptic effect rather than by 5-HT2A agonism, and that the data suggest that subcortical, but not cortical, binding might recover after several months of abstinence (abstract, p. 562). The wording is careful: the paper explicitly declines to use the word neurotoxicity for its own data (p. 571) and states that the recovery calculation rests on comparisons between people rather than within them (p. 570). The mechanistic conclusion nonetheless rests on a comparison of two self-selected groups that also differ in amount and recency of every drug they used.

timeline.event: First [11C]DASB study, with the same cortical pattern but no subcortical reduction
Largest [11C]DASB study, cortical and hippocampal reductions with normal striatum
Independent study with arterial input: cortical reductions, no subcortical change, no relation with abstinence
No difference in men abstinent for at least a year
Review treats the subcortical relation with abstinence as part of the evidence that binding recovers over 40 to 200 days

replication.where_it_stands: The cortical reduction and the dose relation agree with the other [11C]DASB studies; this study is the only one of them to find a subcortical (pallidostriatal and amygdala) reduction, and the only one to find a positive relation between binding and time since last use, which the New York study with the same tracer did not.

funding.funder: Rigshospitalet, the Lundbeck Foundation, the Danish Medical Research Council, the H:S Research Council, the Sawmill owner Jeppe Juhl and Wife Ovita Juhls Foundation, and the John and Birthe Meyer Foundation (p. 574).
funding.declared_conflicts: Financial disclosure: none reported (p. 574).
funding.affiliations_note: Neurobiology Research Unit, Copenhagen University Hospital Rigshospitalet; hair analyses by the Section of Forensic Chemistry, University of Copenhagen.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated scanning of the same people over a year or more of abstinence, with exposure verified in hair at each point, and a comparison group of people who use other drugs but not MDMA; that design would turn the between-person dose and abstinence relations into within-person change.

domains.note: The MDMA-preferring group smoked more, had less education and had used amphetamine and cocaine more recently; covariates were tested one at a time in small groups rather than adjusted jointly.

Hair analysis confirmed recent MDMA in 13 of 14 in the MDMA-preferring group and urine confirmed short-term abstinence, but lifetime tablet counts are self-reported, powder was converted to tablets by an average content, and the counts span two orders of magnitude.
Small self-selected groups defined after the fact by the ratio of their exposures; no pre-use measurement.
None.
Receptor data missing for 4 of 45 because of a technical failure; transporter data complete.
Selective tracers and model-based quantification, but cortical transporter binding is low and noisy, and the receptor outcome is sensitive to two outlying control values.
Regional comparisons Tukey-corrected, null results and the fragile receptor finding reported in full.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A carefully analysed cross-sectional study whose main threats are its small, self-selected groups and their differences in other drug use; it can be cited for the group difference, for the graded relation to lifetime use, and for a between-person relation between binding and time since last use in subcortical regions, not for causation, for recovery within a person, or for the cortical 5-HT2A difference.

key_findings.finding: Transporter binding differed between the three groups in pallidostriatum (F=7.89, p=0.001), neocortex (F=23.05, p<0.001) and amygdala (F=16.58, p<0.001), with the thalamus borderline (F=2.6, p=0.08) and the midbrain unchanged.

Compared with the group that used neither drug, the MDMA-preferring group had binding lower by 19% in pallidostriatum, 32% in amygdala and 56% in neocortex (40% orbitofrontal, 47% parietal, 48% superior temporal, 51% medial inferior temporal, 53% medial inferior frontal, 61% superior frontal, 66% sensory-motor, 73% occipital); the hallucinogen-preferring group did not differ from controls in any region.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'SERT binding', 1st paragraph (continued p. 567); Figures 1 and 2
key_findings.note: The hallucinogen-preferring group had nonetheless used MDMA (median 24 lifetime tablets), so it is also a light-use group, as the paper notes (p. 571).

key_findings.finding: Binding fell with the logarithm of lifetime MDMA tablets in every region but the midbrain: a doubling of tablets corresponded to a fall of 0.021 binding-potential units in neocortex (95% CI -0.029 to -0.014, p<0.001), 0.062 in pallidostriatum (-0.103 to -0.021, p=0.005), 0.067 in thalamus (p=0.006) and 0.075 in amygdala (p<0.001).
key_findings.note: The printed intervals for thalamus (-0.113 to 0.022) and amygdala (-0.106 to 0.045) have positive upper limits that contradict their p-values; the minus signs appear to be missing (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Binding was higher in people whose last MDMA use was longer ago, in pallidostriatum (0.14 per doubling of days, 95% CI 0.05-0.23, p=0.004), amygdala (0.12, 0.04-0.21, p=0.008) and thalamus (0.11, 0.002-0.22, p=0.046), but not in neocortex (0.005, -0.021 to 0.032, p=0.67); after adjustment for lifetime tablets the pallidostriatal, amygdala and midbrain relations held and the thalamic one did not.
key_findings.note: This is a comparison between people scanned once, not a follow-up; the paper says so (p. 570).

key_findings.finding: From the log-logistic model, pallidostriatal binding in a person with the median lifetime use would be expected to reach the control average about 212 days after the last dose (lower 95% limit 91 days; the upper limit is beyond a human lifespan).
key_findings.note: The Comment rounds this to approximately 200 days (p. 570). The upper limit shows how weak the estimate is.

key_findings.finding: Cortical 5-HT2A receptor binding was 9% lower in the combined drug group than in controls (medians 1.51 vs 1.66, p=0.03), but the difference was no longer significant (p=0.10) when two controls with very high values were excluded, and the three-group comparison was not significant (p=0.07).
Neither the dose-response relation nor the abstinence relation appeared for hallucinogen use, and no relation was found between 5-HT2A binding and lifetime use or time since last use of either drug.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'SERT binding', last paragraph (p. 568); Results, 'Serotonin2A receptor binding' (p. 570)

key_findings.finding: Age, body mass index, daylight on the scan day, education and recent amphetamine, cocaine and cannabis use were tested as covariates one at a time and none was significant or changed the group effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The dose-response intervals printed for thalamus (-0.113 to 0.022) and amygdala (-0.106 to 0.045) include zero although the same sentence gives p=0.006 and p<0.001; the intervals for neocortex and pallidostriatum are printed with both limits negative.
reporting_issues.consequence: The upper limits are almost certainly missing a minus sign (-0.022, -0.045); as printed, two of the four dose-response results are internally inconsistent. Checked on the rendered page: the printed text matches the extraction.

reporting_issues.issue: The 5-HT2A outcome is defined in the Methods as the binding potential of specific binding (BPP) but is reported in the Results text as BPND.
reporting_issues.consequence: Mixed labels for the same measure; the values (medians 1.51 and 1.66) belong to the altanserin steady-state analysis described in the Methods.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 4 states that the partial residual plot is adjusted to a median lifetime use of 314 tablets, while Table 1 (p. 564) gives medians of 635 in the MDMA-preferring group and 24 in the hallucinogen-preferring group; the pooled median is not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot check which group the 212-day estimate describes; it is an extrapolation from a between-person model in 24 people.

reporting_issues.issue: The thalamic group difference is reported as borderline (F=2.6, p=0.08) with a note that it became p=0.04 when one woman with no MDMA in hair was excluded.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single participant moves this result across the conventional threshold; the thalamic finding should not be counted as established.

reporting_issues.issue: The group labelled by preference for hallucinogens had itself used MDMA (median 24 lifetime tablets, 9 of 10 had used it), so the contrast between the two drug groups is not MDMA versus no MDMA but heavy versus light MDMA use.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mechanistic conclusion (that hallucinogen-type 5-HT2A agonism does not lower transporter binding) is supported, but the group labels overstate the contrast; the paper acknowledges this.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 562-576 (all pages; Tables 1-4 read in the extraction, the dose-response intervals on p. 568 checked on the rendered page; Figures 1-6 are images and no values were read from them)

design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (Brain 2010;133:1779-1797) of serotonin transporter binding with [11C]DASB in 49 people who used ecstasy and 50 people who did not, recruited by advertisement in Toronto, with scalp-hair toxicology to confirm ecstasy use and detect other stimulants. Binding potential (BPND) was estimated with the Logan graphical method using cerebellar cortex as reference, in 13 regions, with partial-volume correction, two further kinetic models, manual as well as automatic region drawing, and a whole-brain voxel-wise analysis. Structural MRI (volumes and cortical thickness), a battery of cognitive tests, mood scales, blood hormones and serotonin-transporter promoter genotyping were collected in the same people.
can_establish: That in this sample, with ecstasy use confirmed in hair, transporter binding was lower in every cerebral cortical region and in the hippocampus, that it was unchanged in striatum, globus pallidus, thalamus and midbrain, that the cortical reduction was not explained by brain volume, cortical thickness, hormones, genotype, sex or hair-confirmed use of methamphetamine, cocaine or cannabis, and that lower binding went with more years of use and a higher maximum dose.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused the reduction (one scan per person, no pre-use measurement); that the reduction means loss of serotonin terminals rather than lower transporter expression; that the cognitive differences are caused by it (correlational, uncorrected); or anything about recovery, since abstinence was typically only 1-2 months and showed no relation with binding.

sample.recruitment: Advertisements in the Toronto area; full assessment interview with SCID for DSM-IV, health questionnaire, brief neurological examination, mood and sleep questionnaires, drug-history questionnaire, urine screens at each visit and before the scan, and a scalp-hair drug screen (pp. 1781-1782).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both groups: 18-40 years, no psychotropic medication, no first-degree family history of DSM-IV Axis I disorder, no medical illness or brain trauma that could affect the serotonin system. Comparison group: no illicit drug use on hair or urine testing except cannabis. Ecstasy group: hair positive for ecstasy plus self-report; an Axis I condition was an exclusion only if it began before ecstasy use (p. 1781).
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group 28 men, 21 women, mean age 25.9 (SEM 0.8); comparison group 25 men, 25 women, 26.0 (0.9), p=0.90. The ecstasy group had fewer years of education (14.6 vs 16.0, p=0.002), lower premorbid IQ (107.4 vs 111.6, p=0.002) and slightly lower body mass index (23.4 vs 24.7, p=0.04); 30 vs 5 were current smokers and 25 vs 1 used cannabis at least monthly (both p<0.0001) (Table 1, p. 1784).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single session). Scans of three participants were corrected for head movement; some cognitive and hormone data are missing for a few people (Ns given per test in Table 4).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers for a study of ecstasy, with a comparison group screened to be free of illicit drugs other than cannabis; the ecstasy group was therefore also a group with much heavier tobacco, cannabis and stimulant use. The authors describe the sample as typical low-to-moderate ecstasy use (median 1.5 tablets per session, about 2 sessions a month, median 126 lifetime tablets).

exposure.measurement: Self-report questionnaire plus scalp-hair analysis for ecstasy, MDA, methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine and opioids (hair grows about 0.5 inch a month, so it covers roughly 5 months in men and about 21 months in women in this sample), urine screens at interviews and before the scan (pp. 1781, 1784).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: All oral except one person who used crushed tablets intranasally. Mean 4.1 years of use (range 0.5-12); 206 (SEM 31) lifetime tablets, median 126, range 4-922; typical monthly dose median 2.3 tablets; dose per session median 1.5 tablets (80% typically 1-2); maximum dose per session median 3, range 1-20 (Table 2, p. 1785).
exposure.polysubstance: Hair confirmed MDMA in all 49; MDA in 40 (82%); methamphetamine or amphetamine in 32 (65%); cocaine in 23 (47%). Only 9 of the 32 with methamphetamine-positive hair reported recent use (p=0.016). Self-reported co-use in the previous 6 months included alcohol (84%), cannabis (76%), ketamine (37%) and GHB (20%) (Table 2, p. 1785). Binding differences were analysed separately in those positive and negative for methamphetamine and cocaine in hair and were similar (p. 1787).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Reported abstinence from illicit drugs for at least 14 days; mean 45.2 days since last ecstasy (SEM 4.7; median 38, range 11-194) (Table 2, p. 1785).

comparison.controls: 50 people recruited by the same advertisements with no illicit drug use on hair and urine testing except cannabis (p. 1781).
comparison.matching: Matched on age, sex and ethnicity; not matched on education, premorbid IQ, smoking, alcohol or cannabis, which all differed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measurement; the paper states explicitly that a premorbid difference in transporter levels is one of the possible explanations of the finding (p. 1791).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Cannabis in 1 of 50 at least monthly, 5 of 50 current smokers; no other illicit drugs on hair or urine.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB PET on a high-resolution head-dedicated camera (in-plane resolution 2.8 mm), 90-min scans; BPND by Logan graphical analysis with cerebellar cortex as reference, also SRTM2 and MRTM2; geometric transfer matrix partial-volume correction; T1 MRI for CIVET volumes and cortical thickness; cognitive battery (WASI, NART, PASAT, Digit Ordering, Trails, Symbol Digit, Consonant Trigrams, CVLT, Warrington, Denman); mood scales (IDS, HAM, SIGHD/SAD); blood oestradiol, testosterone and FSH; 5-HTTLPR genotyping (pp. 1782-1783).
outcomes.validity_norms: [11C]DASB is selective for the serotonin transporter; cerebellum is nearly free of it. Cognitive tests have published norms, and both groups' IQ scores were in the normal range (p. 1789). A binding potential is a surrogate for terminal integrity.
outcomes.operationalization: Serotonin neuron status is operationalized as regional BPND; cognitive deficit as a lower group mean on a test, tested one-tailed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni-corrected least-significant-difference tests for the 13 regional binding comparisons, and false-discovery-rate correction in the voxel-wise and cortical-thickness analyses; Bonferroni correction for the cognitive tests, which were tested one-tailed; the correlations between binding and cognition are reported uncorrected (pp. 1783, 1786, 1790).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Manual regions of interest were drawn by a research assistant blinded to group; the automatic segmentation is group-blind by construction (p. 1782).

analysis.effect_sizes: Region-by-group interaction F(12,1152)=7.24, p corrected <0.0001. Reductions in the ecstasy group were confined to the cerebral cortices and hippocampus (p corrected <0.001), largest in occipital cortex (-46%); after partial-volume correction, occipital -39%, temporal -34%, hippocampus -31%, cingulate -30%, insular -27%, parietal -19%, frontal -17% (all p<0.01). No difference in caudate, putamen, ventral striatum, globus pallidus, thalamus or midbrain; the three kinetic models agreed (occipital -46%, -46%, -41%; hippocampus -21%, -21%, -15%; striatum +3%, +2%, +8%). Voxel-wise: largest cluster in occipital cortex, peak magnitude -62% (false-discovery-rate corrected p<0.0001). Effect sizes for binding: occipital 1.14, insular 1.10. In the insular cortex 51% of the ecstasy group fell below the lowest control value. Regression within the ecstasy group: only years of use and maximum dose predicted lower cortical binding, F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001; years of use also predicted lower caudate binding, F(1,41)=4.91, p=0.032. No correlation between days since last use and binding. Cognition: lower scores in the ecstasy group on the CVLT (group F(1,93)=8.53, p=0.004, short-delay free recall -17.8%), PASAT, Digit Ordering, Trails B and Symbol Digit, with effect sizes 0.43-0.86, after adjustment for education or verbal IQ; no difference on Denman or Warrington memory tests. Binding in insular cortex and hippocampus correlated with CVLT short-delay free recall (rho=0.38, p=0.004) and Trails B (rho=-0.38 and -0.35).
analysis.covariates: Education and verbal IQ as covariates for the cognitive comparisons; analyses of binding repeated within subgroups defined by hair results for methamphetamine and cocaine, by self-reported cannabis, ketamine, LSD, mushrooms and tobacco, by sex, body mass index, Axis I diagnosis, hormone levels and genotype (p. 1787).
analysis.selective_reporting: Regions, models and subgroup analyses are reported in full in text and supplement; several supplementary tables (manual regions, model comparison, subgroup binding, volumes) were not read here.
analysis.power: Stated for the striatum: with this sample and a coefficient of variation of 16%, a difference as small as 8% would have been detected with 80% power (p. 1793).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Group means of cortical and hippocampal transporter binding were about a fifth to a half lower in people with hair-confirmed ecstasy use, with striatum, pallidum, thalamus and midbrain unchanged; the difference was not explained by the structural, hormonal, genetic and other-drug factors tested; individual values overlapped heavily except in insular cortex; and binding related to years of use and maximum dose but not to time since last use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reads the finding as a 'highly selective mild to marked loss of serotonin transporter' comparable in size to that in Parkinson's disease, and speaks of susceptibility of cortical serotonergic neurons. The Discussion is more careful, listing lower transporter concentration in intact neurons, loss of terminals and a premorbid difference as alternatives (p. 1791). The cognitive section is also careful: it notes near-total overlap with controls and that people may have drifted to a poorer-performing peer group (p. 1790).

timeline.event: First [11C]DASB study reporting the same cortical pattern in 23 people
Same group's follow-up in 16 people with the same tracer (McCann et al., Psychopharmacology 200:439-450); not read here.
Independent study with the same tracer reporting cortical, pallidostriatal and amygdala reductions and a dose relation
Independent study with arterial input confirming the cortical pattern and adding higher 5-HT2A binding
Review counting 14 of 16 human imaging studies with significantly lower transporter binding

replication.where_it_stands: This was the first independent replication of the cortical pattern reported by the Baltimore group with the same tracer, and the only large study with hair verification of exposure; the sex difference reported from SPECT (Reneman et al., 2001) was not reproduced here, where reductions were of similar size in men and women.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health (NIDA DA017301), Canadian Institutes of Health Research MOP-49538, Canadian Psychiatric Foundation (Funding, p. 1794).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (searched in the text extraction of all pages).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and University of Toronto; the senior author has published critiques of the field's interpretation of transporter imaging, including in methamphetamine (Kish et al., 2017).

what_would_settle_it: Repeat scanning of the same people over years of abstinence with a selective tracer and verified exposure, together with a measure able to separate lower transporter expression from loss of terminals (for example transporter protein and other terminal markers post mortem in people with documented use, or a second serotonin terminal marker in vivo).

domains.note: The ecstasy group smoked more, used more cannabis and alcohol, had less education and lower premorbid IQ; two thirds had methamphetamine-positive hair. Subgroup analyses address these one at a time rather than adjusting jointly, and the comparison of binding is unadjusted.

Hair confirms recent exposure for all participants and detects undisclosed stimulant use, which is a strength; amounts, years and abstinence remain self-reported, and hair covers only about 5 months in men.
Self-selected volunteers; no pre-use measurement, so a premorbid difference cannot be excluded, as the paper says.
None.
Few missing data; Ns are given per test.
Selective tracer, high-resolution camera, three kinetic models, partial-volume correction, blinded manual regions and a voxel-wise check; the outcome remains a surrogate for terminal integrity.

Regional comparisons corrected, voxel-wise analyses false-discovery-rate corrected, negative findings reported; the cognitive tests were one-tailed, and the binding-cognition correlations are uncorrected.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Technically the strongest of the imaging studies read here (largest sample, selective tracer, hair verification, several analyses that could have overturned the finding), but still a cross-sectional comparison of self-selected groups differing in education, IQ, tobacco, cannabis and stimulant use, with no pre-use measurement. It can be cited for the size and regional pattern of the group difference and for its relation to years of use and maximum dose, not for causation or for a loss of nerve terminals.

key_findings.finding: Serotonin transporter binding was lower in the ecstasy group throughout the cerebral cortex and in the hippocampus (region-by-group interaction F(12,1152)=7.24, p corrected <0.0001; regional p corrected <0.001), with the occipital cortex most affected (-46%), and was unchanged in caudate, putamen, ventral striatum, globus pallidus, thalamus and midbrain.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 2nd paragraph; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: After partial-volume correction the reductions were of similar size: occipital -39%, temporal -34%, hippocampus -31%, cingulate -30%, insular -27%, parietal -19%, frontal -17% (p<0.01).
key_findings.note: The parietal and hippocampal figures are printed without a minus sign although described as decreases. The abstract's range (-19% to -46%) mixes partial-volume-corrected and uncorrected values; the uncorrected regional values are not printed in the text.

key_findings.finding: Three kinetic models gave the same answer (occipital -46%, -46%, -41%; hippocampus -21%, -21%, -15%; striatum +3%, +2%, +8%), and the voxel-wise analysis found its largest cluster in occipital cortex with a peak magnitude of -62%.
key_findings.locator: Results, same section, last paragraph; Results, 'Voxel-wise analysis'; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Individual values overlapped between groups in most regions; in the insular cortex 51% of the ecstasy group fell below the lowest control value. Effect sizes for binding were 1.14 (occipital) and 1.10 (insular).
key_findings.locator: Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 4th paragraph (p. 1787, overlap); Discussion, 'Preferential SERT changes…' (p. 1792, the 51% figure, also in the Abstract on p. 1779); Discussion, cognitive section (p. 1793, effect sizes)

key_findings.finding: Within the ecstasy group, only years of use and maximum dose predicted lower cortical binding (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001); years of use also predicted lower caudate binding (F(1,41)=4.91, p=0.032). There was no relation between days since last use and binding, with abstinence typically 1-2 months.
Reductions were of similar size in men and women (occipital -51% vs -40%; insular -22% vs -31%; hippocampus -21% in both), unlike the sex difference reported from SPECT.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 'Preferential SERT changes occurred in cerebral cortex and hippocampus'

key_findings.finding: The reduction held in subgroups defined by hair-confirmed methamphetamine (interaction F(12,1140)=4.28, p=0.002) and cocaine, by cannabis, ketamine, LSD, mushrooms and smoking, and was unrelated to sex, body mass index, Axis I diagnosis, hormone levels or serotonin-transporter genotype.

Brain structure did not explain the finding: no group difference in whole-brain, ventricular, white-matter, cortical or subcortical volumes; cortical thinning in the ecstasy group was mostly accounted for by co-use of methamphetamine and, in the rest, by IQ; thickness and volume were unrelated to binding (p>0.05).

The ecstasy group scored lower on verbal memory (CVLT group F(1,93)=8.53, p=0.004; short-delay free recall -17.8%), working memory (PASAT, Digit Ordering), Trails B and Symbol Digit, with effect sizes 0.43-0.86 after adjustment for education or verbal IQ, but not on the Denman or Warrington memory tests; scores of both groups were in the normal range.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 1790); Results, 'Neuropsychological testing' (pp. 1789-1790); Discussion, cognitive section (p. 1793, the effect-size range)
key_findings.note: Cognitive tests were run one-tailed because only deficits were of interest (p. 1783).

key_findings.finding: Lower insular and hippocampal binding went with poorer short-delay verbal recall (rho=0.38, p=0.004) and slower Trails B (rho=-0.38 and -0.35), uncorrected for multiplicity.

Hair toxicology showed MDMA in all 49 participants, MDA in 82%, methamphetamine or amphetamine in 65% and cocaine in 47%; only 9 of 32 people with methamphetamine-positive hair reported recent use (p=0.016).
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Demographic characteristics and drug profiles', 2nd paragraph (p. 1784); Table 2 (p. 1785)

reporting_issues.issue: The length of hair tested is given in the Results as 2.3 inches in men and 10.5 inches in women (about 5 and 21 months) and in the Discussion as 2.6 and 10.3 inches (5 and 20 months).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the hair window is the basis for the claim that recent methamphetamine use does not explain the finding; the two figures should agree.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the cortical range as -19% to -46% and the hippocampus as -21%, while the Results list partial-volume-corrected values of -17% to -39% with a hippocampal value of -31%; the uncorrected regional values other than occipital (-46%) and hippocampus (-21%) are not printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot reconstruct the abstract's range from the printed numbers, and later sources quote the two sets interchangeably (the 2016 review lists the corrected values as the study's result).

reporting_issues.issue: Partial-volume-corrected decreases are printed as 'parietal, 19%' and 'hippocampus, 31%' without minus signs in a list where the other values carry them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographic only; the direction is given in the sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: Subcortical grey-matter volumes were below normal in the 17 people whose hair was negative for methamphetamine but normal in those whose hair was positive.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper calls this apparently paradoxical and explains it by above-normal striatal volume reported in people who use methamphetamine; it shows that the subgroup comparisons are not straightforward to interpret.

reporting_issues.issue: Cognitive comparisons used one-tailed tests, chosen because only deficits were of interest, and the correlations between binding and cognition are reported without correction for multiplicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cognitive p-values are half the two-tailed values, and the binding-cognition correlations (rho about 0.35-0.38) are the weakest part of the paper; the Discussion does not rest its conclusions on them.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 1779-1797 (all pages; Tables 1-4 and the text read in the extraction, Figure 1 checked on the rendered page 1786; supplementary tables and figures not read)

design_detail: Cross-sectional quantitative PET study (Neuropsychopharmacology 2005;30:1741-1750) in which 23 people abstinent from MDMA and 19 people who had never used it were each scanned twice on the same day, about 135 min apart, with two serotonin transporter radioligands, [11C]McN5652 and [11C]DASB, using arterial blood sampling and a single-tissue compartment model. Three binding measures were compared in 15 regions of interest drawn on co-registered MRI by a neurologist blind to group: total distribution volume (DV), specific distribution volume (DVspec, regional DV minus cerebellar DV) and the ratio (DVR).
can_establish: That in this sample, binding of both radioligands was lower on average in the group abstinent from MDMA, with the largest and most consistent differences in neocortical regions, and that the two tracers agreed closely within the same people.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the difference (one scan per person, no pre-use measure, more other-drug use in the MDMA group); that the difference means loss of nerve terminals rather than lower transporter expression; that people with lighter exposure are affected (the group had used on average 97 occasions); or that transporters recover with abstinence, which is tested here only as a correlation across different people, with one-tailed tests.

sample.recruitment: Advertisements in newspapers, fliers, radio and the internet, and word of mouth from previous participants; telephone screen, then face-to-face assessment with the SCID-IV, physical examination, blood chemistry and drug screens (pp. 1742-1743).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MDMA group: use on at least 25 separate occasions; comparison group: never used MDMA. Both groups could have used other recreational drugs but none in the 2 weeks before the study. Excluded: psychiatric disorders in which serotonin has been implicated, past or present alcohol use disorder, current drug dependence; negative urine and blood drug screens other than cannabis (p. 1742).
sample.demographics: MDMA group 10 women, 13 men, mean age 22.04 years, 13.7 years of education; comparison group 11 women, 8 men, mean age 26, 13.68 years of education (Table 1, p. 1744). No standard deviations or tests are given for age or education.
sample.attrition: Not reported; both scans were obtained in all 42 participants (one group's data for some 'other drug' items are based on 22 of 23).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers answering advertisements for a study of ecstasy; the MDMA group had used the drug on average 97 times, so the findings describe people at the heavier end of recreational use. The comparison group had far less experience of other drugs, so group membership tracks a general pattern of drug use, not MDMA alone.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug history at telephone and face-to-face screening; urine and blood drug screens for current drugs only; no hair analysis (p. 1742).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Mean 96.96 MDMA exposures (range 28-324) over 2.97 (SD 2.2) years; 3.12 (1.59) exposures per month; usual dose 1.79 (0.49) tablets, maximum dose 5.83 (3.92) tablets (Table 1, p. 1744). Route not stated; tablet content not verified.
exposure.polysubstance: The MDMA group used more of every other drug class: cannabis 96% vs 37% lifetime, hallucinogens 83% vs 11%, cocaine 52% vs 5%, opioids 43% vs 5%, other stimulants 48% vs 5%, ketamine 57% vs 0%, alcohol 100% vs 79%, tobacco 87% vs 67% (Table 1, p. 1744). The authors state that matching on other drugs proved impossible and that an effect of other drugs cannot be excluded (p. 1748).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks of self-reported abstinence from all illicit drugs, with negative urine and blood screens (cannabis exempted); mean time since last MDMA 4.74 months (SD 8.71) (Table 1, p. 1744).

comparison.controls: 19 people recruited the same way who reported never using MDMA (p. 1742).
comparison.matching: Described as well matched for age and education; no statistical test is given, and the mean ages differ by about 4 years (22.0 vs 26.0).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; the paper notes that an unidentified condition predisposing to drug use could contribute to the reductions (p. 1748).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Lower on every class (Table 1, p. 1744); 37% had used cannabis, 11% hallucinogens, 5% cocaine.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]McN5652 and [11C]DASB PET (GE Advance, axial resolution 5.8 mm), 95-min dynamic scans with arterial input function corrected for metabolites; single-tissue compartment model; 15 regions of interest drawn on MRI by a neurologist blind to group; cerebellum as reference region for DVspec and DVR (pp. 1742-1743).
outcomes.validity_norms: Both tracers are serotonin transporter ligands validated in baboons; the authors note that PET measures underestimate transporter loss measured in vitro, being about half of it in baboons (p. 1748). No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Neurotoxicity' is operationalized as lower regional binding; recovery as a positive correlation between global binding and months since last use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None: 15 preplanned regional comparisons for each of 3 binding measures and 2 tracers, plus correlational analyses with use variables, are reported without adjustment (pp. 1743, 1745).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The neurologist who drew the regions was blind to group, worked from MRI anatomy, and viewed PET images normalized to their own maximum (p. 1743).

analysis.effect_sizes: ANOVA main effect of group: [11C]McN5652 DV F=5.3 (p=0.028), DVspec F=6.6 (p=0.014), DVR F=5.9 (p=0.02); [11C]DASB DV F=4.1 (p=0.05), DVspec F=5.0 (p=0.031), DVR F=7.4 (p=0.01); no group-by-region interaction for either tracer (p=0.16 to 0.45) (Table 2, p. 1746). Regional percent differences in DVspec (Table 3, p. 1748; editors' calculation of standardized differences from the printed means and SDs, Hedges g with 95% interval): [11C]DASB occipital cortex -68% (g -2.16, -2.98 to -1.43), temporal -48% (-2.06, -2.86 to -1.33), parietal -51% (-1.83, -2.60 to -1.13), dorsolateral prefrontal -55% (-1.64, -2.38 to -0.96), hippocampus -40% (-1.26, -1.96 to -0.62), thalamus -23% (-0.62, -1.26 to -0.01), midbrain -21% (-0.48, -1.11 to 0.13), caudate -14% (-0.40, -1.03 to 0.20), putamen -13% (-0.35, -0.97 to 0.26). Correlations (one-tailed): global [11C]McN5652 DVspec with months of abstinence r=0.418, p=0.026; DVR with abstinence r=0.494, p<0.010; global DVR with typical monthly dose r=0.38 and 0.37 for the two tracers, p=0.04 (described in the text as inverse) (p. 1745).
analysis.covariates: None: no adjustment for age, sex, education or other drug use.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 15 regions are shown for DVspec (Table 3) and plotted for all three measures (Figure 4); the DV and DVR tables are not printed, and the counts of significant regions appear only in the text.
analysis.power: Not formally reported; the authors state the study was not powered to demonstrate correlations between binding and use variables and call those analyses preliminary (p. 1748).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Group means of serotonin transporter binding were lower in the MDMA group with both tracers and all three binding measures, most clearly in neocortical regions and hippocampus, with substantial overlap of individual values and no group-by-region interaction; and binding was higher in people who had been abstinent longer, in a correlation across people tested one-tailed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the data provide "strong evidence of reduced SERT density" in some people who use MDMA recreationally, and that exploratory analyses suggested that transporter measures recover with time (abstract, p. 1741). The Discussion calls MDMA-induced toxicity 'the most parsimonious explanation' (p. 1746). The design is cross-sectional with large differences in other drug use, the recovery analysis compares different people at a single time point, and the authors themselves list pre-existing differences and other drugs as unexcluded (p. 1748).

timeline.event: The same group's first PET study with [11C]McN5652 reported a large global reduction (McCann et al., Lancet 352:1433-1437), which this paper describes as having had high variability and needing logarithmic transformation.
Follow-up by the same group in 16 people, again with [11C]DASB, reporting cortical and hippocampal reductions and no striatal change (McCann et al., Psychopharmacology 200:439-450); not read here.
Independent replication in 49 people with hair verification: cortical and hippocampal reductions, normal striatum
Independent study finding reductions in neocortex, pallidostriatum and amygdala, with a dose relation
Independent study with arterial input and a selective 5-HT2A tracer: lower cortical binding, higher 5-HT2A binding
No difference in men abstinent for at least a year

replication.where_it_stands: The cortical finding has been reproduced by three independent laboratories with the same tracer; the subcortical findings have not been consistent, and this study's thalamic reduction was not found by the Toronto or New York groups.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA10217 (McCann), AA11653 (Szabo), DA00206 (Ricaurte) and NCRR grant M01RR002719 (Acknowledgements, p. 1749).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state that none has a financial or other conflict of interest that might bias the work (p. 1749).
funding.affiliations_note: Johns Hopkins; the same laboratory published the 1998 PET study and the 2002 primate report later retracted (Ricaurte et al., 2002), which is a reason for close reading rather than to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A study of the same people scanned before first use and repeatedly through use and abstinence, with biological verification of exposure and a comparison group with the same other-drug use, plus a measure that can distinguish lower transporter expression from loss of terminals.

domains.note: The MDMA group used every other drug class far more often, and no analysis adjusts for this or for the 4-year age difference; age lowers transporter binding, which here runs against the finding, while other stimulant and hallucinogen use runs with it.
Exposure, dose and abstinence are self-reported; no hair analysis; tablet content unverified; the standard deviation of time since last use (8.71 months) is nearly twice its mean.
Volunteers answering advertisements for a study of ecstasy, with a comparison group of people with much less drug experience; no pre-use measurement.
None.
Both scans in all participants; a few self-report items missing for one person.
Quantitative PET with arterial input, two tracers in the same people, blinded region drawing; cortical signal is small and noisy, which the authors discuss.

Ninety regional comparisons without correction; correlations tested one-tailed on a stated directional hypothesis; the significance counts for DV are given only in the text and differ from those for DVR and DVspec.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The imaging is of high technical quality, but the comparison is between groups that differ in every drug class and in age, with self-reported exposure and no correction for 90 comparisons. It supports a group difference in transporter binding, strongest in cortex; it cannot support a causal or quantitative statement, and its recovery analysis is a between-person correlation with one-tailed tests.

key_findings.finding: Main effect of group on binding was significant for both tracers and all three binding measures (DV, DVspec, DVR): [11C]McN5652 F=5.3 (p=0.028), 6.6 (p=0.014), 5.9 (p=0.02); [11C]DASB F=4.1 (p=0.05), 5.0 (p=0.031), 7.4 (p=0.01); no group-by-region interaction.
Preplanned regional comparisons of DV were significant in 12 of 15 regions for [11C]McN5652 and 9 of 15 for [11C]DASB; with DVR and DVspec, 10 of 15 regions for both tracers.
key_findings.note: No correction for 15 comparisons; the interaction term that would license regional comparisons was not significant.

key_findings.finding: Percent differences in DVspec with [11C]DASB were largest in cortex: occipital -68%, dorsolateral prefrontal -55%, parietal -51%, temporal -48%, hippocampus -40%, and smallest in putamen (-13%), caudate (-14%) and midbrain (-21%); the [11C]McN5652 pattern was the same (occipital -54%, putamen -20%).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation of standardized differences from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g, 95% interval): occipital -2.16 (-2.98 to -1.43), temporal -2.06 (-2.86 to -1.33), parietal -1.83 (-2.60 to -1.13), hippocampus -1.26 (-1.96 to -0.62), thalamus -0.62 (-1.26 to -0.01), midbrain -0.48 (-1.11 to 0.13), caudate -0.40 (-1.03 to 0.20), putamen -0.35 (-0.97 to 0.26).

key_findings.finding: Global [11C]McN5652 binding was higher in people with longer abstinence (DVspec r=0.418, p=0.026; DVR r=0.494, p<0.010), and global DVR was lower with higher typical monthly dose (r printed as 0.38 and 0.37, described as inverse; p=0.04 for both tracers).
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph ('Exploratory analyses evaluating a possible relationship…')
key_findings.note: One-tailed tests on a directional hypothesis, across different people at one time point, in a sample the authors say was not powered for these analyses (p. 1748).

key_findings.finding: Binding of the two radioligands agreed closely: across regions overall r=0.97 (controls 0.96, MDMA group 0.98), and within individual participants overall r=0.55.
Group means of the delivery parameter K1 did not differ ([11C]DASB F=1.68, p=0.125; [11C]McN5652 F=1.599, p=0.162), so differences in tracer delivery do not explain the binding difference.

The MDMA group had used MDMA on average 97 times (range 28-324) over about 3 years, at a usual dose of 1.79 tablets and a maximum of 5.83, and had last used it a mean of 4.74 months (SD 8.71) earlier.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives mean ages of 22.04 (MDMA group) and 26 (comparison group) with no standard deviations and no test, while the text states that the groups were well matched for age.
reporting_issues.consequence: A 4-year age difference is not negligible for a measure that declines with age; here it would bias towards higher binding in the MDMA group, so it does not explain the finding, but the claim of matching is not supported by a test.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations between binding and typical monthly dose are described in the text as inverse while the coefficients are printed as positive (r=0.38 and 0.37).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction has to be taken from the text; the sign of the printed coefficients is wrong or the word 'inversely' is.

reporting_issues.issue: The percent differences in Table 3 are printed without signs although every value is a reduction, and the table's title prints the tracer as '[11C]McN56652'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographic; the direction is unambiguous from the means, but values copied from this table can be reported with the wrong sign, as happens in later reviews.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints one cell of the ANOVA as '1.4 (0 = 0.25)' instead of a p-value.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor misprint; the corresponding DV and DVR cells give p=0.25.

reporting_issues.issue: Regional comparisons were run although the stated condition for them (a significant group-by-region interaction, or a main effect) was met only by the main effect, and 90 comparisons across regions, measures and tracers are reported without correction; the correlations are one-tailed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pattern of significant regions, and the two correlations near p=0.03 to 0.04, are less secure than the printed p-values suggest; the cortical differences are large enough to survive, the subcortical ones are not.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that reductions were found 'in selected cortical and subcortical structures' and that measures recover with time, without noting that the abstinence analysis is a between-person correlation with one-tailed tests in a sample the Discussion says was underpowered for it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the abstract alone would take recovery as observed in people over time.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 1741-1750 (all pages; Tables 1-3 read in the text extraction, Figure 4 panels not read numerically)

design_detail: Cross-sectional SPECT study (Lancet 2001;358:1864-1869) of [123I]beta-CIT binding, recruited through flyers at Amsterdam 'rave' venues with a harm-reduction agency. Four groups recruited from the same scene: 15 people with moderate ecstasy use (up to 50 tablets lifetime), 23 with heavy use (50 tablets or more), 16 who had used at least 50 tablets and had stopped for at least a year, and 15 who said they had never used ecstasy but used other drugs. One scan per person; binding expressed as the ratio of region-of-interest counts to cerebellar counts 4 h after injection, in midbrain, thalamus and four cortical regions; analysed in a mixed linear model with group, sex, region and group-by-sex terms.
can_establish: That, in these four groups scanned once, overall and regional [123I]beta-CIT binding ratios were lower in the women with heavy use than in the women in the control group, that the moderate-use groups did not differ from controls, and that women who had stopped for a year or more had higher ratios than women currently using heavily and did not differ significantly from controls.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused the lower binding (no pre-use scan; the groups differ in other drug use); that the higher binding in people who had stopped is recovery (different people, scanned once, not the same people followed); that men are unaffected (the paper's own power calculation shows the male comparison could not detect the difference it looked for); or that the signal is specific to serotonin, since the tracer also binds dopamine transporters.

sample.recruitment: Flyers at venues of the Amsterdam 'rave scene', with the harm-reduction agency UNITY; controls recruited from the same community source (p. 1865).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18-45, otherwise healthy, no psychiatric history. Group thresholds: up to 50 lifetime tablets (moderate), 50 or more (heavy), 50 or more plus at least 1 year without use (stopped). Agreed abstinence from all psychoactive drugs for at least 3 weeks, then urine screening; excluded for a positive drug screen, pregnancy, severe medical or neuropsychiatric illness, or medication binding the serotonin transporter (p. 1865).
sample.demographics: Age 22.7-29.3 years by subgroup; men 3.1 years older than women (95% CI 0.6-5.6). Verbal IQ (Dutch adult reading test) 102.0-112.2, no group difference (p=0.10). Current depression in 11 of 69 participants, no group difference (p=0.86) (Table 1, p. 1865).
sample.attrition: Not applicable: one scan per person, no follow-up.
sample.selection_effects: Groups are self-selected by their own drug histories and recruited in one scene; the group that had stopped is made up of people who both used heavily and then stopped, which may differ systematically from those who continued. Exposure is self-reported, with only a urine screen at entry.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported drug history questionnaire (validated against urine testing in a Dutch survey, 93% agreement, n=594, as the authors cite, p. 1868); urine enzyme immunoassay before enrolment (p. 1865).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported means (Table 2, p. 1865): duration 4.1-4.6 years in all three ecstasy groups; usual dose 1.4 (SD 0.5) tablets in the moderate group, 2.2 (0.7) in the heavy group, 2.1 (1.0) in those who had stopped; lifetime tablets 28.6 (17.8), 530.0 (621.1) and 268.1 (614.3). Route not stated (tablets).
exposure.polysubstance: All groups used other drugs. Amphetamine use in the past 3 months differed between groups (p=0.04) and cocaine use nearly so (p=0.09); the ecstasy groups reported more of both than controls. Cannabis, alcohol and tobacco did not differ by group (Table 1, p. 1865). The authors argue that none of these is a known human serotonin toxin (p. 1868).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 3 weeks from all psychoactive drugs, self-reported and checked with one urine screen. Time since last tablet: 3.6 (SD 5.9) months (moderate), 2.3 (2.4) months (heavy), 29.0 (20.4) months (stopped) (Table 2, p. 1865).

comparison.controls: 15 people recruited from the same subculture who said they had never used ecstasy but used other drugs (p. 1865).
comparison.matching: Not individually matched; groups did not differ in age, verbal IQ, alcohol, tobacco or cannabis use, but did differ in amphetamine use.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan and no measure of serotonin transporter levels before use; the authors note that people with low transporter density might be more likely to use ecstasy (p. 1868).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls used other recreational drugs but reported no amphetamine or cocaine use in the past 3 months (Table 1, p. 1865).

outcomes.instruments: [123I]beta-CIT SPECT, 12-detector brain-dedicated scanner, resolution about 7.5 mm; binding ratio = region counts / cerebellar counts, 4 h after injection of about 140 MBq; regions of interest placed from a standard template by an investigator unaware of the participant's history (p. 1866).
outcomes.validity_norms: The tracer binds both serotonin and dopamine transporters; the authors argue that at 4 h in these regions binding is predominantly serotonergic, and note that striatal ratios at 24 h did not differ between groups (p. 1868). No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Neurotoxic effect' is operationalized as a lower binding ratio; 'reversibility' as a higher ratio in a separate group of people who had stopped.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported: an overall mixed model, then 5 group contrasts in each of 6 regions separately for men and women (Tables 3 and 4, pp. 1866-1867).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The investigator who drew the regions of interest was unaware of the participant's history (p. 1866).

analysis.effect_sizes: Mixed model: group p=0.041, group-by-sex p=0.022 (p. 1866). Overall binding ratio differences, control minus group (Table 3, p. 1866): women, heavy use 0.168 (95% CI 0.078-0.259, p<0.01); men, heavy use 0.025 (-0.067 to 0.117, p=0.587); women, moderate use 0.058 (-0.046 to 0.162, p=0.269). Women who had stopped versus women with heavy use -0.137 (-0.227 to -0.046, p=0.004), i.e. higher binding in those who had stopped; versus controls 0.031 (-0.067 to 0.129, p=0.524). Regional results in women with heavy use versus controls (Table 4, p. 1866): midbrain 0.154 (0.034-0.274, p=0.013), thalamus 0.221 (0.022-0.421, p=0.030), frontal cortex 0.148 (0.073-0.223, p<0.01), temporal cortex 0.134 (0.006-0.262, p=0.040), parieto-occipital 0.177 (0.096-0.259, p<0.01), occipital 0.175 (0.090-0.260, p<0.01). In women who had stopped, binding was still non-significantly lower than in controls in the parieto-occipital (p=0.059) and occipital cortex (p=0.107). Correlation of overall binding with log lifetime tablets: women r=-0.33, p=0.048; men r=0.07, p=0.699 (p. 1867). No percentage changes are given; the outcome is a ratio.
analysis.covariates: Age and current depression added to the model; neither significant (age p=0.492, depression p=0.539) and neither changed the group effect (p. 1867).
analysis.selective_reporting: All six regions and both sexes are tabulated. The paper reports that excluding participants with depression did not change the result but gives no numbers ('data not shown', p. 1868).
analysis.power: A retrospective power calculation states that detecting the reduction seen in heavy use with 80% power would need 7 women but 393 men per group (pp. 1867-1868), so the null result in men is uninformative.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In one scan per person, women with heavy ecstasy use had lower [123I]beta-CIT binding ratios than women in the control group across all six regions; men did not differ; moderate use did not differ; and women who had stopped for a year or more had higher ratios than women currently using heavily and no significant difference from controls, with non-significant differences remaining in the two posterior cortical regions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title and summary speak of 'toxic effects of MDMA on brain serotonin neurons' and conclude that heavy use 'is associated with neurotoxic effects on serotonin neurons' and that the MDMA-induced neurotoxic changes in several brain regions of the women who had stopped are reversible (summary, p. 1864). The results are a cross-sectional difference in a radioligand ratio between separately recruited groups: neither toxicity nor reversal was observed in anyone. The Discussion itself concedes that a prospective design would be needed to establish reversibility (p. 1868) and that pre-existing differences cannot be excluded (p. 1868).

timeline.event: First PET report of lower serotonin transporter binding in people who had used MDMA (McCann et al., Lancet 352:1433-1437), with a large global reduction later not replicated.
Quantitative PET with two radioligands finds lower binding, largest in cortex, and a positive association with time abstinent
Prospective SPECT with the same tracer in people who had just started using finds no difference in transporter binding
PET in men abstinent for at least a year finds no difference from controls
PET with a selective tracer and hair testing finds cortical and hippocampal reductions but normal striatum, and no sex difference in their size
PET finds reductions related to lifetime dose and a positive relation with time since last use in subcortical regions only
Review of molecular imaging counts 14 of 16 human studies with significantly lower transporter binding and judges the evidence on sex differences unsettled

replication.where_it_stands: Lower transporter binding in people who use ecstasy heavily is reported by several independent groups, but this study's two distinctive claims are not settled: the sex difference was not reproduced in the largest PET study (Kish et al., 2010, where reductions were of similar size in men and women), and 'reversibility' rests here and elsewhere on comparisons between different people at one time point.

funding.funder: Partly supported by a grant from the Netherlands Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sports (GVM grant 43894) (Acknowledgments, p. 1869).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (searched in the text extraction of all six pages).
funding.affiliations_note: Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam, and Leiden University Medical Center. The same group later ran the prospective NeXT cohort (de Win et al., 2008), which used the same tracer and found no transporter difference after low doses.

what_would_settle_it: Repeated scanning of the same people with a serotonin-selective tracer: before first use, during use and across years of abstinence, with a retested comparison group who do not start, biological verification of exposure, and enough men and women to test a sex difference rather than infer it from a null result in one sex.

domains.note: The ecstasy groups used more amphetamine (p=0.04) and cocaine (p=0.09) than controls; only age and depression were entered as covariates, and the model does not adjust for other drug use.

Lifetime tablets, dose and abstinence are self-reported, with one urine screen and no hair analysis; tablet content was not verified, and lifetime estimates reach hundreds of tablets with standard deviations larger than their means.
Four self-selected groups from one scene; the group that had stopped consists of people who used heavily and then stopped, which cannot be separated from any pre-existing difference.
None.
One scan per person; no missing imaging data reported.

Region drawing was blinded and the measure is objective, but the tracer is not selective for the serotonin transporter and the outcome is a cerebellar ratio from a scanner with about 7.5 mm resolution.
Six regions, four groups and two sexes are reported without correction; one sensitivity analysis is reported without numbers.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A cross-sectional comparison of self-selected groups with unadjusted differences in other stimulant use and self-reported exposure. It can be cited for a group difference in a radioligand ratio and for the dose relation in women, not for causation, for the absence of an effect in men (power), or for recovery, which it did not observe within any person.

key_findings.finding: In the mixed model the overall effect of group (p=0.041) and the group-by-sex interaction (p=0.022) were significant, so all later comparisons are reported separately for men and women.

Overall binding ratio was lower in women with heavy use than in women in the control group (difference 0.168, 95% CI 0.078-0.259, p<0.01) but not in men (0.025, -0.067 to 0.117, p=0.587); moderate use did not differ in either sex (women 0.058, -0.046 to 0.162, p=0.269).
key_findings.note: The outcome is a ratio to cerebellar binding, so these are absolute differences in ratio units, not percentages; mean ratios are shown only in Figure 1 (p. 1866).

key_findings.finding: In women with heavy use, binding was lower than in controls in all six regions: midbrain 0.154 (0.034-0.274, p=0.013), thalamus 0.221 (0.022-0.421, p=0.030), frontal 0.148 (0.073-0.223, p<0.01), temporal 0.134 (0.006-0.262, p=0.040), parieto-occipital 0.177 (0.096-0.259, p<0.01), occipital 0.175 (0.090-0.260, p<0.01). In men no regional difference reached significance.

Women who had stopped for at least a year had higher overall binding than women with heavy use (-0.137, -0.227 to -0.046, p=0.004) and did not differ significantly from controls (0.031, -0.067 to 0.129, p=0.524); in the parieto-occipital (p=0.059) and occipital cortex (p=0.107) they remained non-significantly below controls.
key_findings.note: These are different people from the heavy-use group, scanned once: no one was followed over abstinence.

key_findings.finding: Overall binding correlated with log lifetime tablets in women (r=-0.33, p=0.048) but not men (r=0.07, p=0.699).
key_findings.note: The text extraction renders the coefficient as 'r=20.33'; the rendered page shows r=-0.33 (checked on the image of p. 1867).

key_findings.finding: A retrospective power calculation states that 7 women but 393 men per group would be needed to detect the reduction seen in heavy use with 80% power.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph on sex differences (begins p. 1867, the figures on p. 1868)
key_findings.note: The null result in men therefore bounds nothing; the paper nonetheless reads it as a sex difference.

key_findings.finding: Adding age and current depression to the model changed nothing (age p=0.492, depression p=0.539), and the four groups did not differ in verbal IQ, alcohol, tobacco or cannabis use, but ecstasy groups reported more amphetamine (p=0.04) and cocaine (p=0.09) use in the past 3 months.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 gives the sex difference in usual dose for the moderate group as 4.2 tablets with a 95% interval of -56.7 to 65.1, although the group's mean usual dose is 1.4 (SD 0.5) tablets.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed interval cannot come from these data; the row is unusable and probably a misprint (the log transformation used for other variables is not stated for this row).

reporting_issues.issue: Also in Table 2, the sex difference in lifetime tablets per kg for the heavy group is -7.1 (95% CI -13.8 to -0.35) with p=0.06.
reporting_issues.consequence: An interval excluding zero with a p-value above 0.05 is internally inconsistent; one of the two is wrong.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary and title describe 'toxic effects on brain serotonin neurons' and reversibility, while the measurement is a [123I]beta-CIT binding ratio in groups scanned once, and the tracer also binds dopamine transporters.
reporting_issues.consequence: A surrogate marker and a between-group difference are presented as observed damage and observed recovery; the Discussion's own caveats (no prospective design, possible pre-existing differences) are not carried into the conclusions.

reporting_issues.issue: The null result in men is presented as a sex difference in susceptibility even though the paper's own power calculation shows the male comparison was powered only for an effect about 50 times larger per-group sample.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of a significant difference in men is not evidence of absence; the group-by-sex interaction (p=0.022) supports a difference in the estimates, but the regional male nulls carry no information.

reporting_issues.issue: Six regions, four groups and two sexes are compared without any correction for multiplicity, and one sensitivity analysis (excluding participants with depression) is reported only as 'data not shown'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Several of the regional p-values lie between 0.01 and 0.05 and would not survive correction; the unreported analysis cannot be checked.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 1864-1869 (all pages; Tables 1-4 and the text of Figure 3 checked on the rendered page 1867)

design_detail: RETRACTED PRIMATE REPORT, CARDED AS A RECORD ONLY (METHODS §3.2). Science 2002;297:2260-2263, retracted on 12 September 2003 (the publisher's PDF carries the line 'Retracted 12 September 2003; see last page'). The brief for this batch asked for a card of design 'commentary'; the schema's design list has no such value and the validator's narrative group contains it, so 'narrative-review' is used, as for the retraction notices already carded, and the choice is flagged for the senior author's open decision on a design for notices and withdrawn records (SENIOR-DECISIONS item 29(5)).
