What the report described: squirrel monkeys and baboons given three doses of 2 mg/kg of what the authors believed was MDMA at 3-hour intervals (subcutaneously in squirrel monkeys, intramuscularly in baboons), then examined 2 to 8 weeks later for brain serotonin and dopamine markers, with silver staining and glial staining in two animals and a dopamine-depletion challenge in three. The retraction notice (Ricaurte et al., 2003) states that the drug given to all but one animal was methamphetamine, so the report is a record of what was claimed, never evidence about MDMA.
can_establish: Nothing about MDMA. The card records what the 2002 report claimed, which dose regimen it described, how many animals died or did not complete it, and the public-health conclusions it drew, so that the claim about the retraction can state what was withdrawn.
cannot_establish: Any effect of MDMA on dopamine or serotonin systems in primates or people: the compound given to all but one animal was methamphetamine, as the authors reported a year later. The report also cannot establish which animal received MDMA or what that animal showed, since the notice does not say.

sample.recruitment: Laboratory animals (Saimiri sciureus and Papio anubis) at Johns Hopkins; no further detail given.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated.
sample.demographics: Species only; sex, age and weight are not given in the report text (they may be in the supporting online material, which was not read).
sample.attrition: Of 5 squirrel monkeys, 1 developed malignant hyperthermia and died within hours of the last dose and 1 received only 2 of the 3 doses after becoming unsteady; of 5 baboons, 1 died after only 2 doses, with hyperthermia up to 41.6 C named as an important factor, and 1 more received only 2 doses. So 2 of 10 animals given the regimen died and 2 others did not complete it.
sample.selection_effects: Not applicable; the decisive problem is the compound given, not the sampling.

exposure.measurement: None of the kind the encyclopedia records: the compound was taken from a bottle labelled MDMA, and the laboratory discovered a year later that it contained methamphetamine (Ricaurte et al., 2003).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As described in the report: 2 mg/kg three times at 3-hour intervals, total 6 mg/kg, subcutaneous in squirrel monkeys and intramuscular in baboons. The report argued that these doses, adjusted with interspecies scaling, were lower than those typically taken by people (1.6 to 2.4 mg/kg).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (animals).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Animals were examined 3.5 days (staining), 2 weeks or 6 to 8 weeks after dosing.

comparison.controls: Saline-treated animals of each species (3 squirrel monkeys, 3 baboons).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-dosing measurement in the same animals; all comparisons are between treated and saline-treated animals.

outcomes.instruments: Regional brain serotonin, 5-HIAA, serotonin transporter, dopamine, DOPAC, dopamine transporter and vesicular monoamine transporter by neurochemistry and quantitative autoradiography; immunoreactive axon counts; silver staining for degenerating terminals; glial fibrillary acidic protein staining; a motor challenge with a dopamine-synthesis blocker in 3 animals.
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity operationalized as lasting reductions in axonal markers plus argyrophilic debris and a glial response.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: One-way analysis of variance followed by individual comparisons; no correction described in the report text.

analysis.effect_sizes: As reported for the animal that received only two doses, 6 weeks later: caudate dopamine -65%, DOPAC -77%, dopamine transporter -51%; serotonin -37%, 5-HIAA -48%, serotonin transporter -40%. Group means are shown only in figures, which are images and were not read. No effect on noradrenaline markers was reported. These figures describe animals given methamphetamine and are recorded here only as what the report stated.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable; the report is four pages with most data in figures and a supporting online file that was not read.
analysis.power: Not reported; groups of 3 to 5 animals.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Nothing about MDMA. On the report's own terms it described large reductions in striatal dopamine markers and smaller reductions in serotonin markers in 2 species after 3 doses of a compound believed to be MDMA, with 2 of 10 animals dying during dosing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The report concluded that people who take repeated doses over several hours are at high risk of severe brain dopamine injury, that this may put them at increased risk of parkinsonism and other disorders later in life, and that cognitive problems reported in people who use ecstasy may be related to dopaminergic rather than serotonergic toxicity. It also argued that oral use offers little protection and that the doses used were, after interspecies scaling, lower than those people take, a statement that the same authors contradicted in their 2003 reply to critics, where they wrote that interspecies scaling had not been used in these studies (see card sc_mithoefer_2003).

timeline.event: Publication in Science on 27 September 2002, with national press coverage of the claim that one night's use could cause brain damage
Published criticism in Science (6 June) that the high mortality showed the regimen was not a common recreational one, with the authors' reply

Retraction on 12 September 2003: the authors report that all but one animal received methamphetamine from a mislabelled bottle, and that their own attempts to reproduce the dopamine finding with authenticated MDMA had failed
Review of molecular imaging finds no consistent dopamine effect of MDMA in people

replication.where_it_stands: Retracted and never replicated. Under METHODS §3.2 it is cited only to document the retraction; the dopamine question in people is treated in the claim on human dopamine markers.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service grants DA 5707, DA 13790, DA 09487, DA 00206 and DA 10217 (Acknowledgements, p. 2263).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated in the report.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Neurology, Neurosciences and Psychiatry, Johns Hopkins; the same laboratory produced the 1998 and 2005 human PET studies of the serotonin transporter.

what_would_settle_it: Nothing can repair this report. The underlying question, whether dose regimens resembling human use damage dopamine neurons in primates, would need a new study with authenticated drug, independent verification of the compound and blinded outcome assessment.

domains.note: Not a review; the item is read here as whether the document can be used as a source of evidence at all, and it cannot: it is retracted.
The report's central exposure was never verified; the compound given was established only after publication, by analysis of frozen brains and of the bottle's contents.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The argument for human relevance rests on the same laboratory's earlier primate work and on an interspecies scaling claim the authors later said they had not used.
The conclusions about parkinsonism in people and about cognitive problems being dopaminergic are speculation presented as implications of the findings.

domains.domain: Balance of the account of human relevance (the risks of the regimen are under-represented)
domains.note: Two of ten animals died and two more could not complete the regimen, yet the regimen is described as one commonly used by people.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No instrument is appropriate: the paper is retracted and is read only as a record of what was claimed (METHODS §3.2). The editors' narrative-review checklist is used as the schema's closest available device, with its domains read as questions about the document as a record. It may be cited only by the claim that documents the retraction.

key_findings.finding: The regimen described was 2 mg/kg three times at 3-hour intervals, a total of 6 mg/kg, given subcutaneously to squirrel monkeys and intramuscularly to baboons, and presented as modelling a regimen used by people at all-night dance parties.

Of 5 squirrel monkeys, 1 died of malignant hyperthermia within hours of the last dose and 1 received only 2 doses after becoming unsteady; of 5 baboons, 1 died after 2 doses, with hyperthermia up to 41.6 C named as an important factor, and 1 more received only 2 doses.
key_findings.note: So 2 of the 10 animals given the regimen died. The authors' 2003 reply to critics stated that one of ten monkeys had died (card sc_mithoefer_2003); the report itself describes two deaths in two species.

key_findings.finding: The report claimed lasting reductions in brain serotonin, 5-HIAA and the serotonin transporter, and a larger loss of striatal dopamine markers, with the animal that received only two doses showing caudate dopamine -65%, DOPAC -77% and dopamine transporter -51% at 6 weeks, alongside serotonin -37%, 5-HIAA -48% and serotonin transporter -40%.
key_findings.note: These figures describe animals that, as the 2003 notice states, received methamphetamine; they are recorded only as what the report claimed.

key_findings.finding: Silver staining 3.5 days after dosing was reported to show argyrophilic debris characteristic of terminal degeneration in the striatum, with a glial response in adjacent sections, and no such debris in a control animal; noradrenaline markers were reported unaffected in both species.

The report concluded that people who use repeated doses over several hours are at high risk of severe brain dopaminergic injury, that this could put them at increased risk of parkinsonism later in life, and that cognitive problems in people who use ecstasy might be dopaminergic rather than serotonergic in origin.
The report argued that the individual doses used were lower than those people typically take (1.6 to 2.4 mg/kg) once adjusted by interspecies dose scaling, citing a pharmacokinetics text.
key_findings.note: In the 2003 exchange in Science the same authors replied to critics that interspecies scaling had not been used in these studies; the two statements cannot both be right.

reporting_issues.issue: The compound given was not verified before publication; the identity of the drug is the one measurement on which everything in the report depends.
reporting_issues.consequence: The report is retracted; nothing in it bears on MDMA.

reporting_issues.issue: A regimen that killed 2 of 10 animals and that 2 more could not complete is described as modelling a dose regimen commonly used by people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mortality is reported in the text but not carried into the conclusions, and it was the first point the published critics raised (card sc_mithoefer_2003).

reporting_issues.issue: The claim that the doses were lower than human doses after interspecies scaling conflicts with the authors' later statement that interspecies scaling was not used.
reporting_issues.consequence: The human-relevance argument in the report cannot be reconciled with the authors' own later account.

reporting_issues.issue: Group data appear almost entirely in figures, with numbers given in the text only for the single animal that received two doses.
reporting_issues.consequence: Even setting the retraction aside, the report's quantitative claims could not be checked from the text; figures were not read for values here.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 2260-2263 (the full report text; figures are images and no values were read from them; the supporting online material was not read)

design_detail: Retraction notice, not a study: a letter headed 'Retraction' in Science 2003;301:1479 (12 September 2003), by Ricaurte, Yuan, Hatzidimitriou, Cord and McCann, withdrawing their report of severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity in primates after a common recreational dose regimen of MDMA (Science 2002;297:2260-2263). About 600 words, no data tables. The brief asked for a card of design 'commentary'; the schema has no such value, so 'narrative-review' is used, as for the three 2024 retraction notices already carded, and the choice is flagged for the senior author's open decision on a design for notices (SENIOR-DECISIONS item 29(5)).
can_establish: That the 2002 report was retracted by its authors on 12 September 2003; the reason they gave (a labelling error, so that all but one animal received methamphetamine rather than MDMA); the evidence they give for it (analyses of frozen brains from two animals that died and of the bottle labelled methamphetamine, by three independent laboratories, with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry); the sequence that led them to check (failure to extend the finding to oral dosing, then failure to reproduce it with a new batch of authenticated MDMA); and what the authors say the error does and does not call into question.
cannot_establish: What any animal in the study actually received beyond the labelling error (the original sample was depleted and the bottle labelled MDMA discarded); which animal received MDMA or what it showed; whether other publications from the same supply were affected; whether MDMA damages dopamine neurons in primates or people, which the notice explicitly leaves open; and whether any institutional investigation followed, which the notice does not mention.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (retraction notice).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not applicable.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Not applicable.

exposure.measurement: The notice reports the exposure checks done after publication: gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of brains frozen from two animals that died shortly after dosing, and of the bottle labelled '(+)-methamphetamine HCl', each by three independent laboratories.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not restated in the notice.
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry and other analytical techniques, as described in the notice.
outcomes.operationalization: The outcome is the identity of the compound given.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None.
analysis.selective_reporting: The notice does not say which animal received MDMA, what that animal showed, how many animals were in each affected study, whether other publications used the same supply, or whether any investigation followed.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The authors withdraw the 2002 report because the drug given to all but one animal came from a bottle labelled MDMA that contained methamphetamine, established by analysis of two animals' brains, which contained methamphetamine and amphetamine and no trace of MDMA or MDA, and of the bottle labelled methamphetamine, which was found to contain MDMA.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The notice states that the labelling error does not call into question earlier studies of the serotonin neurotoxic potential of MDMA in several species, that dose regimens in the range used by some people but not yet tested might still produce dopamine neurotoxicity in primates as they do in rodents, that lasting effects of MDMA on dopaminergic function in humans have been reported and that some people with a history of MDMA use have developed parkinsonism, and that the possibility remains uncertain until it can be examined more fully. These are the authors' own statements about what remains open, not findings.

timeline.event: The report is published in Science (27 September) and widely covered
Published criticism and reply in Science (6 June), three months before the retraction
This notice (12 September).
Case study of newspaper coverage: 26 of 50 large US newspapers covered the publication and 20 the retraction

replication.where_it_stands: The retraction stands; the 2002 report is cited only to document it (METHODS §3.2). The notice's own statement that the dopamine question in primates remains open has not been resolved by any later primate study read for this page.

funding.funder: Not stated in the notice; the retracted report was funded by US Public Health Service grants.
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated.
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Neurology, Neurosciences and Psychiatry, Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center.

what_would_settle_it: For the record itself, nothing further is needed. For the open question the notice names, a new primate study with independently verified drug, pre-specified outcomes and blinded assessment, and a systematic search of human dopamine imaging since 2003.

domains.note: Not a review: the notice reports the authors' own withdrawal of one paper, so nothing is selected.
The notice asserts that earlier serotonin studies are unaffected and cites them, but gives no account of which other work used the same supply or over what period.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The authors are the authors of the retracted paper and of most of the work they say is unaffected.

The analytical findings are stated plainly, but the closing paragraph adds unquantified statements about lasting dopaminergic effects in humans and cases of parkinsonism, citing references not examined here.

domains.domain: Balance of the account of what the error affects (the possibility that other work was affected is under-represented)
domains.note: The notice says the error does not call the serotonin literature into question, without describing how far the mislabelled supply reached.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a retraction notice; the editors' narrative-review checklist is used as the closest available, its domains read as questions about the notice as a source. It is the primary record of the retraction and its stated grounds and may be cited for both; its claims about what the error leaves untouched are the authors' own.

key_findings.finding: The authors retract their 2002 report after discovering that the drug used to treat all but one animal came from a bottle that contained (+)-methamphetamine instead of the intended (+/-)MDMA, and note that methamphetamine would be expected to produce the combined dopaminergic and serotonergic pattern they reported.
The retracted report drew on studies done in their laboratory over about 2 years in two species of non-human primates.

The sequence that led to the discovery: they could not extend the dopamine finding to oral dosing; repeated attempts to reproduce it with systemically given MDMA identical to the original regimen failed under a variety of conditions; they then noticed that the failed replications used a new batch of MDMA, authenticated by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry.

Laboratory records showed that the two bottles had been requested from the supplier on the same date, were for the same amount (10 g), were processed by the supplier on the same day and delivered on the same day with different affixed labels, the same delivery reference number and different batch numbers; both were stored in their original containers in a locked safe.
When the bottle labelled '(+)-methamphetamine HCl' was analysed by three independent laboratories, it was found to consist of MDMA with no evidence of even trace amounts of methamphetamine.

The original sample was depleted and the empty bottle labelled MDMA discarded; frozen brains from two animals that died shortly after dosing were analysed by three independent laboratories and contained methamphetamine and its metabolite amphetamine, neither of which is a metabolite of MDMA, with no trace of MDMA or MDA.

Review of the laboratory records showed that all but one animal in the study had been treated with drug from the bottle labelled MDMA, which had been processed on the same date as the bottle labelled methamphetamine.
key_findings.note: The notice does not identify the one animal that received MDMA or report what that animal showed.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the labelling error does not call into question earlier studies demonstrating the serotonin neurotoxic potential of MDMA in several species, including non-human primates.

They add that it remains possible that dose regimens in the range of those used by some people, but different from those tested so far, produce dopamine neurotoxicity in primates as they do in rodents; that lasting effects of MDMA on dopaminergic function in humans have recently been reported and that some people with a history of MDMA use have developed parkinsonism; and that the possibility remains uncertain until the dopamine neurotoxic potential of MDMA in primates can be examined more fully.
key_findings.note: The supporting citations (their references 9-14) were not read here; the statement is recorded as the authors' own.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice does not say which animal received MDMA, what that animal showed, or how many animals were affected in each of the studies spanning about 2 years.
reporting_issues.consequence: The one uncontaminated data point in the programme is unreported, so nothing survives from the report even in principle.

reporting_issues.issue: It asserts that earlier serotonin studies are unaffected without saying when the mislabelled supply was received or which other work used it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot judge the scope of the error from the notice; a request for an investigation of the laboratory's work since the supply arrived is recorded in the media case study (card sc_barnett_2021), not here.

reporting_issues.issue: The notice gives no account of how the mislabelling arose at the supplier or in the laboratory beyond the delivery records, and names no corrective measure.
reporting_issues.consequence: It documents the error without documenting its handling; the project records it as the primary source for the fact and the stated grounds of the retraction only.

verification.source_read: PDF, p. 1479 (the whole notice, read in the text extraction and checked on the rendered page; the remaining pages of the PDF are unrelated Science letters and were not read)

design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (British Journal of Psychiatry 2009;194:355-359) at Hammersmith Hospital, London, comparing serotonin transporter binding with [11C]DASB and arterial input in three groups of men: 12 who had used MDMA on at least 25 occasions but not in the past year, 9 who used a range of other recreational drugs and had never used MDMA, and 19 who reported no illicit drug use. Binding potential was derived from the total distribution volume relative to cerebellum in 10 regions and compared by repeated-measures analysis of variance with age as covariate.
can_establish: That in these 40 men, transporter binding in the regions measured did not differ significantly between men who had stopped using MDMA at least a year earlier, men who used other drugs and men who used none, and that no variable of MDMA use correlated with binding.
cannot_establish: Whether binding had ever been lower in these men (no earlier scan and no group of people currently using MDMA); whether cortical binding is normal in regions other than frontal cortex (only frontal cortex was analysed, because of low signal); whether the groups are equivalent (a non-significant test in 12 against 19 people, with no regional values or intervals printed); or anything about women.

sample.recruitment: Newspaper or magazine advertisement and word of mouth; diagnostic assessment by psychiatrists using the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (p. 355).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Men aged 25-60; no psychotropic medication; no major psychiatric or neurological problem; no history of drug dependence; no more than three units of alcohol in the 24 h before testing; no recreational drug use for at least 3 days before testing. MDMA group: at least 25 occasions of use, none for at least 1 year. Two people were excluded after hair analysis was positive for MDMA (p. 355).
sample.demographics: Men only. Mean age: no illicit drug use 30.5 (range 25-45), formerly used MDMA 28.2 (25-36), other drugs 35.6 (25-50); the groups differed (p=0.03), so age was a covariate. No group differences in depression, anxiety, neuroticism or premorbid IQ (p>0.2) (pp. 356-357).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one scan per person); 2 people excluded before analysis for MDMA-positive hair.
sample.selection_effects: Men who had stopped using MDMA and volunteered for a study a year or more later; people who went on to heavier use or developed problems are less likely to be in such a sample, and the groups were recruited separately rather than followed.

exposure.measurement: Semi-structured drug-history interview; urine screen on the scan day for MDMA, cocaine, amphetamine, opiates and benzodiazepines; hair samples covering a mean of 2.7 months (SD 0.9) tested for MDMA, cocaine and amphetamine, with two MDMA-positive people excluded (pp. 355-356).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Former MDMA group: mean 243.75 lifetime occasions (SD 244.4, range 60-864), 2.75 tablets in a typical session (1.9, range 1-8), 4.75 use days a month, 4.33 years of regular use, first use at 18.1 years (Table 1, p. 356).
exposure.polysubstance: Both drug-using groups continued to use other drugs and were matched on them: cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine and LSD use did not differ between the MDMA and polydrug groups, with or without correction for multiple comparisons (Table 1, p. 356; Results, p. 357).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 3 days from recreational drugs, with urine and hair screening; mean time since last MDMA 2.74 years (SD 1.46; range given in days as 390-1825) (Table 1, p. 356).

comparison.controls: Two comparison groups: 9 men using a range of recreational drugs but never MDMA, and 19 men reporting no illicit drug use, of whom a random half gave urine and hair samples (pp. 355-356).
comparison.matching: The two drug-using groups were matched on reported drug and alcohol use; age differed across the three groups and was used as a covariate.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; the paper notes that a retrospective design cannot control for pre-existing differences (p. 357).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The polydrug group used cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine and LSD at rates similar to the MDMA group; the drug-naive group reported none.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB PET on a high-sensitivity scanner, 90-min dynamic scan, arterial plasma input with metabolite correction, total distribution volume by graphical analysis, binding potential as the ratio to cerebellum; regions defined on co-registered MRI with a probabilistic atlas: amygdala, caudate, anterior and posterior cingulate, dorsal raphe, frontal cortex, hippocampus, insula, putamen, thalamus (pp. 356-357).
outcomes.validity_norms: [11C]DASB is selective for the transporter; the authors restrict cortical analysis to frontal cortex because of the low signal-to-noise ratio in neocortex. No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: Integrity of serotonin neurons is operationalized as regional binding potential; 'no long-term damage' as the absence of a significant group difference.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not needed for the primary analysis, which is a single repeated-measures model across regions; no regional post-hoc tests are reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Repeated-measures analysis of variance with age as covariate: main effect of brain region F=7.84 (df 9,324, p=0.002), no main effect of group (F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31) and no region-by-group interaction (F=0.36, df 18,324, p=0.81); no effect of age (F=0.18, p=0.66). Cerebellar distribution volume did not differ (F=0.76, p=0.47), nor did injected dose or specific activity. No significant correlations between any variable of MDMA use and binding. The paper reports no regional means, differences or confidence intervals: the only regional data are the bar chart of Figure 1. A power statement says the study could have detected a 15-20% difference in binding potential in most regions at 80% power with p<0.05.
analysis.selective_reporting: Group results are reported only as a figure; the text gives no regional estimates, so a reader cannot see how close to or far from equality the groups were.
analysis.power: Stated as sufficient to detect a 15-20% difference in most regions at 80% power (p. 357); no observed effect sizes or intervals are given to check this, and the claim rests on unpublished variance estimates.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 12 men who had not used MDMA for at least a year, transporter binding did not differ significantly from that of 9 men who used other drugs or 19 men who used none, in 10 regions of which only one was neocortical.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the findings suggest MDMA use 'may not result in long-term damage to serotonin neurons when used recreationally in humans' (abstract, p. 355). The Discussion offers the alternative that binding recovered during abstinence and favours it, citing other studies. Neither can be distinguished here: there is no earlier measurement in these men, no group currently using MDMA and no equivalence analysis, and the one cortical region measured is not among those where other studies find the largest differences.

timeline.event: Lower binding in people abstinent on average 5 months, with a positive relation to months abstinent
Lower cortical and hippocampal binding at a median of 38 days of abstinence, with no relation to time since last use
Lower binding with a positive relation to days since last use in subcortical regions but not neocortex
Independent study noting that this study had no group of people currently using MDMA, so recovery cannot be inferred from it
Review counts this study among the evidence that binding recovers after abstinence

replication.where_it_stands: This is the only [11C]DASB study of people who had stopped, and the only one of six not to find lower cortical binding; whether that is recovery or a difference between samples is unresolved, since no study has scanned the same people during use and after long abstinence.

funding.funder: Medical Research Council; one author supported by an MRC studentship (Funding, p. 359).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declared: one author has received occasional consultancy from GlaxoSmithKline, Merck, Pfizer and GE Healthcare; one is an MRC clinical scientist; one is a GlaxoSmithKline employee and shareholder; one has served on speakers' panels for BMS, AstraZeneca and Janssen (p. 355).
funding.affiliations_note: MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, Hammersmith Hospital, with Oxford and University College London; the regions of interest were taken from the Baltimore group's earlier study.

what_would_settle_it: Scanning the same people while they are using MDMA and again after a year or more without it, with the occipital and temporal cortex included, and reporting regional estimates with intervals so that a null result can be read as equivalence rather than as absence of significance.

domains.note: Age differed between groups and was covaried; the polydrug comparison group addresses other drug use better than most studies in this field, but the groups are small and other confounders are not adjusted.

Lifetime occasions are self-reported; hair testing covered about 2.7 months and excluded two people with MDMA-positive hair, which supports the claim of abstinence but says nothing about historical doses.
Men only, recruited by advertisement a year or more after stopping; people with ongoing problems are unlikely to be represented, and the group that stopped may differ from those who continued.
None.
Complete scans in all analysed participants.
Fully quantitative PET with arterial input, but only frontal cortex among neocortical regions, and the regions most affected in other studies (occipital, temporal) were not analysed.
No regional estimates or intervals are printed; the result is reported as a figure and a non-significant omnibus test, which makes the stated power claim uncheckable.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A null result from a small cross-sectional study whose regional values are not reported. It can be cited for the absence of a detectable group difference in men abstinent for at least a year, in the regions measured, and not for equivalence, for recovery, or for the neocortical regions it did not analyse.

key_findings.finding: No group effect on transporter binding (F=1.22, df 2,36, p=0.31) and no region-by-group interaction (F=0.36, df 18,324, p=0.81); the only significant term was brain region (F=7.84, df 9,324, p=0.002).
Cerebellar distribution volume, injected dose and specific activity did not differ between groups (p=0.47, 0.13, 0.93), so the null result is not explained by tracer delivery.
No variable of MDMA use (lifetime occasions, typical session dose, duration, time since last use) correlated with binding.

The 12 men who had stopped had used MDMA on a mean of 244 occasions (SD 244, range 60-864), about 2.75 tablets per session, for a mean of 4.33 years, and had last used it a mean of 2.74 years earlier (SD 1.46).
Cortical analysis was restricted to the frontal cortex because of the low signal-to-noise ratio of [11C]DASB in neocortex.
key_findings.locator: Method, 'Magnetic resonance scans and definition of volumes of interest', last paragraph
key_findings.note: Occipital and temporal cortex, where other [11C]DASB studies report the largest reductions, were not measured.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the study could have detected a 15-20% difference in binding potential in most regions at 80% power.
key_findings.note: No regional estimates, standard deviations or intervals are printed, so this cannot be checked; the only regional data are Figure 1, a bar chart with within-group standard deviations.

key_findings.finding: The groups did not differ in depression, anxiety, neuroticism or premorbid IQ (all p>0.2), and the two drug-using groups did not differ in cannabis, amphetamine, cocaine, LSD or alcohol use.

reporting_issues.issue: The one-way analyses of variance (age, cerebellar distribution volume, injected dose, specific activity) are reported with 2 and 39 degrees of freedom, which implies 42 participants, while the sample described is 40 (12 + 9 + 19) and the repeated-measures analyses use 2 and 36.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either two further people (perhaps the two excluded after MDMA-positive hair) were included in these tests, or the degrees of freedom are wrong; the group comparison of age, which justified using age as a covariate, is affected.

reporting_issues.issue: No regional means, group differences or confidence intervals are reported anywhere in the paper; Figure 1 is the only source of regional values.
reporting_issues.consequence: A null finding cannot be read as equivalence without estimates and intervals; the paper's own power claim cannot be checked, and later sources can only record 'no difference'.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives time since last MDMA use as a mean in years with the range in days (390-1825, by footnote).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the range corresponds to about 1.1 to 5 years, consistent with the inclusion criterion.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion that MDMA 'may not result in long-term damage' is drawn from a null result in 12 men, while the Discussion prefers the opposite explanation, that binding had recovered.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract and the Discussion point in different directions; the study cannot distinguish them, since no one was scanned while using.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 355-359 plus the data supplement page (all pages; Figure 1 inspected on the rendered page 358 and no values read from it)

design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (Neuropsychopharmacology 2012;37:1465-1473) at Columbia University comparing presynaptic serotonin transporter binding ([11C]DASB) and postsynaptic 5-HT2A receptor binding ([11C]MDL 100907) in 13 people who used ecstasy regularly and 13 matched people who did not. Both scans were acquired, where possible on the same day, with arterial input functions and a two-tissue compartment model; binding potential (BPND) was compared in 17 regions drawn on each person's MRI, with a linear mixed model across all regions, cortical regions and subcortical regions, and a voxel-wise analysis for confirmation.
can_establish: That in this sample, after at least 2 weeks of monitored abstinence, transporter binding was lower and 5-HT2A receptor binding higher in the ecstasy group across cortical regions but not subcortical ones, that the two changes were largest in the same regions, and that non-specific binding (cerebellar distribution volume) did not differ, so the comparison is not an artefact of tracer delivery.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused either difference (cross-sectional, 13 people per group, other drug use allowed); that the percentage reductions are meaningful in cortex, where binding in both groups is near zero; that abstinence restores binding (no relation with length of abstinence, in a sample with a narrow range); or that the changes mean loss of terminals rather than lower transporter expression, as the authors state.

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond approval by the New York State Psychiatric Institute review board and written informed consent; diagnoses assessed with the PRISM and/or SCID (Subjects and Methods, 1st-3rd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ecstasy group: at least 15 lifetime uses and regular use for at least 12 months before enrollment; occasional use of other drugs permitted; 2 weeks' abstinence from all drugs before scanning, monitored twice weekly by urine toxicology and confirmed on the scan day; use in the previous 3 months confirmed by hair analysis. Excluded: any other lifetime Axis I disorder, current substance abuse or dependence other than alcohol or nicotine, past cannabis abuse permitted. Comparison group: same criteria, no Axis I diagnoses and no substance abuse or dependence (Subjects and Methods, 2nd-3rd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group: 8 men, 5 women, mean age 30.8 (SD 3.8); [11C]DASB comparison group 8 men, 5 women, 27.3 (7.5), p=0.15; [11C]MDL comparison group 9 men, 4 women, 31.1 (10.1). Both groups predominantly white (Table 1).
sample.attrition: Fourteen people who used ecstasy were recruited; one was excluded after the scans because of a technical problem during the receptor scan, leaving 13. Eighteen comparison participants were scanned, of whom 8 had both tracers and 5 had only one; 13 were matched to the ecstasy group for each tracer (Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: A small volunteer sample with a decade of ecstasy use and no psychiatric disorder, which the authors say is hard to find without other drug use; people who develop problems or who use other drugs heavily are excluded by design.

exposure.measurement: Self-report assessed with the PRISM and/or SCID; twice-weekly urine toxicology during the 2-week abstinence and on the scan day; hair analysis confirming use in the previous 3 months (Subjects and Methods, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime sessions mean 142, median 50, range 15-1050; duration of use mean 93 months, median 84, range 4-216; frequency mean 1.9 sessions a month, median 0.8, range 0.3-6.3. Doses per session are not reported (Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: All 13 used alcohol regularly and 2 met criteria for alcohol abuse or dependence; 10 of 13 used cannabis regularly; 6 were smokers; 5 had more than 10 lifetime exposures to hallucinogens; more than 10 lifetime exposures to cocaine in 1, ketamine 1, amphetamine 3, opiates 1 (Results, 3rd paragraph). The authors discuss that lower binding has been reported in people who use methamphetamine and that 3 of their participants had used amphetamine (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks monitored; mean 5.7 weeks, median 8, range 2-8 weeks (Results, 2nd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Healthy people matched by age, ethnicity and gender, with no DSM-IV Axis I diagnosis and no substance abuse or dependence (Subjects and Methods, 3rd paragraph).
comparison.matching: Matched on age, ethnicity and gender; not matched on cannabis, alcohol or tobacco use, which were much higher in the ecstasy group (6 smokers versus 1).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measurement; the authors note that lower cortical serotonin function could predispose to use and that their design cannot refute this (Discussion, 5th paragraph).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded for any substance abuse or dependence; only one was a smoker.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB (100-min scan) and [11C]MDL 100907 (90-min scan) PET on an ECAT EXACT HR+, with arterial input functions, two-tissue compartment modelling and BPND as outcome; regions drawn on each person's MRI by published criteria; simplified reference tissue analysis as a check; voxel-wise confirmation with 12-mm smoothing (Subjects and Methods, 4th-7th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Both tracers are selective; the authors note that cortical transporter binding is very low, so the specific signal is small, and that no group difference in cerebellar distribution volume validates the use of BPND. No normative values.
outcomes.operationalization: Presynaptic integrity as transporter BPND; postsynaptic adaptation as 5-HT2A BPND; the hypothesis is a fall in the first and a rise in the second.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None applied to the 17 regional comparisons per tracer; the authors state that no pairwise regional comparison survives correction for multiple comparisons and rest their conclusion on the mixed model (Results, 6th and 9th paragraphs).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: Transporter binding: lower in the ecstasy group across all regions (F=27.07, p<0.001) and across cortical regions (F=25.65, p<0.001), not subcortical (F=1.99, p=0.16), with no region-by-group interaction. Regional BPND (ecstasy versus comparison group, Table 1): occipital -0.01 (SD 0.08) versus 0.10 (0.11), p=0.01; medial prefrontal 0.07 (0.05) versus 0.13 (0.08), p=0.04; temporal 0.07 (0.09) versus 0.15 (0.09), p=0.04; parietal 0.00 (0.05) versus 0.04 (0.07), p=0.09; dorsolateral prefrontal 0.01 (0.06) versus 0.06 (0.09), p=0.16; caudate 0.77 (0.18) versus 0.77 (0.15), p=0.99; putamen 1.21 (0.33) versus 1.19 (0.16), p=0.86; thalamus 0.94 (0.22) versus 0.99 (0.15), p=0.53; midbrain 1.97 (0.56) versus 1.95 (0.39), p=0.92; hippocampus 0.31 (0.15) versus 0.32 (0.09), p=0.97. Editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g with 95% interval): occipital -1.11 (-1.98 to -0.31), medial prefrontal -0.87 (-1.71 to -0.09), temporal -0.86 (-1.70 to -0.08), thalamus -0.26 (-1.04 to 0.51), hippocampus -0.08 (-0.85 to 0.69), caudate 0.00 (-0.77 to 0.77). 5-HT2A receptor binding: higher across all regions (F=12.73, p<0.001), cortical (F=14.55, p<0.001) and subcortical (F=7.38, p=0.007); dorsolateral prefrontal 2.48 (0.47) versus 2.13 (0.33), p=0.04 (editors' calculation g 0.83, 0.06 to 1.67); parietal 2.38 (0.49) versus 2.00 (0.38), p=0.03 (g 0.84, 0.06 to 1.67). Across the seven cortical regions, the size of the receptor difference tracked the size of the transporter difference (r2=0.54, p=0.057). Correlations with use: dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal transporter binding with lifetime uses r=-0.46 (p=0.12) and -0.46 (p=0.11); with duration of use, occipital r=-0.47 (p=0.12) and parietal -0.44 (p=0.14); none significant, and none with duration of abstinence.
analysis.covariates: None reported; no adjustment for smoking, cannabis or alcohol.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 17 regions are tabulated for both tracers, including the null subcortical results and the non-significant correlations.
analysis.power: Not reported; the authors list the small sample as a weakness and note that the narrow range of abstinence may explain the absence of a relation with abstinence (Discussion, 3rd and 8th paragraphs).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 13 people with about 8 years of ecstasy use and 2 to 8 weeks of monitored abstinence, cortical transporter binding was lower and cortical 5-HT2A binding higher than in 13 matched people, with subcortical transporter binding unchanged; no regional comparison survives correction, and the two changes were largest in the same regions.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that, in light of the animal literature, 'the most parsimonious interpretation' is that repeated exposure in humans, even in moderate amounts, 'leads to damage in 5-HT neuron terminals innervating the cortex'. The data are a cross-sectional difference in two binding measures in 13 people; the Discussion itself says that PET cannot determine whether lower binding is loss of terminals or down-regulation, and that a predisposing difference cannot be refuted.

timeline.event: First [11C]DASB study with the same cortical pattern
Largest [11C]DASB study, same cortical pattern, normal striatum
Study with the same tracer finding cortical and some subcortical reductions and no 5-HT2A difference with a different receptor tracer
No difference in men abstinent at least a year, with no current-use group for comparison
Review notes that the very large percentage reductions reported here follow from near-zero cortical binding values

replication.where_it_stands: The fifth of five [11C]DASB studies in people currently using ecstasy to find lower cortical binding, as the paper's own Table 2 sets out; its 5-HT2A finding is the opposite of the altanserin result in the Copenhagen study, which the authors attribute to more hallucinogen use in that sample.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01 DA015806-02; the work was carried out at the New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University Medical Center (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Declared in full: five authors report no support beyond their employers; others report consultancy or research support from ONO, Sunovion, Lilly, Amgen, Pfizer, GlaxoSmithKline, Pierre Fabre, Bristol-Myers Squibb-Otsuka, Boehringer-Ingelheim, Lundbeck, Otsuka, Shire, Merck and Forest (Acknowledgments).
funding.affiliations_note: Columbia University; no author is from the Baltimore or Toronto groups whose results are being confirmed.

what_would_settle_it: A longitudinal study of the same people during use and after long abstinence, with both tracers and a comparison group matched on cannabis, alcohol and tobacco, large enough that regional differences survive correction.

domains.note: The ecstasy group drank, smoked and used cannabis far more; no covariates were used, and the groups are too small for adjustment.
Hair analysis confirms recent use and urine confirms abstinence, but lifetime sessions are self-reported and range from 15 to 1050, and doses per session are not reported.
Thirteen volunteers with a decade of use and no psychiatric disorder, compared with people screened to have no substance problems; no pre-use measurement.
None beyond the required abstinence.
One participant excluded for a technical failure; the control group differs in composition between the two tracers, which the table footnote states.

Fully quantitative PET with arterial input and two selective tracers; cortical transporter binding is near zero in both groups, so the measure has little room and percentage changes are uninformative.
All regions reported, but 34 regional comparisons without correction; the paper states that none of the regional differences survives correction.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, technically careful study whose group difference is robust at the level of the mixed model but not at the level of any single region. It can be cited for the cortical pattern of lower transporter and higher 5-HT2A binding, and for the absence of subcortical differences, not for causation, for a quantitative size of the cortical reduction, or for the absence of a relation with abstinence.

key_findings.finding: Transporter binding was lower in the ecstasy group over all regions (F=27.07, p<0.001) and over cortical regions (F=25.65, p<0.001), but not over subcortical regions (F=1.99, p=0.16), with no region-by-group interaction.

Region by region, binding was significantly lower in occipital (-0.01 vs 0.10, p=0.01), medial prefrontal (0.07 vs 0.13, p=0.04) and temporal cortex (0.07 vs 0.15, p=0.04), and no regional comparison survived correction for multiple comparisons; in several cortical regions the ecstasy group's specific binding could not be detected at all.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed means and SDs (Hedges g, 95% interval): occipital -1.11 (-1.98 to -0.31), medial prefrontal -0.87 (-1.71 to -0.09), temporal -0.86 (-1.70 to -0.08).

key_findings.finding: Subcortical binding was the same in both groups: caudate 0.77 vs 0.77 (p=0.99), putamen 1.21 vs 1.19 (p=0.86), thalamus 0.94 vs 0.99 (p=0.53), midbrain 1.97 vs 1.95 (p=0.92), hippocampus 0.31 vs 0.32 (p=0.97).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: thalamus g -0.26 (-1.04 to 0.51), hippocampus -0.08 (-0.85 to 0.69), caudate 0.00 (-0.77 to 0.77); the intervals are wide, so these nulls bound rather than exclude a difference.

key_findings.finding: 5-HT2A receptor binding was higher in the ecstasy group over all regions (F=12.73, p<0.001), cortical (F=14.55, p<0.001) and subcortical (F=7.38, p=0.007), reaching significance region by region in dorsolateral prefrontal (2.48 vs 2.13, p=0.04) and parietal cortex (2.38 vs 2.00, p=0.03), neither surviving correction.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: dorsolateral prefrontal g 0.83 (0.06 to 1.67), parietal 0.84 (0.06 to 1.67).

key_findings.finding: Across the seven cortical regions, the regions with the largest fall in transporter binding had the largest rise in 5-HT2A binding (r2=0.54, p=0.057, 5 degrees of freedom); the two medial regions changed least on both measures.
key_findings.locator: Results, 10th paragraph; Figure 4 and its caption

key_findings.finding: No correlation between binding and any use variable reached significance, including duration of abstinence; the closest were transporter binding with lifetime uses in dorsolateral prefrontal and parietal cortex (both r=-0.46, p=0.12 and 0.11) and with duration of use in occipital (-0.47, p=0.12) and parietal cortex (-0.44, p=0.14).

Cerebellar distribution volume did not differ between groups for either tracer (9.7 vs 10.1 ml/g, p=0.63; 19.2 vs 20.4, p=0.46), which the authors give as validation of using BPND for a between-group comparison.

The ecstasy group reported a mean of 142 lifetime sessions (median 50, range 15-1050) over a mean of 93 months (median 84), at 1.9 sessions a month, and had been abstinent 5.7 weeks on average (median 8, range 2-8).

The paper's own summary of the five [11C]DASB studies in people currently using ecstasy records lower cortical binding in all five, unchanged striatum in four of five and unchanged midbrain in all five, with the only study of people who had stopped (12 men) showing no difference anywhere.

reporting_issues.issue: The accounting of the comparison group does not add up: 18 people were scanned, 8 with both tracers and 5 with only one, which is 13, yet 13 are reported for each tracer and the footnote says five in each control group differed between tracers.
reporting_issues.consequence: The identity of the 13 controls per tracer, and what became of the remaining 5 of the 18, cannot be reconstructed from the paper; the two tracer comparisons are not independent, since 8 people appear in both.

reporting_issues.issue: Cortical transporter binding potentials are at or below zero in the ecstasy group (occipital -0.01, orbitofrontal 0.00, parietal 0.00), so percentage reductions computed from them are not interpretable.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2016 review that tabulates this study reports reductions of 83% to 100% in these regions from exactly these values; the absolute differences (0.04 to 0.11 binding-potential units) are the only interpretable statement.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion attributes the original finding of a large global reduction to a 1995 methods paper on the radiotracer rather than to the 1998 study that reported it.
reporting_issues.consequence: A citation error; the finding in question is McCann et al. (1998), which the same paragraph cites correctly earlier.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's conclusion that the most parsimonious interpretation is damage to cortical serotonin terminals is stronger than the Discussion, which states that PET cannot distinguish terminal loss from down-regulation and that a predisposing difference cannot be refuted.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract is the part most often cited; its causal reading is not supported by the design.

reporting_issues.issue: Thirty-four regional comparisons are reported without correction, and the paper says none survives it, yet the regional results are presented in the abstract as significant differences in cortical regions.
reporting_issues.consequence: The mixed-model result is the defensible finding; individual regional p-values of 0.03 to 0.04 should not be quoted as established.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3327851 (whole article including Tables 1 and 2, read in a tab opened by this reader; Figures 1-4 are images and no values were read from them)

design_detail: Review with a stated search and explicit selection criteria (Psychopharmacology 2016;233:3473-3501), read as the PubMed Central full text. One database (PubMed) searched to 14 November 2015 with a PICO-derived string; 88 records found, 33 included after applying inclusion criteria (in vivo imaging of a neurotransmitter system; a comparison group naive to MDMA or a baseline measurement before use) and exclusion criteria (case reports, reviews, single-challenge studies, re-analyses of published data). Data were extracted into tables by receptor or transporter, and the reviewers themselves computed percentage differences and Cohen's d from printed means and standard deviations where possible. No risk-of-bias assessment, no protocol, no meta-analysis.
can_establish: What the molecular imaging literature up to late 2015 contains and how it distributes: which studies measured which marker, in how many people, with which radioligand and after what abstinence, together with the reviewers' own calculations of percentage change and effect size for each comparison, and the authors' count that 14 of 16 human transporter studies found a significant reduction and that human dopamine studies mostly found none.
cannot_establish: Whether the included studies are sound (none was appraised); whether lower binding means neurotoxicity, which the review says repeatedly cannot be settled by imaging; the size of any pooled effect (no meta-analysis); or whether binding recovers within a person, since every 'recovery' study it cites compares different people or different groups at one time.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (review of published studies). Participants in the human studies included range, as the review states, from 14 to 116 people per study.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: in vivo imaging findings on a neurotransmitter system, with a comparison group naive to MDMA or a baseline measurement in an MDMA-naive state. Excluded: case reports and reviews, studies giving MDMA as a single challenge, and re-evaluations of previously published data (Methodology, 'Selection of studies').
sample.attrition: Not applicable; the flow from 88 records to 33 included studies is shown only in Figure 1, which is an image and was not read.
sample.selection_effects: One database and no grey literature or registry search, so unpublished null findings cannot enter; the inclusion rule requiring an MDMA-naive comparison excludes within-person designs without a naive baseline.

exposure.measurement: As reported by each included study; the review tabulates the exposure check for every human study (self-report, urine screening, hair analysis) and the minimum abstinence required (Tables 2-10).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Tabulated per study. For context the review states that a Dutch ecstasy tablet contained about 138 mg of MDMA, which it converts to 2-4 mg/kg in a person of 70 kg, and that animal studies used 20-141 mg/kg, mostly twice daily for 4 days, usually intraperitoneally (Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter').
exposure.polysubstance: Treated as a central problem: the review devotes a section to it, concluding from two studies that cannabis, cocaine and hallucinogen use do not appear to change the transporter findings, and showing with a dopamine study that a significant difference against drug-naive controls disappeared against polydrug controls (Discussion, 'MDMA and additional drug use').

comparison.controls: Varies by study: drug-naive controls, polydrug controls who had not used MDMA, or the same people before use.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The review notes that almost all human studies are cross-sectional and cannot exclude premorbid differences; only the Dutch prospective cohort had pre-use measurements.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Tabulated per study; the review repeatedly stresses that a polydrug comparison group is needed and that findings can disappear when one is used.

outcomes.instruments: SPECT and PET imaging of the serotonin transporter ([123I]beta-CIT, [11C]McN5652, [11C]DASB, [18F]ADAM), 5-HT2A receptor, 5-HT1A receptor, serotonin synthesis ([11C]AMT), vesicular monoamine transporter, dopamine D2/3 receptor and release, dopamine transporter and decarboxylase activity ([18F]dopa).
outcomes.validity_norms: Discussed at length: the review explains that [123I]beta-CIT binds both the dopamine and serotonin transporter so striatal serotonin binding cannot be assessed with it, that ratio methods are sensitive to tracer delivery, that scanner resolution causes partial-volume underestimation, and that no PET or SPECT tracer measures toxicity directly.
outcomes.operationalization: Change in receptor or transporter binding, expressed as the percentage difference from the control condition and as Cohen's d, both computed by the reviewers from printed means and standard deviations.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no pooling). The review records which primary studies corrected for multiple comparisons and marks those p-values in its tables.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimate. Counts: 14 of 16 human transporter studies found a significant loss of binding, with effect sizes from -0.05 to -2.17; 9 of 11 animal studies (the Discussion says 10 of 11), with effect sizes from -0.38 to -20.03. Of 10 human studies measuring occipital cortex, 6 found their largest reduction there (effect sizes -0.21 to -2.17); 3 of 4 found lower hippocampal binding; 11 found lower thalamic binding but only 3 significantly. Five human 5-HT2A studies split 3 increases against 2 decreases. One animal and five human dopamine studies found almost nothing: of three dopamine transporter studies one found a 13% increase against polydrug controls (p=0.045, d=2.92) and the other two no difference; decarboxylase activity was 9% higher in the putamen of people who had stopped than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021, d=1.10) but no different from polydrug controls; dopamine D2/3 binding and release did not differ.
analysis.selective_reporting: The tables report all extracted outcomes per study, including non-significant ones, and mark which p-values were corrected for multiplicity.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the review notes that human studies ranged from 14 to 116 participants and animal studies from 1 to 26 animals.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A tabulation of 33 imaging studies: lower serotonin transporter binding in most human studies of heavier ecstasy use, largest in occipital cortex; inconsistent 5-HT2A findings; and no consistent dopamine effect in humans. Several studies report higher binding in people with longer abstinence, all of them comparing different people or different groups.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that in people abstinent from the drug, significant recovery of transporter binding was found over time, and the 'Current knowledge' box states that after 40 to 200 days transporter binding recovers. The 40 days comes from a baboon study and the 200 days from one cross-sectional extrapolation for the pallidostriatum in a study that found no recovery in neocortex; no study followed people over abstinence. The conclusions elsewhere are careful: the review says repeatedly that imaging cannot show whether lower binding is neurotoxicity, and that it is unclear whether any recovery of binding means functionally intact neurons.

timeline.event: A systematic review of neuroimaging in moderate MDMA use (Mueller et al.) found no convincing evidence of neurotoxicity at moderate doses; this review cites it in its introduction.
This review.
A later systematic review and meta-analysis of neurocognitive outcomes after sustained abstinence reaches a different question but overlaps in the primary studies

replication.where_it_stands: The most complete tabulation of molecular imaging in this field that the project has read; it is a catalogue with the reviewers' own effect-size calculations rather than an appraisal, and its headline statements about recovery go beyond the designs it tabulates.

funding.funder: The authors state that they received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication (Funding).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (Conflict of interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of Nuclear Medicine and Radiology, Academic Medical Center, Amsterdam. Two of the three authors are authors of several of the included primary studies (the SPECT studies of 2001 and 2008 and the serotonin-synthesis study of 2014), which the review does not flag.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with two databases or more, duplicate screening and extraction, a risk-of-bias instrument applied to the primary studies, and separate synthesis of within-person designs, so that the recovery question is answered from studies that measured the same people twice rather than from cross-sectional comparisons.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (humans and animals exposed to ecstasy or MDMA), intervention, comparison (MDMA-naive group or pre-use baseline) and outcome (in vivo imaging of a neurotransmitter system) are stated in the Methodology.
No protocol or registration is mentioned.
Animal, human cross-sectional and prospective studies are pooled into the tables without an explanation of the choice of designs.
PubMed only, to 14 November 2015; no second database, no reference-list searching, no grey literature, registries or contact with authors reported.
Not described; the Methodology says only that full-text articles were obtained and criteria applied.
Extracted items are listed but not who extracted them or whether two people did.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Only Figure 1, a flow chart, is offered; it is an image that was not read, and no list of excluded studies with reasons appears in the article.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Tables 2-11 give technique, author, group sizes, inclusion criteria, exposure check, outcomes and the reviewers' effect sizes; setting, funding, recruitment and the exact dose or abstinence of each group are not consistently given.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: No instrument is applied; methodological problems are discussed in general terms in the Limitations.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported for any included study.
No pooling; the reviewers compute per-study percentage changes and Cohen's d only.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No pooled result exists.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Limitations discuss sample sizes, washout, tablet purity and uncorrected multiplicity, but with no risk-of-bias assessment the conclusions treat studies as interchangeable, and the counts of significant findings give each study equal weight.
Sources of variation are discussed at length: radioligand selectivity, quantification method, scanner resolution, abstinence, polydrug use, age at first exposure and sex.
Not investigated or discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: The review reports no funding and no conflicts; it does not note that two authors wrote several included studies.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are not met (no protocol, a one-database search, no list of excluded studies, no risk-of-bias assessment) and publication bias was not investigated. The review is a reliable map of what imaging studies exist and what they reported, and its per-study calculations are useful, but its counts of significant findings carry no weighting by study quality, and its conclusions about recovery go beyond the designs tabulated. Claims may cite it for the shape of the literature and for its own extracted figures, not as evidence for a magnitude.

key_findings.finding: Of 33 included studies, 27 measured the serotonin transporter: 16 in humans, of which 14 found a significant reduction, with effect sizes from -0.05 to -2.17; and 11 in animals, of which the abstract says 9 and the Discussion says 10 were significant, with effect sizes from -0.38 to -20.03.
key_findings.locator: Abstract, Results; Results, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st paragraph; Discussion, 'Serotonin transporter', 1st and 2nd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The counts of significant animal studies differ between the abstract (9 of 11) and the Discussion (10 of 11).

key_findings.finding: Of 10 human studies that measured occipital cortex, 6 found their largest reduction there (effect sizes -0.21 to -2.17); 3 of 4 studies found lower hippocampal binding; 11 studies reported lower thalamic binding but only 3 significantly.

The table of human transporter studies records, among others: Kish et al. (2010), 49 against 50 people, hippocampus -31% and occipital -39%; Erritzoe et al. (2011), neocortex -56%, pallidostriatum -19%, amygdala -32%; McCann et al. (2005), occipital -68% with [11C]DASB and -54% with [11C]McN5652; Selvaraj et al. (2009), no difference; de Win et al. (2008), no significant difference in any region.
key_findings.note: The values listed for Kish et al. are that study's partial-volume-corrected figures, not the uncorrected values its abstract reports (occipital -46%, hippocampus -21%).

key_findings.finding: Five human studies of the 5-HT2A receptor divide 3 increases against 2 decreases, with abstinence ranging from 1.6 to 169.8 weeks, and no consistent relation between receptor binding and time since last use; the review concludes that these findings are inconsistent.

One animal and five human studies of the dopamine system found almost no effect: of three dopamine transporter studies, one reported striatal binding 13% higher than in polydrug controls (p=0.045, d=2.92) and 20% lower in people who also used amphetamines (p=0.007), and two found nothing; decarboxylase activity was 9% higher in the putamen than in drug-naive controls (p=0.021, d=1.10) but no different from polydrug controls; D2/3 binding and dopamine release did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Dopamine system' with Tables 8, 9 and 10; Discussion, 'Dopamine system'
key_findings.note: The authors of the transporter study read their own result as showing that amphetamine use, not MDMA, is associated with lower striatal dopamine transporter binding.

key_findings.finding: The review lists four explanations for lower binding that imaging cannot separate: down-regulation or internalization of the transporter, loss of the neurons expressing it, reduced protein expression, and competition from released neurotransmitter; and states that no PET or SPECT tracer directly assesses toxicity or degeneration.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 'Alteration in receptor binding and neurotoxicity'

key_findings.finding: On recovery, the review cites a baboon study (binding higher 40 days to 9 months after dosing in pons, midbrain and hypothalamus but still low in cortex), two SPECT and PET studies of people who had stopped, a positive correlation with abstinence, and the estimate that pallidostriatal binding returns to normal after about 200 days; it then asks whether recovered binding means functionally intact neurons and notes a study in which memory scores remained low although binding had normalized.

Its 'Current knowledge' box states that heavy use decreases transporter binding and that after 40 to 200 days binding recovers, that the dopamine system does not seem to be affected in humans, and that cannabis, cocaine and hallucinogen use do not seem to influence the transporter findings.

Limitations acknowledged by the authors: no imaging studies of systems other than serotonin and dopamine; small samples (animals 1 to 26, humans 14 to 116); some included studies required only 1 week of abstinence; varying tablet content over the years; and not all studies corrected for multiple comparisons.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 9 of 11 animal transporter studies found a significant loss; the Discussion says all 11 found lower binding and 10 reached significance.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two counts is wrong; the direction of the animal literature is not in doubt, but the figure quoted from this review depends on which sentence is read.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 lists partial-volume-corrected percentages for Kish et al. (2010) (hippocampus -31%, occipital -39%) although that study's primary outcome was the uncorrected measure (hippocampus -21%, occipital -46%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Anyone citing the review for that study's figures will quote the secondary analysis; the editors' claims should take such figures from the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Percentage changes are computed from binding values close to zero: for the prospective SPECT cohort the table gives occipital grey matter -40% from ratios of 0.05 against 0.03 in a study that found no significant difference anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader scanning the table sees a 40% reduction where the study reports a null result; the review flags the same problem for another study's 100% reductions but not here.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated range of human sample sizes, 14 to 116, does not match the review's own tables, in which the smallest human studies total 17 participants (10 and 7; 9 and 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the point that the studies are small stands.

reporting_issues.issue: One row of Table 4 describes its comparison group as polydrug controls in the sample column and as drug-naive controls in the outcome column.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which control group a difference refers to matters in this literature, as the review's own dopamine section shows; the row cannot be used without checking the primary paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Two of the three authors wrote several of the included studies, and the review neither says so nor weights its counts accordingly.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a conflict of interest in the declared sense, but the count of 14 of 16 includes studies by the reviewers themselves.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC5021729 (whole article including Tables 1-11, read in a tab opened by this reader and saved to the reader's folder; Figure 1, the flow chart, is an image and was not read)

design_detail: Retrospective pharmacokinetic analysis of two laboratory phases in 14 men with recreational MDMA experience, none of which was designed to test dose proportionality (Discussion, 3rd paragraph). Pilot phase: six men took one oral dose of racemic MDMA, two each at 50, 100 and 150 mg. Second phase: eight men in a double-blind, randomized, balanced 4 x 4 Latin-square crossover took 75 mg MDMA, 125 mg MDMA, 40 mg amphetamine and placebo, so the 75 and 125 mg comparison is within person (n=8). Plasma MDMA, MDA, HMMA and HMA were measured at 13 times to 24 hours and urine over 0-24 hours, and the analysis compares dose-normalized exposure, clearance and urinary recovery across dose levels. Plasma HMMA was re-measured in five men, one per dose level, and blood pressure at the time of peak concentration is plotted for the same five.
can_establish: Whether, in eight men who are extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers, 125 mg of MDMA gives a peak concentration and exposure that rise by more than the 1.67-fold increase in dose from 75 mg, with a fall in non-renal clearance, and what the urinary metabolite pattern looks like across five doses.
cannot_establish: A dose-response curve between 50 and 150 mg (three of the five doses rest on two men each, different men at each dose); whether the same holds in women, in people who metabolize MDMA slowly or at intermediate speed, or at repeated or recreational dose patterns; whether the cause is saturation or self-inhibition of CYP2D6, which no measurement here separates; or anything about toxicity, which was not analysed.

sample.recruitment: Men recruited by word of mouth and interviewed; the protocol was approved by an institutional ethics committee and authorized by the Spanish Ministry of Health, which also supplied the MDMA; volunteers gave written consent and were paid (Methods > Patients and study design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Recreational MDMA use on at least five occasions; interview to exclude other conditions; major psychiatric disorder (structured clinical interview for DSM-IV) excluded; physical examination, blood and urine tests and 12-lead electrocardiogram; no history of drug abuse or dependence by DSM-IV other than nicotine; no medical or psychiatric reaction to earlier MDMA. In the second phase everyone was phenotyped with dextromethorphan and classed as an extensive CYP2D6 metabolizer; the paper does not say separately whether the six pilot men were phenotyped (Methods, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: All men; mean age 26.5 years (range 21-31), weight 74.4 kg (66-83), height 178 cm (169-186). All but two were current smokers; average alcohol intake 2 units a day (1 unit = 8 g ethanol); all had previously used cannabis, cocaine and methamphetamine (Methods, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: None reported: all 14 are analysed; the second MDA value at 50 mg was below the quantification limit (Table 1 footnote).
sample.selection_effects: Men only, young, healthy, experienced with MDMA, and (in the second phase) all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; women, people with slow or intermediate CYP2D6 activity and people with liver or other disease were not studied. The 150 mg dose caused cardiovascular and subjective side effects in the volunteers who took it, which is why higher doses were not given (Results, 3rd paragraph), so the top of the dose range comes from two men who tolerated it.

exposure.measurement: MDMA given in the laboratory and measured directly: MDMA, MDA, HMMA and HMA in plasma (13 times to 24 hours) and urine (2 or 3 collection periods) by gas chromatography with nitrogen-specific detection, directly or after hydrolysis of glucuronide conjugates, by a method described in an earlier paper (Methods > Analytical methods).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: single oral doses of racemic MDMA of 50, 75, 100, 125 and 150 mg; 75 and 125 mg were taken by the same eight men in randomized order, the other three doses by two different men each.
exposure.polysubstance: No other drug was given in the MDMA conditions; the amphetamine and placebo conditions of the crossover are not reported. The paper does not describe drug screening or abstinence rules before sessions.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not described; the interval between crossover sessions is not stated in the paper.

comparison.controls: No placebo comparison is used for the pharmacokinetic analysis. The comparison is across dose levels: within person for 75 against 125 mg (n=8) and between persons for 50, 100 and 150 mg (n=2 each).
comparison.matching: Randomized Latin-square order for the second phase; no matching for the pilot volunteers.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a pharmacokinetic comparison, except that the pilot and crossover men are different people whose enzyme activity and body size could differ at each dose.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma and urinary MDMA, MDA, HMMA and HMA; pharmacokinetic parameters (peak concentration, time to peak, area under the curve, half-life, total, renal and non-renal clearance); urinary recovery. Psychomotor performance, subjective effects, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, pupil diameter and electrocardiogram were also measured in the second phase but only diastolic blood pressure at the peak time is reported, for five men (Methods; Results, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: The assay is cited to an earlier paper; precision and limits of quantification are not given here beyond the footnote that one MDA value was below the limit.
outcomes.operationalization: Non-linearity is judged from dose-normalized area under the curve (AUC divided by dose), from the recovery of unchanged MDMA and of HMMA in urine, and from the split of clearance into renal and non-renal parts; no dose-proportionality model is fitted.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Separate tests are reported: a paired t test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) at 75 and 125 mg (P<0.03), a Kruskal-Wallis test across five doses (P<0.1), a bioequivalence interval, and analyses of variance of renal clearance (not significant) and non-renal clearance (P<0.03).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The second phase is described as double-blind; the pilot phase is not described as blinded. Plasma assays are objective.

analysis.effect_sizes: Printed in Table 1 (mean and SD for n=8; two individual values for n=2): 75 mg, peak 130.9 (SD 38.6) ug/L, AUC(0-24 h) 1331.5 (646.0) ug.h/L, dose-normalized AUC 17.8 (8.6), half-life 7.7 (3.2) h, total clearance 86.9 (74.4) L/h; 125 mg, peak 236.4 (58.0), AUC 2623.7 (572.9), normalized AUC 21.0 (4.6), half-life 8.6 (3.2), total clearance 51.1 (14.1) L/h, non-renal clearance 38.1 L/h against 74.0 at 75 mg (the SDs are cut off in the image). Editors' calculation from the printed means: a 1.67-fold dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the AUC, which is 18% above proportionality on dose-normalized AUC. Only one interval is given: a 90% interval of -0.3 to 89.3% for the within-person ratio.
