analysis.preregistration_detail: A trial authorized by the Spanish Ministry of Health (General Directorate of Pharmacy and Health Products, no. 95/297); no registry entry is mentioned. The authors call the non-linearity an unexpected observation made retrospectively.
analysis.selective_reporting: The second phase measured effects, psychomotor tests and cardiovascular variables and the amphetamine and placebo conditions, none of which is reported except diastolic pressure in five men. Table 2 and the text do not say how the five men for the HMMA re-analysis were chosen.
analysis.power: No sample-size reasoning. n=8 within person for 75 against 125 mg and n=2 for each of the other doses.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In eight extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers, 125 mg gave a peak concentration 1.8 times and an exposure 2.0 times those after 75 mg (a 1.67-fold dose; editors' calculation), non-renal clearance about halved (74.0 to 38.1 L/h), more unchanged MDMA in urine (71.2 to 169.6 micromol, 2.4-fold) and about the same total HMMA recovery. The two men at 150 mg had an exposure of about 5,100 and 5,200 ug.h/L, about twice the mean at 125 mg for a 1.2-fold dose, but each of the 50, 100 and 150 mg points rests on two men, and the two men at 50 mg differ 8-fold in exposure (100.1 and 813.9). The five-dose comparison was only marginally significant (P<0.1).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the lack of linearity is "a more general phenomenon" concerning the whole population independent of CYP2D6 genotype, and that small dose increases give disproportionate concentration rises so that people are more prone to acute toxicity. The main comparison was in extensive metabolizers only, so independence from genotype was not tested; no toxicity outcome was analysed; the observation was retrospective, from studies not designed for it; and the authors themselves say saturation of metabolism cannot be excluded and that the same people were not tested at every dose. The abstract's results sentence is worded with more care (concentrations that did not follow proportionality, which could be indicative of non-linearity).

timeline.event: Same group: a second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first gave 77% higher exposure than the first dose (see the card for Farre et al.)

Narrative review by the same group on MDMA, methamphetamine and CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics: describes MDMA as an inactivator of its own main metabolizing enzyme, which this paper offers as one of two possible causes, and takes the share of clearance handled by that enzyme from this paper and a 2005 study
Same group: 50 mg two hours before 100 mg raised the peak concentration to 311 from 203 ng/mL, 12.8% above dose proportionality

Independent group: pooled analysis of 139 healthy people in which seven with no CYP2D6 function had a peak MDMA level 15% higher than people with normal function, in the first three hours only, which the authors read as MDMA blocking the enzyme in everyone

replication.where_it_stands: More-than-proportional exposure after a larger or a repeated dose has been seen again in controlled studies, mostly by this group (authors overlap with Farre et al. 2004) and in a booster design by another group, so the direction is supported; the size at a given dose, the role of genotype and the cause (self-inhibition against saturation) are not settled by this paper, which rests on eight men for the key comparison.

funding.funder: Grants FIS 97/1198, CIRIT (1997SGR00077), ISCIII 97/4344 and Plan Nacional sobre Drogas, Madrid; the Spanish Ministry of Health supplied the MDMA (Methods; Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors de la Torre, Farre, Ortuno, Roset and Cami also wrote Farre et al. (2004), so later repeated-dose studies from this group are not independent of this one. The page text does not give affiliations.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study in which the same volunteers take at least four single doses in randomized, blinded order with washouts, including women and people with slow and intermediate CYP2D6 activity (genotyped and phenotyped), large enough to fit a dose-proportionality model with intervals, with an intravenous or a probe-drug measure of CYP2D6 activity after each dose to separate self-inhibition from saturation and absorption from clearance.

domains.note: In the second phase conditions were randomly assigned in a balanced Latin square, but sequence generation and allocation concealment are not described, and the pilot doses were not randomized; the comparison across five doses is between persons for three of them.
The Latin square balances order, but the washout between sessions is not stated.
Plasma and urine concentrations are objective and do not depend on the blind; no deviations are reported.

All 14 men are analysed, but plasma HMMA and blood pressure were re-analysed in one man per dose level (five men), selected without a stated rule, and one MDA value at 50 mg was below the limit of quantification.
Chromatographic assay for MDMA and metabolites with a published method; precision is not reported here.

An unplanned retrospective analysis of studies with other aims; the five-dose test is only P<0.1; the printed dose-normalized AUC(0-24 h) values cannot give the reported paired P<0.03 (see reporting issues); the pharmacodynamic data collected were not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The within-person randomized comparison of 75 and 125 mg gives a clear and plausible signal of more-than-proportional exposure with halved non-renal clearance, and the direction has been seen in later controlled studies. The overall judgment is set by the unplanned retrospective analysis, the dependence of the wider dose range on two men per dose, a statistical description with inconsistencies, and a Table 2 misprint. The source can be cited for more-than-proportional MDMA exposure between 75 and 125 mg in eight men who are extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers and for lower non-renal clearance at 125 mg; it cannot be cited for the shape of the curve from 50 to 150 mg, for genotype-independence, for women, for people with slower metabolism, or for toxicity.

key_findings.finding: Fourteen men took part: six in a pilot phase (two each at 50, 100 and 150 mg) and eight in a double-blind, randomized, Latin-square crossover of 75 mg MDMA, 125 mg MDMA, 40 mg amphetamine and placebo; all had used MDMA at least five times; in the second phase all were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers. The 150 mg volunteers had side effects that ruled out higher doses, and 50 mg was judged low.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Patients and study design, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Abstract (Methods)

key_findings.finding: In the same eight men, 125 mg gave a higher dose-normalized exposure than 75 mg: peak 236.4 ug/L (SD 58.0) against 130.9 (38.6); AUC(0-24 h) 2623.7 (572.9) against 1331.5 (646.0); dose-normalized AUC 21.0 (4.6) against 17.8 (8.6); half-life 8.6 (3.2) against 7.7 (3.2) h. A paired t test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) gave P<0.03, and the 90% interval of the within-person ratio was -0.3 to 89.3%, so the authors judged the 125 mg dose not bioequivalent to the 75 mg dose scaled by dose. Editors' calculation: 1.67 times the dose gave 1.81 times the peak and 1.97 times the AUC.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (image; MDMA rows for 75 and 125 mg); Results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Urinary clearance of MDMA was roughly constant across doses (analysis of variance not significant) while non-renal clearance depended on dose (P<0.03) and, in the same eight men, was about halved at 125 mg (38.1 L/h) against 75 mg (74.0 L/h), which the authors read as impaired hepatic clearance; total clearance was 86.9 (SD 74.4) against 51.1 (14.1) L/h. The SDs of non-renal clearance are cut off at the edge of the table image.

Across the five doses (50 to 150 mg, a 3-fold range) the AUC(0-24 h) of MDMA varied more than 10-fold: two men at 50 mg had 100.1 and 813.9 ug.h/L, two men at 150 mg 5132.8 and 5232.0, with peak concentrations 441.9 and 486.9 ug/L at 150 mg against a mean of 236.4 at 125 mg. A Kruskal-Wallis test of dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity) across the five doses was only marginal (P<0.1).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (image; 50, 100 and 150 mg rows); Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: About half the dose was recovered in urine in 24 hours at every dose (Table 2: 51.0 SD 16.2 and 53.7 SD 11.4 percent in the two groups of eight). Unchanged MDMA recovery rose from 71.2 (SD 13.7) micromol at 75 mg to 169.6 (69.5) at 125 mg (editors' calculation: 2.4-fold for a 1.67-fold dose), while HMMA recovery stayed in the same range (128.3, SD 21.8, then 148.3, SD 102.8 micromol). The authors take the roughly constant HMMA with rising MDMA to point to saturation or inhibition of the demethylenation step, and say unchanged MDMA recovery rose by a factor of nearly 20 across the dose range.

In five men, one per dose level, plasma HMMA exceeded MDMA at 50, 75 and 100 mg and the reverse held at the higher doses; diastolic blood pressure at the time of peak concentration followed MDMA's peak concentration, with a clear non-linearity at 150 mg. Figures 2 and 3 show single men and their values were not extracted.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 legends and images

key_findings.finding: The authors name two explanations: saturation of MDMA metabolism (the simplest, which they say cannot be excluded) and inhibition of CYP2D6-mediated demethylenation by MDMA, and perhaps by its metabolite HMMA; they cite in vitro work showing MDMA is both a substrate and an inhibitor of CYP2D6, with inhibition increasing after preincubation (up to 95% of control activity at 1.5 micromolar, as worded in the paper), at concentrations they say are compatible with those in the body.

Authors' stated limits: the observations were made retrospectively and the clinical studies were not designed to detect the phenomenon, so bias cannot be excluded from the fact that the same individuals were not tested at each dose level; they still say acute toxic effects reported after recreational doses should be read in the light of dose-dependent kinetics.

reporting_issues.issue: The image of Table 1 in the PMC copy is cut off at its right edge: the last column (non-renal clearance) shows 74.0 (71.1 and 38.1 (13.3 for the 75 and 125 mg groups, and the 50 mg range ends 734.1-56.5, with the closing digits missing.
reporting_issues.consequence: The standard deviations of the non-renal clearances on which the 'reduced by one half' statement rests cannot be read in this copy; their values were not extracted and should be checked in the journal's printed page.

reporting_issues.issue: Footnote 2 of Table 1 says the MDMA concentrations of the second volunteer were under the quantification limit, but it is attached to the MDA row at 50 mg (n=1) while MDMA values for both 50 mg men are printed (19.8-82.8 ug/L).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: MDA is evidently meant; the MDA values at 50 mg rest on one man.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 2 the second man at 50 mg has MDMA 40.9, MDA 1.0, HMMA 89.2 and HMA 4.2 micromol, which sum to 135.3 micromol (52.2% of the 259 micromol dose), but the printed dose excreted for him is 38.3%. With 4.9 in place of 40.9 the sum is 99.3 micromol, which is 38.3%. Every other individual and group value reconciles with its printed percentage (editors' arithmetic). The text's 'factor of nearly 20' for MDMA recovery fits 4.9 (group means 12.8 against 246.8 micromol, 19.3-fold) and not 40.9 (30.8 against 246.8, 8.0-fold).
reporting_issues.consequence: A likely lost decimal point; the 50 mg urinary MDMA values should not be quoted, and the statement of a nearly 20-fold rise holds only if the value is 4.9.

reporting_issues.issue: The paired t test is reported as P<0.03 for dose-normalized AUC(0-infinity), a quantity not printed anywhere. The printed dose-normalized AUC(0-24 h) values (17.8, SD 8.6, and 21.0, SD 4.6, n=8 each) cannot give P<0.03 in a paired test at any within-person correlation: the smallest two-sided P that these means and SDs allow is about 0.06, at a correlation of 1 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The significance claimed for the key within-person comparison cannot be checked from the paper; the more-than-proportional rise is better described by the ratio of means (1.97 times the AUC for 1.67 times the dose) than by the P value.

reporting_issues.issue: A Kruskal-Wallis test and an analysis of variance across the five dose levels treat 75 and 125 mg as independent groups although they are the same eight men (16 of the 22 observations).
reporting_issues.consequence: The assumptions of both tests are not met; the five-dose P values (P<0.1 and P<0.03) are not valid as stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The text calls the roughly constant HMMA recovery almost constant at around 100 micromol, but Table 2 shows individual HMMA recoveries from 59.8 to 152.0 micromol and a group SD of 102.8 micromol at 125 mg (mean 148.3, against 128.3 at 75 mg); no test of HMMA recovery against dose is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The constant-HMMA part of the saturation argument describes group means with a wide spread and no statistical test.

reporting_issues.issue: Clearances are computed from oral doses, so they are dose divided by AUC and include bioavailability; the paper reads the fall in non-renal clearance as impaired hepatic clearance, yet also uses the words higher bioavailability for the 125 mg dose.
reporting_issues.consequence: Without an intravenous dose, a fall in clearance and a rise in absorption cannot be told apart; the finding should be quoted as more-than-proportional exposure, not as a mechanism.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the non-linearity concerns the whole population independent of CYP2D6 genotype, but in the second phase everyone was an extensive metabolizer, and it says people are therefore more prone to acute toxicity although no toxicity outcome was analysed.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both statements go beyond the data; the paper supports a more-than-proportional rise in exposure in extensive metabolizers only.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC2014905 (all sections and the reference list read as text). Tables 1 and 2 and Figures 2 and 3 are images and were read on screen; the right-hand edge of the Table 1 image is cut off in the PMC copy.

design_detail: Narrative review (Frontiers in Genetics, 12 November 2012, volume 3, article number 235, as printed in the citation line on the PMC page) by four authors from one research group, using MDMA and methamphetamine as two examples of how CYP2D6 genetics might matter for amphetamine-type drugs. About 3,300 words of main text in ten headed sections (editors' count), one table of 21 compounds with in vitro enzyme constants (Table 1, read as text), two metabolic schemes (Figures 1 and 2, images not viewed) and 56 references. No methods section: no databases, search dates, terms or selection rules; no pooled estimate. The four sections on MDMA alone hold about 1,300 words and the three on methamphetamine alone about 700; the rest is shared (introduction, background, conclusions). The methamphetamine sections were read and are summarized only briefly, because the library claims built from this card concern MDMA.
can_establish: What one research group concluded about how MDMA interacts with CYP2D6 (as substrate and as an enzyme-inactivating inhibitor), which primary studies it points to for genotype comparisons, for the effect of CYP2D6-blocking antidepressants on MDMA levels and for severe reactions with ritonavir, and how it reads that evidence as a whole.
cannot_establish: The size of any effect of CYP2D6 genotype or of CYP2D6-blocking medicines on MDMA exposure or on harm (almost no numbers are given for the genotype comparisons); how many people have their enzyme blocked by one dose (the two fractions given are 67% of men and 100% of women, from two studies not read here); whether MAOIs cause life-threatening reactions with MDMA (no MAOI source can be told from the citations); or whether CYP2D6 genotype changes the risk of death.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). No databases, search dates, terms or inclusion criteria are reported. The Introduction says the review will look at available clinical data against three postulates and chooses MDMA and methamphetamine as two archetypes (Introduction, 4th paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated.
sample.demographics: Not applicable. Sample sizes of cited studies, where the text gives them: nine extensive metabolizers (six *1/*1, three *1/*4) compared with poor metabolizers (*4/*4) after two consecutive doses (MDMA and CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics, 1st paragraph; the reference-list title of one source says one poor metabolizer and nine extensive metabolizers); for methamphetamine, 8 extensive and 3 poor metabolizers given 10 mg by mouth, 202 patients and 337 controls in a Japanese genotype study, 18 autopsies and 52 people who use methamphetamine.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: No stated search, so completeness cannot be judged. At least 15 of 56 references are by the authors' group, including the studies behind the figures for enzyme inactivation, the paroxetine probe study and the ritonavir case. The authors state their belief (no data) that poor metabolizers are under-represented among people who use MDMA because of the strong effects they feel (section 'CYP2D6, MDMA, and methamphetamine: background considerations', 4th paragraph); if true, genotype comparisons in such groups are biased.

exposure.measurement: Not applicable. Cited studies describe CYP2D6 status by genotype (alleles such as *4/*4, *1/*4, *1/*10) or by activity group (poor, intermediate, extensive, ultrarapid); genotyping and phenotyping methods are not given.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single dose and two consecutive doses of MDMA, 10 mg of methamphetamine by mouth, and antidepressants given before MDMA. No milligram doses are given for the MDMA studies.
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed for the intoxication series and the ritonavir and MAOI reports.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not discussed.

comparison.controls: Not applicable. Comparisons described are between genotype groups (poor against extensive metabolizers after two doses; reduced-activity genotypes against others for sodium and cortisol) and, for methamphetamine, patients against controls.
comparison.matching: Not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors suggest that people with strong effects (poor metabolizers) stop or limit use, so genotype frequencies among people who use MDMA may differ from the general population (their belief, not tested).

outcomes.instruments: Not applicable (cited studies). Quantities mentioned: plasma MDMA and its metabolite HMMA; recovery of urinary thioether adducts; plasma osmolality, sodium and vasopressin; plasma cortisol; CYP2D6 activity after a dose (the basis of the 'phenocopying' figures); neuropsychological performance after methamphetamine.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Phenocopying' is used for the measured activity of CYP2D6 falling, after a dose of MDMA, to the level typical of poor metabolizers whatever the genotype (section 'MDMA CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibition and the phenocopying phenomenon', one paragraph).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Figures quoted from other work: enzyme inactivation within about 2 hours and recovery to the starting level after at least 10 days; phenocopying in 67% of men and 100% of women; metabolic clearance about 75% of plasma clearance, of which about 30% regulated by CYP2D6 (also written 'less than 30%', and 'lower than 50%' of metabolic clearance); MDMA concentrations changed by 15 to 30% (the sentence lacks a verb) and the metabolite HMMA 40 to 50% lower with paroxetine, reboxetine or duloxetine; in vitro intrinsic clearance of the *1 enzyme variant 123 times that of *10 for MDMA O-demethylenation (67 and 157 times for two methamphetamine reactions); Km 2.2 against 39.6 micromol/L for MDMA and methamphetamine (Table 1).
analysis.selective_reporting: Not assessable: no search or selection method. The Introduction promises to see how far three postulates were confirmed; the Concluding remarks do not go through them one by one.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: As described by the review, two laboratory studies (one in men, one in women) found CYP2D6 activity reduced to a poor-metabolizer level after one dose of MDMA in 67% of the men and in all of the women. A few small studies compared genotype groups for blood levels, temperature, sodium and cortisol; in a series of poisonings the authors say poor-metabolizer genotypes were not over-represented. Antidepressants that block CYP2D6 raised MDMA levels by a fraction of the order of 15 to 30% and lowered HMMA, and severe or fatal reactions with ritonavir are cited to case reports. No numbers are given for the genotype comparisons.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that everyone, whatever the genotype, is turned into a poor metabolizer by MDMA, that the CYP2D6 share of clearance is substantially lower than in vitro work predicts, and that the clinical relevance of CYP2D6 genetics is lower than predicted. The Concluding remarks add that carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects and acute toxicity, including death, and that MAOIs and ritonavir are the main cause of life-threatening interactions with MDMA. 'Everyone' is stronger than the 67% found in men; the in vitro expectation is never stated, so 'lower than predicted' cannot be checked; and no data on toxicity or deaths by genotype, or on MAOIs, accompany the last statements.

timeline.event: De la Torre et al.: MDMA exposure rises more than in proportion to dose; the review takes from it and from a 2005 paroxetine study the figures of about 75% metabolic clearance and 30% CYP2D6 share
Segura et al. gave paroxetine as a CYP2D6 probe, and de la Torre et al. compared one CYP2D6 poor metabolizer with nine extensive metabolizers (both as cited in this review; neither read)

O'Mathuna et al. gave dextromethorphan as a CYP2D6 probe to 15 healthy men before and after MDMA: the urinary ratio rose above the poor-metabolizer cut-off in 10 of 15 men (the review's 67%), the first probe dose was given 4 hours after MDMA, and the ratio had not fully recovered at 10 days (read in full for this library, see its own card)
Yubero-Lahoz et al. in women (phenocopying in all, as described in this review; not read)
Schmid et al., pooled analysis of 139 healthy people: peak MDMA 15% higher in seven poor metabolizers, in the first three hours only
Sarparast et al. systematic review of medicine interactions with MDMA, which repeats the self-inhibition account second-hand

replication.where_it_stands: The main message (a small effect of CYP2D6 genotype on MDMA exposure, because MDMA blocks the enzyme itself) agrees with the 2016 pooled analysis, which was read in full for this library, and the enzyme-blocking finding agrees in direction with the 2008 probe-drug study in 15 men, also read in full. The 67% figure is 10 of 15 men; the 100% for women and the 2011 study were not read. The review's 'within 2 hours' timing is not what the 2008 study measured (first probe dose at 4 hours). The review's figures for antidepressants rest on four primary studies, of which only the 2007 paroxetine trial was read for this library (it gives a 16% rise in peak MDMA and 38 to 49% lower HMMA); the fractions of people whose enzyme is blocked and the reports of severe reactions rest on this narrative review and on case reports and studies not read here.

funding.funder: No funding statement appears in the page text read.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a conflict of interest.
funding.affiliations_note: Affiliation numbers 1 to 3 are printed beside the authors' names; the affiliation text was in a collapsed panel and was not read. The authors are members of the group that ran several of the clinical studies reviewed (at least 15 of 56 references). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A genotyped, blinded crossover in which women and men with no, reduced and normal CYP2D6 function take the same MDMA dose once and, in another arm, twice in a session, with CYP2D6 probe activity measured before, at 2 hours, at 1 day and at 10 days; temperature, sodium and vasopressin recorded; and a registry of emergency presentations with genotype and co-taken medicines.

domains.note: No databases, search dates, terms or inclusion rules; the review does not say how its 56 references were chosen.

None. Small or single-person studies are written in the plural (poor-metabolizer 'subjects'), results are given without numbers, and an in vitro paper is cited for an observation in people (Kreth et al., 2000, by its reference-list title).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: At least 15 of 56 references are by the authors' group, including the sources of the phenocopying fractions, the paroxetine probe study and the ritonavir case.

Several statements are marked as belief or 'probably' (poor metabolizers under-represented; effects lowered by transporter competition), but the Concluding remarks state higher risk of toxicity, including death, in reduced-function carriers without any data, and the abstract states that everyone is phenocopied against the text's own 67% in men.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against a clinical role of CYP2D6 genetics
domains.note: Findings pointing both ways are named (sodium and cortisol differences by genotype; no excess of poor-metabolizer genotypes in poisonings), but none is weighed with numbers, and the conclusion leans to the small-effect reading.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used. The review can be cited for the authors' account of MDMA as an enzyme-inactivating inhibitor of CYP2D6 and for pointers to primary studies; every number in it is second-hand and unchecked, so a claim that rests on it alone stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: CYP2D6 is a small part of liver enzyme content (1 to 2% of total cytochrome P450) but handles an estimated 20 to 30% of marketed medicines, which the review lists as tricyclic and SSRI antidepressants, opioids, antipsychotics, antiemetics, antiarrhythmics and amphetamine-like drugs. About 5 to 10% of white people are poor metabolizers (lack two functional alleles); the four activity groups are poor, intermediate, extensive and ultrarapid metabolizers.
key_findings.locator: CYP2D6, MDMA, and methamphetamine: background considerations, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: MDMA is both a substrate of CYP2D6 (O-demethylenation to HHMA, then methylation to HMMA) and a potent mechanism-based inhibitor: the review gives metabolic clearance as about 75% of MDMA plasma clearance, with about 30% of its metabolism regulated by CYP2D6 (citing the 2000 non-linear pharmacokinetics paper and a 2005 paroxetine-probe study). Elsewhere the share is written as less than 30% (Drug-drug interactions, 1st paragraph) and, for metabolic clearance of both drugs, lower than 50% (Concluding remarks, 5th paragraph).
key_findings.locator: MDMA pharmacology and metabolic disposition, 4th paragraph; Drug-drug interactions, 1st paragraph; Concluding remarks, 5th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Mechanism-based inhibition happens shortly after a single dose, inactivating most liver CYP2D6 within about 2 hours with activity back to its starting level only after at least 10 days (citing studies from 2008, read separately for this library, and 2011, not read). The review says phenocopying (the enzyme behaving as in a poor metabolizer whatever the genotype) was seen in 67% of male subjects in one study and 100% of females in another, and infers that people who take repeated doses in a session face a higher chance of relative overdose and of adverse effects from other CYP2D6 substrates (citing a 2004 repeated-dose study). No clinical outcome of that inference is shown.
key_findings.locator: MDMA CYP2D6 mechanism-based inhibition and the phenocopying phenomenon, paragraph 1

key_findings.finding: Genotype comparisons are described without numbers: poor metabolizers (*4/*4) are said to show higher MDMA levels and more hyperthermia after a single dose (no citation on that sentence), extensive metabolizers (six *1/*1, three *1/*4) after two consecutive doses are said to resemble poor metabolizers, reduced-activity genotypes are linked to larger falls in plasma sodium and rises in vasopressin (a 2012 study) and some poor/intermediate genotypes to larger rises in cortisol (a 2012 study), and in a series of poisonings an excess of poor-metabolizer genotypes was not found.

Other enzymes contribute: CYP1A2 and, less, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 can oxidize MDMA and MDA; CYP1A2 activity rose after MDMA in a 2012 study while CYP2D6 fell; in a paroxetine trial MDMA was still converted to HHMA, suggesting alternative pathways.

Antidepressants that block CYP2D6 (paroxetine, reboxetine, duloxetine) are said to change MDMA concentrations by 15 to 30% (the sentence has no verb; the direction is read as an increase from the next sentence and from the cited trials) and to lower the metabolite HMMA by 40 to 50%, while the effects of MDMA are lower, 'probably' because of competition for the uptake transporter (four citations: 2005, 2007, 2011, 2012).

The review states that ritonavir (an antiretroviral and CYP2D6 inhibitor) and MAO inhibitors have been reported as the main cause of life-threatening interactions with MDMA, citing three items from 1998, 1999 and 2012; by their titles two are about ritonavir and one is a letter on a fatal MDMA intoxication, and none names an MAO inhibitor.
key_findings.locator: MDMA drug-drug interactions, 3rd paragraph; reference list (Henry and Hill 1998; de la Torre et al. 1999; Papaseit et al. 2012)

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: the polymorphism and co-administered CYP2D6 inhibitors may have less impact on the risk of acute toxicity than previously thought, because other enzymes and renal excretion matter and because MDMA phenocopies everyone; clinical relevance of the polymorphism is called lower than predicted by in vitro studies. The Concluding remarks also say that carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects, and that with environmental factors this may lead to acute toxicity including death.

In vitro background (Table 1 and the background section, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs): MDMA binds CYP2D6 with Km 2.2 (SD 1.6) and Ki 0.6 (SD 0.6) micromol/L, methamphetamine with Km 39.6 (SD 4.7) and Ki 25.0; the *1 enzyme variant clears MDMA 123 times faster than the *10 variant in vitro, and the review states without citation that *10 is carried by about 75% of Asian populations.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, MDMA and methamphetamine rows; CYP2D6, MDMA, and methamphetamine: background considerations, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Methamphetamine sections (summary only): CYP2D6 reduced-function genotypes were associated with lower odds of methamphetamine dependence in 202 Japanese patients against 337 controls (odds ratio 0.62 for intermediate metabolizers); extensive metabolizers did worse on cognitive tests in 52 people; bupropion, a CYP2D6 inhibitor, raised methamphetamine levels and lowered its effects in two trials.
key_findings.locator: Methamphetamine and CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Methamphetamine drug-drug interaction, 1st paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: No methods are reported: the review does not say how studies were found or chosen. The Introduction promises to see how far three postulates (on abuse risk, neurotoxicity and toxicity in poor metabolizers) were confirmed, but the Concluding remarks do not give a verdict on each.
reporting_issues.consequence: Completeness cannot be judged and the conclusions cannot be traced to a stated body of evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says everyone, irrespective of genotype or phenotype, is turned into a poor metabolizer by MDMA, and the Concluding remarks say all subjects are put at risk; the body reports phenocopying in 67% of men and 100% of women, with no denominators, from two studies by the authors' group. The 67% is 10 of 15 men in the 2008 study (read separately): after MDMA their urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio was above the poor-metabolizer cut-off, and 5 men stayed below it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline fraction is stronger than the numbers given: in the one study that was read a third of the men did not reach poor-metabolizer values; the figures should be cited as the review's account of two small studies, not as a finding for everyone.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the CYP2D6 share of clearance is substantially lower than expected from in vitro studies, but the in vitro expectation is never stated. The share itself is written three ways with different denominators: about 30% of metabolism, less than 30%, and lower than 50% of metabolic clearance (itself about 75% of plasma clearance).
reporting_issues.consequence: 'Lower than predicted' cannot be checked from the review; the share of MDMA clearance that depends on CYP2D6 is an approximate figure of the order of a quarter to a third, second-hand.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says MDMA is oxidized at almost 100 times the rate of methamphetamine and points to Table 1, but Table 1 gives affinity constants (Km 2.2 against 39.6 micromol/L, about 18-fold; Ki 0.6 against 25.0, about 42-fold), not rates. The 'almost 100-fold' difference between enzyme variants is a spread of 123 (MDMA) and 67 and 157 (two methamphetamine reactions). The figure of about 75% for the *10 variant in Asian populations has no citation.
reporting_issues.consequence: The in vitro comparisons are loosely summarized and should not be quoted as rates; they say nothing about the size of the effect in people.

reporting_issues.issue: A sentence says poor-metabolizer subjects show higher MDMA concentrations and a higher risk of hyperthermia after a single dose and has no citation; the next sentence cites a 2000 paper whose reference-list title is an in vitro study of the enzymes involved (Kreth et al.) for 'a similar observation' with MDE, another drug. The comparison of nine extensive metabolizers with poor metabolizers appears to rest on a 2005 paper whose title names one poor metabolizer.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim of higher hyperthermia risk in poor metabolizers has no identifiable source in people; a single person is described in the plural.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence on antidepressants that block CYP2D6 reads 'produce 15-30% of MDMA concentrations' with no verb, names no outcome (peak or exposure) and gives no per-medicine figures; the explanation of the lower effects ('probably' transporter competition) is a hypothesis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The range cannot be matched to a medicine or measure without the primary papers; the library reads the direction as an increase from the following sentence and from the review of trials.

reporting_issues.issue: MAO inhibitors are named, with ritonavir, as the main cause of life-threatening interactions with MDMA, but the three citations do not name an MAO inhibitor by title, no cases or denominators are given, and the paragraph does not say what the reactions were.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about MAO inhibitors is unsupported in this review; the ritonavir part rests on case reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The Concluding remarks state that carriers of reduced-function alleles are at higher risk of heightened effects and, with environmental factors, of acute toxicity including death, while the body reports no excess of poor-metabolizer genotypes in a series of poisonings and says the enzyme is blocked in everyone after a dose. The belief that poor metabolizers are under-represented among people who use MDMA is offered without data.
reporting_issues.consequence: The conclusions pull in opposite directions; neither is backed by genotype-specific data on toxicity or deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: For methamphetamine, an odds ratio of 0.62 with a 95% interval of 0.51 to 0.76 is printed beside p = 0.02. That interval implies p well below 0.001, and an interval this narrow is not possible from a simple two-group comparison of 202 patients with 337 controls (the narrowest possible at that odds ratio is about 0.44 to 0.88, editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The interval or the sample sizes are misreported in the review; it concerns methamphetamine only and no MDMA claim uses it.

reporting_issues.issue: The review says MDMA inactivates most hepatic CYP2D6 'within 2 h' and that subjects show the poor-metabolizer phenotype within 2 hours, and gives the 2008 and 2011 studies as the source. In the 2008 study the first probe dose was given 4 hours after MDMA, so it cannot show the state of the enzyme at 2 hours; the review also writes that activity returned to a basal level 'after at least 10 days', whereas that study's own Discussion says the ratio had not fully recovered by 10 days although its abstract says it recovered.
reporting_issues.consequence: The timing of enzyme blockade (2 hours) and its end (10 days) are the review's wording, not the measured times of the cited men: the early rise in probe-drug exposure at 4 hours mixes competition for the enzyme with its inactivation, and the recovery half-life depends on the model (46.6 hours one-phase, 103 hours two-phase).

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3495276 (abstract, all ten headed sections, Table 1 and the reference list read as text in the reader's own browser tab; Figures 1 and 2, the metabolic schemes, were not viewed as images; the page text had no affiliations or funding statement). The article number 235 is printed in the citation line (Front Genet. 2012 Nov 12;3:235); the reference record for de-la-torre_2012 holds the volume but not the number. The 2008 study cited for the phenocopying figures was read in full separately (see its own card) and is used above to check the review's account of it.

design_detail: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover laboratory trial in 12 healthy men (a 13th withdrew after two paroxetine doses and never took MDMA). Each man attended two 3-day sessions 15 days apart: paroxetine 20 mg a day or placebo on days 1 to 3, and MDMA 100 mg by mouth on day 3, 3 hours after that day's paroxetine or placebo capsule. Both day-3 conditions contained MDMA; there was no day-3 session with paroxetine and placebo MDMA, but days 1 and 2 give paroxetine-only against placebo-only comparisons. Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, pupil diameter, a psychomotor battery and three sets of subjective scales were recorded for up to 24 hours; plasma MDMA and its metabolite HMMA for 27 hours after MDMA.
can_establish: Whether, in 12 healthy men who are extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers and have used MDMA before, three days of paroxetine 20 mg before a single 100 mg MDMA dose lowers MDMA's physical and subjectively rated effects (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, pupil size, 'high', liking, stimulation, sociability) and changes MDMA and HMMA concentrations (MDMA peak and exposure higher by about 16% and 22%, HMMA lower by about 49% and 39%; the printed means give 38% for the exposure).
cannot_establish: What happens in women, in people who take paroxetine or another antidepressant for weeks or months (here 3 days), in people with depression or other illness, at other MDMA doses, or after a second dose (none was given); whether the lower effects come from blocking the serotonin transporter (the authors' reading; not measured here) or from other causes; anything about rare severe reactions (12 healthy men); that people on an SSRI 'take higher doses' of MDMA or what happens to their blood levels if they do (not studied: nobody took more than one dose); the share of MDMA cleared by CYP2D6 (not estimated by this design).

sample.recruitment: Men recruited by word of mouth; consent in writing; compensated; approved by the ethics committee of the Institut Municipal d'Assistencia Sanitaria, Barcelona, and authorized by the Spanish Ministry of Health (Materials and Methods, Subjects, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Recreational MDMA use on at least 5 occasions; excluded: more than 20 cigarettes or 30 g of alcohol a day and major psychiatric disorder by structured interview (DSM-IV); a general physical examination, laboratory tests, urinalysis and 12-lead ECG were done to confirm health; negative urine screen (opiates, cocaine, cannabis, amphetamines) before each session; all participants were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers by dextromethorphan phenotyping.
sample.demographics: All men; mean age 24 years (19 to 34), weight 71.0 kg (56.5 to 84.0), height 177 cm; 8 current smokers and 4 non-smokers; average alcohol 12 units a week; all had used cannabis, cocaine and methamphetamine; none had abuse or dependence (DSM-IV) except nicotine, and none had had a medical or psychiatric reaction to MDMA.
sample.attrition: One of 13 men withdrew on the morning of day 3 after two paroxetine doses, with insomnia, restlessness and anxiety; MDMA was not given and he is not in the results. Twelve are analysed. The subset of 7 with paroxetine and other metabolite measurements was published elsewhere.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, young, experienced with MDMA and with normal CYP2D6 activity, able to take 3 days of paroxetine (one of 13 was not); no one with depression or on long-term treatment. The result describes men like these in a hospital laboratory.

exposure.measurement: Paroxetine (Seroxat, repackaged by the hospital pharmacy in capsules identical to placebo) and MDMA (from the Spanish Ministry of Health, in capsules) given in the laboratory; plasma MDMA and HMMA by gas chromatography with mass spectrometry (method of Pizarro et al., 2002) at 14 time points to 27 hours; urine; paroxetine and other metabolites in 7 men.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: paroxetine 20 mg a day by mouth on days 1 to 3 (about 9 AM, fasting) or placebo; MDMA 100 mg by mouth at about noon on day 3, 3 hours after that day's paroxetine or placebo capsule so that both drugs would peak together (average time to peak 2 hours for MDMA, 5 for paroxetine).
exposure.polysubstance: No other drug was given; participants were asked to abstain from drugs of abuse during the study and were screened by urine test before each session. To limit anticipation, the men were told they would receive two types of drugs, a capsule of paroxetine or placebo and, on day 3, two capsules of different doses of MDMA or placebo.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Negative urine screen required before each session; length of abstinence not stated; overnight fast.

comparison.controls: Placebo capsules on days 1 to 3 followed by MDMA 100 mg on day 3 (the same men in the other session). Days 1 and 2 compare paroxetine alone with placebo alone. There was no day-3 session without MDMA.
comparison.matching: Within person, random order, 15-day washout.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline and trait measures are not reported; CYP2D6 phenotype was extensive in all, with no genotype; no measure of whether the men could tell the two conditions apart.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: All had used cannabis, cocaine and methamphetamine; none met criteria for abuse or dependence except nicotine.

outcomes.instruments: Systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate and oral temperature (Dinamap), pupil diameter (Haab scale), continuous ECG; psychomotor battery (digit symbol substitution, simple reaction time, Pauli test, Maddox wing); subjective scales: 49-item Addiction Research Center Inventory short form (ARCI; five scales), the in-house VESSPA questionnaire (six scales) and 21 visual analog scales; plasma MDMA and HMMA (peak, time to peak, area under the curve to 21 hours, elimination rate, half-life).
outcomes.validity_norms: Spanish validated ARCI; VESSPA is the group's own validated questionnaire (Poudevida et al., 2003); the pharmacokinetic assay is cited to an earlier paper.
outcomes.operationalization: Change from baseline; peak (Emax, 3 to 9 hours) and 6-hour area under the curve (3 to 9 hours) of each variable analysed by one-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Tukey tests, and time courses by two-way ANOVA (condition by time); pharmacokinetics by paired Student t test (peak, area) and Wilcoxon test (time to peak).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across outcomes: about 45 effect measures (editors' count from the Methods), each tested on area, peak and the condition-by-time term; Table 1 lists only the variables that differed significantly.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind with identical capsules; whether the men or staff could tell the conditions apart was not assessed, and paroxetine alone raised systolic pressure on days 1 and 2 (peak difference 8 mm Hg) and caused adverse effects in the 13th man.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2 (n=12; mean and SD): MDMA peak 212.72 (46.74) ug/L with placebo against 246.62 (55.80) with paroxetine (+15.9%, P<0.01), area to 21 hours 2115.26 (470.26) against 2572.21 (661.68) ug x h/L (+21.6%, P<0.01), time to peak 1.50 against 1.75 h, half-life 7.88 against 8.34 h (not marked significant); HMMA peak 193.14 (77.50) against 97.88 (33.83) (-49.3%), area 1923.32 (736.35) against 1189.47 (388.78) (-38.2% from the printed means; the paper's text says 39%), half-life 9.54 against 13.10 h (all P<0.01). Effects (Results and Table 1; paroxetine against placebo, MDMA on day 3): peak systolic pressure rise lower by 12 mm Hg (Emax F=22.20, P=0.001), diastolic by 5 mm Hg (Emax F=1.75, P=0.213; area F=0.27, P=0.613; significant only in the time-by-condition test, F=3.97, P<0.001), heart rate by 14 beats/min (Emax F=7.64, P=0.018; area F=3.39, P=0.093), pupil widening 3.33 to 1.23 mm (F=70.35, P<0.001), oral temperature rise lower by 0.3 C (Emax F=5.33, P=0.041; area F=2.01, P=0.184); VAS 'high' area F=41.66 and peak F=34.16 (both P<0.001), 'liking' F=15.52 (P=0.002) and 22.98 (P=0.001), 'good effects' (P<0.001 for area and peak) and 'stimulated' (area P<0.001, peak P=0.003); ARCI morphine-benzedrine group (euphoria) peak 7.27 to 4 (F=11.98, P=0.005); VESSPA sociability 3.0 to 0.58 (P=0.023), activity 5.91 to 1.21 (P=0.007), anxiety 5.55 to 2.7 (P=0.003). No significant change in 'bad effects', 'fear', 'depression or sadness', hallucination items, sedation scales, or the perception and psychotic-symptom scales; no hallucinations or psychotic symptoms; no serious adverse events; nobody needed treatment. Days 1 and 2: no difference between paroxetine and placebo except a higher systolic pressure with paroxetine (peak difference 8 mm Hg); paroxetine alone improved some psychomotor measures (digit symbol) without subjective change.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A trial authorized by the Spanish Ministry of Health; no registry entry is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Table 1 lists only the variables with a significant difference; the 7-man subset results, hormones and immune measures are published elsewhere (Segura et al., 2005; Pacifici et al., 2004).
analysis.power: No sample-size reasoning; 12 men.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 12 men, three days of paroxetine before 100 mg of MDMA lowered the rise in blood pressure (systolic by 12 mm Hg at peak), heart rate (by 14 beats/min), pupil size and temperature, and lowered ratings of 'high', liking, stimulation, euphoria-type and sociability scales, while MDMA's peak concentration was 16% higher and its exposure 22% higher, and the main metabolite HMMA 49% (peak) and 39% (exposure; 38% from the printed means) lower. Diastolic pressure was not significant by the area (P=0.613) or peak (P=0.213) test, and heart rate was significant by the peak test (P=0.018) but not the area test (P=0.093).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the first paragraph of the Discussion say paroxetine was associated with a 30% increase in MDMA concentrations; Table 2 and the Results give 16% (peak) and 22% (exposure), and the Discussion's second mention of 30% cites an earlier analysis of 7 men (Segura et al., 2005). The abstract says the marked decrease in effects could lead people who use MDMA to take higher doses and so to life-threatening toxic effects, and the closing paragraph says the same of depressed people on SSRIs. Nobody took a second dose, no toxicity was measured and nobody on long-term treatment was studied. The Discussion also says the reduction in systolic pressure, diastolic pressure and heart rate was significant, whereas Table 1 gives diastolic pressure P=0.213 at peak and 0.613 for area.

timeline.event: Case series of four people who had taken fluoxetine before ecstasy: one felt less effect, three felt no change (McCann and Ricaurte; cited here and in the 2000 citalopram paper; not read)
Independent group: citalopram by infusion before MDMA lowered most psychological effects of MDMA by about 60% in 16 healthy volunteers
Another group, cited here: fluoxetine given daily for at least 5 days lowered MDMA's cardiovascular and subjective effects (Tancer and Johanson; not read)
Same group: a single MDMA dose lowers CYP2D6 activity for days, so that medicines cleared by CYP2D6 and taken after MDMA would be affected

Systematic review: duloxetine and reboxetine also lowered MDMA's effects and raised peak MDMA by 15 to 18%; bupropion raised MDMA exposure but did not lower the ratings (as summarized by the review, from trials by the Zurich group of the 2000 citalopram study)

replication.where_it_stands: Blunting of MDMA's effects by serotonin reuptake inhibitors has been found by at least two other groups with other drugs (citalopram, fluoxetine), and a rise of 14 to 18% in peak MDMA with CYP2D6-inhibiting medicines was reported for duloxetine and reboxetine in trials summarized by the 2022 review (from the same laboratory as the citalopram study). All of this is small laboratory work in healthy volunteers over a single dose or a few days; no trial has studied people who take an antidepressant for illness, women in numbers, or a second dose of MDMA after an antidepressant.

funding.funder: Fondo de Investigacion Sanitaria grants FIS 97/1198, 98/0181, 00/0777 and 01/1336; Generalitat de Catalunya grant 2001SGR00407; Area Progetto Droga, Istituto Superiore di Sanita, Rome; one author held a post-training contract from the Instituto de Salud Carlos III (Introduction footnote).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors (Farre, Abanades, O'Mathuna, Torrens, de la Torre) overlap with de la Torre et al. (2000, 2012), Farre et al. (2004) and O'Mathuna et al. (2008), so these are one group's studies, not independent replications of each other.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, double-blind crossover in people who take an antidepressant for illness at steady state, in women as well as men and in matched healthy volunteers, with a session of antidepressant and placebo MDMA, MDMA at more than one dose, plasma MDMA and metabolites, CYP2D6 genotype, a measure of whether the blind held, and a second MDMA dose or a dose-choice task so that what people do after feeling little, and what their blood levels are then, is measured rather than assumed.

domains.note: Conditions are said to be randomly assigned; sequence generation and concealment are not described.
A washout of 15 days between sessions; paroxetine and MDMA are cleared within days.

Identical capsules and a cover story; but blinding was not assessed, paroxetine raised systolic pressure on days 1 and 2, one man left with adverse effects, and the blunted MDMA experience itself may reveal the condition.
12 of 13 analysed; the one who left after two paroxetine doses never took MDMA, so the analysed men are those who tolerated paroxetine.
Plasma levels and most physiological measures are objective; the subjective scales are self-ratings that could be influenced by partial unblinding; there is no day-3 session without MDMA.
About 45 measures with three tests each and no correction; Table 1 lists only significant variables; the headline 30% rise in MDMA is not the trial's own figure (16% and 22%).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover with objective pharmacokinetic outcomes and a consistent pattern across many measures, but only 12 men, no confidence intervals, many uncorrected tests, a blind that may have leaked, and a three-day pretreatment. The source can be cited for lower blood-pressure, heart-rate, pupil, temperature and subjective responses to 100 mg of MDMA after 3 days of paroxetine 20 mg in 12 healthy men, with MDMA's peak 16% and exposure 22% higher and HMMA about half as high; it cannot be cited for the 30% figure, for people on long-term treatment, for what happens with a higher or second MDMA dose, or for any harm.

key_findings.finding: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover in 12 healthy men (mean age 24; all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers; MDMA on at least 5 previous occasions); a 13th man withdrew after two paroxetine doses (insomnia, restlessness, anxiety) and never took MDMA. Two 3-day sessions 15 days apart: paroxetine 20 mg a day or placebo on days 1 to 3, MDMA 100 mg on day 3, 3 hours after that day's capsule.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Days 1 and 2: no difference between paroxetine and placebo in area or peak of effects except a rise in systolic pressure with paroxetine (peak difference 8 mm Hg); paroxetine alone improved some psychomotor measures (digit symbol correct responses) and changed no subjective variable.

Physiological effects of MDMA were lowered by paroxetine: peak systolic pressure by 12 mm Hg (Emax F=22.20, P=0.001), diastolic by 5 mm Hg and heart rate by 14 beats/min, pupil widening from 3.33 to 1.23 mm (F=70.35, P<0.001), temperature rise lower by 0.3 C (P=0.041); the Discussion puts the cardiovascular reduction at about 50% and pupil about 70%. By Table 1 the diastolic area (P=0.613) and peak (P=0.213) and the heart-rate area (P=0.093) were not significant.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 957); Results > Physiological Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 957); Fig. 1 (p. 958); Discussion, paragraphs on cardiovascular effects and pupil diameter (pp. 959 to 960)

key_findings.finding: Subjective effects were lowered: ARCI euphoria scale (morphine-benzedrine group) peak 7.27 to 4, amphetamine scale 5.27 to 3.67; VESSPA anxiety 5.55 to 2.7, sociability 3.0 to 0.58, activity 5.91 to 1.21; VAS 'stimulated', 'high', 'any effect', 'good effects', 'liking' (all P=0.003 or less at peak) and 'different body feeling'. No significant change in 'bad effects', 'fear', 'depression or sadness', hallucination items or sedation scales; no hallucinations or psychotic symptoms, no serious adverse events, nobody needed treatment.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 957); Results > Subjective Effects (p. 957); Figs. 2 and 3 (pp. 959 to 960)

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations of MDMA with paroxetine against placebo (Table 2, n=12): peak 246.62 against 212.72 ug/L (+16%), area to 21 hours 2572.21 against 2115.26 ug x h/L (+22%), both P<0.01; HMMA peak 97.88 against 193.14 (-49%) and area 1189.47 against 1923.32 (-38% from the printed means; the text says 39%), half-life 13.10 against 9.54 hours (all P<0.01); MDMA half-life 8.34 against 7.88 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results > Plasma Concentrations of MDMA and HMMA (pp. 957 to 958); Table 2 (p. 961)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the main result is a marked decrease of physiological and subjective effects 'despite a 30% increase' in MDMA plasma concentration (in the abstract: 30%; in the Discussion: 'approximately 30%' citing the 7-man analysis of Segura et al., 2005); because HMMA fell by more than MDMA rose, CYP2D6 seems to contribute less to MDMA's clearance than the 60% from in vitro work; paroxetine is read as acting at the serotonin transporter (pharmacodynamic) and on CYP2D6 (pharmacokinetic), and not fully counteracting MDMA, which points to other transmitter systems.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Discussion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 959); paragraph on SSRIs and the serotonin transporter (p. 959 to 960)

key_findings.finding: The authors close by suggesting that the marked decrease in the positive effects people seek may lead to higher MDMA doses (with depressed people who take SSRIs as their example) and so to potentially life-threatening toxic effects; the abstract makes the same suggestion. They cite internet forums, and animal studies of neuroprotection, for the idea that SSRIs are combined with MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 954 to 955); Discussion, final paragraph (pp. 961 to 962)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the Discussion (first paragraph) state a 30% increase in MDMA plasma concentrations with paroxetine. The trial's own Table 2 and Results give +16% for the peak and +22% for the area to 21 hours; the Discussion's second mention (30%, and HMMA 40% lower) is attributed to an earlier analysis of 7 of these men (Segura et al., 2005).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite 16% (peak) and 22% (exposure) for this trial; the 30% is not this trial's result.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says paroxetine decreased systolic pressure, diastolic pressure and heart rate 'significantly'; Table 1 gives diastolic pressure P=0.613 (area) and P=0.213 (peak) and heart rate P=0.093 (area), significant only for the peak (P=0.018) and in the condition-by-time term.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 5 mm Hg diastolic difference and the area of the heart-rate response are not supported by the paper's own tests; the systolic, pupil and subjective results are the solid ones.

reporting_issues.issue: Both day-3 conditions contained MDMA, so paroxetine's own effect on that day cannot be separated from its effect on MDMA's, and the paper does not say whether each change from baseline is taken from the value before the day-3 capsule or just before MDMA. Days 1 and 2 show paroxetine alone raising systolic pressure (peak difference 8 mm Hg) and improving a psychomotor measure.
reporting_issues.consequence: A higher baseline under paroxetine would, if anything, work against the finding of a lower systolic response, but day-3 effects of paroxetine alone are not measured and the baseline used is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: About 45 effect measures were each tested on area, peak and condition by time, with no correction; Table 1 lists only the variables that differed, and several values lie close to the threshold (systolic area P=0.033, drowsiness area P=0.049, 'different surroundings' P=0.041 and 0.042).
reporting_issues.consequence: Results at P<0.001 (high, any effect, good effects, liking, stimulated, pupil, systolic peak, euphoria and amphetamine scales) are the dependable ones; the near-threshold ones may be chance.

reporting_issues.issue: A 13th volunteer left after two paroxetine doses (insomnia, restlessness, anxiety); he is described in the Methods but counted nowhere in the safety statement ('serious adverse events were not observed'), and the 12 analysed are the men who tolerated paroxetine.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of 13 men could not take 3 days of paroxetine 20 mg; the trial says nothing about the MDMA and paroxetine combination in him, since he never took MDMA.

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that the lower effects could lead people to take higher doses of MDMA, with life-threatening toxic effects, and the example of depressed people on SSRIs, rest on no data: nobody took a second dose, no toxic effect was measured, and no person on long-term SSRI treatment was studied; the supporting references are an internet forum and animal studies.
reporting_issues.consequence: A hypothesis, not a finding: no study has measured whether people who feel less take more or what their blood levels are if they do. The only related measurements are the higher MDMA peak and exposure in this trial and the more-than-proportional rise after higher or repeated doses in other studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion estimates from the larger fall in HMMA (about 40-49%) than rise in MDMA (16-30%) that CYP2D6 handles less of MDMA's clearance than the 60% reported in vitro.
reporting_issues.consequence: The design cannot estimate that share (paroxetine also lowers the formation of HMMA by other routes, and the numbers differ by analysis); do not cite it as a measurement.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods describe the pharmacokinetic area under the curve as 0 to 27 hours (blood was drawn to 27 hours after MDMA), while Table 2 labels its area 0 to 21 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the printed areas (+22% with paroxetine) are quoted as 'to 21 hours', as the table labels them; the paper does not explain the difference.

verification.source_read: PDF Farre_2007_MDMAParoxetineInteraction.pdf (9 pages, pp. 954-962), text extracted once with pdftotext; Tables 1 and 2 and Figures 1 to 3 checked on rendered pages 4, 7 and 8 (pdf pages). Supplementary material: none.

design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person laboratory study in 16 healthy volunteers (12 men, 4 women), each attending four sessions at least 14 days apart in counterbalanced order: placebo then placebo; citalopram then placebo; placebo then MDMA; citalopram then MDMA. Citalopram 40 mg (or saline) was given by intravenous infusion over 90 minutes, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) or placebo capsules by mouth. Psychological effects were rated 120 minutes after MDMA with the Altered States of Consciousness Rating Scale (ASC) and the Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AM). Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, side effects and startle reflex were also recorded and are reported in other papers. No blood levels of MDMA or citalopram were measured.
can_establish: Whether, in 16 healthy volunteers (13 of them with no previous MDMA experience), a single intravenous dose of citalopram 90 minutes before MDMA lowers the psychological effects of MDMA that they rate 2 hours after the MDMA dose (positive mood, derealization, depersonalization, altered sense of time, thought disorder, loss of control, changed meaning of percepts, self-confidence, extroversion), and which ratings are not lowered (emotional excitability, sensitivity).
cannot_establish: What happens in people who take an SSRI by mouth for weeks (steady state) or for illness, at other MDMA doses, with repeated MDMA doses, or in people who regularly take MDMA (only 3 of 16 had tried it); whether MDMA or citalopram blood levels changed (not measured); whether the longer duration of effect after citalopram (about 5 hours against 3) is real, since no measurement method, spread or test is given for it; the cause of the lower ratings beyond the authors' reading that they reflect action at the serotonin uptake site; whether lower ratings lead people to take more MDMA, or what happens to their blood levels if they do (no one took a second dose); sex differences (4 women).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers recruited at the University Hospital and the Medical School of the University of Zurich, informed in writing and orally about the study, MDMA's psychological effects, side effects, previous toxicology and psychiatric risks; written consent. Approved by the Ethics Committee of the Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich and the Swiss Federal Health Office (Materials and Method; Subjects).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy by history, physical examination and blood analysis; psychiatric interview; excluded: major psychiatric disorder in first-degree relatives, head injury, alcohol or regular substance abuse, and a score more than 2 standard deviations above the norm on the neuroticism scale of the Freiburger Personality Inventory.
sample.demographics: 12 men and 4 women, aged 21 to 39 (mean 27.4, SD 4.4); all with high-school education and all but one university students or physicians. Six had previous recreational drug experience: two had tried ecstasy, three a hallucinogen and one both.
sample.attrition: None reported; every analysis has n=16.
sample.selection_effects: Highly educated, screened, mostly drug-naive volunteers (13 of 16 had never taken MDMA), tested once in a hospital; not typical of people who take MDMA at events or of people on long-term antidepressants. The paper itself says the earlier case series of 4 people on fluoxetine differed in dose and route.

exposure.measurement: Citalopram hydrochloride 40 mg ampoules (supplied by Lundbeck, Switzerland) dissolved in 500 mL sterile saline and infused over 90 minutes (330 mL/h); saline alone as placebo; racemic MDMA from the Swiss Federal Health Office in 10 and 50 mg capsules prepared by a hospital pharmacy, and placebo capsules. No concentrations were measured.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: citalopram 40 mg intravenously once, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg by mouth (mean 100 mg, range about 80 to 120 mg) given after the catheter was removed; a pilot with citalopram 40 to 80 mg before MDMA preceded the study; sessions began at 9 AM or 2 PM.
exposure.polysubstance: No other drug; the volunteers did not eat or drink coffee for 2 hours before each session.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Alcohol or regular substance abuse excluded; abstinence before sessions is not described beyond the 2-hour fast.

comparison.controls: Each volunteer's own placebo-placebo, citalopram-placebo and placebo-MDMA sessions, in counterbalanced order, at least 14 days apart.
comparison.matching: Within person; the method of counterbalancing is not described.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Neuroticism was screened; no genotype (CYP2D6 or serotonin-transporter) and no blood levels.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable beyond the exclusion of substance abuse; six had tried recreational drugs.

outcomes.instruments: Altered States of Consciousness Rating Scale (ASC; 66 visual-analog items in three scales: oceanic boundlessness, anxious ego dissolution, visionary restructuralization; 15 item clusters) and Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AM; 14 scales), both completed 120 minutes after MDMA or placebo; duration of the subjective effect (method not described); side effects assessed during the session and 1 and 3 days later (reported separately).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established German-language scales (Dittrich 1985 and 1998; Janke and Debus 1978).
outcomes.operationalization: MANOVA for MDMA against placebo on the three ASC scales; two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with pretreatment (placebo or citalopram) and treatment (placebo or MDMA) as within-person factors, the interaction showing that citalopram changed the MDMA effect; Tukey post hoc tests for subscores; Wilcoxon matched-pairs tests for the AM scales; significance at P<0.05.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None across the 3 ASC scales, 15 ASC clusters and 14 AM scales (32 outcomes by the editors' count), each with several contrasts; Tukey tests only within ANOVAs.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Described as double-blind; whether the blind held is not assessed; nausea in 6 of 16 after citalopram infusion (and fatigue, headache) could reveal the infusion.

analysis.effect_sizes: ASC item clusters, percent of maximum, mean for MDMA alone against citalopram then MDMA (n=16; Table 1): positive basic mood 40.1 against 16.4; derealization 32.7 against 12.6; depersonalization 24.5 against 10.5; alterations of the sense of time 30.9 against 13.1; mania-like experience 26.6 against 6.7; thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6; loss of thought control 14.1 against 2.8; loss of body control 11.9 against 5.3; changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1; facilitated imagination 27.2 against 6.6 (all marked significant); not significantly lowered: frightening derealization 8.5 against 2.1 (P<0.06), synesthesia 12.8 against 8.0, facilitated recollection 18.4 against 7.6; delusion and hallucinations were not significantly above placebo. Editors' percentage falls for the significant clusters: 55% to 80%. Pretreatment-by-treatment interactions: oceanic boundlessness F(1,15)=22.47, P<.0003; anxious ego dissolution F(1,15)=23.04, P<.0002; visionary restructuralization F(1,15)=12.80, P<.027 as printed (about 0.003 by the editors' calculation). Citalopram alone changed scores little (e.g., positive basic mood 2.3% against 0.6% on placebo). AM scales: MDMA raised heightened mood (P<.03), self-confidence (P<.02), extroversion (P<.01), introversion (P<.05), emotional excitability (P<.01), sensitivity (P<.03) and thoughtfulness (P<.002); citalopram lowered the MDMA-induced increases in self-confidence (P<.04) and extroversion (P<.01) to the level of citalopram alone and efficiency-activation (P<.03); the fall in heightened mood did not reach significance (P=.06); emotional excitability and sensitivity were not lowered at all. Time course: MDMA's subjective effect began 20 to 120 minutes after intake (mean 45), peaked 15 to 30 minutes later and lasted a mean of 3 hours; after citalopram the effect was 'markedly reduced but interestingly prolonged' to a mean of 5 hours (no test or spread given). The authors summarize the lowering as about 60% and note no correlation between citalopram dose per kg and the size of the lowering, and that in a pilot of two people 60 mg and 80 mg of citalopram blocked MDMA's effects to a degree comparable to 40 mg.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A 1999 study; no registry entry is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Cardiovascular, temperature, side-effect and startle results from the same sessions are reported in other papers (cited as submitted); no data are given for the duration finding or the pilot with 60 and 80 mg of citalopram.
analysis.power: No sample-size reasoning; 16 volunteers.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 16 healthy volunteers, mostly with no MDMA experience, 40 mg of citalopram by infusion before 1.5 mg/kg of MDMA lowered ratings of most altered-state clusters by roughly 55 to 80% (the authors say about 60%) 2 hours after MDMA, and lowered self-confidence, extroversion and efficiency-activation, but not emotional excitability or sensitivity; the effect lasted longer by the authors' account (5 hours against 3), without data. Nothing about blood levels was measured.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that citalopram attenuated MDMA's acute psychological effects by about 60% and that this suggests the psychoactive properties are largely dependent on action at the serotonin uptake site, with other mechanisms (dopamine, norepinephrine, receptors) accounting for the rest. They suggest the longer duration may be a metabolic interaction (citalopram inhibits CYP2D6) or competition at the uptake site; neither is tested here, and the study measured no blood levels.

timeline.event: Case series of four people who had taken fluoxetine before ecstasy (McCann and Ricaurte; cited here): one felt less effect and three no change; the authors of this study attribute the difference to the lower, oral fluoxetine dose

Independent group: paroxetine 20 mg a day for 3 days before MDMA lowered blood pressure, heart rate, pupil, temperature and subjective responses in 12 men while raising MDMA's peak by 16% and exposure by 22%

Systematic review: lowered effects were also reported for fluoxetine, duloxetine and reboxetine, with bupropion the exception for subjective ratings (as summarized by the review; the duloxetine and reboxetine trials are from this study's laboratory, the fluoxetine trial from another)

replication.where_it_stands: Blunting of MDMA's effects by serotonin reuptake inhibitors was seen again with paroxetine by an independent group (Barcelona) and, as cited in that paper and summarized by the 2022 review, with fluoxetine by another group; duloxetine and reboxetine trials summarized by the review come from this study's own laboratory. The duration finding (3 to 5 hours) was not examined with statistics here and is not reported as such in the paroxetine trial.

funding.funder: Heffter Research Institute, Santa Fe, New Mexico (Acknowledgments); citalopram ampoules 'kindly provided' by Lundbeck, Switzerland, the maker of citalopram (Substances and Dosing); MDMA from the Swiss Federal Health Office.
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: the article carries no conflict-of-interest statement; the maker of citalopram supplied the drug.
funding.affiliations_note: Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich, research department. Liechti is also the last author of several of the later trials of medicines before MDMA that the 2022 review summarizes (reboxetine, duloxetine, methylphenidate, clonidine and others), so those trials and this one are one laboratory's work, not independent confirmations of each other.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, double-blind crossover in people who take an SSRI for illness at steady state and in matched healthy volunteers, with MDMA concentrations and a measured time course of effects (so that duration can be tested and a pharmacokinetic cause separated from a pharmacodynamic one), more than one MDMA dose, women in numbers, a check that the blind held, and a second MDMA dose or a dose-choice task to find out what people do after feeling little and what their levels are then.

domains.note: Counterbalanced order of four conditions; the method is not described.
At least 14 days between sessions (citalopram half-life about 1.5 days).

Double-blind with saline infusion and placebo capsules, but nausea in 6 of 16 (and fatigue, headache) after citalopram could reveal the condition, MDMA's effects are obvious, and the blind was not tested.
All 16 volunteers are analysed on every outcome.
Self-rated scales at one time point (120 minutes) that could be influenced by partial unblinding; the duration of effect has no stated measurement method.
No registration; 32 scales and clusters tested without correction; cardiovascular and other results from the same sessions are reported elsewhere; no data for the duration finding.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A counterbalanced, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover with a large and consistent effect across many scales, but 16 volunteers who were mostly drug-naive, subjective self-ratings with a blind that may have leaked, uncorrected multiple tests and no blood levels. The source can be cited for a roughly 60% lower rating of most psychological effects of 1.5 mg/kg MDMA 2 hours after an infusion of citalopram 40 mg, in 16 healthy volunteers; it cannot be cited for the longer duration, for people on long-term treatment, for blood levels, or for any effect on the amount taken or on harm.

key_findings.finding: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person design with four counterbalanced conditions (placebo-placebo, citalopram-placebo, placebo-MDMA, citalopram-MDMA), sessions at least 14 days apart; citalopram 40 mg in saline over 90 minutes by infusion, then MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (mean 100 mg, SD 10) by mouth; psychometric ratings 120 minutes after MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Method > Substances and Dosing, 1st paragraph (p. 514); Study Design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 514 to 515)

key_findings.finding: Sixteen volunteers, 12 men and 4 women, aged 21 to 39 (mean 27.4), high-school educated and nearly all university students or physicians; six had previous recreational drug experience, of whom three had tried ecstasy.

MDMA's subjective effect began 20 to 120 minutes after intake (mean 45), peaked 15 to 30 minutes later and lasted a mean of 3 hours; after citalopram the effect was markedly reduced but 'prolonged to a mean duration of 5 hours', with no measurement method, spread or test given; the Discussion says citalopram prolonged the effects 'by up to two hours' and offers a metabolic interaction (citalopram inhibits CYP2D6) or competition at the uptake site as possible reasons.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 515); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Another interesting finding' (p. 519)

key_findings.finding: ASC: MDMA raised all three scales against placebo (Rao R(3,12)=7.25, P<.005) and citalopram pretreatment lowered them (pretreatment by treatment: oceanic boundlessness F(1,15)=22.47, anxious ego dissolution F(1,15)=23.04, visionary restructuralization F(1,15)=12.80); positive basic mood 40.1% of maximum with MDMA against 16.4% after citalopram, derealization 32.7 against 12.6, thought disorder 24.8 against 8.6, changed meaning of percepts 37.3 against 14.1 (P<.05 for each cluster marked in Table 1).

AM: citalopram lowered the MDMA-induced rises in self-confidence (P<.04) and extroversion (P<.01) to the level of citalopram alone and lowered efficiency-activation (P<.03); the fall in heightened mood did not reach significance (P=.06); the rises in emotional excitability and sensitivity were not lowered at all.
key_findings.locator: Results, last paragraph (p. 516); Figure 2 (p. 518); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 517)

key_findings.finding: Citalopram alone lowered some scale scores against placebo, which the authors attribute mostly to its side effects (fatigue, headache, nausea; nausea in 6 of 16); they argue this cannot explain the lowering seen in all subjects, and that in the same subjects citalopram also reduced MDMA's cardiovascular effects (reported elsewhere).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 517); paragraph beginning 'Non-specific untoward effects' (pp. 518 to 519)

key_findings.finding: The authors say citalopram attenuated MDMA's effects by about 60% only, which they do not attribute to too little citalopram: all received 40 mg whatever their weight, with no correlation between dose per kg and the size of the lowering, and in a pilot two people given 60 or 80 mg had MDMA's effects blocked to a degree comparable to 40 mg.

Conclusion: citalopram attenuated the acute psychological effects of MDMA in healthy humans by about 60%, suggesting the psychoactive properties of MDMA are largely dependent on action at the serotonin uptake site; other actions (dopamine, norepinephrine, receptors) are left open. A four-person case series of fluoxetine and ecstasy (one felt less effect, three no change) is discussed as differing in dose and route.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 513); Introduction, last paragraph (pp. 513 to 514); Discussion, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 517 to 518) and concluding paragraph (pp. 519 to 520)

reporting_issues.issue: The duration finding (effect lasting 3 hours with MDMA alone and 5 hours after citalopram; 'up to two hours' longer) has no stated measurement method, no spread and no test, though it appears in the Results and is discussed as a finding.
