reporting_issues.consequence: Treat it as an observation reported by the authors, not a tested result; with no blood levels, whether MDMA stayed longer in the blood (a CYP2D6 effect of citalopram) or its effect was delayed cannot be told.

reporting_issues.issue: The pretreatment-by-treatment result for visionary restructuralization is printed as F(1,15)=12.80, P<.027; that F value corresponds to about P=0.003, and F(1,15)=23.04 is printed with P<.0002 though it corresponds to about 0.00023 (the editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably a dropped zero; the interaction is stronger than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors' lowering of about 60 percent is given without saying how it was calculated; from the printed cluster means the significant falls are 55% to 80% (the editors' calculation), and some clusters were not significantly lowered.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use about 60 percent as the authors' summary, not as a measured average.

reporting_issues.issue: The argument that citalopram's own side effects (nausea in 6 of 16, fatigue, headache) are unlikely to explain the lowering rests on side-effect data that are 'to be reported separately'; the blind was not tested.
reporting_issues.consequence: Partial unblinding of the infusion could have influenced the ratings; the size of any such effect is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Cardiovascular, startle and side-effect results from the same sessions, and a pilot with 60 and 80 mg of citalopram in two people, are mentioned but not shown.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper alone cannot be used for the cardiovascular effects or for the pilot's numbers.

verification.source_read: PDF Liechti_2000_CitalopramAttenuatesMDMA.pdf (9 pages, pp. 513-521), text extracted once with pdftotext; Table 1 read in the text layer (no negative numbers used). Figures 1 and 2 not read as images. Supplementary material: none.

design_detail: Prospective follow-up (a case series) of pregnancies in which a health professional contacted the UK National Teratology Information Service (NTIS) about ecstasy exposure between January 1989 and June 1998: 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up, leaving 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with a known outcome. The enquirer reported the exposure, prescribed and non-prescribed drugs, at the time of the enquiry; the service then contacted the enquirer after the expected delivery date and, where needed, other clinical specialists. There is no unexposed comparison group: the 12 infants with an anomaly among 78 live births are set against external figures (2 to 3% for any anomaly, 5 to 10 per 1000 for heart disease, 1 per 1000 for talipes). A one-page research letter with one table.
can_establish: What was reported to a national teratology service about the outcome of 136 pregnancies exposed to ecstasy, with or without other drugs: 11 miscarriages, 48 elective terminations, 78 live births (66 recorded as normal and 12 with a congenital anomaly), and which anomalies were recorded.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy caused any anomaly: there is no unexposed group; 62 of the 136 mothers also took other drugs; alcohol, smoking, age and illness are not adjusted for; 55% of the enquiries had no known outcome; the anomaly list mixes major findings with minor ones (a toe position, thigh pigmentation, clicking hips); the benchmark percentages are not referenced; no dose or number of tablets is given; anomalies among the 59 miscarried or terminated pregnancies are unknown (no necropsies); nothing is said about development after birth.

sample.recruitment: Enquiries to the NTIS by health professionals, in most cases the patient's general practitioner, about ecstasy exposure in pregnancy, January 1989 to June 1998 (302 enquiries). Follow-up by contacting the enquirer after the expected date of delivery, then other clinical specialists where necessary (Methods paragraphs).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Pregnancies with a reported ecstasy exposure and a known outcome. Excluded: 31 pregnancies not yet completed (10% of enquiries) and 135 (45%) lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.
sample.demographics: Maternal age at exposure known for 82 women (60%): 26 aged 16 to 20, 31 aged 21 to 25, 20 aged 26 to 31 and five aged 31 to 36. Exposure by trimester: 127 women in the first trimester (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs), two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four women were exposed to several drugs of abuse throughout pregnancy. Acute toxicity from ecstasy was reported in two mothers.
sample.attrition: 55% of enquiries (45% lost, 10% not completed) have no outcome and are not in the analysis; the letter does not compare them with the 136.
sample.selection_effects: Enquiries made by clinicians who were concerned enough to contact a teratology service, so mothers who asked, and clinicians who followed up, are a selected group. The rate of elective termination (35%, 48 of 136) is stated to be higher than the UK average, which suggests that the exposure itself led to terminations; the live-born denominator is therefore selected, and the direction of any resulting bias is unclear.

exposure.measurement: Reported by the enquiring health professional at the time of the enquiry (prescribed and non-prescribed drugs, expected date of delivery); not confirmed by any test; the contents of the tablets are not known.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not recorded in the letter; only the trimester (127 of 136 in the first trimester) and, for the infants with an anomaly, the weeks of exposure (for example 4 weeks, 6 to 12 weeks, first trimester).
exposure.polysubstance: 62 of 136 mothers also took other drugs of abuse (ecstasy and amphetamine 37 women; with cocaine 20; with cannabis 16; with alcohol 13; with LSD 9; with other drugs 13; the counts overlap); four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy; one neonatal death was in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None. External reference rates are cited without sources: 2 to 3% for congenital anomalies overall; 5 to 10 per 1000 live births for congenital heart disease (24 to 34% of them ventricular septal defects, 7% atrial septal defects); 1 per 1000 for talipes (idiopathic talipes equinovarus has a 3 to 1 male predominance in the UK).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Age is known for 60%; smoking, alcohol quantity, folic acid, other medicines, socio-economic position, illness and family history of malformations are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: None; other drugs are part of the exposure in 62 of 136.

outcomes.instruments: Clinician report to the service after the expected delivery date: miscarriage, termination, live birth, prematurity, birthweight, sex ratio and congenital anomalies (13 findings in the table: 12 in live-born infants and one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs).
outcomes.validity_norms: No definition of congenital anomaly, no coding system and no examination protocol are given; the table includes minor findings (left fourth toe lying under the third, right-sided plagiocephaly, pigmentation of the right thigh, ptosis, clicking hips) alongside major ones (ventricular septal defects, hydrocephalus, absent upper limbs).
outcomes.operationalization: Proportion of live births with an anomaly, with a 95% confidence interval (the editors reproduce the intervals by an exact binomial method to within 0.1 percentage point), compared informally with the external figures; subgroup rates for heart and 'musculoskeletal' anomalies.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; the subgroups (heart disease, talipes) were chosen after the table was drawn up.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; whoever reported the outcome knew of the exposure.

analysis.effect_sizes: 12 of 78 live-born infants had an anomaly: 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4; the editors' exact interval is 8.2 to 25.3) against an expected 2 to 3%. Two infants had congenital heart disease (ventricular septal defects): 26 per 1000 live births (CI 3.0 to 90.0) against 5 to 10 per 1000. Three infants (all girls) had talipes: 38 per 1000 (CI 8 to 109) against 1 per 1000; this is also the figure the abstract gives as 'musculoskeletal anomalies'. Miscarriage 11 of 136 (8%, within the expected range); elective termination 48 (35%); 8 premature births (25 to 36 weeks, including twins born at 25 weeks); one neonatal death; only three infants under 2.5 kg among those born at term; no effect on sex ratio. By the editors' reading of the table, the three infants with talipes were in the ecstasy-only group, and both infants with a ventricular septal defect had other drug exposure (amphetamine and gamma hydroxybutyric acid in one, alcohol in the other).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A service database, not a registered study; an interim report of 92 pregnancies was published as an abstract in 1998 (cited).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract highlights heart and 'musculoskeletal' anomalies, which rest on 2 and 3 infants and were chosen from the 13 findings in the table; the 'musculoskeletal' rate equals the talipes count and the letter does not say which other findings were counted under it.
analysis.power: No calculation; the authors state that the series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 78 live-born infants whose mothers reported ecstasy in pregnancy, 12 (15.4%) had a recorded anomaly, a higher proportion than the 2 to 3% the authors cite, but the comparison is with an unreferenced benchmark of uncertain definition, in a group where 55% of enquiries had no outcome, 62 of 136 mothers took other drugs and the list mixes minor with major findings. Two infants had heart defects (both with other drug exposure) and three had talipes. The numbers are too small and the comparison too uncontrolled to say whether ecstasy changes the chance of an anomaly.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the drug may be associated with a significantly increased risk of congenital defects (15.4%), with heart and musculoskeletal anomalies predominant; the text calls the data important while stating that the series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly.

timeline.event: Interim report of 92 pregnancies from the same service, published as a conference abstract (cited in this letter; not read)
Dutch teratology service reported 43 pregnancies after ecstasy exposure (cited in this letter; not read); the authors know of one other case of congenital heart disease from it

Prospective cohort of 96 women recruited in pregnancy (28 exposed to MDMA) that compares infant development, not anomalies; its Introduction describes this letter as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies, neither of which the letter prints (its Discussion's 15.4% 'increased risk' echoes the letter's own summary)

replication.where_it_stands: No study read here has repeated a count of congenital anomalies after MDMA with a comparison group. The 2012 cohort studied development at 1 and 4 months instead; one of its 28 exposed infants had a rare genetic syndrome that its authors attribute to a spontaneous mutation.

funding.funder: No funding statement; the letter thanks the patients, the Drug Information pharmacists, health-care personnel and a statistician.
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: the letter carries no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors work at the National Teratology Information Service (Regional Drug and Therapeutics Centre, Newcastle) and the Scottish Poisons Information Bureau; the service that collected the data is the authors' own.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort or registry with an unexposed comparison group matched or adjusted for age, smoking, alcohol, other drugs and illness; enrolment in early pregnancy with few lost to follow-up; a stated definition of major anomalies using a standard coding system; exposure timing and amount from interview and, where possible, biological confirmation; and enough exposed pregnancies (hundreds) to give usable intervals for heart and limb defects.

domains.note: No comparison group at all; 62 of 136 mothers also took other drugs; alcohol, smoking, age, illness and folate are not reported.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Only enquiries to a service, and only those with a known outcome (136 of 302); 35% of the pregnancies were terminated.
Exposure is reported second-hand by the enquirer, without confirmation, dose or tablet contents.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Not applicable: the exposure was not assigned; other drugs are counted under confounding.
45% of enquiries were lost to follow-up and 10% not completed; no outcomes for those pregnancies, and no necropsy data for the 59 miscarried or terminated ones.
Anomalies were reported by whoever enquired, with no definition or coding, no systematic examination, and knowledge of the exposure; minor findings are included.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: The abstract's headline is a crude comparison with an unreferenced benchmark; the heart and 'musculoskeletal' subgroups rest on 2 and 3 infants and were chosen after the table was drawn up.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A case series without an unexposed comparison group, from enquiries to a service, with 55% of enquiries lacking an outcome, other drugs in nearly half the exposures and an undefined anomaly list: it cannot show whether ecstasy changes the chance of an anomaly. The source can be cited for what was reported to the service (136 pregnancies, 78 live births, 12 recorded anomalies and which), with its limits stated; it cannot be cited for a risk, a risk ratio, or any statement that ecstasy causes or does not cause anomalies.

key_findings.finding: The UK National Teratology Information Service followed up 136 pregnancies (one pair of twins) with ecstasy exposure from January 1989 to June 1998; there were 302 enquiries, of which 31 (10%) were not yet completed and 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up because the enquirer could no longer identify the patient or she did not return to the surgery.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 3rd paragraph (opens 'The UK National Teratology Information Service'; the boxed summary counts as the 1st paragraph)

key_findings.finding: The enquirer was asked for drug exposure, prescribed and non-prescribed, at the time of the enquiry and the expected delivery date; follow-up was by contacting the enquirer after the expected date of delivery and, where necessary, other clinical specialists.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 4th paragraph (opens 'In each case the enquirer was asked')

key_findings.finding: 74 women reported ecstasy only and 62 ecstasy with other drugs of abuse (amphetamine 37, cocaine 20, cannabis 16, alcohol 13, LSD 9, other 13); acute toxicity from ecstasy in two mothers; maternal age known for 82 (60%): 26 aged 16 to 20, 31 aged 21 to 25, 20 aged 26 to 31, five aged 31 to 36.

127 women (71 ecstasy alone, 56 with other drugs) were exposed in the first trimester, two in the first and second, two in the second and one in the third; four were exposed to several drugs throughout pregnancy.

11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage (8%, within the expected range) and 48 in elective termination (35%, higher than the UK average; one after prenatal diagnosis of malformations); no necropsy data on the other aborted fetuses.

78 live-born infants: 66 normal and 12 with congenital anomalies, 15.4% (95% CI 8.2 to 25.4), described as significantly higher than an expected incidence of 2 to 3%; the table lists 13 anomaly findings (12 live-born, plus one terminated fetus with absent upper limbs), in groups by drug exposure: ecstasy alone 7 rows, ecstasy with amphetamine and gamma hydroxybutyric acid 1, with alcohol 3 and with amphetamine 2.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 8th paragraph (opens 'There were 78 liveborn infants'); Table (Malformations reported after exposure of fetus to ecstasy and other drugs of abuse)

key_findings.finding: Eight infants were born prematurely (25 to 36 weeks, including twins at 25 weeks; two fetal distress cases thought unrelated to ecstasy); one neonatal death in an infant of a mother who took ecstasy, heroin and methadone throughout pregnancy; no adverse effect on sex ratio; birthweights within the expected range for term infants with only three under 2.5 kg.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 9th and 10th paragraphs (open 'Eight infants were born prematurely' and 'No adverse effects were observed in the sex ratio')

key_findings.finding: Three female infants had talipes (38 per 1000, CI 8 to 109, against an expected 1 per 1000; idiopathic talipes equinovarus is male-predominant 3 to 1 in the UK); two infants had congenital heart disease, ventricular septal defects (26 per 1000, CI 3.0 to 90.0, against an expected 5 to 10 per 1000); the authors say the small series has insufficient statistical power to confirm a causal relation with any particular anomaly but consider the data important.
key_findings.locator: Research letter, 11th and 12th paragraphs (open 'There were three female infants with talipes' and 'The spontaneous incidence of congenital heart disease'); abstract

reporting_issues.issue: The 15.4% is called significantly higher than an 'expected incidence of 2-3%', with no source or definition for the benchmark; the 12 live-born infants with an anomaly include minor findings (left fourth toe under the third, right-sided plagiocephaly, pigmentation of the right thigh, ptosis of the left eye, clicking hips) as well as major ones.
reporting_issues.consequence: The comparison is not like with like: a benchmark for major malformations set against a list of mixed severity. The proportion cannot be read as a risk or a risk ratio.

reporting_issues.issue: Of 302 enquiries, 135 (45%) were lost to follow-up and 31 (10%) not completed; the letter does not compare them with the 136 followed.
reporting_issues.consequence: If outcomes were reported back more often when something was wrong, or when the baby was well, the proportion would be biased in either direction; the size of the bias is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: Elective terminations were 35% (48 of 136) and 11 pregnancies ended in miscarriage; no necropsy data exist for the other aborted fetuses (one fetus had absent upper limbs and was terminated).
reporting_issues.consequence: Anomalies in 59 non-live pregnancies are largely unknown, and the live-born denominator may be selected; the table's count of 12 refers to live births only.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's rate for 'musculoskeletal anomalies' (38 per 1000) is the same figure the text gives for talipes alone (3 infants); the letter does not say which other findings (toe position, clinodactyly, clicking hips) were counted under it, and the abstract's 'cardiovascular' rate rests on 2 infants, both of whom were also exposed to other drugs (amphetamine and gamma hydroxybutyric acid in one, alcohol in the other) by the table's grouping.
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup rates have very wide intervals (3 to 90 and 8 to 109 per 1000) and cannot be attributed to ecstasy alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The expected rate of talipes (1 per 1000) is set against three girls, although the letter says idiopathic talipes is male-predominant 3 to 1; the rate is not tested and the unusual sex distribution is not explained.
reporting_issues.consequence: Three cases cannot establish an excess; the sex pattern is noted by the authors but not interpreted.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract speaks of 136 'babies' exposed; there were 136 pregnancies, of which 78 ended in live births (one pair of twins counts as two).
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 136 pregnancies and 78 live births; the 15.4% has a denominator of 78.

reporting_issues.issue: A later paper (Singer et al., 2012) describes this letter in its Introduction as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies; the letter contains no risk ratio, no adjusted analysis and no such multiples (15.4% is a proportion, which the authors compare informally with 2 to 3%, a ratio of about 5 to 8 by the editors' arithmetic). The 2012 paper's Discussion wording, a 15.4% 'increased risk', echoes the letter's own summary.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 4 to 7 times and two-fold figures should not be quoted from the 2012 paper as findings of this letter.

verification.source_read: PDF McElhatton_1999_CongenitalAnomalies.pdf (2 pages, Lancet 354:1441-1442; the letter and its table are on p. 1441, read as text and on a rendered page; the rest of the PDF is an unrelated letter on tonsillar cancer). Supplementary material: none.

design_detail: Open-label, fixed-order pharmacokinetic study in 15 healthy men with recreational MDMA experience who were all extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers, each acting as his own control. Session 1 (control): dextromethorphan 30 mg with caffeine 100 mg. Session 2 (at least 3 days later): MDMA 1.5 mg/kg by mouth (75 to 100 mg), then caffeine at 4 hours and repeated 30 mg doses of dextromethorphan from 4 hours onward. CYP2D6 activity was read from plasma dextromethorphan and its metabolites and from the urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio (the metabolic ratio), and a recovery half-life was fitted to each man's ratio over 7 to 10 days. A pilot of 3 men used one dextromethorphan schedule, 12 men a second schedule (changed because the ratio had not recovered by 168 hours), and the two were pooled. There was no placebo session and no randomization or counterbalancing: the control session always came first, because the enzyme effect of MDMA lasts for days.
can_establish: Whether, in 15 healthy men with normal CYP2D6 activity, a single dose of 1.5 mg/kg MDMA is followed by a large fall in the enzyme's activity, measured with a probe drug (dextromethorphan exposure about 9 to 10 times higher, its CYP2D6 product about 90% lower, urinary ratio from about 0.006 to 0.43), that has not fully reversed after 10 days, and a rough size of the recovery half-life (about 47 hours from a one-phase fit).
cannot_establish: That the early change is mechanism-based inactivation rather than competition from the MDMA still in the blood (the first probe dose came 4 hours after MDMA, near MDMA's peak, and MDMA is itself a CYP2D6 substrate); how long inhibition lasts (a one-phase fit gives 46.6 hours, a two-phase fit 103 hours with a standard deviation of 70, and activity was not at baseline on day 10); what happens to MDMA blood levels after a second MDMA dose, or to any medicine other than dextromethorphan (not measured); anything in women, in slow, intermediate or ultrarapid metabolizers, at other MDMA doses, or in people who use MDMA often (none was studied); toxicity of any kind.

sample.recruitment: Men recruited by word of mouth; self-reported recreational MDMA use on at least 5 occasions and twice in the previous year (Materials and Methods, Subjects, 2nd paragraph). Interviewed by a physician, examined, laboratory tests, urinalysis and 12-lead ECG; interviewed by a psychiatrist (PRISM for DSM-IV). Approved by the local ethics board (CEIC-IMAS) and authorized by the Spanish Medicines Agency (AEM n. 04-0013); written consent; paid for taking part.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Extensive-metabolizer phenotype by dextromethorphan was required; excluded: history of or current major psychiatric disorder (schizophrenia, psychosis, major affective disorder), abuse or dependence other than nicotine, adverse medical or psychiatric reactions to MDMA, regular medication in the previous month (single symptomatic doses accepted up to the week before). Asked to avoid drugs of abuse for 2 weeks before and during the study (urine screen before each session) and to follow a xanthine-free diet for 48 hours.
sample.demographics: All men; mean age 26 years (19 to 33), weight 69.6 kg (54.2 to 91.2), height 181 cm (171 to 196); on average 26 previous MDMA experiences (range 6 to 100); all but 4 were current smokers; all had used other psychostimulants, cannabis or hallucinogens. CYP2D6 genotypes (Subjects, 3rd paragraph): *1/*1 (1 man), *1/*2 (5), *1/*4 (2), *2/*4 (1), *1/*5 (1), *1/*9 (1), *1/*10 (1), *9/*10 (1), *1/*17 (1), *2/*41 (1), so no man carried two null alleles; 4 carried one (*4 or *5) and several carried reduced-function alleles.
sample.attrition: None reported; all 15 contribute to Table 1. The number of men at each urine time point is not stated: the 10-day point (240 to 248 hours) can come only from the 12 men of the final phase, and the 3 pilot men had no sample after 176 hours.
sample.selection_effects: Men only, young, healthy, experienced with MDMA, selected for normal enzyme activity at baseline (mean baseline metabolic ratio 0.0061, SD 0.0056) and for having no adverse reaction to MDMA before; volunteers took one dose in a hospital laboratory. Results therefore describe men like these.

exposure.measurement: MDMA given in the laboratory and measured in plasma (GC-MS, method of Pizarro et al., 2002): peak 194.3 ng/mL (SD 30.9) at 2.0 hours (SD 1.0), area under the curve to 25 hours 1939.7 (SD 484.7) (printed with the unit mg/mL x h, which cannot be right; probably ng/mL x h), mean residence time 13.3 hours (SD 2.3). The probe drug dextromethorphan was measured in plasma and urine by HPLC with stated limits of detection and precision (about 9 to 15%).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral MDMA dose of 1.5 mg/kg (minimum 75 mg, maximum 100 mg), described as the amount in a single ecstasy pill; probe doses of dextromethorphan 30 mg by mouth at 0 hours in session 1 and at 4, 24, 48 (pilot) or 72 (final), 96, 168 and 240 hours (final) in session 2; caffeine 100 mg.
exposure.polysubstance: No drug other than the probes (dextromethorphan, caffeine) and MDMA; the men were asked to avoid drugs of abuse for 2 weeks before and during the study and were screened by rapid urine test before each session. Tobacco smoking was not permitted for 6 hours after dosing.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Two weeks by request (not verified beyond the urine screen at the start of each session); overnight fast; xanthine-free diet for 48 hours; light meal 6 hours after dosing.

comparison.controls: Each man's own control session with dextromethorphan and caffeine alone (session 1), at least 3 days before the MDMA session. There was no placebo MDMA session.
comparison.matching: Within person, so no matching; the control session always came first (no randomization or counterbalancing).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Genotype is listed for all 15 men; urine pH and creatinine were measured and did not correlate with the metabolic ratio in session 1 (r=0.049 and r=0.214), in a homogeneous sample on similar diets; whether anything else changed between sessions (smoking, diet, time of year) is not described.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not described beyond the urine screen.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma dextromethorphan (DEX), dextrorphan (DOR), 3-methoxymorphinan (MM) and 3-hydroxymorphinan (HM) at up to 12 times over 25 hours; urinary DEX/DOR metabolic ratio (MR) in timed collections from 0 to 248 hours; plasma caffeine and paraxanthine (as a CYP1A2 marker; described as unaffected, not shown); recovery half-life of CYP2D6 from a mono-exponential fit to each man's fold change in MR.
outcomes.validity_norms: The urinary ratio is a standard probe of CYP2D6 activity; the poor-metabolizer antimode of 0.3 comes from a 1985 study cited by the authors. The ratio is sensitive to urine pH and renal clearance, which the authors checked at baseline only.
outcomes.operationalization: Activity change = the fold change of each man's MR after MDMA against his own control MR, fitted over time (weighted by the SD of the MR in each collection period), giving a half-life = ln 2 / Kcyp; corrected half-lives subtract MDMA's mean residence time; a two-phase curve was also fitted because the one-phase fit was thought to underestimate recovery.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; paired Student t tests for peak and area (P<0.05) and the Wilcoxon test for time to peak; the main changes are large against their standard deviations.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Open design, justified by the authors by the objective outcomes; blinding of the laboratory analysts is not described.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (n=15; mean and SD; all P<0.05 by paired t test unless noted): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 (3.6) to 29.7 (18.5) ng/mL and area over 8 hours 15.7 (5.2) to 149.1 (75.6) ng/mL x h, half-life 1.7 (0.1) to 9.0 (5.6) h; dextrorphan peak 464.6 (182.6) to 31.9 (12.6) and area 1877.1 (676.2) to 179.1 (77.6), half-life 2.5 (0.6) to 10.9 (5.7) h; 3-hydroxymorphinan peak 164.1 (58.0) to 16.6 (5.8) and area 764.2 (232.2) to 97.5 (38.0); 3-methoxymorphinan peak 2.7 (2.0) to 6.3 (5.1) and area 16.8 (5.3) to 28.8 (24.2), not significant. Editors' ratios of the printed means: dextromethorphan peak 8.5-fold and area 9.5-fold; dextrorphan peak 93% and area 90% lower. Urinary ratio 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848): the ratio of the two means is 71-fold (the paper says almost 100-fold), and 67% of the men (10 of 15, editors' count) were above the poor-metabolizer antimode of 0.3 after MDMA (collection period not stated). The ratio correlated with the peak DEX/DOR ratio (r=0.594, P=0.002). Recovery: Kcyp 0.016 (SD 0.005) per hour (printed without the per), half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8), r2=0.791; corrected for MDMA residence time 37.4 (SD 11.6) hours; a two-phase fit gave 103.0 (SD 70.3) hours, corrected 93.7 (SD 70.4); the ratio had not recovered fully at 10 days (Discussion).
analysis.preregistration_detail: A trial authorized by the Spanish Medicines Agency (AEM n. 04-0013); no registry entry is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Caffeine and paraxanthine results are described as unaffected with no data shown; MDMA's effects and adverse events are summarized in two sentences; the number of men at each later time point is not given; the probe-dose schedule was changed after the first 3 men and the two groups pooled; plasma values below the assay limit were replaced by the limit (Table 1 title), which affects the baseline dextromethorphan values (mean peak 3.5 ng/mL against a limit of 1.5).
analysis.power: No sample-size reasoning; 15 men; the half-life is reported as a mean and SD only.

interpretation_gap.results_show: After 1.5 mg/kg MDMA, 15 men had about 9 to 10 times the plasma exposure to dextromethorphan and about 90% less of its CYP2D6 product; the urinary ratio rose from about 0.006 to 0.43 on average, with 10 of 15 men above the poor-metabolizer cut-off, and had not returned fully to baseline after 10 days. A one-phase model gave a recovery half-life of 47 hours (about 37 hours after the correction); a two-phase model gave about 100 hours with a standard deviation of 70. All probe doses came 4 hours or later after MDMA, so the first hours cannot be separated from competition for the enzyme by MDMA itself.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says CYP2D6 activity 'recovered after 10 days' (the Discussion says the ratio had not recovered fully at 10 days), that the ratio rose 'almost 100-fold' (71-fold by the printed means) and that people who use MDMA 'must be warned' of the consequences. The Discussion says the risk of acute toxicity with repeated doses and binges is 'drastically increased', that a second dose up to a week later would give higher plasma levels and 'higher risk of acute toxicity', and that people who use MDMA often may have 'permanently compromised' CYP2D6 activity. No second MDMA dose, no MDMA level after a second dose, no toxicity outcome and no person who uses MDMA often was studied, so these are inferences from a probe drug.

timeline.event: Same group: non-linear MDMA kinetics in men, which the authors there attributed either to saturation or to inactivation of CYP2D6
Same group: a second 100 mg dose 24 hours after the first raised MDMA exposure by 77% (cited here as in vivo evidence that MDMA inhibits its own metabolism)
Same group: 3 days of paroxetine before MDMA raised MDMA peak by 16% and exposure by 22%

Narrative review by the same group, which uses this study for the speed of recovery and for a statement of inhibition 'within 2 hours' that this study could not show (the first probe dose was at 4 hours)

Independent group: 7 people with no CYP2D6 function had a peak MDMA level 15% above people with normal function, in the first 3 hours only, which the authors read as MDMA blocking the enzyme in everyone

replication.where_it_stands: No second probe-drug study of MDMA's effect on CYP2D6 has been read. The direction (MDMA lowers CYP2D6 activity in people) is supported indirectly by other controlled studies, mostly from the same group, and by an independent pooled genotype analysis; the size and duration of the effect rest on these 15 men, and the duration is uncertain (one-phase 47 hours, two-phase 103 hours, not back to baseline at 10 days).

funding.funder: NIH grant 1 R01 DA017987; Generalitat de Catalunya grant 2005SGR00032; Spanish Network on Addiction Disorders (FIS-RTA RD06/0001/1009) (Acknowledgments footnote); MDMA supplied by the Spanish Ministry of Health.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors state they have no conflicts of interest to disclose (Author Disclosure Information).
funding.affiliations_note: Most authors belong to the Barcelona group (IMIM-Hospital del Mar) that also wrote the 2000 non-linearity paper, the 2004 repeated-dose study, the 2007 paroxetine study and the 2012 review, so these are not independent of each other. Two authors are at the University of Sheffield and one at Simcyp Limited, a pharmacokinetic simulation company; the paper cites a model of MDMA kinetics from the Sheffield and Simcyp authors (Yang et al., 2006).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, blinded crossover in people of known CYP2D6 genotype who take MDMA or placebo and then a CYP2D6 probe (dextromethorphan or another) at several times from 1 hour to 14 days, with MDMA concentrations measured so that competition and inactivation can be told apart, in women and men and at more than one dose; and a design that gives a second MDMA dose, or a medicine cleared by CYP2D6, at set intervals after the first and measures its levels and effects.

domains.note: Fixed order: the control session was always first and MDMA second. The authors had to do it this way, because the enzyme effect lasts for days, but the design cannot separate MDMA from order or time.

Control and MDMA sessions were at least 3 days apart and nothing was done to check that the control values were stable; the probe schedules and collection windows differ between the control and MDMA sessions and between the pilot and final phases.

Open design, with objective outcomes; the dextromethorphan schedule was changed after the first 3 men; abstinence from other drugs rests on the men's word and a urine screen at the start of each session.
All 15 men are in Table 1, but the number at each urine time point is not given and the 10-day point can come only from 12; plasma values below the assay limit were replaced by the limit.

Chromatographic assays with stated limits and precision (about 9 to 15%) and a selectivity check; the urinary ratio can be moved by urine pH and renal function, which were checked at baseline and not at later times.

No registration; the abstract overstates the recovery ('recovered after 10 days') and the size of the ratio change ('almost 100-fold') against the paper's own Discussion and printed means; some results (caffeine, paraxanthine, MDMA effects) are described but not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The outcomes are objective and the changes are large against their spread, but every comparison is the same men's own control session taken first, without a placebo or randomization, and the first probe dose came when MDMA itself was at its peak concentration, so competition for the enzyme cannot be separated from lasting inactivation in the early hours. The source can be cited for a large, long-lasting fall in the probe-drug measure of CYP2D6 activity after a single 1.5 mg/kg dose in 15 healthy men with normal baseline activity, with the later urine collections (from 24 hours) as the stronger evidence for inactivation; it cannot be cited for the length of recovery as a single number, for what happens to MDMA levels after a second dose, for toxicity, or for people who use MDMA often.

key_findings.finding: Fifteen healthy men (mean age 26, range 19 to 33; on average 26 previous MDMA experiences) who were extensive CYP2D6 metabolizers at screening, recruited by word of mouth and paid; genotypes: 1 *1/*1, 5 *1/*2, 2 *1/*4, 1 *2/*4, 1 *1/*5, 1 *1/*9, 1 *1/*10, 1 *9/*10, 1 *1/*17, 1 *2/*41. No man had two null alleles.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Subjects, 2nd paragraph (eligibility, 15 men, demographics) and 3rd paragraph (genotypes and their metabolic ratios)

key_findings.finding: Open, fixed-order design: session 1 (control, dextromethorphan 30 mg with caffeine 100 mg) then at least 3 days later session 2 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, 75 to 100 mg, then caffeine at 4 hours and 30 mg dextromethorphan at 4, 24, 48, 72, 96 and 168 hours in the 3-man pilot); the schedule was changed to 4, 24, 72, 96, 168 and 240 hours for the other 12 men because the ratio had not recovered by 168 hours; results pooled. No placebo MDMA session.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Drugs, 1st paragraph; Study Design, 1st to 4th paragraphs (the 4th, on the changed intervals, is on p. 527)

key_findings.finding: Plasma probe drug after MDMA against the control session (Table 1, n=15): dextromethorphan peak 3.5 to 29.7 ng/mL (SDs 3.6 and 18.5) and area over 8 hours 15.7 to 149.1; dextrorphan peak 464.6 to 31.9 and area 1877.1 to 179.1; 3-hydroxymorphinan peak 164.1 to 16.6 and area 764.2 to 97.5 (all P<0.05); 3-methoxymorphinan not significantly changed; dextromethorphan half-life 1.7 to 9.0 hours.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 527); Results > Plasma Concentrations of DEX, DOR, MM, HM, and MDMA Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamic Effects, 1st paragraph (p. 528)

key_findings.finding: MDMA kinetics in these men: peak 194.3 ng/mL (SD 30.9) at 2.0 hours (SD 1.0), mean residence time 13.3 hours (SD 2.3); the dose produced the usual laboratory effects (higher blood pressure and heart rate, wider pupils, well-being, euphoria) and no adverse effects were noted.

Urinary dextromethorphan to dextrorphan ratio rose from 0.0061 (SD 0.0056) to 0.4322 (SD 0.2848), described as almost 100-fold (the ratio of the printed means is 71-fold); 67% of the men were above the 0.3 poor-metabolizer antimode after MDMA (10 of 15 by the editors' count; the collection period is not stated); no correlation of the ratio with urine pH (r=0.049) or creatinine (r=0.214) at baseline.
key_findings.locator: Results > Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Recovery of CYP2D6 activity fitted with one exponential curve: rate constant 0.016 (SD 0.005) per hour, recovery half-life 46.6 hours (SD 11.8), r2=0.791 (Figure 2).
key_findings.locator: Results > Urinary DEX/DOR MR and CYP2D6 Recovery Half-Life, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 (p. 528)

key_findings.finding: Discussion: the ratio had not recovered fully to baseline at 10 days; the half-life corrected for MDMA's own residence time is 37.4 hours (SD 11.6), and the authors think it underestimates recovery because activity had not recovered even at 10 days; a two-phase fit gives 103.0 hours (SD 70.3), corrected 93.7 (SD 70.4), though variability and few time points 'question the validity of the biphasic model'.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 528, 'not recovered fully ... at 10 days'); 3rd paragraph (p. 529, half-life estimates)

key_findings.finding: The authors compare the effect with paroxetine, also a mechanism-based inhibitor: a single recreational dose of MDMA is said to inhibit CYP2D6 rapidly and completely whereas several prescription doses of paroxetine are needed for similar inhibition, and they point to MDMA phenocopying poor metabolizers as the reason acute toxicity has not been related to genotype.

Statements in the Discussion that go beyond the data: a dose greater than 50 mg would almost completely inactivate CYP2D6 in the liver (from a model, ref. 17); risk of acute toxicity with repeated doses and binges 'drastically increased'; a second dose up to a week later would give higher plasma concentrations and higher risk of acute toxicity; people who use MDMA often may have permanently compromised CYP2D6 activity; people taking an SSRI with multiple MDMA doses should know that metabolism of both is compromised; SSRIs such as citalopram and paroxetine block MDMA's positive effects (refs. 41, 42); the only fatal interaction reported to date was with ritonavir (ref. 40).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says CYP2D6 activity 'recovered after 10 days with a recovery half-life of 46.6 hours'; the Discussion says the ratio 'had not recovered fully' at 10 days and that activity 'has not recovered fully even after 10 days'.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract overstates recovery. The paper's data support only that the ratio was still above baseline at 10 days; the half-life depends on the model (46.6 hours one-phase, 103 hours two-phase).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Results say the metabolic ratio rose 'almost 100-fold' from 0.0061 to 0.4322; the ratio of those two means is 71-fold, and the average of the individual fold changes (which could be larger) is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the printed means (0.006 to 0.43) rather than a fold figure.

reporting_issues.issue: '67% of the subjects' had a ratio above the 0.3 poor-metabolizer antimode after MDMA, without saying in which urine collection period; with 15 men the share is 10 men, and 5 stayed below the cut-off.
reporting_issues.consequence: The share of men who reached poor-metabolizer values depends on the sampling time, and a third did not reach them; the paper does not support saying that everyone became a poor metabolizer.

reporting_issues.issue: The first probe dose after MDMA was given 4 hours after it, when plasma MDMA was near its peak (mean peak 194 ng/mL at 2 hours), and MDMA is itself a CYP2D6 substrate. The early rise in probe-drug exposure therefore mixes competition for the enzyme with inactivation of it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The study does not show inhibition 'within 2 hours' (as the 2012 review of the same group states); the later collections (24 hours onward) are the evidence for lasting inactivation.

reporting_issues.issue: Units are misprinted: MDMA area under the curve '1939.7 +/- 484.7 mg/mL x h' (the value fits ng/mL x h) and Kcyp '0.016 +/- 0.005 hours' (it is a rate per hour; ln 2 / 0.016 = 43 hours is consistent with the stated half-life).
reporting_issues.consequence: Printed units cannot be taken literally; the values are consistent with the rest of the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The dextromethorphan schedule was changed after the first 3 men because the ratio had not recovered by 168 hours; the pilot and final phases differ in dosing times and urine windows and were pooled. The 10-day point comes from 12 men and the number at each time point is not stated; plasma values below the limit of detection were replaced by the limit (Table 1 title).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled half-life mixes two schedules and a changing number of men; the baseline dextromethorphan values (peak 3.5 ng/mL, limit 1.5) are partly the assay limit, so the roughly 9-fold rise is approximate.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's risk statements (acute toxicity 'drastically increased' by repeated doses or binges; a second dose a week later would give higher levels and higher risk of acute toxicity; people who use MDMA often may have permanently compromised activity) are not tested here: no second MDMA dose, no MDMA level after one, no toxicity outcome and no person who uses MDMA often was studied, and the data show recovery under way by 10 days.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the paper for a probe-drug fall that lasts for days after one dose; the statements about toxicity and people who use MDMA often are the authors' inference.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that people who use MDMA 'may take common SSRIs to modify the effects of MDMA' is referenced (ref. 43) to a rat study of fluoxetine and MDMA nerve damage, which does not show what people do.
reporting_issues.consequence: No evidence of people taking SSRIs to change MDMA's effects comes from this paper; the 2007 paroxetine paper cites internet forums for it.

reporting_issues.issue: 3-methoxymorphinan means roughly doubled (peak 2.7 to 6.3; area 16.8 to 28.8) and the text says they were 'not changed by MDMA'; the SDs were as large as the means.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not significant is not the same as unchanged; the sample is too small to say.

verification.source_read: PDF OMathuna_2008_MDMACYP2D6Inhibition.pdf (7 pages, pp. 525-531), text extracted once with pdftotext; Table 1 and Figures 1 and 2 checked on rendered pages 3 and 4. Supplementary material: none.

design_detail: Systematic review (PRISMA; PROSPERO CRD42021233519) of interactions between psychiatric medicines and MDMA or psilocybin, written as a narrative synthesis: no pooled estimate and no risk-of-bias rating of the included studies. One database (MEDLINE via PubMed), English only, 1958 to 21 December 2020; 163 title-or-abstract terms (22 medication-class terms, 135 medicine names, 6 MDMA or psilocybin terms) with 21 publication-type and human filters gave 455 records; 12 more were added by hand. Flow (Fig. 1): 467 screened, 411 excluded on title or abstract, 56 read in full, 16 excluded (no reasons given), 40 included: 26 trial publications, 3 epidemiologic studies and 11 case reports that are summarized only in a supplement. The 26 trial publications are 17 original trials plus 9 secondary or exploratory analyses of the same samples; 22 are on MDMA (13 distinct trials in Table 5) and 4 on psilocybin. Each trial compared a medicine plus MDMA with placebo plus MDMA, and the review expresses the difference as a percent change by a formula it gives in Methods.
can_establish: What was found, under controlled laboratory conditions, when one dose or a short course of a psychiatric medicine was given before MDMA to healthy adults: the direction and rough size (as the review computes them, with no intervals) of changes in blood levels of MDMA and its metabolites, vital signs and ratings of effects, for adrenergic, antipsychotic, antidepressant (SSRI, SNRI, noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, bupropion), stimulant and NMDA-antagonist medicines, and which classes have no controlled data at all.
cannot_establish: How people who take a medicine for months or years, with the illness it treats, respond to MDMA (every trial used healthy adults given the medicine once or for at most 14 days); whether any combination is safe or dangerous outside the laboratory (no trial measured serotonin toxicity, seizures or death, and street MDMA of unknown content is not covered); how large or precise any effect is (percent changes without intervals, some read off graphs, no risk-of-bias rating); anything controlled about MAOIs, benzodiazepines or lithium with MDMA; or causal effects from the surveillance database, the survey and the case reports.

sample.recruitment: Database search of MEDLINE only; 12 of the 40 included publications (30%, editors' calculation) were found by hand, including two (Cohen et al., 2021; Nayak et al., 2021) published after the search date (Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph). The trial samples were healthy adults, often recruited on university campuses, with 8 to 23 participants per trial in the text (Results, 2nd paragraph); the surveillance study analysed 946 reports, the survey 216 adults and the online-reports analysis 96 accounts (Results > Epidemiologic studies).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: human studies in English, any age, any design (meta-analyses, systematic reviews, randomized trials, retrospective, cross-sectional, case-control and cohort studies, case reports) of a psychiatric medicine taken with MDMA or psilocybin, with outcomes in pharmacokinetics, physiology or subjective effects (Methods, 1st paragraph). Excluded: editorials, duplicates, non-English records and records not addressing the question; 16 full texts were excluded without stated reasons (Fig. 1). Outside the scope by the authors' choice: repeated dosing of MDMA itself, other psychedelics, ketamine (no studies found) and non-psychiatric medicines (Discussion > Limitations). Trial exclusion criteria the authors call common: pregnancy or nursing, age under 18 or over 45, body mass index outside 18.5-25, psychiatric illness in the person or a first-degree relative, and active substance use (Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Of the 13 MDMA trials in Table 5, 11 included women (4 to 8 per trial) and 2 (pindolol, paroxetine) were men only; mean ages 22.9 to 27.4. Previous ecstasy experience ranged from none (duloxetine trial, all ecstasy-naive) through 1 to 6 of 14 or 16 people in eight trials to a mean of 18.8 occasions (memantine), a mean of 28.6 occasions (fluoxetine; the only trial that recruited people who use MDMA recreationally) and at least 5 occasions for everyone (paroxetine). CYP2D6 phenotype is given for 8 trials (mostly extensive metabolizers, 0 to 2 poor metabolizers per trial of 16; all 12 extensive in the paroxetine trial). No trial reported race or ethnicity (Discussion > Considerations for future research, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not reported at review level.
sample.selection_effects: Search: one database, English only, publication-type filters, title or abstract terms; 30% of included publications came from hand selection that the paper does not describe, so the set cannot be reproduced from the stated strategy. Population: young, healthy, mostly ecstasy-naive adults screened for psychiatric illness, given the medicine once or for at most 14 days (Becker et al., 2021, for psilocybin); people who take these medicines because they have the conditions they treat, for months or years, were not studied. Two trials excluded people with high neuroticism scores and two admitted only people with previous ecstasy use (Discussion, 2nd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: As in each primary study: medicine and MDMA given in the laboratory, so doses and timing were known and the MDMA was laboratory-grade (Introduction > MDMA, 4th paragraph); blood levels were measured in some trials. Epidemiologic evidence rests on spontaneous reports to a surveillance database, a self-report survey and self-posted online accounts, with unverified drugs and doses.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only (Table 5): MDMA 75 to 125 mg by mouth once (or 1.5 or 1.6 mg/kg) after the medicine. Medicine conditions: citalopram 40 mg infused intravenously over 90 minutes; fluoxetine 20 mg daily for 5 to 11 days; paroxetine 20 mg daily for 3 days; duloxetine 120 mg at 16 and 4 hours before; reboxetine 8 mg at 12 and 1 hours before; bupropion XR raised to 300 mg over 7 days; methylphenidate 60 mg 1 hour before; haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously; memantine 20 mg 2 hours before; carvedilol 50 mg, pindolol 20 mg and clonidine 0.15 mg 1 hour before; doxazosin 8 mg about 16 hours before after 3 days of run-in. Psilocybin trials used 0.17 to 0.25 mg/kg, or 25 mg.
exposure.polysubstance: Trials excluded active substance use. In the surveillance, survey and case-report data, other drugs and unverified MDMA content were the norm, and the review says drug levels could not be ascertained in most case reports (Discussion > Trends in case studies).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable at review level; trial washouts between sessions ranged from 2 days to 1 month (Table 5).

comparison.controls: Within each trial, the same people took placebo plus MDMA (and usually placebo plus placebo and medicine plus placebo), in counterbalanced order in most trials. Two designs differ: the paroxetine trial had only two sessions (paroxetine plus MDMA, placebo plus MDMA), and in the fluoxetine trial placebo pretreatment was always tested first (Table 5).
comparison.matching: Within-person crossover with washouts of 2 days to 1 month; no matching needed at trial level.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the trials. For the surveillance, survey and case data, the reason for taking the medicine, its dose, duration and adherence are unknown, so the medicine cannot be separated from the illness or the circumstances.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable in the trials. In the surveillance data the comparison is with other reports in the same database.

outcomes.instruments: As in each primary study: plasma MDMA, MDA and HMMA (peak concentration, area under the curve, time to peak, half-life), heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, circulating catecholamines, pupil measures, visual analogue scales, Adjective Mood Rating Scale, 5-Dimensions of Altered States of Consciousness scale, Profile of Mood States, Addiction Research Center Inventory, List of Complaints and cognitive tasks; for the epidemiologic studies, a reported fatal outcome or reported adverse effects (Tables 5-7).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not assessed by the review.
outcomes.operationalization: The review expresses each outcome as the percent change of (medicine plus MDMA) against (placebo plus MDMA) by one formula (Methods > Percent change calculation). Depending on the row the base is the peak effect (Emax), the peak change from baseline (delta Emax), the area under the effect curve, or a time-point value, and values marked with a tilde were estimated by the review's authors from graphs (Tables 6-7 footnotes).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None at review level. Significance marks (p<.05, p<.01, p<.001) are the primary studies' own, are not corrected for the many outcomes each trial measured, and are not shown for every row.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not assessed. Most trials are described as double-blind (Table 5); whether participants could tell a blunted from an unblunted MDMA session is not discussed.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled effect sizes and no intervals; only percent differences between two conditions (key findings). Editors' sum of Table 5: 193 participants across the 13 MDMA trials.
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42021233519 (Methods, 1st paragraph). The year in the identifier (2021) is later than the stated search date (21 December 2020), so the registration appears to follow the search; the registry record was not read, so the registered methods, including whether hand selection, case reports and epidemiologic studies were planned, are unchecked.
analysis.selective_reporting: All identified trials are tabulated, but secondary analyses of one sample are counted as separate publications. Percent changes are shown without the underlying means, so a reader cannot recompute them. The discussion stresses the consistent blunting by reuptake inhibitors and explains the exceptions (bupropion, doxazosin) by mechanism. The supplement with the case reports was not read.
analysis.power: Not applicable at review level. Included trials had 8 to 16 participants for MDMA (5 per group in one psilocybin study); the review does not discuss statistical power.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In single-dose or short-course laboratory trials in 8 to 16 healthy adults, pretreatment with an SSRI (citalopram, fluoxetine, paroxetine), an SNRI (duloxetine) or a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (reboxetine) lowered the effects of MDMA that people rated and that were measured (for example drug liking by about 31% with fluoxetine and about 62% with paroxetine, 'any drug effect' by about 62% with duloxetine and 21% with reboxetine), even though peak MDMA blood levels were 14 to 18% higher with paroxetine, duloxetine, reboxetine and bupropion. Bupropion was the exception: effects lasted longer and were not lower. Haloperidol turned MDMA's pleasant state dysphoric; methylphenidate added to heart rate and complaints without adding psychoactive effects; carvedilol cut heart-rate and temperature responses with little change in ratings; memantine changed nothing measured. There is no controlled study of MAOIs, benzodiazepines or lithium with MDMA; case reports (summary in a supplement not read) describe the worst outcomes with MAOIs; surveillance and survey data give associations that cannot separate the medicine from the circumstances.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract promises only a compilation. The conclusion says there are "clear acute pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic interactions" and then that the literature is not readily applicable to clinical settings. The discussion goes beyond the results in four places: it reads the lower heart rate, blood pressure and temperature responses as a reduced odds of serotonin syndrome (no trial measured serotonin toxicity); it says reuptake inhibitors outcompete MDMA at the transporters (tested only by an ex vivo binding measure in two trials); it proposes that blunted effects may lead people to take larger amounts and so explain the higher odds of death in the surveillance data (no included study tested this); and it says MAOIs cause dangerous serotonin elevations, resting on case reports. It also cites a pooled analysis of phase 2 trials (Feduccia et al., 2020), marked retracted in the PMC reference list, for the statement that people who had tapered antidepressants did worse.

timeline.event: de la Torre et al.: MDMA blood levels rise more than in proportion to dose, the background to the review's statement that MDMA inhibits its own breakdown
Schmid et al.: people with only non-functional CYP2D6 alleles reached higher MDMA levels (cited in the review's pharmacogenetics paragraph)
Cohen et al., surveillance-database analysis of co-ingested drugs and fatal outcomes in reports of ecstasy use, added by hand to this review after its search date
This review, the first systematic review of psychiatric-medicine interactions with MDMA or psilocybin by its authors' account; the only earlier review it names is narrative (Papaseit et al., 2020)

replication.where_it_stands: A compilation of controlled laboratory trials, mostly from one laboratory group by the review's own account (10 of the 13 MDMA trials carry Hysek, Liechti, Hasler or Schmid as first author in Table 5, editors' count), plus case reports and observational reports that only generate hypotheses. The consistent blunting by reuptake inhibitors rests on five trials with different first authors (Liechti, Tancer, Farre, Hysek) but small samples; the review does not establish their independence. The primary papers behind the key numbers (Liechti and Vollenweider 2000; Farre et al. 2007; Tancer and Johanson 2006; Hysek et al. 2011 and 2012; Schmid et al. 2015; Cohen et al. 2021) were not read for this card.

funding.funder: No funder for the review is named. Salary support for the last author came from the US Department of Veterans Affairs, Clinical Science Research and Development (award IK2CX001495); two people are thanked for assisting with abstract review (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: The last author has received payment from the MAPS Public Benefit Corporation for training clinicians in MDMA-assisted therapy; the third author runs a membership service that sells drug-interaction guides, courses and consultation; the other two authors declare none (Declarations).
funding.affiliations_note: The page text does not give affiliations. The reference list shows Thomas K. as last author of the surveillance study (Cohen et al., 2021) that the review added by hand, and the review's author list includes Kelan Thomas; whether they are the same person was not checked. The review cites the MAPS investigator's brochure for MDMA's dose range, onset and adverse effects.

what_would_settle_it: A supervised study of people who have taken an SSRI, SNRI or bupropion for months, given MDMA once with and without a washout of the medicine, with blood levels, CYP2D6 genotype, temperature and documented signs of serotonin toxicity measured, powered for safety outcomes rather than ratings; and a case registry of emergency presentations with toxicology that confirms the MDMA and records the medicine, its class and its duration. For MAOIs only systematic case collection with toxicology is ethical.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: PICOS stated: people of any age taking MDMA or psilocybin with a psychiatric medicine; comparison MDMA or psilocybin alone; outcomes in pharmacokinetics, physiology and subjective effects; study types listed (Methods, 1st paragraph).

A PROSPERO identifier is given, but its year (2021) is later than the stated search date (21 December 2020), the registry record was not read, the review has no risk-of-bias assessment that a protocol could have planned, and the 12 hand-selected records and the late additions are not reported as deviations.

Designs are listed, and the inclusion of epidemiologic studies despite their weaknesses (large samples, hypothesis generation) and of case reports in a supplement is explained (Study selection, 2nd paragraph).

One database (MEDLINE via PubMed), English only without justification, publication-type filters, title or abstract terms only, no grey literature, trial registries or reference-list searching described; 12 of 40 included publications (30%) were found outside the strategy, showing that it missed about a third; the search ended on 21 December 2020.
Each abstract was screened by two independent reviewers with disagreements settled by consensus; how full texts were assessed is not stated (Study selection, 1st paragraph).
How data were extracted and the percent changes computed, and by how many people, is not described.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Fig. 1 gives counts only (411 excluded on title or abstract, 16 on full text) with no list and no reasons; the supplement was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 5 gives design, conditions, washout, sample size, sex, age, ecstasy experience and often CYP2D6 phenotype; Tables 6-7 give outcomes with timing. Setting, recruitment, funding and follow-up are not given, the epidemiologic studies are described in prose without group sizes or intervals, and the case reports are only in the supplement.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: None: neither the trials nor the observational studies were appraised.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Not reported.
Narrative synthesis with percent changes; nothing pooled.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Nothing pooled.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Limits of generalizability are discussed (healthy volunteers, short exposure, unusual routes, Discussion, 2nd paragraph) and the case and epidemiologic data are called much less reliable (Introduction > MDMA, 4th paragraph), but without any appraisal the trial results are interpreted without reference to small samples, uncorrected multiple outcomes, the fixed order in one trial or unassessed blinding.

Differences between medicines are explained by mechanism only (bupropion, doxazosin); differences in route (intravenous citalopram), duration (one dose to 14 days), MDMA dose, sex mix and sample size are not related to the results, and paroxetine's larger cardiovascular effect is noted without explanation.
No quantitative synthesis; publication bias is not discussed. The authors contacted researchers with more than one trial for unpublished data and obtained none (Study selection, 2nd paragraph).

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Two authors' interests and the salary support are declared; no funding for the review itself is stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Five critical items are judged no (2, 4, 7, 9 and 13) and items 11 and 15 do not apply (no meta-analysis); more than one critical flaw gives critically low confidence under AMSTAR 2. This is a judgment about how far the review's summary can be trusted, not about the value of the trials it lists: the question is clear, the trial table is detailed and the review is candid that its evidence does not transfer to patients. The source can be cited for the list of medicines tested with MDMA in controlled settings, for the direction and approximate size (as computed by the review, without intervals) of what each primary trial found, and as a pointer to the primary papers. It should not be cited for precise effect sizes, for the safety or danger of any combination, for MAOI risk estimates, or for people taking medicines long-term. Where the review is the only source of a primary finding, claims should say 'as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022)' and stay at draft until the primary paper is read.

key_findings.finding: 40 publications were included from 467 records screened (455 from MEDLINE via PubMed to 21 December 2020 plus 12 added by hand): 26 trial publications (17 original trials and 9 analyses of the same samples; 22 on MDMA, 4 on psilocybin), 3 epidemiologic studies and 11 case reports kept in a supplement; 411 records were excluded on title or abstract and 16 full texts on unstated grounds.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (Results); Methods > Search strategy, 1st paragraph; Study selection, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 1 (image, read on screen); Results, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The 13 MDMA trials in Table 5 had 8 to 16 healthy adults each (editors' sum 193), nearly all double-blind counterbalanced crossovers; the medicine was given as a single dose or two doses within a day in 9 of the 13 and for 3 to 11 days in the other 4 (doxazosin, paroxetine, bupropion, fluoxetine); the longest pretreatment in any trial was 14 days (escitalopram, psilocybin). The fluoxetine trial always tested placebo pretreatment first, and the paroxetine trial had no placebo-only or paroxetine-only session. Authors state the trials were not designed for clinical extrapolation.

SSRIs lowered the rated and measured effects of MDMA. Citalopram (n=16): oceanic boundlessness about 60% lower, anxious ego dissolution about 63% lower (both p<.05), heart rate 12.3% lower at 60 minutes (p<.05), acute complaints about 46% lower (p<.01). Fluoxetine (n=8): drug liking 31.2%, 'high' 47.6% and 'stimulated' 40.1% lower (all p<.05), heart rate 14.6% lower (p<.05). Paroxetine (n=12): liking about 62%, 'high' about 68% (p<.001), systolic pressure about 41% (p<.001) and heart rate about 42% lower (p<.05). The review summarizes this as 30 to 80% lower subjective effects and 6 to 14% lower physiological effects, with paroxetine's physiological effect (40 to 60%) the exception. Values with a tilde were read off graphs by the review's authors.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, citalopram, fluoxetine and paroxetine rows; Results > MDMA > Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: MDMA blood levels were higher with medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 or related enzymes, at the same time as effects were lower. Paroxetine: peak +16.0% and exposure to 21 hours +21.6% (both p<.01), with the main metabolite HMMA 49.3% lower at peak. Duloxetine: peak +14.6%, exposure to 6 hours +16.2%, HMMA peak 40.5% lower. Reboxetine: peak +17.8%, exposure to 24 hours +8.1% (p<.05). Bupropion: peak +14.3%, exposure to 24 hours +33.1% (p<.001), HMMA peak 75.9% lower. Carvedilol (+4.7%), clonidine (-2.9%), doxazosin (-1.6%), methylphenidate (-3.5%) and memantine (-1.0% at 1 hour) changed the peak by 5% or less. Table 6 has no blood-level row for citalopram or fluoxetine.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, pharmacokinetic rows (Cmax, AUC) for each medicine; Results > MDMA, the paragraphs on bupropion, serotonin reuptake inhibitors, duloxetine and reboxetine

key_findings.finding: Duloxetine (n=16) lowered nearly every effect of MDMA: 'any drug effect' 61.7%, drug liking 57.7% and closeness to others 83.1% (all p<.001), heart rate 57.4% and systolic pressure 63.5% (p<.001), and acute complaints 122.5% (p<.01; above 100% because the base is a change from baseline). Reboxetine (n=16) lowered 'any drug effect' by 20.7% (p<.01), closeness by 38.6% (p<.05), heart rate by 26.2% (p<.05) and systolic pressure by 46.5% (p<.001), but drug liking (-10.0%) and good drug effect (-15.2%) did not change significantly.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, duloxetine and reboxetine rows; Results > MDMA > Serotonin reuptake inhibitors and MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Reboxetine and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Bupropion XR (n=16) did not blunt the rated effects: peak ratings of any drug effect, good effect, 'high' and liking were 5.6 to 17.1% higher (no significance marks) and the areas under their curves over 8 hours were 34.0 to 46.1% higher (p<.05 for any drug effect, good effect, 'high' and liking), meaning the effects lasted longer, while heart rate was 38.7% lower (p<.001) and norepinephrine 65.6% lower (p<.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 6, bupropion rows (Physiological; Circulating catecholamines; Subjective); Results > MDMA > Bupropion and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Haloperidol 1.4 mg intravenously (n=14) did not change heart rate, blood pressure or temperature responses to MDMA but made the state dysphoric: well-being about 31% lower (p<.05), state anxiety about 47% higher at 75 minutes (p<.01), oceanic boundlessness about 59% lower (p<.05).
key_findings.locator: Table 6, haloperidol rows; Results > MDMA > Antipsychotics and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Methylphenidate (n=16) delayed MDMA's time to peak by 45.8% (p<.05) without changing its peak (-3.5%) or exposure (+3.2%), raised heart rate 15.1% and the rate-pressure product 16.8% (both p<.001) and epinephrine 54.6% (p<.01), and raised acute and subacute complaints by 86.5% (p<.01) and 191.9% (p<.001), without adding psychoactive effects (any drug effect -1.4%).
key_findings.locator: Table 6, methylphenidate rows; Results > MDMA > Psychostimulants and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Adrenergic agents (n=16 each unless stated): carvedilol lowered the heart-rate rise 79.0%, systolic 76.9% (both p<.001), diastolic 39.2% and temperature 42.0% (p<.05) with little change in ratings (any drug effect +7.4%, liking +1.5%) while epinephrine and norepinephrine rose; pindolol (n=16, men) lowered peak heart rate about 17.6% (p<.001) and 'dreaminess'; clonidine lowered mean arterial pressure and norepinephrine; doxazosin lowered mean arterial pressure 6.8% (p<.05) but raised heart rate 9.6% (p<.05) and lowered heightened-mood ratings. Carvedilol and doxazosin percentages are changes from baseline, pindolol's is on the raw peak.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, adrenergic-agent rows (carvedilol, pindolol, clonidine, doxazosin); Results > MDMA > Adrenergic agents and MDMA, 2nd to 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Memantine 20 mg (n=15) had no effect on MDMA-induced memory impairment or on mood, per the review; Table 6 lists changes of 0.8 to 41.1% on memory and mood measures without significance marks.
key_findings.locator: Table 6, memantine rows; Results > MDMA > Memantine and MDMA

key_findings.finding: Psilocybin: escitalopram taken for 14 days (n=23) did not significantly lower altered-states ratings (oceanic boundlessness unchanged; anxious ego dissolution -40%, visionary restructuralization -4.7%) but lowered bad drug effects 53.8% (p<.01), fear 50% (p<.01) and systolic pressure 43.8% (p<.001) and left psilocin levels unchanged (+1.0%); buspirone lowered visionary restructuralization by about 44% (p<.001); risperidone 1 mg by about 27% (p<.01); haloperidol raised dread of ego dissolution by about 27% (p<.05); ergotamine had no effect on subjective ratings.
key_findings.locator: Table 7; Results > Psilocybin (antipsychotics, serotonin agonists, serotonin reuptake inhibitors)

key_findings.finding: The 11 case reports are summarized only in a supplement (not read). The main text says the highest rates of morbidity came from MDMA with MAOIs such as moclobemide or phenelzine, with hyperthermia, seizure-like activity and altered mental state suggestive of serotonin syndrome, many ending in death; coronary artery disease was found at autopsy in several; one young man with bipolar disorder who took moclobemide and lithium was left unaccompanied for 4 hours and found dead; drug levels were unknown in most. SSRI cases were described as consistent with blunted effects. The main text gives no count of cases or deaths per drug. No controlled study of MAOIs, benzodiazepines or lithium with MDMA was found.
key_findings.locator: Discussion > Trends in case studies, 1st paragraph; Discussion > MDMA psychopharmacology > Pharmacodynamic interactions, 3rd paragraph; Discussion > Considerations for future research, 3rd paragraph; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Surveillance study (Cohen et al., 2021, as summarized here): 946 unique reports of recreational ecstasy use in the US adverse-event database, 2000-2020 (mean age 28, 70.1% men). Adjusted odds ratios of a fatal outcome when a drug class was also reported: benzodiazepines 2.25, opioids 2.05, ethanol 2.03, amphetamines and stimulants 3.05, antidepressants 1.62. Unadjusted odds ratios for single psychiatric medicines: bupropion 2.82, sertraline 2.36, venlafaxine 1.97, citalopram 1.92, olanzapine 1.86; all 18 reports with metoclopramide ended in death; no deaths were reported with risperidone or lithium. No intervals, numbers of deaths or denominators are given.

Survey (Copeland et al., 2006, as summarized here): 216 adults who took ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug in the past 6 months (mean age 26, 63% men, mean 11 days of ecstasy use in 6 months). Of those who took antidepressants with ecstasy, 76% still felt euphoria, but rates of muscle rigidity (0% vs 45%), nystagmus (0% vs 33%), dizziness (19% vs 42%), headache (21% vs 62%) and heavy sweating (28% vs 53%) were higher; antidepressants were not analysed by class and included MAOIs. Group sizes and the order of the paired percentages are not stated.

Pharmacogenetics and metabolism, second-hand: MDMA is cleared mainly by CYP2D6 to the inactive metabolite HMMA and is thought to inhibit CYP2D6 itself, giving non-linear kinetics; people with only non-functional alleles (*3, *4, *5) had a peak MDMA level 19% higher and early exposure (to 6 hours) 25% higher than people with only *1 and *2 alleles, with faster onset and higher blood pressure (Schmid et al., 2016); pooled trial data show effects follow plasma concentration and higher CYP2D6 activity scores predict lower MDMA levels (Studerus et al., 2021). The review names the strong enzyme blocker ritonavir as having caused significant toxicity with MDMA (Papaseit et al., 2012).
key_findings.locator: Introduction > MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Discussion > Pharmacokinetic interactions, 1st paragraph; Discussion > Pharmacogenetics and MDMA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: No trial gave an SSRI or SNRI for months in people who take one as treatment; the longest pretreatment was 14 days (escitalopram, psilocybin trial) and for MDMA 5 to 11 days (fluoxetine). The authors state that modern MDMA-therapy trials either excluded people taking psychiatric medicines or stopped them first, and that none of the psilocybin trials measured physiology.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion > Considerations for future research, 1st paragraph; Table 5

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the 12 hand-selected articles arose while reading full texts, but Fig. 1 adds them at identification (467 records screened by title and abstract); the 16 full-text exclusions have no reasons in the figure or text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The route by which 30% of the included publications entered is unclear and cannot be reproduced; any claim from this review should be treated as resting on a selected, not an exhaustive, body of evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: Results say plasma MDMA concentrations rose with both fluoxetine and paroxetine, but Table 6 has pharmacokinetic rows only for paroxetine among the SSRIs, none for fluoxetine or citalopram.
reporting_issues.consequence: A rise in MDMA levels is shown for paroxetine, duloxetine, reboxetine and bupropion only; the statement for fluoxetine is not supported by anything tabulated.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says bupropion did affect self-reported complaints from MDMA, but Table 6 lists changes of -5.0% (acute) and -6.0% (subacute) with no significance marks, and the same paragraph then says bupropion prolonged positive mood.
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two statements is probably misworded (the table supports 'did not significantly affect'); the complaints finding should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Percent changes in Tables 6 and 7 mix bases: peak effect, peak change from baseline, area under the effect curve, single time points and graph-read estimates, with no means, SDs, n per outcome or intervals; changes beyond 100% appear (norepinephrine -143.2% with duloxetine and -109.8% with clonidine; acute complaints -122.5% with duloxetine).
reporting_issues.consequence: Sizes in different rows are not comparable (a 79.0% fall in carvedilol's heart-rate change against a 17.6% fall in pindolol's heart-rate peak), none has an interval, and a figure above 100% means the effect reversed, not that it was removed twice.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 states that placebo pretreatment was always tested first in the fluoxetine trial, and the paroxetine trial had two sessions only, yet both are counted among the 26 randomized controlled studies; the 1967 chlorpromazine and 1998 psilocybin trials are described only as placebo-controlled crossovers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Randomization and counterbalancing are overstated for two of the three SSRI trials with subjective outcomes; order and expectancy are confounded with the medicine in the fluoxetine result.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion reads lower heart rate, blood pressure and temperature responses as a reduced odds of serotonin syndrome and says blunted effects may drive larger amounts and the higher odds of death for antidepressant combinations in the surveillance data; no included study measured serotonin toxicity or the amount taken, and the same review reports adjusted odds of death of 1.62 with antidepressants and unadjusted 2.36 with sertraline and 2.82 with bupropion.
