reporting_issues.consequence: Both statements are hypotheses; neither reassurance nor alarm follows from the trials, and the surveillance odds ratios (spontaneous reports, no denominators) cannot show that any antidepressant raises the risk of death.

reporting_issues.issue: The review describes several antidepressant-plus-MDMA combinations as having increased mortality, from odds ratios in a spontaneous-report database.
reporting_issues.consequence: A causal verb is used for a reporting association without denominators, intervals or knowledge of dose, purity or indication.

reporting_issues.issue: Feduccia et al. (2020), marked retracted in the PMC reference list, is cited for reduced efficacy of MDMA-assisted therapy after recent tapering of reuptake inhibitors, including 63.6% against 25.0% still meeting PTSD criteria.
reporting_issues.consequence: A retracted paper is read as a record of what was claimed, never as evidence (METHODS 3.2); the statements that rest on it are not used by any claim built from this card.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives the range of sample sizes as 8 to 23 and Table 5 gives 5 for each of the two haloperidol and risperidone psilocybin groups, with 7 women and 8 men listed for the two groups together; Hysek et al. 2012b, cited in the Results among trials with adrenergic agents, is a study of MDMA and emotion recognition and is not in Table 5; the Table 6 footnote expands SERT as 'sertraline transporter'.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the psilocybin samples are smaller than stated, one citation is wrong and one abbreviation is mis-expanded (serotonin transporter); none changes an MDMA result.

reporting_issues.issue: The survey summary gives pairs of percentages (for example headache 21% vs 62%) without saying which group each belongs to or how many people took antidepressants; the surveillance summary gives no intervals, counts of deaths or denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither study's figures can be turned into absolute risks or checked for chance; they can only be quoted as reported by the review.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC9177763 (all sections and Tables 1 to 7 read as text; the saved page text was cut at 120,000 characters inside the reference list, so only selected reference entries were checked; Figure 1, the PRISMA diagram, is an image and was read on screen; the supplement, a downloadable file with the case reports, was not read)

design_detail: Pooled analysis of eight double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover laboratory studies of MDMA in 139 healthy volunteers (70 men, 69 women), in which people were grouped afterwards by CYP2D6 genotype (activity score; poor, intermediate or extensive metabolizers) and, as a check, by phenotype (dextromethorphan metabolic ratio). The comparison between genotype groups is between persons and the exposure (genotype) is not randomized, although the MDMA sessions were randomized crossovers; the authors call the pooled analysis prospectively designed. Plasma MDMA, MDA and HMMA over time, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, temperature and subjective ratings were compared across groups. The methods, doses, tables and most figures are in a supplement (a PDF file) that was not read.
can_establish: Whether, within healthy adults given MDMA in a laboratory, people with little or no CYP2D6 function differ in blood levels of MDMA and its metabolites and in the timing of blood-pressure and subjective effects from people with normal function, with the size of the difference in the first hours.
cannot_establish: The effect of CYP2D6 genotype at any particular dose (the seven poor metabolizers all took the highest dose and the groups were unevenly spread across studies and doses); effects on toxicity, which no study measured; whether the small difference is caused by MDMA blocking CYP2D6 in everyone, which the authors infer from timing and earlier work and did not test here; or anything about repeated doses, other enzymes or medicines that block CYP2D6.

sample.recruitment: Healthy volunteers from eight earlier studies; recruitment, entry criteria and ages are in the supplement, which was not read. The main text gives only the total (70 men, 69 women) and the genotype groups (Abstract; Results, 3rd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not given in the main text (supplement not read).
sample.demographics: 70 men and 69 women; ages, weights and the sex mix within genotype groups are not given in the main text.
sample.attrition: Not reported in the main text. HMMA was analysed for 76 people (N=76 in the correlation; F with 73 error degrees of freedom) and unconjugated HMMA for about 124 (inferred from the degrees of freedom), against 139 for MDMA and MDA, with no reason stated.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers in controlled studies with their own entry criteria. The seven poor metabolizers were all in the high-dose group, and the genotype groups were not equally represented across studies and doses (Discussion, limitations paragraph), so a genotype difference is mixed with dose and study unless the unreported high-dose-only analysis is used.

exposure.measurement: CYP2D6 genotype converted to an activity score (0, 0.5, 1, 2) and to poor, intermediate and extensive groups; phenotype by the urinary ratio of dextromethorphan to its metabolite (DM/DX). Genotype and phenotype were mostly concordant, with some individual discordance (Results, 5th paragraph). Which alleles were scored is in the supplement.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: MDMA given once in each study; the doses differ between the eight studies and are not listed in the main text (supplement); all poor metabolizers took the high dose.
exposure.polysubstance: Not described in the main text; the volunteers were healthy and studied in controlled sessions.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not described in the main text.

comparison.controls: People with normal CYP2D6 function (extensive metabolizers, activity score 2 in the finer analysis) as the reference group; intermediate metabolizers as a middle group.
comparison.matching: None described. The authors say the groups were unevenly spread across studies and doses and that a high-dose-only analysis gave similar results (not shown in the main text).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Body weight, sex mix and age per group are not given in the main text. Polymorphisms of CYP1A2, CYP2C19 and CYP2B6 were assessed and the authors say they did not moderate the CYP2D6 effects; those results are to be published separately.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma concentrations of MDMA, its active metabolite MDA and its inactive metabolite HMMA (peak, area under the curve to 6 hours, and the MDMA to HMMA ratio as a marker of CYP2D6 activity); systolic blood pressure, heart rate and body temperature; visual analogue ratings of 'any drug effect' and 'drug liking'.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed in the main text.
outcomes.operationalization: Effects of genotype group at each time point by analysis of variance with post hoc comparisons; early against late differences (before and after 3 hours); correlations between the MDMA to HMMA ratio at 0.6 hours and effects.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None described; the key contrast of peak MDMA between poor and extensive metabolizers has P=0.049 within a main effect of P=0.02.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The studies were double-blind and placebo-controlled; whether genotype was concealed from those rating effects is not stated in the main text.

analysis.effect_sizes: Peak MDMA in poor metabolizers +15% (mean ratio 1.15, 7 poor against 111 extensive) and peak MDA +50% against extensive metabolizers; peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower, and HMMA exposure to 6 hours about a quarter (24%) of extensive metabolizers' (Abstract; Discussion). Tests: genotype and peak MDMA F(2,136)=4.19, P=0.02, poor against extensive P=0.049; MDMA area under the curve to 6 hours F(2,136)=5.25, P<0.01; MDA peak F(2,136)=8.82, P<0.01 and area F(2,136)=9.09, P<0.001; HMMA peak F(2,73)=3.50, P=0.03 and area F(2,73)=5.22, P<0.01; MDMA to HMMA ratios F(2,73)=10.98 and 10.08, both P<0.001. Systolic pressure rise at 0.6 h greater in poor than in intermediate (P=0.02) and extensive (P=0.01) metabolizers, F(2,135)=3.50, P=0.03; 'any drug effect' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.05); 'drug liking' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.001) and 1 h (P<0.01); no genotype effect on heart rate or temperature; peak effects did not differ. No absolute concentrations are in the main text.
analysis.covariates: None described in the main text; the supplement may contain them.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the authors call the pooled analysis prospectively designed (Introduction, 2nd paragraph) and put the methods in the supplement.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract's percentages are not tabulated in the main text, and the tables and most figures are in the supplement. The high-dose-only analysis is described as giving similar results without numbers, and the effects of other CYP polymorphisms are deferred to another paper.
analysis.power: Seven poor metabolizers, all in one dose group; no power calculation. The authors call it the first study with a meaningful sample size and several people with relevantly impaired function.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Compared with extensive metabolizers, the seven poor metabolizers had a peak MDMA level 15% higher and a peak MDA level 50% higher, with much less of the inactive metabolite HMMA; the difference in MDMA was present only up to 3 hours after the dose. Blood pressure and the ratings of drug effect and liking rose faster in poor metabolizers during the first 0.6 to 1 hour, but peak effects, heart rate and temperature did not differ. The main contrast for peak MDMA is borderline (P=0.049).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the effects of CYP2D6 variation are small because MDMA inhibits CYP2D6 itself; the discussion adds that poor metabolizers may be at increased risk of toxicity, that HMMA differences could be clinically relevant, and that other enzymes (CYP2B6, CYP3A4, CYP1A2) may matter more. The self-inhibition explanation is an inference from timing and earlier work, not tested in this analysis; no toxicity outcome was measured; the HMMA and other-enzyme points are speculation. The authors' statement that the differences are small and transient is, however, what the numbers show.

timeline.event: De la Torre et al. reported MDMA pharmacokinetics in one CYP2D6 poor metabolizer and nine extensive metabolizers (named in this paper's reference list; not read here)
A physiologically based model (Yang et al.) estimated that having no CYP2D6 function would raise peak MDMA by only 36%, as the authors cite
Review of MDMA and CYP2D6 pharmacogenetics by the group of the 2000 non-linearity paper
A pooled analysis of trials (Studerus et al., as summarized by Sarparast et al.) found that higher CYP2D6 activity scores predicted lower MDMA levels and that effects followed plasma concentration

replication.where_it_stands: The direction (somewhat higher early MDMA exposure with little or no CYP2D6 function) is consistent with the 2005 case comparison, the 2006 model and the later pooled analysis as summarized by the 2022 review, which quotes larger figures than this paper's main text (19% for peak and 25% for early exposure, comparing only poor metabolizers with only functional alleles; possibly from this paper's supplement, not read). The size at any one dose, and whether MDMA's self-inhibition is the reason the difference is small, rest on this paper and the earlier modelling.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation (grant 320030_1449493) (Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared.
funding.affiliations_note: The last author's group ran the eight pooled studies (Hysek, Vizeli and Liechti among the authors); several of the same group's studies appear in the 2022 review as trials of medicines given before MDMA, so the pooled data and those trials are not independent of each other.

what_would_settle_it: A genotype-stratified crossover in which people with no, intermediate and normal CYP2D6 function (genotyped and phenotyped) take the same dose in randomized, blinded order, enough poor metabolizers of each sex to give interval estimates, with CYP2B6, CYP1A2, CYP2C19 and CYP3A4 status and a CYP3A4 or pan-CYP inhibitor arm, and with temperature, sodium and clinical outcomes as well as concentrations.

domains.note: Provisional: dose and study are unevenly spread across genotype groups and all seven poor metabolizers were in the high-dose group; a high-dose-only analysis is said to give similar results but is not shown, and covariate adjustment is not described in the main text. Genotype itself is not open to the usual confounders.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Genotype and phenotype were both measured, with some discordance in individuals; the main results use genotype groups and phenotype was used as a check.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteers from eight studies with their own entry criteria, not described in the main text; healthy adults only; no sign that selection depended on genotype.
The exposure is genotype, which cannot be changed by later events; the MDMA conditions analysed are described as placebo-controlled sessions.

HMMA statistics rest on about 76 and unconjugated HMMA on about 124 of 139 people (counts inferred from the degrees of freedom and the N=76 of the correlation), with no reason or check for differences between genotype groups.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Plasma concentrations are objective; ratings came from double-blind sessions.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Many outcomes and time points without multiplicity control; the key contrast has P=0.049; the abstract's percentages, tables and sensitivity analyses are not in the main text; other CYP results deferred.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The exposure and outcomes are measured objectively and the finding is modest and in the expected direction, but only seven people have no CYP2D6 function, all took the same high dose, and the covariate handling and sensitivity analysis are in a supplement that was not read, so the overall judgment is provisional. The source can be cited for a small and short-lived rise in peak MDMA (about 15%) and a larger rise in MDA, much less HMMA, and faster early blood-pressure and subjective effects in people with no CYP2D6 function, in healthy adults in the laboratory; it cannot be cited for the effect at a given dose, for intermediate metabolizers as a separate group with precision, for toxicity or for the mechanism.

key_findings.finding: Pooled analysis of eight double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies in 139 healthy people (70 men, 69 women): 7 CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, 19 intermediate and 113 extensive metabolizers (111 extensive in one Discussion comparison). Doses and study details are in the supplement (not read); all seven poor metabolizers were in the high-dose group.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Main text, 2nd paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, limitations paragraph

key_findings.finding: Genotype altered MDMA levels only in the first 3 hours (absorption and distribution), not after: genotype main effect on peak MDMA F(2,136)=4.19, P=0.02, with higher peaks in poor than extensive metabolizers (P=0.049); area under the curve to 6 hours F(2,136)=5.25, P<0.01 (poor higher than extensive, P<0.01). Peak MDMA was 15% higher in poor metabolizers (abstract) and the mean ratio was 1.15 (7 poor against 111 extensive).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph

key_findings.finding: The active metabolite MDA was higher and the inactive metabolite HMMA lower in poor metabolizers: peak MDA +50% (F(2,136)=8.82, P<0.01; area F=9.09, P<0.001; higher than both intermediate and extensive, P<0.001); peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower (F(2,73)=3.50, P=0.03; area F=5.22, P<0.01), with HMMA exposure to 6 hours about a quarter (24%) of extensive metabolizers'; MDMA to HMMA ratios higher in poor metabolizers (F(2,73)=10.98 and 10.08, P<0.001). The HMMA tests rest on fewer people than the MDMA and MDA tests (N=76 in the HMMA correlation and 73 error degrees of freedom, against 136).
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Main text, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph; Fig. 1 legend

key_findings.finding: Poor metabolizers had faster early effects but not larger ones: systolic pressure rise greater than in intermediate (P=0.02) and extensive (P=0.01) metabolizers at 0.6 h (F(2,135)=3.50, P=0.03), 'any drug effect' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.05) and 'drug liking' higher at 0.6 h (P<0.001) and 1 h (P<0.01); maximal effects did not differ and there was no genotype effect on heart rate or temperature. The MDMA to HMMA ratio at 0.6 h correlated with systolic pressure rise (Rs=0.41, N=76), any drug effect (0.42) and drug liking (0.40), all P<0.001.
key_findings.locator: Abstract; Main text, 4th paragraph; Fig. 2 legend

key_findings.finding: The authors read the small and short-lived difference as the result of MDMA inhibiting CYP2D6 itself (turning all people into functional poor metabolizers within about 1 hour); they cite a physiologically based model estimating a rise of only 36% in peak MDMA with no CYP2D6 function, and say medicines that inhibit CYP2D6 raised peak MDMA by 15 to 20% and exposure by 10 to 30% (their references 6 and 7: reboxetine and duloxetine). They note that poor metabolizers were not over-represented in ecstasy deaths (their reference 11), that severe or fatal toxicity with high MDMA exposure occurred with ritonavir (which blocks CYP2D6, CYP2B6 and CYP3A4), and suggest that other enzymes and CYP3A4 inhibition may matter more than CYP2D6 genetics.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 'Taken together' paragraph (also the following paragraph on limitations)

key_findings.finding: Stated limits: a pooled sample of different studies and doses, unequal representation of activity groups across studies and doses, only seven poor metabolizers and all in the high-dose group; an analysis of the high-dose group alone is said to give similar results (not shown).

reporting_issues.issue: The percentages in the abstract (peak MDMA +15%, peak MDA +50%, peak HMMA 50 to 70% lower) are not given in the main text except as a mean ratio of 1.15 for MDMA and a 24% HMMA exposure; the tables and group means are in the supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sizes cannot be checked against absolute concentrations from the main text; they are quoted as the authors state them.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion compares 7 poor metabolizers with 111 extensive metabolizers, but the figure legends and the groups sum to 113 extensive metabolizers (7 + 19 + 113 = 139).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: two extensive metabolizers are unaccounted for in one comparison; the reason is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The 2022 review of interactions (Sarparast et al.) states that poor metabolizers with only *3, *4 or *5 alleles had a peak 19% and early exposure 25% higher than extensive metabolizers with only *1 and *2 alleles, citing this paper; the main text here gives 15% against all extensive metabolizers and no exposure percentage.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's figures probably come from the activity-score tables in the supplement; the two sets should not be mixed, and the 15% figure is the one the main text supports.

reporting_issues.issue: A rank correlation of 0.18 between MDMA and MDA exposure is described as showing that higher MDMA levels resulted in higher MDA levels.
reporting_issues.consequence: A weak association (about 3% of rank variance) is given a causal verb; it is a description of co-variation in a pooled sample.

reporting_issues.issue: The main contrast for peak MDMA (poor against extensive) is P=0.049 within a main effect of P=0.02, among many outcomes and time points with no correction for multiplicity; the pooled data come from different studies and doses.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 15% difference in peak MDMA is a borderline finding; the more robust signals are the metabolite differences and the early-time effects.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4949007 (main text, figure legends and reference list read as text; Figures 1 and 2 not viewed as images; the supplementary file, a PDF with the methods and tables, was not read, being a download)

design_detail: Prospective cohort of women in the United Kingdom recruited in pregnancy through midwives, leaflets and magazine advertisements asking for pregnant women who had used recreational drugs (the Drugs and Infancy Study, DAISY): 126 responded and 96 were enrolled. The 28 women who used MDMA in pregnancy or in the month before were compared with 68 who did not (32 of them had used MDMA earlier). Use was taken from interviews (62 during pregnancy and 24 after birth). Infants were seen at about 1 month (neonatal behaviour; 82 infants) and at 4 months (Bayley mental and psychomotor scores, behaviour rating, Alberta Infant Motor Scale; 87 infants) by assessors masked to exposure. Analysis by group comparison and by regression with covariates; MDMA entered as yes or no, as tablets per week, and as three groups (heavier, lighter, none).
can_establish: Whether, in a small volunteer cohort of mostly middle-class women who used recreational drugs, infants whose mothers used MDMA in the month before or during early pregnancy differ at 1 and 4 months on standard neonatal and developmental scales from infants of similar women who did not, and what the pattern of use was (most stopped in pregnancy; median 0.13 tablets a week; one woman used in the third trimester).
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused any difference: the exposed women also used more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, fathers' use was not asked, 22 exposed infants were seen, and the two scale differences are among many tested; development beyond 4 months, any count of congenital anomalies, effects on miscarriage or termination, exposure in the second or third trimester, or a graded dose-response against unexposed infants (the lighter-exposed infants scored above the unexposed on two scales).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers answering midwife referrals, leaflets at prenatal clinics and advertisements in pregnancy magazines that asked for pregnant women who had used recreational drugs (ecstasy, tobacco, cannabis, alcohol and cocaine were named as examples), at Case Western Reserve University and the University of East London, with approval from both universities and National Health Service ethics committees (2.1.1 Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: maternal or child HIV, moderate or severe mental retardation or severe psychiatric or medical illness in the mother, and other major medical illness in the child. Of 126 women who responded, 5 did not meet criteria and 25 did not come to the first visit (4 miscarriages, 1 depression, 2 partner's objection, 1 moved away, 3 gave no reason, 14 could not be contacted), leaving 96.
sample.demographics: Mothers mostly white (84% and 85%), married or with a partner (84% and 79%), some university education (mean 14.9 and 15.3 years), a range of incomes, average intellectual ability on two subtests; age at birth 30.3 and 28.4 years; the exposed group had fewer previous births (parity 1.21 against 1.88). Infants: 71% of exposed infants were boys against 46%; gestation 40.0 against 39.5 weeks.
sample.attrition: Infants seen: 1 month 22 of 28 exposed (79%) and 60 of 68 comparison (88%); 4 months 22 of 28 (79%) and 65 of 68 (96%); reasons not given. Birth length and head circumference were available for only 31 and 10 infants (length) and 39 and 16 (head circumference) in the comparison and exposed groups.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected volunteers who knew the study was about recreational drug use in pregnancy, mostly white, middle-class and in stable relationships; the authors say participants may have had additional concerns about risk that precipitated their involvement. The comparison group is made of women who also used drugs, so it is not a drug-free group.

exposure.measurement: Self-report at interview (trained assistants; an adaptation of the Maternal Post-Partum Interview), asking for use in the lifetime, the year before conception, the month before pregnancy, trimesters 1 and 2 and trimester 3; frequency on a 0 to 7 scale and amount per occasion; average per week. Women were classed as exposed if they said they used MDMA during pregnancy or in the month before; women who had used earlier but not then (32) or never were comparison. 62 women were interviewed during pregnancy and 24 after birth (10 of the 96 are not accounted for). No biological confirmation; tablet contents unknown.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Exposure data, not study conditions: mean tablets per week 1.61 (SD 3.11) in the month before pregnancy (Table 4; the text gives 3.2, SD 5.2, for those who used MDMA during pregnancy), 0.82 (1.58) in the first trimester, 0.08 (0.38) in the second and 0.006 (0.03) in the third; mean total 25 tablets (SD 43.7, range 0.45 to 180) over pregnancy and the month before; median 0.13 tablets a week over pregnancy (Table 2; the text gives 0.14); lifetime average 171 times (range 6 to 936) among the women who had used before and continued in pregnancy, typically about 3 tablets (range 1 to 8) per occasion.
exposure.polysubstance: Common: women who used MDMA in pregnancy more often also used cocaine (71% against 16% of women), cannabis (82% against 54%), tobacco (86% against 62%), amphetamine (18% against 3%), mushrooms (14% against 0), LSD (11% against 0), ketamine (7% against 0) and slightly more alcohol (96% against 91% of women; 9.1 against 6.6 units a week); the comparison women also used several drugs.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Most women stopped MDMA in pregnancy (use fell from the month before to the second trimester); only one used in the third trimester.

comparison.controls: 68 pregnant women recruited the same way who had not used MDMA in pregnancy or the month before (polydrug or non-drug-using; 32 had used it earlier).
comparison.matching: None; the groups were similar in age, education, income, intelligence subtests and ethnicity, but differed in parity and in other drugs. Covariates were retained in regressions if related to the outcome and to MDMA status at P<.20 and significant on entry (P<.10) or if they changed the MDMA coefficient by more than 10%.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Fathers' drug use was not asked; maternal weight gain was not available; postnatal care, feeding and later drug use are not reported; genetic testing was done only for one infant.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison group were also drug-using women, but with less cocaine, cannabis, tobacco, amphetamine, LSD and ketamine.

outcomes.instruments: NICU Network Neurobehavioral Scale (NNNS) at about 1 month corrected age (13 summary scores); at 4 months the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (Mental Development Index, Psychomotor Development Index), the Bayley Behavior Rating Scale (attention/arousal and motor quality factors) and the Alberta Infant Motor Scale (AIMS; percentile rank and below the 10th percentile as at risk); birth data from hospital records.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard, normed instruments; NNNS coefficient alpha 0.56 to 0.82 for the summary scores; AIMS normed on 2,202 infants; habituation on the NNNS was not analysed because too few infants were asleep at the start.
outcomes.operationalization: Group comparisons by chi-square, Fisher exact, t and Wilcoxon tests; regressions (ordinary least squares, Poisson, negative binomial, logistic) with MDMA as yes or no, as average tablets per week over pregnancy, and as heavier, lighter or none (analysis of variance, with post hoc comparisons only when the overall P was below .10); heavier and lighter by a median split (0.14 tablets a week over pregnancy).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; about 13 NNNS scores, 2 Bayley indices, 2 behaviour-rating factors, the AIMS rank and a below-10th-percentile cut-off, 8 birth measures, in unadjusted and adjusted models, with P<.05 as the threshold and P<.10 used to open further analyses.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: The NNNS examiner and the Bayley and AIMS assessors were masked to infant drug exposure; the interviewers who asked about use were not.

analysis.effect_sizes: Birth: boys 20 of 28 (71%) against 31 of 68 (46%), chi-square 5.32, P=0.02; odds ratio of a male birth after adjusting for other drug differences 3.2 (95% CI 1.2 to 8.2, P<.02; the crude odds ratio from the Table 5 counts is 3.0, CI 1.2 to 7.7 (editors' calculation)); gestation 40.0 against 39.5 weeks; birth weight 3537 (SD 500) against 3344 (511) g (P=0.15, adjusted for sex); preterm 1 of 28 against 1 of 68; one exposed infant had Townes-Brocks syndrome (a spontaneous SALL1 mutation, per the authors). NNNS at 1 month (22 exposed, 60 comparison): no difference in any mean score (e.g., lethargy 3.14 against 2.63, P=.22; excitability 1.64 against 2.35, P=.15); trends in the score distributions (lethargy 91% against 73%, hypertonicity 9% against 27%, both P<.069). 4 months (22 against 65): Bayley mental index 99.1 against 98.6 (P=.80), psychomotor index 96.5 against 94.3 (P=.40), attention/arousal 71.2 against 70.9, motor quality 58.9 (SD 20.7) against 74.1 (23.8), t -2.61, P=.009; AIMS percentile 50.4 against 45.8 (P=.51), below the 10th percentile 14% in both groups. After adjusting for alcohol exposure, MDMA still predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.21, P<.05); tablets per week over pregnancy predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.24, P<.042). Three groups at 4 months (none, lighter, heavier): motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (F 3.6, P<.04); AIMS percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (F 3.8, P<.03); psychomotor index 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (F 2.6, P<.08); below the 10th percentile 14%, 0 and 27% (P<.18). Higher alcohol exposure predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.36, P<.005); higher cannabis exposure predicted poorer attention (beta -.28) and regulation (beta -.27) at 1 month (both P<.02).
analysis.covariates: Infant age at testing, maternal demographic and infant birth variables, maternal use of other drugs in pregnancy and maternal psychological distress were considered; the one adjustment named for the motor-quality result is average alcohol exposure.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; the authors say the motor findings were predictable from the animal literature and the sex-ratio finding was unexpected.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports the motor-quality difference, a dose-response and lower milestone attainment, but not the null results for the Bayley psychomotor index, the AIMS percentile and the below-10th-percentile rate in the group comparison. The three-group analyses were opened by an overall P<.10 and, for AIMS, rest on the heavier group alone being lower while the lighter group was above the unexposed. The sex-ratio difference was found after the fact.
analysis.power: The authors state that with alpha 0.05 and power 0.80 the sample could detect moderate effect sizes with up to four predictors in a regression; 28 exposed women (22 infants at follow-up), no calculation shown.

interpretation_gap.results_show: At 1 month no mean score differed (two non-significant shifts in the spread of scores pointed to more lethargic and less hypertonic behavior), and on the cognitive and general motor scores at 4 months, infants of women who used MDMA in the month before or during early pregnancy did not differ from comparison infants. The group difference at 4 months was a lower observer-rated motor quality score (58.9 against 74.1), which remained after adjusting for alcohol; on the AIMS the heavier-exposed infants scored lower than the lighter-exposed, while the lighter-exposed scored above the unexposed. More boys were born to the exposed women (71% against 46%). The exposed women also used more cocaine, cannabis, tobacco and alcohol, and the differences are among many tested in small groups.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say the findings suggest risk to the developing infant, with poorer motor quality, lower milestone attainment and a dose-response relationship, and that more male births and a rare genetic syndrome were found. The Introduction describes the 1999 letter on 136 exposed pregnancies as indicating a 4 to 7 times higher risk of malformations and a two-fold risk even after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies; the letter prints neither figure and makes no such adjustment (the Discussion's 15.4% 'increased risk' echoes the letter's own summary). The authors themselves say they cannot establish whether the sex ratio is caused by MDMA and that the syndrome, a spontaneous mutation, cannot be attributed to the drug.

timeline.event: Case series of 136 exposed pregnancies from a UK teratology service, without a comparison group, reporting 12 anomalies among 78 live births and no effect on sex ratio

This cohort (online 3 March 2012), described by its authors as the first prospective study of MDMA-using women identified in pregnancy; no outcome measure is shared with the 1999 letter except a sex-ratio statement that points the other way

replication.where_it_stands: Not repeated in any study read here. The authors call for continued follow-up of the cohort to see whether the early motor differences persist or resolve; no later paper is in the library's reference list for this question.

funding.funder: Grant DA14910-05 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, US National Institutes of Health (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: no conflict-of-interest statement appears in the manuscript.
funding.affiliations_note: Investigators at Case Western Reserve University, the University of East London and Swansea University; the same group reported the cohort's other early findings (Moore et al., cited).

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective cohort recruited before or in early pregnancy with biological confirmation of exposure (for example hair or meconium), a comparison group handled so that cocaine, alcohol, cannabis and tobacco are dealt with, fathers' use recorded, blinded standard assessments at several ages up to school age, systematic recording of major malformations by a standard code, and outcomes named in advance with correction for the number tested.

domains.note: The exposed women used much more cocaine (71% against 16%), cannabis, tobacco, amphetamine and other drugs and slightly more alcohol; fathers' use and maternal weight gain are unknown; 22 exposed infants with several covariates; alcohol, which was adjusted for, predicted motor quality more strongly than MDMA (beta -.36 against -.21).

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Self-report with no biological check, 24 of 86 interviews after birth, 10 women with no stated timing, unknown tablet contents; exposure includes the month before pregnancy; the authors argue the dose-response suggests the reports are valid.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Self-selected volunteers answering advertisements for women who used recreational drugs; mostly white and middle-class; 25 of 126 responders did not attend a first visit.
Postnatal environment, breastfeeding and later maternal drug use, which could affect 4-month motor scores, are not reported.
Follow-up differed by group (exposed 79% at both visits; comparison 88% at 1 month and 96% at 4 months), with no reasons; birth length and head circumference exist for few infants.

domains.domain: Bias in measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Standardized, normed scales given by assessors masked to exposure.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Many outcomes in unadjusted and adjusted models with no correction; the abstract features the significant motor-quality, dose-response and sex-ratio results and omits the null psychomotor and AIMS group comparisons; three-group analyses opened at P<.10.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, self-selected cohort with a comparison group that differs in other drug use, self-reported exposure, differential follow-up and many uncorrected tests. The source can be cited for what was found in 22 exposed infants (no difference at 1 month or on the Bayley scores and AIMS rank at 4 months, a lower observer-rated motor quality at 4 months that persisted after adjustment for alcohol, more male births) and for the exposure pattern (low average use that mostly stopped in pregnancy); it cannot be cited for a causal effect of MDMA, for a dose-response against unexposed infants, or for any figure about malformations.

key_findings.finding: Recruitment of pregnant women who had used recreational drugs through midwives, leaflets and magazine advertisements; 126 responded, 5 did not meet criteria, 25 did not come to the first visit, 96 enrolled; 82 infants were seen at 1 month and 87 at 4 months.

Exposure from interviews (62 women during pregnancy, 24 after birth); women counted as exposed if they said they used MDMA in pregnancy or the month before; 32 women who had used earlier but not then, and women who had never used, formed the comparison group; 28 exposed and 68 comparison.
key_findings.locator: 2.1.2 Measures of MDMA Exposure and Covariates, 1st paragraph; 2.1.2.1 Prenatal Levels of Drug Exposure, 1st paragraph; 2.1.4 Statistical Analyses, 1st paragraph; Abstract, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Use pattern: mean tablets per week 1.61 in the month before pregnancy (Table 4; 3.2 in the text for those who used MDMA during pregnancy), 0.82 in the first trimester, 0.08 in the second, 0.006 in the third; one woman used in the third trimester; mean total 25 tablets (range 0.45 to 180); the heavier (13) and lighter (15) groups were split at a median of 0.14 tablets a week over pregnancy and differed mainly in the month before pregnancy (3.3 against 0.12 tablets, P<.007; first trimester 1.6 against 0.12, P<.12).
key_findings.locator: 3. Results > 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 3rd to 7th paragraphs; Table 4

key_findings.finding: Women who used MDMA had fewer previous births (parity 1.21 against 1.88) and higher drug-problem scores (DAST 7.7 against 4.6); they used more cocaine (71% against 16%), cannabis, tobacco, amphetamine, mushrooms, LSD and ketamine in pregnancy and slightly more alcohol.
key_findings.locator: 3.1 Maternal Outcomes, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Tables 1 to 3

key_findings.finding: Birth outcomes did not differ in gestation, birth weight, prematurity, length or head circumference (the last two with missing data); exposed infants were more often boys (71% against 46%; adjusted odds ratio 3.2, 95% CI 1.2 to 8.2); one exposed infant had Townes-Brocks syndrome (spontaneous SALL1 mutation), and results did not change without him.
key_findings.locator: 3.2 Birth and Neonatal Child Outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 5

key_findings.finding: At 1 month (22 exposed, 60 comparison) no mean NNNS score differed; non-significant trends for more lethargy (91% against 73%) and less hypertonicity (9% against 27%), both P<.069.

At 4 months (22 exposed, 65 comparison) no difference on the Bayley mental index (99.1 against 98.6), psychomotor index (96.5 against 94.3), attention/arousal factor or AIMS percentile (50.4 against 45.8; below the 10th percentile 14% in both); motor quality factor lower in exposed infants (58.9 against 74.1, P=.009), still significant after controlling for alcohol (beta -.21, P<.05) and predicted by tablets per week (beta -.24, P<.042).

Three-group comparison at 4 months (none, lighter, heavier): motor quality 74.1, 60.8, 57.0 (P<.04); AIMS percentile 45.9, 65.7, 35.1 (P<.03); psychomotor index 94.3, 101.1, 91.8 (P<.08); below the 10th percentile 14%, 0 and 27% (P<.18). Higher alcohol exposure predicted poorer motor quality (beta -.36, P<.005) and higher cannabis exposure poorer attention and regulation at 1 month.
key_findings.locator: 3.4 Child Outcomes at 4-Months-Old, 2nd paragraph; Table 8; 3.5 Other Drug Effects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: voluntary enrolment, self-report that may be unreliable, exposure almost entirely in the first trimester, small exposed sample, fathers not interviewed; they say the cohort had fewer confounders than most recreational drug exposure studies. They conclude the findings suggest risk to the developing child and warrant follow-up, and describe the 1999 letter as finding a 15.4% increased risk.
key_findings.locator: 4. Discussion, 9th paragraph (the 1999 letter); 11th paragraph (limitations); 12th paragraph (conclusion); 1. Introduction, 7th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says exposed infants had 'poorer motor quality and lower milestone attainment at 4 months, with a dose-response relationship'. In the group comparison the Bayley psychomotor index (96.5 against 94.3) and the AIMS percentile (50.4 against 45.8; 14% below the 10th percentile in both groups) did not differ; only the motor-quality rating differed (58.9 against 74.1). The lower AIMS scores rest on the heavier-exposed infants alone: the lighter-exposed infants scored above the unexposed (65.7 against 45.9) and the heavier below (35.1).
reporting_issues.consequence: A graded dose-response against unexposed infants is not shown; the milestone result is a difference between two small exposed subgroups (about 11 infants each), and the finding on motor quality is one rated scale among many.

reporting_issues.issue: The heavier and lighter groups were split at a median of 0.14 tablets a week over pregnancy but differ mainly in use in the month before pregnancy (3.3 against 0.12 tablets a week, P<.007), not in the first trimester (1.6 against 0.12, P<.12) or the second (P>.20).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 'dose' that separates the groups is largely pre-conception use, so the dose-response is not clearly a dose during pregnancy.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes the 1999 letter on 136 exposed pregnancies as showing a 4 to 7 times higher risk of malformations, and, after accounting for higher-risk pregnancies, a two-fold risk; the Discussion calls its 15.4% an 'increased risk', which echoes the letter's own summary. The letter reports a proportion (12 of 78 live births) compared informally with an unreferenced 2 to 3% (a ratio of about 5 to 8 by the editors' arithmetic), with no multiples printed, no adjusted analysis and no comparison group. The same paper also says in its second Introduction paragraph that no prospective studies of prenatal MDMA exposure exist, and in the ninth Discussion paragraph calls the 1999 series the only prior prospective follow-up.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 4 to 7 times and two-fold figures are not findings of the 1999 letter and should not be repeated from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The more-male-births finding (71% against 46%) was unexpected and arose among many comparisons in a small group; the 1999 letter this paper cites reported no effect on the sex ratio; the explanations offered (hormones, heat, other toxins) are speculation.
reporting_issues.consequence: A single unexpected comparison, with a wide interval (odds ratio 3.2, 1.2 to 8.2); it is not a replicated finding and points the other way in the earlier letter.

reporting_issues.issue: The 10th paragraph of the Discussion appears garbled (it runs a statement about the paternal origin of SALL1 mutations into a sentence about fathers' exposure and a statement that the infant 'had the exposure to environmental toxins'), and cites an autism and paternal-age twin study (Lundstrom et al., 2010) in support.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reasoning about the genetic syndrome cannot be followed; the authors' own conclusion is that it cannot be attributed to the mother's drug use.

reporting_issues.issue: Interview timing is stated for 86 of 96 women (62 during pregnancy, 24 after birth), with 10 unaccounted for; the pre-pregnancy mean of 3.2 tablets a week in the text (for those who used MDMA during pregnancy) differs from 1.61 in Table 4 (the 28 exposed women) without the denominators being reconciled.
reporting_issues.consequence: Recall after birth may differ from reports during pregnancy; the exposure figures cannot be compared across the text and the table.

reporting_issues.issue: Printed statistics that do not match: the drug-problem (DAST) comparison is printed with t = -3.09 and P = 0.03, whereas that t value corresponds to about P = 0.003 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Likely a dropped zero; no effect on the conclusions.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3367027 (all sections, Tables 1 to 8 and the reference list read as text in this reader's own browser tab; no figures)

design_detail: Narrative review by three Australian authors (Drug and Alcohol Dependence 2010;107:1-10), read as the published PDF; page numbers are the journal's own (pp. 1-10). It asks whether there is evidence for an ecstasy (MDMA) dependence syndrome. Searches were run in PubMed, PsycInfo and EMBASE with the strings given in footnote 1 (p. 2), but no dates, inclusion or exclusion rules or numbers of records are stated. Structure: theory of dependence and the DSM-IV and ICD-10 classifications (pp. 2-3); animal evidence with pure MDMA (pp. 3-6); human evidence (pp. 6-8): three case reports (Jansen, 1999; p. 6), 14 survey samples in Table 1 (pp. 4-6; editors' count: 3 population-based, 2 sentinel populations, 9 self-selected samples, with sample sizes from 26 to 1,662 and reported prevalence from 3.6% to 73%), the structure of the dependence criteria (p. 7), course, treatment seeking and limitations (p. 8), and a summary (p. 8). The authors state that the studies differ too much in method and sample for a meta-analysis (3.6, p. 8). No effect sizes are pooled and no intervals are given.
can_establish: What studies published up to 2009 found when they asked people who take ecstasy about dependence symptoms, as summarized by three authors: the range of reported prevalence by type of sample, the symptoms most often endorsed, that the dependence reported was often not persistent (one German cohort: 93% no longer dependent after about three years), and that treatment for ecstasy alone was uncommon in Australian records (under 1% of episodes).
cannot_establish: How common dependence on MDMA is in any defined group of people. The prevalence figures come from different instruments (DSM-IV hallucinogen, amphetamine or stimulant criteria, the Severity of Dependence Scale at different cut-offs, a screener, a clinician interview), different time windows (lifetime, past year, past month) and mostly self-selected samples, and pills sold as ecstasy may contain methamphetamine (p. 3), so some of the dependence reported may not be on MDMA. It cannot show that tolerance and withdrawal reported on questionnaires reflect changes in the brain rather than the after-effects of a recent session, or what would happen to people followed from first use.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable to the review itself. In the 14 samples of Table 1 (pp. 4-6): three came from household or population surveys of young adults (Stone; von Sydow; Wu), two from sentinel populations (New York nightclub attendees; Taiwanese juvenile detainees), and nine were self-selected (purposive or snowball sampling, rave attendees, readers of a dance magazine, people in treatment services and students).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Search strings in three databases are given (footnote 1, p. 2). No dates, inclusion or exclusion criteria or counts are given, and the review also draws on government statistics, a monograph and a case-report series (Jansen, 1999).
sample.demographics: Not applicable (narrative review). Table 1 rows range from adolescents and young adults to heavy-using rave attendees.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Stated by the review: most studies recruited people who had recently taken ecstasy by convenience or snowball sampling, so the prevalence cannot be extrapolated to everyone taking ecstasy (3.6, p. 8). Editors' observations: the highest figures come from small samples selected for heavy use or drawn partly from treatment services (Cottler, 52 people; Thomasius, 59 people with at least 250 lifetime tablets); the lowest come from household surveys, where the question was about hallucinogen dependence criteria; the review does not say how it chose which studies to put in Table 1.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported ecstasy use. No study in Table 1 verified by laboratory test what people had taken (p. 3). Dependence was measured with questionnaires or interviews built for other drugs: the CIDI, the Severity of Dependence Scale, DSM-IV hallucinogen items, amphetamine-dependence questions from a children's interview schedule, a three-item arrestee screener and, in one non-representative sample, a clinician-rated SCID interview (Thomasius; p. 6).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Recorded here only as study conditions. Lifetime use was reported as means of about 160 occasions (Winstock), 227 pills (Scheier) and 794 tablets (Thomasius, a sample chosen for at least 250 tablets); use in the preceding weeks or months was a median of 2.5 days (Parsons, window as printed) and 12 days in the past six months (range 2-100; Topp, 1997; Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Not controlled in most samples. Where studies adjusted for other drug use, including methamphetamine (Bruno et al., 2009; Topp et al., 1997), they used self-reported use, not laboratory-verified use (p. 3). Thomasius reports high polydrug use (cannabis, cocaine, amphetamine, LSD) and Tossman's sample was people using ecstasy and/or methamphetamine (Table 1).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported.

comparison.controls: Mostly none. The few comparisons in Table 1 and the text are: ecstasy against LSD, peyote and psilocybin for hallucinogen dependence (Stone), people screening positive against negative (Bruno; Parsons, with median days of use 5 against 2 in the past four weeks) and one German cohort followed for just over three years (von Sydow; p. 8).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed as a limit of the evidence. Scheier found lifetime ecstasy use, motivational factors, criminal behaviour and depression to be independent predictors of dependence (p. 7), so what came before the ecstasy use is not separated from the use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Adjusted by self-reported other drug use in two studies (Topp, 1997; Bruno, 2009); not adjusted in the others reported.

outcomes.instruments: CIDI (computerised and modified versions), Severity of Dependence Scale (cut-offs of 4 and 5), DSM-IV hallucinogen items, amphetamine-dependence questions (Yen and Hsu), the Center for Substance Abuse Research arrestee screener, SCID (clinician-rated).
outcomes.validity_norms: The review notes that all the instruments were first designed for other drugs, and that the Severity of Dependence Scale has shown good reliability and validity for opioids, cocaine and amphetamines, where it is unidimensional, whereas for ecstasy it did not have a single factor (p. 7). Topp and colleagues questioned the validity of the withdrawal items (p. 6), and the review says it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as intended (3.6, p. 8).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Dependence' differs between studies: DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence (Stone; Wu), CIDI ecstasy, hallucinogen and stimulant dependence (von Sydow), Severity of Dependence Scale at 4 or more (Bruno) or 5 or more (Winstock), amphetamine-dependence questions (Yen and Hsu), a three-item 'probable' screener (Yacoubian), latent classes of symptoms (Scheier), clinician SCID (Thomasius). Windows differ too: lifetime, past year, past month, or not specified (Table 1, p. 6, footnote a).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (narrative review).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Prevalence of dependence as reported in Table 1 (pp. 4-6), with no intervals. Population-based samples: 3.8% past year (Stone, 1,199 people who had started ecstasy within the previous two years; hallucinogen criteria), 5.8% lifetime among those who had ever taken ecstasy (von Sydow, 207 young adults), 3.6% past year (Wu, 652; the text gives 4%). Sentinel populations: 19% past year (Parsons, 214 nightclub attendees), 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, 200 detainees). Self-selected samples: 18% past month (Bruno, 1,662, Severity of Dependence Scale 4 or more), 43% lifetime (Cottler, 52), 64% lifetime (Topp 1997, 185), 16% (Tossman, 195, past-year ecstasy and/or methamphetamine; window not specified), 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, 154, 'probable' on a screener), 73% lifetime (Thomasius, 59 people with at least 250 lifetime tablets), 17% (Winstock, 1,106; window not specified in Table 1, lifetime in the text). Hanson and Luciana (26): 14 met abuse or dependence criteria in the text, where Table 1 prints 'N = 2 LT'. Scheier (639): latent classes, no prevalence in the table. Text, p. 7: past-year dependence among all young adults in Germany 0.4% (von Sydow). Course, p. 8: of the people classified as dependent at the start, 93% were no longer dependent after a mean of just over three years; 50% no longer used at all; most of the 43% still using no longer met criteria. Treatment, p. 8: under 1% of Australian treatment episodes.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable to the review; adjustment for other drugs in the cited studies was by self-report.
analysis.preregistration_detail: None; narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: No selection rule beyond the search strings. The review gives different quantities for different studies (lifetime, past year, 'probable', latent-class share) and does not put them on a common scale; the figure for one row (Thomasius, 73%) is in Table 1 only, and the figure of 73% in the text belongs to Scheier's latent classes.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 14 samples that used instruments built for other drugs, the share screening positive for dependence ranged from 3.6% to 73%. About 4 in 100 came from household surveys asking about the past year; 16 to 22 in 100 from nightclub attendees, detainees and regular-use samples; 43 to 73 in 100 from small samples selected for heavy use or including people in treatment. In the one cohort followed, 93% of those classified as dependent no longer were after about three years. Tolerance and withdrawal rest on self-report on questionnaires designed for other drugs; pills sold as ecstasy may contain methamphetamine; case reports are few (three) and mild.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary says the evidence is limited in both scope and design and that further controlled work is needed (p. 8), which matches the content. Two statements go further than the data: the abstract's 'Human evidence supports this proposition' (physical features playing a more limited role than psychological ones) rests partly on the absence of case reports of severe withdrawal, and on questionnaire items from other drugs; and the two-factor structure ('compulsive use' and 'escalating use') is proposed from two studies, both by the review's own authors and both in Australia (p. 7).

timeline.event: Australian sample of 185 regular ecstasy-taking people: 64% met CIDI lifetime criteria, typically in their heaviest period, and the authors questioned the withdrawal items (Topp et al.; as summarized in this review).
German population-based follow-up: 93% of young adults classified as dependent at baseline no longer were after about three years (von Sydow et al.; as summarized in this review).
US household surveys: about 4 in 100 past-year ecstasy-taking people met hallucinogen-dependence criteria (Stone et al.; Wu et al., 2008; as summarized in this review).

Australian sample of 1,662 regular ecstasy-taking people: 18% screened positive on the Severity of Dependence Scale; two correlated factors fitted better than one (Bruno et al.; as summarized in this review).

replication.where_it_stands: A 2010 summary of studies to 2009, usable as a second-hand description of what those studies measured. Later studies are not covered. Its main finding, that dependence-like problems are reported by a minority of people taking ecstasy but the evidence is limited in scope and design, has not been tested here against later work.

funding.funder: The Australian Government Department of Health and Ageing assisted the review; the first author holds an Australian NHMRC Senior Research Fellowship (ID 510279); the acknowledgements also name the NHMRC. The funders had no role in the design, interpretation or write-up (p. 9).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared (p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: National Drug and Alcohol Research Centre (University of New South Wales), University of Tasmania and Justice Health (New South Wales). Two of the authors ran the two studies the review uses for the structure of dependence symptoms (Topp et al., 1997; Bruno et al., 2009), and 11 of the references have at least one of the three authors among their authors (editors' count).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective cohort of people starting ecstasy, recruited from the general population rather than from services, with the content of what they take confirmed, a dependence instrument validated for MDMA and a clinician interview in a subsample, followed at repeated visits so that the share who become dependent, how long it lasts and what use pattern comes before it can be estimated with intervals, and compared with people using other drugs.

domains.note: Three databases and the search strings are given (footnote 1, p. 2), but there are no dates, inclusion or exclusion rules or counts, and the review does not say how studies were chosen for Table 1.

Section 3.6 states the main limits plainly (instruments from other drugs, self-report, lifetime recall, convenience samples), but studies are not appraised one by one and several figures differ between Table 1 and the text (Wu, Winstock, Bruno, Hanson and Luciana).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The structure of dependence rests on two studies by the authors (Topp et al., 1997; Bruno et al., 2009), and 11 of the references have at least one of the three authors among their authors.

The summary labels its own inferences with 'suggests' and calls for controlled studies (p. 8), but 'Human evidence supports this proposition' leans on the absence of case reports of severe withdrawal.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how often dependence is reported
domains.note: The full range of figures is shown (3.6% to 73%) with the sampling frame beside each, and the text says the figures cannot be extrapolated to everyone taking ecstasy.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is candid about the limits of the human evidence and shows the range of figures with their sampling frames, so it can be cited as a second-hand description of what studies up to 2009 reported. It cannot be cited for how common dependence is in any group, because the figures come from different instruments, time windows and mostly self-selected samples. A claim resting only on this review stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: animal evidence suggests MDMA may be a less potent reinforcer than other drugs but has dependence potential; some people report problems with their use, but physical features appear to play a more limited role than psychological ones; tolerance is apparent and withdrawal is self-reported, but it is unclear whether these reports distinguish after-effects of a session from a 'true' withdrawal syndrome; studies of structure suggest two factors, 'compulsive use' and 'escalating use'; a minority of people taking ecstasy become concerned about their use and seek treatment. Further controlled studies are called for.

Method and terms: searches in PubMed, PsycInfo and EMBASE with strings covering abuse, dependence, withdrawal, reward, reinforcement, ICD, DSM and nosology (footnote 1), with no dates or rules for inclusion. The authors use 'dependence' rather than 'addiction', following the two classification systems. No specific ecstasy or MDMA dependence diagnosis exists: a person taking ecstasy can be classed as dependent on hallucinogens and/or amphetamines, which differ in structure and in whether withdrawal is a criterion.
key_findings.locator: 1. Introduction, 2nd paragraph and footnote 1 (search, terms); 1.2, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (classification)

key_findings.finding: Pills sold as ecstasy may not contain MDMA at all, and some or many may contain methamphetamine instead (citing Quinn et al., 2007 and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime), so dependence in people who take 'ecstasy' may be on methamphetamine rather than, or as well as, MDMA. Studies that adjusted for other drug use, including methamphetamine, used self-reported use, not laboratory-verified use.

Animal work with pure MDMA: self-administration in mice, rats and non-human primates, so MDMA is rewarding; but substantial proportions of rats fail to acquire self-administration even after extended training, unlike cocaine, and the point at which animals stop working for MDMA is lower than for cocaine and methamphetamine. The review concludes that although MDMA is rewarding, it may be less rewarding than other illicit drugs, and that the course of dependence may differ from drugs such as opioids.
key_findings.locator: 2.2, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 3); closing paragraph of section 2 (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Human evidence is thin: three case reports (Jansen, 1999) of two people with access to large amounts of high-purity MDMA and one with post-traumatic stress disorder, each with tolerance, increasing time using and recovering, neglect of other activities and mild withdrawal in the 'comedown', all three with other drug use disorders. Few studies have examined dependence; all used instruments first designed for other drugs, and only one (non-representative) involved clinician or psychiatric assessment.

Table 1, population-based and sentinel samples: US household surveys 3.8% past year (Stone, 1,199 people who started ecstasy within the previous two years, hallucinogen criteria; ecstasy more likely than LSD, peyote or psilocybin to lead to dependence) and 3.6% past year (Wu, 652; another 11% reported one or two symptoms); Germany 5.8% lifetime among those who had ever taken ecstasy (von Sydow, 207) with under 10% of those classified lifetime-dependent being past-year dependent at the 42-month follow-up; 19% past year (Parsons, 214 New York nightclub attendees); 22% past year (Yen and Hsu, 200 Taiwanese juvenile detainees, amphetamine-dependence questions); Australia 18% past month (Bruno, 1,662 recruited by purposive and snowball sampling, scale cut-off 4 or more; among those screening positive 49% used 1-2 times per week and 34% 1-2 times per month).
key_findings.note: Wu is 3.6% here and 4% in the text (p. 7); Bruno's monthly group is 1-2 times here and 1-3 times in the text (p. 7); Parsons gives 2.5 days over four months in the details column and 5 days over four weeks in the notes.

key_findings.finding: Table 1, self-selected samples: 43% lifetime (Cottler, 52 people in treatment services and the community; continued use despite problems 63%, withdrawal 59%); 14 of 26 students and community members met abuse or dependence criteria (Hanson and Luciana; prevalence cell reads 'N = 2 LT'); latent classes, no prevalence, mean 227 lifetime pills (Scheier, 639); 64% lifetime (Topp 1997, 185 Australians; at heaviest use 66% used 1-2 days a week and 25% 1-3 days a month; the authors questioned the withdrawal items); 16% (Tossman, 195 people who had taken ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year; 17% self-perceived dependence); 17% lifetime (Yacoubian, 154 Washington rave attendees, 'probable' dependence on a three-item screener); 73% lifetime (Thomasius, 59 rave attendees with at least 250 lifetime tablets, mean 794, clinician-rated SCID).

Table 1, last row: 17% (Winstock, 1,106 readers of a UK dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy; Severity of Dependence Scale 5 or more; mean 160 lifetime occasions); tolerance and continued use despite problems with health, work or relationships were reported by more than half of the sample. Footnote a: timeframe for assessment not specified.

Text figures: past-year DSM-IV ecstasy, hallucinogen or stimulant dependence among all young adults in Germany was 0.4% (von Sydow); 4% of past-year ecstasy-taking people in a US survey met hallucinogen-dependence criteria and 3.82% of those who had started in the previous two years had developed dependence (Wu; Stone); 17% of 154 Washington rave attendees and 16% of a German sample of current ecstasy-taking people were classed as dependent; Taiwanese detainees: 22% dependent and 36% with no dependence symptoms; in the Australian sample of 1,662, financial, legal and work-related harms, sexual risk, overdose and help seeking were more common among those screening positive, independent of problematic methamphetamine use, and only 2% (n = 7) of those screening positive used ecstasy at least every second day.
key_findings.locator: 3.2, from the paragraph beginning 'Seventeen percent of 154 Washington rave attendees' to the end of the section
key_findings.note: In the Australian text the 2% is of the group screening positive.

key_findings.finding: Structure: ecstasy dependence criteria did not behave like a single factor as for alcohol, opioids, cocaine or amphetamine; Topp et al. (1997) and Bruno et al. (2009), both Australian studies by the review's authors, found two factors, 'compulsive use' and 'escalating use'. The review concludes that dependence on ecstasy may differ in nature from dependence on alcohol, opioids and amphetamine and that a separate category deserves consideration.

Course: the only study of prognosis (a German population-based study of young adults, mean follow-up just over three years) found that 93% of those meeting criteria at baseline were no longer dependent at follow-up; of that group 50% no longer used the drug at all, and of the 43% still using, most did not meet criteria for a use disorder; the authors suggested ecstasy dependence might be a 'transient phenomenon'.

Treatment: in Australia, ecstasy accounts for very small numbers of treatment episodes (under 1% of all episodes); in a Texas series of 38,350 treatment episodes between 1988 and 2003 for people admitted with problems with 'club drugs', club-drug clients had more problems at admission and more polydrug use than clients using alcohol or other drugs. The review says routine treatment data cannot be used to estimate treatment need, and that problematic use of ecstasy alone may be a less significant reason for entering treatment.

Limitations: the studies are extremely heterogeneous in how dependence was assessed and in the samples, making meta-analysis inappropriate; assessment was typically self-reported without clinician verification and by lifetime retrospective report; people very commonly reported dependence symptoms despite relatively infrequent use, and it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as intended; prevalence cannot be extrapolated to all people taking ecstasy because most studies recruited people who had recently taken ecstasy by convenience or snowball sampling; information on natural history comes from retrospective reports of convenience samples.

Summary: 'The evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is limited in both scope and design.' Tolerance and withdrawal rest largely on self-report in research studies using questionnaires designed for other drugs; there is a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal; some people clearly become concerned about their use; treatment presentations are uncommon compared with the prevalence of use in the general population but do occur.
key_findings.locator: 4. Summary and implications, 1st, 2nd and last paragraphs

reporting_issues.issue: Winstock et al. (1,106 readers of a dance music magazine, 17%): Table 1 footnote a says the timeframe for assessment was not specified, and the text says the sample screened positive for lifetime ecstasy dependence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The window behind the 17% is not clear; it is not comparable with the past-year figures.

reporting_issues.issue: Wu et al.: Table 1 gives 3.6% past year and the text gives 4%; both describe DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence among past-year ecstasy-taking people, not an ecstasy-specific diagnosis. Stone et al. also used six items for hallucinogen criteria (Table 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: The two household-survey figures measure hallucinogen dependence in people who also took ecstasy, which is not the same as dependence on ecstasy; use the table's 3.6% and 3.8% and say so.

reporting_issues.issue: Bruno et al.: among people screening positive, Table 1 gives 34% using 1-2 times per month and the text gives 1-3 times per month; the text's 2% (n = 7) refers to those screening positive, not to the whole sample of 1,662.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small slip in a frequency band; the 2% must not be read as a share of all 1,662 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Hanson and Luciana: the prevalence cell in Table 1 reads 'N = 2 LT', while the details cell and the text say 14 of 26 met criteria for abuse or dependence.
reporting_issues.consequence: The row cannot be used as printed; 14 of 26 is also a sample of students and community members who used ecstasy, not a prevalence.

reporting_issues.issue: Tossman: Table 1 defines the sample as people who had taken ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year, with a footnote that the window was not specified; the text calls it 16% of people currently taking ecstasy.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 16% may include dependence on methamphetamine.

reporting_issues.issue: Parsons et al.: the sample is defined by ecstasy use in the past four weeks, but the details column gives a median of 2.5 days in the past four months, and the notes column gives a median of 5 days in the past four weeks for the dependent group against 2 for the non-dependent group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The frequency windows are not consistent; the 2.5 days cannot be taken as a typical weekly pattern.

reporting_issues.issue: Scheier et al.: Table 1 says latent-class groupings give no direct prevalence, but the text reports three groups with a greater than 50% probability of multiple symptoms and then '73%'; the same 73% is the prevalence printed for Thomasius et al. in Table 1, a study not discussed in the text.
reporting_issues.consequence: The highest prevalence in the table (73% of 59 heavy-using rave attendees) has no discussion in the text, and the 73% in the text paragraph is a different quantity.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 3.3 says two studies examined the structure of dependence, all involving Australian samples and one also including US samples, but the two studies described (Topp et al., 1997; Bruno et al., 2009) are both listed in Table 1 as Australian only.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample behind the two-factor finding is not reliably described; the conclusion rests on two studies by the review's own authors.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary treats a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal as support for physical symptoms playing a limited role, although the review also reports that three case reports described mild withdrawal and that the literature is mostly survey self-report.
reporting_issues.consequence: Absence of case reports is not evidence of absence; the statement is an inference.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1-10 (PDFs/MDMA/Degenhardt_2010_EcstasyDependence.pdf), full text including the funding statement and reference list; extracted once with pdftotext; Table 1 (pp. 4-6, landscape and rotated pages) was checked row by row against 110 dpi renderings of the pages.

design_detail: Echocardiography study in Brussels and Flanders, Belgium (December 2004 to February 2006): 29 people who had taken MDMA in the past year, recruited through the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and help centres for people with drug problems, compared with 29 age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no history of drug use (Am J Cardiol 2007;100:1442-1445; printed pp. 1442-1445, read as the published PDF). The paper calls itself case-control (p. 1445); because people were chosen by exposure and the outcome was measured once, the editors type it as a cross-sectional comparison. 33 people taking MDMA volunteered; 4 were excluded after scanning (3 for image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse), leaving 29 (p. 1443). Table 1 gives the demographics of the 33 and the echocardiographic results of the 29. Transthoracic echocardiograms of all four valves were stored, randomized and read blind by one of the sonographers and by an independent observer. 'Pathologic' follows the US Food and Drug Administration criteria for appetite-suppressant valve disease: mitral regurgitation of grade 2/4 or more, or aortic regurgitation of grade 1/4 or more. The laboratory mechanism (activation of the 5-HT2B receptor on human valve cells, Setola et al.) is cited, not tested.
can_establish: That in this recruited group a larger share of people who had taken MDMA in the past year (about six years of use on average, by their own account) had mild-to-moderate valve regurgitation, restrictive leaflet motion or strands on a blind-read echocardiogram than a matched group of drug-naive students: 8 of 29 (28%) met the FDA criteria against 0 of 29, and 13 of 29 had tricuspid regurgitation of grade 2/4 or more against 0 of 29.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the findings: there were no scans before use, the comparison group was students with no drug use at all, other drugs the MDMA group took are not reported, and the content of the tablets is unknown. How common valve changes are in people who take MDMA elsewhere (this group came through psychiatry and drug-help services). That the findings are harmful, since no symptoms, events or follow-up are reported. That the changes depend on the amount taken or are reversible: the dose comparison is within one small group and no repeat scans were done.

sample.recruitment: People who had taken MDMA in the past year were recruited by the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and by help centres for people with drug problems in Brussels and Flanders; controls were age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no drug use. All took part voluntarily with written consent (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 1442).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded in both groups: a history of ergot-derived drugs, Chinese herbs, appetite-suppressant drugs, intravenous drugs or any drug known to induce valve disease; any past cardiac disease (endocarditis, contractility abnormalities, hypertension); congenital or degenerative valve disease, including mitral or tricuspid prolapse, found on echocardiography; and poor image quality (p. 1442). Four of the 33 volunteers in the MDMA group were excluded after scanning (3 for image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse; Results, 1st paragraph, p. 1443).
sample.demographics: Table 1 (33 people taking MDMA, 29 controls): women 15 of 33 (45%) and 13 of 29 (45%); mean age 24.3 ± 3.1 and 25.6 ± 2.6 years (p = 0.10). MDMA use in the 33: 3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week for 6.1 ± 3.4 years; all had used for at least 6 months (p. 1443).
sample.attrition: 4 of 33 people in the MDMA group (12%) were excluded after scanning; no exclusions after enrolment are reported for the controls (p. 1443).
sample.selection_effects: The exposed people came from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres and the controls from student advertisements, matched only on age and sex, so differences in other drug use, tobacco, alcohol, medicines and the reasons for seeking care are built into the comparison. The weekly tablet figure (3.6 ± 6.7) has a spread nearly twice its mean, which suggests a skewed distribution with a few much higher values. The authors call the sample small because people were hard to recruit (p. 1445). Exclusions after scanning were reported only for the MDMA group.

exposure.measurement: Self-reported MDMA use in a detailed interview by an experienced psychiatrist about current and past drug use (p. 1442); no biological test, no analysis of tablets. Reported as tablets a week, years of use and, in the text, cumulative tablets (p. 1444).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: 3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week for 6.1 ± 3.4 years in the 33 people recruited (Table 1); on average 943 ± 1,162 cumulative tablets in those with higher grades of regurgitation and 242 ± 212 in those with lower grades (p. 1444). These are descriptions of the group studied, not amounts to take.
exposure.polysubstance: The psychiatrist asked about other drugs because substance use is mostly not limited to one drug (p. 1442), but the paper reports nothing about what else the MDMA group took or how it was handled; the comparison is with people reporting no drug use at all. Use of drugs known to induce valve disease was an exclusion criterion.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. The abstract says 'using or having used' MDMA, the Methods say use in the past year; time since last use is not given.

comparison.controls: 29 students who answered advertisements, matched for age and sex, with no history of drug use and the same exclusion criteria (Methods, 1st paragraph, p. 1442).
comparison.matching: Age and sex. Table 1: women 45% in both groups; age 24.3 ± 3.1 against 25.6 ± 2.6 years, p = 0.10 (editors' note: a standardised difference of about 0.45 for 33 against 29, so close but not equal).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No scans before use (the authors: 'There were no echocardiographic data available before MDMA use'). Not reported or adjusted: other drug use, tobacco, alcohol, blood pressure, body size, psychiatric diagnoses and any medicines taken for them.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Controls reported no drug use of any kind. The other drug use of the MDMA group was asked about but is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Transthoracic echocardiography (GE Vivid 7), all four valves from all possible views; continuous-wave, pulse-wave and colour Doppler; regurgitation graded 1 to 4 by American Society of Echocardiography recommendations; regurgitant jet-to-atrium area ratio for the mitral and tricuspid valves. Images stored digitally, randomized and read blind by one of the sonographers and an independent observer (Methods, p. 1443).
outcomes.validity_norms: FDA criteria were written for appetite-suppressant valve disease (mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more, aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more).
