The authors note that trace or mild mitral and tricuspid regurgitation is common in the general population (p. 1443). Interobserver agreement on the FDA score: kappa above 0.9 (Results, p. 1443). The authors say the scoring system of their earlier pergolide study was built for an older population (p. 1444).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Pathologic' = FDA criteria (mitral 2/4 or more, or aortic 1/4 or more). Other outcomes: tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more, pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more, area ratios, restrictive leaflet motion (leaflets stiffer than normal, tips closing towards the apex) and 'strands' (thin, mobile, filamentous projections on the leaflets). No symptoms, pressures, events or follow-up are reported.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; every test two-tailed at p of 0.05 or less (p. 1443). Editors' count of 12 outcomes: the 10 echocardiographic rows of Table 1, the composite FDA criterion and the combined strand count in the abstract; the within-group cumulative-dose comparison and the demographic tests are not counted. By the paper's rule 7 of the 12 reach p of 0.05 or less.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Reading was blind to group (randomized images, two readers, kappa above 0.9). The sonographers who acquired the images are described as not informed of the patients' identities; whether they knew a person's group is not stated (p. 1442).

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 1 (29 people taking MDMA against 29 controls; percentages and intervals added by the editors from the printed counts, Wilson 95% intervals; the paper's Fisher exact p values were reproduced from the counts). FDA criteria 8/29 (28%, 15-46%) against 0/29 (upper 95% bound about 12%), p = 0.0045. Tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 13/29 (45%, 28-62%) against 0, p < 0.001; tricuspid area ratio 19 ± 9.5% against 9 ± 4.5%, p < 0.001. Mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more 4/29 (14%, 5-31%) against 0, p = 0.11; mitral area ratio 12 ± 9.8% against 5 ± 1.3%, p < 0.007; mitral restrictive motion 7/29 (24%, 12-42%) against 0, p = 0.01. Aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more 4/29 (14%) against 0, p = 0.11. Strands: mitral 1/29, aortic 5/29 and combined 6/29 (21%, 10-38%) against 0, p = 0.02 for the combined count. Tricuspid restrictive motion 5/29 against 1/29, p = 0.19; pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more 14/29 (48%) against 10/29 (34%), p = 0.42. Within the MDMA group, people with higher grades of regurgitation had taken on average 943 ± 1,162 cumulative tablets against 242 ± 212 in those with lower grades, p = 0.03 (p. 1444).
analysis.covariates: None for the valve outcomes: groups matched on age and sex only. Relative risks with 95% intervals are described as from logistic regression (p. 1443) but the paper does not say what was adjusted for; the printed 5.83 for tricuspid restrictive motion equals the crude odds ratio from the counts (editors' calculation).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol mentioned; ethics committee approval only (p. 1442).
analysis.selective_reporting: No primary outcome is named. The abstract reports mitral regurgitation of 1/4 in 6 people (p = 0.002) and combined strands (p = 0.02), neither of which has a row in Table 1; the abstract's mitral area-ratio p of 0.007 is printed '<0.007' in Table 1.
analysis.power: No power calculation; 29 per group. The authors say the size is relatively small because people were hard to recruit (p. 1445).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 29 people who had taken MDMA (recruited through psychiatry and drug-help services) 8 (28%) had valve findings meeting the FDA criteria against none of 29 matched drug-naive students. The largest differences were tricuspid regurgitation of grade 2/4 or more (13 of 29 against 0) and the regurgitant area ratios, with mitral restrictive motion in 7 against 0 and strands in 6 against 0; mitral and aortic regurgitation at the FDA thresholds were found in 4 of 29 each against 0 (p = 0.11 each, not significant on its own). Pulmonary regurgitation was common in both groups (14 of 29 and 10 of 29, p = 0.42). Regurgitation was mostly mild to moderate; no symptoms or outcomes are reported. Within the MDMA group, people with higher grades had taken more tablets in total on average (943 against 242, with a wide spread).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says 'possible association', but the abstract concludes that 'MDMA may lead to mild to moderate valvular heart disease and valvular strands'; the Discussion says severity was associated with cumulative dose ('dose-dependent'), that lesions weaker than with pergolide or fenfluramine-phentermine could be explained by reversibility between weekends of use, that the findings are 'of great clinical importance' and that they argue for endocarditis prophylaxis (pp. 1444-1445). The comparison with drug-naive students, the absence of pre-use scans and unreported other drug use leave the group difference unattributed; the dose comparison is within one small group and cannot separate amount from years of use; reversibility was not tested; no clinical outcome or symptom is reported.

timeline.event: Laboratory study: MDMA and its metabolite activate human 5-HT2B receptors and drive prolonged growth of human valve cells in a dish (Setola et al.; cited in this paper, not tested).
Same group's earlier study of restrictive valve disease with pergolide in Parkinson's disease (Van Camp et al., Lancet; cited in this paper).
This paper: the authors state it is the first report of valve disease in young adults using or having used MDMA (Discussion, p. 1444).

replication.where_it_stands: The paper presents itself as the first report and cites no replication. This card does not review later studies, so the status reflects only what the paper reports and should be checked against later echocardiography work before a claim is published.

funding.funder: The first author received a scholarship from the Fonds voor Wetenschappelijk Onderzoek Vlaanderen (Brussels) for this work; no other funding is stated (p. 1442).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated: the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement. A statistician is thanked for advice (p. 1445).
funding.affiliations_note: Departments of cardiology and psychiatry at two Brussels hospitals (Universitair Ziekenhuis Brussel; CHU St. Pieter). Several authors had earlier reported restrictive valve disease with pergolide in Parkinson's disease (Van Camp et al., 2004), and the paper uses that experience to frame the MDMA findings.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study that scans people before they start MDMA, or follows a representative group of people taking it, with repeat blind echocardiograms, a comparison group from the same community checked for other drugs and medicines, confirmed content of what was taken, symptoms and clinical outcomes recorded, and repeat scans after people stop to test reversibility.

domains.note: Matched on age and sex only; controls were students with no drug use, the MDMA group came through psychiatry and drug-help services; other drugs, tobacco, alcohol, medicines and psychiatric diagnoses are not reported or adjusted for.
Self-report in an interview, no biological test, tablet content unknown, cumulative tablets reported with a spread larger than the mean (943 ± 1,162).
Exposed people from psychiatry departments and drug-help centres against advertised student controls; 4 of 33 exposed people were excluded after scanning and only for the MDMA group.
None described.
4 of 33 (12%) of the MDMA group were left out of the echocardiographic analysis; Table 1 gives the demographics and MDMA use for the 33 and the echocardiographic results for the 29.
Randomized images read blind by two readers with kappa above 0.9 and standard criteria; restrictive motion and strands are the authors' own definitions.
No primary outcome; 12 outcomes without correction; two abstract results (mitral 1/4 and combined strands) have no row in Table 1; printed relative risks are not reproducible from the counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The outcome measurement is the strongest part (blind, independent reader, standard criteria), but the comparison cannot separate MDMA from the other differences between a group recruited through psychiatric and drug-help services and drug-naive students, from other drugs taken, or from the unknown content of the tablets, and there were no scans before use. The study may be cited for a difference in echocardiographic findings between these two recruited groups; it may not be cited for MDMA causing valve disease, for how common it is, for dose dependence or for reversibility.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: 29 people using or having used MDMA and 29 gender- and age-matched controls were evaluated blind by echocardiography. 8 (28%) of the MDMA group met FDA criteria for appetite-suppressant valve disease against none of the controls (p = 0.0045); mitral regurgitation of 1/4 in 6 (21%) and over 2/4 in 4 (14%) against none (p = 0.002); mean mitral area ratios 12 ± 9.8% against 5 ± 1.3% (p = 0.007); tricuspid regurgitation over 2/4 in 13 (45%) against none (p < 0.001), area ratios 19 ± 9.5% against 9 ± 4.5%; mild aortic regurgitation in 4 (14%, p = 0.11); strands in 6 (21%) against none (p = 0.02). Conclusion: 'MDMA may lead to mild to moderate valvular heart disease and valvular strands'.
key_findings.note: The abstract says 'over 2/4'; Table 1 and the Methods use 2/4 or more.

key_findings.finding: Recruitment and criteria: people who had taken MDMA in the past year came from the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and from help centres for people with drug problems in Brussels and Flanders (December 2004 to February 2006); controls were age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no drug use. A psychiatrist interviewed everyone about current and past drug use. Exclusions in both groups: ergot-derived drugs, Chinese herbs, appetite suppressants, intravenous drugs or other drugs known to induce valve disease; any cardiac disease; congenital or degenerative valve disease on echocardiography; poor images.

Echocardiography and analysis: all images were stored, randomized and read blind by one of the sonographers and an independent observer; mitral and tricuspid regurgitant area ratio was also calculated. The FDA criteria were used (mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more, aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more) because trace or mild regurgitation of the mitral and tricuspid valves is common in the general population. Fisher exact, chi-square, Student t and Mann-Whitney tests; relative risks from logistic regression; two-tailed, p of 0.05 or less significant; SPSS 14.

Participants and headline result: 33 people who took MDMA and 29 controls were selected; none had a history of cardiac disease; 4 in the MDMA group were excluded (3 for image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse). Demographics were the same in the two groups; kappa between the two blinded observers was above 0.9; all people in the MDMA group had used for at least 6 months. Eight (28%) of the MDMA group had pathologic results by the FDA criteria and none of the controls (p = 0.0045).

Table 1, demographics (controls against MDMA group): n 29 and 33; women 13 (45%) and 15 (45%); age 25.6 ± 2.6 and 24.3 ± 3.1 years (p = 0.10); MDMA dose 3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week; duration 6.1 ± 3.4 years.
key_findings.note: Demographics are for the 33 recruited, the echocardiographic rows for the 29 analysed.

key_findings.finding: Table 1, echocardiography (n = 29 each; controls against MDMA group): mitral regurgitation 2/4 or more 0 and 4 (14%), p = 0.11; mitral area ratio 5 ± 1.3% and 12 ± 9.8%, p < 0.007; mitral restrictive motion 0 and 7 (24%), p = 0.01; mitral strand 0 and 1 (3%), p > 0.99; aortic regurgitation 1/4 or more 0 and 4 (14%), p = 0.11; aortic strand 0 and 5 (17%), p = 0.05; tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 0 and 13 (45%), p < 0.001; tricuspid area ratio 9 ± 4.5% and 19 ± 9.5%, p < 0.001; tricuspid restrictive motion 1 (3%) and 5 (17%), p = 0.19; pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more 10 (34%) and 14 (48%), p = 0.42.
key_findings.note: Editors recalculated Fisher exact p values from the counts and reproduced the printed ones (for example 0.0045, 0.11, 0.01, 0.19, 0.42, 0.02 for the combined strands).

key_findings.finding: Within the MDMA group, people with regurgitation of 2/4 or more on the mitral or tricuspid valves or any aortic regurgitation had on average taken more cumulative tablets (943 ± 1,162) than those with lower grades (242 ± 212; p = 0.03). The lesions were restrictive leaflet lesions at the mitral and tricuspid valves, regurgitation and strands. The authors cite laboratory work (Setola et al.) showing that MDMA and its metabolite activate human 5-HT2B receptors and induce prolonged growth responses in human valve cells, and conclude that severity was associated with cumulative dose.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: Group sizes within the MDMA group and the method of calculating cumulative tablets are not given.

key_findings.finding: Interpretation: the authors report valve disease for the first time in young adults using or having used MDMA; they explain the milder lesions compared with pergolide or fenfluramine-phentermine by possible reversibility between weekends of use, state that the regurgitations could become more severe with increasing doses and duration, and call the findings 'of great clinical importance', adding that endocarditis prophylaxis should be argued for.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 4th to 6th paragraphs (the 5th, beginning 'The party drug MDMA is more frequently used', runs from p. 1444 to p. 1445; the 6th begins on p. 1445)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: MDMA is illegal, so people were hard to recruit and the size is relatively small; information on the quantity of use came from interviews; there were no echocardiographic data before MDMA use because prospective evaluation was not possible in this case-control study for ethical reasons; there is no pathological evidence because no valve surgery was needed.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (beginning 'This study has some limitations')

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 reports the demographics and MDMA use (3.6 ± 6.7 tablets a week, 6.1 ± 3.4 years) for 33 people but the echocardiographic results for 29; the 4 people excluded after scanning are included in the first and not the second.
reporting_issues.consequence: The exposure description does not strictly describe the people whose valves were analysed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives mitral and tricuspid regurgitation as 'over 2/4' (4 and 13 people), but the Methods and Table 1 define the criterion as 2/4 or more. The abstract's 'mitral regurgitation of 1/4 in 6 (21%)' and its p of 0.002 have no row in Table 1; the abstract's combined strands (6, p = 0.02) are also not a Table 1 row (mitral 1 and aortic 5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Two of the abstract's headline results cannot be traced to the table; the counts can be checked only through the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The mitral area ratio is given as p = 0.007 in the abstract and '<0.007' in Table 1, next to a relative risk of 1.68 whose 95% interval (0.99-2.84) includes 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed p and interval for the same variable point in different directions; the relative risk for a continuous ratio is not explained.

reporting_issues.issue: The relative risks are said to come from logistic regression, but the paper does not say what was adjusted for. The printed 5.83 for tricuspid restrictive motion equals the crude odds ratio from the counts (5 of 29 against 1 of 29), and the printed 1.34 for pulmonary regurgitation matches neither the crude risk ratio (1.40) nor the odds ratio (1.77); relative risks are also printed for sex (0.99) and age (0.85) without units.
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed 'relative risks' cannot be interpreted as risk ratios.

reporting_issues.issue: Cumulative tablets are given only as two subgroup means (943 ± 1,162 and 242 ± 212) with no subgroup sizes, ranges or method of calculation; if 3.6 tablets a week applied to every week of 6.1 years it would come to about 1,100 tablets, above both subgroup means, so the figures may not describe the same people or the same weeks of use (the four excluded people may also differ).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose comparison cannot be checked or reproduced; its spread (standard deviation above the mean) means a few people carry the difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The paper calls the design case-control (limitations), but people were chosen by exposure and the valves measured once, not selected by outcome.
reporting_issues.consequence: The design label suggests a stronger inference than a one-time comparison of two recruited groups supports.

reporting_issues.issue: The strength of the claim rises through the paper: the title says 'possible association', the abstract 'may lead to', and the Discussion 'dose-dependent relation' and findings 'of great clinical importance', with a recommendation about endocarditis prophylaxis that no data in the paper test.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the results and the limitations, not the Discussion's causal and clinical statements.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1442-1445 (PDFs/MDMA/Droogmans_2007_ValvularHeartDisease.pdf), full text including the reference list; extracted once with pdftotext, which garbled symbols; Table 1 (p. 1443) and the abstract symbols were checked against 110 dpi renderings, and the paper's Fisher exact p values were recomputed from the counts.

design_detail: Narrative review, single author (Psychopharmacology 2004;173:234-241), read as the published PDF; the page numbers are the journal's own (pp. 234-241). It aims to estimate, for three historical phases (1970s to early 1990s, mid-1990s, late 1990s to 2002), what share of tablets sold as ecstasy contained MDMA, to report the amount per tablet where measured, and to describe how people who use ecstasy perceived purity (Abstract, p. 234; p. 235). There is no methods section, search, database or inclusion rule. The evidence is arranged in three tables of studies (Table 1, p. 236: seven rows from the mid-1970s to the early 1990s; Table 2, p. 236: nine rows from the mid to late 1990s; Table 3, p. 237: nine rows from the late 1990s to 2002), 25 rows in all (editors' count): 15 laboratory analyses of tablets or capsules, 4 toxicological series of deaths and 6 surveys of what people said about purity. Three series carry the headline estimates (Renfroe, 1986, a Californian anonymous testing laboratory; Spruit, 2001, the Dutch government's Drug Information Monitoring System; Schifano, 2000, forensic laboratories in north-eastern Italy), and the review says so (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 238). The rest are small, are a personal communication, or are described only as 'a majority' or 'almost all'. No quantitative synthesis and no intervals.
can_establish: What laboratory analyses published or reported up to 2002 found in tablets and capsules sold as ecstasy (the proportion containing MDMA, its relatives MDA and MDEA, amphetamines or other substances, and the milligrams of MDMA per tablet where measured), as summarized by one author, and how those findings differ by period and place.
cannot_establish: A proportion of tablets sold as ecstasy that contain MDMA in any year or country: none of the cited samples was random, the review gives no intervals, and its estimates are ranges built from different sampling frames (tablets brought in by people who use drugs, amnesty bins, police seizures, a paid testing service). Also anything after 2002; what any person took, how many tablets, or what they felt; and whether the tablets tested resemble the ones people took.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited analyses drew tablets from samples brought in by people who use drugs (the Dutch monitoring service; Renfroe's anonymous mail-in laboratory; the Dancesafe website), amnesty bins at a London dance venue, police seizures (Italy; UK) and a paid testing service (US$100 a pill). The review states that no study used a random sampling procedure (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 238).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated: no search, databases or dates. The sources include a personal communication (Ramsey, 2003), a short item in a Czech addiction journal (Palenicek et al., 2002), a website listing and book chapters, none of which can be checked from the review.
sample.demographics: Not applicable (narrative review).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The review's own limits (the paragraph beginning 'It should be emphasized that this area is fraught with methodological problems', p. 235; Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 238): no randomized sampling; most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or taken from amnesty bins; police seizures of large uniform batches may overstate how often tablets hold MDMA; the paid service probably over-represented atypical drugs; many studies cover one time point and are small. Editors' observations: no search was made, so absent studies cannot be assessed; the three large series dominate the estimates, and one of them (Italy) is built largely on police seizures; the newest data are from 2002.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory analysis of tablets or capsules, as summarized: thin-layer and gas chromatography (Renfroe), a three-stage quick test followed by laboratory analysis of unidentified pills in the Dutch service (p. 236), gas chromatography and infrared spectroscopy (Czech Republic), high-pressure liquid chromatography (Cole et al.); some entries are only statements that 'a majority' or 'almost all' held MDMA. The review does not appraise the methods.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable as doses: the review reports the milligrams of MDMA measured per tablet or capsule (for example 73-102 mg as UK annual averages, 100-150 mg in Italy, 0-152 mg in one Czech set; pp. 239-240), which describe the tablets, not amounts taken. Recorded here only as study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: The review separates the content of tablets from deliberate polydrug use by people, which it argues is probably a more important confound for research than accidental ingestion of other drugs, without data in this paper (p. 239).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None: the review compares periods and places, not groups of people.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable.

outcomes.instruments: Laboratory identification and, in some series, measurement of MDMA per tablet; surveys and interviews about perceived purity.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed: detection limits and the accuracy of the quick tests are not given.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Contained MDMA' means MDMA identified in the tablet, alone or mixed; the tables do not apply this uniformly (the Dutch series separates 'MDMA only' from 'mixtures', Renfroe's figure counts 'MDMA or MDA', and the 2002 website figure counts MDMA 'alone or in combination').
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages as reported by the cited series, with no intervals. Renfroe: 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy or similar names held MDMA or MDA (printed as 97%). Dutch service, each year 1993-1996: 48-60% MDMA alone, 12-20% MDEA alone, 2-5% MDA alone, 7-13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or others, 1-4% amphetamine alone, 2-7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA, and 6-17% 'other drugs'; 1997: 44% MDMA alone, 14% MDMA plus another drug, 24% MDA, MDEA or amphetamine, 18% other non-amphetamine drugs; 1998: 75% MDMA alone; 1999: 81% (p. 236). North-eastern Italy 1995-2000, at least 20,000 tablets: 85-90% MDMA, 8-10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others; UK 2001, 136 tablets: 100% MDMA; a US website 2002, about 175 tablets: 88% MDMA alone or in combination, 4% MDA or MDE, 4% others, 4% no identifiable drug (Table 3, p. 237). The review's own estimates: 90-98% in the 1980s to early 1990s, 50-80% in the mid to late 1990s (with 5-30% MDA or MDEA and 4-20% others), 80-95% in the late 1990s, near 100% in the early 2000s (p. 238). Amount per tablet: UK annual averages 90-102 mg (1991-1995) and 73-88 mg (1996-2001); Italy mostly 100-150 mg (p. 239); 80 identical white tablets from one 2001 UK seizure 73-89 mg, mean 79 mg; Czech tablets 30-100 mg with outliers of 152 and 0 mg (p. 240).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None; narrative review.
analysis.selective_reporting: No search or inclusion rule is stated, so selection cannot be assessed. The review identifies the Californian, Dutch and Italian series as the only large ones over time (p. 238) and includes a personal communication and a website listing as evidence for the most recent period.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the cited analyses most tablets sold as ecstasy held MDMA in every period, but the share ranged from about half to nearly all: lowest in the Netherlands in the mid-1990s (44-60% MDMA alone in a year; 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999), mostly above 85% in north-eastern Italy in 1995-2000 and in the small samples after 1999 (136 of 136 in the UK; about 88% of 175 on a US website). The tablets without MDMA held MDA or MDEA (related drugs), amphetamines, caffeine, ketamine, dextromethorphan, atropine, 4-methylthioamphetamine and others, or nothing active (about 1% in Italy, 4% on the US website). The amount of MDMA varied from none to about 150 mg across samples and, in the one seizure measured, from 73 to 89 mg within a uniform batch.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the purity problem was predominantly a phenomenon of the mid to late 1990s, that non-MDMA tablets are now very infrequent with purity between 90% and 100%, and that high dose tablets are now seen more frequently; the Discussion says the broad validity of using data from people who use ecstasy to estimate the consequences of MDMA is a key finding (p. 239). The text calls its own estimates very approximate (p. 238). The 90-100% for the early 2000s rests on one police-laboratory sample (136 tablets), a personal communication ('almost all') and a self-submitted website sample at 88%; 'high dose tablets now seen more frequently' rests on one mention of occasional high-dose tablets in 1998 and one website listing in 2002 (p. 240), while the review's own UK averages fell between 1991-1995 and 1996-2001 (p. 239).

timeline.event: Californian anonymous testing laboratory: 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy, MDMA, Adam or XTC held MDMA or MDA (Renfroe; as summarized in this review).
Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System, 1993-1999: MDMA alone in 44-60% of tablets a year in 1993-1997, 75% in 1998, 81% in 1999 (Spruit; as summarized in this review).
UK forensic laboratory sample of 136 tablets, all containing MDMA (Cole et al.; as summarized in this review).

replication.where_it_stands: A 2004 summary of tablet analyses up to 2002, usable as a second-hand description of that period. Later monitoring data are not in this review. A newer European pill-content study (Vrolijk et al., 2022) is not yet in the library; it would add current years, a defined European sample and milligrams per tablet over time.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PDF carries no funding statement or acknowledgements.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, University of Wales Swansea. The author has published on harms attributed to ecstasy and on polydrug use among people who use it, and 11 of its 59 references are his own work (editors' count), including the suggestion, from studies he ran in 1997 at the University of East London, that poor-quality tablets might protect against neurotoxicity (p. 239). The question the review answers, whether research on ecstasy measures MDMA, bears on that work; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Regular, random or systematically sampled purchases of tablets and powders sold as ecstasy, in defined places and years, analysed quantitatively for every active ingredient (MDMA, related drugs, other drugs and adulterants) and reported with the number of tablets, the sampling frame, the milligrams of MDMA per tablet and the spread within and between batches, so that the share with no MDMA and the spread of the amount can be estimated with intervals.

domains.note: No search, databases, dates or criteria; the sources include a personal communication, a website listing and short newsletter items, and selection cannot be assessed.

No appraisal of analytical methods or sampling beyond two footnotes to Table 2 (samples too small for estimates; a paid sample probably over-representing atypical drugs); figures are repeated as reported and several do not agree between the abstract, tables and text (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 11 of the 59 references are the author's own; they are used for perceptions of purity and for the suggestion that poor-quality tablets might protect against neurotoxicity (p. 239), not for the tablet-content data, which come from other groups.

Estimates are labelled very approximate and the sampling limits are stated (p. 238), but the abstract's 'high dose tablets now seen more frequently' rests on one website listing, and the serotonin-syndrome risk of high-dose tablets for first-time people is speculation without data (p. 240).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how often tablets sold as ecstasy contain MDMA
domains.note: Reports of low and of high purity are both given, with the mid-1990s dip described in detail; the explanations offered for the dip (supply of the chemical precursor, the later scheduling of related drugs; pp. 236, 239) are single accounts and are not tested.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is a useful and mostly well-hedged map of what was measured in tablets sold as ecstasy up to 2002 and of why the numbers differ, and it can be cited as a second-hand description of that. It cannot be cited for a population proportion, for any period after 2002, or for the trend in amount per tablet. Every figure should be taken from the primary series (Renfroe, 1986; Spruit, 2001; Schifano, 2000; Cole et al., 2002) once those are read; a claim resting only on this review stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: not every tablet sold as ecstasy contained MDMA. The author describes three phases: few problems until the early 1990s; in the mid-1990s a majority still held MDMA while many held MDA, MDEA or amphetamine mixtures and a small share (stated as 4-20% according to survey, time and place) held non-amphetamine drugs such as caffeine, ephedrine, ketamine, paracetamol or placebo; in the late 1990s MDMA rose to around 80-90%; the latest reports suggest 90-100%. Dosage is described as highly variable, with low dose tablets common in the mid-1990s and high dose tablets now seen more frequently.

Earliest data: of 20,721 street drug samples sent to a Californian laboratory in 1972-1985, 610 were MDA or MDMA pills; 89 of these were submitted under the names MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy, and all but two held MDMA or MDA (the two exceptions: an amphetamine capsule and an almost empty syringe). Table 1 gives 97% (n = 87). Surveys of what people said in 1987-1995 (US, Australia and UK; 100, 100, 20 and 209 people) reported no or few concerns about purity, and toxicology of 22 deaths and acute toxic reactions (Dowling) and of 7 deaths (Henry et al.) found MDMA, MDEA or MDA in each case, with other drugs in the larger series.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy from the 1970s to the early 1990s, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 235); Table 1 (p. 236)

key_findings.finding: Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System (Spruit, 2001, as summarized): in each year 1993-1996, around 48-60% of pills held MDMA alone, 12-20% MDEA alone, 2-5% MDA alone, 7-13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or others, 1-4% amphetamine alone and 2-7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA; over 80% held a ring-substituted amphetamine or amphetamine every year, and 6-17% were 'other drugs' (LSD, DOB, ketamine, 2C-B, atropine, caffeine, paracetamol or unknown compounds). In 1997 44% held MDMA alone and 18% non-amphetamine drugs, a time the review links to high demand and difficulty obtaining the chemical precursor; MDMA alone rose to 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999. Samples were mostly brought in by individual people, with a quick test and, for unidentified pills, laboratory analysis.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s, 1st paragraph (begins p. 235; the figures are on p. 236); Table 2, Spruit rows

key_findings.finding: Other mid-1990s analyses were small (13, 25 and 30 tablets in the UK, of which 77%, 64% and 87% held MDMA, MDEA or MDA, often in low or variable amounts; 107 pills in a paid US service, 63% MDMA, MDA or MDEA, with dextromethorphan, caffeine, ephedrine and salicylates among the others) and are called by the review too small for population estimates. Contents other than MDMA, MDA or MDEA included caffeine, amphetamine or ephedrine with caffeine, paracetamol, ketamine, phenylbutanamine, 2C-B and 4-methylthioamphetamine. The review stresses that the large majority of tablets still held MDMA or another ring-substituted amphetamine, and cites a 1996 WHO meeting calling the term ecstasy virtually generic for those drugs.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 236, ends p. 237); Table 2 (p. 236)

key_findings.finding: Late 1990s to 2002 (Table 3): north-eastern Italy, at least 20,000 tablets in 1995-2000, 85-90% MDMA, 8-10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others; Netherlands 1999, 81% MDMA only; Czech Republic, 120 pills, over 80% MDMA only; UK 2001, 136 tablets, 100% MDMA; a US website in 2002, about 175 tablets, 88% MDMA alone or in combination, 4% MDA or MDE, 4% others, 4% no identifiable drug; a London amnesty bin, tablets 'almost all' MDMA (personal communication, 2003).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Australian people interviewed in Perth in 1998-2000 (Hansen et al., 2001) estimated that around one tablet in every four or five was a 'dud', which the review says approximates the more systematic survey data.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review's own rough estimates of the share of ecstasy tablets holding MDMA: 90-98% from the 1980s to the early 1990s (the remaining 2-10% generally MDA); 50-80% in the mid to late 1990s (5-30% MDA or MDEA, 4-20% others); 80-95% in the late 1990s; near 100% in the early 2000s. It calls them very approximate, says only three reports involved large samples over an extended time (Renfroe, Spruit, Schifano), that no study has employed a randomized sampling procedure, that most samples came from people who use drugs or from amnesty bins, that police seizures of uniform batches may overstate purity, and that the paid US series probably over-represented atypical drugs.

A substantial minority of tablets held other drugs: 6-18% of Dutch samples in 1993-1997 were 'other drugs' not in the amphetamine class; the review names ketamine (very different effects, possibly distressing if taken unknowingly), 4-methylthioamphetamine ('flatliners', described as highly toxic and implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands, as quoted from Ramsey et al.), atropine, opiates, phenylbutanamine and dextromethorphan, and weak substances such as paracetamol, caffeine or placebo. When tablets held MDA or MDEA the review argues people would probably not notice marked differences except possibly in duration.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'However, a substantial minority of ecstasy tablets comprise other psychopharmacological compounds'; the preceding paragraph on MDA and MDEA

key_findings.finding: Perceptions: the review reports that people interviewed said they could tell occasions when they had taken MDMA from their other experiences, using jaw clenching, tooth grinding, the quality of mood changes and initial nausea to gauge the purity and strength of tablets (Hansen et al., 2001); winter 1997 studies in East London found frequent complaints about poor quality supplies and no neurocognitive impairments, which led the author to suggest that poor quality tablets might protect against neurotoxicity. The review gives no measurement of whether such signs match what a tablet held.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'One intriguing question is why the supplies of ecstasy first became problematical'

key_findings.finding: Amount per tablet: north-eastern Italy mostly 100-150 mg in 1995-2000; UK annual averages 90-102 mg in 1991-1995, falling to 73-88 mg in 1996-2001 (Cole et al., 2002). Small mid-1990s UK studies found variable and often low amounts: some tablets 100-140 mg, others around 50 mg, some under 20 mg (Sherlock et al.); Czech tablets 30-100 mg with borderline values of 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose); 80 identical-looking white tablets from one 2001 UK seizure ranged 73-89 mg, mean 79 mg. High dose tablets were occasionally found in the Dutch data in 1998 and an American drug website listed a number of them in 2002 (Green et al., 2003); the Dancesafe site listed various high dose examples, but many were at far lower levels or were mixtures. The review says unknown dosage remains a key area of uncertainty. These are measurements of tablets, not amounts to take.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic' (begins p. 239, ends p. 240)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the author concludes that unknown contents will always be a problem for people buying any illicit drug but that, for ecstasy, this was mainly a problem of the mid-1990s; earlier ecstasy was a drug of high street purity, its reputation has largely been restored, and the most recent surveys suggest MDMA purity rates of around 90-100%. The review states, without data, that high dose tablets may be particularly dangerous for people taking MDMA for the first time. A 1979 death after 840 mg of MDA powder, which the person and others believed was another drug, is given as an example of the danger of unknown contents.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic' (end) and the paragraph beginning 'To summarize'

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives about 80-90% of tablets holding MDMA in the late 1990s; the Discussion gives about 80-95% for the same period, citing the same two sources (Spruit; Winstock et al.).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline figure for the late 1990s depends on which part of the paper is read; the Winstock source is a survey of what people said, not an analysis of tablets.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says a small proportion (4-20% according to survey, time and place) held non-amphetamine drugs, and the Discussion repeats 4-20% for the mid to late 1990s, but the Dutch series shows 6-18% (Table 2) or 6-17% a year, and the only 4% in the review is the 2002 website sample (4% others, 4% no identifiable drug).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower bound of 4% cannot be traced to a mid-1990s source; use the Dutch figures for that period.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says high dose tablets are now seen more frequently. The text supports this only with the Dutch service noting that high dose tablets were occasionally encountered in 1998 and one American website listing a number of high dose tablets in 2002, while the Dancesafe site listed many high dose examples at far lower levels; the review's own UK annual averages fell from 90-102 mg to 73-88 mg.
reporting_issues.consequence: A rising trend in amount per tablet is not shown; the abstract's statement should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the biochemical evidence shows tablets nearly always contained MDMA before the 1990s. The evidence is 89 samples from one US laboratory (87 holding MDMA or MDA, so MDA is counted), surveys of what people said and short death series.
reporting_issues.consequence: 'MDMA or its relative MDA' is what the figure measures for the 1970s and 1980s, from one laboratory's anonymous submissions.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 12% of Renfroe's 610 MDA or MDMA samples were submitted as MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy and then says 89 samples; 12% of 610 is about 73, and 89 is about 15%. Table 1 prints 97% for 87 of 89, which is 97.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small slip, but it shows the figures were not checked against the primary paper; figures should be taken from the source.

reporting_issues.issue: Winstock et al. (2001) are described in Table 3 as a questionnaire survey of 1151 'regular/heavy' ecstasy-taking people, in the text as 1151 dance clubbers including numerous experienced people from the harder end of the scene, and in Degenhardt et al. (2010, Table 1) as 1106 readers of a dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample is not reliably described; it is used in the review only for people's reports that supplies improved.

reporting_issues.issue: Palenicek et al. (2002) are dated 1998-2001 in Table 3 and 1998-2002 in the text; the source is a two-page item in a Czech journal and the quotation about 30-100 mg tablets cannot be checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dates and amounts from this source are uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The Italian series, one of the three used for the headline estimates, is made largely of police seizures in north-eastern Italy, while the review warns that large uniform seized batches may lead to an overestimated level of purity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's own caveat applies to its largest late-1990s series; the 85-90% figure may be too high for tablets in circulation.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 234-241 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2004_IsEcstasyMDMA.pdf), full text including the reference list; extracted once with pdftotext; Tables 1-3 (pp. 236-237) and the Discussion pages (pp. 238-240) were checked against 110 dpi renderings of the pages.

design_detail: Retrospective review of coroners' cases from the Victorian State Coroner, Australia (J Anal Toxicol 2011;35:219-226; printed pp. 219-226, read as the published PDF). Closed cases from January 2002 to December 2008 were found through the National Coroners Information System where postmortem blood held a quantified MDMA result above 0.02 mg/L: 106 cases among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology (p. 223). Pathology, toxicology, coroners' findings and case circumstances were read for each. The authors examined in detail only the 19 cases in which they judged the drug combination able to cause serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction, and sorted them by the risk level given in a drug-interaction database (Table I, p. 220): 4 major (all with moclobemide), 10 moderate (dothiepin, methamphetamine and other amphetamines, tramadol, venlafaxine, methadone, fluoxetine) and 5 minor (citalopram, sertraline, fluvoxamine, doxylamine). The other 87 (MDMA alone or with its metabolite MDA 20; MDMA with ethanol 34; MDMA with other drugs judged unlikely to interact 33) were not analysed further (p. 223). Table II (pp. 221-223) lists, for each of the 19, sex, age, cause of death and autopsy findings, the drugs found with their blood concentrations, and the specimen and estimated postmortem interval. No comparison group and no count of people who took the same drugs and survived.
can_establish: Which medicines and other drugs were found, alongside MDMA, in 19 deaths in Victoria in 2002-2008 that the authors selected for a possible drug interaction, the cause of death and autopsy findings recorded for those 19, and how the 106 deaths with a quantified MDMA result divided into MDMA alone, MDMA with alcohol, MDMA with other drugs judged unlikely to interact, and the 19 selected.
cannot_establish: How often any medicine is present in deaths involving MDMA (the 19 were picked for having such a drug), that any medicine caused or contributed to any death, how risky any combination is (there is no count of the people who took the same combination and did not die), or where the medicines came from (usually not known). It does not show that MDMA caused the death in the 106 cases, 60% of which were deaths from external injury.

sample.recruitment: Not recruited: closed Victorian coroners' cases, January 2002 to December 2008, found through the National Coroners Information System, with a quantified MDMA result above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood (Cohort selection, p. 220). In Victoria all violent, unexpected and suspicious deaths reported to the coroner receive a full medicolegal investigation (Toxicological analysis, p. 220).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: the 106 cases above, among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology. Examined in detail: cases 'demonstrating a risk' of serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction from the drug combination and the circumstances; the others were left out 'because this cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only' (p. 223).
sample.demographics: All 106: 83 (78%) male; ages 17 to 48, median 25; 64 (60%) died by external injury, for example hangings and motor vehicle crashes (p. 223). The 19: 14 male; ages 21 to 45, median 28 (p. 224).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The 19 were chosen by the authors' own judgment of interaction risk from the drugs found and the circumstances, so every one of them has a drug of interest by design; 87 of the 106 were set aside and the contents of the 33 'other drugs' cases are not listed. Only deaths with MDMA quantified above 0.02 mg/L in blood are in the 106, so deaths in which MDMA was not tested for or not found are absent. Because 60% of the 106 died of external injury, they are not all deaths from drug toxicity. Counts of medicines among the 19 describe those 19; they are not a rate for deaths involving MDMA.

exposure.measurement: Postmortem toxicology: an immunoassay screen of blood (ELISA) or urine (CEDIA) for amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cannabis metabolites, cocaine metabolites and opiates, plus a semiquantitative gas chromatography screen for common drugs; positive findings confirmed by quantitative gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (lower limit of quantitation for MDMA 0.02 mg/L). Femoral-vein blood was used unless stated, to limit redistribution (Methods, p. 220). Concentrations are in mg/L, except ethanol (g/100 mL), THC (ng/mL) and carbon monoxide (% saturation) (Table II footnote).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: only concentrations measured after death are given, not how much was taken, when or how. MDMA concentrations in the 19 ranged from 0.02 to 3.5 mg/L (Group 1: 1.0 to 2.6, median 1.85; Group 2: 0.02 to 3.5, median 0.07; Group 3: 0.2 to 1.4, median 0.2; p. 224). These are measurements after death, not doses.
exposure.polysubstance: The study is about combinations: every one of the 19 had at least one other drug (a median of 4 substances other than MDMA, editors' count from Table II). Methamphetamine or amphetamine was found in 15 of the 19, in all three risk groups; THC in 5 and ethanol in 3. The paper does not weigh how much each substance contributed to a death.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None. The only comparison is with the 87 cases set aside, whose contents are counted (20, 34 and 33) but not listed, so the 19 cannot be compared with deaths involving MDMA without these drugs or with people who took the same drugs and survived.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history, prescriptions, the source of the drugs, the timing of medicines relative to MDMA and whether medicines were taken as prescribed are mostly missing (Limitations, p. 225); most deaths were unwitnessed, so symptoms before death are rarely known.

outcomes.instruments: Cause of death and intent as recorded by pathologists and coroners; autopsy in 16 of the 19 with the findings in Table II; clinical signs of serotonin toxicity noted by a paramedic or physician in 3 cases (p. 224); the authors' ratings of interaction risk from Micromedex Drugdex and other references (p. 223).
outcomes.validity_norms: Serotonin toxicity cannot be shown at autopsy; the diagnosis rests on witnessed symptoms, the drugs involved and the circumstances (p. 220). Postmortem redistribution can raise concentrations: cavity blood in cases 1 and 10 and a six-day interval before sampling in case 18; tolerance makes concentrations of morphine hard to interpret (p. 225). Codeine and morphine in Table II are unconjugated drug only.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Interaction risk' means the authors' Group 1 (major), 2 (moderate) or 3 (minor) in Table I. Cause of death is the coroner's wording in Table II.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive counts; no tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; the authors assessed each case individually with the findings in hand (Data analysis, p. 220).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive counts only, no tests or intervals. Of 106 cases: 4 major-risk (moclobemide), 10 moderate and 5 minor; 87 set aside (20 MDMA alone or with MDA, 34 with ethanol, 33 with other drugs judged unlikely to interact), that is about 19, 32 and 31 in 100 of the 106 for the three set-aside groups and 18 in 100 for the 19 examined (editors' arithmetic). Editors' tallies of Table II (19 cases; cases with at least one substance of the class): methamphetamine or amphetamine 15 (methamphetamine 14, amphetamine 7); any antidepressant 13 (moclobemide 4; fluoxetine, sertraline, dothiepin, venlafaxine, citalopram, mirtazapine or fluvoxamine 9); any opioid including the heroin marker 6-MAM 12 (methadone 5, codeine 5, morphine 5, tramadol 1, 6-MAM 3); any benzodiazepine or metabolite 8; benzodiazepine or opioid 14; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; THC 5; ethanol 3. Cause of death: drug toxicity alone 12 (cases 1-5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 19); injury with combined toxicity 2 (cases 13, 17); other causes 5 (drowning, train impact, haemorrhagic shock with incised wounds, hanging, carbon monoxide). Serotonin toxicity was noted by a paramedic or physician before death in 3 of the 4 moclobemide cases (cases 1 to 3). MDMA at or below 0.05 mg/L in 5 of the 10 Group 2 cases (6, 8, 9, 13, 14).
analysis.preregistration_detail: None; descriptive retrospective review with ethics approval from the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine and the Department of Justice (p. 223).
analysis.selective_reporting: The 19 cases are chosen by the authors' judgment, and the risk grouping follows the pharmaceutical drug (Table I rates amphetamine derivatives as moderate, yet they appear in 4 of the major and 3 of the minor cases). The examples of major and minor risk in the text (chlorpromazine and chlorpheniramine) do not appear in Table I or II.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 19 deaths the authors selected from 106 for a possible drug interaction, every one had at least one other drug: methamphetamine or amphetamine in 15, antidepressants in 13 (moclobemide in 4, with signs of serotonin toxicity noted before death in 3 of those 4), opioids in 12 (3 with the heroin marker 6-MAM), benzodiazepines in 8. Twelve of the 19 died of drug toxicity alone; the others died of injury or other causes with drugs present. In the other 87 of the 106 (82 in 100), MDMA was found alone or with MDA (20), with ethanol (34) or with drugs judged unlikely to interact (33).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The authors conclude that some people may combine pharmaceutical drugs with MDMA to enhance the effect or ease the comedown, that this appeared a limited practice in Victoria in 2002-2008, that serotonin toxicity was probably overlooked, that knowledge of interactions is probably limited and that education is needed (pp. 224-225). The case counts and postmortem concentrations do not show intentions, knowledge or whether serotonin toxicity occurred in the cases where it was not recorded; the paper gives a source for the drugs only for two moclobemide cases (witness statements suggesting a friend or family member). The abstract's '43 (41%)' cases of combined use cannot be matched to the results (19 + 33 = 52).

timeline.event: Case report of a death after MDMA and moclobemide (Vuori et al.); one of the cases the authors cite for the combination.
Qualitative review of serotonin syndrome with MDMA and other serotonergic drugs (Silins et al.); the authors take part of their risk grouping from it.
This case series: 19 of 106 Victorian deaths with MDMA in blood, 2002-2008, examined for drug combinations.

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive series from one Australian state; it is not designed to be replicated and the authors say a national search would find more. The four moclobemide cases are examined in a separate publication the authors cite (p. 224), which was not read.

funding.funder: Not reported: there is no funding statement. The acknowledgments thank the National Coroners Information System, the State Coroner's Office, the pathologists, technicians and toxicologists of the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, and a colleague for help with the manuscript (p. 225).
funding.declared_conflicts: None stated; the paper has no conflict-of-interest statement.
funding.affiliations_note: The authors are in the Department of Forensic Medicine at Monash University and at the Victorian Institute of Forensic Medicine, whose staff are thanked for help with the cases (p. 219, p. 225).

what_would_settle_it: A study across all Australian states or several years that counts every death and compares it with a denominator (people presenting to hospital after MDMA, or a cohort of people taking MDMA), with the content of what was taken confirmed, prescribing and dispensing records, the timing of each medicine, clinical data such as temperature, a fixed postmortem sampling site and interval, and a rule for rating interaction risk set in advance and applied without knowledge of the outcome.

domains.note: The 19 were chosen by the authors' judgment of interaction risk from 106; 87 were set aside and the 33 'other drugs' cases are not listed; only deaths with MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in blood are in the 106.

Immunoassay screen and quantitative GC-MS, but postmortem redistribution (cavity blood in cases 1 and 10; six-day interval in case 18), unconjugated-only opiates and tolerance limit what the concentrations mean; MDMA is printed as 0.02 mg/L for case 13, equal to the cut-off.

domains.domain: Judgment of interaction risk and cause of death
domains.note: Risk groups were assigned by the authors from a drug database with the findings in hand; serotonin toxicity cannot be shown postmortem and was recorded before death in only 3 cases.
The source of the drugs, prescriptions, timing, clinical data and medical history are mostly missing (p. 225); most deaths were unwitnessed.
The abstract's 43 (41%) cases cannot be matched to the results; pulmonary oedema is in 4 cases in the text and 5 in Table II; named examples (chlorpromazine, chlorpheniramine) are not in the tables.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a coroners' case series (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The series is a transparent list of what was found in 19 deaths chosen for possible interactions, and the table can be cited as a description of those 19. It cannot be cited for how often medicines are found in deaths involving MDMA, for the risk of any combination, or for any medicine having caused a death. A claim resting only on this series stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: 106 fatalities with a quantified MDMA result were identified in Victorian coroners' closed cases, 2002-2008; the abstract states that 43 (41%) involved MDMA with other drugs, including pharmaceuticals likely to result in an adverse drug reaction or varying risks (4 high-risk cases with moclobemide, 10 moderate-risk and 5 minor-risk); it concludes that potential interactions between MDMA and pharmaceutical preparations, in particular serotonin toxicity, should be recognised and publicised.
key_findings.note: 43 (41%) cannot be matched to the Results (19 + 33 = 52).

key_findings.finding: Methods: postmortem femoral blood was used where possible; immunoassay screening (ELISA blood or CEDIA urine) for amphetamines, benzodiazepines, cannabis metabolites, cocaine metabolites and opiates, a semiquantitative gas chromatography screen, and gas chromatography-mass spectrometry confirmation (MDMA lower limit of quantitation 0.02 mg/L). Cases came from the National Coroners Information System: closed Victorian cases, January 2002 to December 2008, with MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood. Each case was assessed for toxicology, pathology and circumstances, including the risk of serotonin toxicity from monoamine oxidase inhibitors, SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, ethanol, amphetamines and some antihistamines.
key_findings.locator: Methods: Toxicological analysis; Cohort selection; Data analysis

key_findings.finding: Table I, risk groups from Drugdex and other references: major (Group 1), moclobemide, a reversible MAO-A inhibitor (hypertensive crisis and serotonin toxicity); moderate (Group 2), dothiepin (tricyclic), amphetamine and derivatives (amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDA, MDEA), tramadol, venlafaxine and cocaine, and the CYP2D6 inhibitors methadone and fluoxetine; minor (Group 3), doxylamine and the SSRIs citalopram, sertraline and fluvoxamine.

Table II, the 19 cases with sex, age, cause of death and drugs in postmortem blood: cases 1 to 4 (Group 1) all had moclobemide with MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L; cases 5 to 14 (Group 2) and 15 to 19 (Group 3) are listed with their drugs. Editors' tallies: methamphetamine or amphetamine 15; antidepressants 13; opioids (including 6-MAM) 12; benzodiazepines or metabolites 8; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; THC 5; ethanol 3. Sixteen of the 19 had a leg-blood specimen, 2 cavity blood and 1 antemortem serum; the estimated postmortem interval was 2 to 6 days.
key_findings.locator: Table II (cases 1-8 on p. 221; 9-16 on p. 222; 17-19 on p. 223)
key_findings.note: Tallies by the editors from the printed table; the paper does not tabulate them.

key_findings.finding: Selection and counts: the paper examined only cases demonstrating a risk of serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction from the combination; the others were excluded because 'this cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only'. 106 cases among 14,682 coroners' cases with full toxicology; 83 (78%) male; 64 (60%) died by external injury; ages 17 to 48, median 25. 4 major, 10 moderate and 5 minor risk cases were examined; the other 87 were MDMA alone or with MDA as metabolite (20), MDMA with ethanol (34) or MDMA with other drugs not likely to cause an adverse drug reaction (33).
key_findings.locator: Methods: Data analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Results: Basic characteristics, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Toxicology in the 19: 14 male, ages 21 to 45 (median 28). Group 1: all four with moclobemide, MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L (median 1.85), clinical symptoms of serotonin toxicity noted by a paramedic or physician in three (cases 1 to 3). Group 2 (10 cases): fluoxetine, venlafaxine, methadone, dothiepin and tramadol, with methamphetamine and paramethoxyamphetamine; MDMA 0.02 to 3.5 mg/L (median 0.07). Group 3 (5 cases): citalopram, fluvoxamine, sertraline and/or doxylamine; MDMA 0.2 to 1.4 mg/L (median 0.2).
key_findings.locator: Results: Toxicology findings in the 19 cases of interest, 1st paragraph (begins on p. 223) to 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Pathology: 16 of the 19 had a full autopsy; coronary artery disease with significant occlusion in two (cases 2 and 4); ischaemic change in the myocardium in one (case 7); hepatic pathology (hepatitis C or fatty liver) in six (cases 1, 7, 8, 13, 18, 19); pulmonary oedema reported in four cases in the text (five in Table II: cases 1, 2, 4, 5, 7); the autopsy findings were relatively unremarkable in Groups 2 and 3 with no significant natural disease.
key_findings.locator: Results: Pathology findings in the cases of interest

key_findings.finding: Discussion: four cases combined MDMA with moclobemide, described as a high-risk combination for serotonin toxicity; Group 2 cases mostly involved serotonergic antidepressants or opioids; serotonin toxicity was reported before death in only three cases and the authors think it was more likely overlooked in others; several Group 2 cases involved benzodiazepines, which the authors say are often used in the days after ecstasy; methadone and fluoxetine are CYP2D6 inhibitors, which the authors say can raise MDMA concentrations; a 2006 survey found that over a quarter of the sample had used ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug, most often from friends.

Source and limits: in many cases the source of the drugs is unknown; witness statements in a number of cases, including two of the moclobemide cases with fatal serotonin toxicity, suggested the person may have obtained the medicine from a friend or family member. Limitations named: postmortem redistribution (cavity blood in case 10; a six-day interval in case 18), missing information on the source of drugs, prescribing and clinical data, concentrations of drugs with tolerance such as morphine being hard to interpret, and a likely under-recording of non-fatal and serotonin toxicity cases.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (begins on p. 224), 7th and 8th paragraphs (p. 225)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: some people may combine pharmaceutical drugs with MDMA to enhance the high or counteract a comedown, but this appeared to be a limited practice in Victoria in 2002-2008; there is a risk for people using pharmaceuticals therapeutically who take MDMA occasionally, particularly if unaware of interactions; since many deaths were apparently unintentional drug toxicity, the authors consider it likely that knowledge of interactions is limited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 43 (41%) of the 106 cases involved MDMA with other drugs. The Results give 19 examined cases plus 33 cases with other drugs judged unlikely to interact (52), or 86 if the 34 with ethanol are added.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's headline share cannot be traced; use the Results counts.

reporting_issues.issue: The text names chlorpromazine as an example of a major interaction and chlorpheniramine as a minor one; neither appears in Table I or Table II.
reporting_issues.consequence: The examples describe the rating scheme, not the cases examined.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports pulmonary oedema in four cases; Table II lists it in five (cases 1, 2, 4, 5 and 7).
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts from the text and the table disagree by one.

reporting_issues.issue: Table I places amphetamine and its derivatives in the moderate group, but methamphetamine or amphetamine appears in 4 major-group cases (1-4) and in 3 minor-group cases (15, 17, 19). The group follows the pharmaceutical drug.
reporting_issues.consequence: Group labels do not describe how many drugs of each risk were present.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table I says it includes all the drugs detected with MDMA in this cohort, but cocaine, MDEA and MDA appear in none of the 19 cases in Table II, and Table II lists drugs not in Table I (mirtazapine, olanzapine, ketamine, paramethoxyamphetamine, codeine, morphine, 6-MAM and all the benzodiazepines).
reporting_issues.consequence: Table I is a rating scheme, not a list of what was found.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion rule is MDMA above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood, but case 13 is printed with MDMA 0.02 mg/L, and 5 of the 10 Group 2 cases have MDMA at or below 0.05 mg/L (cases 6, 8, 9, 13, 14).
reporting_issues.consequence: Several cases sit at the detection limit; MDMA may have been a minor finding in them.

reporting_issues.issue: The contents of the 33 cases of MDMA with 'other drugs not likely to cause an adverse drug reaction' are not given, although the 19 examined cases are chosen against them.
reporting_issues.consequence: The reader cannot see what the authors judged unlikely to interact.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 219-226 (PDFs/MDMA/Pilgrim_2011_MDMADeathsPharmaceuticals.pdf), full text including the reference list; extracted once with pdftotext; Table I (p. 220) and Table II (pp. 221-223) were transcribed and checked case by case against 110 dpi renderings of the pages.

design_detail: In-depth narrative review by two kidney specialists (Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology, 2008): pharmacology and metabolism (Figures 1 and 2), clinical syndromes (Table 1), acute kidney injury (Table 2), low blood sodium with a table of 32 reported cases (Table 3) and a figure of proposed mechanisms (Figure 3), and a treatment section that is not used here. No search method, dates or inclusion criteria are stated; 88 references, most of them case reports, letters and reviews, a few animal studies and one retrospective series.
can_establish: Which kinds of kidney injury and of low blood sodium had been described after ecstasy in case reports up to 2008, what the authors think are the likely mechanisms, and what they say about who was reported; and, from this card's reporting issues, where their statements go beyond the sources they cite.
cannot_establish: How often kidney injury or low sodium happens (for kidney injury the review itself says the incidence cannot be determined); which factor caused which case (case reports have no comparison); the size of any sex difference (the reports are selected); or anything independent of the primary papers, which the review reports second-hand and this reader has not read.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence base as described: case reports and letters (more than 25 reports of low sodium; single case reports for most kidney problems), a few case series, a human volunteer study of vasopressin, and animal studies; Table 3 lists 32 reported cases of low sodium from 21 sources (p. 1855).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Published case reports show people who became ill and were written up; they say nothing about how many people took ecstasy and were not harmed. 10 of the 32 rows in Table 3 come from one California series and all 10 are deaths, 6 of them with no sodium recorded. The in-text citation range for the low-sodium case reports (references 48-68) includes a kidney-injury report (48), an analysis (59), a rat study (67) and a case series (68).

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited report, as described: by history in case reports; in the one volunteer study cited, a dose given by the study team.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As described in the review, not a study condition: three doses at a rave in the first kidney-injury case (1992); 'a single dose' in the vast majority of low-sodium cases (stated in the text; Table 3 has no dose column, p. 1855); five tablets in the one case described in detail (pp. 1855-1856). In the volunteer vasopressin study cited, a small single dose was given to eight men (p. 1856).
exposure.polysubstance: Table 3 has no column for other substances. The review says attributing vasculitis to ecstasy is difficult because other substances are often taken (p. 1854).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None in the review. Case reports have no comparison; the one controlled human experiment described compared vasopressin before and after a dose in eight men.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Body size, kidney function, fluid intake, exertion, heat, other drugs and genetic differences in metabolism are mentioned as possible factors but not measured in the reports the review describes.

outcomes.instruments: As reported in the cited papers: serum and urine sodium and osmolality, plasma vasopressin, creatine kinase, creatinine; scans. The review states that no case of kidney injury after ecstasy had a kidney biopsy (p. 1854).
outcomes.validity_norms: Low sodium is described as 'usually' below 130 mEq/L (p. 1855); Table 3 includes two rows with a sodium of 130.
outcomes.operationalization: Case reports of kidney injury (Table 2) and of low sodium (Table 3), grouped by the reviewers' reading of the likely cause.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As described, no pooled analysis. Death risk in people taking ecstasy for the first time estimated at 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 50,000 (Gore 1999, as cited, p. 1852). Kidney injury: incidence 'cannot be determined'; CK of 100,000 U/L or more in rhabdomyolysis cases (p. 1854); up to 31% of drug-related acute liver failure attributed to MDMA in one study (Andreu, as cited, p. 1854). Low sodium: more than 25 case reports; sodium 101-130 mEq/L; vast majority female, aged 15-30 (text, p. 1855). Table 3 (checked on a render of p. 1855): 32 rows, 27 F, 1 labelled W, 4 M; ages 14-30; 16 deaths, 15 recoveries, 1 not available; 10 rows (all deaths) from the California series, 6 of them with no sodium; Hartung's UK series (reference 68) is not in the table. The text says more than 85% of symptomatic cases were female (28 of 32 rows). The one detailed case: an 18-year-old woman after five tablets, sodium 136 then 130 mEq/L after 1,700 ml of water, plasma vasopressin 33.7 pmol/L (normal below 5.6) (pp. 1855-1856). Vasopressin in eight volunteers rose from 1.14-1.88 to 2.46-9.16 pmol/L within 1 to 2 hours (Henry 1998, as cited, p. 1856).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection without a stated search. The review says some points against its own mechanism (sweat sodium loss 'likely marginal'; most reports lack significant hyperthermia; the incidence of kidney injury cannot be determined) but states other points more firmly in the abstract and conclusions than the text supports (see reporting issues).
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Case reports and a few series show that rhabdomyolysis with high temperature and exertion is the commonest described route to kidney injury, with single reports of other kinds; and that low blood sodium with brain swelling has been reported after ecstasy, mostly in young women who had drunk fluid, with vasopressin raised in a few cases and in eight volunteers. The review has no incidence figures for either.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the low sodium a 'perfect storm' of vasopressin release, polydipsia and ready fluids, and the Conclusions add drug-induced thirst and say young people who take a single dose are at risk. The text says a primary drive to drink 'is not known but has been hypothesized' (p. 1855), and no denominator is given for 'at risk'. The review says the California study found women had a significantly higher incidence of symptomatic low sodium, coma and death, which that study did not show (it found no clear difference for death).

timeline.event: First case report of kidney injury after ecstasy: three doses at a rave, with seizures, rhabdomyolysis and clotting disorder (Fahal and colleagues, as described in this review).
First report of low sodium after ecstasy named in the review (Maxwell and colleagues, as described).
Vasopressin rises within 1 to 2 hours in eight healthy men given a small dose of MDMA (Henry and colleagues, as described).
UK poisons-service series of 17 people with low sodium after ecstasy (listed among the references, not tabulated).
A woman who drank 1,700 ml of water after five tablets and whose sodium fell from 136 to 130 mEq/L, with very high vasopressin (Brvar and colleagues, as described).
Loss of two transplanted kidneys from one donor with recent ecstasy use (Hurault de Ligny and colleagues, as described).
California poison-centre series of 545 reports, which the review summarises and mis-cites.
This review.

replication.where_it_stands: Kidney injury after ecstasy is known from case reports only; the commonest described route is muscle breakdown after exertion with overheating and too little fluid. Low blood sodium has been reported repeatedly, from single cases to a 545-report series, mostly in young women. Mechanisms (vasopressin release, fluid intake) are plausible and partly measured in volunteers, but no study read in this batch compares people who drank a lot with people who did not.

funding.funder: Not stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: Disclosures: none (p. 1857).
funding.affiliations_note: Two authors from the Division of Nephrology, University of Virginia.

what_would_settle_it: For kidney injury: a prospective registry of people attending emergency departments after MDMA, with creatinine and creatine kinase measured on arrival and at follow-up and a count of everyone who attended, so that an incidence could be estimated; kidney biopsy in unexplained cases. For low sodium: see the other cards in this batch (sodium measured on arrival, fluid intake recorded, comparison with people who drank similarly and stayed well).

domains.note: No search method, databases, dates or criteria; the Table 3 rows come from 21 sources and omit the largest UK series; the citation range for case reports includes papers that are not case reports.
No appraisal; case reports, letters, one retrospective series and animal studies are cited side by side as 'case reports' and 'controlled studies'.
The California series is cited as a 1998 case report; Table 1 is cited for sex data it does not contain; 'a single dose' is stated but not tabulated; six Table 3 rows have no sodium.
Mechanisms are mostly worded as 'likely' or 'hypothesized' in the text, but the abstract and Conclusions state drug-induced thirst as fact.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against
domains.note: Says the incidence of kidney injury cannot be determined and that sweat sodium loss is likely marginal, but concludes that young people taking a single dose are at risk with no denominator, and argues the female predominance is not a reporting bias without data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3). The overall judgment is not milder than its worst domain. Use it for the list of kinds of kidney injury and low sodium that had been described by 2008, for what the authors say is unknown, and for pointers to the primary reports; do not use it for how often either happens, for who is at risk, or for the California findings (read Rosenson 2007 instead).

key_findings.finding: The review says ecstasy toxicity is 'not attributable to overdose' in the usual sense: some people take it without harm, while others taking similar amounts have serious toxicity (Brown and Osterloh 1987, as cited). It gives an estimated death risk of 1 in 2,000 to 1 in 50,000 for people taking it for the first time (Gore 1999, as cited); the spread is 25-fold and no basis is shown.

Metabolism, as described from two other reviews: breakdown depends partly on the enzyme CYP2D6, which varies between people; slow metabolisers are said to be at higher risk because levels stay high; after repeated doses (even as few as two) metabolites can inhibit the enzyme, so there is 'the potential for increased toxicity with repeated dosing'. A metabolite, HMMA, is described as a more potent trigger of vasopressin release than MDMA itself, which the authors suggest could explain why low sodium is not seen in everyone.
key_findings.locator: Pharmacology, 3rd paragraph (p. 1852, continued on p. 1853, left column); p. 1853, right column, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Kidney injury: the review says most of the data come from case reports and that 'the absolute incidence of this complication cannot be determined'. The first case (1992) followed three doses at a rave, with seizures, rhabdomyolysis and a clotting disorder. The commonest described route is non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis (muscle breakdown), mostly in people who had exerted themselves with inadequate fluid, impaired heat regulation and high temperature, made worse by a hot room; creatine kinase of 100,000 U/L or more is described; low volume and low blood pressure add to the injury.
key_findings.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, paragraphs 1-2 (left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: Other kidney problems are single case reports: transient proximal tubule dysfunction in an 18-year-old; necrotizing vasculitis in a 30-year-old man who had used ecstasy 10 days before and went on to kidney failure; loss of both transplanted kidneys from one donor with recent use; bladder-neck obstruction; and kidney injury after accelerated or malignant hypertension. The review says that no case of kidney injury after ecstasy had a kidney biopsy, and that attributing vasculitis to ecstasy is difficult because other substances are often taken. Liver failure after ecstasy is described, with a risk of kidney injury through hepatorenal syndrome; one study attributed up to 31% of drug-related acute liver failure to MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Acute Kidney Injury, right column (p. 1854); Table 2 (p. 1854); p. 1855, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Low sodium: more than 25 case reports since 1993; sodium on presentation 101 to 130 mEq/L; 'the vast majority' of cases were female, aged 15 to 30, and are said to have taken a single dose (not shown in Table 3). The cause is called dilutional and due to several interacting effects. Table 3 lists 32 cases (27 F, 1 W, 4 M; 16 deaths, 15 recoveries, 1 unknown), 10 of them from the California series (all deaths, 6 with no sodium recorded); the UK series of 17 is not tabulated.

Fluid and thirst: excessive water intake 'has been directly associated' with ecstasy, partly through 'chill out' areas offering free or cheap water; ecstasy-related dry mouth and thirst are described; whether ecstasy causes a primary drive to drink 'is not known but has been hypothesized'. The one detailed case: an 18-year-old woman, five tablets, severe headache and thirst, sodium 136 mEq/L, then 1,700 ml of water and a sodium of 130 mEq/L with plasma vasopressin of 33.7 pmol/L (normal below 5.6) and urine osmolality 335 mOsm/kg. The authors say the availability of fluids and thirst are 'likely not enough' on their own, because the kidney can normally excrete water faster than it is drunk; kidney water excretion must also be impaired.
key_findings.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1855, right column); p. 1856, left column, 1st paragraph
