key_findings.finding: Vasopressin: said to rise within 1 to 2 hours of MDMA in controlled settings (eight healthy men given a small dose, from a baseline of 1.14-1.88 to 2.46-9.16 pmol/L, with a slight fall in sodium; other studies cited), and more with the metabolite HMMA; urine osmolality was inappropriately high in case reports (184-970 mOsm/kg). Sweat sodium loss is called 'likely marginal'; most low-sodium case reports lack significant hyperthermia; the authors conclude that increased water intake together with kidney water retention is the main driving force.
key_findings.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, left column, 2nd paragraph; right column, 3rd-4th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sex: said to be highly associated with symptomatic low sodium; 'a review of published case reports' found more than 85% of symptomatic cases were female; the review says this was also documented in a 5-year California case review and that it 'does not reflect a bias' toward more women taking ecstasy because other complications are commoner in men (no data given). Suggested reasons are estrogen effects on the brain's sodium pump and vasopressin response, lower muscle mass and body weight (second-hand).

Conclusions: kidney injury is mostly pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis after rhabdomyolysis; low sodium is called a 'perfect storm' of drug-induced vasopressin release, drug-induced thirst and ready fluids; the authors say young people who take a single dose are at risk. The remaining sentences are advice and treatment and are not used.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says ecstasy leads to polydipsia (excess drinking) through its serotonin effects, and the Conclusions list drug-induced thirst as a main mechanism, but the text says whether ecstasy causes a primary drive to drink 'is not known but has been hypothesized', citing one case and a rat study.
reporting_issues.consequence: Drug-induced thirst is a hypothesis in this review, not a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The California case review is cited as reference 49 (Ajaelo 1998, a case report) when it is reference 82 (Rosenson 2007). The review says it showed a significantly higher incidence of symptomatic low sodium, coma and death in women; that study measured low sodium only in people who had a sodium test, found higher odds of coma in women with low sodium, and found no clear difference for death.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review overstates the California findings; read Rosenson 2007 for them.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 lists 32 cases, but 6 rows (all deaths from the California series) have no sodium recorded, 16 of the 32 rows are deaths, one row has gender 'W', and the UK series of 17 (reference 68) is absent. The text says more than 25 case reports; the rows come from 21 sources.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table is not a count of cases and shows mostly the most severe reports; do not use it for the share of women or the share who died.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the vast majority of cases 'ingested a single dose', but Table 3 has no dose column, and the one detailed case took five tablets.
reporting_issues.consequence: The single-dose statement cannot be checked in the review.

reporting_issues.issue: Female gender is described as 'highly associated' with symptoms, citing Table 1, which lists clinical syndromes and has no data on sex. The share of more than 85% is a count of published reports, and the argument that it is not a bias toward more women taking ecstasy has no data or reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex difference is from selected reports; it is not an estimate of risk.

reporting_issues.issue: The citation range for the low-sodium case reports (references 48-68) includes a kidney-injury report (48), an analysis (59), a rat study (67) and a case series (68). The 'controlled studies' of vasopressin rise within 1 to 2 hours (13, 69-72) include a study of isolated rat hypothalamus (71) and a study of people in a club (72).
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts of case reports and the strength of the human vasopressin evidence are overstated.

reporting_issues.issue: No search method, databases, dates or inclusion criteria are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The set of cases is whatever the authors chose; absence of a kind of case does not mean it has not occurred.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1852-1860 (PDFs/MDMA/Campbell_2008_AgonyOfEcstasyKidney.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3, Figure 3, Conclusions, disclosures and the reference list (read to check the citations noted above). Table 3 and the gender and Conclusions passages were checked on rendered images of printed pages 1855 and 1857.

design_detail: Retrospective case series from the London centre of the United Kingdom's National Poisons Information Service (NPIS). All documented telephone enquiries from December 1993 to November 1995 were screened by an information officer for MDMA use complicated by a serum sodium below 130 mmol/l, and clinical details and blood and urine results were requested from the hospital concerned. From December 1995 to March 1996, service medical staff gave management advice for acute cases and, where possible, asked for serial sodium and osmolality tests; blood and urine samples were obtained for toxicology at the authors' laboratory. One further fatal case, where the authors' advice was sought, is included; the paper says it has since been reported separately (reference 12). 17 patients are described: 15 who recovered (Table 1) and 2 who died (Table 2). Descriptive only: there is no comparison group and no statistical analysis is described (Methods, p. 434).
can_establish: What the picture looked like in 17 young people who developed low blood sodium after taking MDMA and whose cases reached a poisons service over about two years: what the hospital records said they had taken and drunk, how soon they became ill, their sodium and urine tests, the course over the next days and the two deaths; and that no raised temperature is recorded for any of the 17.
cannot_establish: How often low sodium follows MDMA (the 17 cases come from telephone enquiries, not from a count of people who took MDMA); who is at greater risk (no comparison group); whether the amount of fluid or the amount of MDMA brought it on (fluid histories are approximate or missing, and nobody who drank similarly and stayed well is described); or whether MDMA raised vasopressin in these patients (it was not measured in this series).

sample.recruitment: Telephone enquiries to one poisons service's London centre. Screened retrospectively from December 1993 to November 1995; from December 1995 to March 1996, cases arising from requests for management advice; plus one further fatal case where the authors' advice was sought, which the paper says has since been reported (Methods, p. 434; reference 12, whose first author is one of this paper's authors).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MDMA use associated with hyponatraemia, defined as serum sodium below 130 mmol/l; no other criteria are given (Methods, p. 434).
sample.demographics: Seven men and ten women aged 15 to 26. Among the 15 who recovered: 7 men and 8 women. Both who died were female, aged 15 and 18 (Table 1, pp. 432-433; Table 2, p. 435).
sample.attrition: Not applicable; an outcome is given for all 17. Many cells of Table 1 are empty and the paper does not say whether the test was not done or not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Only people whose doctors telephoned the poisons service are included; people with milder low sodium, or whose hospital did not call, are absent, and so is anyone who drank a lot and stayed well. The authors themselves say complications of MDMA may be under-reported (Discussion, 1st paragraph, p. 434).

exposure.measurement: Tablets and fluids as recorded in the clinical details requested from the hospital concerned (Methods, p. 434); the paper does not say who supplied the history. MDMA was confirmed analytically in 8 of the 15 who recovered, and in blood in both who died (0.05 and 0.209 mg/l). A fluid history was not available for 5 of the 15 who recovered (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 434; Tables 1 and 2).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: As recorded in the hospital reports, not a study condition. Among the 13 who recovered and had a stated amount, 12 had taken two tablets or fewer (one had taken three); both who died had taken one tablet, and both had taken MDMA before. Tablet content was not measured (a Table 2 footnote gives only a general range for tablets). Every patient became ill within 12 hours of taking the drug, and the two who died within about 5 hours (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 434; Results, p. 434; Table 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol was drunk by several patients (beer, wine, gin; blood ethanol 0.8 g/l in one of the two who died); one of those who died (the 18-year-old) had smoked cannabis. The authors say they do not know whether the patients smoked tobacco, which matters because nicotine releases vasopressin (Table 1; Table 2; Discussion, pp. 435-436).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Everything that might explain who becomes ill: body weight, kidney function, previous MDMA use, exertion, room temperature, sweat loss, and how many people drank similar amounts and stayed well.

outcomes.instruments: Serum sodium and calculated serum osmolality, urine osmolality (and urine sodium in one patient) from hospital laboratories; presenting features, Glasgow Coma Scale, scans, treatment and outcome from hospital notes; post-mortem findings in the two who died; toxicology at the authors' laboratory (Methods and Results, p. 434; Tables 1 and 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Serum osmolality was calculated from sodium, potassium, urea and glucose in many patients (footnote c of Table 1). The SIADH pattern is defined as low sodium, low serum osmolality and inappropriately concentrated urine (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 434).
outcomes.operationalization: A case is an enquiry in which MDMA use was complicated by serum sodium below 130 mmol/l; the series reports what the patients had taken and drunk, their presenting features, sodium and osmolality values and outcome.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no tests).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; data were abstracted from hospital reports after the event.

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts only. Of 17: 7 men, 10 women; ages 15-26; serum sodium 107-128 mmol/l on day 1 (Table 1 and Table 2); 2 deaths. Of the 15 who recovered (counted on the rendered Table 1, pp. 432-433): MDMA confirmed in the laboratory in 8; 8 known to have drunk a large amount of fluid (water, soft drinks or beer) and 5 with no usable fluid history; seizures in 10; 13 labelled complete recovery, 1 with poor concentration and short-term memory at 2 months after a head injury (extradural haematoma and skull fracture), and 1 needing a tracheostomy after aspiration. Biochemistry fitted SIADH in 6 patients. The abstract gives 10 confirmed, 10 known large fluid intake, 11 with seizures and 14 complete recoveries; the first three equal the text counts plus the patients who died (see reporting issues). Share of ecstasy enquiries: 135 a month of 13,762 enquiries; 17 cases in 28 months, which the paper gives as 0.4% of enquiries about ecstasy (Results, 1st paragraph, p. 434).
analysis.selective_reporting: Descriptive series without hypotheses; cases are selected by their outcome (low sodium), so nothing can be said of those who drank and took MDMA without becoming ill.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: 17 young people, 10 of them women, became ill with low blood sodium within 12 hours of taking MDMA (12 of the 13 survivors with a stated amount had taken two tablets or fewer; each of the two who died had taken one). 8 of the 15 survivors were known to have drunk a large amount of fluid and the history was not available for 5; both who died had drunk a large amount of water. Illness began with vomiting and disturbed behaviour, then drowsiness and agitation, with seizures in 10 of the 15 survivors and drowsiness, mutism or disorientation for up to 3 days. No raised temperature is recorded for any of the 17. 15 recovered (13 labelled complete recovery) and 2 died of brain swelling. In 6 patients the sodium, serum osmolality and urine osmolality fitted the pattern the authors call SIADH.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and Discussion state that MDMA can cause life-threatening hyponatraemic encephalopathy when accompanied by excessive fluid ingestion, that the mechanism involves inappropriate secretion of antidiuretic hormone, and, at the end, that the hyperthermic and hyponatraemic complications appear largely avoidable. The cases are consistent with a link to a large fluid intake, but a series with no comparison group cannot show cause or avoidability, and vasopressin was not measured in these patients; the Discussion itself says the way MDMA causes the hormone release remains to be established (p. 435).

timeline.event: Earliest report of low sodium with stupor after ecstasy in this paper's reference list (Maxwell, Polkey and Henry; reference 10).

A near-fatal case attributed to vasopressin over-secretion (Holden and Jackson; reference 7) and cerebral oedema after unrestricted water intake (Matthai and colleagues; reference 9), as cited by this paper.
A rise in vasopressin after MDMA in eight healthy men (Henry and colleagues; reference 19), as cited by this paper; not read here.
This series: 17 cases from one poisons service, 2 deaths.
A series of 18 people with low sodium after ecstasy, 17 of them women (Budisavljevic and colleagues), as cited in the California series; not read here.
California poison-centre review of 545 reports: 73 with a recorded low sodium, 4 deaths among them.
Narrative review that tabulates published cases of low sodium after ecstasy.

replication.where_it_stands: The same picture, low sodium within hours of taking MDMA, usually with a large fluid intake, was described in earlier case reports (this paper cites about eight) and later in a larger American poison-centre series and a review of published cases, both read in this batch. None of the studies read here compares people who drank a large amount with people who did not, so the size of the risk and the part played by fluid remain untested.

funding.funder: Not stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not stated: no funding or competing-interest statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from hospitals in Dundee, London and Chelmsford, one address in Sydney, and Imperial College. The last author (Henry) also wrote or co-wrote three of the papers this one cites, including the 1998 report of vasopressin after MDMA (reference 19), and one author (Parr) is first author of reference 12, a report of one of the fatal cases in this series.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective registry of everyone attending events or emergency departments after taking MDMA, with sodium measured on arrival, an account of fluids drunk, and a denominator, so that low sodium could be compared across levels of fluid intake, body size and sex; and studies in healthy volunteers that follow sodium, vasopressin and recorded fluid intake over the hours after MDMA.

domains.note: No comparison group: nobody who took MDMA and drank similarly and stayed well, so fluid, MDMA and every other difference are untestable.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Cases found through telephone enquiries to one service, by different routes in two periods, with one further fatal case added because advice was sought.
MDMA confirmed in the laboratory in 8 of 15 survivors; fluid intake by history, approximate, and missing for 5.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Not a trial; treatments were those the hospitals chose and are not the subject of the series.
Many sodium, osmolality and urine values are blank in Table 1; the SIADH pattern could be judged in only 6 patients.
Sodium is a laboratory value; clinical descriptions come from notes requested from the hospitals, and for the two deaths the first sodium was recorded after treatment had started.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Descriptive series with no tests; the abstract counts (10, 10, 11, 14) do not match the tables (8, 8, 10, 13) except by adding the two deaths.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A descriptive series appraised with ROBINS-I as the library does for other case series; it has no comparison group, so the confounding domain is critical by design. It can be cited for what these 17 cases looked like and what they were recorded as having taken and drunk; it cannot be cited for how often it happens, for who is at risk, or for fluid or MDMA as the cause.

key_findings.finding: Case finding: of a mean 13,762 enquiries a month to the service, 135 a month (1.0%) concerned ecstasy; over the 28-month study period 17 cases of low sodium after MDMA were identified, which the paper gives as 0.4% of enquiries about ecstasy: 7 men and 10 women aged 15-26. The percentage is a share of telephone enquiries, not of people who took MDMA.

Presentation: vomiting and disturbed behaviour, then drowsiness and agitation, with seizures in 10 of the 15 who recovered; drowsiness, a mute state and disorientation for up to 3 days; the authors say clinical findings did not necessarily reflect the size of the sodium fall. Serum sodium on day 1 was 107-128 mmol/l. Temperature was recorded as normal in 12 of the 15 who recovered, as 37.5 degrees Celsius in two and 34.8 in one; at hospital presentation it was 32.6 and 33 degrees in the two who died.

Fluid and tablets: 8 of the 15 who recovered were known to have drunk a large amount of water, soft drinks or beer, and for 5 the fluid history was not available; of the 13 with a stated amount of MDMA, 12 had taken two tablets or fewer. Both who died had taken one tablet and had drunk an excessive amount of fluid.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, 'History of MDMA and fluid ingestion' column (pp. 432-433); Results, 1st paragraph and top of right column (p. 434); Table 2 (p. 435)

key_findings.finding: The two deaths, both female and both having taken MDMA before: a 15-year-old (one tablet at midnight; dancing, talking and drinking water, at least 3 litres, in rotation; ill at 05:00 and given a considerable amount of water; serum sodium 125 mmol/l at 12:00 after 1.5 litres of intravenous fluid and 1 litre of saline; brain swelling and herniation; brain dead on day 2; blood MDMA 0.05 mg/l) and an 18-year-old (one tablet at 19:45; smoking cannabis and some alcohol; water from 22:00; ill at 00:15 and drank 6-7 cups of water; serum sodium 126 mmol/l; marked brain swelling; brain dead on day 3; blood MDMA 0.209 mg/l, MDA 0.029 mg/l, ethanol 0.8 g/l). Symptoms of brain swelling began within 5 hours of taking one tablet.

Outcome of the 15 who recovered: 13 are labelled complete recovery in Table 1; one had difficulty in concentration and poor short-term memory at 2 months after an extradural haematoma and skull fracture; one needed a tracheostomy after aspiration pneumonia and tracheitis.

Biochemistry consistent with SIADH (low sodium, low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine) in 6 patients. The authors say the low sodium appears to result from water consumption in excess of the body's requirements, compounded by failure of the kidney's response to a water load, and that the way MDMA causes SIADH remains to be established. A raised vasopressin in one earlier patient, and a rise in vasopressin after MDMA in eight healthy men, are cited from other papers.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 434); Discussion, 1st and 3rd paragraphs (p. 434) and p. 435, left column

key_findings.finding: The authors say that the early public message to those taking MDMA to 'drink plenty of fluids' was aimed at preventing overheating and did not state that a high fluid intake could be harmful without prolonged exertion, and that this was later corrected after publicity about the deaths. They also say symptoms of low sodium came on over a short space of time, and that recovery fitted clearing of MDMA and its metabolite over 24-48 hours.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph beginning 'The acute onset of symptoms' and the paragraph on early public messages that follows it (p. 436, left column)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and the text count differently. Confirmation of MDMA in 10 patients (abstract) against 8 (text and Table 1); a large fluid intake known in 10 against 8; seizures in 11 against 10. These equal the text counts plus the patients who died (2, 2 and 1), which the paper never says, and no denominator is given. The abstract's 14 complete recoveries do not match the 13 labelled complete recovery in Table 1.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use the text and table counts (8, 8, 10 and 13 of the 15 who recovered); the abstract mixes denominators of 15 and 17.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives a single window, December 1993 to March 1996, for screening all enquiries. The Methods describe screening of all documented enquiries only to November 1995, then, to March 1996, cases arising from requests for management advice with serial tests asked for, plus one further fatal case added because the authors' advice was sought.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cases were found by different routes, so the 17 cases and the two deaths cannot be read as a systematic count.

reporting_issues.issue: The share '0.4% of all enquiries about ecstasy' is the number of cases over the number of telephone enquiries.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is not a risk among people who take MDMA and should not be quoted as one.

reporting_issues.issue: For the 15-year-old who died, the sodium of 125 mmol/l was recorded at 12:00, after 1.5 litres of intravenous fluid on transport and 1 litre of 0.9% saline in hospital; for the 18-year-old the 126 mmol/l entry and the saline are in the same cell, so the order is not clear. The paper gives no pre-treatment values for either. Both are higher than several survivors (107 to 118), and the authors say clinical findings did not necessarily reflect the size of the fall.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sodium values recorded for the two deaths may be higher than before treatment and should not be used to compare severity with the survivors.

reporting_issues.issue: Fluid amounts are approximate. One entry carries a question mark (excessive amount of water, 13 bottles?); 'excessive amount' is not defined; several entries give an unknown amount.
reporting_issues.consequence: No dose-response between fluid and sodium can be built from this table.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence saying plasma vasopressin was found inappropriately raised 9 hours after ingestion in one case cites reference 1, which is titled as a report of a fatality with coagulopathy and hyperthermia; the near-fatal case with vasopressin over-secretion is listed as reference 7.
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation for the one earlier vasopressin measurement appears to be wrong; it cannot be traced from the paper alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The received and revised dates are printed in the wrong order (received 2 November 2002, revised 21 February 2002).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the findings; one date is a misprint.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 431-437 (PDFs/MDMA/Hartung_2002_HyponatraemicStates.pdf), full text: summary, Methods, Results, Tables 1 and 2, Discussion and references. Table 1 prints rotated; its rows were read and counted on rotated renders of printed pages 432 and 433 (8 laboratory confirmations, 10 seizures, 13 labelled complete recoveries among the 15), and the less-than sign in the case definition (lost in the text layer) was checked on the rendered pages.

design_detail: Single-author narrative review of what is known about MDMA and body temperature in people, written in 2011: placebo-controlled laboratory studies (Table 1), studies of people at dance clubs and parties (Table 2), hospital case reports and series of severe overheating, thermal self-ratings (how hot people say they feel), proposed mechanisms of heat production and loss, and behavioural and environmental co-stressors (Table 3). Animal work is cited only as background. Method as stated: an extensive personal collection of MDMA papers was scrutinised and then a PubMed search was run with thermal key words; no search string, dates, selection rules, number of papers screened or appraisal method are given (Section 1, 3rd paragraph, p. 2).
can_establish: What one author found when he gathered the human temperature studies up to mid-2011: the size and spread of the temperature rises reported in laboratory and in party settings, examples of severe overheating in hospital series, how much people differ in how hot they say they feel, and a list of hypotheses about what makes overheating worse, with the review's own statement of which are untested.
cannot_establish: The size of the average temperature effect of MDMA (the figures are unweighted averages of studies that used different thermometers, doses and comparisons); whether dancing, crowding, a hot room, too little or too much water, other drugs or low thermal awareness raise the risk of severe overheating (the review itself calls most of these untested or very limited); what share of people who take MDMA overheat; or anything about prevention (the review's treatment passages are not used here).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Evidence base as listed in the tables: laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers; party and club studies of 11 to 41 people; one Internet survey of over 200; hospital series of 48 and 332 admissions; individual case reports (Tables 1 and 2, p. 3; Sections 3-5, pp. 4-6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated. Selection began from the author's personal collection and a PubMed search with unstated key words (Section 1, 3rd paragraph, p. 2).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: The author's own work supplies three of the five party studies in Table 2 (Parrott and Young, 2005; Parrott et al., 2007b; Parrott et al., 2008) and the Internet survey of over 200 people; the party studies are small convenience samples at clubs and parties (11 to 41 people each), and one source is a conference abstract (Tancer et al., 2003) and another is cited as a single page (Morefield et al., 2009). Cases from hospitals show the people who became ill, not how many took MDMA and did not.

exposure.measurement: Varies by cited study. Laboratory: dose given by the study team. Parties: MDMA confirmed by blood (Irvine et al., 2006; Morefield et al., 2009) or saliva (Parrott et al., 2008) in some studies, by self-report in others; doses unknown (Sections 2-3, pp. 2-5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as summarized: oral doses of 0.25 to 2.0 mg/kg, or 75, 100 or 125 mg, in laboratory studies; in party studies, self-obtained tablets, 1 to 5 in one study and on average 6 over a night in another (Section 2, pp. 2-4; Section 3, pp. 4-5).
exposure.polysubstance: Laboratory studies: MDMA alone. Party studies: methamphetamine was found in 41% and cannabis in 33% of one sample, other drugs were taken occasionally in another, and one study asked people not to take other stimulants (Section 3, pp. 4-5). The author suggests stimulants may add to body temperature and cannabis may lower it, on very limited data (Table 3; Section 8).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable to a review; in two party studies the same people were also studied on a weekend without MDMA (Section 3, p. 4).

comparison.controls: Laboratory: placebo sessions in the same people, except the first pilot study (Grob et al., 1996), whose text describes baseline sessions only. Parties: no comparison at all in one study; people who had never taken ecstasy at the same club in one; the same people on a weekend without MDMA in two; the person's own pre-drug baseline in one (Sections 2-3, pp. 2-5).
comparison.matching: Varies. The club comparison of people who took ecstasy that evening with people who had never taken it and with former takers is between people; the two weekend studies are within person.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Parties: dancing, room temperature, crowding, fluid intake, sleep and the time of night are not controlled; the review notes that without a control condition the normal fall of body temperature during the night is uncontrolled (Section 3, Irvine paragraph, p. 4).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not controlled in the party studies.

outcomes.instruments: Oral, axillary, tympanic (ear), rectal and ingested radio-telemetry core temperature and skin temperature in the laboratory; ear or oral temperature at parties; self-rated feeling hot, hot and cold flushes and sweating by questionnaire, interview and Internet survey (Tables 1 and 2, p. 3; Section 5, p. 6).
outcomes.validity_norms: Different body sites do not give the same temperature; the author notes, quoting an animal study, that ear temperature can be lower than and independent of blood temperature (Section 8, p. 8).
outcomes.operationalization: Peak change in temperature against placebo, baseline or a comparison group. Dose tiers in Table 1 are the unweighted means of the rows within each tier; 'higher dose' means 2.0 mg/kg.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no pooled analysis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: As summarized (Tables 1 and 2, p. 3; Sections 2-3). Laboratory peak core temperature change: up to 1.0 mg/kg, from -0.1 to +0.3 degrees Celsius, tier mean +0.1; 1.1-1.9 mg/kg, +0.3 to +0.5, mean +0.4; 2.0 mg/kg, +0.4 to +1.0, mean +0.7 (14 people in two studies by the same three authors, each at two room temperatures). In the two studies that varied room temperature, 18 against 30 degrees: +1.0 and +0.8 (4 people) and +0.4 and +0.6 (10 people). One volunteer in an 8-person study rose 1.9 degrees against a group mean of +0.4. Plasma MDMA and temperature correlated with p<0.0001 in the laboratory (Kolbrich et al., 2008) and r=+0.38, p=0.058 at a party (Irvine et al., 2006). Party studies, peak change: +0.2 (27 people, no control), +1.2 against clubbers who had never taken it (32), +0.3 (12; -0.2 on a weekend without MDMA, +0.15 with), +1.6 (11 people, 6 tablets on average, against a weekend without), +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41 people). Thermal self-ratings, Internet survey of over 200: 16% not hot, 41% slightly, 31% moderately, 12% strongly or extremely hot.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection without a stated search. The review reports small and null results (Grob et al.; Vollenweider et al.; Kolbrich et al.; Irvine et al.), which counts in its favour. Table 3 states that high room temperature was associated with higher core temperature in the laboratory, which the text of the same review does not support.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The review notes where small samples limit a result (14 women in one overview).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In placebo-controlled laboratory studies of 4 to 16 volunteers, core temperature rose on average about 0.1 degrees Celsius at low doses, 0.4 at moderate and 0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg, with one volunteer up 1.9; the two studies that varied room temperature found similar rises at 18 and 30 degrees. At parties, group averages rose between 0.2 and 1.6 degrees in five small studies with different comparisons, the largest (+1.6) in the group that took 6 tablets on average over the night. Severe overheating above 40 degrees is described in hospital series and case reports of people who became ill, with no denominator. How hot people said they felt varied widely (16 in 100 not hot at all). Dancing, crowding, other drugs and thermal awareness as risk factors are hypotheses, and the review says so.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Section 8 state that MDMA is clearly a thermal stressor in people and that its effects were dose related; that real-world variation is possibly due to physical activity, ambient temperature and overcrowding; that moderate hyperthermia can progress to severe hyperpyrexia through a cascade of events; and that low thermal awareness might put people most at risk. The first statement is well supported by the laboratory studies. 'Dose related' is a pattern across studies, not shown within any one study. The cascade and the risk factors are explicitly hypotheses (Section 7, p. 7; Table 3).

timeline.event: Pilot study of six volunteers at four low doses: no significant change in oral temperature (Grob et al., as summarized in this review).
13 volunteers at 1.7 mg/kg: about +0.2 to +0.5 degrees Celsius, not significant; one brief hypertensive crisis (Vollenweider et al., as summarized).
8 men at 75 and 125 mg: peak +0.4 degrees at 2 hours (Mas et al., as summarized).
16 and 14 volunteers at 1.5 mg/kg: +0.3 to +0.4 degrees, significant (Liechti et al., as summarized).
4 volunteers at 2.0 mg/kg at 18 and 30 degrees: +1.0 and +0.8 (Tancer et al., conference abstract, as summarized).

10 volunteers at 2.0 mg/kg at 18 and 30 degrees: +0.4 and +0.6, with delayed onset of sweating (Freedman et al., as summarized); also 32 clubbers who had taken ecstasy, 1.2 degrees above clubbers who had never taken it (Parrott and Young).
27 people at a dance party: +0.2 degrees, no control condition (Irvine et al., as summarized).
8 volunteers: +0.3 to +0.4 degrees, not significant, one person +1.9 (Kolbrich et al., as summarized); 12 clubbers on and off MDMA (Parrott et al.).
41 people at parties, 1 to 5 tablets: +1.1 degrees oral (Morefield et al., conference abstract, as summarized).
166 healthy volunteers in nine controlled studies from one laboratory: highest temperature 39.1 degrees, none above 40

replication.where_it_stands: A rise in core temperature after MDMA at rest has been found by several independent laboratories, in small studies; its average size is a few tenths of a degree at moderate doses. The effects of heat, dancing, crowding and other drugs on that rise have not been tested in people, and the review says so. Severe overheating is known from hospital cases only.

funding.funder: Nothing declared (Role of funding source, p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict declared (p. 8).
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, Swansea University; also author of three of the party studies and the Internet survey reviewed here.

what_would_settle_it: A systematic review with a stated search and appraisal; person-level data from placebo-controlled studies at several doses read with one thermometer type; controlled human studies that change one factor at a time (room temperature, activity, fluid intake, a second stimulant) within ethical limits; and party studies that follow matched people who did not take MDMA at the same event, with temperature logged at fixed times and the blood level measured.

domains.note: Starts from a personal collection plus a PubMed search with unstated key words; no dates, criteria or count of papers.
Informal appraisal in the text (no control condition, borderline significance, pooled time points, a study left out of Table 1 because it had no placebo) but none that is systematic.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: Three of the five party studies in Table 2 and the Internet survey are the author's own.
Untested hypotheses are mostly labelled as such (Table 3; Section 7), but the Table 3 row on room temperature states a laboratory finding that the text does not report.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against
domains.note: Reports null and small results; the cascade of co-stressors rests on animal, survey and case evidence.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No standard risk-of-bias instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3). The review is open about what is untested, but its selection is unsystematic and rests partly on the author's own studies, and one table row contradicts its own text. Use it for the list of studies, the figures it reports for each (cite the primary study where it can be read), and the author's statements of what is untested; do not use it for causes of severe overheating.

key_findings.finding: Method: the author scrutinised a personal collection of MDMA papers and then searched PubMed using thermal key words; laboratory and real-world studies were grouped separately. No search string, dates or selection rules are given.

Placebo-controlled laboratory studies (4 to 16 volunteers each): peak core temperature change by dose tier averaged +0.1 degrees Celsius up to 1.0 mg/kg (rows -0.1 to +0.3), +0.4 at 1.1-1.9 mg/kg (rows +0.3 to +0.5) and +0.7 at 2.0 mg/kg (rows +0.4 to +1.0); the highest tier is 14 people in two studies by the same three authors, each tested at two room temperatures. The tier means are unweighted and use oral, axillary, ear and swallowed sensors.

Room temperature: in the two laboratory studies that tested 18 and 30 degrees Celsius, MDMA raised core temperature by +1.0 and +0.8 (4 people) and +0.4 and +0.6 (10 people, swallowed sensor); the review reads the overall effects as broadly similar in both conditions. MDMA also raised metabolic rate and delayed the start of sweating.
key_findings.locator: Section 2, paragraphs beginning 'Tancer et al. (2003) tested four volunteers' (p. 2) and 'The next study comprised the most comprehensive' (p. 3); Section 6, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 6)

key_findings.finding: Variation between people: in an 8-person laboratory study the group mean rise was +0.4 degrees but one volunteer rose +1.9; blood MDMA correlated with the temperature rise (p<0.0001). At a dance party the two of 27 people with the highest blood levels (0.77 and 0.84 mg/l) had the largest rises (+1.0 and +1.6), with a borderline correlation overall (r=+0.38, p=0.058).
key_findings.locator: Section 2, last paragraph (pp. 3-4); Section 3, 1st paragraph (p. 4); Section 8, 1st paragraph (p. 7); Table 3, row 'MDMA plasma level' (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Party and club studies, peak temperature change: +0.2 degrees (27 people, no control), +1.2 against clubbers who had never taken it (32 people), +0.3 (12 people, on against off MDMA), +1.6 (11 people, 6 tablets on average over the night, against a weekend without), +1.1 oral and +1.8 skin (41 people, 1 to 5 tablets; 25% had blood levels the paper reports as in the toxic to lethal range by forensic guidelines, and the high doses were generally well tolerated, with enjoyment).

Hospital series and cases of severe overheating: a woman at 41.6 degrees Celsius two hours after taking MDMA powder found to be pure with no other substance, who survived (a friend who took the same powder had no reaction); a 16-year-old who died after one tablet, her second time, with blood MDMA 0.424 mg/l and no other drug; she was one of seven deaths with temperatures of 40-43 degrees in United Kingdom poisons-unit enquiries of 1990-91, where blood MDMA ranged from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, which the original authors said did not reflect high dose levels, and where the most severe cases showed overheating, widespread clotting, muscle breakdown and acute kidney failure; 332 emergency admissions to one London hospital over three years, with core temperatures on arrival from 34.1 to 41.6 degrees.
key_findings.locator: Section 4, 2nd-3rd paragraphs (p. 5); 5th paragraph beginning 'Following the early case studies' (p. 5); paragraph beginning 'Halpern et al. (2011) described' (pp. 5-6)

key_findings.finding: Thermal self-ratings: in an Internet survey of over 200 people 16% said they did not feel hot on MDMA, 41% slightly, 31% moderately and 12% strongly or extremely; in the laboratory study with a warm room there was no significant overall drug effect on the ratings, though feeling warm rose 2 to 4 hours after MDMA. One woman at a club shivered and felt cold while her temperature was unchanged. The author suggests, as a hypothesis for study, that people with low thermal awareness might be most at risk of severe overheating because they may not cool down.
key_findings.locator: Section 5, 1st-2nd paragraphs (p. 6); Section 7, paragraph beginning 'An important question' (p. 7); Section 8, 2nd paragraph (p. 8)

key_findings.finding: Factors the review lists as possibly raising thermal stress: higher single doses or repeated binge doses, prolonged dancing, crowded and hot clubs, other stimulants, low thermal awareness; and as lowering it: rests and cooler places, possibly cannabis. In its own Table 3 it notes that crowding and loud music have not been investigated, that data on dancing and on other drugs are very limited, and that age, gender, genetics, hydration and personality need study. Hydration is called a contributory factor in animals that needs testing in people.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, rows 'Dance clubs: prolonged dancing' to 'Other factors' (p. 4); Section 7, paragraph beginning 'An important question' (p. 7)

key_findings.finding: In one sentence the review says that low blood sodium arises when a person drinks too much water as a reaction against feeling too hot, and describes it as dilution of sodium and potassium; no data are given.
key_findings.locator: Section 4, paragraph beginning 'to 1.26 mg/l' (right column, 1st paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Overview: the author concludes that MDMA is clearly a thermal stressor in people; laboratory studies found a dose-related rise (minimal at low doses, about +0.4 at moderate and +0.7 at higher doses), and party studies a wider spread, possibly due to dosing or bingeing, lifetime use, dancing, environment and other drugs.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3, row 'Ambient temperature', says that in the laboratory high ambient temperature was associated with higher core body temperature, with complex combined effects. The text reports the opposite for the two studies that varied it: nearly identical core temperatures under both conditions (Tancer et al.: +1.0 at 18 and +0.8 at 30 degrees) and effects broadly similar (Freedman et al.: +0.4 and +0.6).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table row overstates a laboratory effect of room temperature; the text is the better guide, and it rests on 14 people.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 gives 16 volunteers for Liechti et al. (2000b); the text says 14.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small inconsistency in a sample size.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 lists ear (tympanic) temperature for Tancer et al. (2003), but the text says core temperature was measured with rectal probes.
reporting_issues.consequence: The body site of the highest-dose rows is unclear; it matters because sites differ in accuracy.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 is headed as an overview of placebo-controlled studies, but the text describes the first study (Grob et al., 1996) as comparing post-drug sessions with baseline sessions, and the dose tiers mix doses given as mg/kg and as fixed mg, with oral, axillary, ear and swallowed sensors.
reporting_issues.consequence: The tier means, which carry the 'dose related' conclusion, are unweighted averages of unlike measurements.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 puts three different things under one heading, peak temperature change: change from the person's own baseline (Irvine et al.; Morefield et al.), difference from people who had never taken ecstasy at the same club (Parrott and Young), and difference between a weekend with and a weekend without MDMA (Parrott et al., 2007b and 2008). The +0.3 for Parrott et al. (2008) is not stated in the text, which gives -0.2 on the weekend without MDMA, +0.15 with it, and a borderline difference (p=0.08).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures in Table 2 cannot be ranked against one another; the spread from +0.2 to +1.6 reflects different comparisons as well as different parties.

reporting_issues.issue: The two largest party-based rises in ear temperature (+1.6 and +1.2) come from the review author's own small studies (11 and 32 people), one against a non-using comparison group and one against a weekend without MDMA; the next (+1.1 oral, +1.8 skin) is cited as a single page (Neuropsychobiology 60:216), which suggests an abstract. Tancer et al. (2003) is a conference abstract.
reporting_issues.consequence: Peak party temperatures rest on small, partly unreviewed reports.

reporting_issues.issue: The severity bands from Grunau et al. are printed with reversed signs: severe as '<40.0' and extreme as '<42.0' degrees Celsius, where above is meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: A printing error; the thresholds are above 40 and above 42 degrees.

reporting_issues.issue: Hyponatraemia is described as dilution of sodium and potassium; the condition is a low blood sodium. The sentence cites a hospital series and gives no data.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cannot be used for anything about low sodium; the primary papers should be read instead.

reporting_issues.issue: No search string, dates, databases other than PubMed, inclusion rules or count of papers screened are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: Completeness cannot be judged; a study that did not find an effect may be missing.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1-9 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2012_MDMAAndTemperature.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3, funding and the reference list (read for the conference abstracts); Tables 1 and 2 and the Irvine paragraph were checked against rendered images of printed pages 3 and 4, and the Grunau thresholds against a rendered image of page 6.

design_detail: Review of records in the California Poison Control System (CPCS) database, a 24-hour emergency telephone consultation service, for calls coded ecstasy, MDMA, methylenedioxymethamphetamine or XTC from 1 January 2000 to 9 October 2005. The paper labels the design three ways: a retrospective review (abstract), a 'nonconcurrent, prospective, observational case series' (Methods, p. 165) and a 'retrospective observational case series' (Limitations, p. 168). CPCS staff recorded what the treating hospital reported by telephone; no hospital records were obtained. Two authors reviewed every case; three authors abstracted, on a standard form, the cases with a documented sodium (a number or 'normal') and all cases with a seizure. Women and men were compared with univariate logistic regression, and for sodium values below 130 mmol/L with a Wilcoxon test and a mean difference (pp. 165-167).
can_establish: What 545 reported ecstasy-related poisoning calls to one poison-control system looked like; how many of the 188 with a recorded sodium had a level below 130 mmol/L (73), how women and men compared among those 188, and what happened to the people with low sodium (seizure, coma, intensive care, death), including the 4 deaths among them.
cannot_establish: How common low sodium is among people who take MDMA (the denominator is calls to a poison-control system, and a sodium level was recorded for only about a third); whether women are more likely than men to develop it (testing was not random, no adjustment was made, and fluid, weight, kidney function and the amount of MDMA are not reported); whether MDMA caused each case (no gas-chromatography confirmation, and 35 of 103 people with a drug screen were negative for amphetamines); the part played by fluid, heat or dancing (not recorded); or whether sex changes how low sodium affects coma or seizure (no interaction test, and the intervals for women and men overlap).

sample.recruitment: All records in the CPCS database coded as ecstasy, MDMA, methylenedioxymethamphetamine or XTC (by code or free text), 1 January 2000 to 9 October 2005: 1,436 cases after duplicates were removed. Excluded: 267 managed at home; 616 by outcome code (29 'no effect', 63 'unrelated', 2 'confirmed non-exposure', 3 'judged nontoxic', 167 'minimal clinical effects possible', 352 'unable to follow - potentially toxic'); 5 on manual review with no MDMA exposure (miscoded); 3 with no sex recorded. 545 were included (Methods, pp. 165-166; Results, p. 166; Figure 1, p. 167).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Any ecstasy exposure with an outcome known and some effect; information-only calls and cases managed at home excluded; co-ingestions allowed; no age limit (Methods, pp. 165-166).
sample.demographics: 296 women (54.3%) and 249 men (45.7%); mean age 21.2 years (SD 6.8); the same mean and SD (21.2, 6.76) are printed for women and for men in Table 1 (p. 167).
sample.attrition: 357 of 545 (65.5%) had no documented sodium; of the 188 that did, 134 had a number and 54 were recorded only as 'normal' (Results, p. 166; Limitations, p. 169).
sample.selection_effects: Voluntary calls from hospitals and the public, so a passive surveillance source. A sodium was recorded for 35% of women and 33% of men, so the comparison of women and men is among those a clinician chose to test. The authors say referral bias may make the series represent the more severe cases (Limitations, pp. 168-169).

exposure.measurement: History of use as recorded by CPCS staff. A urine drug screen was documented in 103 of the 188 people with a recorded sodium (68 positive and 35 negative for amphetamines or derivatives); the type of assay was not recorded; no gas chromatography-mass spectrometry was reported; the 35 negative cases were counted as MDMA cases from the history (Results, p. 166; Limitations, p. 169).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported: the amount of MDMA and the amount of fluid drunk are not given. 'Rave party' is recorded as the site of use for 50 of 545 (9.1%), including 3 of the 74 low-sodium cases (4.1%) (Results, p. 166).
exposure.polysubstance: Co-ingestion was allowed. Of 103 urine screens, 35 (34%) were also positive for another drug, most often cocaine, tetrahydrocannabinol and benzodiazepines (Results, p. 166).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: Within the 188 with a recorded sodium: women against men for sodium below 130 mmol/L (55 of 105 against 18 of 83); and, within each sex, people with low sodium against those without (55 against 50 women; 18 against 65 men) for seizure, coma, tachycardia, agitation, hyperthermia and death (Results, pp. 167-168; Tables 2 and 3).
comparison.matching: None; univariate analysis only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Body size, kidney function, hydration and fluid intake, amount of MDMA, time since use, heat and exertion, other drugs. The authors list body habitus, renal function, hydration, co-ingestions and behavioural factors (Limitations, p. 169).

outcomes.instruments: Serum sodium as measured at the referring hospital and relayed by telephone; seizure, tachycardia, agitation, hyperthermia, coma, intensive care admission and death from the CPCS record (codes and free text).
outcomes.validity_norms: Low sodium is defined as below 130 mmol/L; hyperthermia, coma and seizure are not defined; no attempt was made to confirm sodium values from hospital records (Methods of Measurement, p. 166).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary outcome: sodium below 130 mmol/L among people with an ecstasy exposure and a documented sodium. Secondary: seizures, tachycardia, agitation, hyperthermia, coma and death among those with a documented sodium (Outcome Measures, p. 166).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 13 odds ratios are reported (1 for sex and low sodium; 6 outcomes in each sex), plus a Wilcoxon test of sodium values; formal tests were limited to the a priori sex hypothesis (Primary Data Analysis, p. 166).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None; two authors reviewed each case and three abstracted the detailed cases, with disagreements settled by discussion and inter-rater reliability not formally tested (Data Collection, p. 166).

analysis.effect_sizes: Of 545: 296 women, 249 men. Documented sodium in 188 (34.5%); sodium below 130 mmol/L in 73 (abstract, Table 2), 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%); odds ratio for female sex 3.97 (95% CI 2.08-7.59). Median sodium among those with low sodium 122 mmol/L (25th-75th percentile 119-124). Within each sex, low sodium against none, odds ratios: coma women 3.93 (1.20-12.90), men 0.78 (0.15-3.97); seizure women 4.38 (1.74-11.00), men 2.21 (0.69-7.07); tachycardia women 0.33 (0.14-0.81), men 0.13 (0.04-0.51); agitation women 0.41 (0.17-0.98), men 1.3 (0.43-4.00); hyperthermia women 0.58 (0.15-2.17), men 0.29 (0.04-2.40); death women 1.39 (0.22-8.65), men 1.85 (0.16-21.70). Deaths 13 of 545 (2.4%), 4 among the people with low sodium (3 women, 1 man), all 4 with brain swelling on CT scan and low blood pressure needing drugs to support it. Among all 545: tachycardia 43%, agitation 32%, seizure 11%, hyperthermia 40 (7.3%), intensive care 153 (28%).
analysis.selective_reporting: The sex hypothesis is described as a priori. All six secondary outcomes are reported in both sexes. The Discussion stresses the coma and seizure odds ratios in women, although their intervals overlap those in men and no test of a difference is given.
analysis.power: No power calculation. Several cells are small, for example 4 deaths among the 73 with low sodium, giving very wide intervals (death in men 1.85, 0.16-21.70).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 188 people with a recorded sodium after a reported ecstasy exposure, 73 had a level below 130 mmol/L, 55 of 105 women (about 52 in 100) and 18 of 83 men (about 22 in 100); the odds of low sodium were about four times higher in women (3.97, 2.08-7.59). Among women, those with low sodium had higher odds of coma and seizure than those without (3.93 and 4.38); among men the intervals included no difference (0.78 and 2.21), but the intervals for women and men overlap. 4 of the 73 with low sodium died, all with brain swelling on CT. Everything is unadjusted and rests on a third of cases having a sodium recorded.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says female sex was associated with increased odds of low sodium and of low-sodium-associated coma, and that confounders prevent any statement about cause. The Editor's Capsule says women were 'four times more likely' (52 in 100 against 22 in 100 is about 2.4 times; the 4 is an odds ratio), and the Discussion says the study 'provides support that such a sex difference does indeed exist' and that the pattern could fit sex acting as an effect modifier, which no interaction test examines.

timeline.event: Low sodium with catatonic stupor after ecstasy (Maxwell and colleagues; reference 18 of this paper).
Near-fatal coma with raised vasopressin after ecstasy (Holden and Jackson; reference 20), as cited by this paper.
Rise in vasopressin with a fall in sodium in healthy, normally hydrated men given MDMA (Henry and colleagues; reference 25), as cited by this paper; not read here.
28-month series of 17 people from a UK poisons service, 10 of them women, 2 deaths (both women).

Series of 18 people with low sodium after ecstasy, 17 of them women (Budisavljevic and colleagues), and a 3-month Israeli series of 32 emergency patients with 3 low-sodium cases, 2 of them women (Ben-Abraham and colleagues), both as cited by this paper; not read here.
This review: 545 California poison-centre reports, 73 with a recorded low sodium, 4 deaths among them.
Narrative review that tabulates published cases of low sodium after ecstasy, including rows from this series.

replication.where_it_stands: Low sodium after MDMA with seizures and brain swelling has been seen in poison-centre and hospital series on two continents and in many case reports. All are selected reports of people who became ill; none compares people who drank a large amount with people who did not. The sex difference rests on this one study (among people who were tested) and on the mostly female make-up of case reports (17 of 18 in one earlier series, 10 of 17 in another), which reflects who was reported rather than who is at risk.

funding.funder: No funder for the study is stated. One author (Blanc) was supported in part by a National Institute on Drug Abuse grant (DA 14935).
funding.declared_conflicts: None printed in the PDF.
funding.affiliations_note: Emergency physicians and toxicologists at California hospitals and universities; several authors work for the California Poison Control System, whose records are analysed.

what_would_settle_it: A sodium measured on arrival in every person presenting after MDMA (not only those a clinician chose to test), with laboratory-confirmed MDMA, recorded fluid intake, body weight, time since use and setting, and an analysis adjusted for these that tests whether sex changes the link between low sodium and coma or seizure.

domains.note: Univariate analysis only; no fluid intake, MDMA amount, body size, kidney function, heat or exertion, so women and men (and people with and without low sodium) differ in unmeasured ways.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Voluntary calls; a sodium was recorded for only 34.5%, and who was tested is not random; 352 potentially toxic cases 'unable to follow' were set aside.
MDMA exposure by history; urine screen in 103 of 188, 35 negative for amphetamines and still counted; no confirmatory assay.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Not a trial; treatment not the subject.
No sodium recorded for 65.5% of cases; 54 of the 188 recorded only as 'normal'; timing of the sodium not consistent.
Sodium values relayed by telephone and never checked against hospital records; coma, seizure and hyperthermia not defined.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Sex hypothesis stated in advance and all secondary outcomes shown, but the interpretation leans on the women-only coma and seizure odds ratios and the text and tables disagree on several counts.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A retrospective, unadjusted analysis of voluntary telephone reports, appraised with ROBINS-I as the library does for other case series. Cite it for what these 545 reports and the 73 low-sodium cases looked like and for the unadjusted women-against-men counts among those tested; do not cite it for how common low sodium is, for risk by sex, or for cause.

key_findings.finding: Source and method: the CPCS is a 24-hour emergency telephone service; staff recorded what callers reported; sodium levels were measured at the referring hospitals and recorded as reported by telephone, with no attempt to confirm them from hospital records; two authors reviewed each case and three abstracted the cases with a sodium (numeric or 'normal') and all cases with a seizure; inter-rater reliability was not formally tested.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 'Study Design and Setting', 'Data Collection and Processing', 'Methods of Measurement'

key_findings.finding: Selection: 1,436 cases identified; 545 included after excluding 267 managed at home, 616 by outcome code, 5 miscoded and 3 without sex. A serum sodium was documented in 188 (34.5%): 105 of 296 women (35%) and 83 of 249 men (33%); 134 as a number and 54 as 'normal'. 357 (65.5%) had no sodium recorded.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph and 'Characteristics of Study Subjects' (p. 166); Figure 1 (p. 167)

key_findings.finding: Main comparison among the 188: sodium below 130 mmol/L in 73, 55 of 105 women (52.4%) and 18 of 83 men (21.7%); odds ratio for female sex 3.97 (95% CI 2.08-7.59). Among the 115 without low sodium, 50 were women and 65 men. The median sodium among those with low sodium was 122 mmol/L (25th-75th percentile 119-124).

Within each sex, low sodium against none (unadjusted odds ratios, Table 3): coma women 3.93 (1.20-12.90), men 0.78 (0.15-3.97); seizure women 4.38 (1.74-11.00), men 2.21 (0.69-7.07); tachycardia women 0.33 (0.14-0.81), men 0.13 (0.04-0.51); agitation women 0.41 (0.17-0.98), men 1.3 (0.43-4.00); hyperthermia women 0.58 (0.15-2.17), men 0.29 (0.04-2.40); death women 1.39 (0.22-8.65), men 1.85 (0.16-21.70). Low sodium was linked to lower odds of tachycardia in both sexes; the authors call the reason unclear.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 and the paragraph below it; Discussion, last paragraph (p. 171)

key_findings.finding: Deaths: 13 of 545 (2.4%). 4 occurred among the people with low sodium (3 women, 1 man): all had a urine test positive for amphetamines or derivatives (1 specifically for MDMA), low blood pressure needing drugs to support it, and brain swelling confirmed by CT; 2 had seizures, 1 presented with a body temperature of 34.4 degrees Celsius and 2 had fluid on the lungs. Of the 9 deaths without low sodium (6 women, 3 men): 5 had asystole or ventricular fibrillation, 3 hyperthermia, 1 severe acidosis with brain death and 2 fatal bleeding in the head (categories overlap).
key_findings.locator: Results, last two paragraphs (left and right columns)

key_findings.finding: Among all 545: tachycardia 232 (42.6%), agitation 174 (31.9%), coma 54 (9.9%), seizure 61 (11.2%), hyperthermia 40 (7.3%; women 16, men 24), intensive care 153 (28.1%), death 13 (2.4%). 'Rave party' was recorded as the site of use for 50 (9.1%), including 3 of the 74 low-sodium cases (4.1%).

MDMA confirmation: urine drug screening was documented in 103 of the 188 (54.8%); 68 positive and 35 (34%) negative for amphetamines or derivatives, and the 35 were still counted as MDMA cases from the history; 35 were also positive for another drug (cocaine, THC and benzodiazepines most often). Among the 73 with low sodium, 43 had a drug screen, 39 positive and 4 negative. No gas chromatography-mass spectrometry was reported and the assay type was not recorded. The paper reports neither the amount of MDMA nor fluid intake.

The authors' own limits: passive surveillance subject to reporting bias; telephone-recorded data; referral bias that may make the series represent more severe cases; MDMA unconfirmed in a large share; no sodium in 65.5% of cases; timing of the sodium not consistent; low sodium may be a mild, self-correcting process in some people; and confounders (body habitus, kidney function, hydration, co-ingestions, behaviour) prevent attributing cause.

Discussion, as hypotheses: sex hormones (estrogen) may shape vasopressin release and the brain's response to low sodium; cited evidence is from rats, from postoperative patients, from a 1998 letter on vasopressin in eight healthy men and from case reports, all second-hand. The authors say women were no more or less likely to have a sodium test (35% against 33%) and that confounders preclude any definitive statement on the nature and mechanisms of the sex difference.

reporting_issues.issue: The count of low-sodium cases differs: 73 (38.8% of 188) in the abstract, Table 2 and Table 3, against 74 (39.4%) in the Results text, and '3 of the 74' for the rave-party figure.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 73, which agrees with the sex counts (55 + 18) and the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Women's share of the 545 is 54.3% in the abstract and Table 1 but 54.6% (and men 45.4%) in the text; 296 of 545 is 54.3%.
reporting_issues.consequence: Small printing error in the text.

reporting_issues.issue: Deaths by sex: Table 1 gives 8 women and 5 men (13 in all), but the Results text (3 women and 1 man with low sodium; 6 women and 3 men without) and the appendix list of the 13 deaths give 9 women and 4 men.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex split of the 13 deaths is uncertain; the paper's own sources disagree.

reporting_issues.issue: The odds ratio for seizure in men with low sodium is 2.11 in the text but 2.21 in Table 3; the confidence interval (0.69-7.07) is centred on 2.21.
reporting_issues.consequence: Use 2.21 from Table 3.

reporting_issues.issue: The sentence giving medians of 124 mmol/L for women and 137 mmol/L for men (all quantified values, Figure 2) is followed by a Wilcoxon P of .77 and a mean sex difference of 0.07 mmol/L (-2.2 to 2.1). These cannot describe the same values; the Methods say the comparison was for values below 130 mmol/L.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sentence is unclear; the medians say nothing about the size of the fall in those with low sodium. Do not quote the two medians as a sex difference in sodium.

reporting_issues.issue: The Editor's Capsule says women were 4 times more likely to have low sodium. The proportions (about 52 in 100 against 22 in 100) give a ratio of about 2.4; the 4 is an odds ratio.
reporting_issues.consequence: Report the proportions first; do not describe the odds ratio as 'times more likely'.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods list the outcome codes excluded but not 'unable to follow - potentially toxic', which the Results and Figure 1 show as the largest coded exclusion (352 of 1,436 cases, about one in four).
reporting_issues.consequence: A quarter of all calls were set aside by a rule not described in the Methods; whether they were more or less severe is not known.

reporting_issues.issue: The design is called a retrospective review in the abstract, a 'nonconcurrent, prospective, observational case series' in the Methods and a retrospective observational case series in the Limitations.
reporting_issues.consequence: It is a retrospective analysis of a database that was kept prospectively; no protocol or registration is described.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says the pattern could be consistent with sex acting as an effect modifier, but no test of interaction is reported and the intervals for women and men overlap (coma 1.20-12.90 against 0.15-3.97).
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding that low sodium is linked to coma 'in women but not in men' is not shown as a difference between women and men.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the same mean age and SD (21.2, 6.76) for women and for men; coma, seizure, hyperthermia and tachycardia are not defined.
reporting_issues.consequence: Probable copying error in Table 1; outcome definitions cannot be checked.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 164-171.e1 (PDFs/MDMA/Rosenson_2007_HyponatremiaCalifornia.pdf), full text including Tables 1-3, Figures 1-2, Limitations, Discussion, references and Appendix E1. Tables 1-3 and the less-than sign in the sodium definition (lost in the text layer) were checked on renders; Appendix E1 was used only to check the sex of the 13 deaths and is not cited in any claim.

design_detail: Pooled analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover phase I studies run in one laboratory at the University Hospital Basel: seven studies of 16 people each who took 125 mg MDMA twice, once alone and once after a pretreatment medicine (112 people); one unpublished study of 24 people who took 125 mg once; and one study of 30 people who took 75 mg once. At least seven days separated sessions. Only the sessions of MDMA alone against placebo are analysed in the paper (166 MDMA sessions); the 112 pretreatment sessions are in a supplement. Analysis: repeated-measures analyses of variance with drug (MDMA against placebo, within person), dose (75 against 125 mg, between people) and sex; Fisher's exact tests for the share of people crossing a clinical line; paired t tests of kidney, liver and blood-count tests at screening against an end-of-study visit. The two doses were given in different studies to different people, so the 75 against 125 mg contrast is between studies and was not randomised.
can_establish: What one oral dose of MDMA did, against placebo in the same people, to blood pressure, heart rate, ear temperature, self-rated drug effects and complaints in 166 healthy young adults sitting at rest in a hospital research unit with a research assistant present; how many of them crossed common clinical lines (systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg, heart rate above 100 a minute, temperature above 38 degrees Celsius); and that creatinine, estimated kidney filtration and liver enzymes were unchanged on average about a month later. It also records how 141 of the 166 rated the overall experience, and whether they would consider taking MDMA again, when asked at the end of the study.
cannot_establish: What happens when people dance, are in a hot or crowded place, drink little or a lot, take other drugs, take pills of unknown content or take further doses (all absent by design); risks in people with heart disease or mental health conditions (excluded); how often rare events (under 1 in 100) such as a temperature above 40 degrees Celsius occur (the authors' own calculation allows up to 1.3% for no event in 278 sessions); anything about blood sodium (not measured); changes in the kidney in the hours and days after a dose (blood was taken about a month later); and a dose-response for temperature or heart rate that is not mixed up with differences between studies. Why people take MDMA or what they seek from it: the volunteers did not choose the dose or the setting, four in five were new to MDMA, and their answers about taking it again come after one or two hospital sessions.

sample.recruitment: Mostly recruited from the University of Basel campus and paid for taking part (Methods > Subjects, 1st paragraph, p. 577; Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph, p. 577).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy European or Caucasian adults aged 18-45, psychiatrically screened. Excluded: a history of psychiatric disorder or physical illness, illicit drug use on more than five occasions in a lifetime (past cannabis use allowed), illicit drug use in the past two months or during the study (urine tests before sessions); the detailed criteria are in the earlier papers of each study (Methods > Subjects, 1st-2nd paragraphs, p. 577).
sample.demographics: Age 24.5 (SD 4) years, body weight 69 (SD 10) kg (range 46-95), equal numbers of women and men (83 each). 59 people had used a drug 1-5 times before, of whom 34 had used MDMA 1-4 times; 80% were MDMA-naive (Methods > Subjects, p. 577; Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph, p. 582).
sample.attrition: Not described for the pooled sample. Two people lacked kidney and liver tests and five lacked blood counts at the end-of-study visit (Table 4 footnotes, p. 583); four people reported no subjective effect and were left out of the timing analysis (Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph, p. 578); 141 of 166 answered the end-of-study questions (Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit, p. 578).
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy, paid volunteers, screened for illness and drug use, mostly new to MDMA. People with heart disease or psychiatric illness are absent by design, and the authors say so (Discussion > limitations paragraph, p. 585). A sample chosen to be healthy cannot show who is more at risk.

exposure.measurement: Dose given by the study team as gelatin capsules of MDMA hydrochloride from a pharmaceutical supplier; peak plasma MDMA and the area under the curve to 6 hours were measured in every person (Methods > Study drug, pp. 577-578; Methods > Plasma concentrations of MDMA, p. 578; Table 1, p. 581).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: oral MDMA 75 mg (30 people) or 125 mg (136 people), once or, in 112 people, twice at least seven days apart (once alone, once after a pretreatment medicine). Doses were not adjusted for weight: dose per body weight averaged 1.7 (SD 0.4) mg/kg overall, with 125 mg working out at 1.7 (SD 0.2) in men and 2.1 (SD 0.3) in women (Methods > Study drug, p. 578).
exposure.polysubstance: No illicit drug use in the two months before or during the study, checked by urine tests before sessions; the sessions with a pretreatment medicine are excluded from the main analysis (Methods > Subjects, 2nd paragraph, p. 577; Methods > Study design, p. 577).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least two months free of illicit drugs by history, with a urine screen before each session; at least seven days between sessions (Methods > Study design and Subjects, p. 577).

comparison.controls: Placebo session in each study, in the same people (double-blind crossover). For the dose comparison, the 30 people given 75 mg and the 136 given 125 mg are different people in different studies.
comparison.matching: Within-person for MDMA against placebo. Between the dose groups there is no matching and no randomisation; the paper does not report whether the order of sessions was randomised or counterbalanced in each study (the original reports hold that).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable for MDMA against placebo, which is within person. For the dose comparison, differences between the studies are unmeasured: the placebo sessions of the 75 mg study averaged a highest ear temperature of 37.0 degrees Celsius and those of the 125 mg studies 37.4 (Table 2, p. 582), and the 75 mg study lacked two temperature time points.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded by screening and urine tests.

outcomes.instruments: Blood pressure and heart rate by automatic oscillometric device, in duplicate one minute apart after at least 10 minutes' rest; core (ear, tympanic) temperature by a two-ear infrared thermometer; each at 0, 0.33, 0.67, 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 4, 5 and 6 hours; visual analogue scales for any, good and bad drug effect; the 66-item List of Complaints at 3-6 and 24 hours; adverse events from 24 hours to 14 days; kidney and liver tests (creatinine, Cockcroft-Gault estimated filtration, enzymes) and blood counts at screening and an end-of-study visit; an end-of-study questionnaire (Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, p. 578; Blood sampling and EOS visit, p. 578).
outcomes.validity_norms: Clinical thresholds: systolic pressure above 140, 160 and 180 mm Hg and diastolic above 90, 100 and 110 for grades I-III of hypertension, heart rate above 100 a minute for tachycardia, temperature above 38 and 40 degrees Celsius for hyperthermia and hyperpyrexia (Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 3rd paragraph, p. 578). Ear temperature is a convenient, not a reference, measure of core temperature; the paper does not discuss its accuracy.
outcomes.operationalization: Table 2 takes each person's highest value in the 6 hours and reports the average of these highest values and the number of people whose highest value crossed each line, so the shares are shares of people who crossed a line at least once. The more readings are taken, the likelier one crosses a line.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated for the many comparisons (editors' count of 60: Table 1, 8; Table 2, 15; Table 3, 28 complaint comparisons; Table 4, 9 blood tests); Tukey post hoc tests followed significant analysis-of-variance effects; significance was set at p<0.05 throughout (Methods > Statistical analyses, p. 578).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind in design. The paper does not report whether people or staff could tell MDMA from placebo, which with 125 mg is likely. Blood pressure, pulse and temperature are device readings; drug effects and complaints are self-ratings.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2 (p. 582), average of each person's highest value, MDMA against placebo. 125 mg (n=136): systolic 157 (SD 15) against 133 (15) mm Hg; diastolic 93 (10) against 79 (8); heart rate 95 (17) against 76 (12) beats a minute; temperature 37.7 (0.5) against 37.4 (0.5) degrees Celsius. People above each line, MDMA against placebo: systolic >160 51 (38%) against 8 (6%); >180 7 (5%) against 0; heart rate >100 45 (33%) against 3 (2%); temperature >38 32 (24%) against 12 (9%). Highest single values 196 against 175 mm Hg systolic, 145 against 117 beats a minute, 39.1 against 38.7 degrees. 75 mg (n=30): systolic 145 (14) against 131 (11); diastolic 84 (8) against 77 (5); heart rate 83 (17) against 69 (9); temperature 37.2 (0.3) against 37.0 (0.3); above the lines: systolic >160 3 (10%) against 0; heart rate >100 3 (10%) against 0; temperature >38 0 against 0. Over all 166: systolic >160 in 54 (33%), >180 in 7 (4%), heart rate >100 in 48 (29%), temperature >38 in 32 (19%), highest 39.1 degrees; no temperature above 40 and no hypertensive urgency (Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, p. 580). Drug effect on every vital sign F >44, p<0.001; drug-by-dose interaction significant for systolic (F 15.2) and diastolic (F 17.9) pressure and not for heart rate (F 2.38) or temperature (F 2.43). Editors' calculation: at 125 mg, extra people above the line with MDMA against placebo 32 in 100 for systolic >160, 31 in 100 for heart rate >100 and 15 in 100 for temperature >38.
analysis.covariates: Sex and dose as factors; dose per body weight and peak plasma MDMA entered as covariates to test whether sex differences were due to dose per kilogram or blood level (Methods > Statistical analyses, p. 578).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Each of the nine studies is listed with a ClinicalTrials.gov number (NCT00886886, NCT00990067, NCT01136278, NCT01270672, NCT01386177, NCT01465685, NCT01771874, NCT01951508, NCT01616407); the pooled safety analysis is not described as preregistered (Methods > Study design, p. 577).
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract gives the shares above each line for MDMA only, without the 9% of placebo sessions at 125 mg that also crossed 38 degrees Celsius, and says all three shares were greater at 125 than at 75 mg, while the dose-by-drug tests for heart rate and temperature are not significant. The pretreatment sessions are in a supplement that was not read. About 60 outcomes were tested without correction.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors call 166 a large sample next to earlier laboratory studies of 6-30 people, and state that it cannot rule out events at 0.1-1% or below; for no temperature above 40 degrees in 278 sessions the binomial upper bound is 1.3% (Introduction, p. 577; Discussion > limitations paragraph, p. 585).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 166 healthy volunteers sitting in a laboratory at about 22.7 degrees Celsius, a single dose of 75 or 125 mg raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo. At 125 mg, 38 in 100 reached a systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg (6 in 100 on placebo), 33 in 100 a heart rate above 100 (2 in 100) and 24 in 100 a temperature above 38 degrees (9 in 100); the highest values were 196 mm Hg and 39.1 degrees, with no hypertensive urgency and no temperature above 40. Dry mouth, loss of appetite, trouble concentrating, sweating and jaw clenching were common; creatinine, estimated filtration and liver enzymes did not change on average at about a month; women gave higher bad-drug-effect ratings and reported more complaints. Blood sodium was not measured. Asked at the end of the study, 95 of 141 volunteers (67%) called the overall experience positive, 25 (18%) neutral and 21 (15%) disappointing or bad.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusion say MDMA was overall safe in physically and psychiatrically healthy subjects in a medical setting, that all three shares above the lines were significantly greater at 125 than at 75 mg, and that risks are likely higher in people with cardiovascular disease. The Conclusion also recommends a fixed dose for women; that recommendation rests on comparing different studies (30 against 136 people) and is not reproduced here. The Discussion also says the study showed clearly greater positive than negative acute subjective effects, that psychological distress was minimal and that there were no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks; no measure of distress other than the 'bad drug effect' rating and the one-item anxiety complaint is reported.
