timeline.event: Earlier analysis of laboratory studies in 74 volunteers from the same group (Liechti et al.), as cited by these authors: systolic pressure at or above 160 mm Hg in 32% and at or above 180 in 9%.

An independent laboratory (Freedman et al.), as summarized in a narrative review: core temperature up 0.4 and 0.6 degrees Celsius in a cool and a warm room, in 10 volunteers given a weight-based dose.
An independent laboratory (Kolbrich et al.), as summarized in the same review: ear temperature up on average 0.3-0.4 degrees in 8 volunteers, not significant, with one person up 1.9.
Parrott's review gathers the human temperature studies and finds a dose-related rise in laboratory studies

replication.where_it_stands: A rise in blood pressure, heart rate and temperature after a single dose at rest is seen in this laboratory's nine studies and, as summarized second-hand in a review, by independent laboratories. The nine studies share site, team and methods, so they are one team's replication. The shares above each line for 75 against 125 mg rest on this paper alone.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation (grants 323230_126231, 32323B_144996 and 320030_149493) (Funding, p. 586).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared (Declaration of conflicting interests, p. 586).
funding.affiliations_note: University Hospital Basel and University of Basel; all nine studies come from the senior author's laboratory, which also ran the studies behind most of the papers it cites for comparison.

what_would_settle_it: A within-person comparison of two or more doses, order randomised, with every temperature taken at the same time points by the same method and a warm-room condition, plus blood sodium, creatinine and a muscle enzyme measured in the first day after dosing, and a sample that includes older people and people with a raised blood pressure at the start.

domains.note: Described as double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover; the sequence generation and any counterbalancing are not described in this paper and no period effect is reported.
At least seven days between sessions, which the authors judge enough to exclude carry-over.
With 125 mg and a 4-hour drug effect, blinding probably did not hold, and no check is reported; the main outcomes are device readings, which expectation affects little.

The 75 mg study lacks temperature at 0.33 and 2.5 hours and one 125 mg study (24 people) lacks it at 2 hours; the highest temperature came on average at 2.4 hours (SD 1.2), so a person's true peak may be missed, more often in the 75 mg group.

Ear temperature is an indirect measure; placebo sessions averaged 37.0 degrees in the 75 mg study and 37.4 in the 125 mg studies, and 9% of placebo sessions at 125 mg crossed 38 degrees, so the line is crossed by chance and by measurement.

The pooled analysis was not preregistered; about 60 outcomes were tested without correction; the abstract features threshold shares that favour a dose effect which the continuous tests for heart rate and temperature do not show.

domains.domain: Dose comparison, 75 against 125 mg (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Different people in different studies, not randomised, with different time points and placebo temperatures; every dose-response statement in the paper rests on this contrast.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The comparison of MDMA with placebo in the same people (the first six rows) is at some concerns at worst, and its effects on blood pressure and pulse are large (F 292-486) next to the sources of bias named. The overall judgment is set by the dose comparison, which is between studies and was not randomised. The source can be cited for what a single dose of 125 mg did to blood pressure, pulse and ear temperature against placebo in healthy volunteers at rest, for the highest values seen, and for unchanged kidney and liver tests about a month later; it should not be cited for how temperature or heart rate change between 75 and 125 mg, for settings with heat, activity or crowding, or for people who are not healthy.

key_findings.finding: Nine double-blind placebo-controlled crossover studies from one hospital in Basel were pooled: 166 healthy volunteers (83 women, 83 men), 75 mg in 30 people and 125 mg in 136; aged 18-45; 80% new to MDMA. Room temperature averaged 22.7 degrees Celsius (SD 0.6) and a research assistant was always present.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Study design and Subjects (p. 577); Figure 1 legend (p. 579); Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (p. 580); Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (p. 582); Discussion > paragraph beginning 'The present safety data' (p. 585)

key_findings.finding: MDMA alone raised blood pressure, heart rate and ear temperature above placebo. Of the 166, 54 (33%) reached a systolic pressure above 160 mm Hg and 7 (4%) above 180; 48 (29%) a heart rate above 100 a minute; 32 (19%) a temperature above 38 degrees Celsius, up to 39.1. There was no hypertensive urgency and no temperature above 40; the highest systolic and diastolic pressures were 196 and 130 mm Hg.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (left column to the top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: At 125 mg (n=136) the average of each person's highest reading was 157 mm Hg systolic (placebo 133), 93 diastolic (79), 95 beats a minute (76) and 37.7 degrees Celsius (37.4). The share above each line was 38% against 6% on placebo for systolic >160, 33% against 2% for heart rate >100 and 24% against 9% for temperature >38.

At 75 mg (n=30) the averages were 145 mm Hg systolic (placebo 131), 84 diastolic (77), 83 beats a minute (69) and 37.2 degrees Celsius (37.0); 3 people (10%) went above 160 systolic and 3 (10%) above 100 beats a minute, against none on placebo, and nobody was above 38 degrees on MDMA or on placebo.

Dose comparison: the drug-by-dose test was significant for systolic and diastolic pressure (F 15.2 and 17.9, p<0.001) but not for heart rate (F 2.38) or temperature (F 2.43); the shares above the lines were higher at 125 than at 75 mg (systolic >160 p<0.01, heart rate >100 p<0.05, temperature >38 p<0.01). The doses were given in different studies to different people.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph (p. 580); Table 2, columns 'Drug x dose' (p. 582)

key_findings.finding: Timing: effects began on average 33 minutes (SD 24) after the dose, peaked at 1.6 hours (SD 0.8) and lasted 4.2 hours (SD 1.3; range 1.4-8.2), with no difference in duration by dose or sex; the highest systolic pressure came at 1.7 hours (SD 0.9), the highest heart rate at 2.0 (SD 1.4) and the highest temperature at 2.4 (SD 1.2).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph; Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Ratings of any and good drug effect were higher at 125 than at 75 mg (good drug effect, highest rating out of 100, average: women 82 against 60, men 77 against 57); bad drug effect was not dose-dependent and was higher in women (24 at 125 mg and 35 at 75 mg) than in men (13 and 7). Four of the 166 reported no subjective effect at all and were left out of the timing analysis; the paper does not say which dose they had or what their blood pressure, pulse or temperature did.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph (p. 578); Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA (p. 580); Table 1 (p. 581)

key_findings.finding: Peak blood MDMA was on average 1.8 times higher after 125 than after 75 mg (224.1 against 124.5 ng/mL), more than the 1.67-fold dose increase, significant in women only; at 125 mg women had about 1.3 times the peak level of men.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, Cmax rows (p. 581); Results > Plasma concentrations of MDMA (p. 582)

key_findings.finding: Sex: no overall sex difference in vital signs; after allowing for the lower dose per kilogram in men, men showed the bigger rise in systolic pressure (F 6.08, p<0.05). Women reported more complaints (acute rise 8.8 against 6.4 points; the day after 5.4 against 3.0).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute effects of MDMA on vital signs, 1st paragraph; Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Most frequent acute complaints with MDMA (of 166), against placebo: lack of appetite 59%, dry mouth 55%, difficulty concentrating 46%, cold feet 42%, sweating 41%, jaw clenching 40% (of 134 asked), restless legs 37%, dizziness 34%, hot flushes 31%, palpitations 24%; no serious adverse event occurred.
key_findings.locator: Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 2nd paragraph (p. 580); Table 3 (p. 583)

key_findings.finding: Kidney and liver tests at screening against the end-of-study visit (29 days on average after the last dose, SD 22; 164 people): creatinine 74 (SD 13) against 73 (12) micromoles a litre, estimated filtration 122 (22) against 125 (24) mL a minute, neither significantly changed; liver enzymes AST and ALT unchanged; GGT 19 against 18 U/L (p<0.01). Red cells and haemoglobin fell and platelets rose, which the authors put down to 400-600 mL of blood taken for analysis.
key_findings.locator: Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit (p. 578); Results > Effects of MDMA on kidney and liver function, 1st paragraph (p. 582); Table 4 (p. 583); Discussion, paragraph beginning 'In the present study, MDMA did not influence' (p. 585)

key_findings.finding: The authors note that no controlled clinical study of MDMA has reported hyperpyrexia (above 40 degrees Celsius), possibly because participants took moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded environment, unlike some recreational settings. This is their suggestion, not a tested result.

Acute tolerance: the authors argue that subjective effects fall although blood MDMA stays high, so that adding more MDMA might not lengthen the effect and may add adverse effects; in their data the duration at 75 and 125 mg did not differ. This is an interpretation citing other studies.

Limits stated by the authors: kidney and liver tests only about a month later (short-lasting changes not excluded); sodium low after MDMA, which is frequently seen in intoxications, was not assessed; 278 sessions are too few to exclude events at 0.1-1% (no temperature above 40 degrees, binomial upper bound 1.3%); only healthy young people, and older people with cardiovascular risk factors may be treated in future.

Highest self-rating after the dose (Emax on a 0 to 100 line, mean (SD)), MDMA against placebo. Any drug effect: 125 mg women 85 (20) against 4 (8), men 73 (24) against 4 (13); 75 mg women 59 (29) against 3 (6), men 56 (32) against 6 (9). Good drug effect: 125 mg women 82 (25) against 3 (10), men 77 (23) against 4 (15); 75 mg women 60 (28) against 6 (13), men 57 (33) against 7 (12). Bad drug effect: 125 mg women 24 (24) against 2 (10), men 13 (22) against 2 (10); 75 mg women 35 (33) against 4 (13), men 7 (11) against 6 (16). Groups: 68 women and 68 men at 125 mg, 15 and 15 at 75 mg; drug effect F(1,162) 652, 585 and 44, p < 0.001 (the 125 and 75 mg groups are different people in different studies).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, rows 'Any drug effect', 'Good drug effect' and 'Bad drug effect'; Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 580)
key_findings.note: Read on a rendered image of the printed page; the means for men and women at each dose are as printed.

key_findings.finding: Tests on the self-ratings (F(1,162)): drug-by-dose for any drug effect F 20 (p < 0.001), good drug effect F 20 (printed p < 0.01) and bad drug effect F 0.001 (not significant); drug-by-sex for any drug effect F 3.4 (p = 0.068), good drug effect F 0.9 (not significant) and bad drug effect F 16 (p < 0.001); drug-by-dose-by-sex for bad drug effect F 3.6 (p = 0.059). Women gave higher bad-drug-effect ratings after MDMA than men, also after allowing for dose per kilogram (F 20.0, p < 0.001) and for blood MDMA level (F 21.5, p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns 'Drug x dose', 'Drug x sex' and 'Drug x dose x sex' (p. 581); Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 580)

key_findings.finding: Complaints on the List of Complaints up to 6 hours after the dose, MDMA against placebo, n (%) of 166: lack of appetite 98 (59%) against 3 (2%); dry mouth 91 (55%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 76 (46%) against 10 (6%); cold feet 69 (42%) against 7 (4%); sweating 68 (41%) against 0; jaw clenching 54 (40%, of 134 asked) against 1 (1%); restless legs 62 (37%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 57 (34%) against 2 (1%); hot flushes 52 (31%) against 0; heart palpitations 40 (24%) against 2 (1%); lack of energy 38 (23%) against 23 (14%); nausea 19 (11%) against 2 (1%); anxiety 9 (6%) against 0; headache 42 (25%) against 27 (16%, not significantly different). Both doses (75 and 125 mg) are pooled in this table.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, columns 'Acute, up to 6 h' (placebo and MDMA)
key_findings.note: Read on a rendered image of the printed page. The complaints were rated 3 to 6 hours after the dose for the period up to 6 hours.

key_findings.finding: Complaints 24 hours after the dose, MDMA against placebo, n (%) of 166: lack of appetite 52 (31%) against 1 (1%); dry mouth 37 (23%) against 3 (2%); difficulty concentrating 35 (22%) against 4 (2%); headache 55 (33%) against 25 (15%); lack of energy 49 (30%) against 5 (3%); jaw clenching 19 (14%) against 1 (1%); hot flushes 12 (7%) against 0; restless legs 12 (7%) against 2 (1%); dizziness 12 (7%) against 3 (2%); heart palpitations 11 (7%) against 1 (1%); cold feet 10 (6%) against 2 (1%); nausea 9 (6%) against 1 (1%); sweating 7 (4%) against 0; anxiety 3 (2%) against 0 (not significant). The authors name headache, lack of energy and lack of appetite as the most frequent at 24 hours.

No serious adverse event occurred. Acute anxiety on the List of Complaints was reported by 9 people (6%) after 125 mg and none after 75 mg. Adverse events reported from 24 hours to 7 to 14 days included depressed mood in 4% after 125 mg MDMA (none listed after placebo or 75 mg) and headache in 6% after 125 mg, 7% after 75 mg and 5% after placebo; none was reported significantly more often after MDMA than after placebo. In the studies using 125 mg, 12 people (9%) reported 'flashbacks' (not defined in the paper) 1 to 3 times, one of them eight times, on average 26 hours (SD 15; range 8 to 50) after the dose; no sex differences; of 141 asked at the end of the study, 12 (9%) reported them, all within 8 to 50 hours.
key_findings.locator: Results > Adverse effects of MDMA, 2nd paragraph (p. 580, continued on p. 582); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 584)

key_findings.finding: Asked at the end of the study (141 of the 166 volunteers; 80% new to MDMA, the rest with at most four earlier exposures): 95 (67%) reported a positive overall experience, 25 (18%) neutral and 21 (15%) disappointing or bad, with no sex differences. Would they consider taking MDMA again: 27 (19%) probably not under any circumstances; 66 (47%) not recreationally but possibly in another controlled study; 48 (34%) possibly in a recreational setting but only if identity, purity and dose were known, of whom 24 had earlier taken illicit drugs including MDMA; only 13 considered a club setting. The controlled setting had no impact on the experience for 51 (36%) and was important for the type of experience, reassuring and made them feel safe for 90 (64%); women rated the setting as more important (F(1,139) 12.4, p < 0.001). Their retrospective rating of the duration of the effect was 4.0 hours (SD 2.9).
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjects' interest in using MDMA again, 1st paragraph (pp. 582 to 584); Results > Acute subjective effects of MDMA, 1st paragraph (p. 580)
key_findings.note: Volunteers were given MDMA by researchers; the 25 not asked are not explained.

key_findings.finding: The authors read the data as showing clearly greater positive than negative acute subjective effects and a state of predominantly positive mood across laboratories, with modest apprehension anxiety in some volunteers, no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks and minimal psychological distress; they contrast this with panic attacks and agitation or aggression described in people who use ecstasy and present to emergency departments (cited from other papers, not read).

The authors state that similar amounts of MDMA are found in ecstasy pills (citing Brunt et al. 2012, not read) and are used in clinical studies in patients; the capsules were pharmaceutical MDMA hydrochloride of known amount.
key_findings.note: Second-hand comparison with pill content; no pill analysis was done in this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 19% of subjects above 38 degrees Celsius with MDMA and 33% and 29% above the blood pressure and heart rate lines, without the placebo shares. Table 2 shows that at 125 mg 12 of 136 placebo sessions (9%) also crossed 38 degrees, 8 (6%) crossed 160 mm Hg systolic and 3 (2%) crossed 100 beats a minute.
reporting_issues.consequence: The excess caused by MDMA at 125 mg is smaller than the headline for temperature: 24% against 9%, about 15 in 100 more (editors' calculation), and the temperature line is partly crossed by chance and by measurement.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the shares with raised blood pressure, fast pulse and temperature above 38 degrees were all significantly greater at 125 than at 75 mg. The continuous dose-by-drug tests for heart rate (F 2.38) and temperature (F 2.43) are not significant, 0 of 30 people at 75 mg crossed 38 degrees against 24% at 125 mg, the 75 mg study lacks temperature readings at 0.33 and 2.5 hours, and the placebo sessions of the two doses differ (37.0 against 37.4 degrees on average).
reporting_issues.consequence: The dose contrast for temperature and heart rate is between studies and partly an artefact of readings and baseline; it should not be quoted as a dose-response for those two measures.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says liver enzymes were similar at screening and at the end-of-study visit, but Table 4 shows GGT 19 (SD 8) against 18 (SD 8) U/L with t=2.73, p<0.01. The interval from the last dose to the end-of-study visit is 29 (SD 22) days in the Methods and 30 (SD 22) in the Results.
reporting_issues.consequence: The GGT change is statistically significant and clinically trivial; the text and table disagree, and the interval is stated two ways.

reporting_issues.issue: Acute anxiety is given as 9 people (6%) after 125 mg in the Results and Table 3 (9 of 166 is 5%), and as 7% in the Discussion (9 of 136 is 7%).
reporting_issues.consequence: Small slip in a percentage; the count of 9 is consistent.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods sentence that defines the blood pressure grades is garbled (the thresholds are listed without saying which belong to systolic and diastolic readings in full); Table 2 shows that the thresholds used were systolic above 140, 160, 180 and diastolic above 90, 100, 110.
reporting_issues.consequence: Thresholds must be read from Table 2, not from the sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion recommends a fixed dose for women on the strength of a comparison between 15 women given 75 mg in one study and 68 given 125 mg in other studies, with bad-drug-effect ratings not dose-dependent.
reporting_issues.consequence: A recommendation about amounts that the between-study design cannot support; not reproduced in any claim.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1 the drug-by-dose test for 'any drug effect' and for 'good drug effect' is printed with the same F (20) but p < 0.001 for the first and p < 0.01 for the second; F(1,162) = 20 gives p of about 0.00001 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: A printing slip; the dose effect on the good-effect rating is stronger than printed. The two doses were given to different people in different studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The end-of-study questions (overall experience, interest in taking MDMA again, setting) were put to 141 of the 166 volunteers; the 25 who were not asked are not explained, and the answers come from people given MDMA by researchers, 80% of them new to it.
reporting_issues.consequence: The shares calling the experience positive (67%) or disappointing or bad (15%) are shares of volunteers, not of people who choose to take MDMA, and may differ for the 25 not asked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says psychological distress was minimal and that there were no cases of severe anxiety or panic attacks, but the Results report no distress scale: the only measures are the 'bad drug effect' rating (mean 7 to 35 out of 100 across the four groups, with SDs of 11 to 33, so some volunteers rated it much higher) and the one-item anxiety complaint (6%); no distribution or highest value is given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper does not say what the statements rest on beyond those two items; how high the highest bad-drug-effect ratings went is not stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The end-of-study visit, where the overall-experience and interest-in-taking-MDMA-again questions were put, took place on average 29 days (SD 22) after the last MDMA dose and after one or two doses; 112 of the 166 volunteers received 125 mg twice, once alone and once after a pretreatment medicine. The paper does not say which session the answers refer to.
reporting_issues.consequence: The shares calling the experience positive (67%) or disappointing or bad (15%) could describe the first session, the last or both together, and for 112 volunteers one of the two sessions followed another drug; they are a summary given weeks later, not ratings taken during a session.

reporting_issues.issue: Five of the 84 percentages in Table 3 are one point above the count over its group when rounded in the usual way (editors' calculation): acute anxiety 9 people printed as 6% (5.4% of 166), 24-hour dry mouth 37 as 23% (22.3%), 24-hour difficulty concentrating 35 as 22% (21.1%), 24-hour nausea 9 as 6% (5.4%) and placebo bruxism at 0 h 2 of 134 as 2% (1.5%). The Results give acute anxiety as 9 people (6%) 'after the 125 mg dose' and the Discussion as 7% after 125 mg (9 of 136 is 6.6%).
reporting_issues.consequence: A rounding slip of one point in a few cells; the counts are the same in all three places (9 people, all after 125 mg), and the printed share for anxiety depends on which group it is taken from.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 576-586 (PDFs/MDMA/Vizeli_2017_SafetyPharmacologyAcute.pdf), full text: abstract, Methods, Results, Tables 1-4, Figure 1 legend, Discussion, limitations, conclusion, funding. Tables 1-4 were read in the layout extraction and checked against rendered images of printed pages 581-583 (including the negative t values -1.95 and -4.27 in Table 4); the supplementary tables (pretreatment sessions, Supplementary Tables S1 and S2) were not read. Findings and reporting issues on the subjective ratings (Table 1), complaints (Table 3), the end-of-study questions and the Discussion of mood were added on 2026-10-18 by AI reader 64 (first reader) from the same PDF (printed pp. 577 to 585; Tables 1 and 3 read again on rendered images of pp. 581 and 583); nothing from the first pass was removed or changed except the text added to can_establish, cannot_establish and the interpretation gap.

design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person laboratory brain-imaging study in 9 healthy volunteers (7 men, 2 women) who had used ecstasy before, at the University of Chicago: three sessions at least 6 days apart (on average 10.7 days, SD 7.2) with MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 1.5 mg/kg given in ascending order and placebo placed at random among the sessions; sessions began at noon and volunteers stayed in hospital at least 4.5 hours. About 85 minutes after the capsule they lay in a 3-tesla scanner and viewed angry, fearful, happy and neutral faces (and a motor-visual control task). Measures: Drug Effects Questionnaire (DEQ; the 'feel drug' item reported), a 7-item visual analogue scale (VAS; the 'sociable' item reported), the Profile of Mood States (POMS; the Friendliness scale reported), blood pressure and heart rate, and brain response in a priori regions (amygdala, ventral striatum). Peak changes and repeated-measures analyses of variance with paired t tests; alpha .05 for the analyses and .01 for post hoc tests; brain tests at voxel p < .005 uncorrected, with small-volume correction in the a priori regions.
can_establish: Whether, in 9 healthy volunteers with earlier ecstasy use, a single oral dose of MDMA raised peak 'feel drug' ratings, systolic pressure and heart rate above placebo (F(2,16) 98.6, 41.9 and 21.9), with 'feel drug' and systolic pressure also higher at the higher dose; whether 1.5 mg/kg raised the 'sociable' rating from baseline at 135 minutes more than 0.75 mg/kg did (p < .01); and, as an early report, that left amygdala response to angry faces was lower at 1.5 mg/kg and ventral striatum response to happy faces higher at 0.75 mg/kg than on placebo.
cannot_establish: That MDMA raises sociability against placebo (the difference from placebo was p = .04, which the paper's own post hoc cut-off of .01 and its text call marginal); that sociability rises with dose (dose and session order are mixed up, since doses were given in ascending order); that the brain changes cause feeling more sociable (no link is tested); that the amygdala result is firm (corrected p = .052); that the brain results are not a general effect of MDMA on blood flow (activity also fell in visual and motor cortex); anything about people new to MDMA (all had used it, 2 to 300 times); unwanted effects beyond one sentence (the anxious, sedated, down and nauseated ratings were collected but not reported); plasma levels (not measured).

sample.recruitment: Online advertisements and word of mouth (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy, right-handed volunteers aged 18 to 29 who reported ecstasy use at least twice. Excluded: lifetime psychotic or bipolar disorder; past-year other Axis I disorder; medical or neurological illness (medical examination, electrocardiogram and clinical interview); body mass index outside 18 to 30; an earlier adverse response to ecstasy; any reason not to be scanned (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.demographics: Mean age 24.0 (SD 3.2); two of nine women; six identified as Caucasian. Lifetime ecstasy use 2 to 300 occasions (mean 63.9, SD 94.9), first use at about 17.4 years, last use 0.5 to 24 months before the study (mean 10.2); four had used ecstasy in the past year. In the past month five smoked daily (about 10 cigarettes a day), five used cannabis at least once and eight drank alcohol; all nine had used cannabis, eight stimulants and seven hallucinogens in their lifetime (Results > 1st paragraph; Table 1).
sample.attrition: None reported for the self-report data; three emotion-recognition runs and three motor-visual runs were excluded from the imaging data for head movement (Materials and Methods > Imaging).
sample.selection_effects: Nine volunteers with earlier ecstasy use, recruited by advertisement, screened for health and for any earlier bad response; the authors say all had prior exposure for ethical reasons and that exposure varied widely. A sample this small and this heterogeneous cannot show how most people respond.

exposure.measurement: Opaque size 00 gelatin capsules with MDMA and lactose, or lactose placebo; no plasma concentrations were measured, which the authors name as a limitation. The source of the MDMA is not stated in the text read.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral dose of 0.75 mg/kg or 1.5 mg/kg (ascending order) or placebo, one per session, at least 6 days apart; no food for 2 hours before each session.
exposure.polysubstance: Abstinence required from cannabis for 7 days, alcohol for 24 hours and other recreational drugs for 48 hours before sessions, checked by urine, saliva and breath tests; five volunteers smoked cigarettes daily.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Cannabis 7 days, alcohol 24 hours, other recreational drugs 48 hours; verified by urine test (Rapid Check 9 Panel), saliva test (Oratect III) and breathalyser; a pregnancy test for women at each session.

comparison.controls: Placebo and both doses in the same people (double-blind); placebo placed at random among the three sessions, the two doses in ascending order.
comparison.matching: Within person. The authors say session order had no effect on the subjective, cardiovascular or brain results, citing the partial randomisation and the interval between sessions; no statistics are printed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Plasma MDMA not measured; earlier ecstasy use varied from 2 to 300 occasions and the authors checked it against brain signal by correlation (none found).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Abstinence rules and tests; current cannabis, alcohol and tobacco use was allowed outside those windows and is reported.

outcomes.instruments: Drug Effects Questionnaire (four visual analogue items: feel any drug effect, like the drug effect, feel high, want more; 'feel drug' reported); a 7-item visual analogue scale (stimulated, anxious, sedated, down, elated, sociable, nauseated; 'sociable' reported); Profile of Mood States (72 adjectives, 8 subscales; Friendliness reported); blood pressure and heart rate; functional magnetic resonance imaging during an emotion-recognition task and a motor-visual task. DEQ and VAS at 0, 30, 60, 135, 210 and 240 minutes after the capsule; POMS at 0, 60 and 240 minutes (Materials and Methods > Protocol, 3rd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established scales cited (Johanson and Uhlenhuth 1980; Folstein and Luria 1973; McNair and Droppleman 1971); the choice of 'sociable' and 'Friendliness' as the subjective outcomes was made on the basis of the hypotheses stated in the Introduction.
outcomes.operationalization: Peak change from before the capsule for blood pressure, heart rate and 'feel drug'; change from baseline over time for 'sociable' and Friendliness, with drug-by-time interaction and then the 135-minute point. Brain: a priori regions as 10 mm spheres (amygdala; ventral striatum).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Editors' count of 11 rows in Table 2 (3 cardiovascular, 1 'feel drug', 2 sociability, 1 friendliness, 4 emotion recognition), plus the imaging tests: whole-brain voxel tests at p < .005 uncorrected in a priori regions, followed by small-volume correction, and p < .001 uncorrected for exploratory whole-brain maps. Post hoc subjective tests used alpha .01.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double blind; no check of the blind is reported. A 1.5 mg/kg dose with a 'feel drug' rating averaging 92 of 100 is unlikely to have been concealed.

analysis.effect_sizes: Table 2, mean (SD as printed) for placebo, 0.75 and 1.5 mg/kg. Peak change from before the capsule: systolic pressure 4.8 (19.0), 34.8 (13.5), 48.1 (11.6) mm Hg, F(2,16) 41.9; diastolic 3.6 (13.9), 15.8 (13.4), 26.0 (5.1), F 8.0; heart rate -5.3 (11.0), 19.7 (16.2), 35.3 (19.9), F 21.9; DEQ 'feel drug' 14.5 (5.0), 57.1 (4.6), 91.8 (4.0), F 98.6 (all p < .05); the SDs for 'feel drug' look like standard errors (editors' calculation: t(8) = 16.1 for 1.5 mg/kg against placebo implies an SD of the difference of about 14). VAS 'sociable' change at 135 minutes -6.3 (17.7), -9.5 (13.5), 19.7 (24.7), F(2,16) 7.3; placebo against 1.5 mg/kg t(8) = 2.5, p = .04 (called marginal; post hoc alpha .01); 0.75 against 1.5 mg/kg t(8) = 3.8, p < .01; drug-by-time F(8,64) 3.1, partial eta-squared .28. POMS Friendliness F(2,16) 1.3, not significant. Emotion recognition accuracy .89, .91, .86 (F 0.9) and reaction time (F 3.1) not significantly changed. Imaging: left amygdala to angry against neutral faces F(2,16) 9.64, p < .005; placebo greater than 1.5 mg/kg t(8) 4.41, p < .005; small-volume corrected p = .052; no effect for fearful faces; ventral striatum to happy against neutral faces F(2,16) 9.75, p < .005; 0.75 mg/kg greater than placebo t(8) 6.13, p < .001, corrected p < .05; 1.5 mg/kg against placebo t(8) 2.72, not surviving correction.
analysis.covariates: None (within person); lifetime ecstasy use and time since last use were correlated with extracted brain signal (no correlations).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration is mentioned; three directional hypotheses (self-rated sociability up; amygdala response to threat down; ventral striatum response to happy faces up) are stated at the end of the Introduction.
analysis.selective_reporting: Four DEQ items, 7 VAS items and 8 POMS subscales were collected but the paper reports three subjective measures; anxious, sedated, down, nauseated, 'like the drug effect', 'feel high' and 'want more' are not reported, nor are the other POMS subscales. The abstract says 1.5 mg/kg increased sociability against placebo as well as against 0.75 mg/kg, and that MDMA attenuated amygdala response to angry faces; the text calls the placebo difference marginal (p = .04 against a post hoc alpha of .01), and the amygdala result is p = .052 after correction.
analysis.power: No power calculation. Nine volunteers; the authors say the sample was small and the findings need replication in a larger sample. They suggest the non-significant Friendliness effect may reflect sample size, citing a large effect size for the main effect of drug (partial eta-squared above .23); that statistic is not printed, and the printed drug-by-time F(2,16) 1.3 gives a partial eta-squared of 0.14 (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 9 volunteers with earlier ecstasy use, MDMA raised 'feel drug' ratings in a dose-related way (peak change 14.5 on placebo, 57.1 at 0.75 mg/kg, 91.8 at 1.5 mg/kg) and raised blood pressure and heart rate; no serious adverse effects were seen. The 'sociable' rating at 135 minutes changed by -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 mg/kg and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg; the 1.5 mg/kg rating was above 0.75 mg/kg (p < .01) and, by the paper's own account, only marginally above placebo (p = .04); the POMS Friendliness scale did not change significantly. Left amygdala response to angry faces was lower at 1.5 mg/kg than on placebo (uncorrected p < .005, corrected p = .052) and ventral striatum response to happy faces higher at 0.75 mg/kg (corrected p < .05); activity in visual and motor cortex also fell. Accuracy and speed of recognising faces did not change.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says MDMA at 1.5 mg/kg increased self-reported sociability compared with placebo and with 0.75 mg/kg, that it attenuated left amygdala response to angry faces, and that the data are the first evidence that MDMA may increase sociability by diminishing responses to threat and enhancing responses to reward; the Discussion says the findings are preliminary and need replication.

timeline.event: Hysek et al. (Basel, 32 volunteers): MDMA 125 mg raised ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others against placebo, and lowered recognition of several negative faces; they cite this study for the lower amygdala response to threat.

Kirkpatrick et al. (pooled Chicago, San Francisco and Basel, 220 volunteers): similar peak ratings of drug effect and drug liking at three sites; closeness to others higher at San Francisco than at Basel.

replication.where_it_stands: Raised self-rated feelings of closeness and good mood after MDMA are reported by other laboratories; the brain-imaging results (amygdala, ventral striatum) were not tested again in the papers read here. The sociability rating against placebo is a marginal result in this study.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse (DA02812) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: None (Disclosures/Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The senior author is also the senior author of the Chicago studies pooled by Kirkpatrick et al. (2014); whether these nine volunteers are among those 95 is not stated.

what_would_settle_it: A larger preregistered study with randomised dose order (or different people at each dose), plasma MDMA at the time of imaging, a control region and a cerebral blood flow measure analysed in the same model, correction across brain regions, a placebo comparison for sociability that meets its own threshold, and behaviour toward other people rather than ratings.

domains.note: Placebo placed at random; MDMA doses given in ascending order for safety; how the placement was generated is not described.
At least 6 days between sessions (average 10.7, SD 7.2); the authors say a longer gap may have been needed to exclude carry-over, and report no order effect without statistics.
Double blind, but the dose-related effect at 1.5 mg/kg is obvious; no check of the blind.
All 9 are described; three emotion-recognition and three motor-visual imaging runs were excluded for movement without saying whose.

Self-ratings by people who could feel the drug; brain signal may reflect blood-flow effects of MDMA (activity in visual and motor cortex also fell); plasma MDMA not measured; printed SDs for 'feel drug' look like standard errors.

Three of the collected subjective measures reported; the abstract's sociability result against placebo does not meet the paper's own post hoc threshold (p = .04 against .01); the headline amygdala result is p = .052 after correction; no registration.

domains.domain: Dose comparison, 0.75 against 1.5 mg/kg (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Ascending order mixes up dose and order; nine volunteers; the dose-dependence of sociability rests on this contrast.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The large dose-related changes in 'feel drug' ratings, blood pressure and heart rate in the same people are at some concerns at worst. The overall judgment is set by the selective reporting of the sociability and brain results and by the ascending dose order. The source may be cited for the design, the sample, the dose-related feel-drug ratings and cardiovascular changes, and as a small early report of a rise in a 'sociable' rating at 1.5 mg/kg that was marginal against placebo; it should not be cited as showing that MDMA raises sociability against placebo, a dose-response for sociability, or the brain findings as established.

key_findings.finding: Design: 9 healthy, right-handed volunteers aged 18 to 29 with earlier ecstasy use (at least twice), recruited by advertisement and word of mouth; a three-session within-person double-blind design with MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 1.5 mg/kg in ascending order and placebo placed at random, at least 6 days apart, sessions at noon, at least 4.5 hours in hospital; abstinence from cannabis for 7 days, alcohol 24 hours and other drugs 48 hours, checked by urine, saliva and breath tests.
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Protocol, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Sample: 7 men and 2 women, mean age 24.0 (SD 3.2); lifetime ecstasy use 2 to 300 occasions (mean 63.9, SD 94.9), 4 of 9 in the past year; all had used cannabis, 8 stimulants and 7 hallucinogens; in the past month 5 smoked daily.

Peak 'feel drug' rating (change from before the capsule, DEQ) 14.5 on placebo, 57.1 at 0.75 mg/kg and 91.8 at 1.5 mg/kg (F(2,16) 98.6); peak systolic pressure rose 4.8, 34.8 and 48.1 mm Hg and heart rate -5.3, 19.7 and 35.3 beats a minute; there were no serious adverse effects.
key_findings.note: The printed SDs for 'feel drug' (5.0, 4.6, 4.0) look like standard errors.

key_findings.finding: 'Sociable' rating (VAS), change from baseline at 135 minutes: -6.3 on placebo, -9.5 at 0.75 mg/kg and +19.7 at 1.5 mg/kg; drug-by-time F(8,64) 3.1 (partial eta-squared .28); 1.5 against 0.75 mg/kg t(8) 3.8, p < .01; 1.5 mg/kg against placebo t(8) 2.5, p = .04, described as marginal against the post hoc alpha of .01. POMS Friendliness showed a similar pattern that was not significant (F(2,16) 1.3).
key_findings.locator: Results > 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Imaging: left amygdala response to angry against neutral faces was lower at 1.5 mg/kg than on placebo (uncorrected p < .005; corrected p = .052) and not changed for fearful faces; ventral striatum response to happy against neutral faces was higher at 0.75 mg/kg than on placebo (corrected p < .05) and at 1.5 mg/kg did not survive correction; activity in visual and motor cortex fell at 1.5 mg/kg; accuracy and speed of recognising faces did not change.

Limits stated by the authors: findings preliminary and the sample small; only two a priori brain regions; possible blood-flow effects on the signal; all volunteers had earlier ecstasy exposure, varying widely; doses in ascending order for safety, 6 days minimum between sessions, no order effect found; no plasma MDMA measured.

The Introduction says increased sociability and decreased defensiveness are cited by people who use ecstasy as a motivator to use it (citing a survey, Sumnall et al. 2006) and that human laboratory studies of 1 to 2 mg/kg report increased extroversion, friendliness, sociability, talkativeness and closeness, with some studies not finding them; this paper's data do not address why people take MDMA.
key_findings.note: Second-hand statement; Sumnall et al. (2006) was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 1.5 mg/kg increased self-reported sociability compared with placebo. Table 2 gives placebo against 1.5 mg/kg as t(8) 2.5, p = .04, and the text and Figure 2 legend call it a marginal difference, against the paper's own post hoc alpha of .01.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's sociability result against placebo is not significant by the paper's own rule; only the contrast with 0.75 mg/kg (p < .01) is.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 1.5 mg/kg attenuated left amygdala response to angry faces compared with placebo; after small-volume correction for the a priori region the result is p = .052.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline imaging result does not meet the conventional threshold once corrected; the paper calls its findings preliminary.

reporting_issues.issue: For POMS Friendliness the text says the main effect of drug was large (partial eta-squared above .23), so a missing significance may reflect sample size; the main-effect statistic is not printed, and the printed drug-by-time F(2,16) 1.3 gives a partial eta-squared of 0.14 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The effect-size statement cannot be checked against Table 2; the Friendliness result is not significant by any printed test.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'feel drug' values in Table 2 are printed as standard deviations (5.0, 4.6, 4.0) but behave like standard errors: t(8) 16.1 for 1.5 mg/kg against placebo implies an SD of the paired difference of about 14 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The spread of 'feel drug' ratings between volunteers is larger than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: Anxious, sedated, down, nauseated, 'like the drug effect', 'feel high' and 'want more' were collected but are not reported, nor are seven of the eight POMS subscales; unwanted effects are covered by one sentence (no serious adverse effects).
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot say how often unpleasant feelings occurred at either dose.

reporting_issues.issue: MDMA doses were given in ascending order, so dose is mixed up with session order; the authors report no order effect without statistics.
reporting_issues.consequence: A dose-response for sociability or for brain responses cannot be separated from order, practice or carry-over.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC3328967 (author manuscript), read in the app's browser: abstract, Introduction, Materials and Methods, Results, Tables 1 to 3, figure legends, Discussion, acknowledgments. Figures 1 to 4 are images and were not read for values.

design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover laboratory study (random order stated in the abstract only) in 32 healthy volunteers (16 women, 16 men) at the University of Basel: one session with a single oral dose of MDMA 125 mg (mean 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30) in gelatin capsules and one with identical placebo capsules (64 sessions), at least 10 days apart. The paper lists two ClinicalTrials.gov numbers (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685). Measures: visual analogue scales (happy, open, close to others) and the 60-item Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS) repeatedly; the Multifaceted Empathy Test (MET, 120 trials) 3 hours after the dose; the Social Value Orientation (SVO) test, a paper money-allocation task, 4 hours after; a dynamic Face Emotion Recognition Task (FERT) 2 hours after; plasma oxytocin, copeptin, cortisol, prolactin and testosterone; plasma MDMA. Peak changes from baseline were analysed with analyses of variance (drug within person; sex between people), Tukey post hoc tests and correlations; session order and past cannabis use were tested as extra factors.
can_establish: Whether, in 32 healthy young adults (22 with no earlier MDMA use, 10 with fewer than five uses), a single oral dose of MDMA raised self-ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others and several mood scales (well-being, extroversion, activity, emotional excitation, dreaminess; also inactivity and introversion) against placebo; raised ratings of feeling for people shown in photographs (emotional empathy) across all volunteers; lowered accuracy in naming fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised faces but not happy faces; and raised plasma oxytocin, cortisol and prolactin, as measured in laboratory sessions (where they took place is not stated) over the hours after the dose (the tasks at 2 to 4 hours).
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA changes how people treat others outside the laboratory (the tasks are photographs, a computer test and a paper allocation of sums whose size is not stated, with real payment to two volunteers); whether the effects on empathy and prosocial behaviour exist in women or only in men, or differ between the sexes at all (the sex-specific results are post hoc subgroup tests of 16 people each, among at least 42 uncorrected tests); whether results are free of expectancy (the authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had); the exact size of each effect (the text prints test statistics, not means; approximate means can be read from the figures, and Supplementary Table S1 was not read); anything about other doses, repeated doses or MDMA taken in a social, party or therapy setting; whether oxytocin carries the effect (no correlation was found).

sample.recruitment: Recruited from the University of Basel campus and paid for taking part (Materials and Methods > Participants; Experimental protocol).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded: a personal or first-degree relative history of psychiatric disorder; chronic or acute physical illness; smoking; a lifetime history of more than five uses of illicit drugs (past cannabis allowed); any illicit drug use including cannabis in the last 2 months or during the study (repeated urine tests at screening and before each session). Women were tested in the follicular phase (days 2 to 14) of the cycle (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.demographics: Mean age 25 (SD 3), range 20 to 31; 16 men and 16 women. 22 completely new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier experiences; 19 had used cannabis more than five times and 15 other illicit drugs one to four times (Materials and Methods > Participants).
sample.attrition: None reported; every analysis is described for the 32. The inequality-aversion test has 20 error degrees of freedom and the plasma MDMA comparison between sexes 15, the inequality-aversion test in volunteers 'with a prosocial orientation' (how many is not given), the plasma comparison without saying how many were analysed.
sample.selection_effects: Young university volunteers, screened for health, mostly new to MDMA, tested in laboratory sessions (the place is not stated); people with psychiatric disorders, regular drug use or smoking are absent by design. Paid volunteers who agreed to take MDMA for research.

exposure.measurement: MDMA (Lipomed AG, Arlesheim, Switzerland) in gelatin capsules with mannitol filler, identical mannitol placebo; plasma MDMA measured repeatedly by high-performance liquid chromatography with tandem mass spectrometry (Cmax 209 ng/mL in men and 269.9 in women, SEM 6.4 and 9.3; AUC0-6h 926.8 and 1146.5 ng/mL h, SEM 29.3 and 37.9; Tmax 2.10 and 2.75 h).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: a single oral dose of 125 mg in one session (1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30; 1.68 in men and 2.09 in women) and placebo in the other, at least 10 days apart; the tasks were run 2 hours (faces), 3 hours (empathy test) and 4 hours (money allocation) after the dose (Study drug; Experimental protocol; Measures).
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drug use including cannabis excluded for 2 months before and during the study (urine tests at screening and before each session); smokers excluded; no information on alcohol.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 months free of illicit drugs by history, with repeated urine tests (TRIAGE 8) at screening and before each session.

comparison.controls: Placebo in the same people (double-blind, random order, washout at least 10 days); the sexes are compared with each other (16 against 16, different people).
comparison.matching: Within person for MDMA against placebo. The authors say order effects were excluded with session order as a factor and that past cannabis use did not confound the sex-by-drug interaction; no statistics are printed for either.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Trait empathy was measured once (Interpersonal Reactivity Index) and did not change the response to MDMA; mood and expectation before the sessions are not reported.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded by screening and urine tests.

outcomes.instruments: Visual analogue scales (happy, open, close to others); AMRS (60 items); Multifaceted Empathy Test (40 photographs of people in emotionally charged scenes, each tested for cognitive empathy as percent correct, explicit emotional empathy and implicit emotional empathy rated 1 to 9, 20 positive and 20 negative scenes); Social Value Orientation (six primary and nine secondary slider items; the angle of the mean amount allocated to the other person against self; allocated funds had real value for two randomly drawn volunteers); dynamic Face Emotion Recognition Task (accuracy and detection threshold per emotion); Interpersonal Reactivity Index (trait empathy); plasma oxytocin, copeptin, cortisol, prolactin, testosterone (Measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Tasks cited to earlier work (Dziobek 2008; Murphy 2011; Domes 2008); the dynamic FERT is described as novel; the paper cross-checked the MET against the FERT after placebo (r = 0.42).
outcomes.operationalization: Repeated measures as peak change from baseline; single-time-point tasks compared between drug sessions. The 60-item AMRS is reported only for the scales that changed, and for anxiety, which did not; the number of scales is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated; Tukey post hoc tests after significant analysis-of-variance effects. Editors' count of 42 tests with a printed statistic in the Results (3 visual analogue scales, 7 AMRS scales and 1 sex interaction, 6 empathy tests and 2 post hoc, 4 SVO tests, 16 face-recognition tests, 3 hormone tests); the supplement, not read, holds more. The authors name the number of comparisons as a limitation (Discussion, 7th paragraph).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double blind with identical capsules, but the authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had during the session and that this may have biased task performance. Outcomes are self-ratings and tasks; no blinding check is reported.

analysis.effect_sizes: No means, SDs or effect sizes are printed in the text; Supplementary Table S1 was not read. Approximate means read from the PDF's vector figures (editors' readings by two readers, placebo then MDMA): explicit emotional empathy (1 to 9 scale) all 4.40 and 5.01, women 4.96 and 5.15, men 3.84 and 4.87; implicit all 4.30 and 4.81, women 4.79 and 4.79, men 3.81 and 4.83; cognitive empathy 62.3% and 61.9%; prosocial angle all 31.2 and 36.9 degrees, women 36.8 and 36.6, men 25.7 and 37.2; inequality-aversion index all 0.48 and 0.38; change in oxytocin 12.2 and 65.9 pg/mL. Printed test statistics, F(1,31) unless stated: happy 120.59, open 80.77, close to others 67.52, AMRS well-being 37.00, extroversion 40.58, emotional excitation 28.46, dreaminess 25.48, activity 24.48 (all p < 0.001), introversion 10.05 (p = 0.003), inactivity 7.72 (p = 0.009); anxiety scale not raised (no statistic). Emotional empathy, all volunteers: explicit 6.05 (p = 0.019), implicit 4.29 (p = 0.047); positive scenes explicit 8.60 (p = 0.006) and implicit 5.02 (p = 0.032); negative scenes not significant; treatment-by-sex interaction implicit 4.68 (p = 0.039) and explicit 3.03 (p = 0.092); post hoc in men explicit p = 0.025 and implicit p = 0.022, in women not significant; cognitive empathy unchanged. SVO angle 4.42 (p = 0.044), by sex 5.52 (p = 0.026), post hoc men p = 0.008, women not significant; inequality-aversion F(1,20) 3.39 (p = 0.079). Face recognition accuracy overall 28.63 (p < 0.001), by sex 6.04 (p = 0.020), women p < 0.001, men not significant; fearful 14.90, angry 18.60 (p < 0.001), disgusted 5.81 (p = 0.022), surprised 9.79 (p = 0.004), happy 0.27 (p = 0.607); in women only fearful (p < 0.001), angry (p = 0.007) and sad (p = 0.010); fear detection threshold 4.92 (printed P < 0.032). Hormones: oxytocin 19.84, cortisol 98.70, prolactin 127.81 (p < 0.001); copeptin and testosterone not changed; no correlation of hormones with empathy or prosocial effects. Women's peak plasma MDMA 269.9 against men's 209 ng/mL (F(1,15) 35.73).
analysis.covariates: Drug within and sex between people; session order and past cannabis use as extra factors (stated, no statistics); trait empathy as a median split for the empathy test; no adjustment for dose per kilogram, although women received 2.09 and men 1.68 mg/kg.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The paper states the study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685). The registry records were not read, so whether the empathy, prosocial and face-recognition outcomes reported here match the registered outcomes is not known.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract and Discussion state sex-specific results (empathy and prosocial behaviour 'in men'; impaired recognition 'particularly in women') as findings; they are post hoc tests after interactions at p = 0.020 to 0.039 (explicit empathy interaction p = 0.092) among at least 42 uncorrected tests. The 60-item AMRS is reported for 8 scales only, out of a number this paper does not state. No means are printed in the text.
analysis.power: No power calculation. The authors argue that the within-person design gave more power than a parallel design (n above 64); the sex-specific tests rest on 16 people each, and the inequality-aversion test on about 22 (20 degrees of freedom; n not stated).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 32 healthy volunteers, mostly new to MDMA, a single oral dose of 125 mg raised self-ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others and several mood scales against placebo (F(1,31) from 37 to 121 for the three ratings and well-being), raised explicit and implicit emotional empathy ratings for photographs overall (p = 0.019 and 0.047, driven by positive scenes), lowered accuracy in naming fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised faces, and raised plasma oxytocin, cortisol and prolactin. Increases in empathy ratings and in the money-allocation measure were significant in men only by post hoc test; the lowering of accuracy for fearful, angry and sad faces was significant in women only. Hormone changes did not correlate with any emotional or prosocial change. The authors state that most volunteers realised which treatment they had.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say MDMA enhanced emotional empathy and increased prosocial behaviour, altering emotion recognition, empathy and prosociality in a sex-specific way, that these effects likely enhance sociability when MDMA is used recreationally, and that they may be useful in psychotherapy; the Discussion says men showed more empathic concern and less competitive behaviour and that oxytocin is a candidate mediator, while reporting no correlation.

timeline.event: Bedi et al. (Chicago): MDMA impaired recognition of fearful faces and did not improve emotion recognition overall. These authors cite Bedi et al. (2009 and 2010) together for raised self-rated sociability; in Bedi et al. (2010) only methamphetamine raised self-rated sociability significantly (MDMA raised loving and friendliness ratings), so the citation holds for the 2009 study only.
Hysek, Domes and Liechti (same Basel group), as cited: MDMA impaired reading of negative emotions and improved reading of positive emotions in the Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test.

Vizeli and Liechti: pooled analysis of nine Basel studies (166 volunteers), whose registrations include both of this study's; positive mood with MDMA across laboratories is reviewed in its Discussion, which also cites this paper for impaired recognition of negative emotions.

replication.where_it_stands: Raised ratings of feeling happy, open and close to others after MDMA are reported by other laboratories as well; the lowered recognition of negative faces was reported earlier by two other studies as cited here. The sex-specific findings and the money-allocation result rest on this study alone and on post hoc subgroup tests.

funding.funder: Swiss National Science Foundation (grants 320030_138481 and 32323B_144996) and the University of Basel (DPH 2053 and DPH 2064) (Acknowledgments).
funding.declared_conflicts: None declared (Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: The senior author leads the Basel laboratory whose studies are pooled by Vizeli and Liechti (2017); both registrations cited here appear in that analysis, so the data are probably part of it.

what_would_settle_it: A larger, preregistered study with a check of whether volunteers could tell the capsules apart, equal numbers of women and men sized for the sex-by-drug interaction, outcomes that are behaviours with real consequences, more than one dose, and a setting with other people present, followed by the same measures outside the laboratory.

domains.note: Random order is stated only in the abstract (the Methods describe a double-blind, placebo-controlled cross-over without mentioning randomization); how the sequence was generated and concealed is not described, and the washout was at least 10 days.
Washout of at least 10 days; the authors say order effects were excluded (no statistics printed).
Identical capsules, but the authors say most volunteers realised which treatment they had and that this may have biased task performance; no check of the blind.
All 32 are described, but degrees of freedom of 20 and 15 appear without saying who was analysed; no dropout figures.
Self-ratings and tasks by people who knew the condition; the FERT is described as novel; SVO payments were real for two randomly drawn volunteers (amounts not stated).
Registered, but the registered outcomes were not checked; at least 42 tests without correction; the text prints no means; AMRS reported for 8 scales only.

domains.domain: Sex-specific findings (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Post hoc tests of 16 people each after interactions at p = 0.020 to 0.039 (0.092 for explicit empathy), uncorrected; the sex-specific results are the paper's headline in the abstract.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The comparison of MDMA with placebo in the same people on the self-rated scales is at some concerns at worst, with very large effects (F 68 to 121) next to the biases named. The overall judgment is set by the sex-specific subgroup findings. The source may be cited for the design and sample, for the rise in self-rated happy, open and close to others and in the listed mood scales, for lowered accuracy in naming fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised faces in all 32 volunteers, and for the unblinding the authors report. It should not be cited as showing that empathy or prosocial behaviour rise in men and not in women, for the size of any effect, or for behaviour outside the laboratory.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 32 healthy volunteers (16 women, 16 men), mean age 25 (SD 3), recruited at the University of Basel; 22 completely new to MDMA and 10 with fewer than five earlier uses; double-blind, random-order crossover, MDMA 125 mg (mean 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.30) and identical placebo capsules at least 10 days apart; registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT01386177 and NCT01465685).
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; Experimental protocol, 1st paragraph; Study drug, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Self-rated effects: MDMA raised visual analogue ratings of feeling happy (F(1,31) = 120.59), open (80.77) and close to others (67.52), all p < 0.001, and AMRS scores for well-being (37.00), extroversion (40.58), emotional excitation (28.46), dreaminess (25.48) and activity (24.48), all p < 0.001, and for inactivity (7.72, p = 0.009) and introversion (10.05, p = 0.003); anxiety was not raised. The text prints no means; they are in Figure 1 and Supplementary Table S1 (not read).

Sex and self-rated happiness: a sex-by-treatment interaction for 'happy' (F(1,31) = 10.49, p = 0.003), but post hoc tests found no difference between men and women after MDMA; no other sex-by-treatment interaction on the self-ratings.
key_findings.locator: Results > Subjective effects, 1st paragraph (last two sentences)

key_findings.finding: Empathy test: MDMA raised explicit and implicit emotional empathy ratings across all volunteers (F(1,31) = 6.05, p = 0.019; 4.29, p = 0.047), significant for positive scenes (8.60, p = 0.006; 5.02, p = 0.032) and not for negative scenes; interaction with sex for implicit empathy (4.68, p = 0.039) and a trend for explicit (3.03, p = 0.092); post hoc, the rises were significant in men only (p = 0.025 explicit, 0.022 implicit); cognitive empathy was unchanged.

Money allocation (Social Value Orientation): the prosocial angle rose after MDMA (F(1,31) = 4.42, p = 0.044) with a sex interaction (5.52, p = 0.026); post hoc significant in men (p = 0.008) and not in women; men's level after MDMA equalled women's after placebo; the inequality-aversion index tended to fall (F(1,20) = 3.39, p = 0.079).
key_findings.locator: Results > Social Value Orientation, 1st paragraph; Figure 3

key_findings.finding: Face recognition: accuracy fell after MDMA overall (F(1,31) = 28.63, p < 0.001) and for fearful (14.90), angry (18.60), disgusted (5.81, p = 0.022) and surprised (9.79, p = 0.004) faces but not happy faces (0.27, p = 0.607); the fall was significant in women (p < 0.001) and not men; in women only, fearful (p < 0.001), angry (p = 0.007) and sad (p = 0.010) faces were named less accurately; the detection threshold for fearful faces rose (F(1,31) = 4.92, printed P < 0.032). MDMA's effect on recognising fearful and sad faces differed between women and men (sex-by-treatment F(1,31) = 6.61, p = 0.015, and 9.42, p = 0.005). In women, fear recognition accuracy was lower the higher the plasma MDMA (Cmax Rp = -0.62, P = 0.014; AUC0-6h Rp = -0.66, P = 0.006; n = 16; editors' calculation: P = 0.014 fits 15 women, P = 0.006 fits 16).
key_findings.locator: Results > Facial emotion recognition, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Hormones: plasma oxytocin (F(1,31) = 19.84), cortisol (98.70) and prolactin (127.81) rose after MDMA (p < 0.001); copeptin and testosterone did not; no correlation between the hormone changes and the empathy or prosocial changes. Peak MDMA level was higher in women (269.9 ng/mL) than in men (209) at the same 125 mg (1.68 mg/kg in men, 2.09 in women). Printed pharmacokinetics (mean, SEM): AUC0-6h 926.8 (29.3) ng/mL h in men and 1146.5 (37.9) in women, F(1,15) = 20.77; Tmax 2.44 h (0.14) overall, 2.10 (0.20) in men and 2.75 (0.17) in women.
key_findings.locator: Results > Endocrine effects and pharmacokinetics of MDMA, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limits stated by the authors: one dose only, relatively high with obvious subjective effects; although the design was double blind with identical placebo, most volunteers realised which treatment they had, which may have biased task performance; a relatively large number of statistical comparisons; the authors call the dose relevant to recreational and clinical use, citing earlier papers. The limitations give avoiding exposure of mostly drug-naive volunteers to more than two doses of MDMA as the reason no dose-response study was done, although the Methods describe one MDMA session per person.

The Introduction states, citing earlier laboratory and clinical papers rather than a survey, that enhanced empathy and sociability are also considered a major reason for recreational use of MDMA; this paper presents no data on why people take MDMA.
key_findings.note: Second-hand statement of the authors; the cited papers were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: Tests of the treatment-by-sex interaction are printed with 1 and 31 degrees of freedom, though sex is a between-person factor with 32 volunteers, which leaves 30 error degrees of freedom (editors' calculation); the printed p-values fit 30 (for example F 4.68 gives p = 0.0386 with 30 and 0.0383 with 31; printed 0.039), and the fear detection threshold F(1,31) = 4.92 is printed 'P < 0.032' where p = 0.034.
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on any conclusion; the models are not described precisely.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison of peak plasma MDMA between women and men is printed with 1 and 15 degrees of freedom (F 35.73 and 20.77), and the inequality-aversion test with 1 and 20; the latter was run in volunteers 'with a prosocial orientation' (p. 1647), without saying how many.
reporting_issues.consequence: Who contributed plasma and inequality-aversion data is unclear; with 32 volunteers a sex comparison would have 30 error degrees of freedom.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion give the sex-specific effects as results (empathy and prosociality 'in men', impaired recognition 'particularly in women'); they rest on post hoc tests after interactions at p = 0.020 to 0.039 (p = 0.092 for explicit empathy) among at least 42 uncorrected tests, in 16 people per sex.
reporting_issues.consequence: Treat the sex differences as hypotheses; the paper's own limitation (a large number of comparisons) applies most to them.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors state that most volunteers realised which treatment they had, yet no check of the blind and no active placebo are reported, and the empathy, money-allocation and face tasks followed the drug effect by 2 to 4 hours.
reporting_issues.consequence: Task results may partly reflect expectancy; self-ratings of drug effect cannot be blind by nature.

reporting_issues.issue: No means or SDs for the task and rating outcomes are printed in the text (the pharmacokinetic means are, with SEM); the values are in the figures and a supplement.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes can only be read approximately from the figures (given under analysis); the supplement was not read.

reporting_issues.issue: The printed areas under the plasma MDMA curve (AUC0-6h 926.8 ng/mL h in men, 1146.5 in women, p. 1648) do not match Figure 4E: the area under its plotted mean curves is about 866 (men) and 921 (women) ng/mL h (editors' trapezoid calculation from the plotted means; the area under a mean curve equals the mean of the individual areas). The curves peak at about 183 (men) and 194 (women) ng/mL at 2.5 h, below the printed mean Cmax of 209 and 269.9, which by itself is expected, since people peak at different times.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the sex difference in plasma levels is uncertain (about 20% smaller in women by the figure); the paper does not explain the gap.
reporting_issues.locator: Results > Endocrine effects and pharmacokinetics of MDMA, 2nd paragraph; Figure 4E

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes 'a trend reduction in inequality-aversion' (p. 1648), but by the paper's own definition (index 0 = perfect inequality aversion, p. 1646) a lower index after MDMA means a shift towards inequality aversion, as the Results say (p. 1647).
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of this non-significant trend is stated the wrong way round in the Discussion; the Results and Figure 3 are consistent with each other.
reporting_issues.locator: Methods (definition of the index); Results > Social Value Orientation, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
