design_detail: Secondary pooled analysis of placebo-controlled, double-blind laboratory studies of oral MDMA run separately at three sites: San Francisco (45 people), Chicago (95) and Basel (80), 220 healthy volunteers in all. Volunteers received placebo or MDMA (1.5 mg/kg at San Francisco and Chicago; a fixed 125 mg at Basel); the models carry participant as a random effect, which implies placebo and MDMA sessions in the same person, but the paper does not say so outright and gives no number of sessions per person, order or spacing. Some of the original studies had further sessions (other doses, an active comparison drug, a pretreatment medicine) that are not analysed. Peak change from baseline in heart rate, blood pressure and five 100-mm visual analogue ratings was compared across sites with multilevel linear models (fixed effects drug, site and sex; random effects past MDMA use and participant). A second analysis related each person's lifetime number of earlier MDMA uses (log of 1 plus the number) to the peak rating or reading after MDMA, site by site. Some San Francisco and Chicago data were unpublished at the time.
can_establish: Whether, in 220 healthy volunteers tested at three sites, a single oral dose of MDMA raised heart rate, blood pressure and ratings of drug effect, drug liking and stimulation to a similar degree at sites that differed in participants' MDMA experience, instructions, whether staff were in the room and whether people lay in bed; that ratings of closeness to others and of anxiety after MDMA differed between some sites; and, as an association between different people, that a higher number of earlier MDMA uses went with a lower 'any drug effect' rating at the two sites that tested experienced people (significant in Chicago, a trend in San Francisco).
cannot_establish: That the sites are equivalent (no equivalence test; a non-significant site difference in groups of 45 to 95 does not show the effects are the same); the size of any effect (the text prints no means, SDs or effect sizes for MDMA against placebo; they are in Figure 2, an image not extracted); anything about doses other than about 1.5 mg/kg (Basel's fixed 125 mg averaged 1.89 mg/kg, 26% more per kilogram than 1.5 mg/kg; editors' calculation); that earlier use made the response weaker (the use-history analysis compares different people; age, other drugs, why people kept using and recall of past use are not controlled; the decline is significant at one site only, Chicago, with San Francisco at trend level, and Basel shows a significant rise in the opposite direction); the response of people new to MDMA outside Basel (the other two sites required earlier use); sex differences (the paper says sex changed no result and prints no statistics); events outside the laboratory such as heat, dancing, crowding, other drugs or pills of unknown content.

sample.recruitment: Not described beyond healthy young adults screened for psychiatric and medical problems at all three sites; the source of volunteers and any payment are not stated in this paper (Methods and Materials > Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Similar across sites with differences in current drug use: current alcohol and nicotine use allowed at all sites (smoking limited to fewer than 7 cigarettes a day in Basel and fewer than 10 in Chicago); current cannabis use excluded in Basel only; some earlier MDMA use required in Chicago and San Francisco but not in Basel; a negative test for alcohol and other drugs before each session at every site. Excluded: a current Axis I disorder including substance dependence (DSM-IV) and any cardiovascular or neurological disorder that would raise risk (Methods and Materials > Participants, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Age 25.4 (SD 5.2) years and weight 68.8 (SD 11.6) kg overall; 44% women; lifetime MDMA use from 0 to 200 occasions. By site (Table 1): age 28.0 (6.7), 24.3 (4.5) and 25.4 (5.2); lifetime uses 32.8 (37.0), 13.1 (13.5) and 0.6 (0.6) for San Francisco, Chicago and Basel. 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory. Other drug histories were not available for San Francisco; in Basel 79 of 80 drank alcohol and 69 had used cannabis at least once; in Chicago 89 of 95 drank alcohol and 75 currently smoked cannabis (about 10 days a month) (Results > Participants).
sample.attrition: The paper counts the 220 who completed the study procedures; how many were enrolled and how many dropped out are not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers screened to be healthy. At San Francisco and Chicago they were chosen because they had used MDMA before; at Basel most were new to it, so site and experience are mixed up. Chicago volunteers were told they might receive a stimulant, sedative, cannabinoid or placebo (the Discussion also lists an opioid; Table 1 does not) and were alone; San Francisco and Basel volunteers were told MDMA or placebo and had researchers in the room. People who completed the study are the only ones described.

exposure.measurement: Oral capsules given double blind: placebo or MDMA by weight (1.5 mg/kg at San Francisco and Chicago) or a fixed 125 mg (Basel). Abstinence from drugs and alcohol checked by urine (all sites) and breath (San Francisco, Chicago) before each session; pregnancy test for women. The paper does not say where the MDMA came from or whether its content was checked.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one oral dose per session, 1.5 mg/kg (San Francisco, Chicago) or 125 mg (Basel; Table 1 gives 1.89 mg/kg, SD 0.33), given in the morning (Table 1: 11 am San Francisco, 9:30 am Chicago, 8 to 9 am Basel). Lifetime earlier MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions, by self-report.
exposure.polysubstance: Volunteers tested negative for alcohol and other drugs before each session; current alcohol and nicotine use allowed everywhere, current cannabis use in Chicago and San Francisco but not Basel; no data on other drugs for San Francisco. Other drug use is not an adjustment variable in the models.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Urine tests at all sites and breath tests at San Francisco and Chicago before each session; no minimum time since the last MDMA use is stated.

comparison.controls: Placebo in the same people (participant as a random effect); some sites' studies also had other conditions. Sites are compared with each other: different people.
comparison.matching: No matching between sites. Sites differ in age, MDMA experience, nationality, language, dose per kilogram, time of day, instructions about possible drugs, whether researchers were present and whether people lay in bed or walked about.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Why people had used MDMA, the amounts and the content of pills in earlier use, other drug use outside Basel and Chicago, and personality are not measured; the use-history analysis has no measurement from before the first use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group); people who currently used cannabis were included in Chicago and San Francisco and excluded in Basel.

outcomes.instruments: Heart rate and blood pressure; five visual analogue scales on a 100-mm line from not at all to extremely: any drug effect, liking the drug effects, stimulated, anxious, closeness to others; measured at baseline and repeatedly for several hours; analysed as peak change from baseline (Methods and Materials > Procedure, Dependent Measures, and Drug; Data Analysis).
outcomes.validity_norms: Single-item visual analogue scales; no validation or norms given; the cardiovascular devices are not described.
outcomes.operationalization: One peak value per person and condition. Earlier MDMA use was transformed to the log of 1 plus the number of occasions (base not stated) to reduce non-normal residuals.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None stated; p < 0.05 for all analyses. Editors' count of 8: heart rate, systolic and diastolic pressure and the five visual analogue ratings; the text says some data are not shown.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double blind by design; no check of whether volunteers could tell MDMA from placebo; they were told different things about the possible drugs (MDMA or placebo at San Francisco and Basel; stimulant, sedative, cannabinoid or placebo in Chicago).

analysis.effect_sizes: The text prints no means, SDs, effect sizes or test statistics for MDMA against placebo or for the site comparisons, only p-value ranges: cardiovascular site comparisons p = 0.15 to 1.00; peak ratings of any drug effect, drug liking and stimulation after MDMA p = 0.07 to 1.00; values are in Figures 1 and 2 (images, not extracted). Printed for use history: use-by-site interaction for any drug effect F(2, 218) = 4.74, p = 0.010; the rating fell by 6.8 points (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7) for each unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago, by 5.8 (CI -1.00 to 12.53; p = 0.094) in San Francisco and by 6.1 (CI 2.18 to 10.0) in the two together; in Basel it rose by 13.5 points (CI 1.63 to 25.3). No other relation between past use and an acute effect was significant.
analysis.covariates: Drug, site and sex as fixed effects; past MDMA use and participant as random effects; the authors state sex altered no result (no statistics). Age, other drug use and dose per kilogram are not adjusted for.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The paper reports no registration of this pooled analysis and cites none for the source studies. It says some of the data were published before (Harris et al. 2002; Bedi et al. 2010; Hysek et al. 2012) and some, from San Francisco and Chicago, were not; by authorship the three papers belong to the San Francisco, Chicago and Basel groups.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract and Conclusion present the sites' agreement as established, but the drug-against-placebo statistics are not printed; subjective results are given as p-value ranges and by figure, and the text says some data are not shown. Only one of five ratings was related to earlier use. The abstract says the inverse relation held at the sites that tested more experienced people; in San Francisco alone it was at trend level (p = 0.094).
analysis.power: No power calculation; the authors treat 220 individual-level records as a strength. Sites of 45 to 95 people can miss moderate differences, and the slope intervals are wide (0.9 to 12.7 points in Chicago).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 220 healthy volunteers at three sites a single oral dose of MDMA raised heart rate, blood pressure and subjective ratings. The text reports no significant site difference in peak ratings of any drug effect, drug liking or stimulation after MDMA (p = 0.07 to 1.00), higher peak anxious ratings in Chicago, where people were tested alone, than at the other two sites, and higher closeness to others in San Francisco than in Basel; after placebo, Chicago volunteers rated drug effect and liking higher than the others. A higher number of earlier MDMA uses went with a lower any-drug-effect rating in Chicago (significant) and San Francisco (trend) and a higher one in Basel (fewer than three earlier uses). No size of any effect is printed in the text.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusion say MDMA's effects are robust and reproducible across settings, that cardiovascular and subjective effects were very similar at the sites, and that there is modest evidence of tolerance in people who use it regularly; the Discussion calls the data the strongest support so far for repeated use weakening the subjective experience and says they give little support for a much stronger first response.

timeline.event: Harris et al., subjective and hormonal effects of MDMA (cited here as earlier publication of some data; by authorship the San Francisco group).
Bedi et al., prosocial feelings and identification of emotions (cited here as earlier publication of some data; by authorship the Chicago group).
Hysek and Liechti, pupillary light reflex after MDMA alone and after pretreatments (cited here as earlier publication of some data; by authorship the Basel group).
Pooled analysis of nine Basel studies in 166 volunteers; it probably overlaps this paper's Basel group of 80 (five studies of 16 fit that number) but neither paper says so.

replication.where_it_stands: A rise in heart rate, blood pressure and positive ratings after one oral dose in laboratory settings is reported by several independent laboratories, and this paper is itself the cross-laboratory comparison; its statement of similarity is not quantified in the text. The link between earlier use and a weaker any-drug-effect rating rests on this paper alone and on one of five ratings.

funding.funder: Grants DA02812 and DA026570 (Chicago, H. de Wit principal investigator), DA017716 and DA016776 (San Francisco, J. E. Mendelson) and SNSF320030_138481 and SNFF32323B_144996 (Basel, M. E. Liechti), as printed (Acknowledgements); the paper does not spell out the funders' names (editors' reading of the prefixes: the US National Institute on Drug Abuse and the Swiss National Science Foundation).
funding.declared_conflicts: None (Conflict of Interest Statement).
funding.affiliations_note: The authors include the principal investigators of the three sites whose data are pooled, so the paper reports on the groups' own studies; the Basel data probably also feed Vizeli and Liechti (2017).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study that gives the same measured dose, with the same instructions and setting, to volunteers who are new to MDMA and to volunteers with a range of earlier use, at more than one site, with pre-specified equivalence margins for the subjective ratings and earlier use recorded in detail (number, amounts, last use, content of pills); and a within-person repeat of the laboratory session in people who go on to use MDMA outside the laboratory.

domains.note: Double blind is stated; whether session order was randomised or counterbalanced, and the gap between sessions, are not given in this paper, and some of the original studies had further sessions (other doses, an active drug, a pretreatment).
Washout intervals are not reported here, so carryover cannot be judged.

Volunteers were told different things about the possible drugs; placebo ratings of drug effect and liking differed by site, which the authors link to expectancy; whether people could tell MDMA from placebo was not checked.
Only the 220 who completed the procedures are described; enrolment and dropout are not reported.
Single-item self-ratings by people who may have known the condition; devices not described; sites differed in time of day and setting (in bed or ambulatory; researchers present or absent).
No registration; p-value ranges printed in place of effect sizes; some results not shown; only one of five ratings related to earlier use; no correction for multiple tests.

domains.domain: Use-history and between-site analyses (added by the editors; not a RoB 2 domain)
domains.note: Correlational and between different people: age, other drug use, recall of past use and site are mixed up (the sites differ in age and in how much earlier use they allowed); the sign is opposite in Basel; the log base is not stated.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The comparison of MDMA with placebo in the same people is at some concerns at worst, but its numbers are not printed in the text, so the source cannot give the size of effects. The overall judgment is set by the cross-site and use-history analyses, which are observational. The source may be cited for the design and sample; for the statement that three sites reported similar peak ratings of drug effect, drug liking and stimulation, with named differences in closeness to others and anxiety; and for the observation that the any-drug-effect rating was lower with more earlier use at two sites. It should not be cited for the size of effects, for equivalence between sites, for tolerance as a cause, or for sex differences.

key_findings.finding: Three sites pooled: San Francisco 45 people (20 women, 25 men; 1.5 mg/kg; researchers present; 11 am), Chicago 95 (37 women, 58 men; 1.5 mg/kg; people alone; 9:30 am; told they might receive a stimulant, sedative, cannabinoid or placebo) and Basel 80 (40 women, 40 men; a fixed 125 mg, 1.89 mg/kg (SD 0.33); researchers present; 8 to 9 am; told MDMA or placebo).

220 volunteers (44% women), age 25.4 (SD 5.2), weight 68.8 (SD 11.6) kg; lifetime MDMA use 0 to 200 occasions, 32.8 (SD 37.0) in San Francisco, 13.1 (13.5) in Chicago and 0.6 (0.6) in Basel; 35 people, all in Basel, had never taken MDMA outside the laboratory. San Francisco volunteers were older and more experienced than the other two groups, and Chicago more experienced than Basel (all p < 0.05).

MDMA raised heart rate and blood pressure to a similar degree at the three sites (site comparison p = 0.15 to 1.00) and produced similar reports on most subjective ratings; peak ratings of any drug effect, drug liking and stimulation after MDMA did not differ between sites (p = 0.07 to 1.00). The values are in Figures 1 and 2, which are images and were not extracted.
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute Effects of MDMA across Sites, 1st paragraph; Figures 1 and 2
key_findings.note: No means or effect sizes in the text; absence of a significant site difference is not equivalence.

key_findings.finding: Site differences: after MDMA, Chicago volunteers gave higher peak anxious ratings than San Francisco and Basel volunteers, and San Francisco volunteers higher peak closeness to others than Basel volunteers (p < 0.05 for each); after placebo, Chicago volunteers gave higher peak drug effect and drug liking than the other two sites (p < 0.01) and Basel volunteers had lower peak systolic and diastolic pressure (p < 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Results > Acute Effects of MDMA across Sites, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Earlier use: the any-drug-effect rating after MDMA related to lifetime MDMA use differently by site (use-by-site F(2, 218) = 4.74, p = 0.010). It fell by 6.8 points (95% CI 0.913 to 12.7) per unit of log(1 + earlier uses) in Chicago, by 5.8 (CI -1.00 to 12.53; p = 0.094) in San Francisco and by 6.1 (CI 2.18 to 10.0) in the two together; in Basel, where people had used MDMA fewer than three times or not at all, it rose by 13.5 (CI 1.63 to 25.3). No other relation between earlier use and an acute effect reached significance.
key_findings.locator: Results > Relationship between acute drug-related effects and MDMA use history, 1st paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: The log base is not stated, so slopes cannot be converted to points per additional use.

key_findings.finding: The authors read the finding as modest evidence of tolerance in people with heavier use and as little support for the idea that the first experience is much stronger than later ones. They offer other explanations: people with heavier use may also use other potent drugs, tolerance may be specific to the setting, and the any-drug-effect rating is a global item that may be more sensitive than the others.

The authors suggest, without testing it, that having researchers in the room (San Francisco, Basel) may have raised prosocial and lowered negative ratings compared with being alone (Chicago), and note that closeness ratings fell with earlier use in San Francisco at trend level (p = 0.07).

Sex: the paper states that participant sex did not alter any result and discusses it no further in the Results; the Discussion notes that other studies found women reported stronger subjective responses.
key_findings.locator: Data Analysis, last sentence; Discussion, 7th paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: The text prints no means, SDs or test statistics for the effect of MDMA against placebo on any rating or on heart rate and blood pressure, and gives site comparisons only as p-value ranges; the values are in figures.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the effects, and how close the sites are, cannot be read from the text; the claim of very similar effects rests on non-significance in groups of 45 to 95.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction says all sites gave comparable, moderate doses (1.5 mg/kg or 125 mg), but Table 1 gives 1.89 mg/kg (SD 0.33) at Basel against 1.5 at the other sites, 26% more per kilogram (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Basel's dose per kilogram was higher; agreement across sites despite this is informative, but the doses are not the same.

reporting_issues.issue: The use-by-site interaction is printed with 2 and 218 degrees of freedom. A model with site, earlier use and their interaction fitted to 220 people has 214 residual degrees of freedom (editors' calculation); 218 would fit a model with one predictor. The printed p (0.010) is the same either way.
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the result; the model is not fully described.

reporting_issues.issue: Earlier use was transformed as the log of 1 plus the number of occasions without saying which base.
reporting_issues.consequence: Slopes of 5.8 to 13.5 points per unit cannot be turned into points per extra use; with base 10 or base e they differ by a factor of about 2.3.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the inverse relation between earlier use and the any-drug-effect rating held at the sites testing more experienced people; Chicago alone was significant (p < 0.05) and San Francisco alone was at trend level (p = 0.094); the two together were significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Evidence of a lower rating with more use rests mainly on Chicago and on pooling two sites; it is one of five ratings tested.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC4161650 (author manuscript), read in the app's browser: abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion, Table 1, figure legends, funding and conflict statements. Figures 1 to 3 are images and were not read for values. No supplementary files exist or were read.

design_detail: Naturalistic prospective field study with repeated measures over one week, no placebo and no random allocation. Three self-selected groups of 15 (ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use; one to nine; never) were tested four times: drug-free at home before a Saturday night out, at a London nightclub 2 to 8 hours after tablets they chose to take (8 of 30 at 8 to 16 hours), and 2 and 7 days later. Outcomes: 16 single-item visual analogue mood scales, a 16-word auditory recall task (two lists per session) and a computerized visual search task. Two-way (mood, memory) and three-way (visual search) analyses of variance, then one-way analyses of variance at each session with Duncan tests of each ecstasy group against the comparison group. Tape-recorded interviews are quoted in the Discussion but not described in the Methods.
can_establish: How self-rated moods and test scores changed from a drug-free session to a club night and over the following week in a small, self-selected London sample of people who chose to take ecstasy, compared with people at the same club who did not.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused any of the changes (no placebo, self-chosen tablets of untested content, alcohol and other drugs on the night, sleep and later drug use not recorded), how large or how common a low mood in the days after is among people who use ecstasy, or anything about lasting memory damage (the ecstasy groups already recalled fewer words before the night, and earlier ability was never measured).

sample.recruitment: Community, snowball sampling: word of the study spread among friends and acquaintances who regularly went to a large nightclub in the Epping Forest area of north-east London; participants were unpaid (Materials and methods › Subjects, p. 262).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Groups defined by self-reported lifetime occasions of MDMA use: ten or more, one to nine, or never (p. 262). The baseline session was held only when people were drug-free by their own account: no MDMA for at least 1 week and no other illicit drug for over 24 hours (Procedures and ethics, p. 262). No other inclusion or exclusion criteria (psychiatric or medical history, medicines, pregnancy) are reported.
sample.demographics: Mean age 21.4 (regular group), 22.8 (novice group) and 21.3 (comparison group) years, range 19 to 30; women/men 8/7, 8/7 and 10/5 (p. 262). Education, employment, IQ, psychiatric history, duration of ecstasy use and lifetime use of other drugs are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not reported: the paper does not say whether all 45 attended all four sessions, and no numbers per session are printed. Eight of the 30 people in the ecstasy groups (four per group) were tested at the club 8 to 16 hours after their tablets instead of the planned 2 to 8 hours (p. 263).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers from the social circle of the experimenters around one club, who were told the study's aims beforehand (p. 263) and knew their own group; groups formed by people's own past and planned drug use. The comparison group were clubbers who mostly drank alcohol that night, not a drug-free group, which the authors name as a limit (p. 266). Not representative of people who use ecstasy in general.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: lifetime occasions of MDMA use for group membership, and the drugs taken that night, noted by each person on a self-rating questionnaire (p. 262). No urine, blood or saliva tests and no testing of the tablets; abstinence before the baseline session also self-reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study condition, as self-reported: 1.80 tablets on average in the regular group and 1.45 in the novice group on the Saturday night; the comparison group took none (abstract, p. 261; p. 262). No spread, range or test of the difference is printed, and the authors describe it as slightly more. Oral tablets (implied, not stated). Lifetime occasions beyond the group cut-offs, frequency and duration of use are not reported. The paper does not discuss tolerance.
exposure.polysubstance: On the night (p. 262): alcohol by 10 of 15 in the comparison group (5.0 drinks per drinker), 5 in the novice group (2.7) and 6 in the regular group (3.7); cannabis by 3, 1 and 2; cocaine by 2, 2 and 4; amphetamine by 1 person in the novice group. The abstract and Discussion call other-drug use at the club similar across groups, without a test. Lifetime and recent use of other drugs, and any drug use between the club night and the 2- and 7-day sessions, are not reported. Nothing was adjusted for.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Baseline: no MDMA for at least 1 week and no other illicit drug for over 24 hours, self-reported, not verified (p. 262). The 2- and 7-day sessions: abstinence since the club night is not reported.

comparison.controls: 15 people from the same social circle who had never taken MDMA, tested at the same club at equivalent times; 10 of them drank alcohol that night, 3 smoked cannabis and 2 took cocaine (pp. 262-263).
comparison.matching: Not matched by design; ages and sex ratios described as similar (21.3 against 21.4 and 22.8 years; women/men 10/5 against 8/7 and 8/7), not tested (p. 262).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of earlier cognitive ability, education, IQ, mood or psychiatric history. At the drug-free baseline the ecstasy groups already recalled fewer words (12.0 and 13.9 against 15.1 of 32) and the novice group already rated itself sadder (31 against 22) (Table 2, p. 264). Sleep, food and fluid intake, and hangover were not measured at any session.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Yes: mainly alcohol on the night (10 of 15; 5.0 drinks per drinker), with cannabis (3) and cocaine (2); lifetime use of other drugs not reported (p. 262).

outcomes.instruments: Auditory word recall: lists of 16 words heard over headphones at one word every 2 s, written free recall after 30 s, two lists per session (maximum 32, per the axis of Fig. 1), eight lists rotated across sessions and matched for word frequency and length (p. 262; Fig. 1, p. 265). Visual search on an Apple Newton Messagepad: target letter L among X (easy) or T (hard) distractors in arrays of 2 x 2 to 5 x 5, of which only 2 x 2 and 4 x 4 were analysed; response time in seconds (p. 262; Fig. 2, p. 265). Sixteen unipolar visual analogue mood scales from 0 (do not feel at all) to 100 (feel completely) on the same device: abnormal, calm, clearheaded, depressed, drowsy, energetic, good tempered, ill, interested, quick witted, sad, sober, steady, unpleasant, unsociable and well co-ordinated (p. 262; Table 2, p. 264). Tape-recorded interviews quoted in the Discussion (pp. 265-267), method not described.
outcomes.validity_norms: The recall task is cited as sensitive to scopolamine and the visual search task to alcohol (earlier work by the first author and others, p. 262). No validity data or norms for the single-item mood scales. The mood list has no items on elation or empathy, which the authors note may have made it insensitive to the effects people seek (p. 267).
outcomes.operationalization: Impairment or a mood difference means a lower or higher group mean than the comparison group at a session on a Duncan test, with p < 0.10 reported as a borderline trend; change over the week is read from the group means at each session and the group-by-session interaction (pp. 263-264).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 21 measures (16 mood scales, word recall and four visual-search conditions) at four sessions, each ecstasy group compared with the comparison group by Duncan's multiple range test, a lenient post hoc procedure: 168 comparisons (editors' count), with p < 0.10 reported as trends. Some results at p < 0.05 would be expected by chance alone.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None reported. The experimenter recruited and knew the participants and their groups and tested them, including at the club; the mood ratings are self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims; who scored the written recall, and whether blind to group, is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Not computable: the paper prints group means only (Table 2, p. 264) and significance symbols (Tables 1 and 2), with no SDs, F values, degrees of freedom or intervals; Figs 1 and 2 show standard-error bars, which were not read as numbers. Key means (comparison, novice, regular): mood on 0 to 100 scales, at the club sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10), abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01), good tempered 85, 90 and 88; 2 days later sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01), depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10), unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); 7 days later no difference on these. Word recall of 32: baseline 15.1, 13.9 (p < 0.10) and 12.0 (p < 0.01); club 13.5, 9.6 and 8.1 (both p < 0.01); 2 days 12.9, 11.9 and 11.1 (p < 0.05); 7 days 13.4, 11.7 and 11.4 (both p < 0.05). Visual search, 4 x 4 hard, at the club 4.1, 6.9 (p < 0.10) and 8.9 s (p < 0.01). Editors' calculation: at the club the novice and regular groups recalled 71% and 60% of the comparison group's mean (the paper says 60-70%).
analysis.covariates: None. No adjustment for age, sex, alcohol or other drugs on the night, sleep, the timing of the club session or the baseline differences.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Study published in 1998; no protocol or registration is reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Only two of the four visual-search array sizes were analysed, by the authors' stated choice of two levels of difficulty (p. 262). All 16 mood scales are reported in Table 2. The novice and regular groups were never compared with each other, although the Discussion ranks them (p. 266). Interview excerpts are quoted with no method and no account of how they were chosen (pp. 265-267).
analysis.power: No power calculation; 15 people per group.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 45 self-selected people around one London club, the two ecstasy groups did not rate their moods clearly better than other clubbers on the night (only p < 0.10 trends for less sadness, and higher 'abnormal' ratings). Two days later they rated their moods lower than the comparison group: sadness and unsociability in both groups; depression, unpleasantness and lower good temper at p < 0.05 in the novice group but only at p < 0.10 in the regular group. Seven days later the groups were alike again. Word recall was lower in the ecstasy groups at the club and, for the regular group, at every session including the drug-free one before the night. No spread, effect sizes or correction for 168 comparisons is reported.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says that two days afterwards the people in the ecstasy groups, taken together, felt significantly more depressed, abnormal, unsociable, unpleasant and less good tempered than the comparison group; at p < 0.05 this holds for the novice group, but for the regular group only for abnormal and unsociable (p. 261 against Table 2, p. 264). The abstract also says both tasks were significantly impaired on-MDMA, while at the club the novice group did not reach p < 0.05 on any visual-search condition (Table 2). The abstract and Discussion read the drug-free memory differences as suggesting MDMA neurotoxicity in humans, and the Discussion finds consistent evidence that they may reflect serotonergic neurodegeneration "directly caused by MDMA self-administration" (p. 266), although the groups were self-selected, already differed before the night and earlier ability was not measured; the alternatives (chance, self-selection, other drugs) are set aside mainly by appeal to other studies, and for other drugs by similar use on the one night rather than lifetime use. The low moods are attributed to serotonin depletion, which was not measured (pp. 266-267). In the paper's favour, it reports plainly that the ecstasy groups showed no mood advantage at the club, calls this unexpected and discusses context, expectancy, the comparison group's drinking and ceiling effects (pp. 266-267).

timeline.event: Curran and Travill (Addiction): 12 people who used ecstasy and 12 who drank alcohol, at a Saturday dance and 1 and 4 days later; better moods on the night and worse in the days after by group-by-time interaction, but no drug-free baseline and no analysis of each session separately (as described in this paper, p. 262). Not read for this card; no reference record yet.
This study: the first, by its own account, to test mood and cognition at a club against a drug-free baseline (p. 267).

Parrott's review of chronic tolerance cites this study's tablet figures correctly (1.45 against 1.80, p. 74) but calls the regular group more than 10 occasions (here ten or more) and treats the figures as an index of chronic tolerance, which this paper does not discuss; it also lists this study among those showing an association between past use and neurocognitive impairment (p. 77), although the novice and regular groups were never compared statistically here.

replication.where_it_stands: For mood, the two-day low agrees in direction with the one earlier club study the paper cites (Curran and Travill, 1997), whose session-by-session differences were not analysed; later field studies of the days after were not read for this card. For memory, the comparison is in effect cross-sectional (the differences were present before the night) and belongs with the contested literature on lasting effects, not as evidence of change. The tablet figures are reported correctly in the 2005 review that uses them.

funding.funder: None stated. The acknowledgements (p. 267) thank Dr Brian Tiplady (Astra Pharmaceuticals) for the loan of his Apple Messagepad cognitive test system, and John Turner for comments and suggestions.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement is printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors: Department of Psychology, University of East London (p. 261). The first author is the sole author of the 2005 review (card sc_parrott_2005) that cites this study's tablet figures. The study was approved by the University Ethics Committee, with written informed consent (p. 263).

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective study at real events in which the pills are drug-checked (content and amount measured) and use is checked biologically, with a comparison group at the same events whose alcohol and other drug use is measured, daily mood ratings for a week on scales that include the effects people seek, sleep and later drug use recorded, raters or analysts blind to group where possible, and spread and effect sizes reported.

domains.note: People chose their own drugs and nothing was adjusted for. On the night the comparison group mostly drank alcohol (10 of 15; 5.0 drinks per drinker) and cocaine was taken by 4 of 15 in the regular group against 2 in each other group; sleep, food, fluids, hangover and drug use after the night were not measured. The drug-free baseline and repeated measures handle stable differences between people for mood, but the groups already differed before the night on word recall and, in the novice group, on sadness; for the memory differences alone, confounding would be very high.
Self-reported tablets of untested content and self-reported lifetime occasions; no biological check of use on the night or of abstinence before the baseline.

Unpaid volunteers from the experimenters' social circle around one club, by snowball sampling; taking part and group membership both depend on people's own drug use; the direction of any bias is unclear.
No intervention after the club night is described; drug use after the night is a confounding problem, noted above.
Attendance at each session and any missing values are not reported; 8 of 30 were tested later than planned at the club.

Single-item self-ratings by people who knew the study's aims and their own group, tested by an experimenter who knew them, at a noisy club for the second session; low moods in the days after ecstasy were already a described expectation (the paper cites it, p. 262). Whether recall was scored blind is not stated.

168 uncorrected comparisons with a lenient post hoc test and p < 0.10 reported as trends; two of four visual-search array sizes analysed; significance symbols only, with no test statistics or spread; interviews quoted without a method.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four domains are at high risk and they act together on the results this card is cited for: tablets of untested content and self-reported use, a comparison group that drank alcohol, sleep and later drug use not recorded, self-ratings by participants who knew the aims and their own group, an experimenter who knew them, and 168 uncorrected comparisons reported as significance symbols only. Under ROBINS-E, high risk in several domains that together substantially lower confidence in the result gives very high overall. The design still has what most studies of people who use ecstasy lack: a drug-free session before the night, a comparison group at the same club, and repeated measures over a week. The card may be cited for what this sample reported: tablets noted on the night, as a study condition, and self-rated moods at the club and 2 and 7 days later against other clubbers, with these limits. It may not be cited for what MDMA itself does, for how large or how common a low mood in the days after is, or for memory damage: the ecstasy groups already recalled fewer words before the night, and earlier ability was not measured.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 45 unpaid volunteers aged 19 to 30, recruited by snowball sampling among friends and acquaintances who regularly went to one large nightclub in north-east London, in three self-selected groups of 15: ten or more earlier occasions of ecstasy use (regular group; mean age 21.4; women/men 8/7), one to nine (novice group; 22.8; 8/7) and never (comparison group; 21.3; 10/5). No placebo and no random allocation; each person was tested four times: drug-free at home before a Saturday night out, at the club, and 2 and 7 days later.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 261); Materials and methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 262); Procedures and ethics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (pp. 262-263)

key_findings.finding: Drugs on the night, as each person noted them on a questionnaire: the regular group 1.80 tablets on average and the novice group 1.45 (the authors: slightly more), the comparison group none; no spread, range or test of the difference is printed and the tablets were not tested. Alcohol: 10 of 15 in the comparison group (5.0 drinks per drinker), 5 in the novice group (2.7) and 6 in the regular group (3.7); cannabis 3, 1 and 2; cocaine 2, 2 and 4; amphetamine 1 in the novice group.
key_findings.locator: Abstract (p. 261); Materials and methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph (p. 262)
key_findings.note: These are the tablet figures Parrott (2005, p. 74) cites, correctly; the review calls the regular group more than 10 occasions (here ten or more) and uses the figures as an index of chronic tolerance, which this paper does not discuss. Study conditions only.

key_findings.finding: Session timing: the baseline was held when people were drug-free by their own account (no MDMA for at least 1 week, no other illicit drug for over 24 hours), at their own or the experimenter's home, before the planned night out; the club session was held in a quieter area of a noisy, crowded venue, planned for 2 to 8 hours after the tablets (the comparison group at equivalent times), but 8 of the 30 in the ecstasy groups (four per group) were tested 8 to 16 hours after; the 2- and 7-day sessions were at venues similar to the baseline.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Procedures and ethics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Mood at the club (0 to 100 self-ratings, means; comparison, novice, regular; Duncan tests against the comparison group): good tempered 85, 90 and 88 (no difference); sad 20, 9 and 9 (both p < 0.10); depressed 31, 22 and 20 (regular p < 0.10); abnormal 36, 64 and 74 (both p < 0.01); energetic 51, 62 and 64 and interested 68, 80 and 82 (no difference). The comparison group was less sober (46 against 78, p < 0.05, and 67) and less steady (50 against 76, p < 0.05, and 71, p < 0.10), which the authors attribute to alcohol.

Mood 2 days later: sad 22, 56 and 53 (both p < 0.01); unsociable 16, 39 (p < 0.01) and 33 (p < 0.05); abnormal 6, 23 (p < 0.05) and 26 (p < 0.01); depressed 36, 59 (p < 0.01) and 48 (p < 0.10); unpleasant 15, 36 (p < 0.01) and 28 (p < 0.10); good tempered 85, 65 (p < 0.05) and 72 (p < 0.10); energetic 72, 62 and 56 (regular p < 0.05); drowsy 23, 33 and 35 (regular p < 0.10); steady 95, 93 and 90 (regular p < 0.05); calm, ill, interested and quick witted did not differ.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, mood-scale rows, columns '2 days after'

key_findings.finding: Mood 7 days later: no difference on sad (22, 25 and 21), depressed (37, 37 and 39), unsociable (22, 18 and 18), unpleasant (14, 18 and 16), abnormal (6, 6 and 5) or good tempered (86, 84 and 87); both ecstasy groups rated themselves less drowsy than the comparison group (28, p < 0.05, and 25, p < 0.01, against 38) and the regular group better co-ordinated (91 against 82, p < 0.10).
key_findings.locator: Table 2, mood-scale rows, columns '7 days after'

key_findings.finding: Before the night (drug-free baseline): the novice group rated itself sadder (31 against 22, p < 0.05) and more depressed (45 against 36, p < 0.10) than the comparison group; both ecstasy groups rated themselves more clearheaded (92 and 94 against 86, p < 0.05), and the regular group less drowsy (27 against 44, p < 0.10).

Two-way analyses of variance (group by session) of the 16 mood scales: interaction p < 0.001 for abnormal, depressed and sad; p < 0.01 for sober, unpleasant and unsociable; p < 0.05 for good tempered and steady; not significant for calm, clearheaded, drowsy, energetic, ill, interested, quick witted and well co-ordinated. Group main effects: abnormal p < 0.001; sad and well co-ordinated p < 0.05; depressed, sober and unpleasant p < 0.10. No F values or degrees of freedom are printed.

Word recall (words recalled of 32; comparison, novice, regular): baseline 15.1, 13.9 (p < 0.10) and 12.0 (p < 0.01); at the club 13.5, 9.6 and 8.1 (both p < 0.01); 2 days later 12.9, 11.9 and 11.1 (p < 0.05); 7 days later 13.4, 11.7 and 11.4 (both p < 0.05). Group and session main effects p < 0.001, interaction p < 0.01. The regular group's lower scores were present before the night, and the novice and regular groups were not compared with each other.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 and Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 263); Table 2, row 'Memory word recall' (p. 264); Fig. 1, axis label (p. 265)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: at the club the novice and regular groups recalled 71% and 60% of the comparison group's mean; the paper says 60-70%.

key_findings.finding: Visual search (response time in seconds; comparison, novice, regular): 4 x 4 hard array at the club 4.1, 6.9 (p < 0.10) and 8.9 (p < 0.01), at baseline 2.5, 2.7 and 2.7, at 2 days 3.2, 3.0 and 3.5 and at 7 days 3.6, 3.6 and 3.5. At the club the regular group was slower than the comparison group in all four conditions (one only at p < 0.10) and the novice group reached p < 0.05 in none. At baseline both ecstasy groups were slower on the easy 2 x 2 condition (1.9 and 1.8 against 1.2; p < 0.01 and p < 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Assessment measures, 2nd paragraph (p. 262); Table 2, visual search rows (p. 264); Fig. 2 (p. 265)

key_findings.finding: The authors' reading of the moods: the lack of better moods in the ecstasy groups on the night was unexpected; they offer as reasons that most clubbers would expect a good night out (earlier studies mostly had no comparison group of other clubbers), the comparison group's own drinking and drug use, ratings such as good tempered already near the top of the scale, and a mood list without items on elation or empathy. They conclude that the good moods of all the clubbers show the importance of context and expectancy, and describe marked mood swings over the week in the ecstasy groups against fairly stable moods in the comparison group, which they attribute to serotonin depletion (not measured).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 6th and 7th paragraphs (p. 266, the 7th continued on p. 267) and 9th paragraph (p. 267)

key_findings.finding: Interview excerpts (method not described): people in the ecstasy groups described difficulty with the tasks at the club, mid-week low moods and crying (their own, and among friends who used more drugs), vomiting after each occasion, paranoid feelings, tingling and involuntary arm movements, and two severe emergencies, one about the speaker's partner, who was taken to hospital, and one in which the speaker collapsed at a dance on holiday. These are individual accounts, not measured outcomes.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 265, continued on p. 266), 7th paragraph (continued on p. 267) and 8th paragraph (p. 267)

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says that two days afterwards the people in the ecstasy groups, taken together, felt significantly more depressed, abnormal, unsociable, unpleasant and less good tempered than the comparison group. In Table 2 this holds at p < 0.05 for the novice group; for the regular group only abnormal and unsociable reach p < 0.05, while depressed, unpleasant and good tempered are at p < 0.10. Sad, significant in both groups, is not in the abstract's list.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two-day low is clearer in the novice group than in the regular group; any claim should give the results by group rather than for both ecstasy groups together.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says performance on both tasks was significantly reduced on-MDMA; in Table 2 the novice group does not reach p < 0.05 on any of the four visual-search conditions at the club (one at p < 0.10). The abstract's on-the-night trend for less sadness/depression is p < 0.10 for sadness in both groups but for depression only in the regular group.
reporting_issues.consequence: The visual-search slowing on the night is shown for the regular group only, against a comparison group that had mostly drunk alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion lists calmness among the moods that fluctuated markedly over the week in the ecstasy groups (p. 267), but Table 1 shows no significant session or interaction effect for calm and Table 2 shows calm between 73 and 86 in every group at every session; Fig. 3, cited for the point, shows neither calm nor depression.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor overstatement of the mood swings; the scales that changed are those in Table 1 with significant interactions.

reporting_issues.issue: The regular group is defined as ten or more earlier occasions in the abstract and Methods (pp. 261-262), but as more than ten occasions in the Discussion (pp. 266, 267); the 2005 review repeats more than 10.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: people with exactly ten occasions belong to the regular group.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Discussion call other-drug use at the club similar across groups (pp. 261, 266), but the counts in the Methods (p. 262) are untested and show cocaine use by 4 of 15 in the regular group against 2 in each other group, and alcohol by 10 of 15 in the comparison group against 5 and 6.
reporting_issues.consequence: Differences in cocaine and alcohol use on the night cannot be excluded as contributors to the differences at the club and two days later.

reporting_issues.issue: Tape-recorded interviews are quoted at length in the Discussion (pp. 265-267), including side effects and two medical emergencies, but the Methods do not mention interviews: who was interviewed, when, how many people and how quotations were chosen are not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: The interview material is anecdote, not study data, and cannot support claims about how often anything happens.

reporting_issues.issue: No SDs, F values, degrees of freedom or exact p values are printed anywhere; Tables 1 and 2 give significance symbols only, and the number of people at each session is not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes and their precision cannot be computed, and attrition cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation slips: Squier et al. is cited as 1995 in the text (pp. 261, 266) and listed as 1996 in the references (p. 268); Maxwell et al. is cited as 1994 (p. 261) and 1993 (p. 267) and listed as 1994 (p. 268); Tiplady (1996) in the text is listed as Triplady (p. 268).
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the findings; noted for anyone tracing the cited cases.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 261-268, all pages (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_1998_SaturdayNightDance.pdf in the senior author's upload folder); Tables 1 and 2 checked on rendered pages; Figs 1 to 3 seen on the rendered page, with values taken from Table 2 rather than read from the figures; no supplementary material exists

design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person sleep-laboratory study with counterbalanced session order (incomplete 12-sequence Latin square): 7 adults with recent recreational MDMA use each completed three 3-night sessions, receiving on the treatment night MDMA with a full night in bed, placebo with a full night in bed, or placebo with a restricted night in bed (a positive control for sleep loss), followed by a placebo recovery night. Overnight polysomnography and next-day multiple sleep latency tests. A separate comparison set the participants' first laboratory night and placebo-day sleepiness tests against 13 age-matched people without drug use drawn from a general-population sleep study.
can_establish: Within these 7 people, how MDMA compared with placebo changes polysomnographic sleep that night and the next night, and whether next-day objective sleepiness after MDMA resembles that after placebo or after a night of restricted sleep.
cannot_establish: Effects of MDMA at other doses, taken at parties with dancing, heat, other drugs or no sleep opportunity; effects after repeated use; whether next-day sleepiness after MDMA truly differs from either comparison (it differed from neither, in 7 people); and whether the differences between the MDMA group and the controls were caused by MDMA (cross-sectional, different recruitment and schedules).

sample.recruitment: Public advertisements (MDMA group); comparison group selected from a concurrent southeastern Michigan general-population study of sleep and daytime sleepiness.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 18 to 35; at least high-school education; weight under 91 kg; at least 6 lifetime uses of recreational stimulants including at least 3 recent MDMA uses, one in the past 6 months; no current or past Axis I disorder including drug or alcohol dependence (other than nicotine), abuse allowed if in remission for a year; no more than 100 MDMA uses or 50 uses of stimulants, opioids, phencyclidine or sedatives; not pregnant or lactating. Comparison group: no illicit drug use history, no shift work, sleep disorder, serious illness, substance abuse or psychiatric diagnosis.
sample.demographics: MDMA group: 5 white men, 1 white woman, 1 African American woman; age 19 to 34 (mean 25.3); lifetime MDMA uses mean 27 (range 3 to 75); cannabis 6 of 7, cocaine 1, other stimulants 2, other hallucinogens 2. Usual home schedule (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index): late bedtime and late rising, 7.8 hours of sleep, 17 minutes to fall asleep, Epworth score 6.8. Comparison group: 10 men and 3 women, age-matched.
sample.attrition: Two further participants withdrew (one after the restricted-sleep session; one after the placebo and MDMA sessions) and are not analysed; three planned participants could not be recruited, leaving the Latin square incomplete.
sample.selection_effects: Light-to-moderate MDMA experience (mean 27 uses, against 112 in an earlier study the authors cite), screened free of psychiatric disorders and dependence; the laboratory bedtime was much earlier than the participants' usual one, which the authors note may have lengthened sleep onset in all conditions.

exposure.measurement: Doses given by the investigators under double-blind conditions in a supervised sleep laboratory; urine drug screens and breathalyser negative at the start of every session.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: racemic MDMA hydrochloride (from David Nichols, Purdue University) 2 mg/kg by salt weight, by mouth in a gelatin capsule filled with dextrose, at 18:00 on the treatment night (night 2); identical dextrose placebo capsules otherwise. Time in bed 23:00 to 07:00 (8 hours) on placebo and MDMA nights; 03:00 to 07:00 (4 hours) with placebo on the restricted-sleep night; placebo at 18:00 and 8 hours in bed on the recovery night (night 3). Multiple sleep latency tests at 10:00, 12:00, 14:00 and 16:00 on days 2 and 3. Sessions at least 1 week apart. Participants agreed not to use illicit drugs between sessions, cannabis for 2 days and alcohol for 12 hours before sessions; usual coffee and tobacco allowed at breaks at least 1 hour before each nap test.
exposure.polysubstance: Cannabis (6 of 7) and other drug use history recorded; abstinence before sessions instructed and checked by urine screens (people who used cannabis regularly were tested on the 2 days before and the day of each session).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Negative urine drug screen and breathalyser at the start of each session; supervised throughout sessions.

comparison.controls: Each participant's own placebo session (a full night in bed) and restricted-sleep session (placebo, a shortened night in bed; exposure field). Separately, 13 age-matched people without illicit drug use, recorded on a single night and next day with no capsule.
comparison.matching: Within-person comparisons with counterbalanced order; the comparison group was matched on age only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sleep before any MDMA use is unknown; the authors note it would be important to know whether the disturbances in the MDMA group predated stimulant use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The comparison group had no illicit drug use; the MDMA group's cannabis and other drug use is a confounder for the between-group comparison.

outcomes.instruments: Nocturnal polysomnography (central and occipital EEG, EOG, chin EMG, ECG; Rechtschaffen and Kales scoring by experienced scorers with 90% reliability): total sleep time, latency to persistent sleep, wake after persistent sleep, percentages of stages 1, 2, 3/4 and REM, REM latency. Multiple sleep latency test (four naps): mean sleep latency and sleep-onset REM periods.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard, validated sleep measures; the comparison group's values matched published norms according to the authors.
outcomes.operationalization: Sleep disruption as shorter total sleep, longer sleep latency and shifts in stage percentages; next-day sleepiness as a shorter mean sleep latency on the nap tests.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (eight polysomnographic and two nap-test measures, each in several analyses).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not stated for the scorers; drug administration double-blind (the restricted-sleep condition cannot be blinded).

analysis.effect_sizes: Repeated-measures general linear models (mean and SEM reported). MDMA against placebo over treatment and recovery nights (df 1 and 6): total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes on the treatment night, F = 8.6, P = 0.026; latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes, F = 7.0, P = 0.038; stage 1 8.4 against 6.6%, F = 9.49, P = 0.022; REM 3.5 (2.1) against 19.2 (2.0)%, F = 14.28, P = 0.009, drug by night interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003 (reduced on the treatment night only); stage 2 P = 0.267, stage 3/4 P = 0.119, REM latency P = 0.589, wake after sleep onset not significant. Treatment nights of all three conditions (df 2 and 12): total sleep F = 17.272 (printed P = 0.005); REM F = 15.036, P = 0.001. Next-day nap tests: treatment by day interaction F = 4.63 (df 2 and 12), P = 0.032; condition means only in a figure. MDMA group against comparison group (df 18): first-night total sleep 376.21 (26.7) against 433.43 (13.1) minutes, t = 2.59; stage 3/4 4.8 (0.7)% against 15.7 (3.4)%, t = 2.90; placebo-day mean nap latency 15.6 (1.76) against 10.9 (4.39) minutes, t = 2.84. Editors' arithmetic: MDMA shortened sleep on the treatment night by about 126 minutes, restricted sleep by about 218 minutes.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All polysomnographic measures are tabulated; nap-test values by condition are given only in a figure.
analysis.power: Not addressed; the authors call the study preliminary and name the small sample as a limitation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: MDMA on the treatment night, compared with placebo, cut total sleep by about two hours, mainly by delaying sleep onset, raised light (stage 1) sleep and almost abolished REM sleep (3.5% against 19.2%), with sleep back to placebo levels on the next night. Next-day sleepiness after MDMA did not differ from placebo, but it did not differ from restricted sleep either; restricted sleep made people sleepier than placebo. Against 13 people without drug use, the MDMA group's first laboratory night was shorter with much less slow-wave sleep, and their nap latencies were longer, with more sleep-onset REM periods.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says acute MDMA "reduced stage 3/4 sleep", that MDMA-related sleep loss was not associated with next-day sleepiness, and that people in the MDMA group showed hyperarousal and impaired REM function, likely due to the deleterious effects of MDMA on catecholamines. Gaps: (1) the drug comparison found no effect on stage 3/4 (P = 0.119); the stage 3/4 difference is between the MDMA group and the comparison group; (2) 'not associated with sleepiness' rests on a non-difference in 7 people from a condition that also did not differ from sleep restriction; (3) hyperarousal, impaired REM function and a catecholamine mechanism are inferred from a cross-sectional comparison with a differently recruited group on a different schedule, which cannot show that MDMA caused the differences, as the authors partly concede.

timeline.event: This preliminary study; the authors describe their results as consistent with an earlier placebo-controlled study by McCann et al. showing sleep disruption with MDMA (not read).

replication.where_it_stands: The only placebo-controlled polysomnographic study of MDMA and next-day sleepiness read for the library; its next-night findings are large and plausible but rest on 7 people, and the next-day sleepiness question is unresolved.

funding.funder: NIDA grant R01-DA14874 (Tancer).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not an industry-supported study. Johanson is an employee of CRS Associates LLC, a for-profit consulting company; the other authors report no financial conflicts.
funding.affiliations_note: Wayne State University and Henry Ford Hospital sleep researchers (Roehrs); the laboratory was at Detroit Receiving Hospital.

what_would_settle_it: A larger placebo-controlled crossover study of MDMA at doses and times people actually use, with polysomnography, next-day nap tests and performance and mood measures over the following days, people's own sleep schedules respected, and a pre-registered analysis.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three sessions)
domains.note: Counterbalanced with a 12-sequence Latin square, of which only 7 sequences were completed; order effects cannot be fully balanced.
Sessions at least a week apart, each beginning with a baseline night; baseline nights did not differ between conditions.
MDMA against placebo was double-blind, but MDMA's effects are noticeable and blinding was not checked; the restricted-sleep condition was necessarily unblinded.
Two of nine who began withdrew and were excluded, one of them after the placebo and MDMA sessions.
Objective polysomnography and nap tests scored by experienced scorers to standard criteria; scorer blinding is not stated, but these measures leave little room for interpretation.
No registration; the abstract reports a stage 3/4 effect the results do not show, and nap-test values appear only in a figure.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Some concerns in four domains, none high; the outcomes are objective, and the large REM and total-sleep effects are unlikely to be artefacts of order or blinding. The between-group comparison with people without drug use is observational and not covered by RoB 2: it is confounded by recruitment source, cannabis and other drug use, sex mix, habitual late sleep schedules and the number of laboratory nights, and should not be cited as an effect of MDMA. May be cited for the treatment-night and recovery-night sleep effects of a single laboratory dose in 7 experienced adults, and for the unresolved next-day sleepiness comparison.

key_findings.finding: Seven adults with recreational MDMA experience completed all three sessions (5 white men, 1 white woman, 1 African American woman; mean age 25.3; lifetime MDMA uses mean 27, range 3 to 75); two others withdrew and three planned participants could not be recruited.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Experimental Procedures, 1st paragraph; Results › Demographics; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Treatment night, MDMA against placebo: total sleep 310.6 (SEM 45.3) against 437.1 (8.1) minutes (F(1,6) = 8.6, P = 0.026), latency to persistent sleep 112.3 (46.1) against 14.9 (5.0) minutes (F = 7.0, P = 0.038), stage 1 sleep 8.4 against 6.6% (F = 9.49, P = 0.022); no significant effect on wake after sleep onset, stage 2 (P = 0.267), stage 3/4 (P = 0.119) or REM latency (P = 0.589).
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3

key_findings.finding: REM sleep was 3.5% (SEM 2.1) of sleep on the MDMA night against 19.2% (2.0) on the placebo night (F(1,6) = 14.28, P = 0.009), reduced on the treatment night only (drug by night interaction F = 23.70, P = 0.003); it was also lower than after restricted sleep (19.3%; post hoc P = 0.004), so the authors read it as a specific REM-suppressing effect rather than a result of sleep loss.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3; Figure 3 legend

key_findings.finding: On the placebo recovery night after the MDMA session, total sleep was 403.6 (34.4) minutes and REM 22.2% (1.5), close to the recovery night of the placebo session (431.9 minutes; 20.6%); apart from REM, no main effects of night or night-by-drug interactions were found.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3, recovery column

key_findings.finding: Next-day objective sleepiness: a treatment by day interaction (F(2,12) = 4.63, P = 0.032); after restricted sleep, mean sleep latency on the nap tests was shorter than after placebo (falling to about 6 minutes), while after MDMA it differed neither from placebo nor from restricted sleep; on the following day the three conditions did not differ. Sleep-onset REM periods: 2.14 after restricted sleep, 1.43 after MDMA and 1.00 after placebo, not significantly different.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend; Discussion, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Compared with 13 age-matched people without drug use, the MDMA group's first laboratory night had less total sleep (376.21, SEM 26.7, against 433.43, 13.1, minutes; t = 2.59, df 18, P < 0.02) and less stage 3/4 sleep (4.8% against 15.7%; t = 2.90, P < 0.01), with similar REM; on the placebo day their mean nap latency was longer (15.6 against 10.9 minutes; t = 2.84, P < .01) and they had more sleep-onset REM periods (5 of 7 had at least one).
key_findings.locator: Results › Nighttime Sleep: MDMA Users Compared With Control Subjects; Results › Effects on the MSLT, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors name the small sample and the laboratory schedule, which was earlier than the participants' usual sleep times, as limitations, and say it would be important to know whether the disturbances in the MDMA group predated stimulant use.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says acute MDMA reduced stage 3/4 sleep, but the results report no effect of MDMA on the stage 3/4 percentage (P = 0.119; Table 3: 5.0% against 5.7% on the treatment night); the reduced stage 3/4 sleep is in the comparison between the MDMA group and people without drug use.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Measurements and Results; Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Reduced slow-wave sleep should not be cited as an acute effect of MDMA from this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The post-hoc P values for total sleep conflict: the text gives MDMA against placebo P = 0.031 and MDMA against restricted sleep P = 0.093, while the Figure 2 legend gives restricted sleep against placebo P = 0.031 and MDMA against placebo P = 0.001.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects on NPSG, 2nd paragraph; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: The exact significance of the MDMA effect on total sleep in the three-way comparison is uncertain; the two-factor analysis (P = 0.026) is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: F = 17.272 with df 2 and 12 is printed with P = 0.005, and F = 15.036 with P = 0.001; the editors' calculation gives p of about 0.0003 and 0.0005.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects on NPSG, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; both effects are significant either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The between-group t of 2.59 for total sleep cannot be reproduced from the printed values (editors' calculation: about 1.9 to 2.2 if the spreads are SEMs, as in Table 3, and about 6.5 if they are SDs), while the nap-latency t of 2.84 roughly fits the values only if they are SDs; the paper does not say which.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Nighttime Sleep: MDMA Users Compared With Control Subjects; Results › Effects on the MSLT, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The between-group statistics cannot be checked; treat their significance as uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The comparison group's mean number of sleep-onset REM periods is printed as 0.008 (SD 0.28), which is impossible for 13 people (the smallest possible non-zero mean is about 0.08); the printed t of 4.51 is reproduced only with 0.008 (editors' calculation; with 0.08, t is about 4.2). The MDMA group's placebo-day value is given as 1.00 with a spread of 0.82 in one paragraph and 0.71 in the next.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects on the MSLT, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical or calculation errors; the conclusion (more sleep-onset REM periods in the MDMA group) holds either way.

reporting_issues.issue: The Table 3 footnote says the data came from a general-population database of Michigan residents, which describes the comparison group, not the MDMA-group data in Table 3; and the text says values 'may differ from Table 1', which holds drug-exposure data (Table 3 seems meant).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3 footnote; Results › Nighttime Sleep: MDMA Users Compared With Control Subjects
reporting_issues.consequence: Editorial errors that obscure which data come from which group.

reporting_issues.issue: The Figure 3 legend reports a main effect of night on REM percentage (P = 0.001), while the text says there were no main effects of night apart from the REM interaction.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Figure 3 legend; Results › Effects on NPSG, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the REM analysis.
