verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC2768958 (all sections and Tables 1 to 3 rendered as text, disclosure and acknowledgments read; Figures 1 to 4 are images and their values, including the nap-test means by condition, were not extracted)

design_detail: Naturalistic field study of two self-selected parallel groups followed over five days, without a measurement before the drug night: 12 people who said they had taken ecstasy (MDMA) on a Saturday night at one London club and 12 who said they had drunk alcohol but taken no illicit drug, tested that night in a quiet room in the club while intoxicated (day 1), at home the next afternoon (day 2) and at home on the Wednesday evening (day 5). Measures: Beck Depression Inventory, 16 Bond-Lader mood visual analogue scales, 14 bodily-symptom visual analogue scales, serial sevens and Rivermead prose recall (immediate and delayed). Repeated-measures ANOVA with group (between) and day (within).
can_establish: How self-rated mood, bodily symptoms and two simple cognitive tasks changed over the five days after a Saturday night of self-reported ecstasy use, compared with a Saturday night of heavy drinking, in 24 young adults from one club.
cannot_establish: Whether ecstasy caused the mid-week changes (no pre-drug measurement, intake not verified, self-selected groups that differed in other drug use, unblinded assessor, testing time and place changing with the day), how many people developed low mood (no individual counts above any cut-off are given), or anything about known doses of pure MDMA.

sample.recruitment: Club setting on successive Saturday nights over four months, snowball technique (p. 823). The assessing psychologist had previously worked as a part-time disc jockey at the club, which made testing there possible (p. 822).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Volunteers who reported taking only MDMA or only alcohol (apart from caffeine or nicotine) on the night; people reporting other drugs, or a combination of MDMA and alcohol, were not included (p. 823). Ages 20 to 27.
sample.demographics: Eight men and four women in each group; ecstasy group six degree students and six employed, alcohol group seven students and five employed (p. 823).
sample.attrition: None: all 24 were tested on all three occasions and re-consented on day 2 (p. 823).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected club-goers willing to be tested in a club and at home; snowball recruitment; groups formed by what people said they took that night. The ecstasy group reported more regular use of several drugs (alcohol, cannabis, MDMA, cocaine); 7 of the 12 in the alcohol group had also used MDMA (3 about monthly, 4 occasionally) (p. 824). The authors had no drug-free volunteers in that setting (p. 822).

exposure.measurement: Self-report on day 2 of what had been taken the previous night; no blood, urine or tablet testing (pp. 824, 829). The authors argue that the acute mood profile matched earlier studies of pure MDMA (p. 829).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: tablets sold as ecstasy, number and content not recorded; 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group also drank 1 to 3 units of alcohol (mean 1.8), mostly before arriving; the alcohol group drank 4 to 14 units (mean 10.8) (p. 824). Usual frequency in the ecstasy group: 2 about weekly, 6 about monthly, 4 occasionally (p. 824).
exposure.polysubstance: Alcohol on the night in 7 of 12 in the ecstasy group (acknowledged as a limitation, p. 829); lifetime use of cannabis, cocaine and other drugs higher in the ecstasy group, not quantified or adjusted. Participants were asked not to drink or use illicit drugs between testings; one person drank 3 units between days 2 and 5 and none reported illicit drugs (p. 824); not verified.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Day 1 was measured during intoxication in both groups; days 2 and 5 after self-reported abstinence, unverified.

comparison.controls: 12 club-goers who reported drinking alcohol but no illicit drug that night.
comparison.matching: Same sex split and similar ages and occupations; no formal matching or adjustment.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure of mood, sleep, cognition, psychiatric history or life events before the drug night; usual mood is unknown in both groups.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The alcohol group drank about ten times as much that night and was itself hung over on day 2 (the authors read its U-shaped course as a hangover, p. 826); most of its members had used MDMA before.

outcomes.instruments: Beck Depression Inventory at each testing point; 16 Bond-Lader mood visual analogue scales (100 mm); 14 bodily-symptom visual analogue scales; serial sevens (correct subtractions and errors in 120 seconds); Rivermead prose recall, immediate and delayed, three versions balanced across people and days (pp. 823-824).
outcomes.validity_norms: The paper cites BDI scores below 9 as normal and above 16 as indicating clinical depression (p. 825); the visual analogue scales have no norms.
outcomes.operationalization: Low mood was read from BDI totals and mood ratings; no diagnostic interview. A reanalysis dropping the BDI's sleep and appetite items was reported (p. 829).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Editors' count from Tables 1 to 3: 4 cognitive scores, the BDI, 16 mood scales and 14 bodily scales, each with group, day and interaction tests; the authors mention 34 variables and that 1.7 results would be significant at 0.05 by chance (p. 826).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: one psychologist recruited and tested everyone and knew who had taken what.

analysis.effect_sizes: The paper gives only significance levels (stars or p thresholds) for group, day and group x day effects, with no F values, degrees of freedom, effect sizes or simple-effect tests. BDI means (SD) on days 1, 2 and 5: ecstasy 3.5 (3.5), 8.7 (3.8), 11.8 (7.2); alcohol 6.4 (5.3), 8.3 (5.2), 6.9 (4.1); group x day p<0.001, group not significant (Table 2, p. 827). Editors' calculation from these means and SDs (independent t-test, 12 per group): the day-5 difference is 4.9 points, 95% CI -0.1 to 9.9, t(22) = 2.05, p = 0.053, d = 0.84; on day 2 the groups do not differ (8.7 against 8.3). Serial sevens: group p<0.01, group x day p<0.05 (pp. 824-825).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable for a 1996 field study; no protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 35 measures are tabulated (Tables 1 to 3), but only with significance marks; no exact statistics or individual counts above BDI cut-offs.
analysis.power: Not addressed; 12 per group. The authors say a delayed-recall difference might have reached significance with a larger sample (p. 829).

interpretation_gap.results_show: The ecstasy group felt elevated on the night and its mood ratings then fell across the next days, while the alcohol group dipped on day 2 and recovered. On day 2 both groups were similar on the BDI (8.7 against 8.3) and many mood scales; the ecstasy group was markedly more tired and lacking in energy. By the Wednesday the ecstasy group's mean BDI was 11.8 against 6.9, with higher ratings of sadness, depression, anxiety, agitation and irritability; the day-5 BDI difference taken alone is borderline (editors' calculation p = 0.053) and the interaction is partly driven by the ecstasy group's low score while intoxicated on day 1. The ecstasy group made fewer correct subtractions on all three days.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says some participants scored within the range for clinical depression on day 5 and that weekend MDMA use may lead to depressed mood mid-week (p. 821); the Results say some were in the mild to moderate range (p. 825) without a count, and the day-5 group mean lies between the normal and clinical cut-offs the paper cites. The abstract presents the serial-sevens result as an impairment from MDMA, although the ecstasy group was lower on every day, including mid-week, so a pre-existing difference cannot be excluded without a baseline. The discussion is open about the field design's limits (pp. 829-830) and offers three explanations (temporary serotonin depletion, neurotoxicity, a psychological reaction to the high) without testing any.

timeline.event: This study: first field report of a mid-week low after weekend ecstasy use, against people who had been drinking.

Scott et al.: people who used ecstasy at the weekend did not differ from people who use ecstasy but abstained that week on distress, mood or clinician ratings one and three days later, against each person's own baseline.

replication.where_it_stands: A small, early, influential field study. A later study with a pre-use baseline and an ecstasy-using comparison group did not find a group difference (Scott et al., 2013). Parrott and Lasky (1998; card sc_parrott_1998) also measured mood two and seven days after a Saturday night and should be read together with these two.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychology, University College London. The second author, who did the testing, had worked as a part-time disc jockey at the club where everyone was recruited (p. 822).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people who already use ecstasy that measures mood and sleep before a planned weekend of use and daily for a week afterwards, against people from the same scene who go out, dance and stay up without taking ecstasy, with tablet testing or urine confirmation, blinded assessment, objective sleep measures and counts of how many people cross a depression cut-off.

domains.note: No measurement before the drug night; the groups differed in lifetime drug use and in how much alcohol they drank that night, and sleep loss and dancing were not measured; nothing was adjusted.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Self-reported intake, tablets of unknown content, and 7 of 12 in the ecstasy group also drank.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Snowball recruitment of volunteers at one club, grouped by what they chose to take that night.
Abstinence between testings was requested but not checked; sleep between testings not recorded.
All 24 completed all three sessions.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-rated scales collected by an assessor who knew the groups; setting and time of day changed with the day (club at night, home at midday, home in the evening), and practice effects were large.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: 35 measures without correction, results reported only as significance marks, and no simple-effect test for the mid-week day.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The study can be cited for the pattern of self-rated mood and tiredness over five days in these 24 people, and for the contrast with a group recovering from heavy drinking. It cannot be cited as showing that ecstasy causes low mood mid-week: there is no pre-drug baseline, the comparison group differs in what it drank and in drug history, intake was not verified and the assessor was not blind. Very high risk of bias for any causal reading.

key_findings.finding: Beck Depression Inventory, means (SD) on days 1, 2 and 5: ecstasy group 3.5 (3.5), 8.7 (3.8), 11.8 (7.2); alcohol group 6.4 (5.3), 8.3 (5.2), 6.9 (4.1). Group not significant, day p<0.001, group x day p<0.001. The text gives the ecstasy day-5 mean as 11.75 and says the spread was larger on day 5, with some people in the normal range and others in the mild to moderate depression range; no count is given.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, BDI row (p. 827); Results, Beck Depression Inventory paragraph (p. 825, left column); Fig. 2 (p. 826)

key_findings.finding: With the BDI's somatic items (sleep, appetite) removed, the pattern and the group x day interaction (p<0.001) remained: ecstasy 2.25, 6.91, 9.92 and alcohol 5.08, 6.83, 5.49 on days 1, 2 and 5.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 826, the reanalysis on p. 829, left column)

key_findings.finding: Mood scales (0-100 mm): 11 of 16 showed group x day interactions; the strongest (p<0.001) were contented-discontented, happy-sad and interested-bored. Sad: ecstasy 7.0 (9.9), 33.5 (20.7), 54.6 (27.7); alcohol 26.9 (21.8), 41.6 (18.5), 35.1 (16.9). Bored: ecstasy 14.4, 49.6, 62.8; alcohol 41.9, 55.9, 39.4. On day 2 the two groups were broadly similar; the authors liken the ecstasy day after to an alcohol hangover in some respects.
key_findings.locator: Results, Mood rating scale paragraphs (p. 825, right column); Table 2 (p. 827); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 826)

key_findings.finding: Bodily symptoms (0-100 mm), days 1, 2 and 5. Lack of energy: ecstasy 10.6 (9.7), 82.2 (11.4), 68.6 (15.1); alcohol 38.8 (22.5), 65.8 (8.5), 48.7 (23.8). Physical tiredness: ecstasy 15.1, 78.9 (11.7), 60.0; alcohol 41.9, 64.5 (5.9), 46.1. Both group x day p<0.001. Headache rose on day 2 in both groups (ecstasy 58.3, alcohol 50.2; interaction not significant).
key_findings.locator: Results, Bodily Symptoms Scale paragraph (p. 826, left column); Table 3 (p. 828)

key_findings.finding: Day 5 bodily ratings, ecstasy against alcohol group: depression 56.3 (24.4) against 20.7 (13.6); anxiety 52.2 (21.2) against 26.9 (18.7); agitation 60.8 (21.1) against 24.5 (15.4); irritability 63.6 (17.6) against 44.1 (18.3). Group x day interactions p<0.01 for depression, anxiety and agitation and p<0.05 for irritability; in the ecstasy group these rose progressively over the days.
key_findings.locator: Results, Bodily Symptoms Scale paragraph (p. 826); Table 3 (p. 828)

key_findings.finding: Serial sevens, correct subtractions in 120 s, means (SD) days 1, 2, 5: ecstasy 2.7 (1.9), 14.2 (6.7), 25.1 (7.1); alcohol 6.3 (3.4), 26.6 (10.7), 31.1 (11.1). Group p<0.01, day p<0.001, group x day p<0.05; the ecstasy group made fewer subtractions at every point, most clearly on day 2; errors did not differ. Prose recall showed only a trend for lower scores in the ecstasy group (p<0.06) and improvement over days in both groups.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (p. 824); Results, Prose recall and Serial sevens paragraphs (pp. 824-825); Fig. 1 (p. 825)

key_findings.finding: Alcohol on the night: 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group also drank, far less than the alcohol group (amounts in the exposure field); one person drank between days 2 and 5.
key_findings.locator: Results, Participants' reported drug use, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Most of the ecstasy group reported lack of sleep on day 2; the authors cannot say whether the day-2 subtraction deficit was a drug effect or due to lost sleep. Sleep was not measured.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, paragraph continuing from p. 829 (p. 830, left column, top)

key_findings.finding: Testing times: day 1 in the club at night; day 2 at home between 12:00 and 16:00; day 5 at home between about 17:30 and 20:30.

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion rule excluded anyone who had combined MDMA and alcohol (p. 823), but 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group reported drinking 1 to 3 units that night (p. 824).
reporting_issues.consequence: The ecstasy group is an ecstasy-plus-some-alcohol group; the authors acknowledge this as a limitation (p. 829).

reporting_issues.issue: The text says two bodily-symptom scales had group x day interactions at the 0.05 level (p. 826), but Table 3 marks three at p<0.05 (irritability, impaired concentration, dry mouth) (p. 828).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the table is the record to cite.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says some participants scored within the range for clinical depression (p. 821); the Results say mild to moderate range (p. 825); no number of people above either cut-off is reported anywhere.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper cannot be cited for how many people had depressed mood; only the group means can be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The authors mention 34 variables (p. 826) while Tables 1 to 3 hold 35 measures (editors' count); none of the tests is reported with a statistic or degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: Effect sizes and simple effects cannot be checked from the paper; the editors' day-5 calculation from the printed means and SDs is borderline (p = 0.053).

reporting_issues.issue: The PDF is a scanned copy with an optical-character text layer; Tables 2 and 3 are printed sideways and their text layer is unreadable, so all values were read from rendered page images.
reporting_issues.consequence: A second reader should check the table values against the page images, not the text layer.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent; AI reader 121, first reader)
verification.source_read: PDF DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/MDMA/Curran_1997_WeekendHighMidweekLow..pdf (uploads folder), pp. 821-831 (the published version, as a scanned copy with an OCR text layer; Tables 1 to 3 and Figures 1 and 2 read from rendered page images; no acknowledgements or funding statement in the article)

design_detail: Prospective study with a baseline before use: 56 people who use ecstasy, drawn from a Melbourne cross-sectional study of 184, were assessed face to face after at least a week without ecstasy, then by telephone the day after a weekend (Day 1, mostly Sunday) and two days later (Day 3, mostly Tuesday). 35 chose to take ecstasy that weekend and 21 chose not to. Outcomes: Kessler-10 distress (rephrased to the present day), a 1-10 rating of the day's mood, and the depression, anxiety and hostility items of the clinician-rated Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale; self-reported hours and restlessness of sleep, drug use (Timeline Followback) and stressful events. Two-way repeated-measures ANCOVA (group x time) and correlations of mood change with possible risk factors.
can_establish: Whether, against each person's own baseline, people who chose to take ecstasy over a weekend reported more distress or lower mood one and three days later than people from the same group who chose not to, and which self-reported factors went with mood change.
cannot_establish: Causal effects (use was self-chosen and the groups differed in age, sex and other drug use), effects of known MDMA doses (tablets not tested), effects beyond three days, or the absence of a small effect (35 and 21 people, 47 at Day 3).

sample.recruitment: Subsample of a cross-sectional study of 184 people aged 18-35 who had used ecstasy in the past 12 months, recruited in Melbourne through university and dance-music websites, newsletters, magazines, newspapers, flyers in cafes, music stores and dance events, and snowballing; 63 consented, 56 provided follow-up data (pp. 54, 56).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methods: regular ecstasy use (at least monthly over the last six months) and planning to take ecstasy the following week; excluded pregnancy, self-reported psychotic disorder and poor English. Asked to abstain from ecstasy for 7 days, other drugs for 24 h (except tobacco and caffeine) and alcohol for 12 h before baseline (pp. 54, 56). Reimbursed AUD 25 for the baseline interview.
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group 20 men and 15 women, mean age 24.2 (SD 5.2); abstainers 6 men and 15 women, 21.1 (2.1); history of depression or anxiety disorder 20.0% and 19.0%; mostly Caucasian and with post-school education (Table 1, p. 56).
sample.attrition: One ecstasy-group member was not reached on Day 1; on Day 3, 5 of 35 and 4 of 21 were not reached (86% and 81% followed up); 7 of the 63 who consented provided no follow-up (pp. 56, 60).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected community volunteers; the comparison depends on who chose to take ecstasy that weekend. The groups differed in age, sex, duration of ecstasy use and lifetime cocaine and cannabis use (pp. 56-57). The authors note that people with worse mood might have been harder to reach and that abstainers might be more sensitive to after-effects (p. 60).

exposure.measurement: Self-report of tablets taken and of other drugs (Timeline Followback); tablets were not analysed; 91.4% of the ecstasy group rated it highly or definitely likely that they had taken MDMA (pp. 55, 60).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: mean 1.91 tablets (SD 1.23; range 0.5-5) on the night (Day 0); the Day 1 interview came on average 21.74 h (SD 6.64; 12.5-40) after the last tablet (p. 57). Usual pattern (Table 3, p. 57): typical 1.90 tablets per occasion, lifetime mean 422 tablets (SD 1002) in the ecstasy group and 149 (355) in abstainers; about 1.4 days of use in the past month in both groups.
exposure.polysubstance: On Day 0, 30 of 35 in the ecstasy group drank alcohol (mean 9.52 standard drinks) against 10 of 21 abstainers (5.07); cannabis 34.3% against 14.3%; 6 took amphetamines; mean number of substances 2.51 against 0.71 (p<0.001). Between Days 1 and 3 the ecstasy group used more alcohol and cannabis (Table 5, p. 58). Number of substances, Day 0 sleep, age, sex and duration of ecstasy use were entered as covariates.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence before baseline by self-report only; the authors note the baseline questionnaire covered the past week, which may overlap with after-effects of earlier use (p. 60).

comparison.controls: 21 people from the same sample of people who use ecstasy who chose not to take it that weekend, interviewed on the same days.
comparison.matching: None; group differences in age, sex, drug use and Day 0 sleep were handled as covariates.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Baseline mood was measured, which most earlier studies lacked; why people abstained, recent trauma or stress beyond the follow-up, and objective sleep were not measured.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Abstainers also used alcohol, cannabis and other drugs (Table 4), but fewer substances that weekend.

outcomes.instruments: Kessler-10 (K10), timeframe changed from the past month to the present day; subjective mood 1 (worst ever) to 10 (best ever); BPRS depression, anxiety and hostility items rated 1-7 by the interviewer; MASQ short form at baseline only; hours of sleep the previous night from reported sleep and wake times minus waking periods, and restlessness of sleep 1-10 compared with normal (pp. 55-56).
outcomes.validity_norms: The K10 cut-off of 17 or more is validated for the past-month version; its use on a present-day version is untested. BPRS reliability is cited for trained raters; follow-up ratings were made by telephone.
outcomes.operationalization: Mood change = baseline score minus Day 1 or Day 3 score (p. 55); clinically significant distress = K10 of 17 or more.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None for the 10 group comparisons (K10, mood and three BPRS items at Day 1 and Day 3); for the correlation analyses a modified Bonferroni threshold of p = 0.001 was set from the effective number of variables (matSpD) (p. 55).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: one doctoral candidate conducted all interviews and arranged follow-up calls around planned use, so knew who had taken ecstasy.

analysis.effect_sizes: No effect sizes or confidence intervals. K10: no main effect of group and no group x time interaction; a time effect at Day 1 (F(1,53) = 4.94, p = 0.03, lower distress than baseline) that disappeared with covariates. Subjective mood: no group or group x day effect; lower than baseline at Day 1 (F(1,52) = 4.60, p = 0.04) and Day 3 (F(1,45) = 6.52, p = 0.01) in both groups; the Day 1 effect disappeared after adjusting for Day 0 sleep. BPRS change scores: no group differences (p > 0.05, values not shown). Means in Table 2 (p. 56). Editors' calculation: K10 of 17 or more at Day 3 in 7 of 30 against 2 of 17, Fisher exact p = 0.45.
analysis.covariates: Sex, age, duration of ecstasy use, hours of sleep on the night of use (or before Day 3), and number of substances, entered one at a time or together (pp. 57-58).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: BPRS results are given only as not significant; correlation results are reported as significant at p = 0.001 or as trends, with some trends at p = 0.01 although trends were defined as p < 0.01.
analysis.power: Not calculated; the authors note that low rates of mood disorder in the sample may have limited power (p. 59).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against their own baseline a week earlier, people who took ecstasy did not differ from people who abstained in distress, mood or clinician-rated symptoms one or three days later; mood ratings fell a little in both groups. The ecstasy group slept about two hours less on the night of use. Across the whole sample, fewer hours of sleep before Day 3 went with a rise in distress and restless sleep with a drop in mood, and in the ecstasy group restless sleep went with a rise in distress; the number of pills, dancing, overheating, sex and baseline mood were not associated with mood change.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that ecstasy use was not associated with subacute depressive, anxiety or aggressive symptoms and that lowered mood was associated instead with sleep (p. 53). This rests on non-significant differences in 56 people, without intervals, so a small effect cannot be excluded; and adjusting for sleep on the night of use removes part of any effect that runs through lost sleep, which ecstasy nights produced (5.9 against 8.1 hours). The discussion is more careful, calling any subacute effects likely modest, naming low power and calling for larger studies (pp. 59-60).

timeline.event: Curran and Travill: field study reporting lower mid-week mood after weekend ecstasy than after a night of drinking, without a pre-use baseline.
Parrott and Lasky: Saturday-night field study with a drug-free baseline, cited by Scott et al. among the studies that found elevated low mood in the following days.

Pirona and Morgan: cited by Scott et al. as finding no difference against an ecstasy-using comparison group on the Beck Depression Inventory, and effects on negative mood that disappeared after adjusting for sleep.
This study: no group difference against ecstasy-using abstainers, with sleep associated with mood change.

replication.where_it_stands: One of the few studies with both a pre-use baseline and a comparison group of people who also use ecstasy. Its null result disagrees with the earlier field studies that compared people who took ecstasy with people who did not use it (as cited, p. 59), and agrees with Pirona and Morgan (2010) as Scott et al. describe it.

funding.funder: The first author held an Australian Postgraduate Award; the project was funded by the School of Psychology and Psychiatry, Monash University; two authors were supported by the Colonial Foundation (p. 60).
funding.declared_conflicts: The author declares no conflict of interest (as printed, in the singular, for four authors) (p. 60).
funding.affiliations_note: Monash University, King's College London, Queensland University of Technology, Turning Point Alcohol and Drug Centre.

what_would_settle_it: A larger prospective study of people who use ecstasy, with daily mood ratings from before a planned weekend to a week after, objective sleep measurement (actigraphy), tablet testing, and a comparison group who go out and lose sleep without taking ecstasy, analysed with sleep as a mediator rather than a covariate.

domains.note: Self-chosen exposure; groups differed in age, sex, duration of ecstasy use and other drug use; covariates were added singly or in small sets, and adjusting for sleep after use may remove part of the effect rather than confounding.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Self-reported tablets of unknown content, though most participants believed they had taken MDMA.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Volunteers from a larger study; the authors raise self-selection of abstainers who may be more sensitive to after-effects.
More alcohol and cannabis in the ecstasy group between Days 1 and 3.
16% not reached at Day 3, similar in both groups; those not reached may have felt worse.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-reports and an interviewer who knew the groups; baseline face to face, follow-up by telephone; K10 timeframe changed.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: BPRS values not shown; many correlations, with trends reported at p = 0.01 despite the stated threshold.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A stronger design than earlier field studies because each person had a baseline and the comparison group also used ecstasy, but the exposure was self-chosen, the groups differed, the sample was small and the outcome measures were self-reported. It can be cited for finding no detectable group difference in mood one and three days after ecstasy in this sample, and for the association of poorer sleep with worse mood; not for the absence of an effect or for sleep as the cause.

key_findings.finding: K10: no main effect of group and no group x time interaction; a main effect of time at Day 1 (F(1,53) = 4.94, p = 0.03), with lower distress than at baseline, not significant after covariates (sex, age, Day 0 sleep, number of drugs on Day 0, duration of ecstasy use). The items depressed and nervous did not differ between groups.
key_findings.locator: Results, Group comparisons: mood, 1st paragraph (right column)

key_findings.finding: Subjective mood: no group or group x day effect; both groups lower than baseline at Day 1 (F(1,52) = 4.60, p = 0.04) and Day 3 (F(1,45) = 6.52, p = 0.01). The Day 1 time effect remained after adjusting for sex, age or duration of use but not after adjusting for hours of sleep on the night of use; the Day 3 effect did not survive adjustment for age, sleep before Day 3 or other drug use. After covariates there was still no group effect or interaction; an age x time interaction (F(1,51) = 3.93, p = 0.05) indicated lower mood in younger participants, especially at Day 1.
key_findings.locator: Results, Subjective mood paragraph (p. 57, right column, continuing on p. 58, left column)

key_findings.finding: Clinician-rated BPRS depression, anxiety and hostility change scores did not differ between groups (p > 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Results, BPRS clinician ratings paragraph (left column)

key_findings.finding: K10 of 17 or more (clinically significant distress): ecstasy group 5 (14.3%) at baseline, 4 (11.8%) at Day 1, 7 (23.3%) at Day 3; abstainers 4 (19.0%), 3 (14.3%), 2 (11.8%), with one abstainer at 30 or more at Day 3. Not tested statistically.
key_findings.locator: Results, Follow-up mood: clinically significant symptoms (left column)

key_findings.finding: Sleep the night before Day 1: ecstasy group 5.85 h (SD 2.14) against abstainers 8.06 h (1.93), p<0.001; restless sleep 2.85 (2.64) against 3.76 (2.81). The night before Day 3: 7.98 h (1.80) against 7.93 h (2.89); restless sleep 3.14 against 2.94.
key_findings.locator: Table 5, hours of sleep and restless sleep rows

key_findings.finding: Sleep and mood change, alpha 0.001: across the whole sample, hours slept before Day 3 correlated with the Day 3 K10 change score (r = -0.49, p = 0.001), described as fewer hours with more distress, and restless sleep correlated with the Day 3 drop in mood (r = 0.45, p = 0.001); in the ecstasy group, restless sleep correlated with the Day 3 K10 change (r = -0.59, p = 0.001), and restless sleep (r = 0.55, p = 0.002) and fewer hours (r = -0.46, p = 0.01) with a drop in mood at Day 3. Stressful life events were not associated with mood change.
key_findings.locator: Results, Sleep and Stress paragraphs (left column)
key_findings.note: Minus signs checked on the rendered page. See reporting issues for the direction of the K10 correlations.

key_findings.finding: No association of mood change with the number of tablets taken, total drugs or alcohol and cannabis on Day 0, feeling hot or time spent dancing, rating of the experience, confidence that MDMA was taken, sex, age, past depression or anxiety, or baseline MASQ symptoms; a trend for more substances used between Days 1 and 3 with a drop in mood at Day 3 (r = 0.37, p = 0.01, whole sample; r = 0.55, p = 0.002, ecstasy group).
key_findings.locator: Results, Correlational analyses: demographics, lifetime drug use, Days 0-2 drug use and ecstasy factors (p. 58, right column, to p. 59, left column)

key_findings.finding: Drugs on the night of use (Day 0): alcohol in 30 of 35 in the ecstasy group against 10 of 21 abstainers, with more drinks in the ecstasy group; cannabis 12 against 3; mean number of substances 2.51 against 0.71 (p<0.001). The Day 1 interview came on average 21.74 h after the last tablet. Amounts are in the exposure field.
key_findings.locator: Results, Follow-up drug use and sleep (p. 57, left column); Table 5 (p. 58)

key_findings.finding: Group differences at baseline: the ecstasy group was older (t(54) = -3.07, p = 0.004), more often male (chi-square(1, 56) = 4.31, p = 0.04), had used ecstasy for longer (t(54) = -2.25, p = 0.03) and had more often tried cocaine; no differences on baseline mood, lifetime ecstasy pills, typical dose or time since last use.
key_findings.locator: Results, Sample characteristics and follow-up, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 56, right column, to p. 57)

reporting_issues.issue: With change scores defined as baseline minus follow-up (p. 55), a negative correlation between hours of sleep and the K10 change (r = -0.49) and a positive one between lifetime amphetamine use and the Day 1 K10 change (r = 0.36, p. 58) imply the opposite of the direction the text gives (fewer hours, or more amphetamine use, with more distress), whereas the negative correlation with restless sleep (r = -0.59) matches its text.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the K10 change was computed the other way for some analyses or a sign is wrong; the direction of the sleep-distress association should be cited from the text with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 5 prints 30 of 35 as 87.7%; 30 of 35 is 85.7%. Its footnote defines a standard drinking unit as equivalent to 10 mg of ethanol, a unit error (presumably grams).
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the counts are usable.

reporting_issues.issue: Comparisons of alcohol and cannabis between Days 1 and 3 are reported as t(47) (p. 57), but with 30 and 17 people an independent t-test has 45 degrees of freedom.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; suggests the analysis used a different n or the df is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: Inclusion is described as at least monthly ecstasy use over six months (p. 54) and, in the abstract, as use at least once in 12 months (p. 53); Table 3 shows times since last use of up to 120 days in the ecstasy group and 94 in abstainers (p. 57).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample is less regular in its use than the Methods suggest.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says one ecstasy-group member could not be contacted on Day 1 (p. 56) and also that two participants were assessed two days after use because they could not be contacted on Day 1 (p. 57).
reporting_issues.consequence: Day 1 timing differs for some participants; minor.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations at p = 0.01 are reported as trends (p. 59) although trends were defined as p < 0.01 (p. 58); results at p = 0.001 are called significant with alpha set at 0.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sleep associations sit at, not below, the authors' own threshold.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent; AI reader 121, first reader)
verification.source_read: PDF DrugEncyclopedia/PDFs/MDMA/Scott_2013_SubacuteMoodRiskFactors.pdf (uploads folder), pp. 53-61, the published version (downloaded copy with a text layer); Tables 3 and 5 and every negative test statistic checked on rendered pages

design_detail: Pooled analysis of the raw data of 10 double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover laboratory studies of MDMA in 194 healthy volunteers at the University Hospital Basel (2009-2018), asking which characteristics measured before dosing predict the acute response. Only the MDMA-alone and placebo sessions are used. The MDMA-placebo comparison was randomized within each source study, but the predictors (sex, age, CYP2D6 genotype, previous MDMA use, personality, mood just before intake) vary between people and were not randomized, so the analysis is observational. Each of 20 predictors was related to each of 25 response variables in linear mixed models with a random intercept for study, unadjusted and adjusted for dose per body weight, with standardized coefficients, semi-partial R2 and Benjamini-Hochberg correction; LASSO models ranked predictors. Missing data were multiply imputed (20 imputations). All coefficients are shown in two figures (images) and a supplementary figure; the main text reports the significant ones.
can_establish: Which characteristics measured before dosing were associated, at a given dose per body weight, with the size of MDMA's acute physiological and subjective effects in young, healthy, mostly MDMA-naive volunteers who took one oral dose of 75 or 125 mg per analysed session lying in a quiet hospital ward, and roughly how much variance each explained (semi-partial R2 of 0.05 to 0.12 for the personality and mood predictors).
cannot_establish: Whether a trait or mood causes a stronger or more anxious response (the predictors were not randomized and each was tested with dose per weight as the only covariate); anything about people with psychiatric disorders, people over 45, people with more than five previous MDMA uses, repeated doses, or settings such as parties, therapy or crowds (absent or not varied by design); or whether sex matters apart from dose per kilogram, since everyone received a fixed dose and women weighed less, so sex and dose per kilogram move together.

sample.recruitment: Paid volunteers recruited from the University of Basel campus into ten earlier crossover studies, each registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (Methods › Study design, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy adults aged 18-45. Excluded: a history of psychiatric disorder or physical illness; lifetime illicit drug use more than 10 times (past cannabis use excepted); illicit drug use in the 2 months before or during the study; drug screens before test sessions (Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph).
sample.demographics: Age 25.1 (SD 4); 97 women; body weight 69 (SD 10) kg, range 46-97. 75 had used illicit substances 1-8 times: MDMA 41 (1-5 times), amphetamine or methamphetamine 18, cocaine 15, LSD 10, psilocybin 15; 79% had never used MDMA. NEO-FFI openness 33.2 (SD 6.3) against 24.5 (SD 5.5) in a normative sample, t = 19.7, p < 0.001 (Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not reported. Missing predictor and response data, mostly from the differing designs of the pooled studies, were multiply imputed; their extent is in Supplementary Table 1 (not read). One genotyping sample was missing and three participants did not consent to genotyping.
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy, screened, paid campus volunteers with little drug experience and markedly higher openness than a normative sample; the authors note that trials may attract open people. Excluding psychiatric disorders narrows the range of neuroticism and trait anxiety, and the narrow ages (SD 4 years) narrow age, both of which tend to weaken associations rather than create them.

exposure.measurement: Characteristics measured before dosing: sex; age; body weight; CYP2D6 genetic activity score; number of previous MDMA uses (self-report); mood immediately before intake on the Adjective Mood Rating Scale (AMRS; 60 adjectives rated on 4-point scales: performance-related activity, general inactivation, extraversion, introversion, general well-being, emotional excitability, anxiety-depressiveness); personality at screening on the NEO Five Factor Inventory (60 items: neuroticism, extraversion, openness to experience, agreeableness, conscientiousness) and the trait scale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-T, 20 items), whose timing is not stated. Dose per body weight was the covariate; MDMA plasma concentration was examined only in unadjusted models, because it is unknown at the time of dosing (Methods › Predictor variables, 1st to 6th paragraphs; Results, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one oral dose of MDMA hydrochloride per analysed session, as gelatin capsules of 25 or 100 mg, 125 mg (164 people) or 75 mg (30 people), the same for women and men regardless of weight; 112 of the 164 also took 125 mg in a second session after a medication pretreatment (not analysed; the order of sessions is not given); dose per body weight 1.7 (SD 0.4) mg/kg, range 0.8-2.7; at least 7 days between sessions. Session conditions: a quiet hospital research ward with no more than two participants per session, lying in hospital beds, mostly listening to music and not physically active; the drug was given in the morning to fasting participants and a small standardized lunch was served about four hours later (Methods › Study design, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Study drug, 1st paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: No illicit drug use in the 2 months before or during the study, with drug screens before sessions; sessions combining MDMA with a pretreatment medication or another substance were excluded from this analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 months without illicit drugs by history, checked by screens before sessions; at least 7 days between drug sessions.

comparison.controls: Placebo sessions in the same people (double-blind crossover within each source study). How the placebo data enter the response variables (for example as MDMA-minus-placebo differences) is not stated in the main text. For the predictors, the comparison is between people with higher and lower values of each characteristic.
comparison.matching: None for the predictors. Each predictor was entered alone (unadjusted) or with dose per body weight (adjusted); predictors were not adjusted for one another except in the LASSO models, which used single imputation and ignored clustering by study (Methods › Statistical analyses, 2nd and 4th paragraphs).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Expectations about MDMA and reasons for taking part were not measured; setting was standardized and could not be studied (the authors say so).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (within-person placebo; the same screening applied to all sessions).

outcomes.instruments: Plasma MDMA (area under the curve 0-6 h from samples up to 6 h); peak mean arterial pressure, heart rate and tympanic temperature (readings up to 6 h); visual analogue scales for any, good and bad drug effect, high mood, drug liking and stimulated, and bidirectional scales for closeness, openness and talkative (area under the effect curve over the day); the AMRS at 1.25, 2 and 5 h; the 5D-ASC at 6 h, rating the whole session in retrospect: oceanic boundlessness, dread of ego dissolution, visionary restructuralization, plus the subscales impaired control and cognition and anxiety. All subjective measures rated by the participant (Methods › Response variables, 1st to 4th paragraphs).
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard instruments of this laboratory; the 5D-ASC subscales follow Studerus et al. (2010). Tympanic temperature is an indirect measure of core temperature.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Unpleasant or anxious reactions' are continuous self-ratings: the 5D-ASC dread of ego dissolution (called anxious ego dissolution in the Discussion), impaired control and cognition and anxiety scores, and the VAS bad drug effect; no threshold for a clinically relevant reaction is used. 'Pleasant and prosocial effects' are the VAS good drug effect, closeness and related scales and 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate correction across all 500 tests of the adjusted models (20 predictors by 25 responses; Figure 1 legend), with the unadjusted models handled in the same way; the text reports associations that survived correction and flags uncorrected ones.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double-blind sessions; whether participants could tell MDMA from placebo is not reported (at 125 mg it is likely; editors' note). The trait questionnaires and the outcome ratings are both self-reports, so a person's general rating style could contribute to trait-outcome associations, especially if outcomes were not placebo-corrected.

analysis.effect_sizes: Standardized coefficients (beta), Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected p and semi-partial R2. Unadjusted, plasma MDMA with: any drug effect beta = 0.48 (corrected p < 0.001, R2 0.35); mean arterial pressure 0.35 (R2 0.25); liking 0.36 (0.17); good drug effect 0.35 (0.19); stimulated 0.3 (0.44); high mood 0.29 (0.43); AMRS introversion 0.24 (0.21); 5D-ASC oceanic boundlessness 0.25 (0.06); significant for 16 of 24 responses uncorrected and 8 after correction. Adjusted for dose per body weight: CYP2D6 activity with plasma MDMA beta = -0.19 (corrected p < 0.001, R2 0.1); age with heart-rate rise -0.27 (p = 0.019, R2 0.07); openness with general inactivation -0.25 (p = 0.042, R2 0.06), closeness 0.28 (p = 0.019, R2 0.08), oceanic boundlessness 0.22 (p = 0.042, R2 0.06) and visionary restructuralization 0.27 (p = 0.006, R2 0.09); neuroticism and trait anxiety with dread of ego dissolution 0.32 each (p = 0.001 and 0.004; R2 0.12 and 0.11) and with impaired control and cognition 0.26 each (p = 0.014 and 0.042; R2 0.08 and 0.07); anxiety-depressiveness and introversion just before intake with 5D-ASC anxiety 0.25 and 0.23 (p = 0.042 each; R2 0.06 and 0.05). Sex and previous MDMA use: no significant association after adjustment. LASSO: 8.6 predictors selected per response on average (5-13); dose per body weight selected for 21 of 25 responses and largest for 12.
analysis.covariates: Dose per body weight in the adjusted models; random intercept for study.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Each of the ten source studies is registered (NCT00886886, NCT00990067, NCT01136278, NCT01270672, NCT01386177, NCT01465685, NCT01771874, NCT01951508, NCT01616407, NCT03019822); the pooled predictor analysis is not described as preregistered.
analysis.selective_reporting: All adjusted and unadjusted coefficients are said to be displayed in Figure 1 and Supplementary Figure 1 (images, not viewable or not read here), so selective reporting of results is limited; the text describes the corrected-significant findings. The 5D-ASC was limited to its three general dimensions to reduce testing, and two subscales were added because adverse reactions were of most interest.
analysis.power: No power calculation. 194 people, but 85% received the same dose and ages were narrow, limiting the analysis of dose and age; the authors call earlier studies too small for such analyses.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In young, healthy, mostly MDMA-naive volunteers at rest in a hospital ward, the amount of MDMA in the blood was the strongest correlate of most effects, especially the pleasant and stimulant ones. Allowing for dose per kilogram, higher openness went with more closeness, oceanic boundlessness and visionary restructuralization; higher neuroticism or trait anxiety with more dread of ego dissolution and impaired control and cognition; and a more anxious-depressed or introverted mood just before dosing with higher 5D-ASC anxiety scores; each explained 5 to 12% of the variance. Older age went with a smaller rise in heart rate and, in LASSO, more bad drug effect. Sex and previous MDMA use (five times at most) showed no significant association after adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say openness “increased the intensity of pleasant and prosocial effects of MDMA” and that neuroticism, state anxiety and an anxious or depressed mood before intake increased the likelihood of unpleasant or anxious reactions, and that the response was largely unaffected by age, sex and previous use. Gaps: (1) causal verbs for between-person associations adjusted only for dose per kilogram; (2) the anxiety predictor was trait anxiety (STAI-T), not state anxiety; (3) age predicted the heart-rate response after correction and was the most important LASSO predictor of bad drug effect, so 'largely unaffected by age' understates the age findings; (4) the explanation that women's stronger unadjusted response came from their higher dose per kilogram is an inference the fixed-dose design cannot cleanly separate from sex (dose per kilogram ranged from 0.8 to 2.7 mg/kg, so the two are correlated, not inseparable); (5) the Discussion's suggestion that patients may benefit progressively over several therapy sessions as they become more open was not tested here. The abstract describes the significant findings accurately and its practical conclusion is hedged.

timeline.event: Kirkpatrick et al. pooled 220 volunteers from three laboratories and found no sex differences in acute responses; the authors cite it as in line with their sex finding.
Schmid et al., CYP2D6 genotype and MDMA response in eight pooled studies from the same laboratory, overlapping with the present sample.

Vizeli and Liechti, safety pharmacology of nine pooled studies from the same laboratory; all nine registration numbers recorded on that card appear among the ten here. The editors' card for it records higher bad-drug-effect ratings in women after allowing for dose per kilogram; this paper says it could not confirm such sex differences (Discussion, 4th paragraph).
Haijen et al., prospective naturalistic predictors of psychedelic responses, cited here for parallels with psychedelics.
This analysis.
Vizeli et al. applied the same approach to LSD in 213 volunteers; one source study (NCT03019822) appears in both analyses.

replication.where_it_stands: The only pooled analysis of predictors of the MDMA response found for this page. It shares its source studies with other Basel pooled analyses (Schmid et al., 2016; Vizeli and Liechti, 2017), so those papers are not independent confirmation of each other, and its LSD counterpart (Vizeli et al., 2024) shares one study and several authors. No independent laboratory has tested personality and pre-dose mood as predictors of the MDMA response, and none outside a laboratory.

funding.funder: The paper states that the authors received no financial support for the research, authorship or publication of this article. Funding of the ten source studies is not stated in this paper.
funding.declared_conflicts: M.E. Liechti is a consultant for Mind Medicine, Inc.; the other authors declare no conflicts of interest. Knowhow and data associated with this work and owned by the University Hospital Basel were licensed by Mind Medicine, Inc. after study completion; the statement says Mind Medicine had no role in financing, planning or conducting the study or the publication.
funding.affiliations_note: E. Studerus at the Division of Personality and Developmental Psychology, University of Basel; the other authors at the Division of Clinical Pharmacology and Toxicology, University Hospital Basel, which ran all ten source studies. E. Studerus and P. Vizeli contributed equally.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered prospective study across several laboratories and in clinical settings that measures openness, neuroticism, trait anxiety and mood before MDMA, includes a wider age range and more varied MDMA experience, sets dose per kilogram independently of sex, uses placebo-corrected outcomes, and tests whether these predictors improve prediction beyond dose in data not used to build the model.

domains.note: Each predictor was adjusted only for dose per body weight, with a random intercept for study; correlated predictors (neuroticism and trait anxiety, sex and weight, mood and personality) were not adjusted for one another in the inferential models. Adequate for prediction; not for the causal wording of the Conclusions.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the exposure
domains.note: Validated questionnaires taken before dosing (NEO-FFI personality at screening, mood immediately before intake; the timing of the STAI-T is not stated), genotype, and recorded dose and weight.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study (or into the analysis)
domains.note: Healthy, screened, paid campus volunteers with high openness and narrow ages; entry did not depend on the response, but the restricted ranges limit what the associations can show.
Standardized sessions; sessions with co-administered substances excluded.
Provisional: multiple imputation assuming data missing at random, mostly by design across studies; the extent is in a supplement that was not read.

domains.domain: Bias arising from measurement of the outcome
domains.note: Self-ratings in sessions where blinding probably did not hold; the main text does not say whether ratings were placebo-corrected, so trait-outcome associations could partly reflect general rating style.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: All 500 adjusted tests are displayed and false-discovery-rate corrected; not preregistered, but the reporting is complete in the figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The MDMA-placebo contrast in each source study was randomized, but this paper's question, which personal characteristics predict the response, is answered by between-person comparisons that were not randomized, so ROBINS-E is used, as on the editors' card for Schmid et al. (2016) from the same studies. Measurement is good and reporting complete; the concerns are adjustment for dose per weight only, restricted samples, uncertain placebo correction and probable unblinding. The source can be cited for associations, in healthy volunteers given MDMA in a hospital ward, of openness with more pleasant and connected effects, of neuroticism and trait anxiety with more anxious ego dissolution and impaired control, and of an anxious-depressed mood just before dosing with more acute anxiety, each modest (R2 0.05 to 0.12), and for dose per kilogram and blood level as the main correlates of the response. It should not be cited for causal effects, for people with psychiatric disorders or heavier MDMA histories, for settings outside a laboratory, or as showing that sex does not matter.

key_findings.finding: Design facts: 10 crossover studies (2009-2018), 194 healthy volunteers (97 women); one oral MDMA dose per analysed session, 125 mg (164) or 75 mg (30), made up as gelatin capsules of 25 or 100 mg, as study conditions; 112 of the 164 (seven studies of 16) took 125 mg in two sessions, alone and after a medication pretreatment, and only the MDMA-alone session was analysed (the order of sessions is not given); dose per body weight 1.7 (SD 0.4) mg/kg, range 0.8-2.7. Sessions were in a quiet hospital ward with at most two participants, lying in beds, mostly listening to music and not physically active; the drug was given in the morning after fasting, with a small lunch about four hours later.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Study design, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Study drug, 1st paragraph; Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Without adjustment, MDMA plasma concentration was the strongest predictor: significant for 16 of 24 responses uncorrected and 8 after correction, most strongly any drug effect (beta = 0.48, corrected p < 0.001, semi-partial R2 0.35), then mean arterial pressure (0.35), liking (0.36), good drug effect (0.35), stimulated (0.3), high mood (0.29), AMRS introversion (0.24) and oceanic boundlessness (0.25).
key_findings.note: The semi-partial R2 values here (0.44 for stimulated, 0.43 for high mood) do not track the coefficients; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Adjusted for dose per body weight: lower CYP2D6 activity predicted higher plasma MDMA (beta = -0.19, corrected p < 0.001, R2 0.1), and older age a smaller rise in heart rate (beta = -0.27, corrected p = 0.019, R2 0.07).

Adjusted for dose per body weight, higher NEO-FFI openness predicted a larger decrease in general inactivation (beta = -0.25, corrected p = 0.042, R2 0.06), more closeness (0.28, p = 0.019, R2 0.08), more oceanic boundlessness (0.22, p = 0.042, R2 0.06) and more visionary restructuralization (0.27, p = 0.006, R2 0.09).

Adjusted for dose per body weight, higher neuroticism and higher trait anxiety (STAI-T) each predicted more 5D-ASC dread of ego dissolution (beta = 0.32 each; corrected p = 0.001 and 0.004; R2 0.12 and 0.11) and more impaired control and cognition (0.26 each; p = 0.014 and 0.042; R2 0.08 and 0.07).

Mood rated on the AMRS immediately before intake: more anxiety-depressiveness and more introversion predicted higher 5D-ASC anxiety scores (beta = 0.25 and 0.23; corrected p = 0.042 each; R2 0.06 and 0.05); the 5D-ASC was completed 6 h after dosing, rating the session retrospectively.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Predictor variables, 5th paragraph; Methods › Response variables, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: LASSO: 8.6 predictors selected per response on average (range 5-13); dose per body weight was selected for 21 of 25 responses and was the most important for 12, including any drug effect, good drug effect, high mood, stimulated, liking and oceanic boundlessness, but was less important for unpleasant or anxious reactions. For bad drug effect the most important predictors were older age, then trait anxiety, then anxiety-depressiveness before intake; neuroticism was the most important for dread of ego dissolution and impaired control and cognition.

Sex was not significantly associated with any response after adjustment for dose per body weight; the authors attribute women's stronger unadjusted response to their higher dose per kilogram (fixed doses, lower body weight), and say this does not confirm earlier studies that reported sex differences after adjusting for body weight; among studies suggesting women may be more vulnerable to acute negative effects they cite Vizeli and Liechti (2017), which the Methods name as a report of safety data from these studies, while a three-laboratory study of 220 people (Kirkpatrick et al., 2014) detected no gender differences.
key_findings.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Methods › Study drug, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study design, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Previous MDMA use showed no association with the response; 79% had never used MDMA and the rest at most five times, so heavier use could not be assessed.
Uncorrected only (not surviving correction): older age with a smaller rise in body temperature, less liking and good drug effect, a smaller decrease in general inactivation and more bad drug effect.

Anxiety responses to MDMA were small relative to other effects; citing the same laboratory's safety analysis, the authors state that 7% of participants reported anxiety as an acute adverse effect at 125 mg.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figure, from Vizeli and Liechti (2017), not computed in this paper.

key_findings.finding: Authors' limitations: young, healthy, mostly MDMA-naive participants; two doses only, 85% at the higher one; the physical and social setting was standardized and could not be studied; nothing about longer-term effects.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions name 'state anxiety' among the predictors of unpleasant or anxious reactions, but the measure analysed was the trait scale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI-T), as the Methods, Results and Discussion say.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Conclusions; Methods › Predictor variables, 6th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the finding as trait anxiety; the state measure in this study is the AMRS anxiety-depressiveness scale.

reporting_issues.issue: In the unadjusted plasma-concentration results the semi-partial R2 values do not track the standardized coefficients: stimulated beta = 0.3 with R2 0.44 and high mood 0.29 with 0.43, against any drug effect 0.48 with 0.35. With one standardized predictor the share of variance would be near the squared coefficient (about 0.09, 0.08 and 0.23; editors' calculation); in the adjusted models R2 and squared coefficients are close.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Kenward-Roger semi-partial R2 depends on the model's degrees of freedom; these unadjusted values should not be quoted as shares of variance explained.

reporting_issues.issue: Drug-experience statements conflict: Subjects says 75 participants had used illicit substances 1-8 times under an exclusion of more than 10 lifetime uses, while Predictor variables says all had no or very limited previous experience with psychoactive substances (0-5 times). The editors' card for Vizeli and Liechti (2017), drawn from nine of the same ten studies, records an exclusion threshold of more than five lifetime occasions.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Subjects, 1st paragraph; Methods › Predictor variables, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The eligibility threshold for prior drug use in these studies cannot be stated with confidence from the Basel pooled papers; check the source trials.

reporting_issues.issue: The main text does not say how the placebo sessions entered the analysis (for example whether responses are MDMA minus placebo, or change from the pre-dose value); outcomes are described as area under the effect curve and peak values in response to MDMA.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Study design, 1st paragraph; Methods › Response variables, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: If outcomes are not placebo-corrected, associations between traits and self-ratings may partly reflect rating style rather than the drug response; the supplement may answer this.

reporting_issues.issue: One 5D-ASC dimension is called dread of ego dissolution in the Results and anxious ego dissolution in the Discussion; the mood scale is abbreviated AMRS in the Methods and ARMS in the Results; 'MDMD' appears once for MDMA.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Discussion, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the same scales are meant.

reporting_issues.issue: PMC marks a cited reference as retracted: Mithoefer et al. (2019), a pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy (DOI 10.1007/s00213-019-05249-5; retraction notice linked on the page as PMC11513733).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Introduction, 1st and 5th paragraphs; References
reporting_issues.consequence: Cited only as background on MDMA-assisted therapy and phase 3 trials; no finding of this paper depends on it.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC8155734 (DOI 10.1177/0269881121998322 confirmed on the page): structured abstract, all sections, figure legends, author contributions, conflict-of-interest and funding statements and the reference list; there are no tables in the article; Figures 1 and 2 (all coefficients and the LASSO rankings) are images and the figure images were not viewable in this reading, so only values given in the text were extracted; the two supplementary Word files were not opened. No correction, comment or reply to this article is linked; the only retraction flag on the page belongs to a cited reference (reporting issues).

disagreements.first_pass: 194 healthy volunteers (97 women), one oral MDMA dose of 125 mg (164) or 75 mg (30) as study conditions;
