design_detail: Narrative review (journal section 'Review') by six authors from the Laboratory of Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Porto, on hyponatraemia (low plasma sodium) after synthetic phenethylamines, mainly MDMA but also other amphetamines and synthetic cathinones. It covers the physiology of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin), the types of hyponatraemia, a table of 52 published cases (Table 3), proposed mechanisms (serotonin-driven ADH release, hyperthermia and sweating, water intake, metabolic activation, genetic variability, sex and ovarian hormones), prevention and hospital treatment. A search is described (PubMed to October 2019 with three search terms, plus reference lists; 168 publications reviewed), but no screening procedure, formal appraisal of the cited studies or quantitative pooling is reported. Most mechanistic evidence comes from animal and in-vitro studies; the human evidence is case reports and two small experiments as described by the review.
can_establish: What this narrative review selected and reported about hyponatraemia after MDMA and related phenethylamines: its case table, proposed mechanisms and mostly animal/in-vitro mechanistic basis. Its search does not establish a complete inventory of published cases.
cannot_establish: How often hyponatraemia occurs in people who use MDMA (no denominators); whether women are more susceptible (case counts are not set against the number of women and men who use MDMA); what share of deaths it causes; or whether any advice on fluids, settings or exertion prevents it (the review presents no comparative evaluation of these recommendations; the cited primary studies were not independently read for this card).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). PubMed searched up to October 2019 with cathinone, amphetamine and mdma, each AND hyponatraemia, with no restriction on year; reference lists of retrieved papers were checked; only publications that emphasized hyponatraemia or plasma sodium, cerebral oedema or nephrotoxicity were considered; 168 publications were reviewed (p. 2, Methods). One author was mainly responsible for the literature search and data collection (p. 12, Author's contribution).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Only the emphasis criterion above; no other criteria, no description of screening and no list of excluded publications. Table 3 is presented as summarizing all clinical cases in the literature of hyponatraemia associated with phenethylamines (p. 7).
sample.demographics: Table 3 (editors' count of rows): 52 cases, 46 women and 6 men; ages 13 to 49 where given (one unknown); MDMA in 50 rows (with other substances in some), methamphetamine in 1, ethcathinone with methylone in 1 (pp. 5–6).
sample.attrition: Not applicable.
sample.selection_effects: Published case reports are selected by severity and by what clinicians chose to write up; the search used one database and three terms, with one author mainly responsible for searching and collecting data; whether other authors independently screened or checked records is not described. Table 3 includes cases with no measured sodium and three fatal cases with no hyponatraemia among the listed effects, and appears to count two patients twice (see reporting issues). A case series of hyponatraemic states after MDMA held in the project's library (Hartung et al., 2002, QJM) is not cited, so the table is not complete.

exposure.measurement: Ascertainment of drug exposure is not consistently described across the case rows. Table 3 gives numeric drug concentrations in 4 of 52 rows and leaves the amount unknown or blank in 30 (editors' count); that does not show that all other exposures were history-only or untested. The review says phenethylamines/metabolites were detected in most cases (p. 7). Two human experiments are described second-hand with their study conditions: oral MDMA 40 mg in healthy hydrated men (Henry et al., 1998), and 125 mg in 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover (Simmler et al., 2011), p. 10.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesizable from the cases. Doses appear only as study conditions of the cited experiments (see measurement) and as the case reports' own descriptions in Table 3.
exposure.polysubstance: No formal analysis of other substances is reported. The review says only phenethylamines and their metabolites were detected in most cases (p. 7). In Table 3, nine MDMA-labelled rows list at least one additional substance: six have an additional label other than MDA (cannabinoids, benzodiazepines, benzylpiperazine, promethazine/codeine or insulin), while three list MDA alone in addition to MDMA. Numeric drug concentrations appear in four rows. These labels do not establish timing, separate co-use, metabolic origin or causal contribution for each case.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None for the cases (case reports have no comparison group). The cited experiments compared MDMA with placebo or with baseline (as described, p. 10).
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: In the cases, the amount of water and other drinks, exertion, ambient heat, time since the drug was taken, other drugs and medicines, and body size are mostly not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma sodium (mmol/L) and clinical course in case reports; plasma ADH, copeptin and urine osmolality in the human experiments; ADH release and body temperature in animal and in-vitro studies.
outcomes.validity_norms: Hyponatraemia is defined in three ways: plasma sodium below 136 mmol/L (p. 1, Introduction), below 135 mmol/L for diagnosis after phenethylamines (p. 11), and below 130 mmol/L as severe (abstract, p. 1).
outcomes.operationalization: Cases were listed as 'involving hyponatraemia' without a stated sodium criterion; 16 of 52 rows give no sodium value (editors' count).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No pooled estimates. Editors' count from Table 3 (pp. 5–6): 52 rows, 46 women (88.5%, editors' calculation; the review prints 89%); 21 deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown, 1 blank; plasma sodium given in 36 rows, lowest per-row values 101 to 130 mmol/L (one of those 36 rows has 137 on day one and 129 on day three; all printed values range from 101 to 137); in the 10 deaths with a value, 109 to 126 mmol/L, within the range of those who recovered (101 to 130). Human experiments as described (p. 10): after 40 mg MDMA in healthy hydrated men, plasma ADH rose sharply within 1–2 h with a slight fall in sodium and a rise in urine osmolality (Henry et al., 1998; the number of volunteers is not given); a later reanalysis found a significant negative correlation between MDMA and ADH concentrations (Forsling et al., 2001). After 125 mg in 8 men and 8 women, copeptin rose in women but not in men, with no significant differences reported in ADH or sodium; the review does not identify that statistical contrast (Simmler et al., 2011). From outside drug use: in postoperative hyponatraemic encephalopathy, menstruant women were about 25 times more likely to die or have permanent brain injury than men or postmenopausal women (Ayus et al., 1992) (pp. 11–12; postoperative setting established by the Ayus reference title).
analysis.selective_reporting: Selection of cases and studies is not described beyond the search/emphasis criteria. The review reports the small crossover study's copeptin result and no significant ADH/sodium differences, without identifying the latter contrast; its inference of female predisposition is instead drawn from selected case counts without exposure denominators.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: The human case table has 52 rows, not verified unique patients, from 1991–2018: 50 labelled MDMA, 46 female, 21 deaths, with lowest sodium values of 101–130 mmol/L in the 36 rows reporting sodium. One of those rows also reports an earlier value of 137. Two small human experiments are described second-hand as reporting ADH or copeptin responses. Mechanistic arguments also draw on animal and in-vitro studies; the authors acknowledge limits to extrapolation on p. 12.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that hyponatraemia may become fatal "particularly in women", that drinking copiously at raves to counteract hyperthermia "often precipitate water intoxication", and that people should be advised to control fluid intake (p. 1). Gaps: (1) the female excess is a share of published cases (46 of 52), from which the review infers a "probable predisposition of the female gender" (p. 7) without the number of women and men who use MDMA, without considering reporting bias, and while its small controlled human study is described as finding no significant ADH or sodium differences without specifying the contrast (p. 10). (2) The role of water intake rests on anecdotal reports, from which the body says it 'could be speculated' (p. 7); no study measuring fluid intake is cited. (3) The prevention section (p. 11) recommends particular drinks, settings and rest without citing any study that tested them. (4) The single-dose statement specifically concerns most deaths or permanent neurological injuries reported in women aged 15–30 (p. 10). Table 3 cannot verify it: the amount is unknown in 14 of 21 fatal rows, and it supplies no aggregate count for permanent injury. (5) Extension to synthetic cathinones rests on one case and a hypothesis the authors say still needs testing (p. 10).

timeline.event: Cited by this review, with others, for hyperthermia being frequent after MDMA (p. 8)

Henry et al. (1998, Lancet letter, 'Low-dose MDMA ("ecstasy") induces vasopressin secretion'): the main human evidence of ADH release after MDMA, as described by this review (p. 10); not read for this card.
Case series of hyponatraemic states after MDMA in the project's library; not cited by this review
California case series; contributes 10 of the 21 deaths in Table 3
Review of MDMA and the kidney, cited by this review for sodium loss in sweat, the role of oestrogen and treatment

Simmler et al. (2011): randomized placebo-controlled crossover study in 8 men and 8 women; copeptin rose in women only, no significant ADH or sodium differences reported without an identified contrast, as described by this review (p. 10); not read for this card.
Review of MDMA's thermal effects in humans, cited by this review for the frequency of hyperthermia

replication.where_it_stands: A useful map of the case literature and of proposed mechanisms up to 2019, but not a reliable count: its case table has probable duplicates, citation mismatches and fatal rows without recorded low sodium, and its search missed at least one case series in the project's library. The claims it supports best (that severe and sometimes fatal hyponatraemia with cerebral oedema has been reported after MDMA, mostly in young women, and that MDMA can raise ADH in people) should be anchored in the primary sources (Rosenson et al., 2007; Hartung et al., 2002; the human experiments), and its prevention advice should not be cited as evidence.

funding.funder: Fundo Europeu de Desenvolvimento Regional (FEDER) through the COMPETE 2020 – Operational Programme for Competitiveness and Internationalisation (POCI), and Portuguese funds through Fundação para a Ciência e a Tecnologia (FCT), project POCI-01-0145-FEDER-029584 (p. 12, Acknowledgements). Role of funding source: 'Nothing declared.'
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 12).
funding.affiliations_note: All six authors from UCIBIO, REQUIMTE, Laboratory of Toxicology, Faculty of Pharmacy, University of Porto (p. 1). The group's own papers are cited mainly for general amphetamine toxicology and animal work, not for the human hyponatraemia evidence. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective studies of people using MDMA in real settings (festivals, clubs), measuring plasma sodium together with fluid intake, sweating, exertion and heat, separately for women and men and with denominators; a systematic review of case reports with duplicate screening and a case definition based on measured sodium; and studies that test fluid-intake advice against measured sodium outcomes.

domains.note: A search is stated (PubMed only, three terms, reference lists, one author mainly responsible for searching/data collection; independent screening not described), but selection is by a vague emphasis criterion with no screening or exclusion record, and the claim that Table 3 holds all published cases is not met (at least one case series in the project's library is missing).

No formal appraisal is reported. The table appears to count two patients twice, attributes one case to an unrelated laboratory-methods reference, includes fatal rows without recorded hyponatraemia/sodium, and leaves one outcome blank despite a death in the reference title. These observations identify reporting problems without establishing whether an author checked the table.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The hyponatraemia evidence comes from other groups; the authors' own work is cited for background toxicology and animal studies.

Some speculation is labelled ('it could be speculated', 'we hypothesise'), but the abstract states as fact what the body calls speculation (water intoxication at raves), and the prevention section gives recommendations on drinks, settings and exertion with no supporting study.

domains.domain: Balance of explanations for the excess of women among reported cases
domains.note: Biological explanations (oestrogen, muscle mass) are developed at length; reporting bias, the share of women among people who use MDMA, and differences in drinking or exertion are not considered, and the small controlled study's ambiguous ADH/sodium contrast is not clarified when case counts are used to infer predisposition.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3). The review states a search but does not select or appraise systematically, its case table contains errors that change the counts, and its prevention advice and its claim of female predisposition go beyond the evidence it cites. The overall judgment follows the worst domains. Cite it for the existence and character of the published case literature and for the mechanisms proposed (as proposals), with counts taken from the editors' recount or from primary sources; do not cite it for the frequency of hyponatraemia, for sex differences in susceptibility, or for the effectiveness of any preventive practice.

key_findings.finding: Search as stated: PubMed up to October 2019 with cathinone, amphetamine and mdma, each AND hyponatraemia, plus reference lists of retrieved papers; publications that emphasized hyponatraemia or plasma sodium, cerebral oedema or nephrotoxicity were considered; 168 publications reviewed. One author was mainly responsible for the search and data collection.

Editors' count of the rows of Table 3, presented as all published cases of hyponatraemia associated with phenethylamines: 52 rows (1991 to 2018), 46 women and 6 men, ages 13 to 49; MDMA in 50 rows; 21 deaths, 27 recoveries, 3 unknown, 1 blank; plasma sodium given in 36 rows, lowest per-row values 101 to 130 mmol/L (one of these 36 rows has 137 on day one then 129 on day three; the range of all printed values is 101 to 137); the 10 deaths with a value had 109 to 126 mmol/L, within the range of those who recovered.
key_findings.note: The counts include two rows that appear to duplicate two others and three fatal rows without hyponatraemia among the listed effects (see reporting issues); they describe the table, not the literature.

key_findings.finding: The review states that 89% of the cases in Table 3 concerned young women and takes this to indicate a probable predisposition of women.
key_findings.note: 46 of the 52 rows are female: 88.5% by editorial calculation, whereas the review prints 89%. If the two probable duplicate female rows are omitted, the conditional recount is 44/50=88.0%, not a verified unique-patient count. Without exposure denominators, none of these shares demonstrates greater susceptibility.

key_findings.finding: Human evidence on ADH, as described by the review: after 40 mg of MDMA in healthy hydrated men, plasma ADH rose sharply within 1–2 h, with a slight fall in plasma sodium and a rise in urine osmolality, and no direct correlation between MDMA and ADH levels (Henry et al., 1998); a reanalysis reported a significant negative correlation between MDMA and ADH concentrations (Forsling et al., 2001). The number of volunteers is not given.

Sex differences in a controlled study, as described by the review: in a randomized placebo-controlled crossover study of 8 healthy men and 8 healthy women given 125 mg of MDMA, copeptin (a marker of ADH secretion) rose in women but not in men, with no significant differences reported in ADH or plasma sodium; the review does not identify that contrast (Simmler et al., 2011).
key_findings.locator: Section 5.1.5 Gender susceptibility and hormonal influence, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review's support for a greater risk in women once hyponatraemic encephalopathy develops comes from a study of postoperative patients: menstruant women about 25 times more likely to die or have permanent brain injury than men or postmenopausal women (Ayus et al., 1992); the other arguments (oestrogen, muscle mass) come from physiology and animal studies.
key_findings.locator: Section 5.1.5, second and third paragraphs (p. 11; second begins on p. 10); Ayus et al. (1992) reference entry (p. 12).

key_findings.finding: Water intake: the review says people using phenethylamines drink large amounts to counter hyperthermia and dry mouth and that, from these anecdotal reports, it could be speculated that thirst and sodium loss in sweat raise the risk of oedema; it also says people using ecstasy are often advised to drink copious amounts (citing a 2016 review). No study measuring fluid intake is cited.

The prevention section recommends particular drinks in place of water, avoiding alcohol and caffeinated drinks, avoiding hot crowded venues, and less dancing with rest periods, and says young women should be warned of their risk; none of these recommendations is supported by a study cited as testing it.
key_findings.locator: Section 5.2 Measures to prevent hyponatraemia, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: The authors' opinion; reported here as what the review says, not as advice.

key_findings.finding: Hospital treatment as described (citing Traub et al., 2002, and Campbell & Rosner, 2008): diagnosis requires a history of use and plasma sodium below 135 mmol/L, with usual values of 115–125 mmol/L; fluid restriction is the treatment of choice, high-volume intravenous fluids are to be avoided unless the person is hypovolaemic (then 0.9% sodium chloride), and 3% hypertonic saline is given for acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or altered mental status; sodium normally returns to normal in about 24 hours.
key_findings.locator: Section 5.3 Treatment, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (the 2nd continuing on p. 12)

key_findings.finding: Mechanistic evidence is mostly from animals and in-vitro work: for example, in isolated rat hypothalamus the MDMA metabolites HMMA and HHA stimulated ADH release more than MDMA itself; the authors hypothesize that cathinone metabolites act similarly, which they say has yet to be shown, and caution that animal data extrapolate poorly to humans.
Definitions used: hyponatraemia as plasma sodium below 136 mmol/L (Introduction) and severe hyponatraemia as below 130 mmol/L (abstract).
key_findings.note: Section 5.3 uses below 135 mmol/L for diagnosis after phenethylamines (p. 11).

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 attributes an MDMA case (woman, 23, sodium 123 mmol/L) to 'Chen and Viola, 1991', and the same citation is among the cases behind the 89% figure, but the reference list gives Chen and Viola (1991) as a method to detect ras point mutations in small subpopulations of cells (Anal Biochem 195:51–56).
reporting_issues.consequence: The source of this case cannot be traced from the review; it should not be counted without the original report.

reporting_issues.issue: Two pairs of Matthai (1996) and Wilkins (1996) female table rows have matching ages 15/16, sodium 119/112 mmol/L and recovery outcomes; one Matthai row also lists MDA. The Wilkins reference has a matching cerebral-oedema/unrestricted-water topic and an author reply. This suggests correspondence and probable repeated entries, but the bibliography does not expressly label it a letter and the primary reports were not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two patients are probably counted twice. Omitting those two rows conditionally gives 50 rows and 44 women (88.0%, editors' calculation); primary reports and the letter were not read, so 50 is not established as the number of distinct patients.

reporting_issues.issue: One fatal case is cited only as '(2001)', and the reference list's first entry has no author ('2001, 2001. A fatal case of Ecstasy poisoning. Paediatr Child Health').
reporting_issues.consequence: The authorless row is traceable through the anonymous first reference, which provides journal details, DOI and PMCID. That primary report was not read; authorlessness alone does not make the case untraceable.

reporting_issues.issue: The O'Connor et al. (1999) row leaves the amount, sodium and outcome blank, although the reference title reports a death from hyponatraemia-induced cerebral oedema.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table has 21 rows explicitly labelled Death and one blank outcome. The reference-title death is an internal inconsistency; it is not substituted into a corrected 22-death count without the primary report.

reporting_issues.issue: Three fatal rows in a table of 'cases involving hyponatraemia' (Karlovsek et al., 2005, two cases; Libiseller et al., 2005) list no hyponatraemia among the effects and give no sodium value; 16 of the 52 rows give no sodium value at all.
reporting_issues.consequence: The table does not establish confirmed hyponatraemia for every fatal row. Missing measurements and absent effect labels do not establish the true number or causes of hyponatraemia deaths, so no corrected death count or proven inflation is inferred.

reporting_issues.issue: Section 5 says hyponatraemia and cerebral oedema were written on the death certificates of several fatal intoxications, citing Farah and Farah (2008), Ghatol and Kazory (2012), Libiseller et al. (2005), Rosenson et al. (2007) and Wilkins (1996); in Table 3 the Farah, Ghatol and Wilkins cases are recoveries, and the Libiseller row lists no hyponatraemia.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement about death certificates is supported, within this review, only by the Rosenson series; it should not be cited as evidence of how such deaths are certified.

reporting_issues.issue: The review states that only phenethylamines and metabolites were detected in most described cases, and treats the absence of other drugs that may induce hyponatraemia as support for a phenethylamine contribution (p. 7). The table itself has numeric concentrations in four rows, six MDMA rows with an additional non-MDA label, and three further MDMA rows listing MDA alone as an additional substance.
reporting_issues.consequence: Define the six-row count as excluding MDA-only labels: nine rows have any additional substance label. A detected label is not proof of separate ingestion or causal contribution; four numeric concentrations do not establish the testing coverage or methods in the other rows. Primary reports remain unread.

reporting_issues.issue: Hyponatraemia is defined as sodium below 136 mmol/L in the Introduction, below 135 mmol/L for diagnosis in Section 5.3, and 'severe' as below 130 mmol/L in the abstract; the Conclusions say hyponatraemia is generally hypervolaemic, while Section 4.2 and Table 1 class SIADH, the mechanism the review proposes, as euvolaemic.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; thresholds should be taken from primary sources when claims depend on them.

reporting_issues.issue: The first row of Table 3 labels Salathe et al. (2018) as methamphetamine, whereas its reference title names ecstasy and SIADH/water intoxication.
reporting_issues.consequence: Record the mismatch; the primary paper was not read and the compound is not corrected from its title alone.

reporting_issues.issue: The review prints a female share of 89% on p. 7. Counting all 52 Table 3 rows gives 46 female rows, or 88.5% to one decimal; 46/52 does not conventionally round to 89% at integer precision.
reporting_issues.consequence: Distinguish the printed percentage from the editorial recount; no alternative author denominator is assumed.

reporting_issues.issue: Ten Table 3 deaths cite Rosenson et al. (2007), and nine of those ten rows are female.
reporting_issues.consequence: Both the fatal count and the female share overlap the California cohort already used by the claims. The table must not be added as an independent 52-person series.

reporting_issues.issue: The Introduction describes the Boulanger-Gobeil et al. (2012) cathinone-associated case as fatal (p. 2), but Table 3 labels recovery and the p. 7 narrative describes resolution of severe hyponatraemia during a six-day hospital stay.
reporting_issues.consequence: This is an internal outcome inconsistency. The primary case report was not read, so the actual patient outcome is not independently adjudicated.

design_detail: Case series from the National Poisons Unit, Guy's Hospital, London. All enquiries to the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) London about suspected 'ecstasy' or MDMA use from January 1990 to December 1991 were recorded; clinical details and outcomes were requested from the hospital and, where appropriate, the pathologist or coroner; and the Unit's laboratory records were searched for samples in which 'ecstasy' was mentioned or detected (p. 385, Methods). Reported: monthly NPIS enquiries (figure); 7 deaths with analytical confirmation of MDMA (Table I); 5 survivors with severe complications (Table II); one person reported to have taken a large number of tablets, with a high plasma concentration and mild symptoms (text only); 5 people from 4 road traffic accidents in whom MDMA was detected, 2 of whom died (Table III); and 7 cases of liver injury after reported 'ecstasy' use, without analytical confirmation, 1 of whom died (Table IV). Plasma concentrations measured in the Unit's laboratory or, for fatal cases 1–4, in other laboratories. No denominator, no comparison group, no statistics.
can_establish: That in 1990–1991 enquiries to the London poisons information service about MDMA rose, and that a recognisable severe pattern (temperature 40–43°C, seizures, disseminated intravascular coagulation, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure) was recorded in 7 people aged 16–21 who died after reportedly taking 1 to 5 tablets, or an unstated number, at clubs, parties or a concert, with MDMA confirmed in each and plasma concentrations of 0.11–1.26 mg/l where measured, while one person who reportedly took far more had a much higher concentration (7.72 mg/l) and mild symptoms. Conditional on the conventional decimal readings: the fatal 0.11 and severe-survivor 0.2/0.7 entries have missing or faint decimal points in the supplied scan; clearer source images are needed to confirm them.
cannot_establish: How often MDMA use leads to death or severe toxicity (no count of people using it); that heat, dancing, crowding or fluid intake caused the deaths (none was recorded; the authors propose it); what plasma concentration is dangerous (sampling times and collection settings incompletely described, unclear scan decimals, no ordinary-use comparison group); that MDMA caused the liver injuries (not confirmed analytically in any of the 7, and other causes not fully excluded); or that MDMA caused the road accidents (presence only).

sample.recruitment: Cases came to the National Poisons Unit as telephone enquiries from hospitals to the NPIS London or as samples sent to its laboratory, January 1990 to December 1991; outcomes were requested from the hospitals and, where appropriate, pathologists or coroners (p. 385).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Table I: deaths with analytical confirmation of MDMA ingestion. Table II: 'severely symptomatic' cases, criteria not stated. Table III: people whose samples from the scene of four road traffic accidents contained MDMA. Table IV: liver injury associated with reported 'ecstasy' ingestion, criteria not stated. No rule is given for which enquiries were tabulated, and the number of enquiries with known outcomes is not reported.
sample.demographics: Deaths (Table I): 5 men and 2 women aged 16–21. Severe survivors (Table II): ages 1 (an accidental ingestion) to 25, 3 male and 2 female. Road traffic cases (Table III): 4 men and 1 woman aged 18–23. Liver injury (Table IV): 6 men and 1 woman aged 19–29.
sample.attrition: Not applicable; how many enquiries lacked outcome information is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Only cases in which a hospital called a poisons service or sent a sample to one laboratory, and of these mainly the most severe; the mild cases that the authors say made up most enquiries (p. 386) are not counted or described in numbers. Enquiry numbers reflect clinicians' use of the service as well as cases, so a rise in calls is not by itself a rise in harm. Deaths without a call or sample, and deaths outside hospital, are missed.

exposure.measurement: Reported tablets or capsules taken, as recorded in the case circumstances; plasma MDMA and other substances measured in the Unit's laboratory or, for fatal cases 1–4, in other laboratories (Table I footnote); MDA, a metabolite, cannot be told apart from co-ingested MDA in biological samples (p. 385). The time of sampling relative to ingestion or admission is not given, and the screening scope behind 'other drugs were not detected' is not described. Liver cases: reported use only, with no analytical confirmation because use had stopped (p. 386).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Reported intake as study data, tablet content unknown. Deaths: 3 tablets (case 1), 2 (2), 5 (3), 1 (4), 'tablets' (5), not stated (6), 3 (7). Survivors: 3 tablets, 1 tablet (a child, accidental), 2 tablets sold as amphetamine, 3 capsules, 2.5 tablets over 4.5 h. Plasma MDMA (mg/l): deaths 0.36, detected, detected (blood and urine), 0.424, 0.11, 1.16, 1.26; severe survivors 0.2, 0.7, 0.97, 0.24, 0.21; road traffic cases 0.1, 0.13, 0.05, 0.34, 0.15; the person with mild symptoms 7.72 (pp. 385–386). Conditional on the conventional decimal readings: the fatal 0.11 and severe-survivor 0.2/0.7 entries have missing or faint decimal points in the supplied scan; clearer source images are needed to confirm them. The plasma table headers do not establish that every value was collected in hospital or before death.
exposure.polysubstance: Deaths: amphetamine at a low concentration in one (the footnote says case 5; the table places it, with MDA, in case 6) and no ethanol or other drugs detected in any. Severe survivors: amphetamine in cases 1 and 4, MDA in cases 3 and 4, MDEA in the urine of case 4; case 3 had taken tablets sold as amphetamine. Road traffic cases: MDA and amphetamine in cases 4 and 5, with ephedrine (and triprolidine in case 4) in urine; case 3 reportedly took alcohol, but ethanol was detected in none; an amyl nitrite bottle was found on case 5. Liver cases: psilocybe, cocaine and cannabis (case 1), LSD and cannabis (case 5) (Tables I–IV).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None. The contrasts are inside the series: one person with a plasma concentration several times higher than any fatal case had only mild symptoms (p. 385), and the plasma values of the 8 people who survived in Tables II and III (0.05–0.97 mg/l) overlap those of the deaths in Table I (0.11–1.26 mg/l) (editors' comparison, pp. 385–386). Conditional on the conventional decimal readings: the fatal 0.11 and severe-survivor 0.2/0.7 entries have missing or faint decimal points in the supplied scan; clearer source images are needed to confirm them.
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Medical history is reported only in passing (haemophilia in fatal case 6; in the liver cases, no history of regular alcohol or injecting drug use and no evidence of paracetamol overdose). Physical activity, ambient temperature, clothing, fluid intake and time spent dancing are not recorded for any case (editors' observation from Tables I–II).

outcomes.instruments: Clinical course and outcome from hospital records and, where appropriate, pathologists or coroners: temperature, pulse, blood pressure, seizures, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure, liver tests and hepatitis serology, treatment, time to death or discharge (Tables I–IV).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable.
outcomes.operationalization: A death enters the 'fatal cases of MDMA toxicity' (Table I) with analytical confirmation of MDMA and the clinical course shown; the cause of death is the authors' reading ('probably' heatstroke with DIC, p. 386), and no certified cause, post-mortem finding or coroner's conclusion is reported. One of the 7 died of graft rejection 18 days after a liver transplant (Table I, case 5). 'MDMA hepatotoxicity' is jaundice or hepatitis after reported 'ecstasy' use with hepatitis A and B (and in 4 cases C) serology negative.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics. Editors' summaries from the tables: in the 5 deaths with a measured plasma MDMA, 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, against 7.72 mg/l in the person with mild symptoms; recorded temperatures in the deaths 40 to 43°C; deaths 2.5 h to 60 h after admission, plus one 18 days after a transplant. Enquiries (editors' approximate reading of the figure, no values printed): about 64 in 1990 and about 343 in 1991. Conditional on the conventional decimal readings: the fatal 0.11 and severe-survivor 0.2/0.7 entries have missing or faint decimal points in the supplied scan; clearer source images are needed to confirm them.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Not reported: the number of enquiries, how many had known outcomes and how many were mild; post-mortem findings or certified causes for any death; sampling times; and any detail of the person with 7.72 mg/l beyond one sentence.
analysis.power: Not applicable.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A two-year series from one poisons service: rising enquiries about MDMA; 7 deaths in people aged 16–21 after reportedly taking a few tablets at clubs, parties or a concert, with temperatures of 40–43°C, seizures, DIC, rhabdomyolysis and renal failure, and plasma MDMA of 0.11–1.26 mg/l where measured; 5 severely ill survivors; one person with 7.72 mg/l and mild symptoms; 5 road traffic cases with MDMA present (2 died); and 7 liver injuries after reported use, none confirmed analytically (1 died). Conditional on the conventional decimal readings: the fatal 0.11 and severe-survivor 0.2/0.7 entries have missing or faint decimal points in the supplied scan; clearer source images are needed to confirm them.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reports a recent increase in severe toxicity following recreational use of small amounts of MDMA (p. 384); the series shows more enquiries and laboratory detections, with no count of people using MDMA, and the amounts are reported tablets of unknown content. The discussion attributes the deaths 'probably' to heatstroke and proposes that sustained activity, high ambient temperature and inadequate fluid replacement at crowded venues add to a direct drug effect on thermoregulation (p. 386), citing animal studies; none of these was recorded in any case, so this is the authors' hypothesis, and the conclusion that the acute toxicity 'may be due mainly to the circumstances' of use (p. 387) rests on it. The liver injuries are presented as MDMA hepatotoxicity, although MDMA was not confirmed in any case and the authors themselves list a metabolite, a contaminant or an additive as possible causes (p. 386). The statement that all fatal cases were at crowded parties or clubs fits Table I except case 7 (a pop concert) and case 6 (found in the street after a party), and crowding is not recorded. The abstract counts 7 fatalities while the paper describes 10 deaths. The road traffic cases are presented neutrally as MDMA identified, which is what they show.

timeline.event: Brown & Osterloh reported multiple severe complications after recreational MDMA ingestion (JAMA; cited as reference 4; not read).
Chadwick et al. (1991) and Campkin & Davies (1992) reported single UK deaths with coagulopathy and hyperthermia; the paper marks its fatal cases 4 and 7 with these references (not read).

This series. Two Lancet letters in reply, named in the project's search log as reporting further complications (Rittoo et al., doi 10.1016/0140-6736(92)92261-d; Ellis, no DOI), are not among the files and were not read.
Milroy analysed MDMA concentrations in deaths attributed to MDMA toxicity against deaths from trauma (as described on the project's drug-deaths list; card written by another reader in this round).
Parrott reviewed the thermal effects of MDMA in humans (title as listed; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: A landmark early UK description of the hyperthermic pattern of fatal MDMA toxicity; a descriptive series, so replication in the usual sense does not apply. Its environmental explanation was a hypothesis here: the project's before-and-during list records that the evidence on heat and dancing is one laboratory study of room temperature, field surveys and reviews, with no trial of cooling, rest or chill-out areas (search-logs/BeforeDuring_DOI-LIST.md, section 11, Known gaps). Overlap between concentrations in fatal and non-fatal cases is taken up in later work (Milroy, 2011).

funding.funder: Not reported (no funding statement).
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported (no conflict-of-interest statement). The acknowledgement thanks the doctors who provided details of patients and four named individuals for their help (p. 387).
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors at the National Poisons Unit, Guy's Hospital, London (p. 384), which ran both the enquiry service and the laboratory from which the cases came.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective surveillance of people treated for MDMA toxicity with timed blood samples, analysis of any remaining tablets, and recorded setting, ambient temperature, activity and fluid intake, compared with people using MDMA in the same settings without harm, with a denominator of use from concurrent surveys; for the liver, analytically confirmed cases with full exclusion of other causes.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Calls to one poisons service and samples sent to one laboratory are not a frame for MDMA toxicity in the population.
No rule is given for which enquiries became tabulated cases; mild cases are not described.
7 deaths, 5 severe survivors, 5 road traffic cases and 7 liver cases; adequate to describe a pattern, not to estimate any frequency.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Each case has age, sex, circumstances, reported amount, clinical course, analytical results and outcome.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: The number of enquiries, and how many had known outcomes, is not reported.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: MDMA was analytically confirmed in the deaths and severe cases, but not in the liver cases; the road traffic cases show presence only; the cause of each death is the authors' reading, without post-mortem findings.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: Analyses in different laboratories, sampling times not given, some results 'detected' without a concentration, hepatitis C serology missing in 3 liver cases.
Description suits a case series, but the claimed increase in severe toxicity rests on raw enquiry counts without a denominator.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: Clinical details were requested from hospitals; how many responded is not reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI checklist, as the round brief directs for case series without a comparison. The cases are clearly tabulated with analytical confirmation, but they were assembled from calls and samples sent to one poisons service, without inclusion rules, denominators, sampling times or any record of the circumstances the authors invoke, so the editors summarise the risk of bias as high for anything beyond description. It may be cited for: the clinical pattern recorded in the 7 deaths (temperature 40–43°C, seizures, DIC, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure); their settings and reported tablet numbers as recorded; the plasma MDMA concentrations in these cases alongside one higher concentration with mild symptoms, as an illustration that concentration and outcome did not line up; the 5 road traffic cases as presence of MDMA; and, attributed to the authors, the heat-and-exertion hypothesis. It may not be cited for a death rate, for heat, dancing or fluids causing the deaths, for a dangerous concentration, or for MDMA causing liver injury.

key_findings.finding: Methods: all enquiries to the NPIS London about suspected 'ecstasy' or MDMA use from January 1990 to December 1991 were recorded and collated; clinical details and outcomes were requested from the hospital and, where appropriate, the pathologist or coroner; and the National Poisons Unit laboratory records were searched for samples in which 'ecstasy' was mentioned or detected.

Enquiries were few until the second half of 1991, when a striking increase in calls was noted; laboratory detections of MDMA and MDA rose similarly, MDMA being found more often. What was sold as 'ecstasy' usually contained MDMA, but MDA or amphetamine were also identified; mixtures were uncommon.
key_findings.note: Editors' approximate reading of the figure bars (no values printed; 300-dpi crop): at most about 15 calls a month in 1990 (about 64 in the year), rising from February 1991 to about 51 in October 1991 (about 343 in 1991); the rise began in the first half of 1991 (about 124 calls) rather than only in the second (about 219).

key_findings.finding: Seven deaths with analytical confirmation of MDMA (Table I): 5 men and 2 women aged 16–21; reported intake 3 tablets in a club, 2 tablets at a party, 5 tablets at a party, 1 tablet in a club, 'tablets' at a party, not stated (a man with haemophilia found collapsed in the street after a party) and 3 tablets at a pop concert. Recorded temperatures 40°C to 43°C (41.8, 41, 42.1 within 4.5 h of ingestion, 40, 41, 40 and 43°C); seizures recorded in 5, DIC in 5, rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure in 3. Deaths 2.5 h to 60 h after admission (two at 14 h and 15.5 h after ingestion); one woman had a liver transplant after 4 days and died of graft rejection after 18 days.
key_findings.note: Table I is an image without a text layer; values read on 150-dpi renderings and 300-dpi crops. Counts are editors' tallies: seizures from two columns (case 4's seizure is recorded under circumstances, cases 2, 5, 6 and 7 under clinical course); DIC (cases 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7) and rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure (cases 5, 6 and 7) from the clinical-course column.

key_findings.finding: Plasma concentrations in the deaths (mg/l): MDMA 0.36 (case 1), detected (2), detected in blood and urine (3), 0.424 (4), 0.11 (5), 1.16 with MDA 0.06 and amphetamine 0.10 (6), 1.26 (7). Samples for cases 1–4 were analysed in other laboratories; the footnote says that, apart from a low concentration of amphetamine in case 5, ethanol and other drugs were not detected in any case.
key_findings.locator: Table I, analytical amounts column and footnote
key_findings.note: Read on the rendered page; the decimal points in 0.11 and 0.10 (and in 6.5 h for case 7) are not visible in the scan and were read by analogy with the other values. The amphetamine is in the row of case 6, not case 5 (reporting issues). Sampling times are not given. The 0.11 fatal-range endpoint and comparisons using it are conditional readings, not independently resolved decimal values.

key_findings.finding: One analytically documented overdose, of allegedly 42 tablets taken at home, with plasma MDMA 7.72 mg/l, was accompanied by no symptoms other than a 'hangover', with tachycardia and hypertension. The authors write that doses were difficult to establish but that in most cases only a few tablets or capsules seemed to have been taken, and the pattern of toxicity did not seem to result from overdose.
key_findings.locator: Results (single paragraph), left column continuing in the right column
key_findings.note: The OCR text layer reads '7-72 mg/1'; the printed page reads 7·72 mg/l (300-dpi crop). No age, sex, sampling time or other detail is given for this person.

key_findings.finding: Five survivors with severe complications (Table II): a man of 23 after 3 tablets in a club (convulsion, temperature 40°C, DIC, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure; MDMA 0.2 and amphetamine 0.1 mg/l; 20 days of veno-venous haemofiltration, 33 days in hospital); a boy recorded as aged 1 after accidentally swallowing 1 tablet (convulsions for 30 min; MDMA 0.7 mg/l; symptom-free by 6 h); a woman of 19 after 2 tablets sold as 'amphetamine' in a club (coma, temperature 39.7°C, thrombocytopenia; MDMA 0.97 and MDA 0.05 mg/l; recovered); a man of 20 after 3 capsules in a club (pulse 210, temperature 40°C, DIC, rhabdomyolysis, acute renal failure; MDMA 0.24, MDA 0.02, amphetamine 0.02 mg/l, MDEA in urine; 21 days in hospital); a woman of 25 after 2.5 tablets over 4.5 h at home (subarachnoid haemorrhage on CT; MDMA 0.21 mg/l; neurosurgery, full recovery).
key_findings.note: Table II is an image; values read on the rendered page, with decimal points in 0.2, 0.7 and 39.7 not visible in the scan. The first two MDMA entries are visibly separated digits in the scan; the conventional 0.2 and 0.7 readings remain conditional.

key_findings.finding: Samples from the scenes of four road traffic accidents contained MDMA in 5 people (Table III): the driver (21, multiple fractures; MDMA 0.1 mg/l) and a passenger (23, multiple skull fractures; 0.13) of the same car in a head-on collision both died; a man of 21 who had taken 'ecstasy' and alcohol (0.05) discharged himself; a woman of 23 who denied drug use (0.34, with MDA, amphetamine, and ephedrine and triprolidine in urine) recovered fully; a pedestrian of 18 hit while staggering across a road, with an amyl nitrite bottle in his pocket (0.15, with MDA, amphetamine and ephedrine), was discharged after 11 days with a minor residual deficit. Ethanol was not detected in any.
key_findings.locator: Results (single paragraph), right column (p. 385); Table III and footnote (p. 386)

key_findings.finding: Seven cases of liver injury after reported 'ecstasy' use (Table IV; 6 men, 1 woman, aged 19–29): reported use from one tablet three weeks earlier to regular use for 3 or 10 months and escalating use to 4 tablets weekly; one fulminant hepatic failure treated by a successful liver transplant, one death (a man of 20 who had also used LSD and cannabis for 2 years, with encephalopathy, coagulopathy and adult respiratory distress syndrome), the others recovering or resolving. Hepatitis A IgM and hepatitis B surface antigen were negative in all, hepatitis C antibody negative in the 4 tested; liver biopsy in 2 showed eosinophilic infiltration. MDMA could not be confirmed analytically because use had stopped; the authors say whether MDMA, a metabolite, a manufacturing contaminant or a tablet additive was responsible was not yet clear.
key_findings.locator: Results (single paragraph), right column (p. 385); Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 386); Table IV and footnote (p. 387)

key_findings.finding: Most cases on which the Unit was consulted had mild symptoms (agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, widely dilated pupils, trismus, sweating); the most severe were characterised by hyperthermia, DIC, rhabdomyolysis and acute renal failure, and death was probably due to heatstroke with DIC. The authors note that this pattern can follow amphetamine sulphate overdose but had only recently been seen with MDMA in the UK, for reasons not clear.

The authors found no evidence that an impurity or manufacturing variation was responsible and suggested a combination of direct drug effects and circumstances: most serious and all fatal cases they encountered were among people at crowded parties or clubs, where sustained physical activity, a high ambient temperature and inadequate fluid replacement could all reduce heat loss and add to a direct effect on thermoregulation (citing animal studies in which hyperthermia is greater at high ambient temperature). On this basis they suggested early medical management with intravenous fluids and intravenous dantrolene, untested in the series, noting that their fatal cases already had established heatstroke when first seen, and speculated that some people developing severe toxicity may have a metabolic myopathy.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column)
key_findings.note: Activity, ambient temperature and fluid intake were not recorded for any case in Tables I–II (editors' observation).

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that MDMA can cause severe toxicity and that its acute pattern in this series may be due mainly to the circumstances in which it is used; they argue for publicity because 'ecstasy' was widely seen as safe, for clinicians to include MDMA in the differential diagnosis of severe hyperthermia, for analytical confirmation in young people with behavioural disturbance or after accidents when circumstances suggest MDMA, and for hepatotoxicity to be recognised as a complication; the frequency and degree of long-term effects on the brain and mental function were unknown.

Conditional editors’ comparison across Tables I–III, if the conventional readings of unclear decimals are correct: eight survivor values (five severe complications, 0.2–0.97 mg/l, and three after road accidents, 0.05, 0.15 and 0.34) span 0.05–0.97 mg/l and overlap five quantified fatal values, 0.11–1.26 mg/l; all five severe-survivor values lie within that fatal range. The two road-accident deaths have 0.10 and 0.13 mg/l, respectively below and within that conditional range. The headers say plasma, not the timing or collection setting for every measurement; they do not establish that all samples were taken in hospital during life.
key_findings.locator: Table I (p. 385); Tables II and III (p. 386)
key_findings.note: Values read on 150-dpi renders and 300-dpi crops; the decimal points in 0.2 and 0.7 (Table II) are not visible in the scan. The survivors were seen in hospital after severe complications or accidents, and one was a child of 1 who swallowed a tablet, so none of these values describes ordinary use without harm.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table I says the low amphetamine concentration was in case 5, but the table lists amphetamine 0.10 mg/l (with MDA 0.06) in the row of case 6; case 5 has MDMA only.
reporting_issues.consequence: Which death had amphetamine is uncertain; the table row is the more specific source.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract counts 7 fatalities, but the paper describes 10 deaths: the 7 in Table I, the 2 road traffic deaths in Table III and the liver-injury death in Table IV.
reporting_issues.consequence: Counts of deaths involving MDMA drawn from this paper depend on which tables are used; the three other deaths are not discussed as deaths.

reporting_issues.issue: Table IV gives bilirubin in mmol/l (40 to 530), a unit in which these values would be impossible; µmol/l is presumably meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Unit error; the bilirubin values should not be quoted with the printed unit.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says none of the liver cases had a history of heavy alcohol or intravenous drug use and none had evidence of infectious hepatitis, and that hyperthermic liver toxicity can be excluded; Table IV records past intravenous drug use (more than 5 years earlier) in case 4, reports no hepatitis C antibody result for cases 2, 5 and 7, and gives no temperatures.
reporting_issues.consequence: Other causes of the liver injuries were excluded less completely than the text states.

reporting_issues.issue: The text places the rise in enquiries in the second half of 1991, but the figure shows monthly calls rising from February 1991 (editors' reading).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the timing of the rise is earlier than stated.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion says all fatal cases were among people at crowded parties or clubs; Table I records a pop concert (case 7) and a person found in the street after a party (case 6), and crowding is not recorded for any case.
reporting_issues.consequence: The setting statement is a generalisation slightly beyond the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The case with plasma MDMA 7.72 mg/l appears only in one sentence of the results. It reports a hangover, tachycardia and hypertension, but gives no age, sex, sampling time, detailed clinical course, follow-up or table entry.
reporting_issues.consequence: The extreme concentration/outcome contrast has only a brief description and unknown sampling time, limiting its assessment. It is an illustration from one selected case, not a validated ordinary-use range or a boundary between survival and death.

reporting_issues.issue: The footnote to Table III says ethanol was not detected in any case, while case 3 is recorded as having taken 'ecstasy' and alcohol.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not a contradiction if the alcohol had been eliminated, but it shows that negative results depend on unreported sampling times.

reporting_issues.issue: The fatal entry conventionally read as 0.11 and the first two severe-survivor entries conventionally read as 0.2 and 0.7 have missing or faint decimal points in this scan. Plasma headers do not establish collection setting or timing for every value.
reporting_issues.consequence: Retain the table readings and overlap calculation only conditionally pending a clearer source. Do not describe all values as hospital samples taken during life or infer a fatal cutoff.

design_detail: Single-author retrospective case series from the files of one forensic pathology department (Medico-Legal Centre, Sheffield, UK): 77 medico-legal autopsies, 1992–2008, in which MDMA, MDEA or MBDB was detected on post-mortem toxicology. Every death had a full autopsy with histology; femoral blood, urine and stomach contents were analysed in one hospital laboratory (GC–MS with selected ion monitoring). Deaths were grouped by the cause of death given (MDMA or related-drug toxicity, polydrug use, trauma), and blood MDMA was described for each group by range, mean and median (Table 1), without statistical tests or individual values. The Discussion compares the results with published series from New York, a US medical-examiner survey, Melbourne, Sydney and Taiwan, and with one study of paired ante-mortem and post-mortem samples. Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist because it describes the distribution of a measurement in defined groups of deaths; there is no living comparison group.
can_establish: The range, mean and median of femoral blood MDMA concentrations at autopsy in one English centre's deaths attributed to MDMA toxicity, to polydrug use and to trauma between 1992 and 2008, and that the three ranges overlap widely.
cannot_establish: A fatal or toxic MDMA threshold, the concentrations found in living people after ordinary use (trauma deaths are an assumed, not a measured, non-fatal baseline), how far post-mortem redistribution or survival time shifted any value, or whether the cause-of-death groups were assigned independently of the measured concentrations.

sample.recruitment: Records: deaths in which ring-substituted phenethylamines were detected on post-mortem toxicology, identified from the files of the Department of Forensic Pathology at the Medico-Legal Centre, Sheffield, UK, for 1992–2008 (p. 249, Materials and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). How the files were searched, and how many autopsies were tested for these drugs, is not described.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Inclusion: positive post-mortem toxicology for MDMA, MDEA or MBDB. No exclusions stated. Table 1 includes only deaths with MDMA measured in blood (59 of 77); deaths with MDMA in urine only, with only liver available (one decomposed body) or with MDEA or MBDB alone are outside it (pp. 248–249).
sample.demographics: Not reported: no age, sex or other characteristics are given for the series or for any group. Place of collapse: for the MDMA-toxicity deaths, most often at home and next most often at a nightclub; for the polydrug deaths, 27 of 30 at home and 3 at a nightclub (p. 249, Results, 1st and 3rd paragraphs).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). 18 of the 77 deaths have no value in Table 1 (editors' count from p. 249): 4 of the 17 MDMA-toxicity deaths (apparently the water-intoxication, myocardial-necrosis, delayed-hyperpyrexia and decomposed cases, which the paper does not say outright), 8 of the 30 polydrug deaths, 4 of the 28 traumatic deaths (MDMA found in urine only) and the two deaths outside the three groups.
sample.selection_effects: Only deaths that reached a medico-legal autopsy with toxicology in one English centre, and in which an amphetamine derivative was found, are included; the series cannot show how many MDMA-related deaths were missed elsewhere. The trauma group is not a sample of people who use MDMA without harm: it is people who died by homicide, vehicle collision, fall or drowning with MDMA present, in some of whom MDMA may have contributed to the event, and whose time since use is unknown. The cause-of-death groups were assigned by unnamed certifiers on unstated criteria, with knowledge of concentrations unreported. If higher values influenced placement in the MDMA-toxicity group, part of the difference between groups would be built into that classification (editors’ inference).

exposure.measurement: MDMA concentration (mg/l) in femoral blood taken at full autopsy; urine and stomach contents also analysed; GC–MS with selected ion monitoring after butyl acetate extraction and acetylation, by the Department of Clinical Chemistry, Royal Hallamshire Hospital, Sheffield (p. 249, Materials and methods, 1st and 2nd paragraphs). No validation data, limits of detection or method changes over the 16 years are reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: no data on amounts, timing, route or pattern of use. The Discussion notes that the number of tablets taken and what tablets sold as MDMA contain both vary (p. 250).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drugs are counted, without concentrations, for the polydrug group (cannabinoids 16, ethanol 13, heroin 11, benzodiazepines 9, amphetamine 8, antidepressants 6, methadone 5, cocaine 5, GHB 2) and the trauma group (ethanol 17, cannabinoids 10, amphetamine 5, cocaine 4, antidepressants 2, ketamine 1) (p. 249). They are not reported for the MDMA-toxicity group, which the abstract describes as deaths from MDMA alone. MDA, the metabolite, is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (post-mortem samples). The time from use to death and from death to sampling is not reported for any death; one MDMA-toxicity death was a delayed death from hyperpyrexia.

comparison.controls: No living comparison group. The comparison is between cause-of-death groups: the 24 traumatic deaths with MDMA in blood (from homicide, vehicle collision, fall from height and drowning) are treated by the author as a baseline for non-fatal concentrations (p. 250, Discussion, 5th paragraph).
comparison.matching: None.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance, pattern of use, time of last use, survival interval, interval from death to autopsy, condition of the body and natural disease are not reported for any group.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Trauma group: ethanol in 17, cannabinoids in 10, amphetamine in 5, cocaine in 4, antidepressants in 2 and ketamine in 1 of the 28 deaths (p. 249, Results, 4th paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: Femoral blood MDMA concentration at autopsy; cause of death as given (MDMA or related-drug toxicity, polydrug use, trauma), with the mechanism named for the atypical MDMA-toxicity deaths (water intoxication, myocardial necrosis, delayed hyperpyrexia).
outcomes.validity_norms: No criteria are given for attributing a death to MDMA toxicity rather than to polydrug use, and who attributed it (pathologist, coroner) is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: MDMA death: MDMA (or related-drug) toxicity given as the cause of death. Polydrug death: polydrug use given as the cause. Trauma: a traumatic death. Fatal against non-fatal concentration is operationalized as MDMA-toxicity deaths against traumatic deaths with MDMA present.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: no statistical tests.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; whoever gave the cause of death is likely to have known the concentrations (editors' inference; the paper does not say).

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only (Table 1, p. 250): MDMA toxicity (N=13) range 0.478–53.9 mg/l, mean 8.43, median 3.49; polydrug (N=22) 0.04–41.5 mg/l, mean 2.90 (2.78 in the Results text), median 0.76; trauma (N=24) 0.035–4.81 mg/l, mean 0.862, median 0.483. No test, interval or individual values. Editors' calculation: the MDMA-toxicity median is about 7.2 times the trauma median and 4.6 times the polydrug median; from the printed medians and ranges, at least 7 of the 13 MDMA-toxicity values lie inside the trauma range and at least 12 of the 24 trauma values lie inside the MDMA-toxicity range. The MDMA-toxicity mean is more than twice its median, so a few very high values dominate it.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: Individual concentrations, other drugs found in the MDMA-toxicity group, MDA concentrations and the values for the 18 deaths outside Table 1 are not reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive); groups of 13, 22 and 24 values.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Of 77 Sheffield deaths with an amphetamine derivative detected, 17 were attributed principally to MDMA, 30 to polydrug use and 28 to trauma. Femoral blood MDMA ranged 0.478–53.9 mg/l (median 3.49) in the 13 MDMA-toxicity deaths with a blood value, 0.04–41.5 mg/l (median 0.76) in 22 polydrug deaths and 0.035–4.81 mg/l (median 0.483) in 24 traumatic deaths. The ranges overlap widely, while the medians differ about sevenfold between MDMA-toxicity and traumatic deaths.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and conclusion state that no specific concentration can determine death without the history and full autopsy findings, and that there is no specific toxic or fatal MDMA concentration (pp. 248, 251); the key points say fatal MDMA concentrations overlap with non-fatal ones (p. 251). The overlap is supported, and if higher concentrations influenced assignment to MDMA-toxicity categories, that could partly build the observed separation into the groups (editors’ inference, not a documented feature of classification). The step from trauma deaths to non-fatal or tolerated concentrations is an assumption: the Discussion says trauma concentrations are “likely to equate with those of normal recreational use” (p. 250), but no living people were studied, the timing of use is unknown, and MDMA may have contributed to some falls, drownings and collisions. The abstract first identifies59 blood-positive cases and then gives13,22,24, which can reasonably be read as the blood-value subsets; it omits the full category totals17,30,28 and calls the MDMA-toxicity deaths deaths from MDMA alone, which the results do not document.

timeline.event: Early UK report of toxicity and deaths after ecstasy, cited by Milroy among reports of collapse at raves and nightclubs (ref. 26).

Gill et al., New York 1997–2002: 22 deaths with MDMA; MDMA and its metabolites the only drugs in just two autopsied cases; mean blood MDMA 1.04 mg/l in acute MDMA intoxication deaths and 0.97 mg/l in trauma deaths (as summarized by Milroy, p. 249).

Patel et al.: survey of US medical examiner offices (8% response), 102 deaths with MDMA; heart blood used in 66%; mean MDMA 2.02 mg/l in heart and 1.12 mg/l in femoral blood, difference not significant (as summarized, p. 250).

Elliott: MDMA in ante-mortem and post-mortem samples from deaths after hospital admission; one case with heart blood 28.39 mg/l against femoral 6.19 and 7.25 mg/l two days after death (as summarized, p. 250). Also listed by Borra et al. (2026) among ante-mortem/post-mortem comparison studies.
Ferner's review of post-mortem clinical pharmacology records published lethal MDMA ranges spanning 40–8500 µg/L (as recorded on its study card).

Pilgrim et al. (Melbourne), Kaye et al. (Sydney) and Lin et al. (Taiwan, 59 deaths, ketamine in 28): wide, overlapping MDMA ranges across cause-of-death groups; in Melbourne the trauma median (1.03 mg/l) exceeded the drug-overdose median (0.05 mg/l) (as summarized, p. 250).
Review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research lists MDMA and MDA among drugs found higher in femoral blood after death than in samples taken before death.

replication.where_it_stands: Overlap of blood MDMA between deaths attributed to MDMA and other deaths with MDMA present is consistent across the series Milroy summarizes (New York, Melbourne, Sydney, Taiwan), all small and retrospective; in the editors' reading the causes of death were probably given with the concentrations known, but neither this paper nor its summaries say so. Henry et al. (1992), read in this round, give plasma MDMA in 8 people who survived after severe complications or road accidents (0.05–0.97 mg/l) that overlaps the levels in their deaths (0.11–1.26 mg/l); no study read here compares post-mortem femoral blood MDMA with levels in living people after ordinary use. Redistribution reviews (Borra et al., 2026) report MDMA among drugs whose femoral concentrations after death exceed those measured before death.

funding.funder: Not reported: no funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement in the article. The acknowledgment thanks a member of the Royal Hallamshire Hospital clinical chemistry department for information on analytical techniques (p. 251).
funding.affiliations_note: The author is at the Eastern Ontario Forensic Pathology Unit (Ontario Forensic Pathology Service, The Ottawa Hospital) and the University of Ottawa; the cases come from the Sheffield Medico-Legal Centre files. Whether the author performed or certified any of these autopsies is not stated. Several cited papers are his own (refs. 17, 22, 30).

what_would_settle_it: A multi-centre post-mortem series reporting individual femoral blood MDMA values with the interval from use to death and from death to sampling, with causes of death assigned by pathologists who did not see the concentrations or by prespecified criteria, set against MDMA concentrations measured in living people (emergency department or roadside samples) and in deaths from causes clearly unrelated to MDMA with known timing.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to address the target population
domains.note: One centre's medico-legal autopsies with an amphetamine derivative detected, 1992–2008: suits the question for that centre, not for MDMA deaths generally; the share of all autopsies tested is not given.

domains.domain: 2. Study participants sampled in an appropriate way
domains.note: Apparently every positive case in the department's files, but how the files were searched and whether the list is complete is not described.
13, 22 and 24 blood values; a single value (53.9 mg/l) can move a group mean by several mg/l.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: No age, sex, circumstances, survival time, hospital treatment or interval from death to autopsy for any group.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: 18of77 deaths are outside Table1; the text describes four atypical MDMA-attributed deaths but does not explicitly map each to the blood-value exclusions. Reasons for absence from Table1 are given only in part.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used for identification of the condition
domains.note: The cause-of-death category was given by unnamed certifiers on unstated criteria; their knowledge or use of concentrations is not reported. Possible incorporation bias if levels influenced classification is an editors’ inference. The trauma group is defined by mechanism of death, not absence of an MDMA effect.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: Femoral blood at full autopsy and one laboratory and method for all, but no validation data, no account of method changes over 16 years, and no interval from death to sampling.
Ranges and medians are appropriate for skewed values, but there are no individual values, intervals or tests, and the polydrug mean is printed two ways.

domains.domain: 9. Response rate adequate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Records, not respondents.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI prevalence checklist for a descriptive case series. Editors' summary: high risk of bias, because the groups are small, unstated certifiers assigned the causes of death on unstated criteria with their knowledge or use of concentrations unreported, the trauma group is an assumed rather than a measured non-fatal comparison, and the timing of use and of sampling is unknown. If higher concentrations influenced classification, the apparent separation could partly reflect that decision; this is a possible bias, not an established assignment process. The descriptive overlap is directly supported by Table1. Citable for: the ranges and medians in Table 1 with their group sizes; the overlap between groups; the share of deaths with an amphetamine derivative present that were attributed to MDMA (17 of 77); the drugs found alongside MDMA in polydrug and trauma deaths. Not citable for: a fatal or toxic concentration; trauma-death concentrations as the levels of ordinary recreational use; the polydrug mean without noting the two printed values.

key_findings.finding: How deaths entered the series and were grouped: deaths with ring-substituted phenethylamines detected on post-mortem toxicology, from the files of the Department of Forensic Pathology, Medico-Legal Centre, Sheffield, 1992–2008; each had a full autopsy with histology, and femoral blood, urine and stomach contents went to the Royal Hallamshire Hospital clinical chemistry department for GC–MS. Deaths were divided by the cause of death given: MDMA or related-drug toxicity, polydrug use, or trauma. Who gave the cause and on what criteria is not stated.

Seventy-seven deaths had positive toxicology: MDMA in 73, MDEA in 4 (2 of them with MDMA) and MBDB in 2. 17 deaths were attributed principally to MDMA, 30 to polydrug use and 28 to trauma, with one hypothermia death (traces of MDMA and amphetamine in urine) and one attributed mainly to ischaemic heart disease (several drugs at relatively low concentrations, MDMA among them). Editors' calculation: 22% of the deaths with an amphetamine derivative present were attributed principally to MDMA, 39% to polydrug use and 36% to trauma.

Of the 17 deaths attributed to MDMA, one was from water intoxication, one from myocardial necrosis, one a delayed death from hyperpyrexia, and one body was decomposed with only liver available; in the other 13 death was known or presumed to have been rapid. Collapse was most often at home, next most often at a nightclub.

Polydrug deaths: in 28 of 30 MDMA was the main drug (one each MDEA and MBDB); MDMA was in blood in 22 (0.04–41.5 mg/l, median 0.76). Other principal drugs: cannabinoids 16, ethanol 13, heroin 11, benzodiazepines 9, amphetamine 8, antidepressants 6, methadone 5, cocaine 5, GHB 2. Collapse was at home in 27 and at a nightclub in 3, the three each involving amphetamine with MDMA, MDEA or MBDB.
key_findings.note: The polydrug mean is 2.78 mg/l in this paragraph and 2.90 mg/l in Table 1 and the abstract (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Traumatic deaths: 28 (homicide 8, vehicle collision 10, fall from height 6, drowning 4); MDMA in blood in 24 (0.035–4.81 mg/l, mean 0.862, median 0.483) and in urine only in the rest; other drugs found: ethanol 17, cannabinoids 10, amphetamine 5, cocaine 4, antidepressants 2, ketamine 1.

Blood MDMA at autopsy (Table 1): MDMA-toxicity deaths (N=13) 0.478–53.9 mg/l, mean 8.43, median 3.49; mixed-drug deaths (N=22) 0.04–41.5 mg/l, mean 2.90, median 0.76; trauma deaths (N=24) 0.035–4.81 mg/l, mean 0.862, median 0.483. No individual values or tests are given.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the printed medians and ranges: at least 7 of the 13 MDMA-toxicity values lie within the trauma range and at least 12 of the 24 trauma values lie within the MDMA-toxicity range; the MDMA-toxicity median is about 7.2 times the trauma median.

key_findings.finding: The author concludes that there is no specific toxic or fatal MDMA concentration, that a post-mortem concentration cannot give the cause of death without the history and the other autopsy findings, and that concentrations were nonetheless higher in MDMA-toxicity deaths than in polydrug and trauma deaths; he likens MDMA to cocaine and methamphetamine in the overlap between tolerated concentrations and concentrations seen at death.

The author treats trauma deaths as a baseline for non-fatal concentrations and as likely to reflect ordinary recreational use, and names two main problems in reading fatal cases: whether post-mortem concentrations reflect those before death, and post-mortem redistribution of MDMA (high volume of distribution), with heart blood showing the highest concentrations.

Paired samples cited from Elliott (second-hand): in 5 deaths after hospital admission, ante-mortem MDMA was 0.55–4.33 mg/l and post-mortem values ran from 0.47 to 28.39 mg/l; in one case, post-mortem samples taken 2 days after death gave heart blood 28.39 mg/l, right femoral 6.19, left femoral 7.25 and vitreous 11.93 mg/l, against ante-mortem serum of 4.33 mg/l taken a day before death.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: in that case heart blood was about 3.9–4.6 times femoral blood, and femoral blood about 1.4–1.7 times the serum value from the day before death. Serum and whole blood differ, so this ratio is indicative only.

key_findings.finding: Other series as summarized (second-hand): Patel et al., 102 deaths from 38 US medical examiner offices (8% of offices responded), heart blood in 66% of cases, mean MDMA 2.02 mg/l (SD 2.84) in heart and 1.12 mg/l (SD 1.23) in femoral blood, not significantly different; Melbourne, drug overdose median 0.05 mg/l and trauma median 1.03 mg/l; Sydney, MDMA-only deaths median 0.7 mg/l (0.3–64.0) and combined-toxicity deaths 0.9 mg/l (0.03–93.0); Taiwan (Lin et al.), 59 deaths, ketamine in 28, MDMA-only deaths median 2.77 mg/l and trauma deaths with ketamine median 0.97 mg/l.
key_findings.note: Second-hand figures; the Melbourne heart-disease median (0.3 mg/l) lies below its own printed range (0.5–2.6 mg/l), see reporting issues. Cite the primary series.

key_findings.finding: The author notes that MDMA is most often taken with alcohol and other drugs and that mono-intoxication is less common, that deciding which of the drugs present were relevant to death is difficult and has no easy answer (with methadone's effect on the QTc interval as an example), that water-intoxication deaths may show low MDMA because of haemodilution, and that most deaths in this series occurred at home rather than at raves.

reporting_issues.issue: The polydrug group's mean blood MDMA is 2.78 mg/l in the Results text (p. 249) but 2.90 mg/l in Table 1 (p. 250) and the abstract (p. 248); range and median agree.
reporting_issues.consequence: One mean is misprinted; cite the median (0.76 mg/l) and range, or both printed means.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 13 MDMA-toxicity, 22 polydrug and 24 trauma deaths; these are the deaths with MDMA measured in blood. The Results give 17, 30 and 28 deaths in these categories (p. 249).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract attributes the 13 deaths to the toxic effects of MDMA alone, but the paper lists other drugs only for the polydrug and trauma groups and reports nothing on other drugs in the MDMA-toxicity group.

reporting_issues.issue: Who assigned the cause of death (pathologist, coroner), on what criteria, and whether the measured concentration entered that decision is not stated, although the three groups are defined by it (Materials and methods, 3rd paragraph).
reporting_issues.consequence: Possible incorporation bias: if high concentrations led to an MDMA-toxicity verdict, the groups' difference in medians is partly built in. The overlap finding is not weakened by this.

reporting_issues.issue: The intervals from use to death and from death to sampling are not reported for any case, although the Discussion names the gap between post-mortem and ante-mortem concentrations and post-mortem redistribution as the main problems of interpretation (p. 250).
reporting_issues.consequence: How far redistribution or survival time shifted the values in each group cannot be judged.

reporting_issues.issue: In the summary of the Melbourne series, 5 deaths associated with heart disease are given a range of 0.5–2.6 mg/l and a median of 0.3 mg/l, a median below the minimum. In the Elliott summary, post-mortem values are printed as 0.47 and 28.39 mg/l, apparently a range.
reporting_issues.consequence: Second-hand figures with a printing error; take them from the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes 77 deaths in which MDMA was detected; the Results say MDMA was found in 73, the other 4 having MDEA or MBDB without MDMA (p. 249).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the series is of deaths with any of three amphetamine derivatives.
