design_detail: Brief narrative review (Journal of Psychopharmacology, Reviews section) of how the use of other drugs alongside ecstasy confounds research on MDMA's long-term effects in people, with sections on stimulant amphetamines (neurotoxicity in animals, possible effects in people) and cannabis (psychopathology and cognitive effects in people; neuroprotection at the cellular level and in one rat study). No search strategy, inclusion criteria or quantitative synthesis; 71 references, 6 of them by the authors' group, whose cross-sectional, follow-up and fMRI studies supply much of the human evidence on cannabis co-use. University of Cologne; published 2006.
can_establish: That, by the literature the authors cite up to 2005, most people who use ecstasy also use alcohol, cannabis and stimulants, that many studies compared them with people using no or fewer drugs, and that findings on whether cannabis co-use explains, worsens or offsets problems seen in people who use ecstasy pointed in different directions.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA, stimulants, cannabis or their combination causes any cognitive or psychiatric outcome in people (the cited human studies are cross-sectional or short follow-ups); whether cannabinoids protect people from MDMA-related harm (the evidence is one rat study, cell studies and a pilot of 8 participants in the MDMA-only group,with the comparison-group sizes not given here); or the size of any effect (no pooling or appraisal).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited studies had samples described as up to 234, containing people using ecstasy with other drugs and polydrug controls who did not use ecstasy; the wording does not resolve whether 234 counts only the ecstasy group or the total (p 189); 28 people using ecstasy and cannabis, 28 using cannabis only and 28 using neither (p. 190); 60 abstinent people using ecstasy with other drugs and 30 matched controls, 38 of the former re-examined after 18 months (p. 190); and 8 abstinent people using only MDMA with two matched groups (p. 190).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated; studies chosen by the authors.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. In the cited 18-month follow-up, 38 of 60 people using ecstasy were re-examined (p. 190).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen by the authors. The human studies on cannabis co-use described in most detail are their own (Daumann et al., 2001, 2003, 2004); other groups' contrary findings are cited in one sentence (p. 190). The neuroprotection argument rests on cell studies and one rat study (Morley et al., 2004).

exposure.measurement: Varies across cited studies; mostly self-reported drug histories. The authors note that some earlier studies did not record use of other drugs at all (p. 191).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. One cited survey defined novice ecstasy use as a cumulative 1–9 pills (p. 189).
exposure.polysubstance: The topic of the review: the most commonly co-used substances are alcohol, cannabis and stimulants (amphetamines and cocaine) (p. 189).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Described as 'currently abstinent' for the authors' cited studies, without durations in this review.

comparison.controls: As in the cited studies: people who use no drugs, people who use other drugs but not ecstasy, people who use cannabis only, and people using ecstasy without (pure) or with (combined) cannabis and amphetamines.
comparison.matching: The authors' studies are described as using matched controls; matching variables are not given in this review.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The authors note that findings may reflect pre-existing traits of people prone to drug use, or drug use and lifestyle in general (p. 191), and that stimulant-related deficits may reflect low cognitive ability before use (p. 189); no cited human study had measurements before drug use.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The central issue: polydrug control groups mostly used drugs more moderately than the ecstasy groups (p. 189; p. 191).

outcomes.instruments: As cited: self-reported psychopathology (obsessive-compulsive behaviour, interpersonal sensitivity, depression, anxiety, phobic anxiety, paranoid ideation), memory and learning tests, working-memory fMRI (n-back), PET and SPECT of serotonin and dopamine transporters, PET glucose metabolism, MR spectroscopy; in animals, brain serotonin and 5-HIAA after MDMA with or without cannabinoids.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not appraised.
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity is framed as loss of serotonergic (and, for stimulants, dopaminergic) axon terminals, transporters and transmitter; functional effects as subtle memory deficits and subclinical psychopathology.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no statistical synthesis).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable.

analysis.effect_sizes: None pooled; the review gives prevalence figures and sample sizes but no effect sizes. Co-use: in one survey, everyone new to ecstasy (cumulative 1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis in the previous month and 32% had done so on five or more occasions; earlier studies found 90–100% cannabis co-use (p. 189).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. The stimulant section describes neurotoxicity of stimulants alone and offers synergy with MDMA as theory, describing no study of people who combined MDMA with stimulants (an imaging study of amphetamine use among people who use ecstasy is only listed). The authors' own cannabis studies are described in detail, contrary findings in a sentence.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors call their fMRI study a small pilot (p. 190).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Most people who use ecstasy also use alcohol, cannabis and stimulants, and many cited studies compared them with people using fewer drugs. Studies with polydrug controls linked raised psychopathology to polydrug use in general rather than to ecstasy; the authors' own studies linked self-reported psychopathology mainly to cannabis, while other groups linked it to ecstasy; cognitive findings were mixed. Cannabinoids partly prevented MDMA-induced serotonin depletion in one rat study; in people, the evidence for an offsetting effect of cannabis is a pilot fMRI study of 8 MDMA-only participants,with the comparison-group sizes not stated and one study of people using amphetamine-type stimulants.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that cannabis use was shown to contribute to psychological problems and cognitive failures in people who use ecstasy, that cannabinoids were shown to partly block MDMA-induced neurotoxicity in laboratory animals, and that stimulants may act synergistically with MDMA. In the body, the cannabis literature is called inconsistent (p. 190), the stimulant synergy is labelled theoretical (p. 189), and the animal evidence is a single rat study (p. 190). The summary calls reports of residual effects of ecstasy "alarming, although the evidence cannot be considered definite" (p. 191), while also saying the findings may reflect pre-existing traits or polydrug use in general. The abstract's 'shown to contribute' is causal wording for observational associations.

timeline.event: Positron emission tomography study of 15 people abstinent from methamphetamine, cited by this review as Volkow et al. (2001b), where the drug is given as amphetamine; project id volkow_2001a, appraised in the library.

Daumann et al. (authors' group): 28 people using ecstasy and cannabis, 28 using cannabis only and 28 using neither; self-reported subclinical psychopathology mainly associated with extent of cannabis use (as described here).

Daumann et al. (authors' group) fMRI pilot: 8 abstinent people using only MDMA showed lower working-memory activation than non-using controls and/or people also using cannabis and amphetamines; the combined group did not differ from controls (as described here).

Daumann et al. (authors' group): 60 abstinent people using ecstasy with other drugs and 30 matched controls, 38 re-examined after 18 months; psychopathology tracked cannabis rather than MDMA use (as described here).
Morley et al.: in Wistar rats given a neurotoxic MDMA regimen, THC and a synthetic CB1 agonist prevented acute hyperthermia and partly prevented long-term serotonin depletion (as described here).
This review.

Halpern et al. recruited people who used ecstasy with minimal exposure to other drugs and alcohol, the design that addresses the confound described here; adjusted differences were small and mostly non-significant across 40 cognitive measures (as summarized on the project's card sc_halpern_2011).

replication.where_it_stands: The confound the review describes is documented and is the reason later studies recruited people with little other drug use (Halpern et al., 2011, in the library). The review's suggestion that cannabis offsets MDMA-related harm in people rests on a rat study, cell studies and a pilot of 8 MDMA-only participants,with the comparison-group sizes not stated, and has not been tested here in a controlled design; the prospective cohort the authors proposed is not known from this review to have been done.

funding.funder: No funding statement printed in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement printed.
funding.affiliations_note: Department of Psychiatry and Psychotherapy, University of Cologne. The authors wrote 6 of 71 references, including the three human studies behind the cannabis-interaction argument (Daumann et al., 2001, 2003, 2004). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: As the authors propose (p. 191): large prospective cohorts of young people who are not or not yet using drugs and may belong to specific risk groups, followed for years with recorded drug histories (ideally verified by hair or urine testing) and repeated psychological and cognitive testing; meanwhile, cross-sectional studies that recruit people who used ecstasy with minimal other drug use, or that match controls on the amount of other drugs used, and animal studies at human-relevant doses for interactions between MDMA, stimulants and cannabinoids.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria; the authors chose the evidence.

No study-by-study appraisal, but the review's subject is a design flaw and it names others (poorly matched controls, earlier studies without data on other drugs, possible pre-existing traits); the authors call their own fMRI study a small pilot.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The human evidence on cannabis co-use described in detail comes from the authors' group (Daumann et al., 2001, 2003, 2004); other groups' contrary findings get a sentence.

The body labels the stimulant synergy theoretical and the protective effect of cannabinoids conceivable, but the abstract turns observational associations into contributions that were shown and gives the rat finding without saying it is a single study.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether findings in people who use ecstasy reflect MDMA or other drugs
domains.note: Both directions are cited for cannabis, but the stimulant section presents only harms and a theoretical synergy, describing no study of people who combined MDMA with stimulants; the one described study with a group using MDMA together with amphetamines and cannabis found no difference from non-using controls, which the authors attribute to cannabis rather than weighing it against synergy; and the possible protective role of cannabis receives more space than its evidence base.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, and the overall judgment can be no milder than the worst domain (no systematic search). The review is useful and largely candid about the confound, but its selection is unsystematic and weighted toward the authors' own studies, and the abstract states more than the body. Citable for: how common use of alcohol, cannabis and stimulants is among people who use ecstasy (as summarized from cited surveys), the ways polydrug use confounds studies of MDMA, and the authors' proposal of prospective designs. Not citable for: any causal effect of MDMA, stimulants or cannabis in people, or for cannabinoid protection in people; claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: The authors call the use of other drugs one of the most important confounds in research on people who use ecstasy: the great majority also use other psychoactive drugs, most commonly alcohol, cannabis and stimulants, so comparisons with people who use no drugs make it difficult to draw conclusions about MDMA’s effects.

In studies with samples of up to 234 people using ecstasy with other drugs and polydrug controls who did not use ecstasy, raised psychopathology appeared to go with polydrug use in general rather than with ecstasy specifically (Parrott et al., 2001; Thomasius et al., 2003; Roiser & Sahakian, 2004); but polydrug control groups mostly used drugs more moderately than the ecstasy groups, which leaves even these comparisons hard to interpret.

Cannabis co-use: in one survey everyone new to ecstasy (cumulative 1–9 pills) had smoked cannabis at least once in the preceding month and 32% on five or more occasions, and more pills went with more frequent cannabis use (Scholey et al., 2004); earlier studies found cannabis co-use in 90–100% of people who use MDMA. Most began cannabis before ecstasy and continued alongside it.
key_findings.note: The Scholey2004 source is titled as a web-based study in the reference list (p192); this review does not state its sample size. The primary survey was not read here.

key_findings.finding: Stimulants: high or repeated doses of amphetamine or methamphetamine damage serotonergic and dopaminergic axon terminals in animal studies; PET and MR spectroscopy studies suggest possible neurotoxicity in people; cross-sectional studies of people using stimulants chronically found deficits in short-term memory, executive control and planning, but whether these are consequences of use or reflect lower ability before use is unclear. The section concludes that co-use of stimulants may enhance MDMA-related serotonergic neurotoxicity and add dopaminergic effects, a synergy the text earlier calls theoretical; the section describes no study of people who combined MDMA with stimulants.
key_findings.locator: Stimulant amphetamines section, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Introduction, 3rd paragraph (theoretical synergy)

key_findings.finding: Cross-sectional study by the authors' group (Daumann et al., 2001): among 28 people using ecstasy and cannabis, 28 using cannabis only and 28 using neither, self-reported subclinical psychopathology was mainly associated with the extent of cannabis use; Morgan et al. (2002) reported similar findings.

Combined cross-sectional and follow-up study by the authors' group (Daumann et al., 2004): 60 currently abstinent people using ecstasy with other drugs and 30 matched controls at baseline, 38 of the 60 re-examined 18 months later; self-reported psychopathology was mainly associated with cannabis rather than MDMA use; those who stopped ecstasy did not differ from those who continued, while those who kept using cannabis regularly reported more problems than those who stopped.
key_findings.note: Whether stopping was chosen or assigned is not stated, so the stop-versus-continue comparison is observational. Editors' arithmetic: 22 of 60 (37%) were not re-examined.

key_findings.finding: Other groups reported clearer associations between psychopathology and the extent of ecstasy rather than cannabis use, or fewer complaints in people using MDMA with cannabis than in those using MDMA alone (Milani et al., 2002; Parrott et al., 2002).

Cognition: several studies related deficits to the extent of MDMA use with little sign of an effect of other drugs; some found an additional effect of cannabis on short- and medium-term memory and learning; a minority found deficits more closely associated with cannabis than with MDMA use in people using both.

In a study of people using amphetamine-type stimulants (Gonzalez et al., 2004), those who also used cannabis showed less cognitive impairment than those who did not; the groups were similar except for more cocaine dependence in the combined group. The authors' fMRI pilot (Daumann et al., 2003) found lower working-memory activation in 8 abstinent people using only MDMA than in matched controls and/or people also using cannabis and amphetamines, while the combined group did not differ from controls; the authors suggest cannabis might offset MDMA-related changes and note that the fMRI literature on cannabis is far from conclusive.
key_findings.note: The review gives the drug in the Gonzalez study as amphetamine; its title in the reference list (p. 191) says methamphetamine. The sizes of the two matched groups in the pilot are not given here.

key_findings.finding: Animal evidence for protection: in Wistar rats given a neurotoxic MDMA regimen, THC and a synthetic CB1 agonist prevented acute hyperthermia and partly prevented the long-term serotonin depletion measured 2 or 7 weeks later; a CB1 antagonist did not block this protection, and the study's authors proposed a CB1-independent, possibly antioxidant mechanism (Morley et al., 2004). Cannabinoids also showed antioxidant and neuroprotective actions in cell and other animal models.
key_findings.locator: Cannabis section, 2nd paragraph (p. 189, continuing on p. 190)

key_findings.finding: Summary: the authors call reports of residual neuropsychiatric effects of ecstasy alarming but not definite; the subtle abnormalities found in cross-sectional studies may reflect serotonergic neurotoxicity but may also reflect pre-existing traits, drug use in general or associated lifestyle; some earlier studies did not record other drugs and many used poorly matched controls. The most consistent finding is a subtle weakening of memory, correlated with the extent of ecstasy use.
key_findings.locator: Summary and perspectives for future research, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Proposed research: since cross-sectional field studies will never be free of the polydrug problem and follow-up studies may not suffice, the authors call for prospective cohorts of young people who are not or not yet using drugs and may belong to specific risk groups, followed for years with recorded drug histories and repeated psychological and cognitive testing, and for animal studies of drug interactions, especially possible cannabinoid protection.
key_findings.locator: Summary and perspectives for future research, 2nd paragraph

reporting_issues.issue: Three studies of people who used methamphetamine are described in the text as studies of people using amphetamine: Volkow et al. (2001b; 15 abstinent participants), Gonzalez et al. (2004) and Voytek et al. (2005); the titles in the reference list say methamphetamine.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims about amphetamine drawn from this review would rest on methamphetamine studies. The review's Volkow et al. (2001b) is the project's volkow_2001a, and its Volkow et al. (2001a) is the project's volkow_2001c; use the DOI when cross-referencing.

reporting_issues.issue: The description of Volkow et al. (2001b) as showing associations of reduced dopamine transporter density with poorer fine-motor and memory performance does not say that these were correlations within the methamphetamine group, with no comparison of test scores against controls (as the project's card sc_volkow_2001a records).
reporting_issues.consequence: The citation can be read as showing impairment relative to people who do not use the drug, which that study did not test.

reporting_issues.issue: An imaging study cited in the text as Renemann et al. (2002) appears in the reference list as Reneman et al. (2002), titled as a study of amphetamine use by people who use ecstasy and striatal dopamine transporter density; it is listed among stimulant imaging studies, but its findings are not described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stimulant–MDMA synergy is presented without summarizing the cited study that bears most directly on it; a reader cannot tell from the review what it found.

design_detail: Cross-sectional anonymous questionnaire survey (June–December 2004) of 116 Australian residents aged 18 or over who had used ecstasy at least once, recruited by convenience and snowball sampling among people known to the researchers (98 questionnaires handed out) and through an advertisement on an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (thanked in the acknowledgements: RaveSafe and Pill Reports), with no record of which route each return came from. Self-completed questionnaire (about 15 minutes, closed and open questions) on demographics, ecstasy use, use of 15 other substances before, during and after ecstasy, pill testing, strategies endorsed from a list to avoid side effects, the 'comedown' and neurotoxicity, and preloading and postloading (pharmaceuticals and natural products taken before or after ecstasy). Descriptive percentages, with t-tests and chi-square tests of correlates. The effectiveness of the practices was explicitly not studied.
can_establish: Which practices before, during and after ecstasy use this self-selected Australian sample reported in 2004 (drinking water, limiting use, breaks, pill testing, preloading and postloading with vitamins, 5-HTP, magnesium and other products, other drugs taken alongside), and which respondent characteristics went with preloading and postloading in it.
cannot_establish: How common these practices are among people who use ecstasy in Australia or elsewhere (convenience and website sample, unknown response rate); whether any practice reduces harm (efficacy was not studied); how often each strategy was used (not asked); or whether the correlates are causes (cross-sectional, about 30 uncorrected tests).

sample.recruitment: Convenience and snowball sampling among people known to the researchers (98 questionnaires distributed) and an advertisement with a downloadable questionnaire on an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter (RaveSafe and Pill Reports, named in the acknowledgements); questionnaires returned anonymously, so the split between the two routes is unknown (p. 169, Method 2.2; p. 175, Acknowledgements).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Australian residents aged 18 or over who had used ecstasy at least once in their lives (p. 169). Data collected June to December 2004.
sample.demographics: 51.3% women; age 18 to 41, mean 26.5 (SD 5.6); 82.5% born in Australia; 50.4% from Victoria, 18.3% New South Wales, 17.4% Western Australia, 10.4% Queensland, 2.6% South Australia, 0.9% Tasmania; 85.1% completed secondary school and 68.2% had further qualifications; 70.2% working and 21.9% studying (p. 170, Results 3.1).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single questionnaire). The number of respondents varies between analyses (101 to 116) without a statement on missing answers.
sample.selection_effects: No sampling frame: acquaintances of the researchers, their networks, and readers of harm-reduction websites. The authors note that respondents found through the Internet may have a particular interest in harm reduction, which would inflate the reported use of harm-reduction practices, and that representativeness cannot be determined (p. 173). Most respondents used recently (79.1% in the past 3 months) and planned to use again (91.2%).

exposure.measurement: Self-report on an unvalidated questionnaire: ecstasy use (age at first use, frequency, usual and highest number of pills, years of use, route, place); use of 15 other substances and whether each was used before, during or after ecstasy; strategies endorsed from a list for three purposes; preloading and postloading, with substances, frequency, sources and reasons in open questions (pp. 169–170, Method 2.3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported pattern of the sample (p. 170): 51.8% used ecstasy at least monthly; 45.7% had used on more than 50 occasions; mean 4.3 years of use (SD 3.3); mean age at first use 22.0 (SD 4.9). Number of pills on a typical occasion, mean 1.9 (SD 1.0); highest number on one occasion, mean 4.7 (SD 4.0), higher in men than women (5.8 against 3.7, t(78.26)=2.78, p=0.007). Mainly oral (96.5%). Main place of use: dance parties or raves 40.8%, bars, pubs or nightclubs 40.8%, at home with others 10.7%.
exposure.polysubstance: Measured, not adjusted for. Every respondent had used at least one other substance with ecstasy. Used before, during and after ecstasy (Table 2, p. 171): alcohol 91.4%, 81.0% and 60.3%; amphetamines 60.3%, 65.5% and 45.7%; tobacco 48.3%, 62.9% and 45.7%; cannabis 36.2%, 51.7% and 62.9%; sedatives such as benzodiazepines 1.7%, 2.6% and 29.3%; antidepressants 0.0%, 0.9% and 11.2%.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None (descriptive survey). Correlates compared respondents who did and did not preload, postload or change their use.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to a descriptive survey; for the correlates, no adjustment of any kind (each variable tested alone).

outcomes.instruments: The authors' own questionnaire; strategies chosen from a list for avoiding (a) negative side effects, (b) the 'comedown' and (c) brain damage or neurotoxicity; open questions on changes in use and on preloading and postloading (pp. 169–170).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not validated; no pilot or reliability data reported. How often each strategy was used was not asked (p. 173).
outcomes.operationalization: A practice counts if ever endorsed (lifetime), except pill-testing frequency and preloading or postloading frequency, which were rated on a five-step scale from 'rarely' to 'always'.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. Ten respondent variables (age, sex, education, years of use, frequency, more or fewer than 50 occasions, average and highest dose, recency, place of use) were tested against three outcomes (changed use, preloading, postloading); alpha 0.05, or 0.025 when normality was violated (p. 170, Data analysis). Editors' count: about 30 tests, 5 significant.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable (self-completed anonymous questionnaire).

analysis.effect_sizes: Proportions without intervals in the paper. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% intervals, n=116): drinking water to avoid negative side effects 95.7% (about 90 to 98); ever preloaded 41.4% (about 33 to 51); ever postloaded 47.4% (about 39 to 56). Correlates (p. 173): preloading with younger age (24.9 against 27.6 years, t(113)=−2.59, p=0.011) and with more than 50 occasions of use (54.7% against 30.2%, chi-square 7.16, p=0.007); postloading with more than 50 occasions (60.4% against 36.5%, chi-square 6.58, p=0.01) and with use at least monthly (55.9% against 36.4%, chi-square 4.38, p=0.036). Changing use in response to dislikes with more than 50 occasions (65.4% against 42.9%, chi-square 5.80, p=0.016) (p. 171). Editors' check: all chi-square values reproduce from the implied counts as uncorrected tests; with continuity correction the frequency–postloading test gives p about 0.057.
analysis.selective_reporting: Sex differences were reported only when significant (p. 170); non-significant correlates are not listed with their statistics.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 116 respondents a prevalence of about 40–50% has an interval of about ±9 points (editors' calculation); comparisons within the 46–55 people who preloaded or postloaded are small.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 116 self-selected adults in Australia who had used ecstasy, recruited partly through harm-reduction websites in 2004, nearly all reported at least one strategy to avoid side effects (drinking water 95.7%, limiting use 70.7%, breaks 62.1%); 38.8% had ever tested pills (editors' calculation from the 61.2% who never had); 41.4% had ever preloaded and 47.4% postloaded, most often with multivitamins, 5-HTP, magnesium and fruit; every respondent had used another substance with ecstasy. Preloading and postloading were more common in respondents with more than 50 occasions of use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that the results indicate that people who use ecstasy are aware of its potential for harm and actively try to minimise it (p. 168); this generalizes from a sample partly recruited through harm-reduction websites, which the authors themselves say may overrepresent interest in harm reduction (p. 173). The Discussion states that most preloading and postloading products are unlikely to cause harm (p. 174), with no data cited, and that pill testing in the Netherlands has reduced deaths, citing a newspaper report (p. 174). It calls this the first study to focus on harm-reduction strategies of people who use ecstasy (p. 173), although the Introduction describes an earlier survey of the same question (Akram and Galt, 1999; p. 169). On the other hand, the paper is explicit that the efficacy of the practices was not its focus (p. 169), that the evidence for protection comes only from rodent studies with injected pre-treatments (p. 174), that the associations are not causal (p. 175), and that some practices, such as 5-HTP with ecstasy, may carry a risk of serotonin syndrome (p. 175).

timeline.event: Sprague et al. (1994): rat study of tryptophan and 5-HTP against MDMA neurotoxicity, cited by this survey as the kind of animal evidence that may underlie preloading (p. 174); on the project's reading list, not read for this card.

Akram and Galt (1999): survey of harm-reduction practices among people using dance drugs in Nottingham, UK, as described in this paper's introduction (82% used one or more strategy; drinking water, chilling out and eating salty snacks most common; women more likely to use strategies) (p. 169).
Copeland et al. (2006), 'Ecstasy and the concomitant use of pharmaceuticals' (Addictive Behaviors), on the project's reading list; not read for this card.
Kelly (2009), 'Mediating MDMA-related harm: preloading and post-loading among ecstasy-using youth' (Journal of Psychoactive Drugs), on the project's reading list; not read for this card.

replication.where_it_stands: Provisional: no later survey was read for this card. The project's reading list notes that preloading and postloading are documented only by surveys and interviews (this paper, Copeland et al., 2006, and Kelly, 2009) and that evidence of protection comes only from rat studies (Sprague et al., 1994; Aguirre et al., 1999); no human study of the efficacy or risks of these products with MDMA was found by the list's search.

funding.funder: "This research was supported by internal funds only" (p. 175, Acknowledgements).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors from the Department of Psychology, Monash University (p. 168). Recruitment was advertised through the harm-reduction organisations RaveSafe and Pill Reports (acknowledgements, p. 175), which shapes who answered.

what_would_settle_it: For prevalence: repeated surveys of people who use ecstasy recruited with a defined frame (for example, sentinel samples at multiple sites) using standard, piloted items on water intake, breaks, pill testing and preloading or postloading, with how often each is done. For effect: controlled human studies of the products most often taken (5-HTP, magnesium, multivitamins) with MDMA, measuring objective outcomes and interaction risks.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: The target is people who use ecstasy in Australia; the frame is the researchers' acquaintances, their networks and readers of two harm-reduction websites.
Convenience, snowball and self-selected web respondents; the authors note a likely interest in harm reduction among the latter.
116 gives intervals of about ±9 points for prevalences near 40–50% (editors' calculation); analyses within the 46–55 people who preloaded or postloaded are small.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex, state, education, employment, patterns and places of use, and other substances described (pp. 170–171).

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Denominators vary (101 to 116) without a statement on missing answers; the counts of people who preloaded differ between text and tables; the two recruitment routes cannot be compared.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Self-report on an unvalidated, unpiloted questionnaire; strategies prompted from a list; lifetime endorsement without frequency.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: The same self-completed questionnaire for all respondents.
Percentages without intervals; about 30 unadjusted bivariate tests without correction for multiplicity.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed
domains.note: 98 questionnaires were handed out but the number returned by that route is unknown, and the web route has no denominator.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI has no overall algorithm; the editors' summary is high risk of bias for prevalence, because the sample has no frame, is self-selected partly through harm-reduction websites and has an unknown response rate, so its percentages describe these respondents, not people who use ecstasy in general. The description is careful and transparent about these limits. Cite it for what this sample reported (practices, substances used for preloading and postloading, other drugs used alongside), labelled as a 2004 convenience sample; not for population prevalence or for whether any practice works.

key_findings.finding: 116 anonymous questionnaires were returned (June–December 2004) from Australian residents aged 18 or over who had ever used ecstasy, recruited through the researchers' acquaintances and their networks (98 questionnaires distributed) and through an ecstasy-related website and e-newsletter; the split between routes is unknown.

Sample: 51.3% women; age 18 to 41, mean 26.5 (SD 5.6); 79.1% had used ecstasy in the past 3 months; 51.8% used at least monthly; ecstasy was mainly taken orally (96.5%), most often at dance parties or raves (40.8%) or in bars, pubs or nightclubs (40.8%).

All respondents had used at least one other substance with ecstasy. Used before, during and after ecstasy: alcohol 91.4%, 81.0%, 60.3%; amphetamines 60.3%, 65.5%, 45.7%; tobacco 48.3%, 62.9%, 45.7%; cannabis 36.2%, 51.7%, 62.9%; cocaine 24.1%, 21.6%, 19.0%; ketamine 10.3%, 19.0%, 16.4%; GHB 8.6%, 11.2%, 9.5%; nitrous oxide 7.8%, 12.9%, 12.9%; 'amyl nitrate' 5.2%, 20.7%, 6.9%; sedatives 1.7%, 2.6%, 29.3%; antidepressants 0.0%, 0.9%, 11.2%.

Strategies endorsed from a list: to avoid negative side effects every respondent used at least one, most often drinking water (95.7%), limiting the amount of ecstasy (70.7%), a healthy lifestyle (59.5%), breaks or 'chilling out' (62.1%) and vitamins or natural products (52.6%); 30.2% took other illegal drugs and 15.5% prescription medicines for this. To avoid the comedown, 4.4% had no strategy (water 67.5%, limiting use 56.1%, vitamins 49.1%); to avoid neurotoxicity, 18.1% had none (limiting use 57.8%, water 54.3%, vitamins 38.8%).

53% had changed their ecstasy use because of what they disliked about it (the comedown was the commonest dislike, 50.0%); among these 61, 68.9% used less often, 16.4% took less per occasion, 13.1% stopped and 3.3% took more. Changing use was more common after more than 50 occasions of use (65.4% against 42.9%, chi-square 5.80, p=0.016).
Pill testing: 61.2% had never tested their pills, 16.4% rarely, 8.6% three-quarters of the time and 6% always.
key_findings.note: The abstract's 'forty percent' corresponds to 38.8% ever (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: 65.5% had heard of preloading and postloading, mostly from a partner or friends (49.4%) or the Internet (36.7%); 41.4% had preloaded and 47.4% postloaded. Preloading products (n=46): multivitamins 50.0%, 5-HTP 41.3%, magnesium 23.9%, fruit or fruit juice 23.9%, vitamin B 15.2%, vitamin C 15.2%, antidepressants 2.2%. Postloading products (n=54): 5-HTP 46.3%, multivitamins 44.4%, fruit or juice 24.1%, vitamin B 16.7%, vitamin C 13.0%, sleeping tablets 5.6%, antidepressants 5.6%, St John's Wort 3.7%.
key_findings.locator: Results 3.4, 4th paragraph (left column, continuing in the right); Table 5

key_findings.finding: Reasons for preloading or postloading (n=55): to reduce the comedown 45.5%, to reduce brain damage or neurotoxicity 32.7%, to increase the pleasurable effects 21.8%, to reduce side effects 18.2%. Frequency: 31.1% always preloaded and 28.9% rarely; 47.3% always postloaded and 20% rarely. Products came from the Internet (34%), supermarkets (32.1%), pharmacies (30.2%) and health stores (28.3%).

Preloading was associated with younger age (24.9 against 27.6 years, t(113)=−2.59, p=0.011) and with more than 50 occasions of use (54.7% against 30.2%, chi-square 7.16, p=0.007); postloading with more than 50 occasions (60.4% against 36.5%, chi-square 6.58, p=0.01) and with use at least monthly (55.9% against 36.4%, chi-square 4.38, p=0.036). No other respondent variable was significant.
key_findings.note: About 30 uncorrected bivariate tests (editors' count); cross-sectional associations, as the authors say (p. 175).

key_findings.finding: No differences between women and men in the use of harm-reduction strategies were found in this sample, unlike the earlier UK survey; men had used more than 50 times more often (60.7% against 32.2%, p=.002) and more often used in public venues (90% against 74.5%, p=0.042).

The authors state that the effectiveness of the practices was not studied, that it is unknown whether preloading and postloading reduce harm in humans, that the protective evidence comes from rodent studies with injected pre-treatments, and that taking 5-HTP, SSRIs or St John's Wort with ecstasy may risk serotonin syndrome.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, last paragraph and Method 2.1 (p. 169); Discussion, 11th to 14th paragraphs (pp. 174–175)

reporting_issues.issue: The number of respondents who preloaded is not stated and the figures imply different counts: 41.4% of 116 (48, consistent with the chi-square tests), n=46 in Table 5, and frequency percentages that fit 45; for postloading 47.4% (55) against n=54 in Table 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; percentages of products refer to those who listed them, not to all who preloaded or postloaded.

reporting_issues.issue: The age comparison for preloading is reported as t(113), implying 115 respondents with data, while the companion chi-square tests use N=116; across analyses n ranges from 101 to 116 without a statement on missing answers.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; missing answers are few but unreported.

reporting_issues.issue: About 30 bivariate tests (10 variables against 3 outcomes) were run without correction; 5 were significant at p from 0.007 to 0.036, and the abstract reports the significant ones as associations of preloading and postloading.
reporting_issues.consequence: The correlates are exploratory; one or two significant results would be expected by chance.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion calls this the first study to focus on the harm-reduction strategies of people who use ecstasy (p. 173), but the Introduction describes an earlier survey of the prevalence and types of such strategies (Akram and Galt, 1999; p. 169).
reporting_issues.consequence: The priority claim should not be repeated; the novelty is the focus on preloading and postloading.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists 'Amyl nitrate' among substances used with ecstasy; the products used as poppers are alkyl nitrites, so the label is presumably a slip for amyl nitrite.
reporting_issues.consequence: A claim on the poppers page citing the 20.7% used during ecstasy should note the table's wording.

design_detail: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, within-person laboratory study with an active comparison drug, at the Human Behavioral Pharmacology Laboratory, University of Chicago. 21 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 38 who had used ecstasy or MDMA at least twice each had four sessions, in randomized order and at least 5 days apart, receiving one opaque capsule per session: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg (a fixed dose, not adjusted for body weight) or placebo (study conditions). Self-ratings: a 15-item visual analogue scale (VAS) at 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 210 and 240 minutes and the 72-item Profile of Mood States (POMS) at 0, 90 and 240 minutes; five outcomes chosen from the hypotheses (VAS sociable, playful, loving and lonely; POMS friendliness), each analysed as peak change from baseline. Emotion-recognition tasks from 65 minutes after the capsule, once per session: a facial emotion recognition task (FER; Ekman faces morphed from neutral to full expression in 10% steps, shown for 500 ms; anger, fear, happiness, sadness and neutral; 170 pictures), the Reading the Mind in the Eyes test (36 items) and the DANVA-2 adult paralanguage test (24 voice clips). Repeated-measures analyses of variance with Bonferroni-adjusted follow-up tests. Participants sat alone in testing rooms with contact only with a research assistant. The PDF read is the NIH Public Access author manuscript (accepted version, pages 1 to 14), not the version of record (Biol Psychiatry 68:1134-1140); anchors cite the manuscript's own page numbers (PDF p.).
can_establish: Whether, in 21 healthy young adults with limited earlier ecstasy use, tested alone in a laboratory, these MDMA doses changed self-rated loving, friendly, playful, lonely and sociable feelings and the accuracy of recognising emotions in briefly shown faces, in eye regions and in voices, compared with placebo and with methamphetamine 20 mg.
cannot_establish: What MDMA does to empathy or social behaviour with real people (participants were alone and the tasks used pictures and recorded voices); whether the loving and friendly feelings are specific to MDMA (after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg they did not differ significantly from those after methamphetamine); effects at other amounts, after repeated doses or in people who had never taken MDMA; or the size of the self-rated effects in natural units (their means appear only in small figures and the VAS range is not stated).

sample.recruitment: Advertisement: internet advertisements and word of mouth; healthy volunteers aged 18 to 38 who reported using MDMA or ecstasy on at least two occasions (PDF p. 3, Methods and Materials > Participants).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Excluded after screening (medical examination, electrocardiogram, structured clinical interview): DSM-IV Axis I psychiatric disorder including substance dependence; signs of medical or neurological illness; body mass index outside 18.5 to 30; cardiovascular illness in a first-degree relative; prior adverse response to ecstasy; pregnancy or lactation (PDF p. 3). Before each session: no cannabis for 7 days, no alcohol or medications for 24 hours and no other recreational drugs (for example ecstasy) for 48 hours, checked with urine, saliva and breath tests; pregnancy test for women at every session (PDF p. 3).
sample.demographics: Mean age 24.4 (SD 4.9); 9 of 21 women; 17 Caucasian, 2 Asian, 1 African-American, 1 mixed race. First ecstasy use at mean age 19.8 (SD 2.7); lifetime ecstasy use on a mean of 15.0 occasions (SD 23.1), 13 participants fewer than 10 times. In the past month 12 smoked cigarettes at least weekly, all drank alcohol and 16 used cannabis; lifetime, all had used cannabis, all but 2 stimulants such as cocaine and all but 1 hallucinogens (PDF p. 5, Results, 1st paragraph).
sample.attrition: No withdrawals are reported. The self-rating analyses had 20 participants ('missing data', reason not given, Figure 1 and 2 legends, PDF pp. 11-12) and the voice task 20 (equipment malfunction, Table 1 footnote, PDF pp. 13-14); whether the same person is missing from both is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: People with earlier ecstasy experience who answered advertisements or heard by word of mouth and passed a health and psychiatric screen; people with psychiatric disorders, drug dependence or an earlier bad reaction to ecstasy are absent by design. Prior experience was required for ethical reasons, and the authors say the findings may not generalize to people new to MDMA, while noting they recruited people with limited prior use (PDF p. 7). Most also used cannabis, alcohol and other drugs.

exposure.measurement: Drugs given in the laboratory in opaque size-00 gelatin capsules: MDMA or methamphetamine with lactose or dextrose filler, or filler only for placebo (PDF p. 3). The source and purity of the study drugs are not stated in the manuscript, and no plasma drug levels are reported.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one oral capsule per session of MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg or placebo, in randomized order, sessions at least 5 days apart, starting at noon after 2 hours without food; tasks from 65 minutes after the capsule; participants stayed in the laboratory at least 4.5 hours and until drug effects had passed (PDF pp. 3-4). The authors describe the MDMA doses as low to moderate and 1.5 mg/kg as within recreational ranges, citing other papers (PDF p. 3).
exposure.polysubstance: Other drug use was common (see demographics). Use before sessions was limited by the abstinence rules above, checked by urine (QuickTox), saliva (Oratect III) and breath alcohol screens (PDF p. 3); drug-use history was not used in any analysis.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Cannabis 7 days, alcohol and medications 24 hours, other recreational drugs 48 hours before each session, with urine, saliva and breath screens (PDF p. 3).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own placebo session (within person), and methamphetamine 20 mg as an active stimulant comparison, included to test whether effects are specific to MDMA (PDF p. 2).
comparison.matching: Within person; capsules given in randomized order. The authors report that session order had no significant effect in any analysis and was dropped from the models (no statistics printed, PDF p. 5).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense (within-person design). Trait sociability, which the authors suggest may shape the response (PDF p. 7), was not measured; expectation was assessed only through participants' guesses of the drug received.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (within person); the same abstinence rules applied before every session.

outcomes.instruments: VAS of 15 adjectives (stimulated, bored, sedated, anxious, insightful, nauseated, loving, dizzy, sociable, confused, lonely, elated, playful, blank, restless); POMS (72 adjectives rated 0 to 4, 8 subscales including friendliness, the mean of 8 items); FER (proportion correct per emotion and number of emotional faces misclassified as neutral); Reading the Mind in the Eyes test, revised (36 items, total correct); DANVA-2 adult paralanguage test (24 clips of one neutral sentence spoken happily, sadly, angrily or fearfully at two intensities; total correct) (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.validity_norms: Established tasks cited to their sources; the FER is described as sensitive to serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition and the Eyes test to oxytocin (PDF p. 4). The range of the VAS is not stated.
outcomes.operationalization: Prosocial feelings as single VAS items and the POMS friendliness subscale, each as peak change from the pre-capsule baseline; emotion recognition as accuracy. Empathy itself was not measured: the authors treat identifying others' emotions as a first step of empathy (PDF p. 2).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial. Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise follow-ups for the self-ratings; for the FER, simple main effects at 0.05 divided by the number of emotion categories, then pairwise tests adjusted for the total number of analyses (PDF pp. 4-5). No correction across the 5 self-rating outcomes or the 3 tasks; the analysis of faces misclassified as neutral is exploratory and uncorrected (PDF p. 6). Editors' count of 13 outcomes: 5 self-ratings, FER accuracy for 5 categories, FER misclassifications as neutral, Eyes total and DANVA-2 total.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Double blind, with four possible drugs. Outcomes are self-ratings and computer tasks. Six of 21 participants guessed ecstasy when they had received methamphetamine; how drug guesses were collected and how often MDMA was correctly identified are not reported (PDF p. 6).

analysis.effect_sizes: Self-ratings, n = 20 (parametric results reported because non-parametric tests agreed, except for VAS lonely): VAS loving F(3,57) = 5.04, p = 0.004, eta squared 0.21 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo); POMS friendliness F(2.7,51) = 6.81, p = 0.001, eta squared 0.26 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo and above MDMA 0.75 mg/kg); VAS lonely, Friedman chi squared(3) = 11.94, p = 0.008, r = 0.54 (MDMA 0.75 mg/kg above methamphetamine and placebo); VAS playful F(3,57) = 8.57, p < 0.001, eta squared 0.31 (MDMA 1.5 mg/kg above placebo and MDMA 0.75 mg/kg; methamphetamine above placebo); VAS sociable F(2.5,47.7) = 3.06, p < 0.05, eta squared 0.14 (methamphetamine above placebo only) (PDF pp. 5-6). Loving and friendliness after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg did not differ significantly from methamphetamine (PDF p. 6). Means are shown only in Figures 1 and 2 (PDF pp. 11-12), low-resolution images read approximately (embedded images enlarged): largest mean change in VAS loving about 0.27 at 120 minutes after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, about 0.15 after methamphetamine and about 0 after placebo; POMS friendliness about 0.68 at 90 minutes after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, about 0.35 after methamphetamine, about 0.03 after placebo and about -0.19 after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg (POMS items are rated 0 to 4; the VAS range is not stated). Emotion recognition, n = 21: FER drug by emotion interaction F(5.2,104.6) = 3.23, p = 0.008; fear F(2.8,56.0) = 4.45, p = 0.008, eta squared 0.18; proportion of fearful faces correctly named 0.63 (SD 0.07) after placebo, 0.59 (0.12) after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, 0.55 (0.10) after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and 0.59 (0.10) after methamphetamine; placebo against MDMA 1.5 mg/kg t(20) = 3.94, significant after Bonferroni correction; placebo against methamphetamine t(20) = 2.59 and MDMA 1.5 mg/kg against methamphetamine t(20) = 1.31, not significant (Table 1, PDF p. 13). Editors' calculation: within-person standardized difference for fear, placebo against MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, dz = 3.94 divided by the square root of 21, about 0.86; mean difference 0.08 (95% CI about 0.04 to 0.12, from the printed t and the rounded means). Other facial emotions did not change after correction (happiness F = 0.96, sadness 3.60, anger 2.0, neutral 2.84; df 3,60). Emotional faces misclassified as neutral: 44.90 (SD 11.31) after placebo against 51.71 (10.58) after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, overall F(3,60) = 3.25 and t(20) = 2.52, each p < 0.05 uncorrected (exploratory). Eyes test total 26.81 (5.14) placebo, 26.10 (2.70) MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, F(3,60) = 0.58; DANVA-2 total 18.05 (1.70) placebo, 17.20 (2.19) MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, 18.70 (2.11) methamphetamine, F(3,57) = 3.01 (Table 1, PDF p. 13).
analysis.covariates: None. Session order was tested and dropped (no statistics). The methamphetamine dose was not adjusted for body weight; post hoc, only methamphetamine's effect on playfulness correlated with body weight (r = -0.45, p = 0.04) (PDF p. 7).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No trial registration or published protocol is mentioned in the manuscript; the five self-rating outcomes are described as chosen from the study hypotheses (PDF p. 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only 5 of the 15 VAS items and 1 of the 8 POMS subscales are reported. Cardiovascular measures taken at baseline and throughout every session are not reported (PDF p. 3). Means and SDs of the self-ratings are not printed (figures only), and the drug-guess data are summarized in two sentences (PDF p. 6).
analysis.power: No power calculation; 21 participants (20 for self-ratings and the voice task). Non-significant results (other facial emotions, the Eyes test, voices, MDMA against methamphetamine) are imprecise and do not show that no effect exists.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 21 healthy young adults with some earlier ecstasy use, tested alone, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg raised self-rated loving and friendliness against placebo but not significantly against methamphetamine 20 mg; only methamphetamine significantly raised self-rated sociability; both MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and methamphetamine raised playfulness; MDMA 0.75 mg/kg raised loneliness. MDMA 1.5 mg/kg lowered the proportion of fearful faces correctly named from 0.63 to 0.55 (the one emotion out of five that passed correction) and did not detectably change recognition of other facial emotions, of complex emotions from the eyes or of emotions in voices; its effect on fear recognition did not differ significantly from methamphetamine's.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Discussion say MDMA increased 'empathogenic' feelings and robustly reduced recognition of fearful faces, findings described as consistent with increased social approach rather than empathy, and call this the first published demonstration of an overt behavioral effect of MDMA in humans (PDF pp. 1, 6). The abstract does not say that the loving and friendly ratings after MDMA did not differ from those after methamphetamine, which the Discussion acknowledges, concluding that MDMA's prosocial effects may be less selective than believed (PDF pp. 6-7). The Discussion adds that ecstasy, while increasing feelings of connection, "can subtly impair interpersonal competence" and may increase social risk-taking, and suggests that reduced fear perception may help MDMA-assisted psychotherapy (PDF pp. 7-8); neither was tested. The statement that expectancy played a minor role rests on a non-significant re-analysis by drug guess in 21 people (PDF p. 6).

timeline.event: Same laboratory, fMRI study: as described here, MDMA altered neural responses to social material but did not change the accuracy of identifying emotions in facial pictures (PDF p. 2).

Hysek and colleagues (Basel), 32 volunteers, MDMA 125 mg against placebo: lower accuracy for fearful, angry, disgusted and surprised dynamic faces, not for happy faces; they cite this paper as consistent, and also cite it for raised self-rated sociability, which this paper did not find for MDMA (only methamphetamine raised sociability significantly).

replication.where_it_stands: Lower recognition of fear in faces after MDMA has been found in two placebo-controlled laboratory studies from different groups (this one, with static faces, and Hysek et al., 2014, with dynamic faces and other negative emotions as well). Whether the loving and friendly feelings are specific to MDMA rather than shared with stimulants rests on this study's comparison with methamphetamine, which found no significant difference either way.

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse (DA02812) (Acknowledgments, PDF p. 8).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest or financial-disclosure statement appears in the author manuscript read; the version of record was not read.
funding.affiliations_note: Human Behavioral Pharmacology Laboratory, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, University of Chicago; the first author also New York State Psychiatric Institute and Columbia University (PDF p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: A larger, preregistered placebo-controlled study in which people interact with real partners (for example, conversations scored for how accurately each reads the other's feelings), with more than one MDMA dose, a stimulant comparison sized to detect a difference from MDMA, plasma drug levels and a reported check of blinding.

domains.note: Capsules given in randomized order; how the order was generated or balanced is not described (PDF p. 3).
Sessions at least 5 days apart to allow drug elimination; session order reported to have no effect in any analysis (no statistics).

Double blind with opaque capsules and four possible drugs, but 6 of 21 guessed ecstasy on methamphetamine; how guesses were collected and how often MDMA was identified are not reported; the re-analysis by guess was non-significant in 21 people.
One participant missing from the self-rating analyses (reason not given) and one from the voice task (equipment malfunction); otherwise complete.
Self-ratings can be shaped by recognising the drug; the computer tasks are objective; the VAS range is not stated.
No registration; 5 of 15 VAS items and 1 of 8 POMS subscales reported (chosen from stated hypotheses); cardiovascular data not reported; the DANVA-2 F(3,57) = 3.01 is printed without its corrected p.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled within-person study with an active comparison drug; the concerns are the undescribed randomization, partial blinding and selective reporting of the subjective scales, none of which is likely to reverse the main findings. The source may be cited for higher self-rated loving and friendliness after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg than after placebo, but not higher than after methamphetamine 20 mg; for lower accuracy in naming fearful faces after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (0.55 against 0.63 after placebo); and for no detectable change in recognising other facial emotions, eye-region emotions or vocal emotions in 21 people. It should not be cited for effects on empathy or behaviour towards real people, for the feelings being specific to MDMA, or for other doses.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 21 healthy volunteers (9 women) aged 18 to 38, mean 24.4 (SD 4.9), who had used ecstasy at least twice (mean 15.0 lifetime occasions; 13 fewer than 10) each had four double-blind sessions in randomized order, at least 5 days apart: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg, MDMA 1.5 mg/kg, methamphetamine 20 mg and placebo (study conditions).
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Participants, 1st paragraph and Experimental Protocol, 1st paragraph (p. 3); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 5)

key_findings.finding: MDMA 1.5 mg/kg raised self-rated loving (VAS; F(3,57) = 5.04, p = 0.004, eta squared 0.21) and POMS friendliness (F(2.7,51) = 6.81, p = 0.001, eta squared 0.26) against placebo; friendliness was also higher than after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg; n = 20.

The loving and friendliness ratings after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg did not differ significantly from those after methamphetamine 20 mg; only methamphetamine significantly raised self-rated sociability (F(2.5,47.7) = 3.06, p < 0.05, eta squared 0.14; methamphetamine above placebo); MDMA 1.5 mg/kg and methamphetamine both raised playfulness (F(3,57) = 8.57, p < 0.001, eta squared 0.31).
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph and 3rd paragraph (p. 5, continuing on p. 6); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (p. 6); Figure 2 (PDF p. 12)
key_findings.note: Read approximately from the low-resolution Figure 2: the mean sociability curve after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (peak about 0.26 at 120 minutes) is as high as methamphetamine's (about 0.22); the analysis used each person's peak change, and only methamphetamine's difference from placebo passed the Bonferroni-adjusted test.

key_findings.finding: MDMA 0.75 mg/kg raised self-rated loneliness against methamphetamine and placebo (Friedman chi squared(3) = 11.94, p = 0.008, r = 0.54).

Fear recognition: the proportion of fearful faces correctly named was 0.63 (SD 0.07) after placebo and 0.55 (SD 0.10) after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (t(20) = 3.94, significant after Bonferroni correction; drug effect on fear F(2.8,56.0) = 4.45, p = 0.008, eta squared 0.18); it was 0.59 after MDMA 0.75 mg/kg and 0.59 after methamphetamine, and MDMA 1.5 mg/kg did not differ significantly from methamphetamine (t(20) = 1.31).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: dz about 0.86 (3.94 divided by the square root of 21); a fall of 8 percentage points, about 3 of the 40 fearful faces.

key_findings.finding: No significant change after correction in recognising happy, sad, angry or neutral faces (F(3,60) = 0.96, 3.60, 2.0 and 2.84), complex emotions from the eye region (Eyes test total 26.81 after placebo, 26.10 after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg; F(3,60) = 0.58) or emotions in voices (DANVA-2, F(3,57) = 3.01; n = 20); no drug by emotion interaction for voices.
key_findings.note: With the uncorrected degrees of freedom printed, DANVA-2 F(3,57) = 3.01 corresponds to p of about 0.04 (editors' calculation); the paper reports no effect, presumably after the sphericity correction it describes, but prints neither the corrected degrees of freedom nor p.

key_findings.finding: Exploratory: MDMA 1.5 mg/kg increased the number of emotional faces misclassified as neutral (mean 51.71, SD 10.58, against 44.90, SD 11.31, after placebo; t(20) = 2.52, p < 0.05 uncorrected).

Expectancy: 6 of 21 participants guessed they had taken ecstasy when they had received methamphetamine; a re-analysis by the drug each participant thought they had received found no significant relation with any measure that was sensitive to the drugs.
Setting: participants were alone in testing rooms, their only social contact a research assistant told not to interact beyond the protocol, without telephone or internet access.
key_findings.locator: Methods and Materials > Experimental Protocol, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Limitations named by the authors: static face photographs may be less ecologically valid than dynamic stimuli; no task compared social with non-social stimuli; the methamphetamine dose was not adjusted for body weight (only methamphetamine's playfulness effect correlated with weight, r = -0.45, p = 0.04); all participants had earlier ecstasy experience, so findings may not generalize to people new to MDMA.

Authors' interpretation: the pattern may be more consistent with increased social approach (sociability) than with increased empathy; MDMA may ease social interaction by reducing the impact of others' negative emotions rather than by improving recognition of, or sensitivity to, them. (The cited Discussion paragraph hedges with 'may be'; only the abstract states it without the hedge.)

reporting_issues.issue: Voice task: Table 1 prints the drug effect on DANVA-2 as F(3,57) = 3.01 without a significance mark; with these uncorrected degrees of freedom p is about 0.04 (editors' calculation). The text says MDMA did not affect DANVA-2 accuracy, and the corrected degrees of freedom and p (the paper interprets Huynh-Feldt or Greenhouse-Geisser corrected levels) are not printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: The null result for voices may be borderline rather than clearly absent; the lowest mean was after MDMA 1.5 mg/kg (17.20) and the highest after methamphetamine (18.70).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract (N = 21) and the Results (9 of the 21 female; 6 of 21 guessed) give 21 participants, but the self-rating analyses (figure legends) and the voice task (Table 1 footnote, p. 14) have 20, without saying who is missing; Table 1 prints uncorrected degrees of freedom (3,60) for the fear effect while the text gives the corrected F(2.8,56.0).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the degrees of freedom printed in the text fit n = 20 for the self-ratings and n = 21 for the face task. (The main Methods section gives no N.)

reporting_issues.issue: The effect size for loneliness is given as r = 0.54 alongside a four-condition Friedman test; how r was derived is not stated. The range of the VAS is not stated, and the figures show mean changes of at most about 0.3 units.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the self-rated effects cannot be expressed in standard units from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Cardiovascular measures were taken at baseline and regularly during every session but are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: No physiological or safety data from these sessions can be cited from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Reference 40, cited for methamphetamine being associated with social and particularly sexual enhancement in some subcultures, is a study of MDMA neurotoxicity in neonatal rats (Meyer et al., 2004). The statement that empathogenic effects are a motivation for recreational use cites a rat study of oxytocin (reference 2) together with a study of ecstasy experiences (reference 3).
reporting_issues.consequence: The methamphetamine statement is not supported by its citation in the manuscript, and the motivation statement rests on reference 3; the version of record was not checked for corrections.
