design_detail: Research letter (The Lancet 351:1784, one page): a non-randomized, single-group before-and-after drug-challenge study, filed as prospective-cohort, the nearest design the schema allows with ROBINS-I ('human-laboratory' is tied to RoB 2, which does not fit a non-randomized comparison; same filing as sc_boehrer_1993). Eight normally hydrated healthy men aged 22 to 32 each took 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (Sigma; equivalent to 40 mg MDMA base) in a capsule with 200 mL water at 10:00 (study conditions); three of them acted as untreated controls on another occasion at least 2 weeks later (the figure legend calls this placebo). Blood was taken before and 30 minutes and 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 24 hours after: plasma MDMA by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, arginine vasopressin (AVP, the antidiuretic hormone) by radioimmunoassay, cortisol and sodium. Before-after comparisons by repeated-measures analysis of variance or paired t test, with one-tailed p values for AVP and sodium. Approved by the UK Home Office (for buying and giving MDMA) and the King's College London Ethics Committee. The text gives ranges and p values; geometric mean AVP and mean MDMA over 24 hours appear only in a small low-resolution figure.
can_establish: That in these 8 healthy men a single 40 mg oral dose of MDMA was followed within 1 to 2 hours by a rise in plasma vasopressin (range 1.14-1.88 pmol/L before, 2.46-9.16 pmol/L at 2 hours) and a fall in plasma sodium of 1 to 3 mmol/L in 7 of the 8, while cortisol did not change significantly.
cannot_establish: That MDMA rather than time of day, posture or fluid intake caused the change (the control occasions were 3 of the 8 men, later and unblinded, and were not compared statistically); what happens at the larger amounts people often take, with dancing, heat or heavy drinking; whether the hormone rise reduced urine output or explains difficulty urinating (urine was not measured); anything about women; or that illness from low blood sodium follows from this effect plus fluid intake (no fluid loading was studied).

sample.recruitment: Not described; eight healthy male volunteers (p. 1784, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Normally hydrated healthy men aged 22 to 32; no other criteria stated.
sample.demographics: Men aged 22 to 32; no other characteristics, and no history of drug use, reported.
sample.attrition: None reported; whether every man gave every sample is not stated, although the 2-hour ranges and the sodium count cover all 8.
sample.selection_effects: Eight healthy young men at rest in a research setting; no women, no dancing, heat or fluid loading; earlier MDMA use not stated.

exposure.measurement: Drug given by the investigators: 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (Sigma), equivalent to 40 mg base, in a capsule; plasma MDMA measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (p. 1784, 2nd paragraph).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: one oral dose of 40 mg MDMA base with 200 mL water at 10:00, samples to 24 hours. The authors call it a relatively small dose and state, without a source, that street ecstasy frequently contains more than 100 mg of MDMA (p. 1784, 4th paragraph).
exposure.polysubstance: Not reported; use of other drugs, alcohol, nicotine or caffeine before or during the session is not described.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported.

comparison.controls: Each man's own pre-dose values; in addition, three of the eight served as untreated controls on an occasion at least 2 weeks after the MDMA session (figure legend: placebo, n = 3). Fixed order, no blinding described, and no statistical comparison between MDMA and control occasions.
comparison.matching: Within person (before and after). Whether the control occasions followed the same clock times is not stated.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Fluid and food intake, posture and activity during the 24 hours, which can affect vasopressin and sodium, are not reported beyond normal hydration and the 200 mL taken with the capsule.

outcomes.instruments: Plasma AVP by radioimmunoassay (method cited to a chapter by the last author, reference 3); plasma MDMA by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry; plasma cortisol and sodium, methods not stated (p. 1784, 2nd paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Reference ranges are not given. The authors note that AVP's initial elimination half-life is about 6 minutes (reference 4), so single samples can miss short peaks.
outcomes.operationalization: AVP rise as the change from baseline (paired t test at 2 hours, one-tailed; repeated-measures analysis of variance across time points for the figure); sodium fall as baseline against 2 hours (paired t test, one-tailed); cortisol baseline against 2 hours.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; one-tailed tests for AVP and sodium. Editors' count of 4: AVP, sodium, cortisol and the AVP-MDMA correlation.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; the measures are laboratory assays.

analysis.effect_sizes: AVP: baseline range 1.14-1.88 pmol/L, at 2 hours 2.46-9.16 pmol/L (paired t test p = 0.006, one-tailed; editors' note: about 0.012 two-tailed); maximum between 1 and 2 hours. Sodium: ranges 139-145 mmol/L at baseline and 140-142 mmol/L at 2 hours; fall of 1 to 3 mmol/L in 7 of 8 men and a rise of 1 mmol/L in the eighth (paired t test p = 0.025, one-tailed; about 0.05 two-tailed, editors' note). Cortisol: mean 331.4 nmol/L (range 208.8-603.4) before and 377.2 nmol/L (268.4-583.3) at 2 hours, not significant (p > 0.05). AVP and MDMA concentrations not correlated (Spearman r = 0.2, p = 0.1). Read approximately from the low-resolution figure: geometric mean AVP after MDMA about 1.5 pmol/L before, about 3 at 1 hour, about 4 at 2 hours, about 2.8 at 4 hours and about 1.5 by 8 hours; on the 3 control occasions about 1.3 before and about 0.6 to 1 pmol/L from 1 to 8 hours; both about 1.75 at 24 hours; mean plasma MDMA about 45 micrograms per litre at 2 hours and 47 at 4 hours, falling to about 23 at 8 hours. No means with SDs, intervals or standardized effects are printed.
analysis.preregistration_detail: None mentioned; a one-page research letter.
analysis.selective_reporting: The text tests only the 2-hour time point for AVP, sodium and cortisol; the control occasions appear only as a line in the figure, with no numbers or test; the figure's asterisks refer to a repeated-measures analysis of variance whose statistics are not given.
analysis.power: Not discussed; 8 men, 3 control occasions.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 8 healthy men, a single 40 mg dose of MDMA was followed by a rise in plasma vasopressin peaking at 1 to 2 hours (one-tailed p = 0.006 at 2 hours) and a fall in plasma sodium of 1 to 3 mmol/L in 7 of 8 (one-tailed p = 0.025), the lowest 2-hour value being 140 mmol/L; cortisol did not change significantly; vasopressin did not correlate with MDMA concentration; on 3 later untreated occasions vasopressin fell slightly.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The title says low-dose MDMA induces vasopressin secretion. The letter concludes that the hyponatraemic illness seen in some people who take ecstasy is likely linked to this effect, that with excessive fluid even a relatively small dose could cause symptoms, that the rise is not part of a generalised stress response because cortisol did not change significantly, and that MDMA-induced hyponatraemia results from a pharmacological effect compounded by excessive fluid intake rather than a rare idiosyncratic reaction (p. 1784, 4th paragraph). No fluid loading, urine output or illness was studied; the stress-response argument rests on a non-significant change in 8 men (cortisol mean 331.4 to 377.2 nmol/L); and the causal title rests on a before-after design whose 3 control occasions were not compared statistically. The closing message, that people who take ecstasy should avoid drinking fluid in excess of the body's requirements, and the statement that MDMA reduces thirst perception and impairs judgment, are not based on data from this study (5th paragraph).

timeline.event: Holden and Jackson: near-fatal hyponatraemic coma attributed to vasopressin over-secretion after ecstasy, the one earlier case with raised vasopressin cited by this letter (reference 2); not read.

Simmler, Hysek and Liechti: a study titled as showing sex differences in the effects of MDMA on plasma copeptin (a marker of vasopressin release) in healthy volunteers, as cited by Hysek et al. (2014); not read.

Hysek and colleagues: in 32 healthy volunteers given MDMA 125 mg in a placebo-controlled crossover study, plasma copeptin measured before and 1 and 2 hours after did not change significantly (no statistic printed; Figure 4B).

replication.where_it_stands: This letter on 8 men is the direct measurement of vasopressin after MDMA that later papers on MDMA-related low blood sodium cite (cards sc_campbell_2008 and sc_rosenson_2007 describe it second-hand). A larger placebo-controlled study measuring copeptin after 125 mg found no significant overall change (Hysek et al., 2014). Whether MDMA raises vasopressin enough to matter, in whom and at which amounts is not settled by these data.

funding.funder: Not reported; the letter thanks Peter Milligan for statistical advice.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Academic Department of Accident and Emergency Medicine, Imperial College School of Medicine, St Mary's Hospital, London (J A Henry); Drug Control Centre and Department of Pharmacy, King's College London; Department of Physiology, United Medical and Dental Schools, St Thomas's Hospital Campus, London. The vasopressin assay method is cited to a chapter by the last author (reference 3).

what_would_settle_it: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in women and men, at doses in the range people take, with standardized fluid intake and repeated measurement of vasopressin or copeptin, plasma sodium and osmolality, urine volume and urine osmolality over the hours after the dose.

domains.note: Before-after design: changes in vasopressin and sodium with time of day, posture and fluid intake are controlled only by 3 later, unblinded, untreated occasions that were not compared statistically; fluid intake after the 200 mL is not reported.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of participants into the study
domains.note: Eight healthy men; recruitment and earlier drug use not described, though selection is unlikely to depend on the outcome.
Dose given and recorded by the investigators; plasma MDMA measured.

domains.domain: Bias due to deviations from intended interventions
domains.note: Not blinded (untreated controls in the text, though the figure legend says placebo); activity, food and fluids during the 24 hours are not described.
The 2-hour ranges and the sodium count cover all 8 men; completeness at other time points is not stated.
Laboratory assays (radioimmunoassay, mass spectrometry) are unlikely to be influenced by knowing the condition; AVP's short half-life makes single samples noisy but not biased.

domains.domain: Bias in selection of the reported result
domains.note: Ranges and one-tailed p values for the 2-hour time point only, chosen after the peak was seen; no comparison with the control occasions; the time course appears only in a figure without statistics.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small uncontrolled before-after experiment with objective measures. The direction of the vasopressin rise is plausible, but without a randomized, blinded comparison the change cannot be cleanly attributed to MDMA, the tests are one-tailed at a selected time point, and the clinical conclusions go beyond the data. It may be cited as: in 8 healthy men, plasma vasopressin rose within 1 to 2 hours of a single 40 mg dose of MDMA while plasma sodium fell slightly (by 1 to 3 mmol/L in 7 of 8). It should not be cited as showing that MDMA causes water retention or low blood sodium in people who use it, or as explaining difficulty urinating.

key_findings.finding: Design and sample: 8 normally hydrated healthy men aged 22 to 32 each took 47.5 mg MDMA hydrochloride (40 mg base) in a capsule with 200 mL water at 10:00; 3 of them acted as untreated controls at least 2 weeks later; blood before and at 30 minutes and 1, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 24 hours for MDMA, vasopressin (AVP), cortisol and sodium.

Vasopressin: plasma AVP peaked between 1 and 2 hours after the dose; the baseline range of 1.14-1.88 pmol/L rose at 2 hours to 2.46-9.16 pmol/L (paired t test p = 0.006, one-tailed), in contrast with a small decrease on the control occasions.
key_findings.note: One-tailed; two-tailed p would be about 0.012 (editors' calculation). The controls are 3 later, untreated occasions, not compared statistically.

key_findings.finding: Sodium: ranges 139-145 mmol/L before and 140-142 mmol/L at 2 hours; 7 of 8 men fell by 1 to 3 mmol/L and one rose by 1 mmol/L (paired t test p = 0.025, one-tailed); the authors call it a small fall.
key_findings.locator: Letter, 3rd paragraph (left column, continuing in the right column) and 4th paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: One-tailed; about 0.05 two-tailed (editors' calculation).

key_findings.finding: Cortisol: mean 331.4 nmol/L (range 208.8-603.4) before and 377.2 nmol/L (268.4-583.3) at 2 hours, a non-significant rise (p > 0.05).
key_findings.locator: Letter, 3rd paragraph (top of the right column)

key_findings.finding: AVP and MDMA concentrations were not correlated (Spearman r = 0.2, p = 0.1); the authors say this is probably because of AVP's rapid clearance (initial elimination half-life about 6 minutes, against hours for MDMA). (Source: 'probably because of'.) Note checked: 8 pairs give p = 0.63; p = 0.1 fits about 64 pooled samples two-tailed, or about 42 if one-tailed like the letter's other tests.
key_findings.note: With 8 independent pairs, r = 0.2 would give p of about 0.6; p = 0.1 fits roughly 64 pooled samples from the 8 men (editors' calculation). How the correlation was computed is not stated.

key_findings.finding: Figure, in the editors' approximate reading of a low-resolution image: geometric mean AVP after MDMA rose from about 1.5 pmol/L to about 4 at 2 hours and was back near 1.5 by 8 hours; on the 3 control occasions it stayed between about 0.6 and 1 pmol/L from 1 to 8 hours; mean plasma MDMA was about 45 micrograms per litre at 2 hours and 47 at 4 hours.
key_findings.note: Approximate values read from a low-resolution figure (a 72-ppi bitmap, enlarged); asterisks for difference from baseline appear beside the AVP points at about 1, 2 and 4 hours.

key_findings.finding: Authors' conclusions: the rise in AVP with a small fall in sodium makes hyponatraemic illness after ecstasy likely to be linked to the drug's ability to stimulate AVP secretion; with excessive fluid intake even a relatively small dose could lead to symptoms; the rise does not seem to be part of a generalised stress response because cortisol did not change significantly; animal studies show that MDMA releases serotonin and that serotonergic pathways regulate AVP secretion. (Source: 'does not seem to be part of'.)

Authors' closing message, not tested in this study: people who take ecstasy or similar drugs may be at risk of hyponatraemia and should avoid drinking fluid in excess of the body's requirements, which may be hard to judge because MDMA reduces thirst perception and impairs judgment.

Background cited: MDMA use had been associated with acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with inappropriate antidiuretic-hormone secretion (Maxwell and colleagues, 1993, reference 1), and raised AVP had been found in one case (Holden and Jackson, 1996, reference 2).
key_findings.locator: Letter, 1st paragraph (left column); references 1 and 2 (right column)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says three volunteers acted as untreated controls at least 2 weeks later, while the figure legend labels this condition placebo (n = 3); no placebo capsule, blinding or statistical comparison with the MDMA occasions is described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The control condition is smaller, later, unblinded and of unclear nature; the MDMA effect rests on before-after change.

reporting_issues.issue: The AVP and sodium tests are one-tailed (p = 0.006 and 0.025) and are given for the 2-hour time point only; two-tailed values would be about 0.012 and 0.05 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sodium change is borderline by conventional two-sided testing; neither result is corrected for the choice of time point.

reporting_issues.issue: The Spearman correlation between AVP and MDMA (r = 0.2, p = 0.1) cannot come from 8 independent pairs, which would give p of about 0.6; it probably pools repeated samples from the same men, which the letter does not say (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The correlation's p value is not interpretable as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: No means, SDs or intervals are given for AVP or sodium, only ranges; the time course and the control occasions appear only in a low-resolution figure, whose legend refers to a repeated-measures analysis of variance without statistics.
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of the effect and its uncertainty cannot be computed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that street ecstasy frequently contains more than 100 mg of MDMA has no source.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not citable from this letter.

design_detail: Qualitative interview study by a single author (School of Sociology and Social Policy, Queen's University Belfast; Substance Use & Misuse 40:1461-1477). Face-to-face, semi-structured, in-depth interviews of 1 to 2 hours, taped and transcribed, with 98 people who currently or formerly used ecstasy in Northern Ireland, October 1997 to November 1998 (106 interviewed; 8 interviews discarded because of recording or transcription problems). Eligibility was any use of ecstasy, with criteria narrowed during the study to reach people outside Belfast and people who had stopped using, and to avoid over-representing groups such as middle-class students. Recruitment through announcements in shops and health centres, advertisements in a club and music magazine, local agencies (youth programmes, universities, sexually transmitted disease clinics, gay and lesbian outreach, young offender programmes, drug services), the interviewers' own contacts and street sources, snowball referral and paid gatekeepers (10 pounds per referral and completed interview, usually up to six); clubs were deliberately not used. The interview covered first, last and usual use, positive and negative experiences, rituals and norms, health and other items; sexuality and sexual risk are reported as themes illustrated by quotations labelled with respondent number, sex and age. Counts are given for the sample (Tables 1 and 2) but not for any finding, and the method of analysis is not described.
can_establish: How these Northern Irish respondents described MDMA's effects on sensuality, sexual desire and sexual performance, and the kinds of sexual risk they reported during MDMA episodes, in 1997 and 1998.
cannot_establish: How common any of these experiences is among people who use MDMA (no finding is counted and the sample is purposive), whether MDMA rather than the alcohol, cannabis or other drugs taken in the same episodes, or individual differences in sexual interest, produced them, or whether sexual risk is greater with MDMA than without it (condoms were rarely used without drugs either).

sample.recruitment: Community, several methods (see design detail). Of the 98: 18% recruited by snowball referral, 26% by one of nine paid gatekeepers, 29% learned of the study through one of its employees and 27% from an advertisement. Each received a music or book gift certificate printed as $15 (US $27) (pp. 1463-1464).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Any lifetime use of ecstasy. After about 4 months, when most respondents were from Belfast, criteria were narrowed to people outside Belfast or people who had stopped using, and at other times adjusted to avoid over-representation, for example of middle-class students (p. 1463, footnote d).
sample.demographics: 69% men and 31% women; age 17 to 45 (mean 25, median 24, mode 23); 16% gay or bisexual (self-defined); 50% lived in Belfast, 46% elsewhere in Northern Ireland and 4% outside it; 49% working class, 46% middle class and 5% between (self-defined); 57% employed (p. 1464; Table 1, p. 1465).
sample.attrition: 8 of 106 interviews (8%) discarded for recording or transcription problems (p. 1463); the 12 pilot interviews were kept (p. 1464).
sample.selection_effects: Purposive sample built through agencies, contacts and paid referral, deliberately avoiding clubs; long and heavy use was common (44% had used ecstasy on at least 100 occasions). How many respondents discussed sex, and how many had sex during MDMA episodes, is not reported.

exposure.measurement: Self-report in the interview. The author notes that tablet content varies, so effects attributed to MDMA refer to what respondents believed they had taken (p. 1463, footnote c).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Lifetime: 44% at least 100 separate episodes. Past 6 months: 8% no use, 50% less than once a month, 37% one to four times a month; about half had used within 2 weeks of the interview. First use at mean age 21 (median 20, range 13 to 35) (p. 1465; Table 2, p. 1466). Amounts per episode not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: All had used cannabis (32% daily in the past 6 months); 90% had used LSD or mushrooms and 93% amphetamines; 45% cocaine or crack and 11% heroin; 84% drank beer, lager, ale or stout weekly (mean 16 pints a week among them); 60% smoked at least 20 cigarettes a day (p. 1465; Table 2, p. 1466). Alcohol and cannabis were often used in the same episodes, and the author says their interactions with MDMA could not be examined (p. 1473).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable.

comparison.controls: None. Respondents compared, in their own words, sex with and without MDMA, MDMA with alcohol, and their reactions with friends'.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Sexual interest, relationship status and sexual behaviour without drugs were not measured systematically; the author suggests individual differences in sexual interest may explain the diverse accounts (p. 1470).

outcomes.instruments: Semi-structured interview guide, piloted on the first 12 respondents and slightly revised, covering use, experiences, rituals and norms, health and other items; demographic and drug-history questions at the end (p. 1464). Questions about sexual risk are mentioned (p. 1473), but the sexuality questions are not reproduced.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not applicable. No coding procedure, coder agreement, saturation criterion or member checking is described.
outcomes.operationalization: Sexual risk is the author's category (multiple partners, partners who were strangers or acquaintances, sex without a condom); the author notes that several respondents needed the question clarified and may not regard these behaviours as risky (pp. 1462, 1473).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis testing).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Four interviewers (two women and two men, two of them the project directors) trained for 2 weeks (p. 1464).

analysis.effect_sizes: None; themes without counts. The quantifiers used are a slight majority (sensuality or deep emotions rather than sexual desire, p. 1467), the majority (sensuality and emotional closeness often without sexual activity, p. 1470), and several, some, a number of or a few elsewhere.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol is mentioned; the interview topics are described in an earlier report (McElrath and McEvoy, 1999, Ecstasy Use in Northern Ireland, as cited on p. 1464).
analysis.selective_reporting: No finding is counted. Quotations carry respondent numbers, which show some themes resting on a few people (respondent 022 is quoted or cited four times, on pp. 1468, 1470, 1471 and 1472, and 018 three times).
analysis.power: Not applicable; no saturation criterion is given.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A slight majority described MDMA mainly as bringing sensuality and emotional closeness rather than sexual desire. Some men who tried to have sex described being unable to get an erection or to ejaculate, reportedly more often among men aged 25 or younger; other men and women described heightened desire and very good sex, and a few used MDMA as a sexual aid with a partner. Some described multiple partners, one-night stands and next-day regret, mostly younger respondents; condoms were rarely used during MDMA episodes with intercourse, but few respondents used them when no drugs had been taken either; views on whether MDMA or alcohol led to more sexual risk were mixed.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says most respondents reported closeness without desire for penetrative sex, where the findings say a slight majority (pp. 1461, 1467). It says gay and bisexual women in particular had used MDMA for sexual enhancement, while the Discussion says the small number of gay and bisexual women in the sample prohibits accurate conclusions (p. 1473). It calls sexual risk taking prevalent among those who had sex during MDMA episodes, without saying how many had sex or took risks, and without the finding that condom use was also rare when no drugs were taken (p. 1472). The statements that heavy drinkers were as likely as others to attempt sex and that feelings did not differ by lifetime use (p. 1471) are impressions without counts.

timeline.event: Buffum and Moser, as cited here: MDMA did not increase the desire to initiate sex but enhanced receptivity to being sexual (p. 1462); not read.

Beck and Rosenbaum, book on MDMA experiences, as cited here: feelings of emotional and physical closeness, and frequent sex with multiple partners in the 1980s Dallas club scene (pp. 1468, 1473-1474); not read.

Zemishlany, Aizenberg and Weizman, retrospective interviews of 35 people in Israel about sex after MDMA: all reported more desire; erections worse in 8 of 20 men and better in 8; orgasm delayed in 16 men and 6 of 15 women.

replication.where_it_stands: Qualitative and survey accounts from the 1980s and 1990s agree that MDMA is often experienced as sensual and emotionally close rather than sexual, with erectile difficulty for some men and heightened desire for others. None of the sources read measures how often these occur among people who use MDMA now, and the author says the scene may have changed since 1997 and 1998 (p. 1474).

funding.funder: Not reported in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, a Reader in the School of Sociology and Social Policy, Queen's University Belfast (pp. 1461, 1476). The interviews were part of a project with two project directors described in a 1999 report (McElrath and McEvoy, Ecstasy Use in Northern Ireland, Stationery Office, as cited); its funder is not named here.

what_would_settle_it: A survey of a defined population of people who use MDMA, with validated measures of sexual function and of sexual behaviour on occasions with MDMA, with alcohol alone and with neither, recording what else was taken, to show how often each experience occurs and whether risk differs from occasions without MDMA.

domains.domain: Research design appropriate to the question (qualitative appraisal, CASP-style)
domains.note: In-depth interviews suit a question about how people perceive MDMA's effects on sexuality and risk.

Purposive multi-method sampling, adjusted during the study to diversify the sample, with paid gatekeepers and clubs avoided for safety; no saturation account; how many respondents spoke about sex is not given.
Trained interviewers, a piloted guide, private settings, taped and transcribed; but the sexuality questions are not reproduced and 8 of 106 interviews were lost.

29% learned of the study through a project employee and some were recruited through interviewers' own contacts; the author notes that researchers and respondents saw risk differently, but gives no account of how the interviewers may have shaped answers.
Confidentiality and anonymity assured, respondents identified by number, an incentive given and clubs avoided for safety; no ethics approval or consent procedure is mentioned.
How the transcripts were analysed (coding, theme development, who coded, any checks) is not described at all.
Themes are illustrated with attributed quotations, but quantifiers such as most, a slight majority and several have no counts, and the abstract states findings more strongly than the text.
The author states plainly that the data are from Northern Ireland in 1997 and 1998 and may not apply now (p. 1474).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the editors' qualitative checklist. A large interview study with careful, diversified recruitment and a frank statement of its time and place, but with no description of how the transcripts were analysed and no counts behind its quantified statements, so the overall judgment follows the analysis domain. It may be cited for the range of experiences described in this Northern Irish sample of 1997 and 1998: closeness without sexual desire, erectile difficulty for some men, heightened desire and use as a sexual aid for others, and sexual risk episodes with regret. It should not be cited for how often any of these occurs, or as showing that MDMA increases sexual risk.

key_findings.finding: Sample: 98 people who currently or formerly used ecstasy in Northern Ireland, interviewed October 1997 to November 1998 (106 interviewed, 8 interviews discarded); 69% men; age 17 to 45 (mean 25); 16% gay or bisexual; 44% had used ecstasy on at least 100 occasions and 92% in the past 6 months.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 1463) and 3rd paragraph (p. 1464); Description of Respondents, 1st paragraph (p. 1464) and 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 1465); Table 1 (p. 1465); Table 2 (p. 1466)

key_findings.finding: Closeness rather than sex: a slight majority described ecstasy as more associated with sensuality or deep emotions than with sexual desire; several men described wanting to hold someone, be with others or dance rather than have sex, and several women described sensual closeness without wanting penetrative sex.
key_findings.locator: Findings > Feelings of Sensuality or Emotional Closeness, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1467) and 3rd paragraph (p. 1468); block quotations not counted as paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Erections: some men who tried to have sex during ecstasy episodes described being unable to get an erection or to ejaculate, which appeared to affect men aged 25 or younger more often than men aged 26 to 38; for these men the author says it was physical inability, not a preference for sensuality.

Heightened desire: other men and women described strongly enhanced desire and very good sex on ecstasy, usually in private homes after clubs or at house parties; a few used ecstasy as a sexual aid with a steady partner, some felt more open to new forms of sex, and some women described exploring bisexuality.
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Arousal, 2nd paragraph (p. 1468), 3rd to 7th paragraphs (p. 1469) and 8th paragraph (p. 1470)

key_findings.finding: Two patterns: the author summarizes that the majority described sensuality, empathy and closeness often without sexual activity, while an apparently distinct group described more desire and sexual fulfilment, possibly reflecting general differences in sexual interest; heavy drinkers were described as just as likely as light drinkers or non-drinkers to attempt sex, and feelings did not appear to differ between people with at least 100 uses and those with few (no counts).
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Arousal, 10th paragraph (p. 1470) and 12th paragraph (p. 1471)

key_findings.finding: Gay and bisexual women appeared more likely than other respondents to use MDMA for sexual enhancement, but the author says their small number in the sample prohibits accurate conclusions.
key_findings.locator: Discussion > MDMA As a Sexual 'Aid', 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Sexual risk: several respondents who had sex during ecstasy episodes described behaviours carrying infection risk, more often those aged about 18 to 25: multiple partners and one-night stands with strangers or distant acquaintances; a number of men and women voiced next-day regret. (Regret is not an infection-risk behaviour.)
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Risk Behaviors, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Condoms: condom use was rare during ecstasy episodes that involved intercourse, but few respondents used condoms during sex when no drugs had been taken either; some used them with strangers but not with partners.

MDMA against alcohol: asked which brought more sexual risk, respondents were mixed; some said risk was greater on ecstasy, others that alcohol was far more likely to lead to risk and that they felt more in control on ecstasy; because a number of respondents took alcohol and other substances in the same episodes, the author says their effects are difficult to disentangle. (Source: 'difficult to disentangle', p. 1472, not 'could not be'.)
key_findings.locator: Findings > Sexual Risk Behaviors, 7th and 8th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated: the data are from 1997 and 1998 and the scene has probably changed (tablet prices, by anecdotal report, fell from about 10 to 5 pounds; researchers in England report more alcohol use in clubs, and the author says similar changes are possible in Northern Ireland), so it is unclear whether the findings apply now; prospective data, with the timing of substance use and sex, might be needed. (pp. 1473-1474: the alcohol change is England's and only 'possible' locally; 'might be needed'.)
key_findings.locator: Discussion > The Role of MDMA, Other Drugs, and Sexual Behavior, 2nd paragraph (p. 1472, continuing on p. 1473); Limitations of the Study and Suggestions for Future Research, 1st paragraph (p. 1474)

key_findings.finding: Context from footnotes: clubs were not used for recruitment because local folklore tied some paramilitary groups to clubs and recruiting there might have raised suspicion and put respondents and researchers at risk; respondents said some clubs turned off water taps in toilets, and in several clubs only bottled water was sold; respondents said they recognised people on MDMA by large black pupils, clenched teeth, an 'irregular' jaw formation and extreme friendliness, particularly with strangers. (Footnote e says 'local folklore suggests', not 'reported links'.)
key_findings.locator: Footnote e (p. 1464); footnote h (p. 1466); footnote i (p. 1467)

reporting_issues.issue: The method of analysis of the transcripts is not reported, and no finding is counted; the abstract turns the findings' slight majority (p. 1467) into most respondents (p. 1461).
reporting_issues.consequence: How themes were derived cannot be judged, and the abstract's quantifiers should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract singles out gay and bisexual women as having used MDMA for sexual enhancement, which the Discussion says their small number does not allow to be concluded (p. 1473).
reporting_issues.consequence: The subgroup statement should not be cited as a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract calls sexual risk taking prevalent among those who had sex during MDMA episodes, but the paper gives neither the number who had sex during episodes nor the number reporting risk, and reports that condom use was also rare when no drugs were taken.
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither the prevalence of sexual risk nor any difference from sex without MDMA can be taken from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2's past-6-month categories (no use 8%, less than once a month 50%, one to four times a month 37%) sum to 95%; the other 5% are not described, and the 77% described as currently using MDMA are not defined, although 92% had used in the past 6 months.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; frequency of use cannot be fully described from the table.

reporting_issues.issue: The incentive is printed as a $15 (US $27) gift certificate, where the conversion implies 15 pounds sterling.
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible typographical error.

No supplement.

disagreements.reviewer: Sexual risk: several respondents who had sex during ecstasy episodes described behaviours carrying infection risk, more often those aged about 18 to 25: multiple partners and one-night stands with strangers or distant acquaintances; a number of men and women voiced next-day regret. design_detail: Short communication (European Psychiatry 16:127-130): a retrospective structured-interview survey, by authors at Geha Psychiatric Hospital, Petah Tikva, and Tel Aviv University, Israel, of 20 men and 15 women who had occasionally used MDMA before a sexual encounter (9 of the 35 interviewed by telephone). Each person rated sexual activity up to 6 hours after taking MDMA against their usual sexual function without it, for desire, erection (lubrication in women), orgasm intensity, orgasm delay and satisfaction, on a scale from -3 (marked decrease) to +3 (marked increase). Results are descriptive percentages plus a table of every participant's age, education and ratings (Table I); no statistical tests or intervals are printed. Recruitment method, place and dates of the interviews are not stated (received by the journal 11 October 1999).
can_establish: How these 35 people, recalling sex after taking MDMA, rated their desire, erections or lubrication, orgasm and satisfaction compared with their usual sex without MDMA.
cannot_establish: How common these effects are among people who take MDMA (a self-selected sample, recruited in an unstated way, of people who had used it before sex), whether MDMA itself caused them (no comparison condition, unknown dose and content of the pills, retrospective recall, expectations, and cannabis used with MDMA by 20 of 35), or anything about sexual risk or long-term sexual function.

sample.recruitment: Not described. The paper says only that 20 men and 15 women who had occasionally used MDMA before engaging in a sexual encounter consented to a structured interview (p. 127, Subjects and methods, 1st paragraph); the setting is Israel by the authors' affiliation.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included only people who were physically healthy, without a major psychiatric disorder or history of sexual disorders, medication-free and, in the paper's word, not abusing alcohol or opiates; all had prior recreational experience with MDMA; the same criteria were checked for the 9 telephone interviews (pp. 127-128).
sample.demographics: Ages 21 to 48 (men 22 to 46, women 21 to 48; editors' calculation from Table I: mean 31.1 years for men, 31.7 for women); 94% had a high-school or academic education (33 of 35 had 12 or more years in Table I); six were full-time university students and the rest steadily employed in professional occupations (p. 128; Table I, p. 129).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single interview); the number of people approached or declining is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected people willing to describe their use of an illegal drug, all of whom had used MDMA before sex; people with sexual or psychiatric disorders excluded; mostly educated and employed. The authors name the non-random sample, retrospective and possibly inaccurate recall, unknown dose and purity, and cannabis use by about half as limitations (p. 129).

exposure.measurement: Self-report of past MDMA use in a sexual setting; what was taken was not confirmed, and the dose and purity of the pills could not be determined (p. 129).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not measured. Use before sex is described as occasional; number of occasions, amounts and time since the last occasion are not reported; ratings refer to sexual activity up to 6 hours after taking MDMA (pp. 127-128).
exposure.polysubstance: Ten men (50%) and ten women (67%) reported occasional use of cannabis with MDMA, mainly, they said, to enhance desire; ratings were said to be restricted to MDMA alone, and the authors report no differences in any sexual rating between those who did and did not add cannabis, without numbers or tests (p. 128). Alcohol use short of the exclusion criterion is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable (retrospective interview); time since last use not reported.

comparison.controls: None. Each person compared sex after MDMA with their own usual sexual function without MDMA, from memory.
comparison.matching: Not applicable.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Usual sexual function was not measured, and relationship status, partners, setting, other substances on the occasions recalled and expectations were not recorded.

outcomes.instruments: A structured interview on four domains (desire; erection in men or lubrication in women; orgasm, assessed for intensity and for ease of achievement; satisfaction), citing the authors' earlier study of amantadine in men with schizophrenia (reference 16) for the domains; each item rated from -3 to +3 against the person's usual function (0 unchanged, 1 mild, 2 moderate, 3 profound or marked; minus a decrease, plus an increase) (p. 128; Table I legend, p. 129).
outcomes.validity_norms: No reliability or validity data; an ad hoc rating scale rather than a validated sexual-function questionnaire.
outcomes.operationalization: Moderate to profound increase means a rating of +2 or +3; impaired sexual performance, in the authors' conclusion, means a decrease in erection rating, delayed orgasm or anorgasmia (p. 129).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (descriptive only; the one comparison, by cannabis use, is reported without a test).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; who conducted the interviews is not stated.

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages only, without intervals. Editors' tallies from Table I with Wilson 95% intervals (editors' calculation): sexual desire increased in 35 of 35, moderately or markedly in 34 (97%; 85.5% to 99.5%); satisfaction moderately or markedly increased in 32 of 35 (91%; 77.6% to 97.0%); erections worse in 8 of 20 men (40%; 21.9% to 61.3%), 4 of them moderately or markedly, better in 8 (40%) and unchanged in 4; lubrication increased in 12 of 15 women (80%; 54.8% to 93.0%) and decreased in 2; orgasm delayed in 16 of 20 men (80%; 58.4% to 91.9%) and 6 of 15 women (40%; 19.8% to 64.3%); no orgasm at all on MDMA in 1 man and 2 women; orgasm more intense in 17 men (85%) and 8 women (53%), less intense in 1 man and 3 women. All 8 men who reported weaker erections and all 3 people who could not reach orgasm rated satisfaction as moderately or markedly increased.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration mentioned; no ethics committee approval is mentioned, only consent.
analysis.selective_reporting: Every participant's ratings are printed in Table I, so the percentages in the text can be checked (they agree, see reporting issues). The comparison by cannabis use is stated without data, and Table I does not show who used cannabis.
analysis.power: Not applicable (descriptive); with 20 men and 15 women, proportions are uncertain by about 20 percentage points either way (for example 40% of 20 men: 21.9% to 61.3%, editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: All 35 recalled more sexual desire after MDMA and 32 rated satisfaction moderately or markedly higher; 16 of 20 men and 6 of 15 women recalled delayed orgasm and 3 people could not reach orgasm; 8 of 20 men recalled weaker erections and 8 stronger ones; 12 of 15 women recalled more lubrication; orgasm felt more intense to 17 men and 8 women.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary and conclusion say MDMA seems to impair sexual performance in spite of enhanced desire and the perception of greater satisfaction, and that the increased desire is associated in most subjects with orgasmic or erectile dysfunction (pp. 127, 129). The summary reports erections impaired in 40% of the men without the other 40% who reported better erections, which the Discussion calls inconsistent effects (p. 128); and the dysfunction counted is mostly delayed orgasm in people who still rated satisfaction higher (editors' tally from Table I: 17 of 20 men and 8 of 15 women had delayed orgasm, no orgasm or weaker erections or lubrication). The links to dopamine and serotonin are hypotheses not tested here, and the authors themselves say expectations (a placebo effect) should not be disregarded (p. 128).

timeline.event: Buffum and Moser, self-rating questionnaires distributed in the San Francisco area, as cited here as the only earlier survey of MDMA and sexual function: MDMA enhanced sensuality, made orgasm more difficult and decreased erectile ability in 46% of men (p. 128); not read.

McElrath, in-depth interviews with 98 people in Northern Ireland (1997-1998): many described closeness without wanting penetrative sex, some men described being unable to get an erection, and others described heightened desire; no counts given.

replication.where_it_stands: Small self-report studies from the 1980s and 1990s agree that desire and sensuality often rise with MDMA while erections and orgasm can be impaired; no study among those read measured sexual function under controlled conditions or in a representative sample.

funding.funder: Not reported.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported.
funding.affiliations_note: Geha Psychiatric Hospital, Petah Tikva, and Sackler Faculty of Medicine, Tel Aviv University, Israel (p. 127).

what_would_settle_it: A prospective diary study in which people who use MDMA rate sexual function with a validated questionnaire on occasions with and without MDMA, with the pills tested and other substances recorded; or a placebo-controlled laboratory study measuring desire, arousal and orgasm.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame is described; how the 35 people were found is not stated.
Self-selected people who had used MDMA before sex and agreed to talk about it; not a random or consecutive sample.
35 people (20 men, 15 women); intervals around the sex-specific proportions span about 40 percentage points.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Age, sex and years of education are given for every person, with occupations summarized; recruitment, place and dates are not described.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: All 35 participants' ratings are shown in Table I and the text's percentages match it.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: An unvalidated retrospective self-rating scale; the exposure (MDMA) is unverified and its dose and content unknown.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One structured interview for all, but 9 by telephone, interviewers not described and recall over unspecified periods.
Descriptive percentages suit a description, but there are no intervals and the comparison by cannabis use has neither data nor test.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A small, self-selected, retrospective survey with an unvalidated rating scale and unverified exposure, whose per-person table at least makes every count checkable. It may be cited for what these 35 people recalled: more desire and satisfaction, delayed orgasm in most men, and erections reported as worse by 40% of men but better by another 40%. It should not be cited for how often these effects occur among people who take MDMA, or as showing that MDMA causes them.

key_findings.finding: Sample and method: 35 people (20 men aged 22 to 46, 15 women aged 21 to 48) who had occasionally used MDMA before sex were interviewed retrospectively (9 by telephone) about sexual activity up to 6 hours after MDMA, rating each domain from -3 to +3 against their usual function without MDMA.
key_findings.locator: Summary (p. 127); Subjects and methods, 1st paragraph (p. 127, continuing on p. 128) and 2nd paragraph (p. 128); Table I (p. 129)

key_findings.finding: Desire: all 35 reported increased sexual desire after MDMA; the increase was moderate to profound in 19 of 20 men (95%) and in all 15 women; most described the experience as more sensual than usual.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 128); Table I, title and rows (p. 129)

key_findings.finding: Satisfaction: moderately to profoundly increased in 90% of men and 93% of women (18 of 20 and 14 of 15 in Table I).
Erection: 40% of men (8 of 20) reported a negative effect and 40% (8) a positive effect, and 4 no change; lubrication was enhanced in 80% of women (12 of 15).
key_findings.note: Editors' tally from Table I: of the 8 men with weaker erections, 4 rated the decrease as moderate or marked (-2 or -3); 2 women reported less lubrication.

key_findings.finding: Orgasm: delayed in 16 men (80%) and 6 women (40%); 1 man and 2 women had not been able to reach orgasm at all on MDMA; orgasm was perceived as more intense by 85% of men and 53% of women.
key_findings.note: Editors' tally from Table I: orgasm felt less intense to 1 man and 3 women, 3 of these 4 being the people who could not reach orgasm.

key_findings.finding: Satisfaction was still rated as increased despite impaired function: all 8 men who reported weaker erections and all 3 people who could not reach orgasm rated satisfaction +2 or +3 (moderately or markedly increased compared with usual). (The ratings are changes from usual function, not levels, so 'stayed high' misdescribes them.)
key_findings.note: Editors' tally from the individual ratings in Table I.

key_findings.finding: Cannabis: 10 men (50%) and 10 women (67%) reported occasional use of cannabis with MDMA and said the main effect of adding it was enhanced desire; ratings were restricted to MDMA alone, and the authors report no differences in any sexual rating between those who did and did not add cannabis (no data or test shown). (Results p. 128 report an effect users noted; the purpose, 'for further facilitation of desire', is the authors' reading in the Discussion.)

The authors compare their results with the only earlier survey they knew (Buffum and Moser, 1986, San Francisco area): MDMA enhanced sensuality, made orgasm harder to achieve and decreased erectile ability in 46% of men (as cited).

Limitations named by the authors: a non-random sample of people willing to describe use of an illegal drug, retrospective recall open to inaccuracy, unknown dose and purity of the pills, and cannabis use by about half; they also say expected effects of the drug (a placebo effect) should not be disregarded, citing alcohol studies in which women felt more aroused while measured arousal fell.

reporting_issues.issue: The summary reports erection impaired in 40% of the men, but not that another 40% reported better erections (both in Results, p. 128), and concludes that MDMA impairs sexual performance.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary overstates the erection finding; the Discussion itself calls the effects on erection inconsistent (p. 128).

reporting_issues.issue: Telephone interviews are given as 9 subjects (25%); 9 of 35 is 26% (editors' calculation). All other percentages in the text match the individual ratings in Table I (editors' check).
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible; the counts are reliable as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that sexual ratings did not differ between people who did and did not use cannabis with MDMA is given without numbers or a test, and Table I does not mark who used cannabis.
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that cannabis did not affect the ratings cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Recruitment method, place and dates of the interviews, the interviewers and ethics approval are not reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample frame and representativeness cannot be judged (JBI items 1, 2 and 9).
